Article.Title: Head movement allocation in freely-moving macaques learning object-context sequences
Article.Authors: Rahman, K. F.; Abbaspoor, S.; Zinke, W.; Tamaki, H.; Hoffman, K. L.
Article.Abstract: Flexible learning and long-term memory are hallmark features of primate cognition that are shaped by interactions with changing environments. A comprehensive understanding of these brain-body-environment interactions requires minimal constraints on behavior, and environments rich with conditional cues that encourage diverse behavioral dynamics. In this study, we introduce a multi-level enclosure (Treehouse) that allows for independent control of spatially distributed touchscreens for studying cognition in freely moving macaques. To test flexible learning, two monkeys completed trials consisting of a regular sequence of conditional object choices (targets) across four distinct spatiotemporal contexts (screens). Both monkeys acquired numerous unique, conditional object-context sequences without detriment to new learning as memoranda accumulated. They also successfully recalled their correct choices after weeks without exposure. To assess how monkeys allocate movement during learning and memory-guided decision making, we tracked their head kinematics and used recurrent neural networks to decode different aspects of their engagement with the environment during the choice epoch of the task. One such model predicted the position of the object about to be touched, including on error trials, tracking overt gaze towards objects. Separate models decoded sequence corner, the ordinal step, and the individual screen stations the monkeys occupied, despite identical stimulus layouts and behavioral demands at each station. Head movements also showed efficiencies that the task did not require: under conditions of uncertainty, monkeys were biased in their initial search locations to the targets that were closest to reach, and across days they made smoother head movements as training progressed, with no change in accuracy. These results demonstrate the potential of immersive 3-D environments, in which body kinematics can shed light on animals' goals, and reveal that situated learning in primates can be rapid, capacious, durable, and flexible.

Article.Title: Revisiting the role of cAMP in Drosophila aversive olfactory memory formation
Article.Authors: Abe, T.; Yamazaki, D.; Hiroi, M.; Ueoka, Y.; Maeyama, Y.; Tabata, T.
Article.Abstract: In aversive olfactory conditioning in Drosophila melanogaster, an odor (the conditioned stimulus, CS) is paired with an electric shock (the unconditioned stimulus, US). Rutabaga adenylyl cyclase, which synthesizes cAMP in Kenyon cells (KCs), has long been proposed to act as a coincidence detector, synergistically activated by calcium/calmodulin in response to odor-evoked KC activity and by Gs downstream of shock-evoked dopamine signaling. This framework implies that CS+ responsive KCs, which receive both CS and US signals, should be distinguishable from the remaining KCs by elevated cAMP levels, such that elevated cAMP would selectively mark these KCs for memory-related plasticity. However, our live imaging revealed that olfactory stimulation alone activates dopaminergic signaling and elevates cAMP broadly across KC axons, with only weak spatial correspondence to sparse local Ca2+ responses, such that CS+ responsive KCs could not be distinguished from the remaining KCs by bulk cAMP levels. This observation challenges a key prediction of the Rutabaga coincidence-detection model. Our findings instead suggest that cAMP concentrations do not selectively mark CS+ neurons. Rather, we propose that the compartmental population dynamics of cAMP across the {gamma} lobe represent a KC-intrinsic expression of valence, integrated across compartments from multiple dopaminergic inputs. Associative conditioning reshaped dopamine responses to the CS+ odor, with corresponding changes in this compartmental cAMP pattern. Simultaneous imaging of cAMP and acetylcholine (ACh) revealed that conditioning establishes an inverse relationship between this pattern and ACh release for the CS+ but not for the CS- odors; this relationship was absent in rutabaga mutants. Pharmacological elevation of cAMP suppressed ACh release from KCs. These findings suggest that cAMP-dependent suppression of ACh release from KCs may shift the valence of the CS+ odor toward a more aversive state in conditioned flies, thereby contributing to aversive olfactory memory formation.

Article.Title: Expertise modifies neural responses to causal inference during language comprehension
Article.Authors: Hauptman, M.; Bedny, M.
Article.Abstract: Linguistic communication relies on shared common ground, yet different individuals in a community have specialized semantic knowledge. As a key example, physicians acquire rich knowledge about the causes of illness. An open question is whether such "causal expertise" influences the neural basis of language comprehension. Here we tested the hypothesis that when understanding everyday language like, "Holly used a grimy faucet during her overseas plane ride. Now she has the stomach flu," medical experts retrieve richer representations in semantic networks of the brain. Physicians (n=16) and age- and education-matched controls (n=16) undergoing fMRI read two-sentence vignettes that elicited implicit causal inferences about illness or object mechanics as well as control vignettes that did not elicit causal inferences. Vignettes were linguistically matched across conditions and were accessible to experts and non-experts alike. Across both groups, causal vignettes about illness engaged a temporoparietal semantic network previously implicated in thinking about animates, i.e., people and animals (precuneus and left temporoparietal junction), whereas causal vignettes about object mechanics engaged a semantic network associated with places and objects. Critically, physicians' responses in the animacy network were more robust and self-similar, suggesting the activation of richer semantic knowledge. Medical expertise effects were specific to biological inferences rather than mechanical or mental state inferences. By contrast, individually localized frontotemporal language and frontoparietal reasoning networks did not respond preferentially to causally connected sentences or show effects of expertise. Our findings suggest that causal expertise alters neural responses to causal inferences that unfold automatically during language comprehension.

Article.Title: A multimodal dataset of EEG, eye-tracking, and physiological signals during naturalistic smartphone interactions
Article.Authors: Mishra, P.; Gandhi, T. K.; Gandhi, S. R.
Article.Abstract: Smartphones have become pervasive tools for communication, information consumption, and digital interaction, yet the neurophysiological dynamics associated with naturalistic smartphone use remain insufficiently characterized. Here, we present a multimodal physiological dataset collected during ecologically valid smartphone interaction and a subsequent relaxation condition. Twenty-three participants engaged with their most frequently used smartphone application (primarily gaming or short form video) for ten minutes, followed by a five-minute passive viewing of a standardized nature video. Simultaneous recordings were obtained from electroencephalography (EEG; 64 channels), wearable eye-tracking, photoplethysmography (PPG), and galvanic skin response (GSR) sensors. Questionnaire-based assessments, including the smartphone addiction scale (SAS) and the mobile phone problematic use scale (MPPUS), are also collected to characterize individual differences in smartphone-related behavioral traits. All data streams are synchronized using transistor-transistor logic (TTL) trigger signals to ensure precise temporal alignment across modalities. The dataset is organized according to the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) specification and is publicly available on OpenNeuro (Accession Number: ds007537). This dataset enables the investigation of neural, ocular, and autonomic responses during smartphone interaction and supports multimodal analysis of diverse smartphone behaviors while preserving ecological validity.

Article.Title: Human single-neuron correlates of somatosensation
Article.Authors: Liu, B.; Bjanes, D.; She, L.; Pejsa, K.; Lee, B.; Liu, C. Y.; Andersen, R. A.
Article.Abstract: Understanding the neural correlates of consciousness poses a central challenge in neuroscience, with longstanding debate over which cortical areas underlie subjective sensory perception. In the tactile domain, posterior parietal cortex (PPC) and primary somatosensory cortex (S1) are candidate cortical substrates for neural correlates of consciousness due to their crucial roles in somatosensory processing. Yet whether and how these regions contribute to conscious tactile perception remains unclear. Here, to address this issue, we leveraged chronic intracortical recordings to simultaneously monitor large ensembles of single neurons in grasp related cortical areas from three participants with tetraplegia while natural vibrotactile stimuli were delivered to a sensate region of the upper limb. We demonstrate that an orchestration of neural activity emerged across the grasp-related parietal-frontal network at near-threshold perception. Within this distributed network, we then focused on PPC and S1. While S1 responses closely tracked the amplitude of the physical stimulus, PPC activity covaried more strongly with awareness and confidence. This single-neuron evidence reveals PPC and S1 have complementary neural codes with PPC transforming physical stimulation into conscious perception whereas S1 is more sensitive to stimulus amplitude.

Article.Title: Dissection of the contribution of bushy cell delays to sound localization in juvenile and adult Mongolian gerbils
Article.Authors: Sierksma, M. C.; Borst, J. G. G.
Article.Abstract: Sound sources along the azimuth generate interaural time differences in arrival (ITDs) at the ears. According to Jeffress hypothesis, ITDs are detected by coincidence-sensitive neurons of the medial superior olive (MSO) for which a differential axonal delay from each ear to the MSO compensates for the ITDs. The origin and development of these delays remain poorly understood. To this end, we made recordings from bushy cells (BCs), which project to both MSOs, in adult and in 2-4-week-old Mongolian gerbils of either sex. First spike latency revealed a frequency-dependent delay likely originating in the cochlea. Latencies were markedly larger for pure tone stimulation than for complex sounds. Combined with our published recordings from the MSO, we observed a developmental decrease in most delays, including the contralateral BC-to-MSO axonal delay. Unexpectedly, the ipsilateral BC-to-MSO axonal delay did not decrease. Anatomical brainstem reconstructions revealed that the inter-MSO distance was stable whereas the cochlear nucleus-to-MSO distance increased during development. Together, this indicated an increase in axonal propagation velocity, particularly for the contralateral projection. The variability in the averaged firing onset between BCs was found to be as large as the variance in bITDs, suggesting that BCs with matching firing onset are selected to converge onto the same MSO neuron. Together, our results indicate that the developmental speedup of ear-to-MSO delays contributes greatly to bringing the bITDs within their ecological range, but that the difference in path length is not overcome, keeping the ITD tuning biased to contralateral sound sources.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: sound localization; medial superior olive; bushy cells; interaural time difference; axonal delay; cochlear nucleus; Mongolian gerbil; ipsilateral and contralateral projections

Article.Title: Resource competition controls the length-dependence of synaptic protein synthesis
Article.Authors: Rubisch, P.; Raak, S. B.; Wodke, J. A. H.; Stefan, M. I.; O'Donnell, C.
Article.Abstract: Synaptic plasticity is dependent on the availability of specific proteins at the synapse with distinct requirements for potentiation and depression. Specifically, experimental evidence suggests an upregulation of short proteins and a downregulation for long proteins during long-term depression (LTD). The mechanism of this length-dependent protein synthesis regulation is yet unknown. In this work, we propose an computational model of ribosomal regulation of protein synthesis than can reproduce the length-dependent shift in protein expression seen during ribosomal elevations. By analysing the model dynamics, we discover that this effect is due to a shift from initiation-restricted to elongation-restricted protein synthesis. This works offers a novel explanation for the loss of ribosomal control of protein synthesis due to saturation in pathological ribosome enriched conditions. This new theoretical model of ribosomal regulation of protein synthesis is capable of explaining length-dependent shifts in protein synthesis.

Article.Title: In-vivo MRI of noradrenergic and dopaminergic nuclei predicts future cognition and Alzheimers disease progression
Article.Authors: Zhao, W.; Guzman, S. J.; Yoo, H. J.; Ruiz, K.; Chen, K.; Moheban, A.; Nation, D. A.; Dahl, M. J.; Mather, M.
Article.Abstract: Noradrenergic and dopaminergic nuclei modulate cognition, and post-mortem data indicate they are affected early in the neurodegenerative cascade of Alzheimers disease. We derived in-vivo locus coeruleus (LC) and substantia nigra-ventral tegmental area (SN-VTA) MRI integrity measures from 739 ADNI participants, examined MRI-histology correspondence in individuals with both in-vivo imaging and post-mortem data, and tested whether these measures reflect early MRI-indexed degeneration predicting later cognitive decline. LC and SN-VTA contrast predicted cognitive and behavioral function 10 years later, despite only weak associations with current function. LC- and SN-VTA-associated brain-wide atrophy patterns aligned with PET-derived norepinephrine-transporter and dopamine-receptor maps, respectively. A one-standard-deviation decrease in baseline LC contrast was associated with 84% higher five-year odds of MCI-to-AD progression, and predictive effects of the catecholaminergic nuclei were mediated by their corresponding atrophy patterns. The SN-VTA pattern was associated with less amyloid PET-related memory decline. Together, these findings establish LC and SN-VTA MRI contrast as markers of early neurodegeneration that forecast cognitive decline years before clinical onset.

Article.Title: Assessing reinforcement learning and vigor with an online decision-making battery
Article.Authors: Wenke, S.; Granwald, T.; Ferrante, A.; Nilsson, M.; Ekström, I.; Papenberg, G.; Guitart-Masip, M.
Article.Abstract: Reinforcement learning and vigor are two fundamental aspects of decision-making modulated by dopamine. Although vigor is highly relevant for mood disorders, it has been overlooked by previous batteries characterizing decision-making abilities. We developed a test battery with two RL tasks (RL/working memory, go/no-go task) and two vigor tasks (physical effort discounting, foraging task) and administered it to an online community sample (N = 162). We used computational modeling and factor analysis to identify two factors reflecting RL and vigor. The RL factor reflected participants' general decision-making ability, while vigor corresponded to a motivational propensity to obtain rewards. Both factors demonstrated moderately strong test-retest reliability (ICC(2,1) = .65 and .67, respectively) over a one-to-two-week interval. Moreover, both factors were meaningfully related to self-report scales. The RL and vigor factors were negatively and positively associated with mania, respectively, although further analyses revealed that vigor was not fully independent of RL. Neither factor was significantly associated with depression symptoms. Collectively, we present preliminary evidence that vigor may represent a separate factor from RL in line with the putative dopamine hypothesis, paving the way for future longitudinal assessments of RL and vigor in mood disorders.

Article.Title: Natural predator-associated chemosignals evoke distinct spatiotemporal patterns of risk assessment and vomeronasal population responses
Article.Authors: Wang, J.; Haran, V.; Meeks, J. P.
Article.Abstract: Natural predator-associated chemosignals elicit diverse defensive behaviors, yet it remains unclear how complex natural cues shape the spatiotemporal organization of risk assessment and activate vomeronasal sensory neurons (VSNs) and downstream circuits in the mammalian accessory olfactory system. Here, we investigated odor-dependent behavioral organization and VSN sensory representations using three-dimensional behavioral tracking, integrative machine-learning analysis, volumetric calcium imaging, and whole-brain FosTRAP2 mapping. We developed a pose-based integrative machine-learning analysis pipeline (PIMAP) to identify behavioral signatures based on posture, spatial exploration, state transitions, and temporal dynamics. We found that common behavioral states were expressed in multiple odor conditions, but their expression rates, spatial positions, and temporal sequencing distinguished responses to snake, tortoise, lizard, and mouse fecal cues. Snake fecal cues elicited sustained direct investigation and distinct patterns of spatial exploration, behavioral transitions, and grooming in both two-chamber and multiple-choice assays. Volumetric calcium imaging in the vomeronasal epithelium revealed distinct patterns of VSN activation by different reptilian cues. Whole-brain microscopy of FosTRAP2 transgenic mice indicated potential differential activity patterns in AOS-associated circuits following snake and tortoise exposure. Furthermore, Trpc2 deletion altered snake-associated behavioral signatures, while odor-discriminative behavioral patterns remained detectable. Together, these findings show that reptilian predator cues activate distinct AOS components and bias exploration patterns towards threat assessment and vigilance.

Article.Title: Sex differences in fear extinction are conditional, not categorical
Article.Authors: Nguyen, M. T.; Didachos, A.; Roozendaal, B.; Henckens, M. J. A. G.; Gulmez Karaca, K.
Article.Abstract: Threat memories are dynamic, and their behavioral expression can change with subsequent experience and the passage of time. Extinction training can reduce conditioned fear responses, yet these responses may re-emerge over time through spontaneous recovery. Although biological sex has been implicated as modulatory factor in fear and extinction memory processes, studies have reported inconsistent findings. Here, we investigated how differences in extinction training and the timing of memory assessment influence extinction memory in male and female mice. Using contextual fear conditioning, we assessed fear acquisition and threat retention, characterized within-session and across-session extinction during repeated training, and compared shorter (3-minute) and longer (6-minute) daily extinction sessions. We subsequently evaluated extinction memory retention and spontaneous recovery at a later time point. Estrous-cycle stage in females was monitored daily throughout the experimental protocol to examine its potential association with fear and extinction behavior. We found that males and females demonstrated comparable fear acquisition and threat memory, as well as similar extinction progression across days. During longer extinction sessions, but not shorter, males showed greater within-session reductions in freezing, whereas females exhibited modestly higher overall freezing. We found no significant sex difference in the magnitude of spontaneous recovery. There was no significant association between estrous-cycle stage and freezing behavior. Together, our findings suggest that sex-dependent differences in contextual fear extinction are not uniformly expressed, but rather depend on the experimental conditions under which extinction is assessed

Article.Title: Feedback reliability modulates learning-related dynamics of midfrontal error monitoring
Article.Authors: Gawlowska, M.
Article.Abstract: Learning from feedback requires the brain to evaluate both performance outcomes and the reliability of the information used for learning. This study examined the dynamics of neural performance monitoring during deterministic (100% reliable) and probabilistic (75% reliable) associative learning using two within-subject tasks with different stimulus materials. Behavioral performance improved under both feedback regimes, but learning was consistently more successful under deterministic feedback. Error-related negativity, feedback-related negativity, and phase-locked midfrontal theta became progressively more pronounced across deterministic learning, particularly in the image-image task, whereas corresponding changes were attenuated under probabilistic feedback. Induced theta showed the opposite pattern, decreasing across deterministic learning while remaining comparatively stable under probabilistic learning. These opposing theta trajectories suggest that phase-locked and induced activity reflect distinct components of learning-related neural adaptation that may be obscured when total theta power is considered alone. Overall, the findings indicate that feedback reliability shapes the progressive tuning of midfrontal performance-monitoring responses during learning.

Article.Title: Endothelin-1 from Tongue Glands Gates 1 Sodium Taste and Intake
Article.Authors: Chen, L.-T.; Xia, X.; Soto, E. R.; Ostroff, G. R.; Zhang, J.
Article.Abstract: Sodium is an essential nutrient. To survive sodium deficiency, animals dramatically increase their appetite for salt. However, whether and how sodium depletion impacts the taste of salt to drive sodium intake is unknown. Here we show that tongue gland-derived endothelin-1 (EDN1) regulates the amiloride-sensitive, sodium-selective salt taste. Edn1 is specifically expressed in the glands embedded within the tongue. Under normal conditions, EDN1 suppresses salt taste by acting on its receptor EDNRB on the projections of salt-sensing taste neurons innervating taste buds. When internal sodium levels drop, EDN1 expression decreases, lifting this inhibition and enhancing responses to salt. Applying EDN1 directly to the tongue, using a nonionic eutectic-based organogel (Neogel) delivery technology that we establish here, dampens the activity of the salt-sensing taste neurons and reduces salt intake and preference. Conversely, genetic deletion of Ednrb in taste neurons mimics the effects of sodium deficiency, enhancing salt-sensing neuron activity and increasing salt consumption. These findings reveal a peripheral mechanism that regulates salt taste and intake in response to internal sodium levels, highlighting a direct role of the taste pathway in maintaining nutrient homeostasis.

Article.Title: Mapping Endogenous Psychedelic Chemistry: Indolethylamine N-Methyltransferase (INMT) Localizes Proximal to the Golgi Apparatus of Human Neurons
Article.Authors: Will, K.; Lazaro Martinez, S.; Reis, S. A.; Haggarty, S. J.
Article.Abstract: N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT) is a serotonergic psychedelic with a history of ethnobotanical use and emerging clinical efficacy for neuropsychiatric disorders. Following Julius Axelrod's pioneering studies showing DMT production in human tissues, DMT has been proposed as an endogenous neuromodulator because it is a serotonin 2A receptor (5-HT2A R) agonist. However, the DMT-producing enzyme, indolethylamine N-methyltransferase (INMT), has not been characterized at the protein level in the human central nervous system. Here, we validated an anti-INMT antibody and used immunocytochemistry to show that INMT localizes in close proximity to other DMT biosynthetic enzymes near the cytosolic face of the cis-Golgi network in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons, with immunoreactivity observed across multiple neuronal Golgi phenotypes. Notably, both DMT-like and 5-HT2A R immunoreactivity also partially localized in close proximity to the Golgi apparatus. Our results establish the first protein-level characterization of INMT in human neurons and identify the cis-Golgi network as a candidate microdomain for psychedelic tryptamine biosynthesis. We propose that INMT catalytic activity at the cis-Golgi network creates an enriched region of membrane-permeable psychedelic tryptamines that can access an intracellular 5- HT2A R pool. These findings provide new tools and insights that can inform efforts to understand the mechanism of action of psychedelics under clinical investigation and to target endogenous tryptamines therapeutically.

Article.Title: LAMA2-related muscular dystrophy alters Schwann cell calcium homeostasis and increases peripheral nerve inflammation
Article.Authors: Wang, J.; Khati, M.; Heron, M.; Munir, A.; Akinyele, O.; Johnson, M. A.; Vockley, J.; Pandey, U. B.; Kemaladewi, D. U.
Article.Abstract: LAMA2-related muscular dystrophy (LAMA2-RD) affects skeletal muscle and peripheral nerves, yet the consequences of LAMA2 deficiency on peripheral nerve integrity beyond early postnatal development remain incompletely understood. We investigated sciatic nerve architecture and molecular alterations across postnatal life in hypomorphic Lama2dy2J/dy2J mice. LAMA2 localizes around the abaxonal surface of myelinating Schwann cells in control nerves. LAMA2-deficient nerves exhibited patchy regions lacking myelinated axons from early postnatal stages into adulthood, including expanded Remak bundles along with axons completely lacking normal Schwann cell ensheathment. In adult nerves, myelin infolding and reduced myelin circularity revealed abnormalities in the architecture of myelin that had formed. Bulk sciatic nerve RNA sequencing identified altered calcium-signaling and immune-related transcriptional signatures. Complementary Fura Red measurements in primary nerve-derived Schwann cell cultures demonstrated decreased intracellular calcium in LAMA2-deficient samples, while ATP-evoked responses were preserved. Older LAMA2-deficient nerves also exhibited increased CD45+CD11b+ myeloid-cell infiltration. Together, these observations extend the characterization of LAMA2-associated neuropathy into adulthood and identify calcium homeostasis and neuroimmune responses as candidate processes relevant to persistent peripheral nerve pathology.

Article.Title: Nucleus accumbens acetylcholine dips track reward value and temporal costs to shape delay discounting
Article.Authors: Cavallaro, J.; Zuelke, D. R.; Maysonet, C. M.; Salazar, R. E.; Setara, R.; Gallo, E. F.
Article.Abstract: As an organism chooses between competing rewards, it must often integrate learned reward value with the changing costs associated with obtaining them. Yet, the brain mechanisms through which these factors jointly guide choice are not well understood. Previous studies have shown that dopamine signals in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) track reward value and are modulated by their associated delay costs. Our prior work further implicated NAc cholinergic interneurons by demonstrating that dopamine D2 receptors in these neurons influence choice under temporal, but not probabilistic, costs. However, whether NAc acetylcholine (ACh) dynamics track reward value and/or delay, and whether they contribute to adaptive choice, remains unknown. Using in vivo fiber photometry during a delay discounting task in which mice choose between a small, immediate reward and a larger, delayed reward, we reveal that cue-evoked ACh dips dynamically track relative reward magnitude and are diminished by increasing delays. Our data further show that optogenetically enhancing these dips attenuates the delay-dependent decline in choice of the larger, delayed reward. These findings identify a previously unrecognized role for NAc cue-evoked ACh dips in shaping adaptive choice as temporal costs increase.

Article.Title: Single-molecule bouncing at a liquid interface governs presynaptic enrichment
Article.Authors: Kudo, K.; Longfield, S. F.; McCann, A. J.; Schoovaerts, N.; Sanchez-Velasquez, J.; Parra-Rivas, L. A.; Roy, S.; Verstreken, P.; Hinde, E.; Millard, S. S.; Bademosi, A. T.; Meunier, F. A.
Article.Abstract: Many cellular processes rely on accumulating highly diffusive cytoplasmic proteins to a specific location within the cell. This spatial enrichment is generally thought to rely on locally immobilizing proteins or slowing diffusion through binding and molecular crowding. Paradoxically, cytoplasmic proteins that are enriched within nerve terminals remain highly diffusive, raising questions about the mechanisms that govern presynaptic enrichment. Here, using in vivo single-molecule microscopy, we tracked the diffusion of a model cytoplasmic protein, -Synuclein (-Syn), and synaptic vesicles (SVs), in motor neuron presynapses of live Drosophila larvae. We demonstrate that -Syn undergoes rapid and frequent "bouncing" events at a presynaptic interface, locally impeding escape from the presynapse. We measured escape probabilities at the interface, and show that impeding escape, without dramatically slowing diffusion, is sufficient to govern presynaptic enrichment. The interface is liquid-like and coincides with the boundary of the SV cluster, which is a necessary scaffold for the presynaptic enrichment of -Syn. Our results provide direct evidence of interfacial reflectivity at the interface of liquid-like compartments, and that this phenomenon can govern the subcellular enrichment of proteins and small organelles at the level of individual particles.

Article.Title: Prolactin Receptor Long Isoform ΔS1 Expression is Reduced in the Dorsal Root Ganglia of Humans with Chronic Pain
Article.Authors: He, L.; Natarajan, K.; Shiers, S. I.; Arendt-Tranholm, A.; Sayani, R.; Jagan, S.; Hossain, A.; Rosenfield, J.; Rodriguez Concepcion, A. J.; Dussor, G.; Akopian, A. N.; Price, T. J.
Article.Abstract: Prolactin receptor (PRLR) isoforms, specifically the short (PRLR-S) and long (PRLR-L), are differentially expressed in pathological conditions and may be involved in the induction and maintenance of pain in females. PRLR sex-dependent actions are well studied in rodent models of chronic pain, but the translatability of these findings have only been assessed in electrophysiology studies that found consistent results with previous sex differences described in mice. To increase our understanding of the sexual dimorphic nature of prolactin actions on sensory neurons and our knowledge of how this body of work applies to the human nervous system, we characterized the expression of the short and long isoforms of PRLR with RNAscope in situ hybridization in human dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons. Based on data in mice, we hypothesized PRLR-S and PRLR-L would be equally expressed in human DRG neurons, with higher expression in females. To test this, we used DRG tissues recovered from male and female organ donors and cervix as a positive control. Expression for both PRLR isoforms in cervix was consistent with previous reports. Article.Abstract: Neurotransmitter receptor and transporter distributions shape neural communication across the cortex and underpin mechanistic interpretations of brain function. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived eigenmodes, low-dimensional spatial patterns that capture the principal axes of cortical organization, are increasingly used to reconstruct brain maps and offer a potential route to approximating molecular topographies in large cohorts where direct measurements are unavailable. Yet whether the type of MRI data used to derive these eigenmodes determines which receptor and transporter distributions can be approximated, and which molecular systems are accessible through this approach at all, remains unknown. Using a spatial reconstruction framework applied to 23 molecular systems spanning neurotransmitter, metabolic, and pathological markers, we show that eight receptor and transporter maps, spanning serotonin, dopamine, histamine, cholinergic, and opioid markers, can be selectively approximated from functional eigenmodes but not structural or geometric ones. To illustrate translational potential in clinical cohorts where molecular imaging is unavailable, we applied individual-level eigenmode decompositions of MRI data projected onto the eight validated molecular systems and detected cross-sectional differences in autism and longitudinal changes in schizophrenia. Together, these findings reveal a difference in how geometric, structural, and functional brain organization relate to molecular architecture, offering a method for approximating validated molecular profiles in population neuroimaging cohorts that lack direct molecular imaging.

Article.Title: Increased Beta-Band Input to Spinal Motor Neurons is Not Confined to the Responding Muscle During a Go/No-Go Task
Article.Authors: Hug, F.; Dernoncourt, F.; Naveilhan, C.; van den Hoorn, W.
Article.Abstract: During movement preparation and inhibition, the sensorimotor cortex shows alpha- and beta-band oscillations that are also expressed in the discharge of spinal motor neurons. Whether this oscillatory activity is confined to the motor neurons innervating the muscles involved in the prepared action is unknown. Here we combined electroencephalography with recordings of spinal motor neurons innervating the tibialis anterior. Alpha- and beta-band power increased after the imperative cue in both cortical activity and motor neuron output, including when the tibialis anterior was not involved in the response. Because power modulations in motor neuron output can be confounded by the concurrent change in discharge rate, we assessed the oscillatory activity shared across motor neurons by calculating coherence between disjoint subsets, which is largely insensitive to discharge rate. We then used simulation-based inference to identify synaptic input modulations compatible with our observations. These analyses indicated that beta-band common input increased whether or not the tibialis anterior was involved in the response, whereas alpha-band input increased only when it was the responding muscle. The concurrent decrease in discharge rate and torque was attributed to reduced net excitatory drive, whereas alpha- and beta-band inputs accounted for the increase in synchronisation. These results demonstrate that cue-related oscillatory inputs reach spinal motor neurons more broadly than classically assumed, and shape motor neuron synchronisation.

Article.Authors: Arab Ahmadi, V.; Nasseri-Moghaddam, S.; Toscani, M.; Metzger, A.
Article.Abstract: Vision can sample objects remotely and over a broad field, whereas touch is restricted to contacted skin and is often spatially serial however might outperform vision in resolution by transforming spatial information to a temporal code. In bimodal exploration, gaze and touch became more spatially similar than during unimodal exploration, while touch changed less than vision between unimodal and bimodal contexts. A temporal overlap analysis further showed that touch preceded gaze on average during the first 5 s of bimodal exploration. We then increased visual discriminability of the textures using cast-shadow illumination. A psychophysical pilot confirmed improved texture discrimination, and a new participant group showed a strong shift towards vision-leading exploration. Article.Authors: Schlosser, G.; Milz, C.; Falb, P.; Graf, S.; Tüchler, S. M.; Murgas, M.; Mayerweg, A.; Schmidt, C.; Pörnbacher, I.; Artmeier, L.; Harouak, A.; Lenz, J.; Sahl, A.; Grohmann, M.; Briem, E.; Reed, M. B.; Marculescu, R.; Nics, L.; Rasul, S.; Rujescu, D.; Hacker, M.; Pruessner, J. C.; Lanzenberger, R.; Hahn, A.

Article.Title: How Well Does Structural MRI Classify Autism? A Leakage-Free, Site-Aware and Externally Validated Machine-Learning Evaluation in Two ABIDE Cohorts
Article.Authors: Akar, B.; Elik, C.; Altıntas, T.
Article.Abstract: Background: Many studies report high accuracy for classifying autism spectrum disorder (ASD) from structural MRI, but small samples, single train-test splits, site effects and information leakage can inflate performance. Methods: FreeSurfer-derived features (n = 280: regional thickness, area and volume; subcortical volumes; Yeo-network composites; asymmetry indices; global measures) from ABIDE II (804 participants; 341 ASD; 12 sites) were used to train logistic regression, linear support vector machine, random forest, XGBoost and multilayer perceptron classifiers. Confound regression (age, age2, sex, brain volume), site-wise centring and standardisation were learned within training folds only. Results: Cross-validated discrimination was modest: the best model (regularised logistic regression on all features) reached an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.60 [0.56, 0.64], significantly above chance (permutation p = .002) but far from clinically useful and below a confound-only baseline using age, sex, brain volume and site (AUC 0.63); non-linear models did not perform better (AUC 0.45-0.60 across models and feature sets). Pooled leave-one-site-out AUCs were 0.54-0.61, with large between-site variation, and AUCs in the external ABIDE I cohort were 0.52-0.58. Age-stratified models did not exceed AUC 0.60. Article.Title: Stimulus Sampling Shapes Estimated Perceptual Geometry in Psychophysical Scaling

Article.Abstract: We used simulations and mathematical analysis to investigate how simultaneous estimation of transducer nonlinearity and perceptual geometry affects bias in maximum likelihood difference scaling (MLDS). These biases were substantially reduced when stimuli were sampled uniformly in response space, distributing observations more evenly across the transducer. Likelihood-surface analysis revealed substantial confounding between sampling-induced distortions and effects attributable to changes in perceptual geometry. Uniform stimulus-domain sampling produced a pronounced trade-off between the parameters governing transducer nonlinearity and perceptual geometry, which was substantially reduced under uniform response-space sampling. Although response-space sampling generally improved the local conditioning of the likelihood surface, parameter identifiability remained dependent on its intrinsic geometry and thus on the underlying transducer. These results show that stimulus sampling can influence whether departures from a Riemannian perceptual metric are detected, highlighting the importance of sampling designs that adequately represent perceptual space. Article.Title: Learning complex temporal dependencies via local synaptic plasticity
Article.Authors: Ng-Kee-Kwong, J.; Tang, M.; Akam, T.; Bogacz, R.
Article.Abstract: The ability to extract and exploit temporal structure across diverse tasks is central to human cognition. Neuroscientists have typically relied on recurrent neural networks (RNNs) trained with backpropagation through time (BPTT) when modelling neural and behavioural processes such as decision-making and motor control. However, this algorithm has limited biological plausibility, hence the computational principles underlying efficient learning of temporal dependencies remain unresolved. Here, we investigate temporal predictive coding (tPC), a recently proposed framework that extends predictive coding to the temporal domain while preserving local Hebbian update rules. We analyse and extend tPC to establish its relationship with several influential computational models of learning in RNNs, including BPTT, reservoir computing, and eligibility propagation (e-prop). We first demonstrate structurally equivalent weight update rules between tPC and tBPTT1, a variant of BPTT in which gradients are propagated only one time step into the past. We then show that tPC can leverage reservoir dynamics to encode short-range temporal context, and simultaneously sculpt neural trajectories in state space to support downstream readout. We further demonstrate that hierarchical recurrent dynamics can facilitate learning of more complex temporal dependencies, while additionally conferring robustness to strong distractors. Finally, we show that tPC networks can be augmented with biologically inspired eligibility traces to solve temporally extended context-dependent tasks. Together, these results reveal that relatively simple recurrent networks governed by local plasticity can support temporal learning in more complex settings than previously appreciated.

Article.Title: Dopaminergic reward signals shape foraging decisions through learned value expectations
Article.Authors: Kingsbury, L. E.; May, H.; Uchida, N.
Article.Abstract: A fundamental function of the nervous system is to direct animals towards life-sustaining resources and enable adaptive strategies for acquiring them. Foraging, the challenge of securing these resources from the environment, requires making decisions that balance local gains against costs, opening a window on value-based decision making in ecological context. Yet despite the centrality of foraging in life, the algorithms and neural mechanisms underlying foraging decisions are not well understood. We studied mice making stay-or-leave patch foraging decisions for water across poor- and rich-resource environments with dynamic local reward outcomes. We found that mice integrate immediate rewards, local reward history, and reward (i.e. value) expectations to guide foraging decisions, favoring greater time investment in rich-environment patches. Computational models revealed influence of a time-varying bias which mirrored the shape of a learned value function. Consistent with a reinforcement learning mechanism, dopamine in the ventral striatum signaled a temporal-difference reward prediction error, which could be used as a teaching signal to construct value functions, and calibrated optogenetic manipulation of dopamine to create fictive reward signals recapitulated the value-related decision bias. Taken together, our results shed new light on the neurocomputational basis of foraging, revealing a novel role for value expectations in dynamic environments. Further, they establish generalized function of biological reinforcement learning in ecological context, demonstrating a specific role for the canonical dopamine reward circuit in shaping temporally resolved value expectations to guide behavior and cognition. The unification of this framework with foraging opens a new avenue to elucidate principles of how animals learn and dynamically adjust cognitive strategies for real-world ecological problems.

Article.Title: The transformer as a candidate canonical cortical microcircuit
Article.Authors: Shah, Y.; Yamins, D. L. K.
Article.Abstract: Neuroscience hypothesizes a canonical microcircuit subserving cortical computation across brain systems. In artificial intelligence, neural networks have become a universal computational substrate. Here, we leverage newly available large-scale data and mapping techniques to compare neural network motifs to the brain. We embedded a spectrum of candidate microcircuit architectures within a common spatial macrocircuit, measuring alignment with an extensive battery of cortical signatures. We find that one specific circuit type--the transformer--uniquely captures fine-grained unit-level circuit details, population-level functional maps and neuronal activity patterns, and systems-level wiring efficiency and behavioral demands. The key ingredient enabling the transformer's success is a learned multiplicative component making relational information available without extensive long-range wiring. These results suggest striking convergence between computational motifs in natural and artificial intelligence.

Article.Authors: Potts, T. C.; McDonnell, E. E.; Levey, J.; Gall, L. G.; Coffinas, E.; Rutley, C. G.; Gururaj, N.; Vindigni, A. K.; Iyer, A. R.; Pericone, K. A.; Gosai, M. H.; Canace, M. E.; O'Brown, N. M.

FishNAP thus enables the identification of conserved modulators of BBB function with translational potential for brain drug delivery.

Setting: Level IV neonatal intensive care unit at Children's National Hospital, Washington, DC. Participants: Of 400 infants screened, 253 preterm infants born before 37 weeks' gestation (128 with NEC and 125 without NEC) were included across neuroimaging, plasma metabolomic, and postmortem cohorts. Exposures: Medical or surgical NEC (modified Bell stage [≥]II). In postmortem tissue (n = 27), white matter pathology qualitatively resembled that of prematurity, whereas the hindbrain showed distinct regional phenotypes. The cerebellum exhibited external granular layer contraction (42% reduction; P = .04), while the pons showed neuronal injury with increased morphological apoptotic burden (P [≤] .05). Brain and intestinal transcriptomics (n = 14), complemented by plasma metabolomics (n = 29), revealed divergent inflammatory and metabolic signatures. The pons showed increased neuroinflammatory and reduced mitochondrial programs, whereas the cerebellum showed reduced metabolic and cell-cycle programs alongside circulating lysophospholipid depletion. Serial ultrasonography (n = 159), anchored to the cohort mean NEC onset age of 29 weeks' postmenstrual age, identified earlier cerebellar dimensional deficits (P = .015) and later pontine growth deceleration (P < .001). These findings support investigation of regional vulnerability and stage-specific neuroprotection; individual injury timing and causal mechanisms remain unresolved.

Article.Authors: Akar, B.; Altıntas, T.
Article.Abstract: Background: Odours reach limbic and prefrontal targets through a uniquely direct pathway and are often claimed to enhance cognition, yet experimental evidence for specific essential oils is mixed and frequently confounded by expectancy. Conclusions: A single brief exposure to peppermint oil was associated with substantially better immediate recall than no odour. Because the peppermint-clove contrast was inconclusive and no placebo odour was used, the data do not establish an odour-specific effect; general arousal and expectancy remain plausible contributors. Article.Authors: Jia, X.; Zeng, C.; Liu, L.; Gao, T.; Bi, J.; Zeng, Z.; Liang, L.; Qi, C.; Lin, F.; Cheng, F.
Article.Abstract: Myelin, the multilamellar sheath wrapping neuronal axons, enables saltatory conduction. Article.Title: Path knockout: an analysis tool for connectome-driven circuit discovery
Article.Authors: McGrath, R.; Hattori, D.
Article.Abstract: Neural circuits in the brain transform sensory information into perceptual, emotional and motor output. The connectome -- a synaptic-resolution wiring diagram of all neurons in a nervous system -- provides a neuroanatomical blueprint for identifying different circuits that mediate specific computations. However, its sheer scale and complexity pose a significant challenge in extracting functionally relevant multi-synaptic pathways. Here we established path knockout, a connectome analysis method that identifies dominant multi-synaptic pathways. Path knockout uses the input fraction of each synaptic connection as a surrogate for the probability that information transfer succeeds across that synapse and calculates approximate probability, or connection strength, that at least one path succeeds among all multi-synaptic paths between defined source and sink neuron populations. It then quantifies the importance of each interneuron by assessing the impact of its removal on the connection strength. We demonstrate that path knockout outperforms other methods for pathway analysis and identifies known and novel interneurons in the Drosophila circuits. Using path knockout, we identified a convergent circuit motif linking sexually dimorphic aggression command neurons to a shared isomorphic visual pursuit pathway. Path knockout is implemented such that it runs in minutes on a standard computer. Thus, path knockout provides a scalable and generalizable framework for connectome-driven circuit discovery.

Article.Title: A medial entorhinal connectome reveals compartmentalized microcircuit architecture
Article.Authors: Shi, T.; Chen, Y.; Jin, H.; Jiang, H.; Chen, X.; Xiong, Z.; Wu, F.; Zhang, R.
Article.Abstract: The medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) transforms multimodal inputs into spatial representations, but the synaptic architecture underlying its computations remains unclear. Here we generated a synapse-resolution connectomic dataset spanning all six layers of mouse MEC and the adjacent parasubiculum with serial electron microscopy, providing a continuous volume for mapping cellular organization and connectivity across layers and regions. We found that clustered pyramidal neurons in MEC layer II extended oblique apical dendrites with a dorsolateral bias and long-range myelinated axons within the layer. Exhaustive reconstruction of one cluster revealed a central exclusion core (ExC) that spatially partitioned basal dendritic architecture and synaptic connectivity. A spatially constrained growth model reproduced the position-dependent dendritic patterns. Within the ExC, pyramidal neurons formed a compact recurrent excitatory network and converged onto shared inhibitory partners. Basket cells (BC) and recurrent Martinotti cells provided perisomatic and apical-dendritic feedback, respectively. Dense, compact reciprocal connectivity between L2P neurons and BCs within the ExC, together with BC axonal bands extending beyond the ExC, suggests a potential circuit mechanism for generating temporally structured inhibitory output from the pyramidal-cell cluster along directionally extended axons. Together, these findings link cellular-scale geometry and synaptic wiring to emergent circuit dynamics that extend from dense computation within individual clusters to region-wide modulation, providing a connectomic foundation for understanding the circuit basis of spatial navigation.

Article.Title: Wolffia globosa -derived nanovesicles as a natural source of bioactive metabolites with neuroprotective potential against methylglyoxal-induced oxidative stress
Article.Authors: Khongkla, E.; Boonsnongcheep, P.; Srisaisup, M.; Charuraksa, T.
Article.Abstract: Plant-derived nanovesicles (PDNVs) have attracted increasing attention for their potential biomedical applications, particularly in oxidative stress-related diseases and neuroprotection. Wolffia globosa, an emerging functional food and potential future food source, is rich in phytochemicals associated with health-promoting properties. Harnessing W. globosa-derived nanovesicles (WGNVs) represents a promising strategy for expanding the biomedical applications of this plant. In this study, WGNVs were isolated and characterized, and their neuroprotective potential was evaluated in vitro. The isolated WGNVs exhibited nanoscale dimensions and a lipid bilayer structure. Biochemical analyses revealed substantial total phenolic and flavonoid contents, alongside intrinsic antioxidant activities. Untargeted metabolomic profiling identified a diverse repertoire of metabolites, including major constituents subsequently validated using independent analytical approaches. These findings provided a foundation for investigating the neuroprotective effects of WGNVs in a methylglyoxal (MGX)-induced model of neuronal oxidative stress. High-resolution confocal microscopy demonstrated the cellular localization of WGNVs within neuronal cells, providing evidence of interactions between plant-derived nanovesicles and neuronal cells. WGNV treatment attenuated MGX-induced free radical accumulation and oxidative stress responses while preserving cellular morphology integrity. Collectively, this study provides foundational evidence of the physicochemical characteristics, metabolite composition, and in vitro neuroprotective potential of WGNVs. These findings highlight WGNVs as a promising naturally derived nanocarrier platform for investigating plant-animal interkingdom interactions and exploring potential therapeutic applications across a broad range of biomedical fields.

Article.Title: Region-dependent regulation of Tau phosphorylation by Glycerophosphodiester Phosphodiesterase 2 in a mouse model of tauopathy
Article.Authors: Jimenez-Ornelas, C.; Sockanathan, S.
Article.Abstract: Hyperphosphorylation of Tau promotes its aggregation and neurofibrillary tangle (NFT) formation, contributing to neuronal dysfunction and neurodegeneration in diseases such as Alzheimer's Disease (AD) and AD-related dementias (ADRDs). However, the mechanisms underlying dysregulated Tau phosphorylation under pathological contexts remain unclear. Glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase 2 (GDE2) is a six-transmembrane enzyme that acts at the cell surface to cleave the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchor that tethers a subclass of proteins to the membrane. Here, we show that in the PS19 tauopathy mouse model, GDE2 disruption modulates Tau phosphorylation by transiently decreasing Tau's propensity for aggregation through region-specific regulation of local kinase environments. In the cortex, GDE2 ablation in 6-month-old PS19 male mice (PS19;Gde2KO) reduces Tau phosphorylation at Serine (S)202/Threonine (T)205, T212, and S396 but increases S262 phosphorylation in the hippocampus of 6-month-old PS19;Gde2KO male and female mice. Consistent with these changes, in males, Glycogen Synthase Kinase-3 / {beta} (GSK3 / {beta}) activity is decreased in the cortex, while AKT activity is increased in both males and females in the hippocampus, with no changes in protein phosphatase 1 (PP1) and protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) activity. Primary cortical neurons from PS19;Gde2KO animals showed reduced Tau phosphorylation at S202/T205, implying cell-autonomous roles for neuronal GDE2 in this process. GDE2 overexpression in heterologous SH-SY5Y cells increased Tau phosphorylation at S202/T205, while a catalytically inactive form of GDE2 did not, suggesting that GDE2 regulation of target GPI-anchored protein surface activity is required to modulate Tau phosphorylation. Taken together, our study identifies GDE2 as a component of the complex regulatory network that controls Tau phosphorylation in the context of tauopathy and provides insight into putative pathways relevant to Tau pathologies observed in disease.

Article.Title: Dissociable norepinephrine and dopamine representations during strategic decision-making and reward learning
Article.Authors: Aloor, J.; Sit, T. P.; Geuter, J.; Tutt, J. O.; Duan, C. A.
Article.Abstract: Adaptive decision-making in competitive environments requires learning from immediate reward outcomes while tracking longer-timescale information to adjust behavioural strategies and remain unpredictable against others. Dopamine (DA) and norepinephrine (NE) have long been implicated in reward-guided behaviours, but their contributions to strategic choice remain unclear. We trained mice to play a zero-sum matching pennies game against a computer opponent that exploited regularities in their choice and reward history, such that optimal performance required stochastic choice decoupled from immediate reward. We combined fibre photometry recordings, behavioural and neural modelling, and a within-subject multi-task design to determine how NE and DA contribute to strategic choice in the matching pennies game versus reward-guided behaviour in a two-armed bandit (2AB) task. DA responses were dominated by trial-by-trial reward outcomes and consistently tracked model-derived reward prediction errors (RPE) across tasks and behavioural states. In contrast, NE activity reflected salient task events, predicted upcoming choice switches, and tracked longer-timescale variables including model-inferred behavioural strategy and average reward rate. In addition, NE responses were selectively enhanced following rewarded switches when these outcomes were informative for deciding whether to stay in or switch from the current strategy; and this enhancement could not be explained by RPE. Incorporating pre-choice NE activity into a reinforcement-learning model to modulate choice generation improved model prediction in matching pennies but not in the 2AB task. Together, these findings reveal complementary neuromodulatory correlates of competitive decision-making across timescales: DA primarily guides learning from immediate outcomes through RPE, whereas NE additionally represents contextual information and choice stochasticity relevant for shaping long-term strategies.

Article.Title: Oscillatory Phase Coding Emerges in Adaptive RNNS for Flexible Working Memory
Article.Authors: Lu, K.; Chu, T.; TUERHONG, A.; Sun, Y.; Luo, H.; Fang, F.; WU, S.
Article.Abstract: Oscillatory phase coding (OPC) is widely observed in neural systems and has been implicated in cognitive functions such as memory and sequence processing. However, its computational role and neural substrates remain largely unclear. Here, we studied OPC by training recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with adaptation to perform sequence working memory tasks with variable delays. After training, we found that OPC emerges in the RNN spontaneously: the memorized items recur at distinct phases of a shared rhythm, with oscillation amplitude encoding item identity and phase encoding serial order. Ablation studies identified three key elements required for OPC: adaptation in neural dynamics, variable delay in memory retention, and flexibility in reading out information. Neuron-type analysis revealed the emergence of content and time cells in the trained RNN, and they process item identity and sequence order separately. Recurrent connectivity analysis revealed phase-organized connections among time cells and structured connections within digit-selective content-cell groups. Inspired by these findings, we proposed a neural circuit model which reproduces OPC through interactions between content units and an adaptive time ring. Together, this study reveals how OPC arises from network structures and task demands, offers insights into the implementation and computational mechanisms of OPC in biological systems, and inspires us to develop computational models for human-like cognitive functions.

Article.Title: Biomarkers indicate altered outer retinal fluid homeostasis in the absence of Kv2.1/Kv8.2 channels.
Article.Authors: Laird, J. G.; Soetedjo, J.; Inamdar, S. M.; Bock, A. R.; Ataman, E. S.; Pufall, M. A.; Berkowitz, B. A.; Baker, S. A.
Article.Abstract: Purpose: Photoreceptor Kv2.1/Kv8.2 voltage-gated potassium channels carry an outward potassium current, helping to set the resting membrane potential and to shape dim light responses. Because potassium flux in the outer retina influences extracellular osmolarity and fluid distribution, we hypothesized that Kv2.1/Kv8.2 channels also contribute to fluid homeostasis in this region of the retina. Methods: OCT imaging was performed in Kv8.2 heterozygous (Het) and knockout (KO) mice aged ~5 weeks under dark- and light-adapted conditions. Light-dark differences in the distance between the external limiting membrane (ELM) and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) ({Delta}ELM-RPE) were calculated to quantify light-evoked outer retinal expansion, a biomarker associated with changes in subretinal space (SRS) fluid handling. As a secondary outcome, outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness was also measured under both lighting conditions. Retinal gene expression was assessed by RNA-seq and droplet digital RT-PCR. Retinal protein expression was determined by western blotting and immunolabeling. Results: {Delta}ELM-RPE was significantly reduced in Kv8.2 KO mice compared with Het controls, indicating altered light-evoked outer retinal dynamics compatible with changes in subretinal space fluid handling. ONL thickness exhibited a small but significant light-dark change that was different between genotypes. Transcriptomic analyses revealed upregulation of osmosensitive genes, including osmolyte transporters and aquaporins. AQP1 protein expression in photoreceptors increased. Conclusions: These findings are consistent with altered outer retinal fluid homeostasis following loss of Kv8.2 and support a model in which photoreceptor potassium efflux contributes to osmotic water movement into the subretinal space.

Article.Title: Integrated metabolomics and proteomics from voxelated cortical hemispheres of adult rhesus monkeys
Article.Authors: Wu, Q.; Brigande, A. M.; Lutz, M. W.; Shi, P.; Disney, A.
Article.Abstract: The spatial organization of molecular networks across cortex likely contributes to differences in local circuit vulnerability in aging and Alzheimer's disease; yet many existing molecular datasets sacrifice spatial structure, sampling only a handful of regions per brain. Here, we present a framework for generating spatially registered, paired metabolomic and proteomic maps across an entire cortical hemisphere of an adult rhesus monkey, at millimeter resolution. One hemisphere each from two animals was harvested under controlled conditions, approximately flattened, and hand dissected at different sampling resolutions (roughly 2.5 and 4 mm/side) into tissue voxels. Each voxel was split after homogenization and extraction to provide matched aliquots for targeted metabolomics and deep untargeted proteomics. To handle these high dimensional data, we developed PChclust, a principal component guided feature clustering algorithm. For cross omic integration, we developed a spatially regularized sparse canonical correlation analysis (sr-sCCA), which incorporates spatial neighborhood structure via graph Laplacian smoothing. We recover meaningful biology: Molecular similarity between neighboring voxels decayed with distance in both modalities, confirming that voxelation captures spatially organized biological variance. The sr-sCCA identified joint proteome-metabolome components with coherent cortical gradients that were conserved across animals. Pathway enrichment analysis recovered brain relevant ontologies and reconstructed complete metabolic circuits from single voxels.

Article.Title: Multi-scale place fields provide a predictive basis for hierarchical control
Article.Authors: Yu, C.; Maimon, S. R.; Rich, P. D.; Eliav, T.; Las, L.; Lee, A. K.; Ulanovsky, N.; Lengyel, M.
Article.Abstract: Hippocampal place cells typically exhibit unimodal spatial selectivity in small enclosures, but express multiple, irregularly spaced fields in environments of naturalistic scale. However, existing predictive-map theories of the hippocampus do not scale well to large environments and do not account for these heterogeneous place field characteristics. Here, we introduce the factorised hierarchical successor representation (fHSR), a predictive map that supports hierarchical control using subgoal-directed subroutines. We show that the fHSR allows efficient generalisation across tasks, scaling favourably with environmental size, and it reproduces key statistical and topological characteristics of multi-scale CA1 place cell activity in rats and bats. Analyses of experimental data further confirmed a novel prediction of the fHSR: population firing rates exhibit spatial periodicity with a characteristic wavelength independent of environmental size. These results identify the integration of hierarchical control and predictive representations as a normative principle that unifies efficient navigation with the spatial organisation of hippocampal activity.

Article.Title: Active vision modulates early cortical stages of visual processing: Evidence from MEG and eye-tracking
Article.Authors: Huber-Huber, C.; De Lange, F. P.
Article.Abstract: Vision is fundamentally active. Humans and other mammals make several saccadic eye movements per second. This feature of mammalian vision has received increasing interest across the last decades and many behavioural and neurophysiological studies have investigated how the visual system accounts for the effects of self-generated motion (efference copy) in perceptual processing. Still, it is often believed that, besides accounting for the efference copy and for the rhythmic modulation of activity due to perpetual saccade-fixation cycles, active vision does not further modulate neural processing of visual input obtained during periods of fixation. In contrast, using a gaze-contingent trans-saccadic change design with concurrent MEG and eye-tracking data recording from human participants, we find sequential history effects in visual cortices. Harnessing the preview effect, we show that primary visual and ventral occipital cortices respond differently when eye-movements bring objects into focus compared to when the same objects appear during steady fixation. Specifically, we find that sequential modulations of cortical processing across saccades, in the form of preview effects, are increased during active vision compared to steady-gaze control conditions. Our data also show that these sequential modulations cannot be explained by any type of adaptation alone. Our study, therefore, provides an update on the role of active vision in modulating cortical function.

Article.Title: BundleMorphometry: Spatially Resolved White Matter Bundle Shape Analysis Using Nonlinear Streamline-based Registration
Article.Authors: Dasanayake, D.; Amit, S. N.; Chandio, B. Q.
Article.Abstract: Diffusion MRI tractometry quantifies microstructural properties along white matter (WM) bundles but does not directly measure their geometry, potentially overlooking localized morphological alterations. Here, we introduce BundleMorphometry, a framework for quantifying local WM bundle shape using the analytical Jacobian of nonlinear streamline-based registration. Individual subject bundles are registered to a reference atlas bundle using BundleWarp, a streamline-based nonlinear registration method. We derive the analytical Jacobian of the resulting deformation field and compute its log-determinant (log det J) to quantify local expansion and compression at each streamline point. To enable spatially resolved group comparisons, these measurements are projected onto the two-dimensional grid, capturing variations along and across each bundle. We evaluated BundleMorphometry using two clinical datasets comprising patients with glioma and Parkinson's disease (PD). In the glioma dataset, BundleMorphometry revealed spatially extensive deformation patterns in lesion-affected WM bundles that were not captured by displacement magnitude alone. Additionally, in a group analysis of the PD dataset (32 patients and 32 healthy controls), we identified significant localized morphological differences in the corpus callosum forceps major, mid-body and right spinothalamic tract, with distinct patterns of expansion and compression. These findings demonstrate the potential of BundleMorphometry to advance conventional tractometry by enabling spatially resolved analysis of bundle morphology.

Article.Title: Circuit regulation along an activity continuum shapes flexible and stable representations during learning
Article.Authors: Yusufi, D.; Ma, Y.; Chen, L.; Wang, G.; Malone, T.; Zhang, K.; Kim, J. H.; Shahid, F.; Cekada, K.; Barcelone, E.; Gu, Y.
Article.Abstract: Learning requires neural representations to flexibly incorporate new information while progressively stabilizing to support enduring memories. How neural circuits balance these demands remains unclear. Here, we identify complementary mechanisms supporting representational flexibility and stability in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC), a key component of the cognitive map for memory-guided navigation. Longitudinal calcium imaging in mice learning novel virtual environments revealed a persistent axis of excitatory neuronal activity associated with distinct representational dynamics. Low-activity neurons exhibited intermittent activation that varied with learning stages and greater learning-dependent representational refinement, flexibly shifting their encoding from landmarks toward reward locations. By contrast, high-activity neurons exhibited more persistent activation and maintained more stable spatial representations. Dopaminergic pre-reward ramping was associated with the emergence of reward encoding in low-activity neurons, whereas interactions with inhibitory interneurons contributed to the stability of high-activity neurons. Notably, interneurons exhibited activity changes opposing those of excitatory neurons during learning, and their transient activation upon novelty exposure delayed excitatory representational remodeling, stabilization, and behavioral learning, suggesting that inhibitory circuits gate learning-dependent representational dynamics. Together, these findings reveal how activity-dependent excitatory neuronal organization and circuit-level regulation enable complementary forms of representational flexibility and stability to coexist, facilitating the incorporation of novel experiences into stable, context-specific cognitive maps that support learning.

Article.Title: Photoentrainment as Bayesian Inference: How the central circadian clock may weight and integrate the intensity and wavelength of natural light to estimate astronomical time
Article.Authors: Ball, D. m.; Walsh, V.; Foster, R. G.; Speekenbrink, M.
Article.Abstract: Synchronising with the Earth's 24-hour rotation using natural light as a timing cue presents a problem for the mammalian brain's central circadian clock. Natural light is highly variable and can take a range of values at any given time of day. For example, it fluctuates due to differences in weather conditions and across seasons. Therefore, an absolute value of light provides an uncertain indication of the time of day. Despite this uncertainty, the central clock maintains close alignment with astronomical time, and here we describe how this may be achieved computationally. We present a Bayesian model in which the clock's endogenous oscillation is used to predict the probability of observing features of light, including intensity and spectral composition, and their co-occurrence given the time of day. These predictions are drawn from a distribution of values typically experienced. When observed light falls outside the predicted range, a prediction error provides evidence that the clock may be misaligned with astronomical time. How much the clock adjusts its phase depends on the relative uncertainty associated with its internal prediction and observed light. These are combined as a weighted average according to their relative reliability, drawing the clock's updated phase towards whichever provides the more reliable estimate of astronomical time. Using natural light measurements collected over one week from 59 human observers and 100 days of environmental spectral measurements, we characterize how the variability of natural light systematically changes across the day and show how the clock may exploit this structure for circadian timekeeping. The model explains how the canonical shape of the phase response curve emerges from the relationship between light distributions and time of day, and how properties of light, including intensity and spectral composition, can be integrated according to their reliability. The central clock's synchrony to light may represent a specific instance of a general computational strategy employed by the mammalian nervous system, whereby sensory information is interpreted relative to an internally generated prediction.

Article.Title: Why probe registration is crucial for infant fNIRS and HD-DOT? An evaluation across 49 newborns
Article.Authors: Perkins, G. A.; Flo, A.; Visibelli, E.; Dognabas, E. N.; Reoyo-Serrano, N.; Benavides-Varela, S.
Article.Abstract: Source-detector probe registration, i.e., the mapping of optode positions on the scalp to their true anatomical locations in head/brain space, is crucial for brain imaging with fNIRS or HD-DOT. While individual, MRI-based registration is desirable, it is not always feasible, motivating the development of alternative registration approaches. This study uses the STORM-Net registration protocol and quantifies the variation of cap alignment in a cohort of 49 newborns to evaluate how this affects reconstructed images using HD-DOT. Relative to a centrally aligned template, the cohort showed a median probe-position error of 10.12 mm, while the least and most misaligned subjects exhibited mean errors of 4.41 mm and 20.60 mm, respectively. The results demonstrate that the level of cap misalignment typically observed in newborn imaging can affect the spatial accuracy of reconstructed functional images, particularly in cases with larger probe displacements. These findings provide a quantitative basis for adopting more conservative interpretations of group-level functional brain activity and functional connectivity results, and strongly support the routine use of registration methods in infant HD-DOT studies.

Article.Title: Integrated Characterization of Proximal and Distal Nerve Stumps in a Model of Chronic Motor Nerve Transection
Article.Authors: Yu, C.; Joe, L.; Newman, A.; Pepper, J.-P.
Article.Abstract: Prolonged peripheral nerve discontinuity subjects the proximal stump to chronic axotomy and the distal stump to chronic denervation, resulting in pathological changes that may compromise regeneration following delayed repair. Although these changes have been investigated in both nerve stumps, much of the existing evidence derives from mixed sensorimotor nerve models, leaving the histopathological changes of chronic motor nerve injury incompletely understood. Addressing this gap requires a well-defined, reproducible model that maintains prolonged motor nerve discontinuity and enables concurrent characterization of both nerve stumps. This study aimed to establish a chronic motor nerve transection model and characterize the distinct structural and microenvironmental changes occurring in both nerve stumps. The buccal branch of the facial nerve was transected in Lewis rats, and the nerve ends were secured to adjacent muscle to prevent spontaneous reconnection. At 10 weeks post-injury (p.i.), proximal and distal stumps were compared with uninjured nerves using histological, immunofluorescence, and morphometric analyses. Persistent functional impairment was observed throughout the study period. The proximal stump exhibited traumatic neuroma formation, altered axonal morphology, and loss of myelin integrity, but largely preserved its underlying nerve architecture and microenvironment. In contrast, the distal stump exhibited reduced neurofilament expression, clusters of small-caliber myelinated axons, and increased myelinated axon density compared to both uninjured nerves and the proximal chronically injured segment. These changes were accompanied by endoneurial tube atrophy, increased collagen I deposition, vascular remodeling, and immune-cell accumulation, indicating extensive structural and microenvironmental remodeling. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that chronic motor nerve transection produces two distinct pathological compartments: a proximal stump characterized by persistent but disorganized regeneration-associated features and a distal stump characterized by pronounced degenerative and microenvironmental changes. This study establishes a reproducible model of chronic peripheral nerve injury and provides a foundation for investigating how these compartment-specific pathologies contribute to regenerative failure and for developing targeted therapeutic strategies to improve regeneration following delayed nerve repair.

Article.Title: Oligodendrocyte precursor cell death does not contribute to lifelong population homeostasis
Article.Authors: Kamen, Y.; Scholand, A.; Hill, R. A.
Article.Abstract: Oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) proliferate and differentiate into myelinating oligodendrocytes throughout life, but it is unclear if their continuous self-renewal is balanced by cell death. We find that OPCs do not die during development or adulthood, nor during remyelination, acute systemic inflammation, or aging. These findings challenge the assumption that spontaneous OPC death is common and reveal that OPC homeostasis does not depend on programmed cell death.

Article.Title: Establishing an assay for visual desensitization in larval zebrafish for understanding synaptic plasticity
Article.Authors: Gorska, O.; Freifeld, L.; Severi, K. E.
Article.Abstract: Synaptic plasticity, the ability of neurons to modify the strength of their connections, is essential for learning. Desensitization is a type of synaptic plasticity during which a behavioral response to a stimulus is reduced after repeated presentations of a weakened version of the stimulus which does not produce the behavioral response and thus is deemed a subthreshold stimulus. Here we explore whether the larval zebrafish escape response from visual threats, such as an expanding dark spot, can act as a potential model to study desensitization. We developed a novel experimental setup to investigate visual desensitization, exposing larvae to looming visual threats of varying contrast, and used high-speed cameras to verify rapid escape movements. First, we established stimuli which reliably acted as subthreshold and suprathreshold stimuli. Next, we quantified the response rate before and after desensitization and compared those data to control larvae who were not desensitized. We observed desensitized larvae reduced their response rate to threatening looming stimuli. By providing an opportunity to explore the plasticity mechanisms governing sensory-motor transformations and behavioral adaptation, this research contributes to our understanding of fundamental principles of learning and neural plasticity across vertebrates.

Article.Title: Transplantation of human iPSC-derived retinal cells in the cone-dominant Northern tree shrew
Article.Authors: Yu, C. T.; Kandoi, S.; Follett, H. M.; Mitra, E.; Periasamy, R.; Allen, K. P.; Summerfelt, P.; Freling, S.; Lipinski, D. M.; Carroll, J.; Lamba, D. A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract: Purpose: To characterize the transplantation and survival of photoreceptors generated from human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived retinal organoids in the Northern tree shrew (Tupaia belangeri, TS). Methods: TS eyes were injected with retinal cells dissociated from GFP-expressing hiPSC-derived retinal organoids (12 animals; n=22 eyes). 15 eyes had prior damage induced by either experimental retinal detachment (n=11) or ATP-induced retinal damage (n=4), and seven eyes were undamaged. Retinal organoids were treated with Notch pathway inhibitor 2 days before transplant. TS retinal structure and cellular details were assessed post-transplantation for up to 8 weeks using scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (SLO), optical coherence tomography (OCT), and adaptive optics SLO (AOSLO). Histological analysis was done at the end of the experiment. Results: Cell transplants in eyes treated with a simple immunosuppression treatment failed to survive for more than 2 weeks (n=10 eyes). Robust cell survival was observed in the eyes treated with a complex immunosuppression cocktail for up to 8 weeks (n=12 eyes). The transplanted cells were confirmed to be subretinally located using OCT imaging and the cell fate was confirmed to be human photoreceptors by histology. Finally, AOSLO imaging captured structures resembling photoreceptor inner segments. Conclusions: Our results demonstrate survival of transplanted cells using a species-specific immunosuppression treatment. Future studies should aim to explore the long-term survival and function of the transplanted cells.
