Article.Title: Donor Aware Reanalysis of Neuronal Nuclei Supports STMN2 Depletion Associated with Nuclear TDP 43 loss in FTD and ALS
Article.Authors: CHAUDHARY, A.; Yao, S.
Article.Abstract: Background. Nuclear TDP-43 depletion is a central pathological feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD), but donor-to-donor variation can obscure transcriptomic associations in small postmortem cohorts. We reanalyzed public RNA-seq data from FACS-isolated NeuN-positive frontal-cortex neuronal nuclei to quantify gene-expression changes associated with nuclear TDP-43 loss while explicitly accounting for donor structure. Methods. The supplied GSE126542-derived matrix contained 62,754 genes across 12 libraries from seven donors, including five complete matched pairs. Source labels TDP-43 positive and TDP-43 negative were harmonized as nuclear TDP-43 retained and lost, respectively. After validation against featureCounts-assigned read counts, 44,225 genes with at least 10 total counts were analyzed using PyDESeq2. The primary model was ~ donor + nuclear_status; status-only and diagnosis-adjusted models were sensitivity analyses. The contrast was TDP-43 loss minus retained. Results. The donor-aware model identified 3,442 genes at false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05: 1,865 lower and 1,577 higher in TDP-43-loss nuclei. STMN2 was consistently depleted (log2 fold change = -1.813, 95% Wald interval -2.229 to -1.396; FDR = 6.22e-15), corresponding to approximately 71.5% lower expression. Normalized STMN2 counts were lower in TDP-43-loss nuclei in all five complete donor pairs. TARDBP expression was also lower (log2 fold change = -0.606; FDR = 4.98e-6). In contrast, UNC13A whole-gene expression was modestly higher in the donor-aware model (log2 fold change = 0.372; FDR = 0.00622) and was not significant in either sensitivity model. Conclusions. Donor-aware analysis supports a robust association between nuclear TDP-43 loss and STMN2 depletion in this neuronal-nuclei cohort, alongside extensive but model-dependent transcriptomic variation. Whole-gene UNC13A expression cannot be used to infer UNC13A cryptic-exon inclusion or functional UNC13A depletion. No splice-junction, percent-spliced-in, isoform, or protein measurements were available; mechanistic claims therefore require junction-level and experimental validation.

Article.Title: Systematic Spike Sorting Errors Revealed by Juxtacellular Ground Truth in the Awake Brain
Article.Authors: Saccomano, Z.; Khaghani, B.; Bullins Shugg, R.; McKenzie, S.; English, D. F.
Article.Abstract: Existing ground-truth data for spike sorting come almost entirely from anesthetized or in vitro preparations. Yet phenomena expected to challenge spike sorting most (spike overlap and bursting) depend on brain state and differ in the awake brain. Therefore, error estimates from existing benchmarks may not transfer to awake recordings, and the types of errors in the awake brain remain largely uncharacterized. To address this, we generated a ground-truth dataset (16 neurons) using paired juxtacellular-extracellular electrophysiology in awake mice, and found spike sorting performance, particularly recall, to be lower than conventional benchmarks might suggest. Generally, false negatives sharply increased with intrinsic physiological factors like bursting, whereas false positives were more strongly associated with extrinsic factors, such as putative spike overlaps. To quantify contributions to errors from intrinsic and extrinsic factors, for each observed juxtacellular waveform we predicted the corresponding extracellular waveform. In the best-performing sorter, we estimate approximately half of false positives were attributable to credulous attempts to resolve putative overlaps. Bursting and putative overlaps were each associated with a roughly doubled false negative rate when they occurred separately, and with a sevenfold increase when they occurred together. These co-occurrences accounted for approximately 40% of a typical neuron's false negatives, despite comprising only approximately a fifth of its spikes. Thus, the moments when spike sorters must rely on the assumption of waveform invariance the most to resolve overlaps are exactly the moments when bursting makes that assumption least valid. We also estimate that three-quarters of false negatives had been detected but assigned to other units. These spikes were not cleanly oversplit: post-hoc merging was not productive because the loss in precision was three times the gain in recall. Because bursting and spike overlaps often co-occur, sorting spikes by waveform similarity and repairing the result by post hoc merging is unlikely to adequately balance precision and recall in the situations of greatest scientific interest. That is, while bursting and spike overlaps may involve only a minority of spikes, the resulting sorting errors may disproportionately distort the interpretation of neuronal population dynamics. We thus conclude that uncertainty quantification in sorters' output is essential.

Article.Title: Sensory neurons gate a cortical plasticity window for immune encoding
Article.Authors: Gursky, Z. H.; Tang, S.; Wu, M.; Liu, C.; Fang, S.-Y.; Farrell, E. K.; Subramanian, S.; Wu, A.; Colom Diaz, P.; Ibrahim, A.; Berto, S.; Che, A.; Favuzzi, E.
Article.Abstract: Activity-dependent plasticity allows brain circuits to encode experience, but this has been established with brief stimuli. Immune responses develop over days and are represented in the insular cortex (IC). How the cortex encodes experiences with this temporal structure is unknown. Here we show that Trpv1+ sensory neurons open a multi-day cortical plasticity window matched to the immune response. Following peripheral immune challenges, Parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory interneurons are activated first, restricting plasticity. Vasoactive intestinal peptide-expressing interneurons respond two days later, disinhibiting IC excitatory neurons. Weaker challenges trigger the first phase but not the second, and preventing the transition blocks immune encoding, whereas lowering inhibition beforehand does not. These results identify a body-to-brain mechanism that gates cortical plasticity on the timescale of slowly evolving physiological experience.

Article.Title: Long term survival of chronically demyelinated axons in the taiep rat
Article.Authors: Edgar, J. M.; Langan, N.; August, B. K.; Chapple, K. J.; Allardyce, H.; Radecki, D.; Duncan, I.
Article.Abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an inflammatory demyelinating disease of the CNS in which neuroaxonal loss underlies permanent neurological disability. Axon loss in MS has been attributed to several causes, including loss of trophic/metabolic support from the myelin sheath. However, the contribution of chronic demyelination to axonal demise has been difficult to ascertain, due largely to the lack of long-lived models and uncertainty about the location of the primary injury site in long fibre tracts in MS patients. Here, we examine chronically demyelinated axons using light and electron microscopy of spinal cord tracts of 1- to 24-month-old taiep rats, in which the gene that is mutated, Tubb4a p.A302T, is expressed highly in oligodendrocytes. We find that small diameter axons in the dorsal column can survive for many months following demyelination. This is associated with significantly increased densities of oligodendroglia, and supernumerary glial cell processes. We hypothesise that trophic and metabolic support, sufficient to support axon survival, can be achieved through close contact between axons and glia. While efforts to restore myelin in MS remain crucial to recovering normal neurological function, myelin per se might not be a prerequisite for axonal survival under all circumstances.

Article.Title: PHASOR: An Open-Source Pipeline for Hidden Markov Model Analysis of Stimulus-Locked Retinal Multielectrode-Array Population Activity
Article.Authors: Shaik, M. J.; Chen, S.; Jin, J.; Babino, D.
Article.Abstract: Multielectrode-array recordings of the retina reveal neural population activity at cellular resolution, but relating recurring population states to stimulus timing and single-unit responses requires several linked analysis steps. We present PHASOR (Population HMM Analysis of Stimulus-locked Output in the Retina), a pipeline that combines stimulus-clock alignment, Fourier-based response classification, hidden Markov modeling with Chow-Liu tree emissions, model-order selection, and state visualization. We evaluated the workflow with synthetic populations and demonstrated its use in ten ex vivo recordings from three wild-type retinas (two male, one female) and one male rd1 retina, including 2 Hz full-field sinusoidal stimulation. Across ten synthetic datasets containing seven generative states, selected model orders ranged from seven to nine, with a mean of 7.9, matching the generative count exactly in three of the ten datasets. A representative confusion matrix showed a near one-to-one correspondence between generative and decoded states, with a single additional low-occupancy state, illustrating the distinction between recovering temporal structure and recovering the exact state count. In a representative retinal recording, response classes differed in stimulus phase and contrast dependence, and decoded states differed in occupancy, dwell time, and active-unit composition. Recordings during L-AP4 application, without projected stimulation, and in a photoreceptor-degenerate rd1 retina illustrated changes in the resulting population-state descriptions. PHASOR integrates established analysis methods into a reusable workflow for relating stimulus-associated population activity to functional response classes. The selected states provide a descriptive model of population activity; their number and correspondence to biological assemblies require separate validation.

Article.Title: Direction-Dependent Encoding of Forward and Inverse Models in the Same Purkinje Cells
Article.Authors: Inoue, J.; Markanday, A.; Thier, P.
Article.Abstract: Saccadic eye movements are too fast to be guided by sensory feedback and therefore depend on precisely calibrated internal models. The cerebellum is widely thought to compute both forward and inverse models, yet how these two computations coexist in the same circuit remains unclear. We hypothesized that the same Purkinje cells (PCs) can serve as a forward model for saccades in one direction and as an inverse model for saccades in the opposite direction, because target neurons on either side of the cerebellar nuclei contribute differently to leftward and rightward saccades. To test this hypothesis, we recorded from PCs in the oculomotor vermis of macaque monkeys during repetitive saccade paradigms that induce adaptation and fatigue. Using the preferred error direction of each PC conveyed by increased complex spike (CS) activity (CS-on direction) as a proxy of the side of the cerebellar nuclei it projects to, we compared population activity for saccades directed against the CS-on direction (CS-on opposed) and along it (CS-on aligned). CS-on opposed saccades, (toward the PC's projection side) were accompanied by a precisely timed, sharp burst of simple spike (SS) activity at saccade onset that scaled with peak velocity, and CS error sensitivity was highest after the saccade. SS activity also changed systematically after adaptation, reflecting the altered kinematics of the adapted saccade. These properties are consistent with a forward model that estimates ongoing movement and updates itself based on post-movement error. In contrast, the CS-on aligned saccades, (away from the PC's projection side) were accompanied by broader SS modulation around saccade offset, and the CS error sensitivity was highest before the saccade. CSs around saccade onset encoded target location and initial eye position, and their occurrence was associated with reduced saccade amplitude. This reduction likely adjusts the motor command to the starting eye position, as expected for an inverse model that pre-programs the motor command before movement begins. Together, these findings provide neural evidence that the same PC population can contribute to both forward and inverse model computations, depending on saccade direction.

Article.Title: Predicting cortical signal mixing in coarse-resolution fMRI: a forward-operator analysis of surface mapping and the conditional benefit of correction
Article.Authors: Velioglu, H. A.
Article.Abstract: Surface-based fMRI projection can mix signals from cortical locations that are close in the volume but distant along the folded cortical sheet. We constructed an anatomy- and acquisition-informed linear forward operator to estimate this mixing and evaluated a regularised surface reconstruction that inverts it. In HCP 7T geometry, the operator-predicted net far-cortex contribution to a standard surface value exceeded 5% in 4%, 10% and 22% of the group-average cortex at 1.6 mm and at emulated 2.4 and 3.2 mm resolution. Including the modelled far component improved predictions of emulated coarser maps and of real coarser StudyForrest sessions in high-leakage regions. Against finer-resolution, cross-run fMRI references, the regularised reconstruction reduced the residual error in HCP development data (n = 15) and in a pre-specified, family-independent confirmatory analysis (158 participants in 86 families). The improvement increased with a response-weighted contamination measure in HCP and in an independent 3T dataset (35 test participants), although a coarse-data-only version of the measure did not generalise to 3T, where an anatomical atlas predicted the gain at twofold coarsening. Overall performance improved at twofold, but not 1.5-fold, coarsening in the 3T sample. Ablation and data-reduction analyses were consistent with an important contribution from local deconvolution but did not uniquely identify the mechanism. Benefits were smaller or absent for multi-run averages, and no robust improvement across separately acquired sessions was established. The leakage maps characterise model-predicted, signed mixing rather than directly measured signal origins, and every gain is measured against an fMRI reference rather than against the true cortical response. Code, analysis plans and group leakage maps (7T and 3T) are provided in a public repository.

Article.Title: Reaction-time asymmetry covaries with shifts in hand choice in macaques
Article.Authors: Holmes, C. D.; Hong, S.; Gepshtein, S.; Snyder, L. H.; Mooshagian, E.
Article.Abstract: How primates choose which hand to reach with remains poorly understood. Humans prefer the hand on the target's side of the body midline, and that preference shifts with biomechanical cost and with head and gaze direction. Earlier monkey studies used only two targets, one per side, too few to fit a psychometric function. Reaction time may also reflect the choice; in humans it is longest at the point of subjective equality (PSE), the target position at which either hand is equally likely to be chosen. We measured hand choice at ten horizontal target positions in two male rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) that chose freely on each trial. For peripheral targets, both animals used the hand on the same side of the body midline, with a well-defined transition in between. Displacing the hands, rotating the head, or displacing gaze to one side each moved the PSE toward that side. Reaction time was longest near the PSE. Hand displacement slowed the hand on the displaced side, and gaze displacement slowed the hand opposite the gaze. In every condition, the farther the PSE lay toward one side, the slower that side's hand was relative to the other. Macaque hand choice thus resembles human hand choice, making the macaque a tractable model for studying how the brain chooses a hand.

Article.Title: Dyskinesia induced by a dopamine 2 receptor-like agonist, but not a dopamine 1 receptor-like agonist, is blocked by sub-anesthetic ketamine
Article.Authors: Parmar, R.; Meredith, J. R.; Bartlett, M. J.; Smith, E. G. E.; Castro, J. M.; Sherman, S. J.; Chattree, G.; Steece-Collier, K.; Falk, T.
Article.Abstract: L-DOPA remains the most effective symptomatic treatment for Parkinson's disease, but chronic administration is frequently complicated by L-DOPA-induced dyskinesia (LID). Our prior work has established that sub-anesthetic ketamine can reduced LID acutely and has a long-lasting neuroplastic effect. This study tested whether low-dose ketamine reduces dyskinesia induced specifically by dopamine D2R-like or D1R-like receptor activation. Male Sprague Dawley rats were primed with daily L-DOPA to establish dyskinesia and then challenged with quinpirole, a D2R-like receptor agonist, or SKF-81297, a D1R-like receptor agonist, to induce abnormal involuntary movements (AIMs). After stable AIM baselines were established, animals received agonist plus vehicle or agonist plus ketamine. Limb, axial, and orolingual AIMs were scored on the acute treatment day (D0) and after washout on D4 and D7. Quinpirole and SKF-81297 reliably produced stable total LAO AIM scores following L-DOPA priming. Ketamine significantly reduced only quinpirole-induced, but not SKF-81297-induced, total AIMs compared with vehicle on D0, demonstrating an acute anti-dyskinetic effect. This reduction persisted after washout, with ketamine-treated animals continuing to show significantly lower AIMs on D4 and D7. Time-course analyses further showed reduced AIMs expression across the post-quinpirole observation period on D0 and at multiple time points on D7. These findings demonstrate that ketamine suppresses quinpirole-induced dyskinesia in L-DOPA-primed male rats and suggest that D2R-like receptor-mediated or indirect pathway-related mechanisms, but not direct pathway-related mechanisms, may contribute to ketamine's anti-dyskinetic effects. Together, these results extend prior work on ketamine by linking its sustained anti-dyskinetic effects to dyskinesia driven by D2R-like receptor stimulation in vivo.

Article.Title: Serial dependence carries the action that produced the previous report
Article.Authors: Qu, C.; Naeve, C.; Shi, Z.
Article.Abstract: Serial dependence pulls current judgments toward the recent past, but what is carried forward is debated: the previous stimulus, the previous decision, or something about the report itself. Three magnitude-reproduction experiments separated these sources. Participants viewed dot arrays that varied independently in duration and numerosity, then reproduced the cued dimension by holding a key while a display accumulated, so that both magnitudes were produced through the same action. A response-history model partitioned the attraction into previous-stimulus and previous-response paths. The previous response predicted cross-dimensional attraction after controlling for the previous and current stimuli: a numerosity report biased the next duration judgment and vice versa (Experiment 1), also when each task used its own response key (Experiment 2). A task switch weakened this carryover without abolishing it. Experiment 3 randomized, trial by trial, whether a reported number required a long or a short key hold. The influence of a previous number on the next duration judgment changed with this mapping, showing that reported value alone did not account for carryover. Conventional stimulus-based measures showed none of this cross-task history. Serial dependence can therefore carry the trace of the action through which a previous judgment was expressed, bounded but not gated by task context.

Article.Title: DPYD links glial lipids and myelination to sleep duration
Article.Authors: Zimmerman, A. J.; Deal, S.; Almeraya Del Valle, E.; Donnelly, J.; Kroll, F.; Guo, X.; Tsundupalli, T.; Shetty, Z.; Doldur-Balli, F.; Keenan, B.; Grant, S. F.; Rihel, J.; Sehgal, A.; Pack, A. I.
Article.Abstract: The regulation of sleep is heritable and conserved across species1,2, but the governing genetic mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the role of DPYD--which encodes the pyrimidine catabolic enzyme, dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase--in sleep. Using a cross-species approach, we show that DPYD and its orthologs act specifically in glia to promote sleep through the regulation of brain lipids. In mouse and zebrafish, we find that DPYD orthologs are enriched in oligodendrocyte lineage cells, and their loss reduces myelination and sleep independent of DPYDs established role in uracil catabolism to {beta}-alanine. Genetic and pharmacological manipulations of myelin in zebrafish show that altering myelination is sufficient to perturb sleep duration. In Drosophila, which lack myelin, we find that the DPYD ortholog acts in ensheathing glia to promote sleep through formation of glial lipid droplets, a proposed evolutionary precursor to myelin. Furthermore, a human GWAS-identified sleep variant2 resides in a conserved cis-regulatory element that selectively contacts the promoter of DPYD within oligodendrocytes, connecting the human genetic association to oligodendrocyte-specific control of DPYD. Together, these results identify a deeply conserved role for glial lipids in sleep regulation and establish DPYD as a mechanistic link between myelin biology and sleep.

Article.Title: Cerebrovascular Structure-Flow Gradients Revealed by Volumetric Ultrasound Localization Microscopy
Article.Authors: Zhu, J.; Kawara, S.; Riemer, K.; Wang, B.; Yan, J.; Morse, S. V.; Schultz, S. R.; Choi, J. J.; Tang, M.-X.
Article.Abstract: Characterizing the joint organization of microscale cerebrovascular structure and flow in vivo is challenging. Volumetric ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM) provides spatially resolved measures of microvascular structure and flow from the same acquisition, but how these features are jointly organized across brain networks remains unclear. Here, we characterized local vascular phenotypes from transcranial volumetric ULM in mice and examined whether they contained reproducible low-dimensional organization. Local measures of vascular structure and flow dynamics were summarized within corresponding brain regions across mice. Subject-specific vascular phenotype similarity matrices were combined into a group-consensus graph and analyzed using diffusion embedding. Two leading gradients, showing distinct spatial distributions across brain networks, were reproducibly recovered across subject and spatial scales. The principal gradient was associated with local vascular density and flow complexity, defining a vascular structure-related axis. The secondary gradient was associated with flow speed and acceleration, defining a flow-dynamics-related axis. These gradients provide a low-dimensional representation of the cerebrovascular structure and flow and provide a reference for studying coordinated vascular changes across disease, aging, and intervention.

Article.Title: A single dose of the antipsychotic drug clozapine has long-term behavioral and functional effects in mice
Article.Authors: Lupori, L.; Heindorf, M.; Kouvaros, S.; Schilling, T.; Schildkamp, A.; Bischofberger, J.; Keller, G. B.
Article.Abstract: Antipsychotic dosing regimens, commonly daily or via slow-release compounds, are designed to maintain steady-state plasma concentrations. They are guided by their plasma half-life, which is typically in the range of several hours. This schedule contrasts with the slow time course of therapeutic efficacy, which takes days to weeks to develop fully. This discrepancy led us to hypothesize that the effects of a single dose of an antipsychotic drug might be detectable well beyond the time window predicted by receptor occupancy. To test this, we administered a single dose of the antipsychotic drug clozapine to mice. We observed long-term behavioral effects and changes to cortical activity patterns up to several days after administration. Specifically, clozapine induced a decorrelation of activity in the dorsal cortex observable up to 9 days post administration. This effect was driven by a genetically and functionally distinct subset of layer 5 intratelencephalic neurons and was accompanied by an increase in the reliability of long-range inhibitory functional influence on a similar timescale. Thus, a single dose of clozapine triggers changes in the function of specific circuits that outlast the presence of the drug. If antipsychotic action depends on slower processes involving plasticity, longer dosing intervals may warrant further clinical exploration.

Article.Title: Multimodal characterization of putative pan-inhibitory viral constructs in macaque monkeys
Article.Authors: Medalla, M.; Boucher, P. O.; Mojica, C. A. R.; Bhatt, H.; Snyder, B.; Zhou, Y.; Sengupta, N.; More, A. I.; Yahaya, M.; Opitz-Araya, X.; Wang, T.; Lee, E. K.; Rosene, D. L.; Rushmore, R. J.; Moore, T. L.; Zemelman, B. V.; Ting, J. T.; Levi, B. P.; Luebke, J. I.; Chandrasekaran, C.
Article.Abstract: Transgenic approaches and validated viral vector toolboxes have advanced our understanding of how inhibitory neurons shape cognition and motor control in mice and other rodents. However, such advances have been elusive in non-human primates (NHPs). While many studies demonstrate expression of reporter proteins, few studies have provided clear quantitative evidence of whether these viral constructs can be reliably used for assessment of in vivo and in vitro function in primates, which, in turn, has hindered widespread adoption by NHP researchers. Here, we characterize putative pan-inhibitory cell targeting vectors engineered with regions from the Dlx5-6 intergenic domain. Pan-inhibitory viral vectors are attractive because they enable ground-truth optotagging and modulation of multiple inhibitory subtypes in the same animal and, when combined with machine learning approaches, enable cell-type classifiers for NHPs. We combined in vivo anesthetized electrophysiological recordings, in vitro slice electrophysiology, and immunohistochemistry across seven rhesus macaque monkeys to assess the specificity, completeness and efficacy of three constructs in multiple sensory and higher-order association cortices. The vectors reliably restricted transgene expression to inhibitory neurons (81-97%). However, of the local GABAergic neurons only 32-64% expressed the transgene, depending on the construct. This incompleteness arose in part from uneven coverage across subtypes, with strong transgene expression in parvalbumin-positive interneurons (~60-90%), sparse expression in calbindin-positive interneurons (~1-7%), and near-complete avoidance of calretinin-positive interneurons. A construct pairing DLX2.0 with ChrimsonR was excellent for in vivo optotagging, while h56D paired with bReaChES most effectively suppressed neural activity in vivo. In the slice, activating terminals of transgene-expressing neurons optically evoked inhibitory currents in coupled pyramidal neurons confirming transsynaptic functionality of these constructs and their use for inhibitory circuit-specific synaptic assessments and manipulation. Collectively, the results provide rigorous functional characterization, and quantitative guidance for NHP researchers seeking to deploy GABAergic cell-type-specific tools in their experiments.

Article.Title: Distinct medial septal GABAergic pathways differentially regulate spatial memory and network activity
Article.Authors: MacLaren, D. A. A.; Saidov, K. M.; Schlesiger, M. I.; Monyer, H.
Article.Abstract: Septal GABAergic projection neurons form distinct pathways to subregions of the hippocampal formation, including the hippocampus proper and the medial and lateral entorhinal cortices. Parvalbumin (PV+) and calbindin expressing (CB+) projections target different types of interneurons and thereby differentially regulate neuronal activity in the downstream area. Consistent with the idea of dissociable functional roles, inhibition of septal PV+ neurons impairs reference memory whereas inhibition of septal CB+ neurons impairs both reference and working memory. Here, we show that these functions are differentially supported by specific projection pathways: PV+ projections to the dorsal hippocampus and medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) support reference memory, whereas CB+ projections to the MEC support both reference and working memory. At the network level, septal PV+, but not CB+, neurons regulate theta oscillations. Together, these findings further define the roles of septal PV+ and CB+ pathways in orchestrating network activity and supporting specific forms of memory.

Article.Title: The anti-dyskinetic and the anti-parkinsonian effects of sub-anesthetic ketamine are also present in female preclinical models
Article.Authors: Parmar, R.; Bartlett, M. J.; Meredith, J. R.; Singh, S.; Ragsdale, S.; Sherman, S. J.; Falk, T.
Article.Abstract: Biological sex is an important determinant of neuropharmacological response, yet females remain underrepresented in preclinical studies of Parkinson's disease (PD) and L-DOPA-induced dyskinesia (LID). We previously demonstrated that sub-anesthetic ketamine reduces established LID, attenuates dyskinesia development, and produces anti-parkinsonian effects in male unilateral 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) rat models. However, whether these therapeutic effects extend to females remained unknown. Here, we evaluated the anti-dyskinetic and anti-parkinsonian effects of sub-anesthetic ketamine in female Sprague-Dawley rats using the attenuation and established models of LID. In the attenuation paradigm, unilateral 6-OHDA-lesioned females received repeated L-DOPA administration with either ketamine (20 mg/kg, i.p.; 10-h dosing paradigm) or vehicle. Ketamine significantly attenuated the progressive development of dyskinesia, indicating that early intervention modified the trajectory of LID expression. In the established LID paradigm, ketamine produced robust significant acute reductions in abnormal involuntary movements (AIMs) after dyskinesia had fully developed, and these significant effects persisted for up to 49 days following treatment, demonstrating sustained suppression of dyskinesia severity. To determine whether ketamine altered therapeutic motor function, forelimb adjusting steps testing was performed in female unilateral 6-OHDA rats. Ketamine did not impair L-DOPA-mediated motor improvement suggesting compatibility with the gold standard medication. Ketamine was also by itself associated with significantly improved stepping performance during ketamine treatment conditions, indicating acute anti-parkinsonian motor benefit. Together, these findings demonstrate that the anti-dyskinetic and anti-parkinsonian effects of ketamine extend to female preclinical models and strengthen the translational rationale for repurposing sub-anesthetic ketamine as a potential therapeutic strategy for individuals with LID.

Article.Title: Electroencephalographic activity patterns distinguish interdigitated default and frontoparietal networks
Article.Authors: Kucyi, A.; Braun, D.; Shareef-Trudeau, L.; Adler, A.; Pantazis, D.
Article.Abstract: The brain is comprised of distributed functional networks that operate on diverse time scales. Evidence from precision fMRI shows that canonical networks, including default (DN), frontoparietal control (FPCN), and dorsal attention (dATN), each fractionate into multiple finely interdigitated networks. However, as fMRI is blind to fast processes underlying neural communication, there remains a need to neurophysiologically characterize individual-level network fractionation. To address this need, we conducted a simultaneous EEG-fMRI study, including multiple sessions per individual, resting-state and task conditions, and carbon wire loop sensors for optimized artifact correction. Using precision network mapping, we discovered dissociable electrophysiological correlates of blood-oxygen-level-dependent activity for two networks within the boundaries of the canonical DN. One (DNa) related more positively with alpha and high-beta power, while another (DNb) related more negatively with theta and low-beta power. Univariate and machine learning analyses further revealed electrophysiological dissociations between networks within the canonical FPCN (FPCNa versus FPCNb) but not dATN. The network-specific electrophysiological activity patterns were reliable across sessions, only modestly variable between resting-state and demanding task conditions, and observable for neighboring nodes of different networks across multiple cortical zones. Our findings provide insight into rhythmic neural processes that fine-grained networks may engage to support divergent cognitive operations.

Article.Title: CD40 ligand and IFN-γ induce proinflammatory activity and microglia-mediated neurodegeneration in human stem cell models
Article.Authors: Hammond, T.; Wirak, G. S.; Ryan, S. K.; Blazier, A.; Liu, D.; Nyarko-Danquah, I.; LaMorte, M.; Khader, S.; Vela, J.; Yang, B.; Wesseling, H.; Zhang, B.; Rapaport, F.; Gandhi, R.; Djukic, B.; Ofengeim, D.
Article.Abstract: The cluster of differentiation 40 (CD40)/CD40 ligand (CD40L) co-stimulatory pathway plays a critical role in the activation and regulation of immune networks involving both adaptive and innate immune cells. Dysregulation of this pathway has been implicated in multiple autoimmune diseases, including multiple sclerosis (MS). MS is characterized by progressive neurodegeneration driven by compartmentalized neuroinflammation within the central nervous system (CNS), sustained low-grade T cell infiltration at the blood-brain barrier, and T cell reactivation at CNS border tissues. CD40L-expressing T cells can activate CD40-expressing microglia, which are a critical effector cell that contribute to neurodegeneration in MS. However, the consequence of this functional interaction in the brain remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that the combination of CD40L and interferon-gamma (IFN-{gamma}), a cytokine produced by activated T cells, induces a robust inflammatory response and cell death in human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSC)-derived microglia. Stimulation with CD40L elicited microglial clustering, morphological transformation, and robust release of proinflammatory cytokines including interleukin-12 (IL-12), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-), and IL-6. Anti-CD40L antibody treatment reversed both cell death and inflammatory response and partially normalized the associated transcriptional changes. Furthermore, using an hiPSC-derived tri-culture system comprising neurons, astrocytes, and microglia, we demonstrated that CD40L and IFN-{gamma} trigger microglia-dependent neuronal dysregulation and death. Anti-CD40L treatment substantially attenuated neuronal injury. Finally, transcriptomic enrichment analysis identified CD40L-mediated microglial gene expression signatures that correlated with CD40 expression in primary progressive MS brain tissue but not in the normal-appearing white matter of healthy controls. Collectively, these findings support a role for the microglial CD40/T cell CD40L axis in MS pathology and suggest CD40L blockade as a potential therapeutic strategy warranting further investigation.

Article.Title: Sensory representation by non-equilibrium flows of neural activity at the mesoscale of cortex
Article.Authors: Braun, J.; Lamb, N.; Ghosh, K. -
Article.Abstract: We present a non-equilibrium theory of sensory perception and the mesoscale of sensory cortex. We propose that local neuron assemblies (cortical columns) toggle spontaneously between activity states (on and off) and that small populations of columns are coupled within and between areas of sensory cortex. The resulting network generates sudden, large-scale fluctuations and represents sensory inputs and perceptions by characteristic patterns of activity flows. The non-equilibrium dynamic is governed by the variational principle of maximal path entropy, or Maximum Caliber. Many current theories, by contrast, posit equilibrium dynamics and representation with activity states Our minimal model of sensory cortex describes populations of columns from two cortical areas and is fully constrained by empirical observations of `reversals' in perceived appearance, which occur spontaneously for visual, auditory, and tactile stimulation. We formalize representation by activity flows with dynamic Hamiltonian functions. Surprisingly, effective representation requires small-number fluctuations of toggling columns, as larger numbers would be dominated by hysteresis. Finally, we detail predictions for the microscale of spiking neurons that follow from on-off toggling and non-equilibrium dynamics. We conclude that the neural levels underlying perception are functionally organized in terms of activity flows. The inherent instability of non-equilibrium ensures active updating and renders all perceptions open to immediate revision. We conjecture that current theories of brain function (such as the Free Energy Principle) could be reformulated in terms of the variational principle of non-equilibrium, Maximum Caliber.

Article.Title: Embodied Dynamic Causal Modelling: Brain and Cardiac Effective Connectivity
Article.Authors: Levy, A. D.; Zeidman, P.; Allen, M.; Friston, K.
Article.Abstract: Brain-body interactions underpin embodied inference and interoception, and are central to both general health and the pathophysiology of mental health disorders. These interactions are orchestrated across a hierarchy extending from the cortex, through the brainstem, to peripheral autonomic effectors. Existing methods either reduce this communication to scalar summaries or lack an invertible biophysical model, and so cannot resolve where in this extended architecture an observed effect originates. To address this, we introduce Embodied Dynamic Causal Modelling, an extension of the generative causal modelling framework that formalises hierarchical message passing across the full brain-body axis. We instantiate the framework for brain-heart interactions with the Brainstem Cardiac Network, a closed-loop neural mass model of brainstem autonomic circuitry and sinoatrial node dynamics. By incorporating five brainstem nuclei, a viscerosensory thalamic relay and the cardiac pacemaker, the network enables estimation of directed effective connectivity across the cortical-brainstem-cardiac axis. As an illustrative case study, representative of the experiments and extended physiological systems that Embodied DCM and the BCN can now interrogate, we applied the framework to simultaneously recorded electroencephalography and electrocardiography during an auditory Go/No-Go paradigm. A multimodal observation model permits joint inversion of electrophysiological and cardiac responses, so that neural and bodily measurements together constrain an account of central and peripheral dynamics. The case study shows how the framework can arbitrate between competing hypotheses about functional cytoarchitecture, distinguishing granular from agranular microcircuits within the viscero-sensorimotor hierarchy. It also shows how time-varying estimates of synaptic efficacy can be recovered alongside continuous latent neuronal dynamics, over extended windows spanning anticipation, target processing and motor inhibition. By linking neural and cardiac signals to a single generative architecture, this work moves the study of brain-heart interactions beyond correlation, providing a framework for testing theories of embodied inference and for identifying circuit-level disruptions in disorders of interoceptive and autonomic regulation.

Article.Title: A hypothalamo-septo-hippocampal circuit for REM sleep-dependent consolidation of social memory
Article.Authors: Qin, H.; Jian, T.; Jin, W.; Liang, M.; Liao, X.; Zhang, K.; Liang, S.; Zhang, C.; He, C.; Jia, H.; Wang, Y.; Han, J.; Chen, X.
Article.Abstract: REM sleep constitutes a critical window for memory consolidation, yet the brain circuits orchestrating this process remain incompletely defined. Here, we identify a lateral supramammillary nucleus (SuM)-medial septum (MS) projection as a REM sleep-specialized pathway essential for hippocampal memory consolidation. Fiber photometry and optrode recordings revealed that lateral SuM-MS projecting neurons were selectively active during REM sleep. REM-specific optogenetic silencing of this projection impaired consolidation of both social and contextual fear memories. Crucially, silencing of its downstream target, the MS-CA2 pathway, during REM sleep selectively disrupted social memory while sparing contextual fear memory. This functional dissection establishes a hypothalamo-septo-hippocampal circuit (lateral SuM-MS-CA2) dedicated to social memory processing, in parallel to the recently-described direct SuM-CA2 pathway. These results also position the SuM as a REM sleep-hub that routes information via parallel septal pathways to consolidate distinct memory modalities.

Article.Title: A vagal-to-sympathetic reflex controls lung vascular leak
Article.Authors: Robinson, E.; Ibanez, E. M.; Santibanez Ocampo, B.; Li, J.; Ballal, N.; Miller, J. M.; Shivdikar, K.; Umans, B. D.; Prescott, S. L.
Article.Abstract: Dynamic regulation of the vascular barrier is required for innate immunity, yet excessive leak endangers vulnerable organs like the lungs, where edema stiffens tissue and threatens breathing. The reflex originates in a previously-uncharacterized population of polymodal, alveolus-innervating vagal sensory neurons marked by Cysltr2. Stimulating CYSLTR2 neurons increases lung fluid within minutes, whereas sustained activation elicits perivascular edema and respiratory dysfunction. Silencing them during allergen challenge reduces leak and improves lung mechanics. Rather than acting locally, CYSLTR2 neurons relay centrally to sympathetic efferents to broadcast effects throughout lung vasculature. This pathway thus forms an axis of organ defense that can go awry in disease, suggesting new ways to control lung fluid balance.

Article.Title: Summed contrasts can conceal reversed regional preferences: directional and dose criteria for screening transcranial direct current stimulation montage pairs
Article.Authors: Bruschi, D. L.; Schiavi, A.; Joseph, I.
Article.Abstract: Background: The regional-matching design evaluated here requires two transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) montages, each stronger in its own target region, with adequate exposure. Summed contrasts can be positive when only one preference holds. Objective: To test whether a summed double-dissociation index (DDI), overlap and cohort-median dose rules identify such pairs, for a focused-attention versus open-monitoring experiment. Methods: Twenty-four montage pairs were simulated in 20 anatomical head models (SimNIBS 4.6, 2 mA). A four-rule screen (DDI, overlap, cohort-median dose) was recorded before cohort results; a post hoc conjunction required both regional contrasts positive in >=80% of heads. Two leading pairs were compared on per-head dose, a second solver and 60 conductivity stress-test draws. Results: Eighteen pairs passed the screen, but 13 failed the conjunction; one with positive median DDI (0.782) reversed the salience-region preference in all 20 heads. The nominated pair (F3-centered 4x1 ring; F8-Fp2 sponges; median DDI 1.561; both preferences in 20/20 heads) brought both anatomical targets to the 0.20 V/m operational floor in 11/20 heads; a conventional sponge pair (DDI 0.627) did so in 20/20, though both passed the cohort-median dose rule. The nominated pair's separation held across a second solver and all 60 stress-test draws, but both network targets reached the floor in 19/60. Conclusions: Summed indices and cohort-median dose rules can pass pairs that fail reciprocal-exposure criteria. Such screens should pre-specify the directional conjunction and report per-head joint dose coverage. These are modeled exposures, not physiological or behavioral effects.

Article.Title: Apolipoprotein E4 Exacerbates Aβ Oligomer-Induced Synaptotoxicity through Promoting Autophagic Degradation of Glutathione Peroxidase 4
Article.Authors: Zhou, J.; Liao, H.; Liang, W.; Liu, S.; Cai, J.; Liu, Y.; Liu, Y.; Zhou, Z.; Wu, S.
Article.Abstract: Extensive synaptic loss and progressive neurodegeneration are defining pathological hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease (AD), primarily driven by soluble A{beta} oligomers and neurofibrillary tangles. The apolipoprotein E4 (APOE4) isoform further aggravates these pathological cascades, yet the precise molecular mechanisms underlying AD pathogenesis remain poorly elucidated. Store-operated calcium entry (SOCE) deficiency in neurons has been proven to exert a detrimental effect on dendritic spine integrity and function. Herein, we investigated whether SOCE dysregulation contributes to A{beta}O-induced synaptotoxicity and how APOE4 modulates this pathological process. In primary neuronal cultures, co-treatment with A{beta}O and APOE4 markedly reduced synapse density and impaired dendritic arbor complexity, compared with A{beta}O treatments combined with APOE3 or APOE2 isoforms. Consistently, neurons exposed to A{beta}O plus APOE4 exhibited significantly lower SOCE amplitudes than those treated with A{beta}O and APOE3. In line with SOCE suppression, the A{beta}O/APOE4 combination specifically downregulated stromal interaction molecule 1 (STIM1) protein expression, with no observable change in STIM2 levels. Mechanistically, A{beta}O/APOE4-mediated STIM1 reduction was dependent on p62-selective autophagic degradation. Notably, exogenous STIM1 overexpression effectively rescued the deficits in dendritic arbor complexity. Furthermore, STIM1 downregulation induced by A{beta}O and APOE4 initiated the autophagic degradation of glutathione peroxidase 4 (Gpx4). This autophagy activation was attributed to decreased Bcl2 expression and occurs independently of STING accumulation. Subsequent Gpx4 insufficiency further triggered excessive accumulation of reactive oxygen species and disrupted mitochondrial cristae morphology in neurons. Collectively, our findings uncover a previously unrecognized mechanism whereby APOE4 exacerbates A{beta}O-induced synaptotoxicity. Specifically, the combination facilitates p62-mediated selective autophagic degradation of STIM1, which suppresses Bcl2 expression and ultimately promotes robust Gpx4 autophagic degradation, driving neuronal synaptic damage.

Article.Title: Association between white-matter lesion volume and heart-rate variability: A comparison of T1w, T1w+T2w and T1w+FLAIR-based segmentations using FreeSurfer SAMSEG
Article.Authors: Robinson, T. D.; Cerri, S.; Zhang, F. E.; van Leemput, K.; Chen, J. J.
Article.Abstract: Background Heart disease is a crucial risk factor for brain degeneration, but the specific mechanisms of this association are still under investigation. Notably, the development of white-matter lesions, a hallmark of cerebral small-vessel disease with connections to progressive neurodegeneration and cognitive decline, has been linked to cardiovascular disease. As such, measures of cardiovascular function such as heart-rate variability may represent accessible indicators of white-matter lesion burden. After controlling for the effect of age on lesion volume, low-frequency heart rate variability specifically was found to interact with age-related lesion volume. Moreover, we showed that the relationship between white-matter lesion volume and heart-rate variability is apparent using T1w+FLAIR or T1w+T2w based lesion estimates could be observed with T1w-based lesion estimation alone, opening new avenues for studying cerebral small-vessel disease. Discussion These results suggest heart rate variability as a factor in the translation between cardiovascular risk and white matter degeneration, as well as an accessible and non-invasive indicator of white-matter lesion burden and associated cognitive impairment in later life. The unique association between reduced low-frequency band heart-rate variability and age-related lesion burden may help to establish the link between autonomic control of cardiac function and brain health in aging.

Article.Title: Human and mouse cerebellar inhibitory circuits in dystonic crisis and their modulation with therapeutic stimulation
Article.Authors: Rey Hipolito, A. G.; Dew, M. P.; Gill, J. S.; Allen, J. E.; Chesky, K. A.; Hull, M.; Sillitoe, R. V.
Article.Abstract: Dystonia is a neurological movement disorder characterized by abnormal muscle contractions that, at their most severe, lead to a life-threatening condition - dystonic crisis. Yet, therapeutic options remain limited by our incomplete understanding of what neural circuits underly the condition. Although cerebellar nuclei neurons are implicated in the origin of baseline dystonic symptoms, it is unclear whether their activity drives dystonic crisis. To explore this role, we found that cerebellar abnormalities and neural inhibition were recurring targets in patients with dystonic crisis, implicating cerebellar inhibitory neurons in its development. Directional optogenetic modulation of iCNNs induced dystonic crises on-demand and alleviated spontaneous crises in mice that mimic spontaneous dystonic crises. To investigate whether iCNNs interact with other motor areas during dystonic crisis, we identified monosynaptic iCNN projections to the centrolateral nucleus of the thalamus (CL). Deep brain stimulation of the CL alleviated dystonic crises induced by iCNN photoactivation. Our data uncover a cell type-specific cerebellar origin of dystonic crisis and highlight its therapeutic potential.

Article.Title: Glider compositionality and information capacity in an E/I-balanced neuronal automaton
Article.Authors: Belluscio, M.; Pajevic, S.; Plenz, D.
Article.Abstract: In cellular automata, localized activity patterns called gliders propagate and interact to carry and transform information. Whether neuronal networks can harness this computational power remains unclear. Here, we demonstrate that a cortical network model with separate excitatory and inhibitory populations, graded cellular activity and uniform local connectivity spontaneously generates diverse, interacting gliders. An analytical reduction identifies the cellular conditions sustaining propagation of the dominant G-glider. Distinct gliders can assemble into growing structures that emit other glider types. Near excitation/inhibition balance, sparse glider dynamics coexist with high computational capacity, measured by input differentiation and generalization, with local capacity varying across space and time. Strong mutual inhibition between interneurons instead permits metastatic proliferation with low computational capacity. These findings connect cellular automata to neuronal information processing and identify interacting gliders as a candidate mechanism for dynamic plasticity: the reorganization of computation within an unchanged synaptic architecture.

Article.Title: Practical Identifiability of a Minimal Adaptive Learning-Gain Model for Binary Feedback: A Simulation Study
Article.Authors: Li, W.; Zhong, J.
Article.Abstract: Social learning is shaped by distinct computational components--baseline beliefs (prior mean), feedback sensitivity (learning gain), and temporal uncertainty (drift)--that empirical designs rarely disentangle. We evaluate practical identifiability and predictive performance of a parsimonious four-parameter adaptive learning-gain model for binary feedback, where a latent belief about positive-outcome probability updates deterministically between observations and an internal confidence-precision state decays each trial. {sigma}, {omega}, and {lambda} are internal, model-defined variables--not validated psychological constructs. Using fixed-seed simulations, we report four findings. Joint maximum-likelihood recovery is poor: on a 24-condition grid (T=80), {sigma} and {omega} show near-zero tolerance-based recovery ([≤]0.002) across tolerances 0.3-1.0, {lambda} recovers at 0.078-0.263, and longer sequences do not improve recovery. Profile-likelihood and trade-off diagnostics show flat regions for {sigma} and {omega} and an asymmetric {lambda} profile, indicating weak practical (not structural) identifiability. A fitting-parity audit fixed a return-order bug in the fixed-gain candidate. After correction, block-level model discrimination is 0.48 (72/150) under common bounds--above chance (p<0.001)--but is driven almost entirely by Rescorla-Wagner (0.88-0.90); the adaptive filter and its nested fixed-gain restriction remain indistinguishable. Across 50 held-out datasets, the model shows no predictive advantage over an empirical-frequency baseline (paired 95% CIs span zero). Ablations show the added update components provide no consistent benefit. These results caution against interpreting individual parameter estimates from this model class in short binary-feedback designs, and specify that mechanistic claims about clinical group differences in {sigma}, {omega}, or {lambda} require graded responses, manipulated volatility, multi-context sequences, and longitudinal replication.

Article.Title: Dog and Human Brains Represent Human Emotional Bodies with Asymmetric Encoding of Happiness and Anger
Article.Authors: Cuaya, L. V.; Hernandez-Perez, R.; Boch, M.; Rumpf, J.; Reyes-Aguilar, A.; Huber, L.; Lamm, C.
Article.Abstract: Dogs live in an environment rich in human emotional signals, yet most of what we know about their visual emotion perception comes from faces. Our study shifts this focus to the body, a central channel of emotional communication in dogs and a source of social information when they observe human emotional expressions. Here, we investigated how the brains of dogs and humans represent emotions conveyed by human bodies. Using fMRI, we examined 24 awake companion dogs and 40 humans viewing videos of bodily happiness, anger, and neutral actions, alongside phase-scrambled controls. Both dogs and humans showed occipito-temporal sensitivity to human bodies, with emotional modulation in the right caudal suprasylvian gyrus in dogs and the right extrastriate body area in humans. Multivariate response patterns also differentiated bodily happiness from anger in both dogs and humans. Emotion-specific RSA further showed a similar representational asymmetry: happiness showed consistent category-specific neural patterns, whereas anger showed no comparable category effect but could still be differentiated from happiness and neutral actions. Despite this shared representational asymmetry, the anatomical distribution differed, with happiness represented across more distributed regions in dogs, whereas anger differentiation involved a broader cortical network in humans. No corresponding effects were found for phase-scrambled controls. Together, these findings provide the first direct neural evidence of how the dog brain represents affective information conveyed by human bodies, while leaving open whether emotions expressed by conspecific bodies evoke similar neural representations. More broadly, our results suggest similar representational relationships between bodily emotions in dogs and humans, despite differences in the anatomical distribution of these effects, while highlighting the role of human bodily expressions in dogs' social cognition, and advancing our understanding of the neural basis of emotional communication across species.

Article.Title: Cognitive reserve depends on cortical neurochemistry to predict memory after partner-inflicted brain injury
Article.Authors: McFarland, C. W.; Lin, A. P.; McComas, S.; Ratai, E.-M.; Gönenc, A.; Denk, A.-L. J.; Nikolaidou, S.; Valera, E. M.
Article.Abstract: Memory problems are commonplace following brain injury (BI). However, it remains unclear why some report memory problems while others do not, especially following repeated neurotrauma. Cognitive reserve has been widely hypothesized to account for this variation, but testing this account has yielded inconsistent results and proven difficult, likely as it requires a sample spanning a wide range of BI burden with concurrent neuroimaging and cognitive measurement. Here, we combined a wide range of cognitive assessments with measures of neuronal health using magnetic resonance spectroscopy across three brain regions in 62 women who had experienced physical intimate partner violence. Among a small subset with high BI exposure ([≥]10 BIs; n = 11), BI count explained 5% of the variance in delayed recall, the primary memory outcome, whereas cognitive reserve, inferred from a measure of premorbid functioning, explained almost half (unadjusted in-sample associations). In the full cohort, cognitive reserve predicted memory only among the most heavily injured participants. In a separate model, cognitive reserve predicted memory only when creatine-referenced total N-acetylaspartate, a marker of neuronal health, was lower in the posterior cingulate gyrus and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Ultimately, our findings provide behavioral and neurochemical evidence consistent with the cognitive reserve hypothesis and shed new light on why, despite a high burden of neurotrauma, memory may remain resilient.

Article.Title: TRPV4 antagonist efficacy in a post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus pig model
Article.Authors: Bentley, R. T.; Mitchell, S. C.; McCain, R. R.; Knipp, G. T.; Audu, D.; Bidgoli, F. O.; Hochstetler, A. L.; Behm, D. J.; Cox, A. D.; Blazer-Yost, B. L.
Article.Abstract: Hydrocephalus occurs across the age spectrum but is particularly prevalent in young and old individuals. One form of this disease is post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus (PHH), which is a life-threatening sequela of intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH). Progress has been limited by the lack of gyrencephalic animal models that exhibit high fidelity to human conditions. The orally bioavailable TRPV4 antagonist GSK2789917 penetrates the blood-brain barrier, and prevents progression to PHH when administered 2 days after IVH. Specifically, GSK2789917 prevents the development of ventriculomegaly, suppresses early ICP elevations and prevents or reverses inflammasome activation. These findings establish a clinically relevant large-animal model of PHH and identify TRPV4 antagonism as a promising treatment for hydrocephalus.

Article.Title: ADRA2B genetic polymorphism modulates vagus nerve stimulation response
Article.Authors: Riley, E.; Mabry, S. A.; MacMillan, M. K.; Ko, L.; Middleton, F. A.; De Rosa, E.; Anderson, A. K.
Article.Abstract: Introduction. Given interest in vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) as a potential therapy for Alzheimer's disease, due to its hypothesized influence on the noradrenergic (NA) system, there is a need to understand the pronounced individual differences in responsiveness to VNS in aging. Article.Title: Socio-demographic gradients in traumatic brain injury disability, severity and nutrition: a two-level analysis of the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 and NHANES 2011-2014

Article.Title: Optimizing non-invasive assessment of gastric activity: a fully automated channel-wise pipeline for multi-electrode electrogastrography
Article.Authors: Iannone, A.; Panasiti, M. S.; Aglioti, S. M.; Della Penna, S.
Article.Abstract: Electrogastrography (EGG) is a non-invasive, and affordable technique for investigating gastric physiology. Article.Authors: Heinrichs, H. S.; Zanoli, C.; Thalji, S. M.; Gagelmann, L.; Kilic, E.; Spitschan, M.

Here, we introduce ultradeep optical coherence tomography (OCT), which combines hardware and computational approaches to enhance the signal from deep tissue regions. Autocorrelation artifacts are measured and subtracted, and multiple frames are coherently averaged to improve the signal-to-noise ratio further. These techniques, along with computational refocusing and bandwidth control, allowed us to extend structural imaging depth in biological tissues. Ultradeep OCT demonstrated physical imaging depths of 2.3 to 2.8 mm (mean 2.5 mm) in the ex vivo mouse brain and 2.5 to 3.0 mm (mean 2.8 mm) in chicken tissue. The resulting volumes in the ex vivo mouse brain samples depict the dorsal hippocampus and its two major subregions with sufficient contrast to allow segmentation and three-dimensional reconstructions. Features in the thalamus could also be discerned. These findings demonstrate the potential of ultradeep OCT as a label-free approach for visualizing deep-brain structures at a spatial scale complementary to magnetic resonance imaging and microscopy. This approach could enable optical imaging studies of hippocampal structural changes in mouse models of neurodegenerative disease.

Article.Title: Hierarchical Uncertainty Transformation During Multimodal Comprehension
Article.Authors: Zhao, W.; Yang, J.; Li, Z.; Du, Y.
Article.Abstract: Human communication requires combining information from different modalities even when each source is incomplete or ambiguous. Yet how uncertainty is coordinated as distinct semantic representations interact and converge remains unclear. Rather than being uniformly reduced as information accumulates, uncertainty changed its computational form across three interdependent levels: uncertainty within modality-specific semantic representations, bidirectional but asymmetric changes during cross-modal interaction, and uncertainty associated with multisensory convergence. These computational distinctions were accompanied by differentiated but temporally overlapping neural associations. Modality-specific uncertainty was expressed relatively early, whereas cross-modal transformation and convergence were most prominently associated with activity in the N400 range. Critically, both the neural expression and statistical coupling of these computational quantities varied with the semantic information available from gesture and speech. Together, these findings show that multimodal comprehension involves a context-dependent reorganization of uncertainty across interacting representations, providing a computational framework for understanding how coherent meaning emerges from heterogeneous and uncertain information.

Article.Title: Neural discrimination of emotional prosody in natural sentences in 2- to 3-month-old infants using OPM-MEG
Article.Authors: Yang, J.; Leija, V. M.; Waitt, A.; Kowalczyk, A.; Bremner, A.; Pomiechowska, B.; Orioli, G.; Jensen, O.; An, K.-m.
Article.Abstract: From birth, infants are sensitive to the emotional prosody of speech, yet it remains unclear when the developing brain discriminates emotions conveyed by natural spoken sentences. Angry prosody also delayed the late auditory response by approximately 15 ms with no detectable changes in amplitude. Compared to non-tagged neurons, AC-to-V1 neurons more often responded to auditory, visual, or audiovisual stimuli. Furthermore, most AC-to-V1 neurons responded to specific sound frequencies; a modest but significant fraction was selective for visual orientations. These results could not be explained by motor responses or single-neuron variations in firing rate, cortical recording depth, or waveform type. These findings show that AC-to-V1 neurons carry sensory-specific signals, as opposed to nonspecific modulations, and exhibit distinctive response profiles compared to non-tagged AC neurons.

Article.Title: Caudate nucleus aging and its association with brain disorders
Article.Authors: Guo, S.; Yang, X.; Dong, Y.; Xu, J.; Sangjizhuoma, A.; Wichmann, T.; Galvan, A.; Smith, Y.; He, J.
Article.Abstract: The caudate nucleus supports cognition and goal-directed behavior, undergoes age-associated changes, and is implicated in substance use, psychiatric, and neurodegenerative disorders. In donors with AUD, age-associated changes appeared earlier, with altered trajectories in lipid metabolism, mitochondrial function, and neuronal signaling. Across comparisons involving AUD, OUD, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and Alzheimer disease, mitochondrial function and fatty acid metabolism emerged as consensus features linking caudate aging to diseases, although the direction and extent of overlap varied by disorder and brain region. Article.Authors: Fuentealba-Villarroel, F.; Bastos, L. M.; Gallas-Lopes, M.; Herrmann, A. P.; Zancan, D.; Piato, A.
Article.Abstract: Unpredictable chronic stress (UCS) produces heterogeneous behavioural outcomes, but identifying resilient individuals remains challenging because post-stress behaviour is multidimensional and classification depends on the analytical framework. De novo Louvain analysis identified lower- and higher-exploration configurations, but correspondence with the control reference was asymmetric: all 44 lower-exploration fish mapped to the lower reference profile, whereas only 22 of 45 higher-exploration fish mapped to the higher reference profile. Thus, higher exploration after UCS was insufficient to define a resilient-like response. Across five analytical frameworks, resilient assignments ranged from 9 to 45 individuals and susceptible assignments from 23 to 68, with partial individual-level convergence. These findings support reference-integrated behavioural stratification for identifying resilient- and susceptible-like candidates for physiological, cellular and molecular validation.

Article.Authors: Szakacs, H.; Gombos, F.; Kringelbach, M. L.; Deco, G.; Kovacs, I.
Article.Abstract: Adolescence is a period of rapid brain development, during which biological maturational timing varies substantially between individuals. This variability may drive specific developmental vulnerabilities to adverse experiences with long-term consequences, warranting early identification of at-risk individuals. First, early maturing adolescents showed persistent reduction in brain hierarchy. Second, those undergoing their fastest phase of development - specifically, decelerated adolescents - showed the strongest disruption in brain hierarchy following the pandemic. These findings suggest that pubertal timing is a critical dimension of individual variation in adolescent brain development and vulnerability. They also emphasize the need for objective maturity measurements to tailor support to individual pubertal timelines, particularly given the secular trend toward earlier puberty and ongoing global ecological crises.

Article.Authors: Reina-Gonzalez, P. J.; Boos, J. R.; Abu-Salah, A.; Anchan, A.; Strazdins, R.; Ay, M.; Shah, A.; Chalupa, D.; Richardson, J. J.; Sarkar, S.; Cory-Slechta, D.

These findings raise significant concerns as to the contribution of PQ exposures to the continued increase in the incidence of PD in the US.

Crucially, decoding analyses across three distinct neural datasets demonstrate that these geometric structures are not merely descriptive but capture behaviorally relevant information rivaling conventional spectral features. Article.Title: Brain-wide representations of olfactory behavior in C. elegans
Article.Authors: Casademunt, H.; Zhang, H.; Laver, J.; Park, C. F.; Kim, S.; Fredenberg, W.; Hung, W.; Calarco, J.; Zhen, M.; Samuel, A. D. T.
Article.Abstract: Olfactory navigation emerges from dynamic interactions between sensory input, brain activity state and the animal's own movements. In C. elegans, a compact nervous system enables brain-wide imaging in behaving animals exposed to controlled olfactory environments, with an undulatory locomotion that reduces navigation to transitions among forward runs, reversals, and turns. Here, we used tracking microscopy to record and compare brain-wide neural activity in crawling worms navigating spatial odor gradients or isotropic environments, and in immobilized worms responding to temporal odor pulses. Across conditions, we identified strongly correlated brain-wide activity patterns spanning olfactory sensory neurons, interneurons, and premotor interneurons. Comparisons between navigation in odor gradients and exploration in isotropic environments revealed a compact functional circuit linking olfactory sensory neurons, interneurons, and premotor neurons. Comparisons between different odors distinguished sensory activity relationships associated with odor identity from a shared sensorimotor circuit for navigational movement. Comparisons between crawling and immobilized animals revealed profound differences in motor-state transitions and brain-wide correlation structure, further demonstrating the dependence of sensory representations and motor decision-making on behavioral context. Our findings reveal a functional organization linking olfactory sensory activity to navigational movement and show how this organization depends on behavioral state and environmental context.

Article.Title: Graph neural network approach for inferring neuronal connectivity
Article.Authors: Gupta, A.; Neveu, C. L.; Byrne, J. H.
Article.Abstract: Understanding the connectivity of neuronal networks is essential for understanding brain function. Current anatomical mapping techniques, such as serial section microscopy and viral tracing, are resource-intensive and cannot capture the efficacy of connectivity. A complementary approach is to infer effective connectivity from single-neuron-resolution population activity. We developed a graph neural network (GNN)-based tool, CircuitGNN, that accurately infers neural effective connectivity from population activity. CircuitGNN accurately inferred the connectivity of several small circuits and detected both the strengthening and weakening of connections, such as those that occur during learning. CircuitGNN outperformed other methods when applied to simulated population activity generated by an invertebrate central pattern-generating circuit and a cortical microcircuit. CircuitGNN was evaluated on networks of varying size, recording duration, and proportion of hidden neurons. Although performance improved with longer recordings, CircuitGNN achieved high precision with recordings as short as 4 min, scaled to large circuits of up to ~750 neurons, and remained robust when 20% or 40% of neurons were hidden. These results establish CircuitGNN as an accurate and robust technique for inferring neural connectivity from activity.

Article.Title: Noise-referenced multi-shell diffusion-weighted imaging for regional cerebrospinal fluid thermometry
Article.Authors: Behler, C.; Breakspear, M.; Ramadan, S.; Dao, T. T.; Close, T. G.; Vos, S. B.; Thienel, R.; Giorgio, J.; Behler, A.; Fay, M.
Article.Abstract: We developed a multi-shell diffusion-weighted imaging approach for separate ventricular and subarachnoid cerebrospinal fluid thermometry. The approach uses measured image noise to assess agreement among temperature estimates. In 12 participants, temperature was estimated from four non-zero diffusion weightings. For each voxel, disagreement between these estimates was compared with that expected from image noise, accounting for their shared reference image. Voxels meeting this consistency criterion were retained for regional analysis. Mean diffusion-derived temperature ({+/-} SD) was 38.4 {+/-} 0.4 {degrees}C in the lateral ventricles and 36.0 {+/-} 1.1 {degrees}C in the subarachnoid space. Ventricular estimates were consistently higher than subarachnoid estimates across all participants, with a mean difference of 2.4 {+/-} 1.2 {degrees}C (95% confidence interval 1.6 -3.1 {degrees}C). This difference persisted under alternative noise models and temperature estimators. Subarachnoid estimates increased with retained voxel count; in a post hoc analysis of the six participants with the largest retained counts, ventricular estimates remained higher by 1.6 {+/-} 0.7 {degrees}C. Absolute temperature accuracy and the physiological origin of the regional difference require independent validation. This approach provides an internal consistency check for CSF thermometry and supports separate assessment of ventricular and subarachnoid temperatures.

Article.Title: Transcranial alternating current stimulation reverses adolescent alcohol-induced cellular and behavioral deficits.
Article.Authors: Sullivan, E. D. K.; Bresnicky, A.; Trevathan, H. B.; Gallagher, L. F.; Solanki, R.; Fröhlich, F.; Robinson, D. L.
Article.Abstract: BACKGROUND: Alcohol is commonly consumed by adolescents in a binge-like pattern that can produce persistent cognitive impairments. Previous work found that adolescent intermittent ethanol (AIE) exposure reduces parvalbumin expressing (PV+) interneurons and increases perineuronal net (PNN) expression in brain regions critical for cognition. Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS), a noninvasive neuromodulation technique, has shown promise for treating psychiatric disorders associated with cognitive dysfunction. Here, we examined whether AIE exposure alters PV+ interneurons and PNN expression in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and impairs cognition, and whether mPFC-targeted gamma tACS can reverse these effects. METHODS: Sprague Dawley rats (N=139, 50% female) underwent AIE or control exposure during adolescence and received Active or Sham mPFC-targeted gamma tACS treatment for three consecutive days in adulthood. Following stimulation, rats either underwent immunohistochemical assessment of PV+ and PNN expression or behavioral testing using the novel object recognition (NOR) task. RESULTS: AIE exposure reduced PV+ cell counts in the prelimbic cortex, an effect that was reversed by active tACS. In contrast, AIE exposure did not alter PNN measures. Interestingly, active tACS affected the prelimbic and infralimbic cortices more than the anterior cingulate cortex. AIE exposure also reduced recognition memory of a novel object, and this deficit was ameliorated by active tACS when assessed one week after stimulation. Additionally, active stimulation decreased anxiety-like behavior in the open-field test. CONCLUSIONS: Together, these results confirm that adolescent alcohol exposure produces lasting cellular and cognitive alterations and supports mPFC-targeted gamma tACS as a potential intervention for alcohol-induced dysfunction.

Article.Title: Parkinson Disease vs Aging Features Impairments in Formation and Release of a Power Grip in Real and Pantomimed String-Pulling
Article.Authors: Kia, M.; Singh, S.; Inayat, S.; Doan, J.; Tata, M.; Luczak, A.; Whishaw, I.
Article.Abstract: Parkinson disease (PD) impairs skilled reaching tasks but less is known about its effects on rhythmic bimanual actions. We used a bimanual hand-over-hand string-pulling task that requires repeated reach, grasp, pull, push and release movements. We predicted that participants with PD would show impairment in making the rotary skilled hand movement of retrieving the string, analogous to impairments observed in single handed target reaching. Nine participants with PD (mean UPDRS-III: 24.6), 16 older adults, and 10 young adults successfully performed a real string-pulling task and then pantomimed the action. Video analyses combined optical-flow estimation of whole-body movement speed, markerless 2D pose estimation of upper-limb kinematics, and expert frame-by-frame scoring of hand and finger shaping. Machine-learning classification then identified the discriminative information carried by these multilevel movement components. Participants with PD showed lower movement speed, a smaller hand workspace, and reduced hand and finger shaping, with older adults showing intermediate values. All participants grasped the real string with a power grip, but participants with PD showed reduced rotary movements of the arm and the wrists and absent of arpeggio-like sequential finger movement during grasp and release. During pantomime, participants with PD moved faster and made larger hand movements, while grasp-related hand opening and finger sequencing was reduced or absent. The findings suggest that PD is expressed across this multicomponent movement manifold, and that the movement organization changes with task demands: real string pulling requires formation and release of a power grip, whereas pantomime does not place demands on grasping ability.

Article.Title: Closed-loop acoustic stimulation promotes local slow oscillation train initiation and persistence in elderly adults
Article.Authors: Capurro, L.; Tassone, L. M.; Radloff, M.; Brusco, L. I.; Ramele, R.; Forcato, C.
Article.Abstract: Slow oscillations (SOs) during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep support memory consolidation and metabolic waste clearance. Aging is associated with reduced SO amplitude and density and disrupted temporal organization, characterized by more isolated events and shorter SO trains. We investigated whether closed-loop acoustic stimulation (CLAS) could enhance the initiation and persistence of rhythmic SO activity in elderly adults. Twenty-seven participants underwent a baseline night followed by an experimental night, during which online-detected SOs were either stimulated using CLAS (STIM; n = 16) or left unstimulated (SHAM; n = 11). We quantified the proportions of isolated and consecutive SOs, train-initiation probability, and SO train length. Analyses assessed local effects around online-detected SOs and global effects across NREM sleep using offline detection. Locally, CLAS reduced the proportion of isolated SOs and increased the proportion of consecutive SOs, train-initiation probability, and mean train length. Global overnight effects were weaker but directionally consistent, primarily reflecting a shift toward longer SO trains. These changes occurred without a significant between-group difference in the change in SO density, and local effects remained significant after adjustment for SO density. Thus, CLAS promoted sustained rhythmic activity beyond changes in SO occurrence. These findings suggest that CLAS can modify the temporal organization of SOs in elderly adults, supporting its potential to mitigate age-related disruptions in SO dynamics. Temporal organization measures may complement conventional amplitude and density measures when evaluating CLAS effects. Further studies should establish whether these changes translate into cognitive benefits or improvements in other aspects of brain health.
