Article.Title: Spinal Noradrenergic Overdrive Promotes Reversible Motor Unit Aging and Sarcopenia
Article.Authors: Wang, Z.; Grinevich, V.; Messi, M. L.; Longo, S.; Muthu, R.; Meeker, W.; Budygin, E.; Delbono, O.
Article.Abstract: Background Sarcopenia is characterized by progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass, strength, and physical function with aging. Motor unit degeneration is a major contributor, but the mechanisms driving age-related deterioration of motor neurons, neuromuscular junctions (NMJs), and muscle fibers remain incompletely understood. Norepinephrine (NE) regulates spinal motor neuron excitability, but its role in motor unit aging has not been established. Methods Whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology, optogenetics, fast-scan cyclic voltammetry, microdialysis, high-performance liquid chromatography, western blotting, and chemogenetics were used in mice aged 1-25 months. Motor neuron intrinsic properties were examined in 135 lumbar motor neurons from 81 mice. NE release dynamics, tissue content, and expression of the NE transporter (NET) and 2A-adrenergic autoreceptor were assessed in adult and aged mice. Descending spinally projecting noradrenergic neurons were selectively inhibited in aged mice using a retrograde chemogenetic approach. Results Aging produced progressive motor neuron hyperexcitability characterized by membrane depolarization, increased input resistance, elevated firing frequency, and altered action potential threshold (all P < 0.005). Optogenetically evoked endogenous NE increased motor neuron excitability by reducing action potential latency (P = 0.0001) and decreasing rheobase (P = 0.0028); these effects were prevented by 1-adrenergic receptor blockade (P = 0.0313). Aging enhanced stimulus-evoked spinal NE release, with greater responses at 20 Hz (P = 0.0223), 30 Hz (P = 0.0022), and 40 Hz (P < 0.0001). NE release elicited by stimulation of locus coeruleus and A5 noradrenergic inputs was also increased in aged mice (P = 0.0349 and P = 0.0016, respectively). Basal extracellular NE concentrations were unchanged, whereas spinal cord NE content increased (P = 0.0403). Aging reduced 2A-adrenergic receptor (P = 0.0009) and NET expression (P = 0.0046). Chemogenetic suppression of descending noradrenergic neurons in aged mice increased hindlimb muscle mass (P = 0.0111-0.0344), muscle fiber cross-sectional area (P = 0.0078-0.0467), NMJ innervation (P = 0.0210), and motor neuron soma size (P = 0.0353). Conclusions Aging promotes spinal noradrenergic overdrive characterized by increased NE storage, enhanced activity-dependent NE release, and impaired autoregulatory control. Excessive noradrenergic signaling contributes to motor neuron hyperexcitability and motor unit deterioration. Suppression of descending noradrenergic activity reverses structural features of motor neuron, NMJ, and skeletal muscle aging, identifying spinal noradrenergic signaling as a potential therapeutic target for sarcopenia.

Article.Title: Brain mitovesicles undergo stage-specific remodelling during the progression of amyloid-β pathology
Article.Authors: Voorbraeck, L.; Alarcon-Gil, J.; Mijalkov, M.; Passaretti, M.; Cao, Z.; Mamand, D. R.; Garcia-Ptacek, S.; Kele, J.; Fowler, S. L.; Ankarcrona, M.; Pereira, J. B.; Naia, L.
Article.Abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is an early feature of Alzheimer's disease that shows nonlinear changes as the disease progresses. However, how these changes are reflected in the mitochondrial material released by brain cells remains poorly understood. Mitovesicles are a recently described extracellular vesicle subpopulation of mitochondrial origin that provide a unique insight into mitochondrial alterations in the brain and could potentially show how nonlinear changes evolve across disease stages of amyloid-beta pathology. Here, we isolated forebrain-derived small extracellular vesicles and mitovesicles from wild-type and Amyloid precursor protein (App) knock-in (AppKI) mice, carrying familial AD mutations and progressively accumulating amyloid-beta plaques, at presymptomatic (2-month) and symptomatic (12-month) stages using high-resolution density gradient fractionation. Vesicle identity and composition were assessed by morphological, biophysical and quantitative proteomic analyses, and mitovesicle respiratory function was measured by extracellular flux analysis. We show that mitovesicles carry a distinct, predominantly mitochondrial inner membrane proteome that is remodelled by age and disease in a stage-specific manner. Compared with small extracellular vesicles, mitovesicle proteomic profiles captured disease progression more clearly, with symptomatic AppKI mice forming the most molecularly distinct group. At the presymptomatic stage, AppKI mitovesicles showed reduced mitochondrial protein representation, most notably of fatty acid {beta}-oxidation and lipid-metabolism proteins associated with astroglial and vascular signatures, preceding any detectable respiratory impairment. At the symptomatic stage this reversed: AppKI mitovesicles were enriched for oxidative phosphorylation, mitochondrial membrane and transporter proteins, yet showed reduced Complex IV-linked respiration, revealing a dissociation between mitochondrial cargo abundance and respiratory function. Selected cargo changes were not mirrored in whole-brain tissue, indicating selective remodelling of mitovesicle content. Comparison with mitovesicles from post-mortem human Alzheimer's disease frontotemporal cortex and hippocampus identified a conserved 62-protein mitovesicle core, dominated by oxidative phosphorylation subunits and mitochondrial carriers. In addition, 25 of these proteins were enriched in mitovesicles derived from Alzheimer's and AppKI forebrains, defining a conserved mitovesicular disease signature. Together, these findings establish forebrain-derived mitovesicles as a dynamically remodelled vesicle population that reflects progressive mitochondrial dysfunction in the Alzheimer's disease brain and provides a cross-species resource for future biomarker and mechanistic studies.

Article.Title: Structure-Based Discovery of GTP-Enhanced Rab10 Modulators and Their Effects on Alzheimer Disease-Relevant Cellular Phenotypes
Article.Authors: Malasala, S.; Cox, N.; Sellman, G.; Chen, Y.-H.; Lu, Q.
Article.Abstract: Rab10-mediated membrane trafficking has been implicated in Alzheimer disease (AD), but pharmacological tools for investigating its function remain limited. Here, we screened more than 80 million compounds using structure-based virtual screening and prioritized five candidate Rab10 modulators (R1-R5). These compounds exhibited favorable docking scores, stable modeled protein-ligand complexes in molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and predicted acceptable ADME/toxicity profiles. Comparative docking against Rab5, Rab8, and Rab11 predicted preferential interactions with GTP-associated Rab10. R1 and R2 yielded the most favorable Rab10 scores, whereas R3 showed the largest differences between GTP-associated, GDP-containing, and nucleotide-free Rab10 models. Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) revealed micromolar apparent affinities of R1-R4 without added GTP and nanomolar apparent affinities under GTP-containing conditions, generally favoring GTP-bound Rab10 over Rab5. In a cell-based GTP quantification assay, R1, R2, R3, and R5 reduced GTP-bound Rab10, whereas R4 increased it. R3 produced dose- and time-dependent reductions in GTP-bound Rab10 and was selected for functional studies. R3 altered endosomal organization and reduced EEA1 and LAMP1 expressions. In amyloid precursor protein (APP)/presenilin-1-expressing CHO cells, R3 redistributed intracellular APP, reduced APP carboxyl-terminal fragments (APP-CTFs), and decreased enlarged endosome-like structures. In neuronal differentiated PC12 cells, R1-R3 attenuated NGF withdrawal-induced cytoskeletal disruption and cell death, accompanied by reduced APP-CTF accumulation and tau phosphorylation. These studies highlight novel Rab10 modulators and support their further validation as candidate pharmacological probes for investigating Rab10-associated trafficking and AD-relevant cellular phenotypes.

Article.Title: Mapping brain networks underlying abstract perceptual decision formation and its EEG signatures
Article.Authors: Asadpour, A.; Steinemann, N. A.; Kalou, K.; Kelly, S. P.; O'Connell, R. G.; Wong-Lin, K.
Article.Abstract: Perceptual decisions have been proposed to involve a common mechanism of evidence accumulation operating across sensory modalities and motor contexts. In human EEG, the centroparietal positivity (CPP) tracks evidence accumulation in such a supramodal motor-independent manner, but its cortical sources are uncertain. Here we combined fMRI and EEG, acquired in separate sessions of the same supramodal change-detection paradigm, with individualized finite element head modeling to identify decision-related networks. A conjunction analysis across visual and auditory modalities and across motor and non-motor required tasks revealed consistent activation of bilateral postcentral, supramarginal, and superior parietal lobules, precentral gyrus, central operculum, middle frontal gyrus, and cerebellum. Forward modeling of fMRI-defined sources indicated that parietal-opercular regions were the dominant contributors to the response-locked and non-motor-required peak-locked CPP signal. These results implicate a network of brain areas in supramodal, motor-independent target-detection decisions, whose specific functional roles can be interrogated in more complex decision tasks in future.

Article.Title: Evolution Shapes Cortical Interneuron Migration
Article.Authors: Bonafina, A.; Boutsen, A.; Cheng, H.-Y.; Javier-Torrent, M.; Coumans, B.; Epifanova, E.; Cardenas, A.; Close, R.; Bruce, H.; Rasetto, N.; Tielens, S.; Kune, C.; Gallego-Lopez, I.; Iwata, R.; Le Bail, R.; Perrier d'Hauterive, S.; Firquet, A.; Cappello, S.; Vanderhaeghen, P.; Mazzucchelli, G.; Janke, C.; Lakaye, B.; Raty, J.-Y.; Borrell, V.; Nguyen, L.
Article.Abstract: The cerebral cortex comprises excitatory neurons and inhibitory interneurons originating from distinct forebrain regions. During migration, cortical interneurons (cINs) interact dynamically with neighbouring cells and their microenvironment, contributing to cortical architecture. However, how evolutionary changes in cIN migration shape species-specific cortical development remains unclear. Comparative analyses in mouse, ferret, and human models revealed a conserved migratory sequence but distinct behaviours: human cINs migrate slower, display increased leading-process branching, and exhibit more frequent homotypic repulsive interactions than their mouse and ferret counterparts. These features promote dispersed cortical invasion of cINs in humans and ferrets, contrasting with the stream-like migration observed in mice. Mechanistically, elevated expression of the cytosolic carboxypeptidase CCP1 in human cINs reduces microtubule glutamylation and doublecortin recruitment, thereby facilitating leading-process branching. These findings identify a CCP1-dependent mechanism regulating cIN dispersion and suggest that evolutionary changes in cIN migration contribute to divergent patterns of cortical morphogenesis across mammals.

Article.Title: Distinct processing of visual motion by transcriptomic cell types in the superior colliculus
Article.Authors: Chen, C.; Liu, Y.; Eaves, D. G.; Lagas, C. I.; Ren, J.; Kipcak, A.; Chen, H.; Erisir, A.; Cang, J.
Article.Abstract: How the brain organizes visual processing across distinct neuron types is a fundamental yet unresolved question. Here we study how visual motion is processed by transcriptomically defined cell types in the superior colliculus (SC). We generated or identified transgenic mouse lines to target three transcriptomic types of neurons in the superficial SC, the Cbln4+, Vip+, and Grp+ neurons. We find that each of these cell types encodes distinct ranges of stimulus direction, speed, size, and spatial and temporal features. In response to ecologically relevant visual flows, the three cell types occupy partitional spaces in the encoding manifold. The three cell types also show unique morphology and connectivity, including their retinal and intracollicular input and projection patterns. Together, these results reveal a genetic logic for visual motion processing in the SC, where transcriptomic cell types are likely the basic computational units with their specific feature selectivity, morphology, and input-output connectivity.

Article.Title: Stable large-scale network architecture and structured individual variability in the awake mouse brain
Article.Authors: Zou, Y.; Tu, R.; Zhang, C.; Hu, D.; Hou, X.; Wang, W.; Ji, Y.; Jiang, Y.; Wang, Q.; Yue, Y.; Zhong, S.; Wu, Q.; Wang, X.
Article.Abstract: Large-scale functional networks provide a scaffold for brain activity, but their population architecture and inter-individual variability remain poorly defined in the awake mouse brain. Here we introduce the Awake Mouse Connectome Project (AMCP), a population-scale multimodal MRI resource comprising 212 sex-balanced awake mice. Using this dataset, we generated high-precision in vivo tissue probability maps, derived a reproducible whole-brain functional network atlas and quantified structured variability in network connectivity across animals. The resulting atlas defined a stable large-scale architecture aligned with structural topology, while inter-individual functional connectivity variability followed organized connectional gradients rather than random dispersion. We further benchmarked the clustering-derived scaffold against conventional group independent component analysis (GICA) and release the GICA network atlas as an accompanying resource. AMCP further provides empirical scaling relationships linking sample size, scan duration and connectome precision. These analyses indicate that mean functional connectivity and functional connectivity variability have distinct sample-size requirements, providing a protocol-specific guidance for studies focused on group-average connectivity and inter-individual variability. Individualized network parcellations derived from the AMCP scaffold improved behavioural prediction relative to group-average features for selected behavioural domains, indicating functional relevance of subject-specific network architecture. Together, AMCP establishes an open dataset, tissue-template resource, clustering-derived and GICA functional atlases, and analysis toolbox for reproducible awake mouse connectomics and for translational studies linking circuit mechanisms to large-scale brain organization.

Article.Title: APP functions at the endomembrane system
Article.Authors: Wang, Z.; Fu, Z.; Lai, G.; Zheng, Q.; Li, W.; Lei, Z.; Xia, X.; Zhu, X.; Lou, Y.; Liu, D.; Du, X.; Liu, Q.; Zheng, B.; Li, N.
Article.Abstract: INTRODUCTION: APP is a type I transmembrane protein, and its intracellular domain (AICD) interacts with FE65, X11, and mDAB1, et al., through the YENPTY motif. Accordingly, it has been proposed that the functions of APP are similar to Notch, which regulates gene expression through releasing NICD after combining with its ligands. However, the detailed underlying mechanisms of how FE65 is regulated by APP, as well as their target genes, remain unknown. METHODS: We overexpressed APP695 in N2a cells, and deleted/mutated APP in H4 cells by CRISPR-Cas9, respectively. The impacts of APP overexpression and ablation were detected by proteome comparison and immunoblotting. Thereafter, the subcellular localizations of APP and its binding protein FE65 were examined by immunofluorescence. RESULTS: APP overexpression not only resulted in its retention in Golgi apparatus (GA) and Endoplasmic reticulum (ER), but also induced FE65 clustering. In addition, it significantly reduced the protein level of ATF4 in N2a cells. On the contrary, knockdown of FE65 restored the protein level of ATF4. More importantly, APP overexpression also impaired autophagy. In contrast, knockout of APP rescued LC3 conversion. Of note, the APP Swedish mutant did not impact ER stress or the autophagic flux. Nevertheless, it facilitated the cleavage of APP-CTFs by gamma-secretase. DISCUSSION: The evidence presented in the current study demonstrates that APP is involved in stabilizing the endomembrane system and the subcellular transport of FE65. More importantly, the role of APP in regulating autophagy indicated that full-length APP could be considered a therapeutic target for preventing the development of AD.

Article.Title: Reducing the Risk of Gradient Induced EEG Hardware Heating During Simultaneous EEG-fMRI
Article.Authors: Ingram, B. T.; Waggoner, R. A.; Uji, M.; Ueno, K.; Suzuki, C.; Sato, F.; Li, X.; Mayhew, S. D.; Bagshaw, A. P.; Tamaki, M.; Mullinger, K. J.
Article.Abstract: Simultaneous electroencephalography (EEG) and functional MRI (fMRI) has the potential to provide a more complete characterisation of brain function. Acquiring these data simultaneously requires the EEG hardware to be MR safe, since the EEG cap, amplifiers and powerpacks must be located within the MR environment. Placing them in this environment exposes them to both static and varying (radiofrequency (RF) and gradient) magnetic fields, presenting a potential heating risk. Previous studies have typically positioned the amplifiers and powerpacks outside of the bore, meaning that this risk is largely limited to the EEG cap. However, current guidelines recommend positioning the amplifiers within the bore. This reduces the distance between the EEG electrodes and amplifier, improving EEG signal quality and reducing risks of RF heating at the electrodes, but presents a potential heating risk for the amplifiers and powerpacks from the varying magnetic field gradients. In this study, we demonstrate that placing the amplifiers and powerpacks in the bore presents a significant heating risk, both at 7T and 3T. At 7T, we show that EPI sequences with a slew rate of at least 88 T/m/s resulted in significant heating of the EEG amplifiers. This heating effect could be negated by reducing the slew rate to 61 T/m/s. At 3T, we replicate the EEG amplifier heating and show that an alternative approach to reducing the gradient slew rates experience by the hardware is to increase the distance between the EEG amplifier/powerpacks and the isocentre of the magnet. Increasing the distance between the EEG hardware and MR isocentre by 30 cm mitigates the heating risk to the amplifiers and powerpacks, regardless of sequence parameters (e.g., slew rate). Therefore, whilst reducing the distance between the electrodes and amplifiers may improve EEG signal quality and reduce the potential for electrode RF heating, we show that risk of heating of hardware by gradient switching is greatly increased. This is particularly important to consider with the faster gradient slew rates available on modern MRI scanners, desired to increase spatial resolution. Experimenters must make careful decisions about hardware placement to ensure that the EEG-fMRI setup they use is safe, taking account of the varying risks that are posed by different approaches.

Article.Title: Fast rate coding in heterogeneous spiking networks
Article.Authors: Smeets, K.; Wang, S.; Schmutz, V.; Gerstner, W.
Article.Abstract: A network of spiking neurons is said to operate in the rate coding regime if its dynamics can be accurately described by a continuous rate network. But how can discrete spike-based communication between neurons give rise to continuous rate-based dynamics? Computational studies showing that heterogeneous spiking networks can approximate the dynamics of recurrent neural networks (RNNs), a special case of rate network, assume that spikes are approximately Poisson or that network dynamics are slow. Here, we show that neither assumption is necessary: heterogeneous networks of non-Poisson neurons can produce fast rate-based dynamics. To demonstrate this, we show that signal transmission in feedforward networks of integrate-and-fire-type neurons can be described by a history-dependent rate network that is asymptotically exact as network size grows, even if heterogeneity persists, while linear-nonlinear rate networks fail. By providing a constructive model of fast rate coding in heterogeneous networks, this work lays the foundation for extending rate-based analyses of neural recordings beyond the assumption of slow dynamics or Poisson rate codes.

Article.Title: Self-Other Neural Representational Distinction is Associated with Distorted Social Predictions in Social Anxiety
Article.Authors: Qi, Y.; Chen, Y.; Hu, Y.; Fan, Q.; Wang, L.; Yang, G.; Hein, G.; Wu, H.
Article.Abstract: Background: Social anxiety (SA) is characterized by distorted negative expectations about the future. Because optimism bias is inherently comparative, the extent to which these predictions reflect a fundamental disruption in self- versus other-referential processing remains poorly understood. Methods: Across two experiments, we investigated the mechanisms underlying social predictions in SA. In Experiment 1, individuals with high (n = 52, LSAS > 65) and low SA (n = 51, LSAS < 35) rated the future likelihood of positive and negative social outcomes for themselves or for a protagonist. In Experiment 2, 35 adults spanning a continuous spectrum of SA completed the task during fMRI. Behavior was analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. Neurally, multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) quantified self-other representational distinctions, while a parametric general linear model (GLM) tracked neural sensitivity to likelihood predictions. Results: Behaviorally, higher SA was characterized by an attenuated optimism bias: individuals predicted a lower likelihood of positive outcomes, but a higher likelihood of negative outcomes, for themselves compared to others. Neurally, higher trait SA correlated with greater self-other representational distinction within the left pregenual anterior cingulate cortex (pgACC). Concurrently, the precuneus exhibited stronger parametric tracking of self-negative predictions versus others. Crucially, pgACC representational distinction during positive outcome processing significantly mediated the association between SA severity and heightened prediction-tracking in the precuneus. Conclusions: These findings offer a novel mechanistic framework, suggesting that an exaggerated neural segregation of the self from others drives hyper-vigilant, risk-sensitive social predictions in SA. This candidate circuit-level dynamic warrants further replication in clinical cohorts.

Article.Title: Diagnose Harmonisation (DHARM): An open-source tool for the harmonisation and analysis of batch effects in MRI-derived measures.
Article.Authors: Turnbull, J.; Bhalerao, G.; Nichols, T. E.; McCarthy, P.; Gillis, G.; Blane, J.; Zhaoyi Mo, B.; Warrington, S.; Sotiropoulos, S. N.; Besenczi, R.; Alfaro-Almagro, F.; Smith, S. M.; Griffanti, L.
Article.Abstract: Technical differences between scanners, acquisition protocols, machine hardware and processing pipelines can introduce systematic variation into MRI-derived measures. Numerous harmonisation methods have been developed to reduce these effects. However, validation of these methods is often performed using different criteria depending on the method itself, the datasets used and the study design. Consequently, determining whether harmonisation is required, selecting an appropriate method and establishing whether or not technical variation has been sufficiently removed without compromising biological signal remain challenging. In this manuscript, we introduce Diagnose Harmonisation (DHARM), an open-source Python toolbox for diagnosing batch effects, applying harmonisation and evaluating harmonisation performance in cross-sectional and repeated-measures settings. DHARM is user-friendly, comes with GUI-based and command-line interfaces, and has graphical reporting. It provides standardised reporting workflows combining complementary measures of batch-associated differences in feature location, scale, empirical distributions, covariance and multivariate structure, together with measures assessing preservation of biological covariate effects and repeated-measures consistency. The framework includes several established harmonisation approaches, but its evaluation workflow is method-agnostic: users can also supply data harmonised using external or newly developed methods and benchmark their outputs using the same common set of diagnostics. We demonstrate DHARM using multisite cross-sectional MRI measures from UK Biobank, Cam-CAN and OxBAC as well as travelling-heads data from the ON-Harmony dataset. Across the cross-sectional datasets, harmonisation substantially reduced additive batch effects, while residual differences in variance and empirical distributions varied between methods. Multivariate diagnostics further demonstrated that reduction of batch-associated structure can coexist with preservation or increased detectability of biologically relevant variation. In the repeated-measures example, harmonisation reduced batch-associated and within-subject variability, while broadly preserving subject-level and biological relationships. DHARM provides a reproducible framework for diagnosing batch effects, applying different harmonisation methods and evaluating harmonisation as a multi-criteria problem rather than relying on a single measure of success. By jointly characterising technical variation and preservation of biologically meaningful information, DHARM can support dataset- and objective-specific selection, benchmarking and validation of harmonisation strategies.

Article.Title: Strategy-dependent causal relationships between large-scale cortical activity and perceptual decisions
Article.Authors: Mohammadi, Z.; Pillow, J. W.; Pinto, L.; Glaser, J. I.
Article.Abstract: Animals can adopt different internally generated strategies to solve decision-making tasks, but whether cortical regions distinctly contribute to decisions under different strategies remains unknown. To address this problem, we analyzed three datasets comprising either cortical widefield imaging, or optogenetic inactivation of dozens of cortical locations in 54 mice, all performing the same sensory-evidence-accumulation task. Using Generalized Linear Model-Hidden Markov Models (GLM-HMMs), we found that the mice adopted one of three underlying strategies: an engaged, stimulus-driven state, and two disengaged states characterized by large side biases. The specific effects of inactivation of cortical regions depended on behavioral strategy: during engaged states, inactivation tended to increase side bias, while the opposite was true in biased states. For engaged states, these effects were most prominent when frontal regions were inactivated. Moreover, neural decoding analyses from cortex-wide activity revealed that frontal regions preferentially encode the animals' choices during engaged states relative to biased states. Our results suggest that distinct patterns of large-scale cortical dynamics underlie decisions under different task strategies and identify the frontal cortex as an important substrate of engaged-strategy control.

Article.Title: Differential effects of chronic hypertension and sex on vascular density along the septotemporal axis of the hippocampus in a rat model of VCID
Article.Authors: Luchetta, J.; Schellinger, E. D.; Bolton, Z.; DeMarco, G. M.; Chapman, A. C.
Article.Abstract: Background: Chronic hypertension is a major modifiable risk factor for vascular contributions to cognitive impairment and dementia (VCID), yet vascular changes that precede cognitive dysfunction remain poorly understood. This is particularly relevant for the hippocampus, a deep brain structure critical to memory function, which differs along its septotemporal axis functionally and in its susceptibility to hypoxic/ischemic injury. The impacts of hypertension and sex on hippocampal vascularization remains unclear and could contribute to the development/progression of VCID. Methods: In this study, adult male and female Wistar and spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR) were used at 5 months old, an age before memory impairments. Vascular density and morphometric parameters in dorsal and ventral hippocampus were quantified using high-resolution confocal microscopy and 3D vascular reconstruction. Results: In SHR, vascular density was increased in the dorsal hippocampus in males and across dorsal and ventral hippocampus in females compared to normotensive rats. Diameter and length of the microvasculature shifted to be smaller and longer during hypertension in males, but not females. Conclusions: These findings demonstrate chronic hypertension increases vascular density differentially by sex along the septotemporal axis of the hippocampus in mid adulthood that may increase vascular resistance and potentiate perfusion deficits or increase sites of blood-brain barrier disruption and contribute to VCID.

Article.Title: Metabolic complexity in the human brain supports metastable network dynamics and declines in normative ageing
Article.Authors: Deery, H.; Liang, E.; Moran, C.; Egan, G. F.; Jamadar, S. D.
Article.Abstract: The adaptive capacity of the brain is tied to the complexity of its neural activity. While entropy of brain signals has been used to characterise this complexity in haemodynamic and electrophysiological systems, it remains unknown whether entropy contributes to the temporal dynamics of the metabolic signals of the brain (glucodynamics) and how metabolic entropy may relate to network organisation, brain ageing and cognitive decline. Here, we combined dynamic functional PET (fPET) with 18F-fluoroedeoxyglucose and simultaneously acquired functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) in 84 adults to investigate multiscale entropy (MSE) in the brain. We report that metabolic complexity measured with PET MSE represents non-linear, high-frequency complexity, whereas hemodynamic complexity reflects non-linearly constrained neurovascular phase dynamics. Greater metabolic complexity was associated with greater network metastability, particularly in unimodal and higher-order associative networks. Greater regional metabolic complexity also correlated with greater cortical thickness, cerebral metabolic rates of glucose (CMRglc) and cerebral blood flow, and was lower in older than younger adults. In contrast, global and network haemodynamic MSE was not significant associated with network dynamics. Higher global metabolic complexity was associated with better cognitive performance, and voxel-level derived MSE clusters were \associated with cognitive performance in both modalities, with varied cluster sizes and spatial locations. However, these associations were largely accounted for by age variance. We conclude that temporal complexity in cerebral glucose is associated with the dynamics of the underlying metabolic signals, enables metastable network states and declines in ageing. Entropy of metabolic brain signals offers promise as a neurobiologically grounded metric of brain ageing.

Article.Title: Norepinephrine inhibits Afferent activation of NTS Catecholamine Neurons in Mice
Article.Authors: Fernandes, L. G.; Jara, J. I.; Appleyard, S. M.
Article.Abstract: The nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) integrates visceral sensory input to regulate feeding behavior, with catecholaminergic (CA) and neuropeptide Y (NPY)-expressing neurons playing key roles in energy homeostasis. Recent evidence suggests functional heterogeneity among CA-NTS neurons, including distinct subpopulations that either suppress or promote feeding. In this study, we investigated how norepinephrine (NE) modulates excitatory synaptic transmission from solitary tract (ST) afferents onto tyrosine hydroxylase-positive (TH) NTS neurons in mice. Using patch-clamp electrophysiology in horizontal brainstem slices, we found that NE inhibits ST-evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (ST-EPSCs) in a concentration-dependent manner, with maximal effects at 10 microM and an EC of ~3.4 microM. This inhibition was mediated by alpha-adrenergic receptors and was independent of GABAA receptor activity. NE also suppressed asynchronous glutamate release and attenuated CCK-induced increase in spontaneous EPSC frequency, suggesting a presynaptic mechanism. NPY similarly reduced ST-EPSC amplitude via Y2 receptor activation, and co-application of NE and NPY produce additive or synergistic effects, even at subthreshold concentrations. Together, our results reveal a novel mechanism by which noradrenergic and peptidergic systems interact to regulate visceral sensory processing in the brainstem.

Article.Title: A Preventive Effect of Exercise in a Mouse Model of Essential Tremor
Article.Authors: Constantopoulos, S.; Bergdahl, A.; Courtemanche, R.
Article.Abstract: The effects of exercise have not been widely studied for potential benefits in essential tremor (ET), while this has been growing for other neurodegenerative disorders. This study examines the effects of two types of exercise [high-intensity interval training (HIIT) and resistance training (RT)] on mice that were subjected to harmaline injections to trigger tremor. We employed a repeated-measures design with three groups: a HIIT group, a RT group, and a sedentary (SED) control group. Each group received an injection before and after the intervention. Tremor kinetics (power within the 8-14 and 14-29 Hz bands) were assessed using accelerometry. Tremor kinematics were also assessed using high-speed video analysis, for validation. As potential signalling molecules from exercise, we also tested for blood lactate and BDNF in each group. Compared to pre-intervention measurements, we found a significant decrease in power within the 8-14 Hz band combined with an increase in the 14-29 Hz band, for the HIIT group, but not in the RT or SED groups. We also found a change in BDNF concentration for the HIIT group. These results suggest that the HIIT protocol may have helped the animal to shift tremor frequency to higher bands, thereby offering functional resistance to harmaline-induced tremor. This study supports high intensity aerobic physical exercise as a potential therapeutic/preventive intervention for ET, with translational implications for human studies.

Article.Title: Chronic hypertension disrupts the blood-brain barrier in the ventral hippocampus in females but not males in a rat model of vascular cognitive impairment
Article.Authors: Luchetta, J.; DeMarco, G. M.; Thaqi, A.; Bernstein, G. A.; Chavara, S. E.; Schellinger, E. D.; Chen, D.; Chapman, A. C.
Article.Abstract: Background: Chronic hypertension is a leading cause of cerebrovascular disease, ischemic stroke, and cognitive impairment. In addition, anxiety and hypertension often co-exist, however, little is known about the relationship between the two. Understanding how chronic hypertension impacts limbic brain regions such as the ventral hippocampus may provide insight into how cerebrovascular contributes to altered emotional behavior. Methods: An open field task was used to quantify locomotion, exploratory behavior, thigmotaxis, rearing and risk assessment behaviors in adult (7-month-old) male and female normotensive Wistar rats and spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR; n=8/group). Blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability was assessed by measuring extravasation of sodium fluorescein, 3 kDa Texas red dextran and 10 kDa cascade blue into the ventral hippocampus. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays were used to measure markers of vascular signaling, inflammation, and central nervous system-specific proteins indicative of neuroaxonal and glial injury in serum from separate groups of male and female SHR (n=6/group). Main effects and interactions between two independent variables (sex and hypertension) were determined using two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey's post-hoc tests. Circulating factors were compared using a Welch's t-test. Relationships between BBB permeability and anxiety-like behavior were determined using Pearson's correlations. Results: Chronic hypertension increased circulating inflammatory factors and BBB permeability in female but not male rats. BBB permeability did not differ by sex in male and female normotensive rats. There was an anxiolytic effect of chronic hypertension on exploratory-related anxiety-like behavior, including less thigmotaxis, lower latency to cross through the center of the arena, and increased unsupported rearing. Risk assessment behavior, quantified as stretch-attend posture, was increased in female SHR. BBB permeability in the ventral hippocampus was correlated with anxiety-like behavior in females, but not in males, suggesting sex-dependent mechanisms of hypertension-induced changes in emotional behavior. Conclusions: These findings implicate a role for chronic hypertension-induced BBB disruption in neuropsychiatric disorders in the female sex and advances our understanding of cerebrovascular vulnerability in deep limbic brain regions.

Article.Title: Lesion-Derived Estimated Functional and Structural Connectomes Predict Post-Stroke Recovery Outcomes
Article.Authors: Gillies, C.; Jamison, K.; Boes, A.; Kuceyeski, A.
Article.Abstract: Accurate prognosis after stroke remains challenging, limiting the ability to predict individual recovery. While advanced connectome MRI can provide further prognostically-useful information regarding affected brain networks, its impractical nature has given rise instead to lesion-based estimates of network disruptions. Here, we present a novel pipeline that leverages our recently developed connectome analysis tools to estimate structural disconnection (eSDC) and functional connectivity (eFC) directly from N=96 patient lesion masks for use in predicting motor, language, attention and memory outcomes at multiple timepoints after stroke. Our approach jointly leverages our Network Modification (NeMo) Tool, a database of white matter tractography results that estimates structural disconnectivity (eSDC), and the Krakencoder, a joint autoencoder that estimates functional connectomes (eFC) from the NeMo Tool's output. Models based on eSDC and eFC predicted almost all outcomes, particularly motor outcomes, significantly better than models that used patients' fMRI-based observed FC (oFC) and models based on only lesion information and covariates. Estimated connectome measures also i) retained meaningful inter-individual variability when compared to observed functional connectomes, ii) reflected population-level, stroke-related changes in functional connectomes, and iii) resulted in outcome prediction models with feature importances that aligned with expected networks of relevance to the given outcome. Feature importance analyses also identified distinct predictive signatures across both modality and outcome domain, indicating that eSDC and eFC capture non-redundant, biologically meaningful information about post-stroke network disruption. Together, these findings establish our lesion-based estimates of post-stroke structural and functional connectomes as a practical, information-rich alternative to advanced imaging in patients. This approach allows for probing an individual's affected neural circuitry underlying stroke impairment and recovery, paving the way toward more efficient, accessible, and personalized approaches to post-stroke prognosis and intervention.

Article.Title: Striatal and frontal signatures of social context and cost-benefit decision making in developmental stuttering
Article.Authors: Neef, N. E.; Winter, E.; Obrig, H.; Neef, A.; Mildner, T.; Haj Mohamad, S.; Riedel, C. H.; Scholze, K.
Article.Abstract: Developmental stuttering is usually framed as a sensorimotor disorder, yet it manifests in communicative situations that engage motivational, self-referential, and regulatory processes. In this case-control study, we combined a socio-economic decision task outside the scanner with a socially modulated speech task during functional MRI to test how listener presence and self-referential speech shape neural activity in 34 adults who stutter and 32 controls. Both groups valued talking with another person about themselves more than talking with another person about someone else or talking to themselves. On the neural level, listener-directed (vs. private) speech and self-disclosure (vs. guessing the preferences of a famous other) elicited stronger responses in the ventral striatum and medial prefrontal cortex, with no significant group differences in the central listener-directed versus private contrast. Within the stuttering group, individual differences revealed a systematic reweighting of socially modulated activation as a function of symptom burden: higher anticipation of stuttering and greater self-reported impact of stuttering on everyday life were associated with stronger engagement of motivational circuitry, greater recruitment of frontal evaluative-control regions, and reduced contextual differentiation within speech-language cortex. Stuttering anticipation and lived experience gradually shift the balance between control, language, and motivational salience-processing systems, contributing to the disorder's marked heterogeneity and context sensitivity. These findings indicate system-level signatures of the interaction between social context and symptom severity in developmental stuttering, extending accounts based on sensorimotor deficits.

Article.Title: A medial entorhinal connectome reveals compartmentalized microcircuit architecture
Article.Authors: Shi, T.; Chen, Y.; Jin, H.; Jiang, H.; Chen, X.; Xiong, Z.; Wu, F.; Zhang, R.
Article.Abstract: The medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) transforms multimodal inputs into spatial representations, but the synaptic architecture underlying its computations remains unclear. Here we generated a synapse-resolution connectomic dataset spanning all six layers of mouse MEC and the adjacent parasubiculum with serial electron microscopy, providing a continuous volume for mapping cellular organization and connectivity across layers and regions. We found that clustered pyramidal neurons in MEC layer II extended oblique apical dendrites with a dorsolateral bias and long-range myelinated axons within the layer. Exhaustive reconstruction of one cluster revealed a central exclusion core (ExC) that spatially partitioned basal dendritic architecture and synaptic connectivity. A spatially constrained growth model reproduced the position-dependent dendritic patterns. Within the ExC, pyramidal neurons formed a compact recurrent excitatory network and converged onto shared inhibitory partners. Basket cells (BC) and recurrent Martinotti cells provided perisomatic and apical-dendritic feedback, respectively. Dense, compact reciprocal connectivity between L2P neurons and BCs within the ExC, together with BC axonal bands extending beyond the ExC, suggests a potential circuit mechanism for generating temporally structured inhibitory output from the pyramidal-cell cluster along directionally extended axons. Together, these findings link cellular-scale geometry and synaptic wiring to emergent circuit dynamics that extend from dense computation within individual clusters to region-wide modulation, providing a connectomic foundation for understanding the circuit basis of spatial navigation.

Article.Title: Impact of acoustic property uncertainty on transcranial ultrasound simulation
Article.Authors: Kosciessa, J. Q.; Webb, T. D.; Martin, E.; Treeby, B.; Butts Pauly, K.; Verhagen, L.; Pichardo, S.
Article.Abstract: Subject-specific simulations of wave propagation are commonly used to plan and report acoustic and thermal exposure during transcranial ultrasound (TUS) interventions. Their accuracy depends on acoustic and thermal tissue property assumptions, including sound speed, density, and attenuation. Reported property measurements vary widely across the literature, precluding consensus point estimates for simulation. How this property uncertainty affects estimated exposure has not been quantified. We compile literature-based bounds for seven acoustic and thermal properties of skull and brain tissue and assess their individual impact on simulated intensity and temperature rise using two independent simulation platforms (PRESTUS/k-Wave and BabelBrain). Variations in skull attenuation and absorption produced the largest outcome uncertainty: peak intensity in the brain varied roughly threefold across the reported range of skull attenuation alone, while absorption most strongly affected temperature rise within the skull. The direction of each parameter's effect was consistent across platforms and, with one exception, across skull thickness. This allowed bounds to be combined into setups that bracket transmission and temperature rise. Compared to these extremes, default property sets of three simulation toolboxes (k-Plan, BabelBrain, PRESTUS) yielded similar brain intensity but divergent skull heating, driven mainly by differing assumptions on skull absorption and heat capacity. These results indicate that uncertainty in skull acoustic properties is a major source of variability in TUS exposure estimates, and that refined measurements of these properties, together with explicit reporting of exposure uncertainty, are needed to support safe, effective, and reproducible transcranial ultrasound planning.

Article.Title: Facing the waves of negative mood: Trait mindfulness moderates the links between physiology and emotion
Article.Authors: Campos, A. M.; Batchalli Maruthy, G.; Cumming, G.; Rodriguez, S.; Himes, L.; Rypma, B.
Article.Abstract: Trait mindfulness is a dispositional ability characterized by awareness, non-judgment, and acceptance of internal and external experiences. Stress is associated with numerous psychological and physical health concerns including depression and anxiety. Mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) have consistently been shown to reduce perceived stress and improve a variety of other health outcomes. However, the mechanisms through which mindfulness confers these benefits are not yet fully understood. This study aimed to examine (1) the relationship between trait mindfulness and changes in cortisol following a negative Mood Induction Procedure (MIP) and (2) whether trait mindfulness moderates the relationship between changes in cortisol and mood reactivity following a negative MIP. Participants were recruited from the Dallas-Fort Worth Metroplex (N = 25 participants) and completed a series of self-report questionnaires, negative and positive mood induction, and mood assessments. Participants provided salivary cortisol samples before and after negative MIPs. Results indicated that, following the negative MIP, sadness and anxiety were associated with greater reductions in cortisol. Trait mindfulness moderated these associations. Overall, these findings contribute to a broader understanding of emotional responses to negatively-valenced stressors and how they are mitigated by mindfulness. They suggest support for future applications of mindfulness-based interventions in high-stress populations.

Article.Title: Cholinergic-dopaminergic synergy and antagonism shape prediction-error broadcasting
Article.Authors: Kiraly, B.; Pillar, V.; Szabo, I.; Schlingloff, D.; Hegedüs, P.; Szigeti, K.; Li, Y.; Hangya, B.
Article.Abstract: Cholinergic and dopaminergic pathways control reinforcement learning, yet how their basal forebrain and midbrain populations interact remains unresolved. We simultaneously monitored both systems using dual-cell-type optogenetic tagging and neurotransmitter measurements in mice engaged in psychometric learning. Their activity contributed synergistically to reward prediction-error signaling. However, punishment-inhibited dopaminergic neurons showed antagonistic interactions with cholinergic neurons as well. Optogenetic stimulation and channelrhodopsin-assisted circuit mapping revealed a cholinergic-to-dopaminergic disynaptic inhibitory pathway through basal forebrain GABAergic neurons consistent with this antagonism. Chemogenetic suppression of cholinergic activity reduced dopaminergic responses to reward-predicting stimuli, attenuated punishment-induced dopamine suppression, and impaired learning. These findings reveal how a common underlying circuit architecture can flexibly shape prediction-error signaling through synergistic and antagonistic interactions, with implications for adaptive learning and neuropsychiatric disease.

Article.Title: Assessing reinforcement learning and vigor with an online decision-making battery
Article.Authors: Wenke, S.; Granwald, T.; Ferrante, A.; Nilsson, M.; Ekström, I.; Papenberg, G.; Guitart-Masip, M.
Article.Abstract: Reinforcement learning and vigor are two fundamental aspects of decision-making modulated by dopamine. Although vigor is highly relevant for mood disorders, it has been overlooked by previous batteries characterizing decision-making abilities. We used computational modeling and factor analysis to identify two factors reflecting RL and vigor. The RL factor reflected participants' general decision-making ability, while vigor corresponded to a motivational propensity to obtain rewards. Both factors demonstrated moderately strong test-retest reliability (ICC(2,1) = .65 and .67, respectively) over a one-to-two-week interval. Moreover, both factors were meaningfully related to self-report scales. The RL and vigor factors were negatively and positively associated with mania, respectively, although further analyses revealed that vigor was not fully independent of RL. Neither factor was significantly associated with depression symptoms. Collectively, we present preliminary evidence that vigor may represent a separate factor from RL in line with the putative dopamine hypothesis, paving the way for future longitudinal assessments of RL and vigor in mood disorders.

Article.Title: Betrayal is worse than loss during cooperation
Article.Authors: Tang, R.; Tan, J.; Gao, Y.; Lin, C.; Gan, J.; Ding, X.; Gao, D.
Article.Abstract: Cooperative behavior refers to activities that benefit another individual or benefit both the person performing the behavior and the recipient. Although both betrayal aversion and loss aversion (the financial detriment incurred from betrayal) are established determinants of cooperative behavior, their relative potency remains undetermined. Here, we investigated these effects by integrating computational modeling and event-related potential (ERP) techniques. In two tasks involving risk and cooperation, participants decided whether to take financial risks or to cooperate under possible betrayal. Our results showed that betrayal aversion had a stronger effect on reducing cooperation compared to loss aversion. Furthermore, ERP data demonstrated a temporal pattern consistent with sequential processing: betrayal was encoded early in decision-making, reflected by increased P3 with weaker betrayal aversion, whereas loss aversion manifested later, marked by increased LPP. By dissociating the contributions of betrayal and loss, our finding provides novel insights into the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying cooperative behavior.

Article.Title: A VTA-pontine GABA pathway biases locomotor direction via local and distal inhibition
Article.Authors: Gonzalez-Cabrera, C.; Kayumova, R.; Guatteo, E.; Berretta, N.; Mercuri, N. B.; Montero, T.; Vila, M.; Henny, P.; Prigge, M.
Article.Abstract: Locomotor direction in mammals is implemented by descending circuits, yet how midbrain selection systems bias directional motor output remains unclear. Here we define a projection-defined inhibitory pathway from the ventral tegmental area to the oral pontine reticular nucleus (VTAPnO) whose activation is sufficient to drive backward locomotion. These TH- VTA neurons form monosynaptic GABAA synapses locally while projecting to PnO, establishing a dual local-projection inhibitory architecture. Somatic activation reliably induced backward locomotion, and selective stimulation of VTAPnO terminals reproduced the effect. Pathway recruitment produced a rapid transient increase in dopaminergic single-unit activity and frequency-dependent increases in dopaminergic population calcium signals in awake mice. During forced locomotion, chronically recorded VTAPnO neurons were preferentially engaged during reverse compared to forward rotations. Together, these findings reveal a projection-defined midbrain pathway that biases locomotor direction through coordinated local inhibition and distal engagement of a brainstem premotor node.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: backward locomotion; ventral tegmental area; GABAergic inhibition; dopaminergic neurons

Article.Title: Disambiguation of two-tone images aligns object representations in the EEG
Article.Authors: Kessler, R.; Finnemann, J. J.; Skeide, M. A.
Article.Abstract: Electrophysiological responses to visual objects carry information about stimulus identity and semantic category, but it remains difficult to know whether such information represents conceptual knowledge or merely regularities in physical image features. Here, we presented two-tone images before and after disambiguation via corresponding photographs to seventeen healthy participants while recording EEG to dissociate the learned image concept from its physical properties. After disambiguation, EEG responses to learned two-tone images became more similar to the responses of their photo counterparts. This effect emerged approximately 100 ms after stimulus onset and peaked at 350 ms. However, we found no evidence for a generalization of the response pattern to the stimulus semantic category. Furthermore, alignment to the photo counterparts was only detectable after explicit visual disambiguation rather than spontaneous recognition. Together, these findings indicate that EEG can capture specific learned conceptual modulations of responses to visually degraded stimuli, while also showing that low-level visual properties dominate the representational structure.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: semantic categories

Article.Title: Turning an object into a scene: buildings activate scene-selective visual cortex independently of visual features
Article.Authors: Zhao, Y.; Hagen, S.; Peelen, M. V.
Article.Abstract: Human visual cortex contains regions that selectively respond to both scenes and large objects, particularly buildings. The cortical overlap between buildings and scenes has been attributed to shared visual features (e.g., cardinal orientations, rectilinearity). Alternative accounts propose that buildings may also activate scene representations indirectly, independently of specific visual features, for example because buildings evoke a sense of space. Here, we tested for such feature-independent activation by comparing EEG and fMRI responses in human participants (both sexes) to buildings and visually-matched boxes, and relating these responses to scene-selective responses. Buildings and boxes were matched using image-based metrics, deep neural networks, and a perceptual similarity task. Time-resolved EEG decoding showed that buildings and boxes evoked discriminable responses from 360ms post-stimulus onset, incompatible with feedforward visual feature processing. Importantly, the building-box classifier generalized to discriminate scenes from chairs, providing the first EEG evidence for a representational overlap between buildings and scenes. Temporal generalization analyses further showed that the late building-selective response corresponded to an earlier scene-selective response, with a temporal offset of ~130ms. Finally, ultra-fast fMRI (TR=140ms) revealed that the scene-selective parahippocampal place area (PPA) similarly showed a feature-independent building-selective response that was delayed and prolonged relative to the scene-selective response. These results clarify the nature of building selectivity in visual cortex by showing that this selectivity is feature-independent and delayed relative to scene selectivity. We propose that intrinsic associations between object categories (e.g., buildings and scenes, tools and hands) may account for part of the categorical organization of ventral temporal cortex.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: parahippocampal place area; ventral temporal cortex; EEG decoding; temporal generalization
Article.TopicFields: Neuroscience > Cognitive Neuroscience > Visual perception and processing mechanisms; Neuroscience > Cognitive Neuroscience > Face Recognition and Perception; Computer Science > Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition > Visual Attention and Saliency Detection

Article.Title: A Biologically Inspired Attention Model for Neural Signal Analysis
Article.Authors: Skatchkovsky, N.; Glazman, N.; Egea-Weiss, A.; Sadeh, S.; Iacaruso, F.
Article.Abstract: Understanding how the brain represents sensory information and triggers behavioural responses is a fundamental goal in neuroscience. Recent advances in neuronal recording techniques aim to progress towards this milestone, yet the resulting high-dimensional responses are challenging to interpret and link to relevant variables. Although existing machine learning models propose to do so, they often sacrifice interpretability for predictive power, effectively operating as black boxes. In this work, we introduce SPARKS, a biologically inspired model capable of high decoding accuracy and interpretable discovery within a single framework. SPARKS adapts the self-attention mechanism of large language models to extract information from the timing of single spikes and the sequence in which neurons fire using Hebbian learning. Trained with a criterion inspired by predictive coding to enforce temporal coherence, our model produces low-dimensional latent embeddings that are robust across sessions and animals. By directly capturing the underlying data distribution through a generative encoding-decoding framework, SPARKS matches or exceeds state-of-the-art decoders across diverse electrophysiology and calcium imaging datasets from the motor, visual and entorhinal cortices. Crucially, the Hebbian coefficients learned by the model are interpretable, allowing us to infer directed functional interactions and recover the known functional hierarchy of the mouse visual cortex. Overall, SPARKS unifies representation learning, high-performance decoding and model interpretability in a single framework by bridging neuroscience and AI, providing a powerful and versatile tool for dissecting neural computations and marking a step towards the next generation of biologically inspired intelligent systems.

Article.Title: Iconic Sound-Shape Correspondences in Aphasia
Article.Authors: Dorsi, J.; Sandberg, C.; Lacey, S.; Nygaard, L.; Sathian, K.
Article.Abstract: Purpose: To examine speech iconicity for shape in aphasia, we compared shape iconicity ratings from people with aphasia to those from neurologically intact individuals and evaluated how these ratings relate to phonological and semantic processing profiles in aphasia. Method: Twelve people with aphasia and twelve age- and gender-matched neurologically intact participants rated how rounded or pointed 50 auditory pseudowords sounded, using a 5 point scale. Ratings from participants with aphasia were compared to predicted shape iconicity ratings derived from reference ratings from prior work and to ratings from neurologically intact participants. For participants with aphasia, correlations between individual ratings and predicted ratings were related to measures of phonological and semantic processing. Results: Ratings from people with aphasia were significantly correlated with both the predicted ratings and the ratings from neurologically intact participants. Relative to ratings from neurologically intact people, ratings from people with aphasia had weaker correlations to predicted ratings. There were indications that greater language impairment was associated with greater disruption of iconicity ratings; in particular, deficits in phonological segmentation and semantic processing were associated with reduced sensitivity to shape iconicity. Conclusion: These findings suggest that sensitivity to shape iconicity is preserved to varying degrees in individuals with aphasia. Disruption of phonological and semantic processing appears to affect shape iconicity processing in aphasia.

Article.Title: Conserved synaptic modifications by humanized tau through diverse isoform- and mutation-specific intracellular interactions
Article.Authors: Nickerson, E.; Pomeroy-Tuck, J.; Pratt, S.; Rodriguez, C.; Zhao, T.; Stodola, T.; Hoffman, B.; Maser, R.; Bloss, E.
Article.Abstract: Mutations in the microtubule-binding protein tau are considered causal for a diverse group of neurodegenerative diseases collectively referred to as primary tauopathies. Specific tauopathies are associated with different mutations, distinct tau isoforms, manifest in unique cellular and circuit-wide patterns of degeneration, and present with specific clinical symptoms and trajectories. The mechanisms that link variations in the primary tau protein structure to distinct forms of neural circuit dysfunction remain largely unknown. Here, we created an orthogonal viral resource to systematically examine the impact of expressing humanized tau isoforms harboring different disease-relevant mutations in excitatory pyramidal cells from the mouse prelimbic cortex. We used these reagents to show that expression of mutant humanized tau (hTau) as either of two isoforms produced very similar patterns of circuit-specific synaptic disconnection on cortical projection neurons. However, mass spectrometry revealed that the interactomes of these different tau species varied markedly as functions of isoform, mutation, and subcellular location. We validated the functional relevance of increased hTau interactions with mitochondrial proteins in induced neurons differentiated from Ngn2-iPSCs expressing different hTau constructs. These results suggest different disease-relevant hTau proteins likely use distinct mechanisms to drive a highly stereotyped form of synapse loss in cortical neurons.

Article.Title: Serial dependence carries the action that produced the previous report
Article.Authors: Qu, C.; Naeve, C.; Shi, Z.
Article.Abstract: Serial dependence pulls current judgments toward the recent past, but what is carried forward is debated: the previous stimulus, the previous decision, or something about the report itself. Three magnitude-reproduction experiments separated these sources. Participants viewed dot arrays that varied independently in duration and numerosity, then reproduced the cued dimension by holding a key while a display accumulated, so that both magnitudes were produced through the same action. A response-history model partitioned the attraction into previous-stimulus and previous-response paths. The previous response predicted cross-dimensional attraction after controlling for the previous and current stimuli: a numerosity report biased the next duration judgment and vice versa (Experiment 1), also when each task used its own response key (Experiment 2). A task switch weakened this carryover without abolishing it. Experiment 3 randomized, trial by trial, whether a reported number required a long or a short key hold. The influence of a previous number on the next duration judgment changed with this mapping, showing that reported value alone did not account for carryover. Conventional stimulus-based measures showed none of this cross-task history. Serial dependence can therefore carry the trace of the action through which a previous judgment was expressed, bounded but not gated by task context.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: serial dependence; duration judgment; numerosity judgment

Article.Title: ROCK inhibitor Ripasudil reduces Alzheimer pathological proteins and enhances cellular bioenergetics
Article.Authors: Li, Y.; Liu, Z.; Cambi, X.; Peterson, J.; Benavides, G.; Ouyang, X.; Candib, A.; Zaia, J.; Darley-Usmar, V.; Zheng, C.; Zhang, J.; Xia, W.
Article.Abstract: Rho-associated kinase (ROCK) inhibitors have been explored as an Alzheimer Disease (AD) therapeutic agent. In this study, we aim to determine the efficacy of a potent ROCK inhibitor, ripasudil, in impacting AD pathological protein tau in mice. The time-course study showed that ripasudil rapidly penetrated mouse brains, reaching maximal concentration half an hour post-injection. To determine the efficacy of ripasudil, we injected AppNL-G-F knock-in mice with ripasudil at 30 mg/kg and sacrificed them after three hours. We used Tandem Mass Tag labels and compared the proteomic profiles of mouse brains exposed to ripasudil to those exposed to saline. We also treated AD-patient-derived Neural Stem Cells (NSCs) with ripasudil and performed a Seahorse Mito Stress Test to evaluate their impact on mitochondrial activity. Bioinformatics analysis of the proteomic profiles revealed differentially enriched components of chromosome. The Mito Stress Test of NSCs revealed significant increases in basal oxygen consumption, ATP-linked respiration, maximal respiration, and reserve capacity oxygen consumption compared to untreated NSCs. Importantly, we found a significant reduction of Tau and pTau 396 in brains of mice treated with ripasudil. Overall, our findings highlight the feasibility and promise of ROCK inhibitor ripasudil as an AD therapeutic agent.

Article.Title: Common variation of cell abundances and gene expression in the human striatum
Article.Authors: Burger, S.; Nemesh, J.; Yoo, O.; Muratoglu, E.; Vanderburg, C.; Yuan, J.; Shakir, K.; Mello, C. J.; Gao, H.; Rayan, N. A.; Finn, E.; Milidantri, J.; Mohsin, A.; Kim, K.; Drouin, S.; Budnik, N.; Goldman, M.; Bratchikov, S.; Fritch, H.; Genovese, G.; Hogan, M.; Catalini, O.; Kashin, S.; Rockweiler, N.; Wysoker, A.; Macaisa, L.; Reese, L.; Flowers, K.; Kraft, A. W.; Fleming, S. J.; Coe, M.; Gunaratne, R.; Spina, L.; Fischer, G.; Crombie, C.; Kamitaki, N.; Macosko, E. Z.; Ichihara, K.; McCarroll, S. A.
Article.Abstract: The cellular and molecular bases of inter-individual variation in the human brain are not yet understood, particularly beyond the neocortex. Here we describe cellular and gene-expression variation in the striatum and prefrontal cortex from single-nucleus RNA-seq analysis of 3.9 million nuclei from 178 adult brain donors. People with more astrocytes, microglia, or oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) in any one brain region tended to have this property in all gray matter regions sampled. OPCs proportions declined by 40% across ages 30-80 in cortex and striatum. Age-associated gene-expression changes differed substantially across cell types. Donor age was predicted from RNA-expression patterns with a median absolute error of 6.6 years across cell types. Common genetic variants were associated with expression of nearly 10,000 genes; these effects were mostly cell-type-specific and distinguished striatal from cortical neurons. These open-access data provide a foundation for future studies of human brain variation and vulnerabilities.

Article.Title: Detecting deception in event narratives: the analysis of response latencies and error rates to unexpected questions.
Article.Authors: Rosa, M. V.; Melis, G.; Sartori, G.; Zangrossi, A.
Article.Abstract: Deception is a central phenomenon in the study of human behaviour, and in forensic and investigative contexts it assumes significance due to its potential consequences. Although the unexpected questions technique has shown promising results, its application to the narration of a false autobiographical event remains underexplored. This study aims to fill this gap using the unexpected questions technique in an investigative interview setting. A total of 60 participants were randomly divided into two groups: the honest group was asked to describe their most recent day trip, while the deceptive group was asked to memorise a narrative describing a day trip. Both groups underwent an audio-recorded interview containing control, expected and unexpected questions. The results showed that both groups exhibited longer response latencies and higher error and inaccuracy rates in response to unexpected questions, but these indices were significantly higher in the deceptive group (p = .022 for response latency, uncorrected for multiple comparisons; p < .001 for error and inaccuracy rates). The findings suggest that longer response times and higher error and inaccuracy rates during unexpected questions may reflect not only the difficulty of the questions, but also additional cognitive demands faced by deceptive participants. Furthermore, these indicators were used to classify a subject as deceptive or honest using machine-learning algorithms. Within the sample, the model showed excellent cross-validated discriminatory performance (AUC = 0.967), suggesting that these indices may have diagnostic potential worthy of further investigation.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: deception detection; error rate; event narratives; investigative interviewing; response latency; machine learning classification

Article.Title: Surprisal contributes little beyond contextual embeddings in high-gamma ECoG encoding
Article.Authors: Sakuma, T.
Article.Abstract: Surprisal and contextual embeddings are both derived from large language models and are widely used to predict neural responses during language comprehension, but it is unclear whether surprisal adds information beyond embeddings. We test this directly: does word surprisal improve out-of-sample prediction of high-gamma ECoG responses after GPT-2 XL contextual embeddings are included? Using public ECoG recordings from natural speech, we fit word-aligned ridge encoding models with baseline stimulus features, GPT-2 XL embeddings, and GPT-2 XL surprisal. Adding one surprisal predictor left held-out correlation essentially unchanged at the primary response window, and the increment stayed within an equivalence margin across alternative lags, residualized surprisal, and frequency-band targets; it did not uniformly meet the same criterion under banded ridge regularization or within labeled temporal subsets. This small increment suggests that surprisal does not act as an independent predictor. It is better understood as a compressed readout of the same broader predictive state that the embeddings already capture.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: contextual embeddings; word surprisal; language comprehension; out-of-sample forecasting

Article.Title: Nociceptive-evoked electroencephalography can predict inter-individual differences in high frequency induced sensitisation of central nociceptive pathways: A test-retest reliability study
Article.Authors: Mugglestone, S.; Hughes, S. W.; Ganis, G.
Article.Abstract: Evoked-EEG can capture changes in cortical responses during experimentally induced sensitised pain states. However, the test-retest reliability of such methods requires validation. The present study applied HFS across two identical sessions in the same individuals to assess the test-retest reliability of EEG dynamics evoked by a 128mN pin-prick stimulator and single-pulse electrical stimuli before and after HFS conditioning. The value of these features for reflecting individual differences in the development of hyperalgesia was also assessed. Results demonstrate poor-to-moderate test-retest reliability and relatively wide agreement at baseline for all features, with lateralised differences often present. This was further reduced when post-HFS changes were considered. -ERD assessed from contralateral central electrodes was significantly strengthened post-HFS for both electrical and pinprick stimuli, consistent with increased sensorimotor engagement in response to hyperalgesic and non-hyperalgesic stimuli. Notably, baseline -ERD was related to the subsequent time course of SHA development. Furthermore, whilst VP magnitude displayed a significant relationship with the general intensity of perceived pain, no specificity for SHA development was evident. Alternatively, {theta}-ERS captured a general habituation effect relative to variations in reported pain intensity between sessions for both stimuli modalities. These findings indicate that evoked EEG responses may be useful for investigating individual differences in the cortical processing of acute pain and the development time course of HFS-induced sensitivity yet may not possess sufficient test-retest reliability for interventional testing.

Article.Title: Automated Segmentation of the Hypothalamus: Associations of Age and Socioeconomic Status with Subunit Volumes in Cognitively Healthy Adults
Article.Authors: Akar, B.; Atasever, U.
Article.Abstract: Background: The hypothalamus regulates sleep-wake cycles, energy balance, and autonomic and neuroendocrine function, yet its small size and poorly contrasted boundaries have long hindered in vivo volumetry. Deep-learning segmentation now allows the hypothalamus to be divided into functionally meaningful subunits. We examined whether hypothalamic subunit volumes are associated with age and socioeconomic status (SES) in cognitively healthy adults. Methods: From the OASIS-1 cross-sectional dataset (n = 416, 18-96 years), 133 participants with a Clinical Dementia Rating of 0 and complete segmentation output were analysed (33-94 years). A FreeSurfer-based convolutional neural network, run on a cloud virtual machine, segmented five subunits per hemisphere. Volumes were normalised to estimated total intracranial volume (eTIV) and related to age and SES (Hollingshead index) using Pearson correlations with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction; partial correlations adjusted for sex (age) and for age and sex (SES) served as sensitivity analyses. Results: Older age was associated with lower normalised volume of the right posterior subunit (r = -.456, q < .001) and the left posterior subunit (r = -.274, q = .007); both associations persisted after adjustment for sex. Lower SES showed a trend towards larger left anterior-inferior volume (r = .242, uncorrected p = .005) that did not survive FDR correction (q = .053). Conclusions: Age-related volumetric differences in the healthy hypothalamus appear to be concentrated in its posterior portion, a region housing arousal-promoting circuitry. Automated subunit segmentation offers a scalable tool for studying the hypothalamus in ageing and in relation to environmental exposures; the cross-sectional associations reported here should not be interpreted as causal or as within-person change.

Article.Title: Gain Control of Peripheral Input by Core Brain Thermosensors Drives Drosophila Thermoregulation
Article.Authors: Lazopulo, S.; Zlatic, M.; Cardona, A.; Garrity, P.; Samuel, A. D. T.
Article.Abstract: Temperature affects all aspects of animal physiology, rendering thermoregulation critical for survival. In Drosophila larvae, well-established peripheral thermosensors detect temperature changes and mediate thermotaxis over a broad innocuous range, but how larvae seek a specific preferred body temperature within this range remains unknown. Here we show that core thermosensors in the brain (LPBT neurons) establish this setpoint by mediating warming-evoked turning at temperatures above it. LPBTs express the warmth-activated thermosensor TrpA1(A), but are not simply cell-autonomous thermosensors. Rather, sustained LPBT responses above setpoint require both peripheral thermosensory input and TRPA1-dependent thermosensing within LPBTs. TRPA1-dependent core thermosensing provides gain control that defines the homeostatic setpoint by tuning the behavioral weights of peripheral inputs. This new conception of thermal preference reveals parallels between Drosophila and mammalian thermoregulation.

Article.Title: Brain Decoding from a Deep Neural Network of Visual Memory Reveals the Maturation Trajectory of Memory Systems across Ages 3-7
Article.Authors: GUO, X.; Leong, Y. C.; Bainbridge, W. A.
Article.Abstract: Memories from the first four years of life are largely inaccessible by adulthood, yet these early experiences profoundly shape cognition throughout development. Understanding this phenomenon of infantile amnesia is critical for revealing the mechanisms of early memory development. Here, we developed a new content-based behavioral measure of memory that quantifies how closely children's memory patterns resemble those of adults, which we term the memory maturation score. Using a movie-watching fMRI dataset spanning age 3 to adulthood, we trained a cross-validated model on adults' movie-evoked brain activity to predict adult's propensity to remember each movie snippet, estimated by ResMem, a deep neural network trained to predict visual memorability. We then applied the model to each child's brain activity while viewing the same movie to assess their memory maturation (i.e., cross-decodability from adult patterns). Children exhibited adult-like neural patterns of memory around age 4, extending prior behavioral findings. Structural analyses showed that the volume of the left posterior hippocampus, but not age or total brain volume, significantly predicted children's memory maturation. Memory maturation around age 4 thus likely reflects age-related neural development of hippocampal memory systems, rather than an age increase itself. Functional searchlight analyses revealed a trajectory of memory maturation: the inferior temporal gyrus reflected mature memory-related processing from age 3 onward, the left posterior hippocampus by age 5, and higher-order regions involved in social-affective processing and multimodal integration by age 7. Together, these findings suggest that hippocampal maturation between ages 3 and 5 drives the maturation of memory patterns.
