Article.Title: SafeLens: A Statistically Controlled Nonlinear Machine Learning Framework for Characterizing Hidden Dynamics in Event-Locked Neural Activity
Article.Authors: Minasi, C. B.; Hassan, U.; Cline, C. C.; Keller, C. J.
Article.Abstract: Machine learning has advanced rapidly over the past decade, yet event-locked neural activity is still analyzed predominantly with traditional statistics and linear models. While traditional linear methods provide computationally tractable statistical control for pre-selected features or trial-averaged waveforms, they miss subtle nonlinear and trial-varying neural dynamics. Nonlinear models can capture these complex patterns, but their feature reliance is opaque and notoriously difficult to threshold statistically. We introduce SafeLens (Searchlight Analysis of Fluctuation Events, Leveraging Extensive Null Sampling) to combine the power of nonlinear machine learning with the rigorous false-positive control of traditional statistical inference. At each position of a sliding window, a random forest learns to discriminate event-locked activity from interleaved resting-state neural activity using multiscale temporal derivatives. Randomized feature ablation inverts slope polarity in held-out trials to map the random forest models' reliance on specific rising versus falling excursions across the time-frequency space. SafeLens then establishes an empirical null by running the same pipeline on separate resting-state recordings, training forests to discriminate rest from rest. This empirical null translates each channel's complex nonlinear resting dynamics into a model-matched noise floor on the map's linear reliance scale, allowing a single threshold to control the family-wise error rate against the channel's own background structure rather than a summary statistic of its baseline. When we injected simulated cortico-cortical evoked potentials (CCEPs) into resting intracranial EEG recordings, SafeLens recovered ~2.5 times as many polarity-resolved deflections as trial-average thresholding and the closest data-driven method, maintaining its advantage under trial-to-trial variability while yielding ~5-11 times fewer false components, ~2-5 times lower mean boundary error, and superior single-trial latency tracking as a timing prior. In eight patients, CCEPs remained detectable above chance until 1,040 ms after stimulation, compared with 570 and 455 ms for those benchmarks. Together, these findings establish SafeLens as a novel solution for enabling nonlinear models to uncover subtle, trial-varying neural dynamics under strict statistical control.

Article.Title: Rapid Detection and Initial Treatment of Life-Threatening Subdural Hematoma in a Sheep Model
Article.Authors: Brody, D. L.; Dengler, B. A.; Angelo, J. P.; Blodgett, D. W.; Cohen, A. B.; Drewry, D. G.; Fitch, M. J.; Goonasekeram, N.; Januszkiewicz, A. J.; Knapp, T.; Kohler, B.; Mark, J.; McAdams, I. S.; Perrino, K. M.; Rodriguez, C. L.; Sleasman, T. A.; Spicer, G. L.; Steiner, N. E.; Vieth, A. P.; Wathen, J. J.; Wolfe, K. C.
Article.Abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is the leading cause of death and disability in people under 40 worldwide. There is an unmet need for detection and treatment of life-threatening TBI when computed tomography (CT) scanners and neurosurgeons are unavailable. We developed a new handheld frequency-domain multidetector infrared hemorrhage detection device. Using the new device, military pre-hospital medics required <4 minutes to detect life-threatening subdural hematoma in a sheep model. We developed a second device that allows non-neurosurgeons to safely create a burr hole and partially remove clotted subdural blood. In sheep, the treatment device reduced intracranial pressure within 20 minutes, and improved post-anesthesia blinded neurological outcomes. With human use adaptation, these devices could allow rapid detection and initial treatment of some life-threatening TBIs in challenging situations.

Article.Title: Intra-individual changes to peak alpha frequency map to pain perception following high frequency sensitisation of central nociceptive pathways: A test-retest reliability study
Article.Authors: Mugglestone, S.; Hughes, S. W.; Ganis, G.
Article.Abstract: Resting-state EEG can capture cortical dynamics relevant to sensitised pain states in the absence of ongoing nociceptive engagement. However, whilst the slowing of global oscillations is evident within various chronic pain conditions, the mechanistic specificity of PAF and -band power remains uncertain. Therefore, the present study assessed these features across two identical test-retest sessions in which HFS was applied to induce the development of SHA as characterised through 128 mN MPS. Crucially, changes in -band features post-HFS were investigated. Blind source separation was also applied to identify independent sensorimotor components relevant to nociception and assess their test-retest reliability. Results demonstrated good test-retest reliability for sensor-level data at baseline, with inter-individual changes in global PAF reflecting MPS post-HFS. However, no specific regional driver of this signal was evident. Alternatively, components identified through sensorimotor template matching revealed a significant influence of -band power on MPS both at baseline and post-HFS. However, only a small number of these components genuinely localised to pre- or post-central gyri, and test-retest reliability of -band power was poor. Together, these findings indicate that resting-state EEG may be useful for tracking changes in cortical -band oscillations alongside the development of pain sensitivity. However, methods of sensorimotor component identification evidenced limited agreement and global PAF slowing could not be linked to a specific electrode grouping.

Article.Title: Matching Corticospinal and Cortical Excitability along the motor cortex: TMS-EMG-EEG study
Article.Authors: Nazarova, M.; Higdon, M.; Rouste, J.; Mutanen, T. P.; Nikulin, V.; Ukharova, E.; Vaalto, S.; Ilmoniemi, R. J.; Lioumis, P.; Renvall, H.
Article.Abstract: There is still no consensus on how to choose intensities for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). The resting motor threshold (RMT), the intensity needed to evoke muscle contractions in the contralateral limb muscles, is a robust muscle-specific index of corticospinal excitability. RMT from one of the hand muscles is commonly used as a reference for TMS neuromodulation interventions and TMS-electroencephalography (EEG) studies. However, it only provides an indirect measure of cortical excitability, and even for the primary motor cortex (M1), we do not understand how cortical and corticospinal excitability correspond to each other. Indeed, it remains unclear whether cortical responses to TMS follow similar location-dependent patterns along the M1, and whether subthreshold stimulation can reliably engage cortical circuits relevant to motor output. Combining TMS with electromyography (EMG) and EEG, TMS-EMG-EEG, enables simultaneous assessment of corticospinal and cortical excitability to answer these questions. We investigated how cortical excitability thresholds (CETs, measured with EEG), relate to corticospinal excitability thresholds (RMTs, measured with EMG) at the hand, arm, and leg hotspots along the M1 in 24 subjects. RMTs and CETs were strongly correlated, and both increased from hand to arm to leg. CETs were generally lower than RMTs, indicating that subthreshold stimulation was enough to evoke robust early TMS evoked potentials (TEPs). Within subjects, CETs differed from the corresponding RMTs at all three M1 hotspots, and this difference increased from hand to leg representations. The findings of the present study argue against using a default hand-muscle RMT to set cortical excitability dosage along the M1 and beyond. Online TMS-EEG can enable real-time dosing and could improve stimulation precision, efficiency, and generalizability, but the site-specific variability calls for adaptive control.

Article.Title: Clustering instantaneous phase-locking states with a rank-two Bures-Wasserstein distance
Article.Authors: Miri, M.; Behjat, H. H.; Van De Ville, D.; Olsen, A. S.
Article.Abstract: Instantaneous phase-locking (iPL) matrices, defined by the cosines of pairwise phase differences between band-limited signals, underpin widely used methods for time-resolved functional connectivity, including Leading Eigenvector Dynamics Analysis (LEiDA). Each iPL matrix has rank at most two and is fully characterized by its two nonzero eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors. Yet, existing methods retain different parts of this decomposition and compare them using distances that do not reflect the geometry of the underlying sample space. We show that weighting the two eigenvectors by the square roots of their eigenvalues recovers each channel's phase relative to the mean phase, and that optimal orthogonal Procrustes alignment of these weighted eigenvector pairs yields the Bures-Wasserstein distance between the corresponding iPL matrices. In EEG, where most channels oscillate nearly in phase, existing distances become insensitive to phase-lag size, whereas the Bures-Wasserstein distance preserves this sensitivity. In simulations, clustering with this distance recovered states differing in both lag size and spatial pattern that existing distances failed to distinguish.In resting-state EEG, it resolved distinct phase-gradient states that other methods merged into a single global in-phase state.

Article.Title: The ontogeny of hippocampal spatial memory is supported by postnatal Cajal-Retzius cells
Article.Authors: Glaerum, I. L.; Salih, R. H. F.; Sachuriga, S.; Roudi, Y.; Quattrocolo, G.
Article.Abstract: The functional capabilities of the adult hippocampus depend on specialized circuits that are established during development. Cajal-Retzius (CR) cells persist in the hippocampus long after their disappearance from the neocortex and contribute to the postnatal maturation of hippocampal circuits, but how this developmental role shapes adult hippocampal function remains unknown. Here, we selectively ablated CR cells from the postnatal hippocampus and examined the consequences for spatial learning, navigation, and CA1 spatial representations. CR-cell ablated animals learned reward locations and adapted to changing task conditions, but learned more slowly and made more errors. Reinforcement-learning models suggest that these behavioral differences reflect less stable internal representations guiding behavior. Consistent with this, CA1 spatial representations remained present but were more unstable and showed reduced differentiation of reward locations, particularly when task conditions changed. Our findings identify postnatal CR cells as key developmental contributors to the stability of hippocampal spatial representations and the adaptive behavior they support.

Article.Title: Late radiation-induced brain injury is associated with functional cerebrovascular impairment without structural vessel loss in mice
Article.Authors: Tamplin, M. R.; Vitale, A. H.; Loureiro, P.; Cunningham, A.; Lee, C.-Y.; Axelson, E. D.; Subramanian, V.; Lin, L.-H.; Thiel, W.; Petronek, M. S.; Grumbach, I. M.
Article.Abstract: Background: Radiation-induced brain injury (RIBI) is a major and often irreversible complication of cranial radiotherapy, affecting up to 90% of long-term survivors. Although cerebrovascular damage is a leading mechanistic hypothesis, whether chronic resting hypoperfusion occurs independently of structural vessel loss remains unknown. The aim of this study was to comprehensively characterize cerebrovascular, structural, and behavioral outcomes in a murine model of late RIBI to determine the primary drivers of vascular dysfunction. Methods: Adult C57BL/6 mice underwent 12 Gy whole-brain irradiation and were assessed one year later using laser speckle contrast imaging (LSCI), 7T MRI, immunohistochemistry, and behavioral testing. Results: Irradiated mice exhibited reduced pial flow velocity and flow area by LSCI, indicative of upstream cerebrovascular dysfunction, while bulk cortical tissue perfusion was preserved. This pial hypoperfusion was accompanied by cerebral atrophy, decreased T2* relaxation time and tissue iron deposition consistent with chronic microhemorrhage across multiple brain regions by MRI, blood-brain barrier disruption reflected by reduced ZO-1 and VE-cadherin expression, and increased anxiety-like behavior. Strikingly, capillary density, pericyte coverage, astrocyte endfeet, and NeuN-positive neuronal nuclei were all preserved. Conclusion: These findings demonstrate that functional vascular impairment - not structural vessel or neuronal loss - drives hypoperfusion and blood-brain barrier disruption in late RIBI. This dissociation between vascular dysfunction and rarefaction reframes the pathophysiology of RIBI and identifies endothelial dysfunction as a tractable therapeutic target for intervention.

Article.Title: Distinct patterns of multisensory integration underly the expression of flavor preferences and aversions in rats
Article.Authors: Allar, I. B.; Berenguer-Nascimento, A. L.; McNally, B. N.; Tang, Y.; Harunani, N.; Maier, J. X.
Article.Abstract: Flavor is an inherently multisensory experience, combining gustatory and retronasal odor signals during consumption. Previous work has shown that rats weight taste and smell components of flavor mixture solutions to express flavor preferences. However, a comprehensive quantitative understanding of taste-smell integration is lacking. Here, we evaluated the validity of the maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) framework for explaining multisensory integration of taste and smell signals toward hedonic flavor judgments. MLE is a dominant framework for explaining multisensory integration in a wide variety of contexts, and states that components of a mixture are weighted according to their relative reliability, resulting in more reliable multisensory judgments. In our experiment, rats expressed preferences for taste, odor and taste+odor solutions in a series of two-bottle preference tests featuring an unpalatable odor component (amyl acetate), and either a palatable taste component (sucrose) or an unpalatable taste component (citric acid). Taste reliability was experimentally varied by presenting taste components at two different concentrations. Reliability of animals' preference judgements was quantified as the variance in preference across repetitions of the same conditions in the same animals. Our results confirm that preferences for mixtures featuring a palatable taste can be described as a weighted average of the component preferences where the weights depend on the relative reliability of the components-a finding that is in line with the MLE framework. However-contrary to MLE-component weighting does not increase the reliability of multisensory preference judgments themselves. In addition, preferences for taste+smell mixtures featuring an unpalatable taste follow a qualitatively different pattern: taste and smell components are combined to enhance flavor rejection judgements. These results demonstrate that the multisensory integrative principles underlying flavor preference differ from other multisensory domains and depend on the valence of the flavor components.

Article.Title: Chronic Sleep Disruption Activates the Transcriptional Unfolded Protein Response and Induces Compartment-Specific Proteomic Changes in Mice
Article.Authors: Espinosa-Garcia, C.; Kour, D.; Srivastava, U.; Malepati, S.; Kumar, P.; Parhizkar, S.; Tobin, B.; Jang, W. E.; Kumari, R.; Campbell, B.; Stagray, J.; Henley, M.; Liu, X.; Wood, L. B.; Faundez, V.; Rangaraju, S.
Article.Abstract: Sleep disruption (SD) is associated with adverse brain health and increased risk of dementia, including Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the pathological mechanisms underlying this association are not fully understood. Preclinical studies have shown that acute SD impairs cognition by altering vulnerable synapses (molecular composition, ultrastructure, and function). However, the cumulative effects of chronic SD on the adult brain and its vulnerable synapses, that might contribute to AD risk, remain poorly defined. Here, we investigated the impact of chronic SD on brain transcriptomic signatures and subcellular compartment-specific proteomic profiles to identify genes, proteins, and signaling pathways that might confer AD risk. Chronic SD induced a modest transcriptional stress response globally, whereas alterations were more pronounced in the synaptosomal (synapse-enriched P2 fractions) and whole-brain proteomes. Remarkably, chronic SD elicited unique proteomic alterations at the synaptic compartment were distinct from whole-brain effects, including increased proteins involved in synaptic vesicle endocytosis, regulation of dendritic spine morphogenesis, and regulation of long-term synaptic depression, compared to increased proteins involved in immune/inflammatory, glial responses and neuronal function at the whole-brain level. Consistent with the chronic SD-induced molecular signatures, we observed subtle ultrastructural changes in vulnerable CA1 hippocampal synapses, including reduced pre-synapse size and decreased synaptic vesicle density, which suggest that chronic SD modifies synaptic transmission and plasticity. Together, our findings indicate that chronic SD differentially impacts the brain and the synaptic proteome, nominating candidate therapeutic targets and signaling pathways for future mechanistic studies of chronic SD and how SD contributes to increased AD risk.

Article.Title: Presynaptic PMCA interacts with Dlg, regulating in vivo synaptic calcium in Drosophila larval NMJ
Article.Authors: Kohler, A.; Lopez, E.; Quiroz, E.; Kobler, O.; Gonzalez-Gutierrrez, A. E.; Thomas, U.; Sierralta, J. A.
Article.Abstract: Precise regulation of presynaptic Ca2+is essential for neurotransmitter release and synaptic function. At the Drosophila larval neuromuscular junction (NMJ), the plasma membrane Ca2+-ATPase (PMCA) mediates presynaptic Ca2+; extrusion and is enriched in peri-active-zone membrane domains. Here, we investigated how PMCA distribution is regulated and contributes to synaptic function. Co-immunoprecipitation and super-resolution STED microscopy revealed that PMCA interacts and co-localizes with the MAGUK scaffold protein Discs large (Dlg) in discrete presynaptic membrane clusters. Neuronal depletion of the DlgS97 isoform disrupted PMCA clustering without substantially altering its abundance, redistributing the pump into smaller membrane puncta. Reporter assays further showed that PDZ-binding motifs in the PMCA C-terminus mediate its interaction with Dlg and are required for normal cluster formation. Electrophysiological analyses revealed that reducing either PMCA or Dlg increased spontaneous neurotransmitter release and enhanced asynchronous release following high-frequency stimulation. PMCA depletion also prolonged postsynaptic current decay during repetitive stimulation, implicating PMCA in the rapid regulation of presynaptic Ca2+; signals. Together, these findings identify Dlg as a key organizer of presynaptic PMCA and establish a link between synaptic scaffold organization and Ca2+; homeostasis in vivo. Our results demonstrate that PMCA contributes to maintaining resting presynaptic Ca2+; levels, restoring Ca2+; homeostasis after repetitive stimulation, and regulating Ca2+; dynamics following a single stimulus. These findings highlight the importance of the nanoscale organization of Ca2+; extrusion machinery in controlling neurotransmitter release at the Drosophila NMJ.

Article.Title: Sensory representation by non-equilibrium flows of neural activity at the mesoscale of cortex
Article.Authors: Braun, J.; Lamb, N.; Ghosh, K. -
Article.Abstract: We present a non-equilibrium theory of sensory perception and the mesoscale of sensory cortex. We propose that local neuron assemblies (cortical columns) toggle spontaneously between activity states (on and off) and that small populations of columns are coupled within and between areas of sensory cortex. The resulting network generates sudden, large-scale fluctuations and represents sensory inputs and perceptions by characteristic patterns of activity flows. The non-equilibrium dynamic is governed by the variational principle of maximal path entropy, or Maximum Caliber. Many current theories, by contrast, posit equilibrium dynamics and representation with activity states Our minimal model of sensory cortex describes populations of columns from two cortical areas and is fully constrained by empirical observations of `reversals' in perceived appearance, which occur spontaneously for visual, auditory, and tactile stimulation. We formalize representation by activity flows with dynamic Hamiltonian functions. Surprisingly, effective representation requires small-number fluctuations of toggling columns, as larger numbers would be dominated by hysteresis. Finally, we detail predictions for the microscale of spiking neurons that follow from on-off toggling and non-equilibrium dynamics. We conclude that the neural levels underlying perception are functionally organized in terms of activity flows. The inherent instability of non-equilibrium ensures active updating and renders all perceptions open to immediate revision. We conjecture that current theories of brain function (such as the Free Energy Principle) could be reformulated in terms of the variational principle of non-equilibrium, Maximum Caliber.

Article.Title: Gut Stem Cell Secretome Therapy Promotes Durable Neuroprotection and Functional Recovery After Stroke
Article.Authors: Mani, K. K.; Alex, A. M.; Pickle, K.; Akbari, Z.; Obhrai, A.; Kavithil, A. S.; Ashokraj, N.; Jadhav, S. R.; Stone, E.; Adlouni, N.; Saksham, G.; Miller, K.; Malik, S.; Sohrabji, F.
Article.Abstract: Background: Stroke causes rapid neuronal death and gut barrier disruption in the acute phase, with persistent cognitive-affective impairment in the chronic phase. We previously showed that transplants of intestinal epithelial stem cells ameliorated the acute and chronic impairment of stroke. The current study tested the efficacy of a cell free strategy, specifically, the secretome of intestinal epithelial stem cells. Methods: Middle aged male and female rats underwent middle cerebral artery occlusion or sham surgery and received intestinal epithelial stem cell secretome from healthy sex-matched adult or control media. Behavioral assays (social interaction, novel object recognition and Barnes maze), gut histology, markers of gut permeability, serum cytokines were performed at acute and chronic time points. Group differences were assessed by two-way ANOVA. Results: In the acute phase, vehicle-treated stroke animals displayed histopathological changes in the gut including villus blunting, loss of goblet cells, increased markers of gut permeability and elevated systemic inflammation. In the chronic phase, stroke resulted in cognitive/affective changes including social withdrawal, recognition memory and spatial memory deficits. In middle-aged males, three doses of IESC secretome treatment 4h/24h/48h after stroke restored mucosal architecture, goblet cells and dampened inflammatory cytokines in the acute phase. Cognitive and social outcomes, tested 4+ weeks after stroke, were significantly improved compared to vehicle-treated stroke animals. However, in middle-aged females treated with the same regimen of intestinal epithelial stem cell secretome, gut architecture was not restored and inflammatory cytokines remained elevated. Long term cognitive impairment was only partially improved in this group. Proteomic analysis of the secretome revealed a largely shared core of proteins between males and females with sex differences in pathway level regulation. Subsequently, another cohort of middle-aged females was administered four doses of secretome 4h/12h/24h/36h after stroke. This regimen restored gut architecture and dampened inflammatory cytokines in the acute phase, and improved long term cognitive outcomes. Conclusions: Collectively, these studies underscore the therapeutic potential of IESC secretome and the importance of tailoring post stroke therapy by demographics such as biological sex. These data further support the hypothesis that gut repair is tightly associated with long-term improvement in stroke outcomes.

Article.Title: An Innate Neuroprotective Reflex Activates NRF2 via Phosphorylation of p62 at Ser351 to Mitigate Traumatic Brain Injury
Article.Authors: Li, C.; Powell, K.; Wadolowski, S.; LeDoux, D.; Dehdashti, A. R.; Ullman, J. S.; Brenner, M.; LeDoux, C.; Rams, K.; Sciubba, D.; Wang, P.
Article.Abstract: Rationale: The oxidative crisis in traumatic brain injury (TBI) has remained therapeutically intractable to direct antioxidant therapies. Activating nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) offers a promising strategy, but its translation is hindered by a key question: whether TBI's depleted antioxidant reserves can accommodate canonical electrophilic activation. The diving reflex (DR) is a potential non-electrophilic alternative, but its efficacy in TBI is unknown and its natural induction is clinically impractical. This study tests whether artificial DR, induced by trigeminal nerve stimulation (TNS), can safely engage this non-electrophilic NRF2 pathway and exert a protective role in the acutely injured brain. Methods: In a rat model of severe TBI, we compared TNS-induced DR, natural DR, and exogenous calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) against the electrophilic NRF2 activator dimethyl fumarate (DMF). To define the mechanism of action, we quantified p62 phosphorylation at Ser351 (NRF2-activating) versus Ser403 (autophagy-related), alongside redox homeostasis, lesion volume, and multi-domain functional outcomes. Results: TNS-induced DR fully recapitulated the neuroprotection of natural DR, an effect mimicked by exogenous CGRP, and prevented by CGRP inhibition, confirming a shared, neuropeptide-driven mechanism. This non-electrophilic pathway operated by selectively phosphorylating p62 at Ser351, which preserved glutathione reserves, halted lipid peroxidation, and reduced chronic lesion volume. In contrast, while DMF activated NRF2, its electrophilic mechanism was associated with a further reduction in the brain's already compromised glutathione pools and increased lipid peroxidation. This mechanistic difference was functionally significant, as only the non-electrophilic approaches delivered multi-domain recovery. Conclusion: The TNS-evoked artificial DR is a mechanistically tailored strategy for activating NRF2 in acute TBI. By engaging the endogenous CGRP-p62-KEAP1 pathway, it circumvents the fundamental limitations of both passively consumed direct antioxidants and redox-costly electrophilic activators. Our findings establish a clear translational roadmap for harnessing an innate reflex as a clinically deployable therapy for hyper-oxidative states.

These molecular changes are accompanied by increased TE elaboration approaching superficial levels, enhanced excitatory synaptic activity, and reduced burst-firing. Together, these findings identify ST18-dependent restriction of an alternative subtype program as a mechanism linking molecular identity to distinct input connectivity patterns and intrinsic firing properties during postnatal circuit maturation.

Article.Authors: Weigel, M. K.; Cooper, M. H.; Zaghi, M.; Gopakumar, J.; Bridges, C. M.; Ho, P. Finally, analysis of post-mortem multiple sclerosis tissue reveals a concordant DAO-like state associated with increased engagement of the FGF/FGFR axis. Collectively, these studies define a regulated mechanism of DAO formation linked to myelin disruption and position mature oligodendrocytes as active contributors to myelin pathology in CNS disease.

Article.Title: Vision-language representations link food perception to subjective valuation
Article.Authors: Aoki, Y.; Toyama, A.; Sugawara, M.; Kojima, H.; Yamashita, Y.; SUZUKI, S.
Article.Abstract: Subjective values of foods guide dietary decisions. Yet, how the brain computes such values from visual input remains unclear. Here, we show that visual food valuation relies on higher-level conceptual representations captured by a multimodal vision-language deep neural network model. Using food images and human ratings (N = 194 and 200), we found that a vision-language model predicted subjective value more accurately than vision-only models. Representational analyses demonstrated that, compared with the vision-only model, the vision-language model preferentially encoded higher-level food attributes, including perceived healthiness, while encoding less image-level visual information. Multivariate analyses of fMRI data (N = 31) showed that embedding features from both models corresponded to activity patterns along the visual pathways. Critically, vision-language features showed greater correspondence than vision-only features in the fusiform gyrus, a downstream region of the ventral visual pathway. Article.Authors: Alipour, M.; van Drongelen, W.; Warnke, P. C.; Issa, N. P.; Lee, K.; Satzer, D.
Article.Abstract: Sleep and epilepsy interact strongly during sleep stages N2 and N3, when synchronization of brain rhythms is increased. Among regions sampled in all participants, thalamic channels performed best (area under the curve [AUC] 0.94 with RF + HMM and 0.93 with SleepSEEG across whole recordings; 0.88 and 0.86 at night). With RF + HMM, thalamic channels outperformed mesial temporal and temporal neocortical channels in all six participants across whole recordings. The advantage persisted against channel-count-matched subsets and a white-matter control with both classifiers. Individual thalamic electrodes reached AUCs of 0.79-0.99 with RF + HMM (10 of 11 at least 0.89). These offline findings support thalamic N2+N3 detection and motivate real-time evaluation for sleep-targeted neuromodulation.

Article.Authors: Mehaffey, T. M.; Smith, R.; Watson, A. M.; Southard-Smith, E. M.
Article.Abstract: Pelvic autonomic neurons are responsible for coordinating pelvic organ function, including storage and emptying of the urinary bladder. To track neural crest progenitor migration, neurogenesis, and formation of mature pelvic ganglia morphology in mice, we imaged intact lower urinary tract tissue from mid-gestational to post-weaning stages at single-cell resolution. The resulting atlas identifies the precise timing and initial routes of neural crest progenitor migration, defines timing for pelvic ganglion neurogenesis, and reveals previously unrecognized neuronal cell bodies outside of the centralized pelvic ganglia structures. The analysis further highlights morphological changes to pelvic ganglion structure that occur in parallel with genitourinary maturation, including the divergence of the major pelvic ganglia and bladder-proximal accessory ganglia. This work acts as the first wholemount imaging atlas of pelvic innervation in the mouse spanning fetal and postnatal timepoints, and thus we present an informative tool for future studies of developmental neurourology and neurogenic bladder dysfunction.

Article.Title: Active manipulation of surface orientation under directional illumination improves color discrimination
Article.Authors: Mohiddin, S. N.; Morimoto, T.; Coupette, F.; Smithson, H. E.
Article.Abstract: Two surfaces that appear different colors under one illumination might appear the same color under another illumination. This phenomenon is known as illuminant metamerism and is thought to limit surface color discrimination. However, real-world lighting environments are not directionally uniform. In theory, surfaces that appear the same color at one tilt might not appear the same color at another tilt where they sample a different illumination spectrum. We tested whether human observers could use this directional variation to improve surface color discrimination. Our results confirm that human color discrimination is improved when observers are able to tilt surfaces to sample directional lighting. Observer sampling motions were spatiotemporally structured and appeared to be directed towards the general lighting geometry rather than systematically maximizing color discriminating information for specific surface pairs.

Article.Title: Connectivity of Implicit Statistical Learning Networks is Associated with Language Impairment Severity in Post-Stroke Aphasia
Article.Authors: Ramage, A. E.; Underwood, B.; Lerner, K.; Ballard, K. J.
Article.Abstract: Rehabilitation of language for individuals with post-stroke aphasia (PSA) requires relearning to use cognitive-linguistic skills, but little is known about how these individuals relearn, or how brain reorganization may support different types of learning. One type of learning critical to language acquisition is implicit-statistical learning (ISL), which supports robust, accurate performance with minimal conscious effort. ISL relies on brain subnetworks that include language areas as well as domain general regions (i.e., salience and cognitive control) with the latter considered less likely to be damaged in individuals with PSA. Using three brain subnetworks associated with ISL, the present study used graph theory metrics to (1) compare their functional connectivity in PSA (n = 30) relative to neurologically healthy controls (n=18), and (2) examine their relationship with aphasia severity in the PSA group. Resting-state functional connectivity was weaker for the language and salience subnetworks in PSA than controls, but not for the cognitive control subnetwork. Additionally, edges within all three networks correlated with aphasia severity, particularly between regions of the right frontal cortex, such that stronger connectivity in these ISL subnetworks were associated with milder aphasia. While it is unsurprising that the damaged left-sided brain regions in the PSA group resulted in connectivity that differed from controls, these differences were also observed in the salience subnetwork. Further, the correspondence to aphasia severity was evident in all subnetworks, highlighting that domain general ISL networks may contribute to variability in language outcomes.

Article.Title: Lipidome of Compact Myelin from Cortical Regions of the Aging Murine Brain
Article.Authors: Liu, V. P.; Johnson, C. E.; Lakhani, S.; Furber, K. L.
Article.Abstract: Age-related cognitive decline has been associated with neurodegeneration in cortical white matter tracts. The trajectory of white matter degeneration over the lifespan follows a similar pattern in humans, primates and rodents including the loss of myelin integrity and concomitant loss in myelinated axonal segments. Previous studies suggest that biochemical alterations in myelin begin to occur well prior to myelin loss. To better understand these biochemical determinants underlying white matter degeneration, we investigated the lipid composition of myelin isolated from young adult, middle-aged and aged murine brain. Compact myelin was enriched from cortical regions using a refined density centrifugation protocol and profiled the lipidome using LC-MS/MS. Over 2000 lipid species were identified, with the relative expression of 414 species changing over the age-span. The myelin lipidome from young mice was biochemically distinct compared to the aging cohorts. Aging was characterized by an overall decrease in high abundant species of glycerophospholipid and sphingolipids, including phosphocholine, phosphoethanolamine, sphingomyelin and cerebrosides. Pathway analysis by LipidSig 2.0 and lipid ontology analysis by LION/web highlighted alterations to lipid metabolism and membrane biophysical properties related to bilayer stability and organization. These data support the concept that myelin lipid compositional changes are apparent by middle age which underly structural changes in myelin at later ages. The findings provide greater insight into age-related biochemical alterations in the myelin sheath and may aid in strategies to mitigate white matter degeneration over the lifespan.

Article.Title: Dissociable Oscillatory Alpha and Aperiodic Neural Dynamics Underlie Atypical Attentional Control in Children With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
Article.Authors: Kong, Y.; Lu, R.; Lee, S.-M.; Zhou, M.; Yu, Z.; Lu, Y.-J.; Sun, X.; Jensen, O.; Sun, L.; Song, Y.
Article.Abstract: Children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) often have difficulty maintaining goal-directed attention when task-relevant and task-irrelevant information compete for processing resources. The present study investigated whether this difficulty reflects distinct abnormalities in demand-related attentional regulation and distractor-related neural responses. We recorded electroencephalography (EEG) signals from 45 children with ADHD and 45 typically developing (TD) children while they performed a visual detection task under low and high visual demands, with simultaneous task-irrelevant standard and deviant sounds. EEG power spectra were parameterized to separate oscillatory alpha activity from aperiodic activity, as putative indices of attentional regulation and cortical excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance, respectively. TD children showed adaptive demand-related alpha modulation, whereas children with ADHD showed an atypical alpha response pattern, including reduced frontal modulation and atypical posterior alpha enhancement; this demand-related group difference was observed in oscillatory alpha activity but not in aperiodic activity. In contrast, ADHD-related abnormalities in responses to auditory distractors were more clearly reflected in the aperiodic slope. Children with ADHD showed atypical distractor-related aperiodic modulation, suggesting reduced stability of neural background activity, potentially reflecting disrupted cortical E/I balance when irrelevant sounds had to be ignored. Furthermore, multivariate machine learning classification demonstrated that relying on these sensitive neural signatures yielded robust discrimination between children with ADHD and TD controls, with significant predictive performance emerging shortly after stimulus onset and sustaining throughout information processing. These findings suggest that oscillatory alpha activity and aperiodic neural dynamics show differential sensitivity to distinct attentional abnormalities in ADHD, with alpha oscillations primarily reflecting demand-related regulatory deficits and aperiodic activity primarily reflecting distractor-related neural instability.

Article.Title: Concurrent metacognitive evaluation is dissociable from perceptual evidence accumulation in the parietal cortex
Article.Authors: Li, X.; Chen, Y.; Su, R.; Yang, T.
Article.Abstract: Adaptive behavior requires not only accumulating evidence toward a choice but also monitoring its reliability in real time. A central question is whether such concurrent uncertainty is read out directly from the circuit that accumulates perceptual evidence, or is computed by a separate process that runs alongside it. We trained two macaques on a perceptual discrimination task in which they could abandon deliberation at any moment and request assistance, so that uncertainty responses were in parallel with, rather than appended to, evidence accumulation. Behaviorally, a race between distinct perceptual and uncertainty accumulators outperformed models in which the opt-out decision was derived from the perceptual decision variable alone. To ask where the second accumulator resides, we recorded single units in the lateral intraparietal area (LIP), a canonical sensory-motor transformation area, and compared population dynamics with recurrent neural networks instantiating two architectures: one in which uncertainty is computed within the perceptual accumulator, and one in which it is computed outside and triggers the uncertainty response there. LIP exhibited all of these signatures for perceptual choices and none for uncertainty responses. Uncertainty-related activity rose late and stereotypically, lacking the coherence-scaled ramp of an accumulator, and separable from the perceptual accumulation. They are all predicted by the segregated architecture. Concurrent uncertainty is thus represented in LIP but is unlikely to be computed within LIP, indicating that metacognitive monitoring during deliberation is a dissociable operation rather than a derivative readout of the LIP perceptual circuit; its anatomical substrate is not localized here.

Article.Title: Interpretable Machine Learning Links Group-Specific Plasma Proteomics to Regional Structural Neuroimaging in Alzheimer's Disease
Article.Authors: Laugi, H.; Hosseinzadehketilateh, M.; Lee, S.; Weisberg, S. M.; Zhu, X.
Article.Abstract: Background: Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology begins years before clinical symptoms, highlighting the need for scalable biomarkers that capture biological changes across the AD continuum. Broader plasma proteomics may capture systemic processes that vary with disease stage, yet their relationship to AD-related brain neurodegeneration remains unclear. We aimed to identify plasma proteomic signatures across cognitively normal (CN), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and AD and evaluate their neuroanatomical associations. Methods: We analyzed 146 plasma analytes from 565 Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) participants (58 CN, 396 MCI, 111 AD). Group-specific proteomic signatures were identified using pairwise classification models with nested 5*5 cross-validation. SHAP quantified feature importance, with the top 15 proteins per comparison being prioritized for MRI association analysis. We analyzed 103 regional structural MRI volumes harmonized across 57 acquisition sites using ComBat. Separate ordinary least squares regression tested protein-MRI associations, adjusting for age, sex, APOE4, diagnosis, and intracranial volume, followed by Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Results: Classification models using proteomic data achieved AUC of 0.956 +- 0.017 for CN vs MCI, 0.963 +- 0.011 for MCI vs. AD, and 0.836 +- 0.085 for CN vs. AD. SHAP identified group-dependent proteomic signatures. No protein-MRI associations survived FDR correction for CN vs. MCI. In MCI vs. AD, higher cortisol was associated with lower left precuneus and superior parietal volumes, while higher osteopontin was associated with lower left paracentral and accumbens volumes. In CN vs. AD, higher vitronectin was associated with lower posterior corpus callosum volume. Conclusion: These findings suggest that plasma proteomics capture group-specific systemic biological signals across the AD continuum. Linking ML-prioritized plasma proteins to regional brain structure provides neuroanatomical context for blood-based biomarker discovery.

Article.Title: Anticipatory Threat of Shock Reduces the Number of Items Reported From a Brief Visual Display: Evidence for Capacity Loss Along the Scanning Order
Article.Authors: Akar, B.; Aydın Karabas, M.; Altıntas, T.
Article.Abstract: Background: Anticipatory anxiety impairs working memory, but whether it also limits the earliest, high-capacity stage of visual storage is unclear. We asked whether the mere expectation of an aversive electrical stimulus reduces how many items people can report from a briefly flashed display, and whether any loss is spatially uniform. Methods: Eighty-eight healthy adults aged 18-25 years were randomly allocated to a threat-of-shock condition (surface electrodes on the wrist and the instruction that a painful stimulus might be delivered; none was) or a control condition (n = 44 each). Participants viewed a 4 x 3 letter matrix for 400 ms and performed untimed written whole report. Correct recall (0-12), intrusions and the position of each reported letter were scored. Groups were compared with Welch's t test, the Mann-Whitney U test, bootstrapped effect sizes, a binomial generalised linear model and a Bayes factor; spatial effects were tested with generalised estimating equations (GEE) accounting for letters nested within participants. Results: The threat group reported fewer correct letters (3.41 +/- 1.09) than controls (4.70 +/- 1.29); Welch t(83.6) = 5.11, p < .001, Hedges' g = 1.08, 95% CI [0.70, 1.53], BF10 ~ 7,549. Intrusions did not differ (p = .376). Recall declined more steeply from left to right under threat (group x column chi2(3) = 11.24, p = .011), with losses confined to the third and fourth letters of the top row (FDR-corrected q <= .003). Conclusions: Anticipatory threat reduced the amount of information transferred from a brief display into a reportable form without increasing guessing. Intact first items and depleted later items along the habitual reading order indicate a reduced number of items read out of a rapidly decaying visual store, rather than a hemifield-specific bias. The single-trial design and the absence of a manipulation check limit mechanistic inference.

Article.Title: Characterising cortical perturbation-recovery dynamics using TMS-EEG: The Brain Dynamic Toolbox
Article.Authors: Qin, W.; Peterson, A.; Burkitt, A. N.; Fitzgerald, P.; Karoly, P.; Naim-Feil, J.
Article.Abstract: Objective: To adapt dynamical measures used in computational and experimental perturbation models to human transcranial magnetic stimulation and electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) and determine whether analysis of the extended post-stimulation trajectory reveals additional features of the cortical response to long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI). Methods: Single pulse and paired pulse LICI TMS-EEG responses from the bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal cortex were re-analysed in 16 healthy adults. At the stimulation site, 75 single-pulse and 75 paired-pulse trials were delivered; paired pulses comprised conditioning and test stimuli separated by 100 ms. Responses from 20 frontocentral EEG channels were analysed from 50-950 ms following TMS using the open source Brain Dynamic Metric Toolbox. Perturbative Integration Latency Index (PILI) indexed cortical resilience via response energy and recovery, Autocorrelation Function Width (ACFW) captured temporal memory, and Lyapunov Exponent (LE) indicated the dynamical stability. Linear mixed-effects models examined temporal, spectral, and time-frequency effects from the measured metrics. Results: LICI altered the temporal evolution of the dynamical measures. PILI distinguished conditions in the earliest post-stimulation window before converging, whereas ACFW differences persisted across a broader early interval. LE showed weaker and less consistent discrimination. Spectral effects were most evident for ACFW, while time-frequency analyses revealed later, frequency-specific LICI effects for PILI and ACFW but not LE. Conclusions: The extended post-stimulation trajectory revealed LICI-related differences in cortical resilience and temporal memory with distinct temporal and spectral profiles, while effects on dynamical stability were less consistent. Significance: The Brain Dynamic Metric Toolbox provides a reproducible framework for quantifying perturbation-recovery dynamics in TMS-EEG and demonstrates that the extended perturbational response contains information about LICI not captured by discrete early response measures.

Article.Title: Basal ganglia output guides decision-making by state destabilization
Article.Authors: Tanimoto, Y.; Torigoe, M.; Islam, T.; Kakinuma, H.; Shiraki, T.; Lange, M.; Isomura, T.; Okamoto, H.
Article.Abstract: To execute learned behavior, the nervous system can undergo an activity-state transition between the current and the learned activity states. After learning the Go/No-go task in virtual reality, the striatal indirect pathway responds to negative values of a conditioned cue and the absence of sensory feedback by different neuronal populations. The pallidal output pathway integrates these negative value signals and then broadcasts the integrated signal to the Dc area in the pallium (fish cortex). Optogenetics and mathematical modeling suggested that this pallidal output activity uniformly destabilizes ongoing Dc activity states, thereby facilitating behavioral state transitions toward the behavioral state with the minimum pallidal output activity. This mechanism explains how pallidal output activity guides goal-directed behavior beyond potential barriers between activity states underlying different behavioral states.

Article.Title: A single day of natural daylight exposure and physical activity does not conclusively change circadian phase: A Bayesian crossover experiment
Article.Authors: Loock, A.-S.; Milanesi, M.; Schwendinger, F.; Garbazza, C.; Schmidt-Trucksaess, A.; Lang, U.; Blume, C.
Article.Abstract: Among the environmental signals that shape human physiology, the daily light-dark cycle is the primary zeitgeber of the human circadian system. Physical activity may provide an additional non-photic time cue and frequently co-occurs with daylight in everyday life. However, their independent and combined effects on circadian phase have rarely been disentangled under naturalistic daylight conditions. In a counterbalanced mixed-design experiment, 41 healthy adults (24 women; mean age = 23.7 years, SD = 4.3) participated in up to three 40-h visits on fixed individual sleep-wake schedules. Each visit comprised an 8-h exposure beginning 1.5 h after wake to natural daylight, daylight attenuated by amber-tinted glasses, or indoor electric light (within subjects; mean photopic illuminances: 1196, 460, and 75 lx), with otherwise dim-light conditions. Participants hiked for approximately 4 h or remained sedentary (between subjects; activity indexed by median heart rate reserve [HRR]; group means: 32.7% and 2.7%). Bayesian hierarchical models used individual photopic illuminance (ActTrust 2) and median HRR to predict change in dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO; primary outcome) and exploratory outcomes (daytime and evening sleepiness, mood, and wellbeing, daytime perceived exertion, and evening psychomotor vigilance). Per standard-deviation increase in log-transformed illuminance and median HRR, estimated DLMO changes were -4.22 min (95% HDI [-10.93, 2.22]; BF = 0.70) and -6.48 min (95% HDI [-13.79, 1.27], BF = 1.56), respectively. Evidence remained inconclusive for both predictors and their interaction. Exploratory findings were largely inconclusive, practically negligible, or favoured the absence of effects. The circadian effects of a single day of natural daylight exposure, with or without physical activity, therefore remain unclear. Resolving this question may require larger samples and brighter, repeated, or habitual exposure timed to phases of greater circadian light sensitivity.

Article.Title: Recruitment of intrasegmental and propriospinal interneuron networks of forelimb motor circuitry in chronic cervical contusion spinal cord injury
Article.Authors: Crowther, K.; Harbeck, A.; Middlesworth, M.; Bosch, M.; Lyttle, M. A.; MacGibbon, C.; Jaffe, D. A.; Michel-Flutot, P.; Fitchett, E.; Li, S.; Lepore, A. C.

The vast majority of regenerative strategies have been studied during the acute and sub-acute phases following SCI, while therapeutic testing remains limited for chronic injury, when persistent barriers significantly limit circuit remodeling. Following C5 hemi-contusion, female rats underwent behavioral testing of forelimb motor function and received PTEN antagonist peptide (PAP) beginning at a chronic time point, and the trans-synaptic tracer, pseudorabies virus (PRV), was injected into ipsilesional triceps to trace forelimb-associated motor circuitry. PAP selectively improved forelimb usage during cylinder paw-preference testing, but not strength, sensorimotor, or gait-related forelimb measures. PAP increased recruitment of PRV-traced local-projecting and propriospinal interneuron networks. In addition, PAP enhanced synaptic input to these recruited propriospinal interneurons, raising the possibility that spared descending pathways may contribute to recovery through spinal relay circuits. Lastly, we mapped the supraspinal connectome providing descending input from brainstem to the lower motor neurons innervating forelimb muscle, and we determined how this connectome was impacted both by SCI and PAP. Together, these findings show that, even in chronic SCI, pharmacological PTEN inhibition can promote forelimb functional recovery and significant circuit remodeling, with spinal interneuron networks emerging as a key site of PAP-induced plasticity.

Article.Title: Mechanisms of impaired cerebral hemodynamics and memory resilience differ by sex: A role for mineralocorticoid receptors in VCID
Article.Authors: DeMarco, G. M.; Bernstein, G. A.; Chen, D.; Bloete, J.; Schellinger, E. D.; Westbrook, M. E.; Baumoel, E. J.; Luchetta, J.; Chapman, A. C.
Article.Abstract: INTRODUCTION: Chronic hypertension is associated with cerebral hypoperfusion and is a primary risk factor for vascular contributions to cognitive impairment and dementia (VCID). METHODS: The effects of MR signaling during hypertension on hemodynamics in two cognition-centric brain regions were determined in both sexes using an established model of VCID (spontaneously hypertensive rat, SHR) and MR antagonist eplerenone. Long-term and spatial working memory were tested, and absolute brain blood flow and brain oxygenation were measured in vivo in CA1 of dorsal hippocampus and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). RESULTS: Hypertension differentially impaired hemodynamics in a sex- and region-dependent manner. Female SHR had more pervasive hypoperfusion than males that did not affect flow-metabolism coupling. Eplerenone treatment in females restored perfusion in mPFC and hippocampus, improved working memory, but did not protect hippocampal-dependent memory. Eplerenone had no effect in male SHR, indicating the MR-dependent mechanism of VCID is sex-specific. DISCUSSION: This study advances our understanding of how chronic hypertension compromises brain blood flow, suggests that resilience of memory function differs by domain, and that efficacy of interventions depend upon sex.

Article.Title: Immersion as inference: An active inference account of induced realities and its relation to the two-competitor model
Article.Authors: Renz, L.; GauthierDickey, K. L.; Vibell, J.; Francis, A. L.; Corona-Strauss, F. I.; Strauss, D. J.
Article.Abstract: Immersive technologies are designed for a single target: the human perceptual system. Engineers of virtual and augmented reality have long recognized that a display does not have to replicate the physical world, it only has to provide the inputs that satisfy the senses at the level at which the brain samples them. This engineering intuition is, in fact, a statement about brain function. Here we develop it into a formal account of immersion within the active inference framework. We treat an induced reality (a virtual, augmented, or mixed reality, but also a book or a daydream) as a candidate generative model that competes with the model of the actual reality for the explanation of a shared sensorium and for the control of action. Immersion is then defined as the ensuant belief that the induced reality best explains the current sensory signals and supports the current perceived reality of the winning model, despite any break in immersion by Bayesian model switching driven by a high-precision prediction error that the induced model cannot absorb. Exogenous and endogenous attention, implemented as weights governing stream selection in our earlier two-competitor model, which treated attention as necessary but not sufficient for immersion, appear as two routes of precision allocation: likelihood precision of evolutionarily entrenched sensory events, and precision that follows the expected free energy of policies. Affect and motivation enter through the pragmatic and epistemic value of remaining in the induced reality and through the rate of change of free energy. We show that the two-competitor attentional focus vector and its angle are recovered from the active inference variables, and we reproduce the two scenarios of the original model, a rewarding and a fatiguing activity interrupted by a slamming door, in a minimal simulation. The account links presence, embodiment, cybersickness, and narrative absorption to a single quantity, and it yields concrete predictions for the psychophysiological assessment and closed-loop control of immersion. We discuss implications for neuroergonomic design in which the evolutionarily entrenched core of perception is non-negotiable while its experience-dependent periphery can be trained.

Article.Title: Differential modulation of the neurocomputational signature of early and late mismatch responses to spoken words by awareness and task relevance
Article.Authors: Harenbrock, J.; Straube, T.; Dellert, T.; Schlossmacher, I.
Article.Abstract: Mismatch responses (MMRs), including the mismatch negativity (MMN) and the P3, are a hallmark of the brains capacity to detect unexpected events. They are discussed to be generated by two main processes: adaptation and prediction error (PE). However, MMR research on underlying mechanisms has mostly relied on simple, non-linguistic stimuli such as tones, and it remains unknown how awareness and attentional conditions affect MMRs to auditory verbal stimuli, that, unlike tones, carry lexical-semantic meaning. Here, we conducted a preregistered EEG study that disentangled influences of awareness, general task-relevance of word stimuli, and specific target-relevance of word oddballs on the MMN and P3. In addition, single-trial neurocomputational models were applied to uncover the underlying generative models of the MMRs. Results show that word-related MMN and P3 were only elicited when words were task-relevant, and the P3 increased with target-relevance. Crucially, no word-related MMN emerged under inattention, in contrast to the pre-attentive MMN typically reported for tonal deviants. Neurocomputational modeling revealed that the early part of the task-relevant MMN reflects adaptation processes. PE processes generated later parts of the MMN under task-relevance, and the entire MMN under target-relevance, as well as the P3 independent of relevance conditions. This suggests that the same temporal generation pattern of adaptation and PE underlie mismatch responses to both words and tones, but that, unlike tonal MMRs, eliciting MMRs to words requires the allocation of attention. This attentional dependency may reflect the additional lexical-semantic and multi-level representational demands that spoken words impose on the auditory system.

Article.Title: Physical sensorimotor contingencies facilitate learning in monkeys
Article.Authors: An, S.-J.; Gabel, J.; Jazayeri, M.; Sohn, H.
Article.Abstract: Animal studies in neuroscience routinely use virtual tasks that deviate significantly from the animals' natural behavioral repertoire. This choice is often necessary for conducting careful and controlled experimentation. However, this approach raises a fundamental question: do virtual tasks expose neural computations and mechanisms associated with naturalistic tasks? In this study, we explore how naturalistic settings influence learning timescale and generalization behavior in rhesus monkeys. By training animals in a maze-solving task and comparing their behavior across two environments, we observe significant differences. Specifically, we found that a realistic setup using physical objects enabled learning that was orders of magnitude faster than the learning timescale observed in a comparable computerized virtual environment. Furthermore, we noted limited transfer of performance between the physical and virtual settings. These findings underscore the need for understanding how task environments shape learning and generalization, with potential implications for the design of future neuroscience and AI experiments.

Article.Title: One digit too many: brain rhythms and autonomic responses at the limits of working memory capacity
Article.Authors: Kotyusov, A. I.; Kasanov, D. A.; Zaitseva, A. I.; Kotchoubey, B.; Pavlov, Y. G.
Article.Abstract: Physiological measures vary with working memory load, but whether they identify when demands exceed a person's working memory capacity remains unclear. Phasic pupil responses increased across serial positions but were smaller in span+1 at late span-matched positions; responses did not differ between conditions at their final digits. Non-baseline-corrected pupil diameter was larger in span+1 before sequence onset and during terminal retention, whereas non-baseline-corrected PWA did not differ. Frontal midline theta increased with serial position and was greater during terminal retention in span+1. Alpha and beta power decreased with serial position, and differed between conditions only at late positions. Terminal beta suppression was greater on correctly recalled span+1 trials. Thus, exceeding calibrated span impaired recall without producing a common physiological breakpoint. The findings suggest that reaching this limit does not immediately lead to resource exhaustion or disengagement. Physiological responses showed shifts in timing consistent with adjustments in preparation for recall of the longer sequence, along with increased effort before and during longer sequences.

Article.Title: Integrative Transcriptomic Meta-Analysis Reveals SIRT1-SNCA Correlation in Parkinson's Disease
Article.Authors: Cimen, H.; Sonmez, E.; Hotaslier, F.
Article.Abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that affects midbrain dopaminergic neurons without any approved therapy. Candidate molecular targets identified in one model are not always traceable across the postmortem, induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC), and cell-based systems used to study PD, which complicates clinical translation. To address this gap, we performed an integrative transcriptomic meta-analysis of 33 publicly available datasets across postmortem human brain, iPSC-derived models, and dopaminergic cell lines of PD. Differential expression and functional enrichment analyses were combined with STRING protein-protein interaction networks, followed by drug-gene interaction screening against a polyphenol panel. Overall, resveratrol was recovered in all 33 comparisons, independent of model system, tissue, and genetic background. We associated resveratrol with 30 distinct target genes, and SIRT1 was itself a recovered target in 6 comparisons spanning all three model systems. Finally, we resolved the SIRT1-SNCA relationship into four directional patterns that differed by model, inverse in postmortem brain and positive in acutely toxin-exposed cells. These findings support a candidate, context-dependent resveratrol-SIRT1 axis in PD.

Article.Title: The behaviour bends, the code holds: working-memory category information in the multiple-demand network across graded interruption
Article.Authors: Leticevscaia, O.; Feredoes, E.
Article.Abstract: Protecting working memory (WM) from interference is essential for goal-directed behaviour, yet its neural mechanisms remain unclear. The multiple-demand (MD) network - a set of frontoparietal regions recruited by diverse cognitive demands - is a candidate system for maintaining WM content under interference. We examined how the MD network represents a memorandum when an unrelated task interrupts maintenance. Participants memorised an image of a tool or animal and, during the delay, performed a digit task whose difficulty was parametrically varied (passive, easy, hard), allowing us to test how task engagement and associated cognitive demands affected concurrently maintained information. Using fMRI and multivariate pattern analysis, we decoded the maintained category (tool vs. animal) from 13 MD regions and early visual cortex. Behaviourally, interruption reduced recall accuracy, while the most demanding interrupter slowed responses. Neurally, category information was present during the delay, most strongly in visual cortex and bilateral intraparietal sulcus. This information was unaffected by task engagement (active vs. passive), consistently across decoding accuracy and cross-validated Mahalanobis (crossnobis) distance, with Bayesian evidence supporting the null effect. Increasing the demand of the active interrupter, however, produced a modest, network-wide reduction in crossnobis distance that was not detectable in decoding accuracy. Together, these findings reveal a dissociation between the behavioural costs of interruption and the neural representation of maintained category information. Although interruption impaired recall, engaging in an interrupter did not measurably alter category-level information in the MD network or visual cortex. Increasing the demand of the interrupter produced only a modest, network-wide reduction in representational distance, without affecting decoding accuracy, suggesting that the behavioural costs of interruption may not be fully explained by changes in the categorical representation of the memorandum.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: multiple-demand network; visual cortex; working memory; intraparietal sulcus; category representation; cognitive demand; task interruption; memory maintenance

Article.Title: Contributions of Site Heterogeneity in Multi-site Brain-Phenotype Predictions
Article.Authors: Chen, G.; Jones, M.; Gadiyar, I.; Satterthwaite, T. D.; Chen, A.; Vandekar, S.
Article.Abstract: Machine learning studies of brain-phenotype associations typically summarize accuracy with a single Pearson correlation, yet in harmonized multi-site data this metric is shaped by training-set size, feature and outcome variability, and true effect heterogeneity. We analyzed structural MRI data from the Reproducible Brain Charts consortium. After preprocessing and quality control, 3486 participants from 9 sites were retained. Three training set compositions were used to understand contributions of site heterogeneity after harmonization: within-site (Local), size-downsampled multi-site (Multi-Down), and full multi-site (Multi-Full). Another site-agnostic strategy (Overall) pooled all sites into a single dataset. All strategies included the target site in the training and testing samples. These analyses separate the contribution of the site effect from that of sample size. Between-site heterogeneity was extensive (age I^2 {approx} 95%). The overall correlation of age prediction (r = 0.73) exceeded the within-site meta-analytic estimate (Multi-Full r = 0.63). The improvement of correlation in the pooled dataset was driven by a mechanical inflation from the larger outcome variance. At matched sample size, within-site training outperformed harmonized multi-site training. Increasing the multi-site training sample size did not yield a significant advantage over within-site training. The apparent advantage of cross-dataset training thus appears to reflect training-set size rather than a benefit of multi-site composition per se. The same pattern generally held for the weaker brain-p-factor signals. Together, these results indicate that between-site heterogeneity in machine learning brain-phenotype prediction persists after harmonization. We recommend reporting site-level prediction accuracy and feature dispersion and standard deviation of the outcome variable alongside any pooled estimate to improve inter-site and inter-study comparison of machine learning prediction accuracy.

Article.Title: Disentangling the effects of Anxious, Autistic and Schizotypal Traits on Perceptual Inference
Article.Authors: Bevalot, C.; Mallevays, M.; Bayon de Noyer, E.; Berkovitch, L.; Meyniel, F.
Article.Abstract: Perception combines sensory information with prior knowledge, but people differ in how they do so. These differences may be associated with psychological traits; however, previous studies often focused on one trait at a time and yielded contradictory results. We measured how anxious, autistic and schizotypal traits relate to perception in two general population samples (original: n=277; replication: n=279, pre-registered). We combined tasks in which priors were either explicitly communicated or implicitly learnt with computational modelling to distinguish the decision and learning stages of perceptual inference. The three traits formed distinct but correlated dimensions. At the decision stage, higher trait anxiety was associated with more optimal choices and greater reliance on sensory information, without any alteration in the reliance on priors, whether explicit or implicit. On the other hand, state anxiety was associated with a reduced effect of sensory information on response speed. When traits were analysed separately, autistic traits showed similar associations, but these associations disappeared once anxiety was taken into account in multidimensional analyses. No other credible or consistent effects emerged for autistic or schizotypal traits, nor for learning parameters. These results highlight the importance of a multidimensional approach, including anxiety measurements, to characterise inter-individual differences in perception.

Article.Title: Scn2a-deficient mice exhibit serotonergic dysfunction and altered behavioral responses to psilocybin
Article.Authors: Deming, B. A.; Zhang, J.; Brown-Leung, J.; Halurkar, M.; Abeyaratna, A. D.; Ranga, R.; Farmer, K.; Ramasamy, D.; Cannon, J.; Yang, Y.
Article.Abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a prominent neurodevelopmental disorder affecting approximately 3.2% of children in the United States. Although ASD has traditionally been considered a polygenic disorder, advances in genetic testing have identified individual genes that can contribute to its development. Large-scale whole-exome sequencing has identified variants in SCN2A, which encodes the alpha subunit of the voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.2, as a leading monogenic cause of ASD. Social deficits are a core feature of ASD, and the serotonergic system has been implicated in the regulation of social behavior. Recent studies have demonstrated that serotonergic psychedelics, such as psilocybin, can increase sociability in mouse models of ASD. However, whether underlying genetic alterations associated with ASD influence behavioral responses to psilocybin remains poorly understood. Therefore, we investigated how Scn2a deficiency affects behavioral responses to psilocybin and whether these differences are accompanied by alterations in the serotonergic system. We found that Scn2a-deficient mice exhibited differential responses to psilocybin compared to wild-type (WT) mice. Specifically, psilocybin increased sociability in Scn2a-deficient mice without affecting anxiety-like behavior, whereas WT mice exhibited decreased anxiety-like behavior without increased sociability. Further behavioral evaluation revealed a reduced head twitch response in Scn2a-deficient mice following psilocybin administration compared to WT mice. To further investigate these differences, we examined serotonin levels and receptor expression in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), a brain region implicated in social behavior and psychedelic action. Although baseline serotonin levels in the mPFC did not differ between genotypes, Scn2a-deficient mice exhibited altered serotonin receptor expression. We further characterized the serotonergic system by evaluating neuronal activity in the Dorsal Raphe Nucleus, a major source of serotonergic projections to the mPFC, and found increased spontaneous firing in Scn2a-deficient mice. Together, these findings highlight serotonergic alterations associated with SCN2A deficiency and the potential for serotonergic interventions to alleviate social deficits associated with SCN2A-related ASD.

Article.Title: Connectome structure constrains neural activity across scales
Article.Authors: Sale, C.; Richardson, M. J.
Article.Abstract: Connectomes can be represented at many resolutions, but coarse-graining risks discarding structure relevant to neural dynamics. Here we ask at what resolution a connectome preserves what it predicts about neural activity. In C. elegans, direct synaptic connectivity poorly predicts whether stimulating one neuron evokes a response in another. A parameter-free predictor based on paths through the connectome performs substantially better, with most predictive information carried by two-step paths and by the arrangement rather than the number of connections. Coarse-graining neurons into biological cell classes preserves these predictions despite discarding path structure, whereas random partitions degrade them. Connectivity alone identifies alternative coarse-grainings that preserve prediction down to about nine groups corresponding to nervous-system subsystems. Partitions inferred from newly hatched animals preserve adult predictions, and lineage-based partitions in Drosophila preserve path structure better than random coarse-graining. Functional prediction can therefore survive at resolutions far coarser than those required to preserve structure.

Article.Title: Neural dynamics become significantly faster and more nonlinear at the peak of information processing
Article.Authors: samiei, t.; Lokray, S.; Ahmed, H. F.; Nozari, E.
Article.Abstract: The temporal scale at which neural populations preserve stimulus information is often treated as fixed, even though population activity changes rapidly during sensory processing. Whether the information-optimal scale changes within a single stimulus-evoked episode, and what determines its evolution, remains unclear. We developed Integration-Split, a decoding-based framework that estimates the time-varying temporal resolution of population spike trains. Across four visual paradigms and throughout the mouse visual hierarchy, the optimal scale contracted after stimulus onset and subsequently re-expanded. This pattern persisted across stimulus temporal frequencies and was largely absent in a hippocampal control. The optimal scale varied inversely with stimulus decodability, reaching its finest resolution when stimulus identity was most accurately decoded. Beyond this association, independently estimating the signal-noise autocorrelation balance across candidate window widths identified the window that maximized the autocorrelation-based signal-to-noise ratio, and this optimal width closely followed the Integration-Split trajectory. Consistent with these findings, stronger nonlinear predictive structure coincided with finer optimal temporal resolution, consistent with the idea that shorter integration windows are needed to preserve informative nonlinear population structure that would otherwise be attenuated by temporal averaging. To test the functional relevance of this organization, we trained a Transformer solely to decode stimulus identity, without providing the optimal temporal-scale pattern or Integration-Split outputs. Its learned attention exhibited a similar contraction-and-recovery profile, and disrupting heads with stronger correspondence produced larger decoding deficits. Together, these findings reveal a dynamically changing, information-optimal temporal scale in population coding, shaped by the evolving balance of signal and noise autocorrelation and by nonlinear population structure, and independently recapitulated in the learned attention of a Transformer trained without temporal-scale supervision.

Article.Title: Amnesia Induced by Suppressing the Focus of Internal Attention
Article.Authors: Satish, A.; Hulbert, J. C.; Anderson, M. C.
Article.Abstract: Our thoughts can recede as we direct attention to the external world. This experience may reflect the suppression of thoughts about past events, future worries, or stray ideas that could otherwise disrupt focus. Such thoughts may arise spontaneously from replay mechanisms supported by the episodic memory system; hence, sustaining external focus may require suppressing these systems to stop internal distraction. Here, periods of high external focus disrupted diverse episodic content activated near in time, inducing an 'amnesic shadow'. This shadow occurred for both novel content and already formed memories and exhibited key markers of active suppression: forgetting beyond expectations from time alone, which generalised to an alternative reminder. External attention therefore automatically engages an active suppression mechanism that appears to broadly inhibit cognitive systems supporting the emergence of distracting thoughts. The findings raise the possibility that people may naturally gravitate toward activities demanding external attention, unwittingly, to regulate unwanted thoughts.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: thought suppression; episodic memory; internal focus; external attention

Article.Title: Context-dependent effects of ketamine on emotional evidence integration
Article.Authors: Rascu, M.; Grohn, J.; Costi, S.; Zangani, C.; Agyapong, S.; Smith, K. A.; Cowen, P. J.; Hunt, L. T.; Klein-Flügge, M. C.; Weber, L. A.
Article.Abstract: Understanding others' emotions requires continuously integrating noisy affective information as emotional states change over time. Research on emotion processing, however, has thus far focused on static environments or discrete events. Here, we developed a continuous emotional evidence integration task in which participants had to track the average emotional state in a rapidly changing sequence of faces under different levels of environmental volatility. This allowed us to examine emotion integration in changing environments. In online (n=92) and in-person (n=29) cohorts, participants integrated emotional information over longer timescales in stable environments while relying more strongly on recent evidence under volatility, consistent with principles established in perceptual decision-making. We further examined whether this process was modulated by ketamine, an NMDA receptor antagonist associated with evidence integration in the perceptual domain. We conducted a double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-subject study and probed emotion integration during the post-acute period, approximately 1.5 hours after the infusion. Ketamine modulated the temporal weighting of emotional evidence, shifting the balance between recent and past information depending on environmental volatility. Together, these findings show that emotional evidence integration dynamically adapts to the statistical structure of the environment and that ketamine can further modulate this process, which may have relevance for affective disorders.
