Article.Title: Simple, static, spiking nonlinearities can account for seemingly complex interactions between visual, motor and cognitive variables in the visual cortex.
Article.Authors: Zajkowski, W. K.; Quinn, K.; Seillier, L.; Bellet, M. E.; Butts, D. A.; Nienborg, H.
Article.Abstract: Neural activity in the visual cortex is driven by the stimulus and modulated by multiple task-related variables, including spatial attention, eye movements, and perceptual decisions. These multiple influences are each typically described as nonlinear interactions such as gain or normalization, raising the question of how these diverse signals can be combined through cellular or circuit mechanisms. Here we address this problem by examining neuronal responses in macaque visual areas V2 and V3 during a visual discrimination task that dissociates spatial attention from motor planning and microsaccadic eye movements. Using a statistical modeling framework, we show that attentional, microsaccade-related, and choice-related influences on neural activity are best explained by a simple additive stimulus-independent input modulation, which manifests as a gain via a spiking nonlinearity. In addition to explaining how interactions between variables might be accomplished mechanistically, this framework also resolves a controversy about the relationship between microsaccades and spatial attention. We find that neither microsaccade direction nor microsaccade-related neural activity accounts for attentional modulation, although these variables are often correlated, leading to apparent interactions. Thus, visual cortex can integrate sensory, motor-related, and cognitive signals through a parsimonious mechanism that preserves stable stimulus representations while supporting flexible, context-dependent modulation.

Article.Title: Acute nicotine exposure produces a spatially organized transcriptional response in mouse olfactory cortex
Article.Authors: Griffioen, M. K.; Lombardi, A.; Milstead, R.; Borski, C.; Zou, S.; Stitzel, J.; Ehringer, M. A.; Hoeffer, C. A.
Article.Abstract: Nicotine acts on nicotinic receptors throughout the forebrain. Most molecular studies of its effects, however, have focused on reward circuitry and have used bulk tissue, which cannot show which cells respond or how responding cells are arranged relative to one another. We previously found that a single nicotine exposure activates hippocampal astrocytes through the astrocyte-expressed kinase AKT2. Here we asked which cells respond to nicotine in the anterior olfactory cortex, a cholinergic-modulated region that encodes odor associations, and whether their astrocytic surroundings change. Male mice received a single intraperitoneal injection of nicotine or saline, and coronal sections spanning the anterior olfactory nucleus, piriform cortex and adjacent isocortex were sequencing 24 h later using Visium HD. Differential expression on nucleus-based segmentation was concentrated in olfactory excitatory neurons. Article.Title: Infant Sensory Over-Responsivity: Relations to Early Life Adversity, Emerging Behavioral Problems, and Sensory Functional Connectivity
Article.Authors: Overschmidt, S.; Luo, H.; Smyser, T. A.; Latham, A.; Warner, B. B.; Rogers, C. E.; Barch, D.; Sylvester, C.; Smyser, C. D.; Luby, J.; Schwarzlose, R. F.

Positive relationships of prenatal PSS with Y3 autism, anxiety, and internalizing problems were partially mediated by Y2 SOR. Greater neonatal FC between the cortical somatomotor hand network and bilateral thalamus was also associated with SOR at one to two years later. Conclusions. Article.Title: Temporal Variability in Brain Connectivity for Estimating Two-Year Clinical Severity in Mild Cognitive Impairment
Article.Authors: Maximov, Y.; Volkov, A.; Chattopadhyay, T.; Thompson, P. M.; Gabitov, I.
Article.Abstract: Resting-state functional MRI measures coordinated activity across brain networks and may reveal early changes relevant to cognitive decline. Conventional static functional connectivity analyses often compute time-series correlations across an entire scan, missing informative fluctuations over shorter timescales. With additional motion covariates, the corresponding errors were 1.70, 1.73, and 1.59. Connectivity variability outperformed both conventional models in all three cross-validation repetitions, while randomized signals preserving the complete cross-spectrum did not reproduce the improvement. Perhaps surprisingly though, most of the gain occurred in participants without subsequent clinical worsening, and results were sensitive to the choice of temporal windows. These preliminary findings suggest that compact measures of connectivity variability may capture clinically relevant information beyond conventional measures of static functional connectivity, motivating larger studies to evaluate their value for predicting future cognitive impairment.

Article.Title: Sex-specific gene and isoform expression characterizes hippocampal aging in rhesus macaques
Article.Authors: Harper-Alexander, V.; Peterson, S.; Sadikova, S.; Kohama, S. G.; Ram, D. R.
Article.Abstract: Aging produces widespread transcriptomic alterations that extend beyond changes in gene expression to include changes at the isoform level. Declining splicing fidelity, including increased intron retention and aberrant isoform expression, has been proposed to contribute to cellular dysfunction; however, the extent and biological significance of isoform-specific changes in the aging brain remain poorly understood. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) further identified sex-specific modules associated with inflammatory, glial, mitochondrial, and hormone-responsive processes. Together, these findings highlight sex-associated differences in hippocampal transcriptomic aging, underscore the importance of isoform-level regulation, and identify shared transcriptional signatures between normal aging and AD-associated pathways.

Article.Title: Decoding and Characterizing the Intracranial Representation of Semantic Information
Article.Authors: Smith, C.; Inchyna, S.; Barrentine, B.; Kana, R. K.; Basilico, D. A.; Nelson, M. J.
Article.Abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have achieved impressive performance by decoding motor and articulatory signals associated with speech production. Beyond neuroprosthetic applications, this work contributes to understanding how conceptual knowledge is represented in the distributed human language network.

Article.Title: Pathology in resected areas of FDG PET hypometabolism in pediatric epilepsy patients with focal cortical dysplasia type II
Article.Authors: Lam, J.; von Ellenrieder, N.; Hamel, M.; Ruan, Y.; Dufresne, D.; Guiot, M.-C.; Karamchandani, J.; Bernhardt, B.; Dudley, R. W.
Article.Abstract: Introduction: [18F]fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) frequently reveals hypometabolism extending beyond MRI-visible focal cortical dysplasia (FCD). Methods: Fourteen children with intractable, extra-temporal focal epilepsy (mean age 9.0{+/-}5.0 years; 9 female) were retrospectively reviewed. Multiple pathological specimens were obtained from the epicentre and surrounding hypometabolic areas. Overall, 136 specimens were analyzed: 64 epicentre (median 4{+/-}3/patient) and 72 border (median 5{+/-}4/patient). Results: Pathology was identified in 75% of epicentre specimens (59% with frank FCD (fFCD) IIa/b, 16% with dysmorphic neurons only (DNO)). Border specimens showed pathology in 62% (31% fFCD IIa/b, 31% DNO). We fitted a Bayesian logistic mixed model with pathology as outcome variable, location as predictor, and subject as a random effect. Compared to negative pathology, the log-odds of fFCD in the epicentre was 1.00 (credible interval (CI) 0.32, 1.77) and -1.25 in the border (CI -2.17, -0.40). The log-odds of DNO vs negative pathology was non-significant in both locations. Exploratory analyses did not show significant associations between pathology and degree of regional hypometabolism or volume. All patients achieved Engel Ia status at one-year follow-up with no long-term neurological deficits. Conclusion: These findings suggest a spatial difference in distribution of histopathology, with fFCD concentrated in the epicentre and DNO present in both the epicentre and hypometabolic borders. Thus, FDG-PET may be used to better detect the histopathological borders of FCD type II, and the high seizure-freedom rate presented here supports the inclusion of these surrounding hypometabolic regions in the surgical resection (when safe to do so), improving the likelihood of removing potentially epileptogenic cells.

Article.Title: Taste preferences are influenced by temperature and the TRPM8 thermoreceptor
Article.Authors: Zumpano, K. T.; Brooks, C.; Lemon, C. H.
Article.Abstract: Oral temperature influences perceptual and behavioral responses to taste stimuli. Whether somatosensory processes contribute to this influence is unknown. Mice were water-restricted or -replete during quinine and sugar tests, respectively, which were conducted separately and examined all possible concentration-temperature pairings across multiple days. Linear mixed model (LMM) analysis revealed that concentration and temperature both individually and additively affected licks emitted to quinine, with higher concentration and higher temperature (30{degrees}C) associated with the greatest reduction in quinine licks in B6 and KO mice. In contrast, LMM analysis indicated that temperature influenced licks to sugar only in KO mice, which made significantly fewer licks to higher than lower temperature sugars. Notably, KO mice also showed significantly reduced avidity to lick concentrated sugars than B6 mice. These data uncover novel roles for oral temperature and the TRPM8 thermoreceptor, and possibly its broader physiological influences, in taste preference behavior.

Article.Title: Neural representations supporting reuse of abstract structural knowledge in humans
Article.Authors: Luettgau, L.; Chen, N.; Erdmann, T.; Veselic, S.; Kurth-Nelson, Z.; Moran, R.; Dolan, R. J.
Article.Abstract: A human ability to adapt to the dynamics of novel environments relies on abstracting and generalizing from past experiences. Consistent with this, a complementary dynamical role decoding analysis revealed enhanced neural decodability, across experiential contexts, for stimuli that adhered to identical structural transition types, specifically when prior experience included the relevant graph structure. Decoding strength for these role representations was positively related to behavioral success in reuse of subprocess knowledge, a relationship that will require future independent replication. The findings provide neural evidence consistent with the notion that abstract role representations may contribute to the reuse of experience within new contexts.

Article.Title: Use of Integrative Proteomic Analysis to Uncover Shared Molecular Signatures Across Distinct Forms of Hydrocephalus
Article.Authors: Mahendran, G.; Kirupaharan, P.; Audu, D.; Blazer-Yost, B. L.
Article.Abstract: Hydrocephalus is a heterogeneous disease characterized by disruption of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) dynamics and can arise from diverse etiologies, including post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus (PHH), hydrocephalus following subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), post-infectious hydrocephalus (PIH), and idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH). Hydrocephalus has high disease burden in pediatric and older populations and a marked increase in prevalence with advancing age. Despite this high incidence, the underpinning molecular and signaling pathway alterations remain incompletely understood. Hence CSF proteomic profiling would enable a robust and high-resolution approach for exploring disease-specific biomarkers and to discover shared molecular mechanisms underlying hydrocephalus. Hemorrhage-associated forms of hydrocephalus (PHH and SAH) demonstrated enriched coagulation and hemoglobin-related pathways, whereas infection associated forms (PIH) showed enhanced immune and inflammatory responses. iNPH exhibited alterations in proteins linked to neurodegeneration, synaptic function, and impaired CSF clearance. Interestingly, our cross-study analyses identified recurrently dysregulated proteins across hydrocephalus subtypes. Collectively, our cross-study proteomic analyses define shared and etiology-specific proteomic signatures across hydrocephalus subtypes and identify potential CSF-based biomarkers for diagnostic stratification and future precision therapeutic approaches.

Article.Title: Dynamic Routing on a Static Structure: Neuromodulatory Gating of Cortical Wave Propagation
Article.Authors: Maran, R.; Shine, J.; Fulcher, B. D.; Muller, E. J.
Article.Abstract: Stimulus-evoked cortical responses range from tightly localized activations to spatially extended traveling waves, yet the mechanisms through which these distinct regimes are flexibly recruited remain unclear. To test this hypothesis, we extend an empirically grounded corticothalamic neural field model to incorporate a diffusely projecting modulatory population, parameterized on the noradrenergic (NA) arousal system of the locus coeruleus (LC) as the best-characterized case. We then examine evoked responses under transient stimulus-locked versus sustained modulation - corresponding to phasic and tonic modulation - with geometry given by distance-dependent connectivity plus additional fast-conducting non-local projections (FNPs). Transient modulation produces spatiotemporally sustained traveling waves of cortical activity, whereas sustained modulation yields temporally prolonged but spatially localized responses; without modulation, waves are weak and dissipative. The model shows that the timing and spatial pattern of modulatory engagement gate wave-onset latency and impose anisotropy, restricting stimulus propagation to modulated territories and halting it across unmodulated gaps. In the presence of FNPs, which capture contributions of long-range white matter fiber tracts in the brain, modulation also enables the rapid non-local activation of distant cortical regions required for selective long-distance routing. Our results identify patterned gain control as a parsimonious mechanism for variability in evoked dynamics, and suggest that ascending modulatory systems such as the NA system could transiently privilege specific pathways over a largely static connectome.

Article.Title: Temporal Progression of Prior Precision, Surprisal, Model Updating and Tone Adaptation in Human Auditory Cortices
Article.Authors: van Haren, J. J. G.; de Lange, F. P.; Kotz, S. A.; De Martino, F.
Article.Abstract: Auditory perception emerges from the continuous integration of incoming acoustic signals with statistical predictions, a process complemented by simpler local adaptation. Spectrally, these components mapped onto diverging oscillatory fingerprints, ranging from theta-alpha modulation during adaptation to beta suppression during surprisal and broad spectral dampening during precision weighting. Together, these findings demonstrate that the brain navigates uncertain auditory environments through a cascade of neural processes, where fast, local sensory gating and mismatch signals precede the hierarchical revision of internal models.

Article.Title: E3 Ubiquitin Ligase Highwire/Phr1 Mediates Endocytic Control of JNK Signaling in Drosophila Neurons
Article.Authors: Pippadpally, S.; Bisht, A.; Choudhury, S. D.; Dwivedi, M. K.; Mushtaq, Z.; Devi, L. B.; Reddy-Alla, S.; Kumar, V.
Article.Abstract: Endocytosis is essential for synaptic membrane retrieval and the trafficking of growth-regulatory signaling components, yet the mechanistic links between endocytic dysfunction and synaptic overgrowth have remained elusive. Here, we uncover a previously unrecognized mechanism by which endocytosis constrains synaptic growth by regulating the neuronal E3 ubiquitin ligase Highwire (Hiw/Phr1), a key negative regulator of the c-Jun N-terminal Kinase (JNK) signaling pathway. We show that loss of endocytic proteins causes Hiw/Phr1 to accumulate in the neuronal cell bodies, leading to elevated MAP3K Wallenda (Wnd)/DLK levels and hyperactivation of JNK signaling. The accumulated Hiw/Phr1 assembles into dynamic punctate structures, as revealed by their rapid and reversible dissolution with 1,6-hexanediol (1,6-HD). Acute blockade of endocytosis using a conditional temperature-sensitive dynamin mutant Shibirets similarly triggered robust Hiw accumulation at restrictive temperatures. We further demonstrate that Rab11-positive recycling endosomes are essential for proper Hiw localization and turnover, directly linking endosomal trafficking to the control of JNK signaling. Finally, we show that both the Bone Morphogenetic Protein (BMP) pathway and JNK signaling are necessary and sufficient to guide synaptic morphogenesis at the Drosophila neuromuscular junction (NMJ), thereby integrating endocytic trafficking with synaptic growth signaling. Our findings establish endocytosis as a critical regulator of Hiw/Phr1-dependent JNK signaling, with implications that extend beyond synaptic morphogenesis to axon injury and degeneration pathways.

Article.Title: Distinct computations underlie movement error parsing during implicit motor adaptation and perturbation detection
Article.Authors: Kim, H. E.; Darley, J. O.; Landy, M. S.; Chua, R.; Fox, D. J.
Article.Abstract: The human sensorimotor system is remarkably effective at automatically parsing total movement error into its constituent parts, the error component due to a perturbation, or externally-generated error (EGE), versus the error component due to motor noise, or internally-generated error (IGE). This implicit error parsing, and its associated perceptual processes, directly contrasts previous work showing that humans will explicitly misattribute motor errors caused by relatively large external perturbations to their own motor variability. While the combined results suggest a dissociation between perception for action---which allows for precise and automatic error parsing---and perception for conscious detection, this must be inferred across studies using different methodologies. Here, we combined a within-subjects study design and computational modeling to shed light on the principles underlying implicit adaptation to a perturbation and explicit perturbation detection. Neuro-typical adults participated in two experiments consisting of pseudo-randomized rotations during reaches to a single target, with one session requiring explicit reports after each reach of whether a perturbation was detected. Participants demonstrated a clear dissociation between implicit responses to a perturbation and explicit detection, with robust adaptation to $1\degree$ EGEs, but an inability to reliably report the presence of an EGE until it reached $\sim4\degree$. Our modeling results explain this behavioral dissociation as a consequence of the sensorimotor system applying distinct computational strategies to these behaviors. For the adaptation task, the best-fitting model assumes the participant compares proprioceptive and visual cues to detect a perturbation and corrects for a proportion of this error. For signal-detection, the best-fitting model used Bayesian causal inference in which sensory cues are optimally integrated with a prior on their cause. Combined, our study sheds light on the dichotomy between perception for action versus perception for recognition in the context of visuomotor control and adaptation.

Article.Title: Auditory Evoked Potentials Differ from Controls and Correlate with Aspects of Cognition in Kabuki Syndrome and Rubinstein-Taybi Syndrome
Article.Authors: Kalinousky, A.; Bucklin, E.; Ng, R.; Meier, L.; Jiddou, H.; Fanara, P.; Ewen, J. B.; Harris, J.
Article.Abstract: Objective Kabuki syndrome (KS) and Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome (RSTS) are two disorders caused by dysfunctional components of the epigenetic machinery and both result in intellectual disability. Mouse models of both KS and RSTS have seen reversal of cognitive impairment with epigenetic treatments. However, a great need exists for biomarkers in these disorders to improve the likelihood of successful clinical trials. This study aimed to investigate cortical auditory evoked potentials (AEPs) in KS and RSTS so that it could potentially be developed into a response biomarker in the future. Methods The amplitude of the N1-P2-N2 complex was measured for passive listening to monotonal auditory stimuli in individuals with KS, with RSTS, and typically developing controls. A standardized cognitive assessment battery was performed and specific subtests were correlated with AEP values. Results Groups differed significantly in P2, N2, and P2-N2 amplitude although RSTS was consistently more different from typically developing controls than was KS. The mid- to late-phase AEP components (P2 and N2) also correlate with cognition within and across these groups particularly with language whereas earlier components N1 and P2 correlate more with measures of executive functioning. Conclusion Late-phase components of AEPs differ in KS and RSTS from each other and from controls. KS and RSTS differ from controls in P2 and N2 amplitude in the same direction and both show a positive correlation between language and P2 amplitude and a negative correlation between language and N2 amplitude. Together they also show an association with N1 and P2 amplitude and executive functioning. Significance AEPs may turn out to be a valuable response biomarker in KS and RSTS individually and together.

Article.Title: Modeling circadian rhythm splitting under chronic light and the asymmetric transition kinetics between lighting conditions
Article.Authors: Goltsev, A. V.; Mendes, J. F.
Article.Abstract: In various vertebrates, chronic light splits the single daily 24-h circadian activity bout into two 12-h behavioral components per cycle, yet the underlying mechanism remains unresolved. Here, we develop a two-lobe biophysical model of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) to understand this phenomenon. By representing the master clock as interacting ventral core and dorsal shell populations of Kuramoto-type oscillators across bilateral lobes, we suggest that chronic light changes the excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance orchestrated by GABA, which either inhibits or excites SCN neurons. Under constant darkness, excitation dominates and provides in-phase synchronization of the populations. Under chronic light, inhibition dominates, and the ipsilateral and contralateral couplings among the core and shell populations become negative. Consequently, the shells in the left and right lobes oscillate in antiphase, producing the 12-h behavioral rhythm in downstream tissues. We suggest that this E/I balance is shifted by a light-induced change in the expression of chloride cotransporters in SCN neurons. Another key novelty is the introduction of the biologically motivated dynamics of chloride cotransporter expression, which explains the sign inversion of ipsilateral and contralateral couplings under time-varying lighting conditions. The model also reproduces the effects of unilateral SCN lesions: if one lobe is abolished, the remaining intact lobe autonomously stabilizes into a single-bout circadian output with a period comparable to that of the intact system. Finally, we compare our results with experimental data and demonstrate a close agreement.

Article.Title: Robust lesion network mapping reveals symptom-specific circuits
Article.Authors: Cui, W.; Zhu, J.; Long, Y.; Wang, F.; Yin, Y.; Wang, X.; Fu, X.; Zhang, B.; Lu, Y.; Zhang, W.; Huang, J.; Li, L.; Luan, G.; Lin, Y.; Gordon, E. M.; Wang, D.; Zalesky, A.; Dosenbach, N. U. F.; Ren, J.; Liu, H.
Article.Abstract: Lesion network mapping (LNM) is a powerful tool for linking distributed brain lesions to symptom-relevant networks, but similar LNM maps across unrelated symptoms have raised concerns about its statistical validity and specificity. Here we introduce robust LNM (rLNM), a statistically principled framework that combines two complementary controls: an anatomy-preserving spatial null model to account for connectome-derived hub bias shared across symptoms, and hypothesis-driven contrasts to resolve selective specificity among related symptoms. rLNM effectively controls both false positives and negatives. Across 10 lesion datasets (384 lesions) and two task-fMRI meta-analyses (339 experiments), rLNM recovers distinct symptom-specific networks (mean r = 0.044), which show significantly reduced similarity to the connectome hub pattern (r = 0.12 vs. 0.33 in conventional LNM). In 56 patients with neurosurgical lesions, rLNM predicts postoperative language decline at the single-patient level. rLNM thus resolves these concerns and lays a unified statistical foundation for network-symptom inferenc.

Article.Title: Neural transformation from image realism to perceived realness
Article.Authors: Orima, T.; Ban, H.
Article.Abstract: Humans readily perceive whether a visual stimulus depicts something that could exist in the real world, yet the neural basis of perceived realness remains unclear. Because differences between real and unreal stimuli are ultimately expressed through visual features, realness might be expected to emerge along the ventral visual stream. Contrary to this prediction, we show that perceived-realness representations emerge in higher dorsal visual areas through a transformation of image-realism-related image-feature representations in early visual and early dorsal visual areas. fMRI revealed this representational shift toward intraparietal sulcus (IPS), with IPS patterns predicting perceived realness beyond image features and decision difficulty; source-localized MEG showed that realness coding in IPS emerged later than feature coding in early visual and dorsal visual areas. Together, these findings reveal a transformation from visual features to perceived realness along the dorsal visual stream. This representation may help guide subsequent actions and interactions with the real world.

Article.Title: A Mathematical Model of Reliability-Dependent Sensory Reweighting in Quiet Standing
Article.Authors: Kobayashi, J.
Article.Abstract: Human quiet standing relies on vestibular, proprioceptive, and visual information whose contributions change with sensory context. Posturography characterizes this reweighting through responses to visual and support-surface perturbations, but a compact account of how sensory reliability propagates from state estimation to postural action remains incomplete. We develop a minimal quiet-standing model in which sensory reliability is encoded by channel-specific precision parameters that weight sensory prediction errors. A one-link inverted pendulum with intrinsic ankle stiffness estimates posture by minimizing an active-inference free-energy objective and selects ankle torque by minimizing the same objective under a restorative sensory goal. A fixed-point analysis predicts in closed form the perturbation-induced belief bias, each channel's state-update contribution, the steady posture, and a linear stability condition from the precisions, goal dynamics, and intrinsic stiffness. Closed-loop simulations in 115 trials matched the predicted equilibria to within 0.001degrees wherever the loop settled, and the two conditions predicted unstable diverged or drifted. Reducing an unreliable channel's precision eightfold reduced perturbation-driven posture shifts by 82%, with a matching decrease in that channel's state-update contribution; intrinsic stiffness left this reduction essentially unchanged for visual and sensory-only perturbations but bounded it for physical support tilts; a global precision reduction did not reduce the shift; and a within-trial precision switch showed belief updating, not a separate action gain, carrying the change to ankle torque. The results give a compact mathematical account of postural sensory reweighting as relative, context-selective precision control in a closed multisensory loop.

Article.Title: Emergent topological structure in spontaneous brain-organoid activity
Article.Authors: Bodnia, E.; Basart, M.; Hai, S.; Ford, L.; Miolane, N.; Kosik, K. S.; Bouwmeester, D.; Carr, L. D.
Article.Abstract: Neural activity is widely held to organize on low-dimensional structure embedded in a high-dimensional state space. Persistent homology reads such structure directly from the pattern of pairwise correlations, without assuming in advance which variables are relevant. We apply persistent homology to microelectrode-array (MEA) recordings of spontaneous activity from human (Lancaster) and mouse (Pasca) cortical organoids, spanning 25-197 sorted units, and ask whether topological data analysis resolves structure at the node counts that neural recordings actually deliver. Building weighted networks in correlation space and characterizing them by Vietoris-Rips filtration, we find that the first homology (H1, loops) rises significantly above a rate- and population-preserving null in 14 of 18 datasets, all of which remain significant after correction for testing 18 datasets. Random removal of neural units leaves the loops largely intact. Removing the units that form the loops disrupts them more than removing equally connected units does. Topological richness grows with network size, and second homology (H2) exceeds the null only in the larger networks. These results show that persistent homology resolves structured topology in neural recordings at the scale experiments actually deliver.

Article.Title: Beyond Terrestrial Carnivores: Olfactory Bulb Anatomy in a Semi-Aquatic Mammal
Article.Authors: Fraga-Abelleira, S. A.; Torres, M. V.; Canales, R.; Ruiz-Rubio, S.; Sanchez-Quinteiro, P.; Ortiz-Leal, I.
Article.Abstract: The organization of the olfactory systems remains poorly understood in mustelids, particularly in lutrines adapted to semiaquatic environments. This study provides the first detailed anatomical, histological, lectin-histochemical, and immunohistochemical characterization of the main (MOB) and accessory (AOB) olfactory bulbs of the Asian small-clawed otter (Aonyx cinereus). Serial transverse and sagittal sections were examined using Nissl and Tolivia staining, a panel of lectins, and neuronal and olfactory immunohistochemical markers. Macroscopically, the olfactory bulbs were prominent and elongated, although no distinct AOB could be identified. Histologically, the MOB displayed a well-developed laminar organization, abundant mitral and tufted cells, and a clearly defined lateral olfactory tract. By contrast, the AOB was small, located dorsocaudally within the olfactory peduncle, and lacked the canonical lamination observed in many other mammals. Its identification was supported by the selective binding of Ulex europaeus agglutinin and strong Gi2 immunoreactivity in glomerular-like structures, whereas Go labeling was weak. LEA and STA labeled the superficial layers of both bulbs, while VVA and SBA recognized only scattered MOB glomeruli. Neuronal markers, including NCAM, NSE, NeuN, PGP 9.5, and {beta}-tubulin III, confirmed the neuronal nature of the AOB, while calretinin strongly labeled its glomerular structures and projection neurons. These findings reveal a marked contrast between a highly developed MOB and a small, poorly laminated but neurochemically differentiated AOB. This organization indicates that the vomeronasal pathway is retained in A. cinereus, although in a structurally reduced form, and provides a comparative basis for investigating chemosensory evolution in semiaquatic carnivorans.

Article.Title: Distinct lifespan trajectories of cortical intrinsic timescales and neural oscillations
Article.Authors: Liu, X.; Harris, B.; Lu, R.; Wang, S.; Yu, Q.; Zhang, M.; Cui, R.; Liang, X.; Fan, T.
Article.Abstract: The brain integrates information over time through the persistence of neural activity, yet how this persistence changes across the human lifespan and the mechanisms underlying these changes remain unclear. Using resting-state magnetoencephalography from three independent cohorts (n = 1,156; ages 6-88 years), we systematically examined lifespan changes in neural temporal dynamics, focusing on cortical intrinsic timescales and alpha oscillatory frequency. We found that cortical intrinsic timescales shortened from approximately 29 ms in childhood to 9 ms in late adulthood, with the steepest decline occurring before age 30. This compression was reproducible across cohorts and observed in all cortical regions, while the sensory-to-association hierarchy of timescales remained preserved throughout life. By contrast, alpha frequency followed a distinct trajectory, peaking in early adulthood before declining after midlife. Individualized corticothalamic models linked timescale compression to stronger intrathalamic inhibition, whereas increased conduction delays partly accounted for alpha slowing. Further network simulations indicated that intrinsic timescales primarily reflect collective network dynamics rather than single-neuron kinetics. Together, these findings reveal distinct lifespan trajectories of neural persistence and oscillatory rhythms, implicating collective corticothalamic dynamics in the temporal organization of the human brain across development and ageing.

Article.Title: Single-cell multi-omics identify OTP and NOVA1 as regulators of leptin action in hypothalamic feeding circuits
Article.Authors: Tan, H. L.; Tan, Y.; Ruiz-Ortiz, J.; Paul, M.; Han, Z.; Kelly, L.; Toci, A.; Plucinska, K.; Tajima, Y.; Shiao, R.; Lee, B.; Ilanges, A.; Darnell, R. B.; Cohen, P.; Friedman, J. M.
Article.Abstract: Leptin acts directly and indirectly on multiple neuronal populations to regulate feeding and numerous other physiologic functions. However, our understanding of how a single circulating signal coordinates diverse neuronal populations across multiple circuits is limited. To further elucidate how leptin reshapes molecular states in its direct and indirect neural targets, we combined time-resolved single-nucleus transcriptomics and chromatin accessibility profiling to map leptin-induced transcriptional and chromatin state changes across individual neurons in two key hypothalamic nuclei: the arcuate nucleus (ARC), which contains the majority of leptin receptor (LepR) neurons, and the paraventricular hypothalamic nucleus (PVH), an established downstream target of ARC LepR neurons. We found that leptin treatment of leptin-deficient ob/ob mice does not alter neuronal identity, but instead induces coordinated, cell-type-specific transcriptional and regulatory state changes that propagate hierarchically from the ARC to downstream PVH neurons. Integrating RNA velocity, cis-regulatory analysis, and cell-cell communication inference revealed that leptin modulates hypothalamic circuit architecture by selectively strengthening specific interactions while pruning broadly distributed, low-specificity signaling. Although leptin broadly activated STAT3 signaling across LepR neuronal subtypes, integrated multi-omic analyses revealed that activation of STAT3 engages distinct downstream regulatory programs in different neuronal populations, often with opposing physiological functions. Functional analyses identified the homeobox transcription factor OTP, a leptin-responsive regulator selectively induced in AGRP neurons, as a critical mediator of leptin-mediated inhibition of hunger-promoting AGRP neuronal activity and feeding. In parallel, unbiased analysis of PVH neuronal state transitions shows that NOVA1, an RNA-binding protein primarily expressed in inhibitory neurons, is regulated by leptin and alterations of NOVA1 expression bidirectionally control food intake and body weight. Together, these findings define a multi-layered regulatory framework through which leptin regulates hypothalamic feeding circuits to control energy balance.

Article.Title: Early AAV9-mediated SLC9A6 gene replacement preserves cerebellar structure and motor function in the shaker rat model of Christianson syndrome
Article.Authors: Dahiya, K.; Sekaran, K.; Hu, L.; Bloomfield, A.; Kapasakis, E.; Henning-Smith, S.; Riley, L. G.; Evans, M.; Haslam, S.; Katakowski, J.; Anderson, D. N.; Gold, W.; Anderson, C. J.
Article.Abstract: Christianson syndrome (CS) is an X-linked neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorder caused by SLC9A6 loss of function, resulting in NHE6 deficiency and epilepsy, intellectual disability, cerebellar atrophy, and ataxia. Following on our prior gene replacement therapeutic development, we preclinically evaluated AAV9-mediated SLC9A6 gene replacement in the context of promoter selection, dosing, and treatment timing. Intracerebroventricular delivery of neuronal-targeted gene replacement at 1 x 10^11 vector genomes (vg) produced substantial improvements in motor coordination and preserved cerebellar volume, quantified through structural MRI. Early postnatal treatment prevented the development of gait ataxia throughout the longitudinal assessment period, statistically indistinguishable from wildtype controls, with molecular analyses demonstrating restored NHE6 expression and preservation of cerebellar markers. Interestingly, later treatments at timepoints corresponding to early neurodegenerative stages yielded strong initial effects, but these effects were largely lost over time, with half-life modelling demonstrating the need for early treatment. This conflicted with more persistent motor benefit shown in prior work with an engineered capsid, suggesting the need to consider the interaction between treatment timing and capsid-specific tropism and/or persistence. Finally, we built models capable of accurately predicting motor coordination from several protein markers. These findings will impact therapeutic development for CS, with relevance across neurodevelopmental genetic disorders.

Article.Title: Personalized Prediction of Differences in fMRI Connectivity Estimates Across Preprocessing Pipelines
Article.Authors: Maximov, Y.; Volkov, A.; Chattopadhyay, T.; Thompson, P. M.; Gabitov, I.
Article.Abstract: Longitudinal functional MRI of the human brain is valuable for tracking changes in functional connectivity (FC) associated with disease progression or treatment response. Even so, measured FC values depend on preprocessing, and nuisance regression and temporal filtering affect individuals differently. We examined whether we could use earlier scans to predict how preprocessing would affect a later scan. In 69 ADNI (Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative) participants scanned three times, we measured how nuisance regression and filtering, alone and in sequence, changed the measured FC. A ridge regression model combined these responses with baseline FC from the third scan to predict the effect of reversing the processing order. Just four coefficients were shared across 79,800 connections. In leave-one-participant-out testing, mean squared error was 0.012, compared with 0.017 for predicting the same average response for everyone. It outperformed the best of seven alternative predictions chosen for each participant (0.013; normalized gain 0.069, 95% bootstrap interval 0.006-0.134), with lower error in 44 of 69 participants. About half the benefit of using each persons earlier responses, rather than the average across participants, came from which connections changed. This advantage persisted after accounting for acquisition variables. The ADNI-trained model reduced mean error in ten Midnight Scan Club participants without refitting. These results support using personal preprocessing history to predict changes in connectivity estimates on newly acquired scans.

Article.Title: Temporal Structure in Resting-State fMRI under Marginal and Cross-Spectral Surrogate Controls
Article.Authors: Volkov, A.; Maximov, Y.; Chattopadhyay, T.; Thompson, P. M.; Gabitov, I.
Article.Abstract: Resting-state functional MRI is commonly analyzed using correlations between regional signals and their frequency spectra, which characterize average connectivity and spectral properties but may miss other aspects of temporal organization. Measures of temporal complexity offer complementary information about the recurrence of signal patterns, how fluctuations vary across timescales, and signal roughness. These properties may reveal disease-related alterations in brain activity, offering opportunities for biomarker discovery and insights into mechanisms of neurological and psychiatric disorders. Here we examined sample entropy (SampEn), multifractal de-trended fluctuation analysis (MFDFA), and Higuchi curve shapes in 732 scans from 270 ADNI participants, including cognitively normal individuals, people with mild cognitive impairment, and people with dementia. Using the seven Yeo resting-state networks (Yeo-7), we compared recordings with randomized signals preserving either each networks amplitude distribution and approximate spectrum (IAAFT), or the complete cross-spectrum across networks. If these properties fully explained temporal complexity, real recordings should resemble their randomized references. We therefore counted how often each real recording was the strongest outlier among itself and 20 references. This occurred in 21.7%, 12.7%, and 44.2% of 5,124 network-visits for SampEn, MFDFA, and Higuchi, versus 5.5%, 5.1%, and 6.3% in surrogate-only controls. Cross-spectrum-preserving references yielded 39.8%, 17.5%, and 49.8%. Simulations showed that changes in sampling or signal processing, including abrupt changes in signal amplitude, can produce similar differences without changing the underlying dynamics. The measures showed repeatability across visits but did not improve retrospective prediction of changes in Clinical Dementia Rating Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) scores. These findings identify temporal features not reproduced by the tested spectral controls and provide a basis for evaluating their potential as disease biomarkers.

Article.Title: An expansive internal chemosensory system in the insect abdomen implicates Gustatory Receptors in diverse aspects of interoception
Article.Authors: Fujii, S.; Amrein, H.
Article.Abstract: Taste and olfactory receptors are gatekeepers that convey chemical information about the external environment. Their role in chemosensory systems has been extensively studied in several model system, which established their role in triggering discrete behavioral as well as physiological responses related to feeding and social interactions. Over time, cases of chemoreceptors expressed internally in organs not linked to the external chemosensory systems of taste and olfaction have been reported. Here, we present the existence of a complex internal chemosensory system in the abdomen of Drosophila melanogaster. We show that the adult fruit fly harbors a complex internal chemosensory system, composed of about 80 to 100 abdominal chemosensory neurons (ACSNs) expressing approximately 20 different Gustatory receptor (Gr) genes, including all sugar receptor and several members of the less conserved bitter receptor genes. The cells expressing specific Gr genes are stereotypically arranged along the entire circumference of the abdominal body wall, in proximity of muscle and fat layers. The ACSN fall into at least nine different subtypes based on co-expression analysis, projection trajectories into the Abdominal Ganglion (AG) and location of cell somata. Identification of different subpopulation of ASCNs expressing discrete combinations of Gr genes indicates that these receptor complexes have new, previously not considered roles in interoception, including monitoring of different nutrients, detection of cell metabolites and their byproducts and chemicals associated with pathogens.

Article.Title: Hyperactivity preferentially disrupts scotopic retinal circuits in the early stages of diabetic retinopathy
Article.Authors: philip, s. a.; Singh, N. P.; Parida, P.; Kakkatt, H.; swaminathaprasath, a.; Padikkappurath, L. K.; Kumaravel, S.; sethuramanujam, s.
Article.Abstract: Diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of blindness worldwide. In this disease, visual impairments result from neurovascular dysfunction in the retina. However, the specific retinal circuits and the mechanisms underlying their dysfunction remain unclear. Here, in mouse models of diabetes, we evaluated scotopic (night vision) and photopic (day vision) retinal circuit function in the early stages of the disease. Using a combination of immunohistochemical, behavioral and electrophysiological techniques, we show that vision impairments early in the disease are not associated with widespread degeneration of the retinal circuitry but with abnormalities localized to scotopic circuits. Specifically, we observed swelling of axon terminals in rod but not cone bipolar cells. Importantly, these abnormalities were closely linked with bipolar cell activity, as rod bipolar cells showed higher intrinsic activity than cone bipolar cells, and inducing hyperactivity in control retinas was sufficient to recapitulate the pathology in diabetic rod bipolar cells. Further, the swollen rod bipolar cell terminals exhibited an increase in oxidative stress, consistent with cellular dysfunction. In line with this notion, electrophysiological measurements demonstrated that the contrast sensitivity of retinal ganglion cells was preferentially attenuated under scotopic conditions. Finally, behavioral experiments showed that visual sensitivity under scotopic conditions was affected earlier in disease progression compared to photopic conditions. Together, these findings reveal that scotopic circuits are preferentially affected in the early stages of diabetic retinopathy and that hyperactivity is sufficient to drive these abnormalities.

Article.Title: A biomimetic deep encoder for auditory restoration by cortical stimulation
Article.Authors: Lamothe, C.; Verdier, A.; Caris, C.; Greer, R.; Oliveira, R.; Mabrouk, E.; Ceballo, S.; Platel, P.; Butt, E.; Callas, E.; San Roman, R.; Mathieson, K.; Serizel, R.; Bathellier, B.
Article.Abstract: Cochlear and auditory brainstem implants are the primary treatments for profound deafness. However, the inherently low resolution of electrical stimulation used by these devices limits information transfer to a small number of independent stimulation channels and results in perceptual difficulties. An alternative approach is to target the auditory cortex, a brain region large enough to accommodate hundreds of stimulation channels and whose stimulation evokes sound percepts. Although modern brain interfaces offer large channel counts and spatial resolution, developing encoding algorithms capable of accurately transmitting interpretable sound information remains challenging. Here we introduce Braincodec, a deep network that optimizes both sound information transmission and the alignment of stimulation patterns with the spatial, temporal, and high-level properties of the auditory cortex neural code. Braincodec operates online and requires only a few hundred channels to transmit sufficient information for the reconstruction of natural sounds with high fidelity, a performance inaccessible to cochlear implant encoders. Moreover, mice equipped with a Braincodec-driven auditory cortical prosthesis matched the accuracy of non-implanted mice in discriminating real sounds. Braincodec therefore enables the development of high-throughput cortical neuroprosthetics with the potential to overcome the limitations of current auditory implants and provides a generic framework applicable to other sensory modalities.

Article.Title: CD300f is required for efficient lipid handling during cuprizone-induced demyelination
Article.Authors: Manich, G.; Rego, N.; de Frutos, E.; Sanchez-Molina, P.; Almolda, B.; Lopez-Vales, R.; Gonzalez, B.; Castellano, B.; Peluffo, H.; Lago, N.
Article.Abstract: Microglia play a crucial role in central nervous system homeostasis and response to demyelination, yet the mechanisms that coordinate the sensing and processing of myelin-derived lipids remain poorly understood. CD300f is a lipid-sensing innate immune receptor expressed by myeloid cells that has been implicated in tissue damage sensing, phagocytosis, and lipid metabolism. Here, we investigated the role of CD300f in the cuprizone-induced demyelination model. Using CD300f-deficient mice, we demonstrate exacerbated demyelination, increased lipid droplet accumulation, impaired microglial responses, and reduced remyelination accompanied by motor coordination deficits. Bulk RNA sequencing of the corpus callosum at the peak of demyelination revealed enrichment of homeostatic, disease-associated (DAM), and foamy microglial signatures, together with increased expression of genes involved in lysosomal function, phagocytosis, inflammation, and lipid metabolism. Notably, these transcriptional changes were associated with marked lipid droplet accumulation in microglia and enrichment of microglial states previously linked to chronic demyelinating lesions. These findings suggest that CD300f is required for efficient handling of myelin-derived lipids and for microglial metabolic adaptation during demyelination. Our study identifies CD300f as a critical regulator of microglial function and lipid homeostasis and highlights this receptor as a potential therapeutic target in demyelinating diseases.

Article.Title: Active eye modeling: a tool for estimating retinal image quality across the visual field in everyday life
Article.Authors: Burlingham, C. S.; Erkelens, I. M.; Spiegel, D. P.; Nicholls, A.; Cossairt, O. S.; Guan, P.
Article.Abstract: Purpose: The "visual diet," the totality of visual experience, shapes retinal image formation and thereby refractive development, but measuring retinal image statistics during everyday behavior is challenging. Limits in mobile eye tracking, egocentric video, and full-field optical measurement leave gaps in our understanding of how environmental and behavioral factors shape image quality across the retina. Methods: We introduce active eye modeling, a computational platform combining optically validated, wide-field, accommodating eye models (Hastings et al. 2024) with realistic three-dimensional virtual environments and gaze behavior derived from human data. This approach enables systematic estimation of retinal blur across the visual field under parametrically controlled conditions, including varying viewing distances, ambient light levels, and environmental depth structure. Inputs may be simulated and/or drawn from real-world measurements: scene depth, video, and gaze/pupil recordings. Results: During simulated far work, peripheral image quality is depth-tolerant, owing to wide depth-of-field from off-axis aberrations. Near work under dim indoor lighting substantially increases peripheral blur, reducing contrast at mid and high spatial frequencies. This contrast reduction is comparable in magnitude to a moderate diffusing filter (Bangerter 0.4 strength) that affects eye growth when imposed experimentally in animal models. A consistency check with eye-tracked virtual driving confirms peripheral depth-tolerance during far work. Conclusions: Active eye modeling provides a flexible framework for investigating how visual experience shapes the retinal image, relevant to refractive development, display and lens design, and peripheral vision. Applied to common visual behaviors, the platform identifies optical conditions during indoor near work that warrant empirical investigation, complementing measurement-based approaches.

Article.Title: Clinical relevance of diffusion tensor imaging-based parameters estimated with deep learning: the effect of model retraining
Article.Authors: Ciupek, D.; Tristan Vega, A.; Malawski, M.; Pieciak, T.
Article.Abstract: Deep learning (DL)-based approaches have recently become powerful tools for characterizing microstructural properties of brain tissue from diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging data. These techniques enable depicting microstructural features with significantly reduced acquisition schemes while preserving relatively high image-quality metrics compared with non-DL-based approaches. Learning-based methods have increasingly been applied to diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and more advanced multi-compartmental biophysical models, with the potential to facilitate multiparameter analyses of brain microstructure in clinical settings. However, independently trained DL models-while maintaining image-quality properties-do not appear to preserve the statistical properties of groupwise analyses across independently trained models. In this study, we systematically evaluate the statistical properties of DL-based DTI parameters across independently trained neural networks under the same architecture to preserve group-level effects in bipolar disorder. We examine the impact of model retraining and its dependence on reducing the number of gradient directions compared with the nonlinear least-squares (NLLS) procedure. Our results show that initializing model weights randomly from a uniform distribution, while keeping the network architecture and training hyperparameters the identical in the experiment, leads to significant variation in the statistical properties of DTI measures inferred from independently trained models. The analyses showed that the true positive rate in groupwise analysis using the DL-based DTI parameters ranges from 0\% to 100\% compared with the NLLS-based analysis. As the number of gradient directions increased, the NLLS procedure yielded more stable groupwise statistical results, whereas independently trained DL models showed greater variability despite similar image-quality agreement with reference maps. The results indicate that the DTI maps retrieved from a single trained network should be treated with great caution before drawing clinical conclusions.

Article.Title: Apparent sequential effects due to trial-to-trial fluctuations in decision criterion
Article.Authors: Vloeberghs, R.; Desender, K.; Urai, A. E.
Article.Abstract: Decision making is shaped by sequential effects, whereby preceding stimuli and responses influence current decisions. Computational models typically explain these effects by assuming that decision parameters are causally updated as a function of experimental history. Here, we challenge this assumption by showing that several hallmark sequential effects can instead emerge from slow fluctuations in the decision criterion. Using simulations based on Signal Detection Theory (SDT), we demonstrate that trial-to-trial criterion fluctuations, independent of experimental history, generate three commonly observed sequential effects: the repulsive effect of the previous stimulus (i.e., a tendency to alternate), the influence of previous response (i.e., choice history bias), and the modulation of choice history bias by previous confidence. To disentangle causal effects from effects driven by criterion fluctuations, we used the Hierarchical Model for Fluctuations in Criterion (hMFC), which simultaneously estimates both processes. Applying hMFC to 14 empirical datasets revealed that the repulsive effect of the previous stimulus was fully explained by criterion fluctuations. Accounting for criterion fluctuations also substantially altered choice history bias estimates: attractive biases disappeared in all four affected datasets, while three datasets revealed a previously masked tendency to alternate and two showed stronger alternation. In contrast, the modulation of choice history bias by previous confidence was largely unaffected by concurrent estimation of criterion fluctuations. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that criterion fluctuations account for a substantial portion of sequential effects and highlight the importance of explicitly modeling them to avoid confounded interpretations of behavioral and neuroimaging data.

Article.Title: Individual differences reveal shared computational structure in perceptual decision-making
Article.Authors: Xue, J.; Feng, S. F.; Xiong, H.-D.; Wang, S.; Wilson, R. C.
Article.Abstract: To discover computational mechanisms of cognition, models typically specify a fixed psychological architecture, treating individual differences as variations within a predefined parameterization. Here, we take a different approach by using the population structure of individual differences to directly drive model discovery. We develop a low-rank neural network that uses this `population geometry' to learn shared computational components and participant-specific weights from trial-level choices, allowing cross-subject variation to constrain the model's architecture. Applied to perceptual decision-making in the Bernoulli Clicks Task across primary and replication datasets, out-of-sample prediction reveals a six-dimensional representation for individual differences: two continuous dimensions of temporal evidence weighting and two of choice-outcome history dependence, alongside participant-specific side bias and signal-to-noise ratio. This low-dimensional organization replicated in an independent dataset. Together, these findings reveal that seemingly disparate decision heuristics reflect different weightings over a small set of shared computational components, and establish a principled methodology for using behavioral variability to discover the mechanistic architecture of cognition.

Article.Title: Dopamine synthesis capacity and tau pathology differentially modulate rest-to-task functional network dynamics
Article.Authors: Morin, T. M.; Chen, H.-Y.; Aghasoltan, S.; Hsu, M. M.; Jagust, W. J.; Berry, A. S.
Article.Abstract: Optimal cognition relies on large-scale functional brain networks which balance segregation at rest with selective integration during task performance. In aging, these network dynamics are altered. We examined two prominent features of brain aging: dysregulated dopamine function and Alzheimer's disease (AD)-related pathology to examine impacts on brain network dynamics. Young adults and cognitively unimpaired older adults completed resting-state and task-based fMRI and PET imaging of dopamine synthesis capacity ([18F]fluoro-m-L-tyrosine). Older adults were classified as {beta}-amyloid negative/positive using [11C]Pittsburgh Compound-B PET(PiB- or PiB+) and underwent tau-PET scanning ([18F]flortaucipir). Greater rest-to-task network stability and task-related network segregation were associated with better subsequent memory. Compared to young adults, PiB+ older adults showed reduced network stability and both PiB+ and PiB- older adults showed reduced segregation during rest. Higher ventral striatal dopamine synthesis capacity was associated with greater stability within associative networks in young adults, but this relationship was attenuated in older adults and absent in PiB+ participants. In PiB+ older adults, higher tau burden was associated with a task-induced collapse of network segregation across large-scale networks. These findings reveal dissociable influences of dopamine and tau on rest-to-task network organization, highlighting the value of integrating neuromodulatory and pathological markers in aging research.

Article.Title: Circuit and cell-type mechanisms of the spectrolaminar motif of cortical oscillations
Article.Authors: Herrera, B.; Ito, S.; Haufler, D.; Dai, K.; Abdaltawab, A.; Li, Y.; Sennesh, E. Z.; Mendoza-Halliday, D.; Bastos, A. M.; Arkhipov, A.
Article.Abstract: Oscillations are a key feature of cortical activity, coordinating spike timing across areas, layers, and cell types. Recent work suggests these rhythms follow a stereotyped organization across cortical depth, the spectrolaminar (SL) motif, with higher-frequency gamma prominent in superficial layers and lower-frequency alpha/beta in deep layers, yet the mechanisms generating it remain poorly understood. Using a bio-realistic model of mouse primary visual cortex, we reproduced the SL motif and found it preserved across diverse visual stimuli. Systematic cell-type- and layer-resolved perturbations showed that the alpha/beta component was intrinsic to every layer, whereas the 50-80 Hz gamma component was predominantly generated within layer 4 (L4) and propagated network-wide through inter-laminar connections. Pvalb interneurons were the principal regulators of gamma, Sst cells shaped low-frequency power, and Vip cells controlled oscillation magnitude. The temporal properties of L4 Pvalb-to-excitatory synapses were especially influential in generating the SL motif. These models and simulation results thus offer a plausible description of circuit mechanisms underlying cortical oscillations and the SL motif and are publicly available to facilitate further studies.

Article.Title: Reinforcement sculpts synaptic ensembles for operant dendritic control
Article.Authors: Albarran, E.; Fushiki, A.; Athalye, V.; Peterka, D. S.; Costa, R. M.
Article.Abstract: Reinforcement learning requires the selective modification of synapses that contribute to outcome-relevant neural activity, yet the principles underlying these selective modifications remain unclear. Here we combined longitudinal two-photon imaging of identified dendritic spines with a closed-loop optical brain-machine interface (BMI), in which activity from selected apical dendrites of layer 5 motor-cortical neurons controlled an auditory cursor, with target acquisition triggering optogenetic reinforcement. Mice learned to reliably generate the specific dendritic activity that leads to reinforcement. Learning was accompanied by selective strengthening and weakening of individual spines on reinforced dendrites. At individual synapses, the direction of plasticity depended on both the timing of activity relative to reinforced dendritic events and the pre-existing temporal organization of that activity. Furthermore, plasticity was enriched in small task-relevant synaptic groups: spines in synergistic groups were preferentially strengthened, whereas those in antagonistic groups were preferentially weakened. These changes were accompanied by the emergence of increasingly reproducible, selectively recruited, and temporally focused synaptic ensembles, and the incorporation of newly formed spines into these ensembles. Finally, blocking striatal dopamine receptor signaling impaired BMI learning and cortical synaptic reorganization of target dendrites, demonstrating a role for striatal reinforcement in cortical plasticity. Together, these findings reveal how reinforcement of specific dendritic activity sculpts synaptic ensembles that support learned operant dendritic control.

Article.Title: Cross-excitation in dorsal root ganglia redistributes coding capacity from stimulus intensity to stimulus location
Article.Authors: Perevozniuk, D.; Koshev, N.; Musienko, P.
Article.Abstract: The phenomenon of cross-excitation between neurons of dorsal root ganglia (DRGs) of mammals is widely known, yet its exact mechanism remains underexplored. In this work, we analyze the phenomenon as part of the signal processing performed by the body's somatosensory system. We argue that, if the mechanism is indeed as prevalent as it is reported in experimental works, it should provide a significant computational advantage. Here, we created a model network in which sensory A-type neurons are interconnected only via a chemical agent and showed that such a connection, when fitted with parameters similar to those observed in experiments, improves the stimulus-localization properties of the ganglia at the expense of intensity-encoding accuracy. Although this exchange is near-neutral in raw bits, it becomes favorable once the logarithmic compression of intensity perception - the Weber--Fechner law - is taken into account, since the sacrificed intensity capacity is largely perceptually redundant. We therefore propose that cross-excitation is not an imperfection of somatic isolation but an effective, chemically mediated pre-processing stage that sharpens spatial localization.

Article.Title: Towards an analytical framework for investigating the neurophysiological influence of social context in speech perception
Article.Authors: Ip, E. Y. J.; Igoe, A.; Cowan, B. R.; Di Liberto, G. M.
Article.Abstract: Social information plays an important role in everyday speech communication, yet existing neurophysiological approaches provide limited means of isolating its contribution during naturalistic speech perception. Here, we present an analytical framework that combines the large language model (LLM) Mistral-Instruct, fine-tuned on conversational language, and temporal response functions (TRFs) to investigate the influence of social context on word-level speech processing. The framework disentangles local context (LC) from speaker-specific social context (SC) when generating LLM-derived lexical expectation measures, enabling such predictions to be generated under either matching or mismatching speaker contexts for the same speech material. This provides a direct way of isolating the contribution of social information to lexical predictions. We first show that speaker-related social context carries information about speech register and conversational role beyond that available from previous local context alone by interrogating Mistral-Instruct. We then demonstrate that lexical expectations generated from socially congruent contexts produce small but reliable improvements in EEG prediction relative to expectations generated from incongruent social contexts. These effects were observed despite identical acoustic input and neural recordings, indicating that the influence of social context on lexical expectations explains dissociable variance in neural responses to speech. Together, these findings provide a proof of concept for using LLM-derived lexical expectations to isolate and measure the influence of social context on speech processing. More broadly, the proposed framework offers a flexible approach for generating and testing hypotheses about how different forms of contextual knowledge shape neural responses during naturalistic language comprehension.

Article.Title: Extended Pavlovian conditioned approach training and devaluation in Long-Evans rats using time-restricted feeding
Article.Authors: Rainer, I. L.; Brooks, K.; Ulrich-Lai, Y. M.; McReynolds, J. R.
Article.Abstract: Pavlovian conditioned approach (PCA) is a useful tool in studying compulsive- and addictive-like behaviors. PCA pairs a cue with reward delivery and rats typically differentiate into three phenotypes (sign-trackers, goal-trackers, and intermediates) based on behavior during the reward-paired cue presentation. Sign-trackers, who preferentially interact with the cue, are more likely to engage in compulsive behaviors and have decreased behavioral flexibility compared to goal-trackers, who preferentially interact with the food cup. However, one limitation to PCA is the use of food deprivation conditions that maintain rats at 80-90% of ad libitum weight, likely increasing stress which may bias animals towards sign-tracking behavior. Furthermore, most behavioral analysis only examines lever pressing and food cup entry, overlooking other behaviors that may better define phenotypes. In the current study male and female Long-Evans rats underwent an extended PCA training paradigm followed by satiety-induced reward devaluation under time-restricted feeding (TRF) conditions. Under TRF, rats continued to gain weight across PCA training and maintained caloric intake relative to ad libitum intake. Expanding the scope of behavioral analysis increased the proportion of ST rats in both early and late PCA training. Rats also increased the time spent interacting with the food cup during the inter-trial interval across extended PCA training. All rats were sensitive to satiety-induced reward devaluation, regardless of sex or devaluation condition. This study helps establish a PCA method optimized for Long-Evans rats with relevance for identifying PCA phenotypes contribution to dysregulated behavior in the context of chronic stress and obesity.

Article.Title: Walking delays auditory processing in humans alongside a global shift in aperiodic neural activity
Article.Authors: Chen, X.; Chen, S.; Zhang, X.; Cao, L.
Article.Abstract: Natural sensory processing unfolds during movement, yet human electrophysiology is usually measured under enforced stillness. Here, we used mobile EEG to test whether walking changes the timing of auditory processing. Thirty adults listened to lateralised pure tones while walking freely or standing. Walking led to a delay in auditory N1 latency (< 10 ms). Control analyses ruled out the possibility that the N1 delay was contaminated by foot strike related noise in EEG. Multivariate decoding further indicated a later emergence of sound location information during walking in the subset of participants with reliable decoding in both states. Walking also produced a scalp wide decrease in the aperiodic exponent of neural responses. A larger global exponent decrease was associated with a larger N1 delay across participants. Together, these findings show that natural walking reorganises the temporal dynamics of human auditory processing and link early sensory slowing to a global change in ongoing cortical state.

Article.Title: Neonatal NMDA receptor blockade disrupts prefrontal cortical regulation of social affective behavior: implications for schizophrenia
Article.Authors: Tachihara, R.; Hayashi, N.; Rosal, C. G. d.; Xiong, T.; Igarashi, K.; Ozawa, T.; Hori, M.; Yamada, K.; Toyoshima, M.
Article.Abstract: Developmental N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAr) hypofunction has been implicated in the pathophysiology of schizophrenia, including cognitive and emotional deficits. However, the neural circuit mechanisms linking developmental NMDAr hypofunction to social affective impairments remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated schizophrenia-related social affective dysfunction induced by neonatal exposure to the NMDAr antagonist MK-801 and examined the contribution of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), a key hub for socio-cognitive function. Sprague-Dawley rat pups received subcutaneous injections of saline or MK-801 (MK-Low: 0.2 mg/kg; MK-High: 0.4 mg/kg) during the neonatal period. These impairments were ameliorated by chemogenetic inhibition of pyramidal cells in the mPFC, whereas activation of these neurons disrupted social affective behavior in naive rats. Histological analyses revealed reduced parvalbumin-positive interneuron (PVIN) density in the mPFC of MK-801-treated rats. Consistent with the involvement of PVIN dysfunction, selective activation of mPFC PVINs alleviated social affective deficits in MK-801-treated rats. These findings identify impaired PVIN-mediated inhibitory regulation within the mPFC as a circuit mechanism underlying social affective dysfunction following neonatal NMDAr blockade, providing insight into the pathophysiology of schizophrenia-related social impairments.

Article.Title: A Framework for SPICE MRSI Reconstruction Posterior Uncertainty Quantification
Article.Authors: Lyu, T.; Jbabdi, S.; Finney, S. M.; Clarke, W. T.
Article.Abstract: Purpose: Low-rank reconstruction methods such as SPICE substantially improve Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopic Imaging (MRSI) reconstruction quality. However, SPICE does not provide an estimate of reconstruction uncertainty. A framework for posterior uncertainty estimation in SPICE reconstruction is proposed, hereafter referred to as the framework. Theory and Methods: A Laplace approximation is used to estimate the covariance of the reconstructed spatial coefficients. This covariance is propagated through the spectral basis and spectral fitting to obtain metabolite concentration uncertainty. Matrix-free Hessian--vector products and voxel-wise conjugate-gradient estimation are used to avoid explicit construction or inversion of the full Hessian, making the method tractable. Results: Validation using repeated in vivo 7 T MRSI acquisitions showed that the estimated posterior uncertainty exhibited spatial and spectral patterns similar to those of empirical repeated-scan uncertainty. Experiments further demonstrated how spatial regularization and k-space undersampling affect the estimated uncertainty. Conclusion: The framework provides a practical framework for uncertainty quantification when using SPICE reconstruction of MRSI. It could be adapted to other regularised low-rank reconstruction methods.

Article.Title: Curved geometry shapes the observability of hippocampal oscillations
Article.Authors: Makarova, J.; Munoz-Arnaiz, R.; Ashouri, F.; Herreras, O.
Article.Abstract: Curved neural architectures reshape the spatial distribution of field oscillations, complicating the identification of their underlying generators. To test these principles experimentally, here we resolve the paradoxical poor expression of theta oscillations in the hilus of the folded dentate gyrus (DG), a region that otherwise exhibits some of the largest FPs in the brain. Using laminar recordings across both hippocampi and computational modeling, we show that theta is locally masked by cancellation of phase-coherent contributions. Theta generators in CA1 and DG produce volume-conducted fields that, due to the curved geometry of the DG, exhibit opposite dipolar orientations in the hilus, leading to regional cancellation. In contrast, beta and gamma generators are only weakly coordinated across hippocampal regions and therefore remain prominently expressed despite the same geometry. These results demonstrate that theta amplitude, local observability, spatial segregation and apparent translocation emerge from the interplay between geometry and temporal coherence among distributed generators, with tissue geometry acting as a spatial filter for coherent activity.

Article.Title: Multi-scale place fields provide a predictive basis for hierarchical control
Article.Authors: Yu, C.; Maimon, S. R.; Rich, P. D.; Eliav, T.; Las, L.; Lee, A. K.; Ulanovsky, N.; Lengyel, M.
Article.Abstract: Hippocampal place cells typically exhibit unimodal spatial selectivity in small enclosures, but express multiple, irregularly spaced fields in environments of naturalistic scale. However, existing predictive-map theories of the hippocampus do not scale well to large environments and do not account for these heterogeneous place field characteristics. Here, we introduce the factorised hierarchical successor representation (fHSR), a predictive map that supports hierarchical control using subgoal-directed subroutines. We show that the fHSR allows efficient generalisation across tasks, scaling favourably with environmental size, and it reproduces key statistical and topological characteristics of multi-scale CA1 place cell activity in rats and bats. Analyses of experimental data further confirmed a novel prediction of the fHSR: population firing rates exhibit spatial periodicity with a characteristic wavelength independent of environmental size. These results identify the integration of hierarchical control and predictive representations as a normative principle that unifies efficient navigation with the spatial organisation of hippocampal activity.

Article.Title: A biological light sheet links cellular voltage to mesoscopic brain dynamics
Article.Authors: Chen, T.-W.; Lin, B.-J.
Article.Abstract: Membrane voltage is the fundamental currency of neural computation, yet cellular-resolution voltage imaging of large neuronal populations in vivo remains limited by trade-offs among imaging speed, field of view, and optical sectioning. We overcome this challenge by encoding a biological light sheet in the brain: Selective Plane Expression (SPress) restricts fluorescent indicator expression to a user-defined, 20-m-thick plane, suppressing background at its source. Following one-time two-photon photoactivation, SPress enables standard widefield microscopes to capture high-contrast kilohertz voltage dynamics from hundreds of densely labeled neurons across millimeter-scale cortical sheets and columns in vivo. These recordings reveal mesoscopic subthreshold waves that flexibly reorganize population-wide spike timing, together with cellularscale wavefront microstructure that preserves stereotyped local recruitment biases. Article.Title: In Vivo Network-Level Cerebrovascular Mapping Reveals the Impact of Flow Topology on Capillary Stalls After Stroke
Article.Authors: Glandorf, L.; Droux, J.; Jessen, E.; Wittmann, B.; Song, D.; Weber, B.; Wegener, S.; Menze, B.; Leitgeb, R.; Schillinger, D.; EL AMKI, M.; Razansky, D.

Despite changes in individual capillary assignments after stroke, the overall proportions of capillary subtype remained largely preserved. Together, these findings identify local flow topology as a marker of capillary vulnerability after stroke.

Article.Title: Persistent hippocampal traces of lifelong spatial memory
Article.Authors: Wu, J.; Meister, M.; Lois, C.
Article.Abstract: Memory presents a biological paradox: the brain changes continuously, yet a brief experience can influence behavior for a lifetime. How such memories are stored in brain circuits remains unclear. Here we show that two days in a binary-tree maze leave mice with spatial memories that survive repeated 90-day absences over as much as a year. Across return visits, mice explored the maze more efficiently than when naive and resumed direct runs to a reward location sooner, both by a factor of 3. Chronic calcium imaging of the same hippocampal CA1 neurons showed that although most neurons had changed their preferred locations, the population activity at a given maze location still resembled the pattern from 90 days earlier. Article.Title: Neural Bases for Working Memory of Natural Sound Textures
Article.Authors: Mohammadi, Y.; Billig, A. J.; Berger, J. I.; Chait, M.; Griffiths, T.
Article.Abstract: Holding sound objects in mind is critical to understanding the sound world around us. In the texture task, participants judged whether two sequentially presented sounds belonged to the same texture type, whereas in the loudness task, participants judged whether the sounds, drawn from the same texture type, had the same loudness. Stimuli were presented for either 0.1s or 2s. Discrimination sensitivity increased with duration in both tasks, but more strongly for texture discrimination. fMRI analysis revealed distinct effects of duration on univariate and multivariate activity in the auditory cortex and medial temporal lobe (MTL) during maintenance. We found no univariate duration effect in the auditory cortex during maintenance, but multivariate patterns encoded texture category more strongly for longer stimuli, regardless of task. In contrast, MTL activity was modulated by sound duration in both tasks, but there was no effect of duration on texture category decoding. There was a task effect in MTL where multivariate patterns in posterior hippocampal and parahippocampal regions distinguished texture from loudness tasks following 2s stimuli.
