Article.Title: Graph-Based Classification of Penetrating Cortical Arteries and Veins in Whole-Mouse Vasculature Datasets
Article.Authors: Farina, S.; Greco, L.; Barra, G.; Boyer, M.; Renier, N.; Schmid, F.
Article.Abstract: Advances in whole-brain imaging have produced large-scale vascular datasets, yet most lack artery-vein annotations. However, this is essential for quantitative analysis of whole brain vascular structure, blood flow simulation and translational cerebrovascular research. For unlabelled datasets, manual labelling is infeasible at network scale, and surface-vessel tracing is hampered by reconstruction artefacts, limiting the insights that can be gained from these datasets. Here, we focus on penetrating vessel trees, i.e. descending arteries (A) and ascending veins (V). A supervised Random Forest classifier is trained on graph-derived morphological and topological tree features, including persistent homology. Topological features alone achieved competitive accuracy without relying on diameter measurements, demonstrating cross-modality portability. The veins show greater branching complexity, allowing low-pressure drainage. These signatures are stable across modalities, supporting their physological relevance. The framework enables A-V label transfer to unlabelled whole-brain TP graph datasets, validated through the V:A ratio as a function of middle cerebral artery (MCA) distance. Article.Title: Striatal Value Signals Track Progress Toward a Goal During Planning

Article.Abstract: When making decisions, we often weigh immediate gains against long-term goals, and the value of the same choices can change over time. We used a novel task in which participants repeatedly chose between two cards, each with an immediate point value and an uncertain prospective value, with the latter reflecting the collection of card sets. Computational modeling showed that the prospective value captured how close participants were to completing a set. This goal gradient could be explained by both a simple progress-weighted heuristic and a forward-simulating planner. Using fMRI, we found that striatal and precuneus activity increased with the prospective value of the chosen card but not with its immediate point value. Activity in the dorsomedial and insular cortices instead increased with the value of the card given up and was highest when participants chose against the model-based value of the options. Activity in all regions of interest provides stronger support for the goal gradient rather than a full forward-planning model. Article.Abstract: The Human Neocortical Neurosolver (HNN) is an open-source biophysical modeling tool for multiscale interpretation of human electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) signals. HNN's foundation is a pre-tuned canonical neocortical circuit model consisting of excitatory pyramidal neurons and inhibitory interneurons in supra- (L2/3) and infragranular (L5) layers. This model was originally developed based on studies in rodent and non-human primate cortices when dynamics of human neurons were poorly characterized. Yet recent advances in recordings from human tissue now provide unprecedented detail to update the model. Here, we present a significantly updated model for use in the HNN software, with electrophysiological properties and synaptic connections tuned to human tissue. Beyond reproducing biologically realistic somatic dynamics, the pyramidal cells simulate dendritic calcium (Ca2+) spikes in the L5 extratelencephalic-projecting (ET) neurons, and shorter dendritic spikes in the L2/3 pyramidal neurons. The model is distributed with workflows to simulate event-related responses and oscillations, and tutorials demonstrating how membrane potentials, Ca2+ dynamics, and synaptic currents can be recorded and visualized. Unlike our previous study, daytime feeding was not suppressed; instead, cKO mice were slightly and variably hypophagic on HFD but not SCD. DIO resistance was not accompanied by increased energy expenditure, activity, or body temperature. Rather, cKO mice showed reduced energy expenditure and activity and lower body temperature on both diets. In the replication cohort, HFD fecal output was lower in cKO mice, whereas the independent bomb-calorimetry cohort showed no genotype difference in fecal mass; fecal energy density and nonesterified fatty acid concentration were unchanged. Article.Abstract: Symptomatic hydrocephalus is a neuropathological disorder of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) homeostasis characterized by abnormal accumulation of CSF and progressive ventricular enlargement. EPO+MLT, RN1734, or triple therapy differentially attenuated these inflammatory responses. The triple combination reduced both TLR4 and NLRP3 protein abundance within the affected periventricular region and ameliorated the structural alterations. These findings support a combined therapeutic approach that addresses ventricular pathology, inflammation and periventricular structural consequences of congenital hydrocephalus.

The rule also switched on incorrectly 1.4-1.8 times per hour outside N2+N3 and remained active during 28-31% of REM in patients, compared with 2% in healthy adults. Translationally, implanted thalamic leads, increasingly used for neuromodulation in epilepsy, could support sleep-stage-dependent stimulation without scalp EEG, while scalp EEG might be used for noninvasive neuromodulation. Closed-loop systems should be evaluated not only by sleep-stage classification accuracy but also by how reliably and promptly they enable and disable stimulation.

Article.Title: Generalizable sex differences in functional brain organization follow the cortical hierarchy in youth
Article.Authors: Luo, A. C.; Hettwer, M. D.; Alexander-Bloch, A. F.; Bagautdinova, J.; Barch, D. M.; Cieslak, M.; Flook, E. A.; Franco, A. R.; Gur, R. E.; Gur, R. C.; Keller, A. S.; Kiar, G.; Milham, M. P.; Pritschet, L.; Raznahan, A.; Salo, T.; Salum, G. A.; Shafiei, G.; Shinohara, R. T.; Somerville, L. H.; Sydnor, V. J.; Vandekar, S. N.; Zhang, X.; Shanmugan, S.; Satterthwaite, T. D.
Article.Abstract: It remains unknown if sex differences in human functional connectivity follow a generalizable overarching principle. Here, we tested whether sex differences in functional connectivity during childhood and adolescence are organized along the sensorimotor-association (S-A) axis, a cortical hierarchy spanning unimodal sensorimotor to transmodal association cortex. We analyzed four large-scale, independent datasets of youth ages 5-23 years (total N = 3,355). Across datasets, males showed greater connectivity between functional networks, whereas females showed greater connectivity within networks, most prominently within the default mode network. More broadly, the sensorimotor and association ends of the S-A axis were more segregated in females and more integrated in males. This difference extended to macroscale cortical organization: the cortical hierarchy was expanded in females relative to males along the principal gradient of functional connectivity. Together, these findings identify the S-A axis as a generalizable organizing principle of sex differences in functional brain organization during youth.

Article.Title: No Evidence of an Effect of a Single Mirror Visual Feedback Session on Subsequent Motor Imagery
Article.Authors: Schwarz, L. J.; Sterr, A.; Kranczioch, C.
Article.Abstract: Motor imagery (MI) and mirror therapy, based on mirror visual feedback (MVF), are recommended as adjuncts to conventional therapies for upper limb rehabilitation after stroke. Both approaches activate sensorimotor cortical networks despite the absence of overt movement, and their concurrent application has been associated with enhanced neural activation. The present study investigated whether a single session of MVF modulates subsequent kinesthetic Motor Imagery (kMI)-related neural activity. EEG data from 38 healthy participants (MVF: n = 18; sham: n = 20) were analyzed in a mixed pre-post design. Participants performed kMI before and after either an MVF or sham intervention. Analyses focused on mu-band (8-12 Hz) event-related desynchronization (ERD) and its hemispheric lateralization. Although kMI reliably elicited stronger contralateral than ipsilateral mu ERD, MVF did not significantly affect subsequent kMI-related mu ERD or its hemispheric lateralization. These findings suggest that previously reported facilitatory effects of MVF on MI may be more closely related to concurrent application than to immediate aftereffects, while potential effects of repeated MVF exposure on subsequent MI remain to be investigated. These findings provide a foundation for future studies investigating how MVF and MI can be combined to optimize upper-limb stroke rehabilitation.

Article.Title: Compositional computations in the primate frontal cortex
Article.Authors: Tang, C.; Jazayeri, M.
Article.Abstract: A hallmark of intelligence is the ability to apply familiar operations to new inputs without relearning. How neural circuits carry a learned computation into states never visited during training remains unclear. Here we combined neural recordings, circuit modeling and human experiments to investigate compositional generalization. Monkeys learned to combine a start location with a displacement specified by the direction and duration of an optic-flow stimulus, then encountered novel combinations of these familiar inputs. Frontal population activity separated the computation into spatial and temporal components: start location and flow direction established the neural state, from which activity evolved along shared timing dynamics. Novel combinations elicited accurate responses when trajectories maintained this organization, whereas departures predicted systematic behavioral biases. Circuit models revealed a three-way alignment problem: input representations, recurrent dynamics and readout operations must jointly implement the required computation. Mismatches produced systematic biases that increased with distance from trained conditions. Humans exhibited similar biases when familiar sensory cues and spatial transformations were linked through an unfamiliar mapping. Together, these findings show how the coordination of reusable neural resources supports new computations, and how its disruption produces predictable failures of generalization.

Article.Title: Increased Cognitive Load Expands, Stabilizes, and Aligns Visual Representation Across the Human Brain
Article.Authors: Qu, S.; Chun, M. M.; Xu, Y.
Article.Abstract: Cognitive load refers to the mental effort required to perform a task. While previous research has extensively examined its detrimental effects on neural and behavioral performance, much less is known about how the brain actively adapts to heightened demands. Across two fMRI experiments involving visual n-back tasks, we identified several fundamental properties of this adaptive process. First, higher load enhanced and expanded visual representations beyond localized visual regions, leading to widespread visual coding. At the global scale, heightened load promoted cross-regional coordination by increasing representational alignment and strengthening information encoded in interregional functional connectivity patterns. Beyond facilitating stronger visual representation, increased load also reduced neural pattern variability, which led to more stable information coding. Finally, load was encoded independently of other task-relevant information as a separate brain state, supporting its overarching role in guiding visual processing. Together, these findings revealed that the brain adapts to heightened cognitive demands by globally reorganizing neural processing to support flexible cognition.

Article.Title: Confidence: Its Measurement, Relation to Behavior, and Neural Representation
Article.Authors: Tsutsumi, M.; Ogawa, T.; Kishi, T.; Kawanabe, M.; Kuroda, T.
Article.Abstract: Confidence (certainty/uncertainty about one's own decision) has attracted considerable attention in psychology, neuroscience, and artificial intelligence. Yet its relation to behavior remains unclear: Some treat confidence as a cause of behavior whereas others view it as a state controlled by environmental variables. The unobservable nature of confidence makes its measurement validation and analyses difficult. To tackle these issues, we developed a novel procedure combining a decision-making task, risk choices, and a post-task open-ended questionnaire. Point-gain/loss amounts for correct/incorrect decisions varied depending on choices between high-risk/high-return and low-risk/low-return. In the questionnaire, 90% of 16 participants reported feelings interpretable as certainty/uncertainty when making those risk choices despite no instruction about confidence, whereas 8% did so when the choices led to identical outcomes/returns. This suggests confidence is a state controlled by environmental contingencies rather than a cause of behavior. We also decoded changes in the state from electroencephalography and functional magnetic resonance imaging.

Article.Title: Deprivation of dietary fiber promotes low-grade neuroinflammation and anxiety-like behavior in mice
Article.Authors: Oyetunde, A.; Pyaram, D. N.; Ngo, V.; Li, C.; Abo, H.; Zou, J.; Mabb, A. M.; Gewirtz, A. T.
Article.Abstract: Background: Intestinal health is an important determinant of brain function in that an array of gut perturbants, especially those targeting microbiota, influence behavior. Fermentable dietary fiber nourishes gut microbiota and, consequently, promotes gut health. We hypothesized that depriving mice of fermentable dietary fiber would impact their brain and behavior. Methods: Male C57BL/6J mice were fed standard grain-based chow (GBC), a compositionally defined diet (CDD) which mimics macronutrient content of GBC but lacks fermentable fiber, or CDD supplemented with the fermentable fiber inulin (CDD+INU). Mice were subjected to behavioral testing 6-8 weeks later followed by analysis of the gut brain axis. Results: Relative to GBC-fed mice, CDD-fed mice exhibited low-grade gut inflammation and a reduction in open-field center exploration, signaling heightened anxiety-like behavior. CDD+INU fully reversed these abnormalities arguing they were a consequence of fiber deprivation. Analysis of the gut microbiome and serum metabolome showed that CDD+INU increased oxidative phosphorylation and immune suppressive metabolites. Flow cytometric and transcriptomic analyses of the brain revealed an array of pro-inflammatory alterations in myeloid cells, CD4+ T-cells, microglia and astrocytes in mice fed CDD but not CDD+INU. Most notably, microglia and astrocytes from mice fed CDD, but not CDD+INU, displayed reduced mitochondrial respiration and greater glycolytic activity. CDD, but not CDD+INU consumption also reduced the abundance of oligodendrocytes and neurons, and increased hippocampal pro-inflammatory gene expression. Conclusions: Deprivation of fermentable fiber results in coordinated changes in brain immune composition and glial metabolic state that is associated with increased anxiety-like behavior.

Article.Title: Phase-locked dual-band vibration bursts strengthen anti-kindling by vibrotactile coordinated reset stimulation in a spiking network model
Article.Authors: Patki, S. A.; SKM, V.
Article.Abstract: Parkinsons disease and related movement disorders are accompanied by pathologically synchronized neuronal activity in cortico-basal ganglia circuits. Coordinated reset (CR) stimulation was derived computationally as a means of suppressing such activity at its source, by resetting the phases of the subpopulations of a synchronized network at staggered times. Under spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP), the resulting decorrelated firing depresses excitatory coupling and establishes a weakly coupled, desynchronized state that outlasts stimulation, a process termed anti-kindling. Sustained post-stimulation benefit has been demonstrated for electrical CR stimulation in parkinsonian primates and in proof-of-concept patient studies, and vibrotactile CR (vCR) stimulation realizes the same principle non-invasively through bursts of fingertip vibration. The deployed vCR protocol employs a carrier frequency of 250 Hz, which preferentially recruits Pacinian afferents. Because Pacinian receptive fields extend substantially beyond the stimulated digit, inputs originating at adjacent fingertips converge on overlapping regions of the target population, which degrades the spatial separation on which CR depends. Here we examine whether the spectral composition of the individual burst, independent of the stimulation schedule, governs the magnitude of anti-kindling. In a Hodgkin-Huxley network with STDP, driven through a two-channel model of fast-adapting afferents, a dual-band burst superimposing a 30 Hz component on the 250 Hz carrier yielded the lowest post-stimulation coupling among eleven vCR patterns, at one third of the carriers drive power. Recruitment of focal Meissner afferents by the 30 Hz component restricts part of the drive to the stimulated subpopulation, and phase locking of that component to the burst envelope generates post-burst pauses that reset the phase of the stimulated neurons. Spectral composition therefore determines both the spatial selectivity of vCR stimulation and its capacity for phase resetting.

Article.Abstract: Objective: To determine whether an -synuclein (-Syn) seed amplification assay (SAA) detects seeding-competent aggregates in endoscopic mucosal biopsies, differs by gastrointestinal region, registers pathology more frequently than immunohistochemistry (IHC), and associates with Parkinson disease (PD) diagnosis, disease duration or severity. Sigmoid SAA positivity increased significantly with PD disease duration (40.00% at <5 years, 73.33% at 5-10 years, and 93.75% at >10 years), independent of motor severity, whereas ileal positivity remained stable across disease stages. Article.Title: Concussion decreases brain signal variability
Article.Authors: Schultz, D. H.; Bouchard, H. C.; Barnwell, B. C.; Muncy, N. M.; Wilcox, R. R.; Savage, C. R.; Neta, M.; Barbey, A. K.
Article.Abstract: Sports-related concussion represents a major public health concern, with millions of cases diagnosed annually. Despite significant methodological advances in functional brain imaging, a clinically meaningful neuroimaging biomarker of concussion has yet to be established. This may be due in part to a reliance on traditional measures. For example, approaches examining mean activation across trials reduce responses to a single measure of central tendency and therefore fail to capture important individual differences. In contrast, blood oxygenation level dependent (BOLD) variability offers a promising new approach to measuring brain function, Specifically, it captures individual differences in the temporal variability in the BOLD signal over time. Further, it is sensitive to neural, vascular, and neurovascular coupling changes that accompany concussion. We collected baseline (prior to injury) and post-concussion (within 48 hours of injury) neuroimaging data in 56 collegiate athletes. Within this longitudinal dataset, we investigated changes in BOLD variability across multiple spatial scales. In addition, we examined their relationships with self-reported symptoms and cognitive performance. As expected, symptoms increased following concussion while computerized cognitive performance declined. BOLD variability decreased from baseline to post-concussion, particularly in the somatomotor and language networks. Moreover, changes in BOLD variability were related to changes in symptom reporting and cognitive performance. Together, these findings advance our understanding of how concussion affects brain function and highlight BOLD signal variability as a promising biomarker to aid ongoing efforts to improve the diagnosis and treatment of sports-related concussion.

Article.Title: Neurons entrain and shape an intrinsic arteriole rhythm that distributes blood across the cortical mantle
Article.Authors: Duckworth, J.; Broggini, T.; Chhabria, K.; Neill, P.; Sancho, M.; Sellier-Prono, M.; Iyengar, S.; Vergassola, M.; Nelson, M. T.; Kleinfeld, D.

Three findings support this: First, suppressing endothelial hyperpolarization left resting-state oscillations intact but weakened the vascular response to neural activity, showing that vasomotion originates within the arteriole network rather than following neuronal drive. Second, arterioles amplify sensory drive selectively rather than faithfully: neural activity near 0.1 Hz is resonantly enhanced to form a strong peak in the vascular response. Third, neuronal frequency sets spatial reach, and areas compete: when two neighboring cortical areas are driven simultaneously, the one nearer fvaso captures more vascular territory. Neurons therefore entrain an intrinsic vascular rhythm and stimulation frequency governs how vasomotion distributes blood, shapes functional brain images, and may influence interstitial fluid transport.

Article.Authors: Paiva, C. D.; Evora, A. J.; Zheng, S.; Carreira-Rosario, A.
Article.Abstract: Genetically encoded fluorescent indicators are powerful tools for monitoring biological processes in live samples (Lin and Schnitzer 2016; Nakai, Ohkura, and Imoto 2001). When combined with a large field of view, a single time-lapse recording has the potential to capture many specimens, facilitating high-throughput data collection. However, this approach generates large, multidimensional datasets that are challenging to process and analyze. We present SNAzzy, a Python package for studying synchronous network activity (SNA) in Drosophila embryos via high-throughput microscopy. SNA is a hallmark of developing nervous systems (Wu, Kourdougli, and Portera-Cailliau 2024; Blankenship and Feller 2009; Akin and Zipursky 2020), often studied using genetically encoded calcium indicators to monitor neural activity in vivo. SNAzzy processes and analyzes time-lapse datasets taken from live samples using fluorescent widefield microscopy. Each dataset contains dozens of individual specimens in the same field of view and thousands of time points. The software offers individual specimen cropping for optimization of storage and processing, adaptive regions of interest for quantification of fluorescence and changes in morphology over time, a custom peak detection algorithm, and a graphical user interface for data visualization, curation, and dataset comparison. The code is available at https://github.com/ACRLab/snazzy.

Article.Title: Probing EEG Foundation Model Attention Maps for Lightweight Interpretable Emotion Recognition
Article.Authors: Arvanitopoulos, L. N.; Dragomir, A.; Fidas, C. A.; Bezerianos, A.
Article.Abstract: Foundation Models (FMs) trained on EEG signals promise subject- and dataset-independent pipelines for brain-computer interface (BCI) applications, but have yet to consistently outperform task-specific architectures, and their large representations are costly to compute and store. As a means of advancing the understanding of the Foundation Models' inner mechanisms, we propose a lightweight alternative that exploits the self-attention mechanism of REVE, a pretrained EEG FM, to derive features similar to weighted Functional Connectivity (FC) without any fine-tuning. Inspired by kernel-based FC matrices, we aggregate the raw first-layer attention weights of a single head over the full duration of dataset trials into weighted channel-to-channel adjacency matrices. These matrices replace standard encoder representation vectors as classification features, substantially reducing computational cost. We further introduce a label-free, symmetry-based criterion, motivated by the emergence of near-symmetric attention patterns in trained encoder-decoder transformers, ranking attention heads by how much discriminative information they carry. Classical machine learning classifiers are then trained on the single most informative head's attention-derived FC matrix and achieve balanced accuracy and F1 scores on the SEED-IV emotion-recognition dataset that are competitive with several fully fine-tuned state-of-the-art EEG Foundation Models, requiring at least two orders of magnitude fewer calculations than the standard use of the encoder. Subsequent cortical region analysis revealed a significant over-representation of frontal region connections by ranking the most discriminative FC matrix connectivity edges, validating our methods as consistent with prior affective-computing literature. These results suggest that interpretable, computationally inexpensive linear probing of attention maps is a viable route to deploying EEG Foundation Models in resource-constrained settings.

Article.Authors: Sharma, A.; Clements, K. J.; D'Ambra, N.; Birnbaum, J.; Kuklin, E.; Reed, M.; Griffith, L.
Article.Abstract: Similar behavioral outcomes in males and females can mask substantial differences in the mechanisms underlying neuronal function. However, to what extent sex influences the abundance and activity-dependent changes of proteins that govern neuronal plasticity remains poorly understood. These sex-specific differences are downstream of the sex determination pathway, implicating somatic sex identity in the regulation of CaMKII abundance and its activity-dependent dynamics. Despite the differences in CaMKII levels between female and male flies, we observed no impairment of plasticity in either sex. Overall, our findings reveal sex-dependent regulation of both steady-state and activity-dependent levels of a highly conserved neuronal plasticity-associated protein across distinct neuronal contexts and development stages. These results further support the idea that females and males can achieve similar behavioral outcomes through different molecular mechanisms. Growing evidence that sexually dimorphic molecular responses contribute directly to sex differences in vulnerability to stress and disease underscores the importance of identifying these mechanisms and understanding their consequences.

Article.Title: Experience shifts value updating from synaptic plasticity to neural dynamics
Article.Authors: Lee, J.; Hennig, J.; Frelih, V.; Gershman, S. J.; Uchida, N.
Article.Abstract: Adaptive behavior requires durable value memories and rapid updating. Mice exposed to repeated reversals of odor-outcome contingencies acquired faster value updating at the cost of faster memory decay. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) trained with continual plasticity revealed two routes to faster learning, one through more efficient synaptic plasticity and one through a transition to value computation by neural dynamics. Context and value signals decayed over prolonged inter-trial intervals, paralleling behavioral forgetting. Conditional deletion of CaMKIIa in Emx1-cre-expressing neurons spared initial associative learning but impaired expert reversal performance, as did freezing the recurrent weights of RNNs, suggesting distinct loci for initial value learning and meta-learning. Together, these findings reveal how experience shifts value computation from synaptic plasticity toward neural dynamics, providing a mechanistic framework for the trade-off between memory stability and behavioral flexibility.

Article.Title: Tree shrews combine panoramic vision with an expanded oculomotor repertoire
Article.Authors: Pal, R.; Kempkes, E.; Aeleti, R.; Tubbs, E.; Biswas, A.; Sedigh-Sarvestani, M.
Article.Abstract: Mammals differ in how they redirect gaze. Primates shift and hold gaze with rapid, precise eye movements that can be decoupled from the head. In lateral-eyed mammals studied to date, gaze is organized around the head: saccades are coupled to head rotation in freely moving animals and typically accompanied by attempted head movements even under head fixation. These observations suggest a trade-off: animals that keep a panoramic field give up the precise, eye-driven control of gaze typical of frontal-eyed animals. But because lateral eyes and head-centered gaze co-occur in every lateral-eyed species studied, it is unknown whether one follows from the other. Here we test this in the tree shrew, an arboreal mammal with laterally placed eyes. Using real-time eye tracking in head-fixed animals, we find that tree shrews saccade frequently under head fixation and that most saccades occur without detectable attempted head movement. Tree shrews make visually evoked saccades, along both the horizontal and vertical axes of the visual field, toward targets. They can also fixate on visual targets. Using widefield calcium imaging, we show that visual cortex over-represents the central visual field. Lastly, we show that extraocular muscles that move the eyes contain specialized nerve endings found in frontal-eyed species. Based on this suite of evidence, we conclude that lateral eyes do not preclude eye-driven gaze control. The two are separable dimensions of visual system design, a combination that may suit animals whose locomotion routinely points the head away from where they need to look.

Article.Authors: Daaboul, D.; Vandensteen, J.; Dascenco, D.; Lorente-Echeverria, B.; Vandenbempt, J.; Leysen, E.; Reverendo, M.; Vlaeminck, I.; Vervloessem, L.; Alcaraz, N.; Wojno, M.; Poovathingal, S.; Davie, K.; Magalhaes, P.; Kempynck, N.; Michel, G.; Spruston, N.; Wierda, K.; Aerts, S.; de Wit, J.

Deep and superficial hippocampal CA3 pyramidal neurons (PNs) differ in intrinsic firing and mossy fiber (MF) input at specialized postsynaptic structures termed thorny excrescences (TEs). Combining developmental single-nucleus multiomics with genetic targeting, morphological analysis and electrophysiology, we identify the transcription factor ST18 as a regulator of deep CA3 subtype identity. ST18 marks sparsely thorny and burst-firing neurons, and gene regulatory analyses predict that it represses a superficial-associated program involved in dendritic spine development, synaptic organization, and electrophysiological properties. Postnatal ST18 loss shifts the transcriptional and chromatin landscape of deep CA3 PNs toward a superficial-like state. These molecular changes are accompanied by increased TE elaboration approaching superficial levels, enhanced excitatory synaptic activity, and reduced burst-firing. Together, these findings identify ST18-dependent restriction of an alternative subtype program as a mechanism linking molecular identity to distinct input connectivity patterns and intrinsic firing properties during postnatal circuit maturation.

Article.Title: Learning to play with spikes: characterizing, predicting, and engineering unsupervised plasticity rules for spiking reservoir computing
Article.Authors: Kania, M.; Confavreux, B.; Vogels, T. P.
Article.Abstract: Spiking reservoir computing, and reservoir computing more generally, is a powerful and efficient framework for neuromorphic and biological applications, in which a fixed random reservoir drives a trained readout. Its performance depends critically on the reservoir initialization, so that enriching the reservoir with adaptive, unsupervised plasticity rules offers a natural solution to this limitation. However, it is unclear which rules work, or why, and how to find the best-suited rules for specific tasks without exhaustive and expensive search. Here, we learn how to play the Atari game Pong in a plastic spiking reservoir network. We systematically characterize a large family of local plasticity rules that were meta-learned in prior work. We then show that their performance is predictable and structured: high-scoring rules are characterized by strong differentiation between neurons encoding the ball trajectory and the background, with stable weight dynamics, and consistent readout alignment across time. These mechanistic signatures are not task-specific and transfer to a delayed-match recognition task. Rule performance can be estimated from rule parameters alone. Finally, conditioning simulation-based inference (SBI) on high scores allows us to sample directly from promising regions of the rule space, to discover rules that exceed the performance of those found in the prior distribution and reveal stable, high-performing configurations. Together, these results offer competitive performance against classical reservoir computing while providing a transparent, interpretable account of what makes a plasticity rule useful for neuromorphic hardware and biological computing.

Article.Authors: Geller, A.; Kwon, M. J.; Simmons, S. K.; Xu, Q.; Martenis, W. E.; Doman, J.; Natarajan, S.; Stalnaker, K. Moreover, when Gpr34 KO mice were crossed with 5xFAD mice, the DAM transcriptional profile of microglia and glial pathology were further exacerbated beyond the already robust DAM signature driven by 5xFAD alone. This occurred without affecting amyloid plaque burden. Human stem cell-derived microglia (iMGLs) lacking GPR34 showed reduced calcium (Ca2+) and phosphorylated ERK (pERK) signaling in response to stimulation with known GPR34 agonists (lyso-phosphatidylserine (lysoPS) and myelin), as well as transcriptomic changes in immune regulation and cell proliferation related pathways. Interestingly, GPR34 KO iMGLs were selectively impaired in phagocytosis of myelin but not amyloid-B; (AB) or E. coli, and showed a diminished transcriptional response elicited by myelin. Together, these findings suggest that GPR34 is important for maintaining microglia in a homeostatic state, promotes phagocytosis of and transcriptional response to myelin, and limits microglial reactivity in neurodegenerative disease conditions.

Article.Authors: Desai, N. P.; Love, K. F.; van Schoor, A.; Freeman, S.; Ali, M.; Richardson, R.; Kovacs-Balint, Z. A.; Tobar Mosqueira, R. A.; Lebovic, R. L.; Acevedo-Polo, J. H.; Vlasova, R. MRI at 3 months revealed larger total cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) volume, reduced visual processing region volumes, and sex-specific brain structural alterations: males exhibited amygdala hypertrophy, whereas females had volumetric reductions in temporal-limbic and temporal-auditory cortices. Article.Title: Uncovering the latent structure of interwoven population and temporal codes
Article.Authors: Friedenberger, Z.; Cao, Y.; Naud, R.
Article.Abstract: Population analysis methods have become standard for navigating the complexity of neural data. However, these methods often assume a rate code, neglecting information encoded in the precise timing of spikes. Critically, additional information encoded in bursts of action potentials may be missed. Here, we develop a probabilistic latent-variable framework that disentangles the factors associated with bursts and individual spikes. This enables burst codes to be investigated directly from the structure of the data, without requiring external covariates. We demonstrate that analyzing firing rates alone obscures the latent structure and factors underlying bursts. Applying our method to simulated and experimental data, we show that it can infer the correct latent structure and be used to test for the presence of burst coding. By merging the population and burst coding perspectives, we provide a framework for linking changes in bursting to internal variables involved in attention, perception, and learning.

Article.Title: Dual kinase inhibition provides early clues to restoration of neuroimmune homeostasis in an AAV-haSyn model of Parkinsons disease
Article.Authors: Chiang, W.; Sandoval, I. M.; Li, H.; Bernal-Conde, L. D.; Squire, R.; Washburn, M. K.; Schwartz, J. L.; Squire, E.; Wagner, E. J.; Manfredsson, F. P.; Gelbard, H. A.
Article.Abstract: Background Previous studies of drugs targeting mixed linage kinase type 3 (MLK3) and/or leucine rich repeat kinase type 2 (LRRK2) in sporadic Parkinsons disease (PD) have failed to meet clinical endpoints despite multiple lines of evidence implicating these kinases in pathogenesis. This has reduced enthusiasm for MLK3 and LRRK2 as druggable targets. Largely overlooked is the evidence that these targets remain valid but must be considered in combination to achieve a therapeutic outcome. This provides the rationale for this study. Methods We conducted a pilot study modeling early, pre-symptomatic PD with subsequent evaluation of therapeutic potential of a multi-kinase inhibitor (URMC-099) in alleviating disease pathology. Sprague Dawley rats received unilateral intranigral injections of low dose AAV-haSyn. After a two-week recovery period, all animals were administered either once-daily intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of URMC-099 or its vehicle control until their terminal endpoint. Induction of early PD, and its alleviation with URMC-099, was evaluated by lateralized motor impairment using the cylinder test and immunohistochemical analysis of neuropathology in the substantia nigra (SN) and striatum. Finally, an in vitro microglial PD model exposed to aSyn pre-formed fibrils and treated with URMC-099 was used to further evaluate the mechanism underlying therapeutic activity. Results A unilateral model of early and progressive AAV-haSyn model for PD was used to demonstrate the therapeutic potential of a targeted multi-kinase inhibitor to attenuate PD-associated neuropathology and prevent the manifestation of lateral motor deficits. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed protection of neuronal cellular integrity along the nigral-striatal pathway with once-daily i.p. URMC-099. The mitigation of degenerative neuropathology was linked to targeted inhibition of MLK3 and LRRK2 and complemented by reduced levels of gliosis in astrocytes and microglia in the SN. Single-microglia segmentation analysis suggested URMC-099 treatment preserved dynamic effector state switching in microglia to enhance autophagic flux to reduce the overall burden of pathologic aSyn. Transcriptomic analysis of a complementary in vitro microglia model corroborated the retention of a homeostatic-like effector state with URMC-099 treatment that was unique to MLK3/LRRK2 dual inhibition. Conclusions Unilateral injection of low dose AAV-haSyn successfully resulted in a lateralized model of early, progressive PD. Dual inhibition of aberrant MLK3 and LRRK2 activity with once-daily i.p. URMC-099 therapy significantly mitigated the development of PD pathology and progression in an early manifest phenotype. Our results present a potential mechanism of therapeutic action dependent on the dual inhibition of MLK3 and LRRK2. This presents a novel therapeutic modality that may be beneficial to a broad population of etiologic PD patients.

Article.Title: Shikonin alleviates bone cancer pain through suppression of spinal IGF2-associated p38 MAPK signaling
Article.Authors: Ma, z.; Jia, J.; Lu, D.; Wanying, Y.; Xiaogeng, H.; Shuyao, Z.; Xinfang, F.; Jing, Z.; Fan, B.; Longsheng, X.; Ming, Y.
Article.Abstract: Background Bone cancer pain (BCP) is a debilitating complication of advanced cancer that substantially impairs physical function and emotional wellbeing. Current pharmacological treatments often provide incomplete analgesia and may be limited by adverse effects. Shikonin, a bioactive naphthoquinone derived from Lithospermum erythrorhizon, exhibits analgesic and anti inflammatory activities, but its effects and underlying mechanisms in BCP remain unclear. Methods A rat model of BCP was established by intratibial inoculation of luciferase labeled MADB106 cells. The analgesic and behavioral effects of intrathecal Shikonin were evaluated using mechanical and thermal nociceptive assays, CatWalk gait analysis, the open field test (OFT), elevated plus maze (EPM), light/dark box (LDB) test, and rotarod testing. Bioluminescence imaging and hematoxylin eosin staining were used to characterize tumor development and bone pathology. Spinal dorsal horn transcriptomic sequencing was performed to identify candidate molecular pathways. Western blotting, quantitative PCR, and ELISA were used to examine IGF2 associated p38 MAPK signaling and proinflammatory cytokines. The functional involvement of IGF2 and p38 associated signaling was further evaluated using intrathecal IGF2 siRNA and the p38 inhibitor Adezmapimod (SB203580). Results Intrathecal Shikonin produced dose and time dependent antinociceptive effects in BCP rats, with an estimated ED50 of 29.80 g/kg, and did not produce an apparent impairment of rotarod performance. Shikonin also improved gait abnormalities and pain related anxiety like behaviors. Transcriptomic analysis identified Igf2 as a candidate gene responsive to Shikonin treatment, and spinal IGF2 and p38 phosphorylation were increased during BCP development. Shikonin significantly reduced IGF2 expression and p38 phosphorylation in the spinal dorsal horn, accompanied by decreased IL 6, IL 1{beta};, and TNF ; expression in spinal tissue. IGF2 knockdown reproduced the analgesic and behavioral effects of Shikonin and reduced p38 phosphorylation, whereas p38 inhibition reproduced key behavioral effects without a marked change in IGF2 expression. Combined treatment with Shikonin and either IGF2 knockdown or p38 inhibition produced no significant additional behavioral benefit. Conclusion Intrathecal Shikonin alleviates nociceptive hypersensitivity, functional impairment, and pain related anxiety like behaviors in rats with MADB106 induced BCP. The phenocopying and non additive effects of IGF2 knockdown and p38 inhibition support the involvement of an IGF2 associated p38 MAPK signaling axis in the analgesic actions of Shikonin.

Article.Title: Feasible closed-loop stimulation for neural latent dynamics control
Article.Authors: Johnsen, K. A.; Lai, Y.; Vivekanandasarma, L.; Berman, G. J.; Pandarinath, C.; Rozell, C. J.
Article.Abstract: Modern neuroscience benefits from powerful computational and experimental methods for studying neural populations, including latent dynamics models that predict behavior with few dimensions. But despite their explanatory utility, latent factors are seldom targeted explicitly with experimental perturbations, leaving causal relationships to behavior and inferred dynamical landscapes untested. A promising solution is closed-loop, multi-channel optogenetic control, which, when paired with model predictions, could steer neural trajectories in real time--a feat impossible for traditional, hand-designed stimulation. However, because closed-loop latent control has not been demonstrated in vivo, the hardware and software requirements remain unclear--particularly the necessary stimulation dimensionality and how limited resources such as implant volume and bandwidth should be allocated between stimulation and recording capabilities. Preliminary experiments would thus help guide ongoing technological development. As large-scale exploration of these design spaces in vivo is prohibitively expensive, we conducted a high-throughput simulation survey using biophysically grounded spiking neural networks. We found that low-dimensional actuation is sufficient: in the reference configuration, ~20% of the stimulation channels achieved ~85% of peak control performance, far fewer than the number of neurons. Furthermore, allocating channels roughly equally between stimulation and recording optimized behavioral control, whereas pairing many electrodes with a single light source--the prevailing practice in experimental labs--performed poorly. Even without heavily optimizing modeling or control, we obtained >60% tracking error reduction and >90% evoked behavior accuracy on average for optimal channel counts. These results held across extensive parameter variations, suggesting that closed-loop latent control is feasible with accessible channel counts and establishing design principles for future tool development and in vivo experiments.

Article.Title: Identification of Kinome Biomarkers and Therapeutic Rescue in cGMP-Linked Retinal Degeneration
Article.Authors: Topcu Okan, I. C.; Ahmadian, M.; Altay, H. Y.; Pal Singh, S.; Kheirandish, G.; Ozer, S.; Gaillard, P.; Bouffard, R.; Neutzner, A.; Esmen, K.; Tschopp, M.; Lawrence, M.; Diril, M. K.; Paquet-Durand, F.; Agca, C.
Article.Abstract: Inherited retinal degenerations, such as Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP) and Leber's congenital amaurosis (LCA), are major causes of progressive and irreversible vision loss. The large number of genes associated with these disorders makes their clinical and molecular characterization difficult, while systemic biomarkers for disease progression or treatment response remain limited. These challenges were addressed by targeting cGMP-associated mechanisms shared by RP and LCA and integrating systemic biomarker profiling with retinal outcomes. Kinase activity analysis (kinome analysis) in peripheral blood mononuclear cells distinguished healthy and diseased states and captured therapy-associated signatures in rd10 mice treated with LP-CN03, a liposomal formulation of the cGMP analog CN03. This first systemic analysis in a therapeutically responsive animal model highlights kinome analysis as a potential translational readout. Given shared cGMP signaling in RP and AIPL1-associated LCA, LP-CN03's therapeutic potential was further evaluated in a new CRISPR-Cas9-generated Aipl1-/- mouse model. Treatment with LP-CN03 preserved retinal structure and function, as shown by electroretinography, longitudinal optical coherence tomography, fundus imaging, optomotor testing, and photoreceptor-specific gene expression. Together, these findings provide independent in vivo evidence for the neuroprotective effect of LP-CN03 in both cGMP-related RP and LCA, also highlighting the translational value of kinome profiling.

Article.Authors: Sakai, K.; Ishida, H.; Pavlenko, D.; Suehiro, M.; Oshea, T.; Dorning, J.; Sanders, K.; Sanchez, C.; Lopez, A.; Talamas, S.; Boulina, M.; Griswold, A. J.; Akiyama, T.
Article.Abstract: Neuroimmune interactions in the skin coordinate immune defense and somatosensory perception, yet how immune cells shape sensory signaling remains poorly defined. LC activation increases neuronal and behavioral responses to thermal, mechanical, and pruritic stimuli without directly exciting sensory neurons, whereas LC inhibition or ablation selectively reduces pruritogen-evoked itch. Semaphorin 7A sensitized cultured sensory neurons to chloroquine and histamine, and neutralizing semaphorin 7A abolished the increase in chloroquine-evoked scratching produced by LC activation. Its receptor PlexinC1 was expressed by most MrgprA3 pruriceptors and blocking PlexinC1 reduced semaphorin 7A-evoked neuronal responses. Together, these findings identify epidermal LCs as local immune-derived amplifiers that regulate the responsiveness of cutaneous sensory circuits and identify semaphorin 7A as a mediator of LC-induced itch potentiation.

Article.Title: Fatty acid desaturation controls cellular fate decisions between senescence and ferroptosis
Article.Authors: Kuehnemann C.; Jezak S.; Mogck B.; Kura N.; Tariq R.; Che Y.; Vaittinen M.; Siokas I.; Deshpande S.; Guthrie C.; Tan X.; Aimontche E.; Kahn A.; Reifsnyder P.; Lee G.; Majidipur A.; Kung A.; Wang Q.; Jurk D.; Zheng T.; Greenberg A.; Wang X.; Kitazawa K.; Dolnikowski G.; Cheng Y.
Article.Abstract: When subject to damage or stress, cells develop responses in order to maintain tissue homeostasis. Here, we show that senescent cells increase import and membrane levels of multiple polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), but a specific intermediate PUFA, dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid (DGLA, 20:3ω-6), is reduced. Senescent cells manifest additional features associated with ferroptosis, including labile iron and expression of lipoxygenases as well as low-level membrane peroxidation. Oral DGLA supplementation lowers markers of senescence in aged mice and improves age-related functional outcomes. Finally, obese humans with lowered DGLA desaturation rates have lower markers of adipose tissue senescence. Together, our data implicate shifts in PUFA metabolism as a driver of decisions between senescence and ferroptosis.

Article.Title: Subsistence transition preceded population turnover in the eastern Colombian Andes
Article.Authors: Sirak K.; Delgado M.; Triana Vega A.; Rivas S.; Argüello P.; Boada A.; Rivera-Sandoval J.; Peña G.; Langebaek C.; Ospina J.; Archila S.; Torres Orjuela S.; Mejía Cano M.; Rodríguez Saza F.; Barton A.; Callan K.; Curtis E.; Frost T.; Iliev L.; Kearns A.; Kellogg J.; Lawson A.; Qiu L.; Workman J.; Mah M.
Article.Abstract: The Altiplano Cundiboyacense in the eastern Colombian Andes preserves one of the Americas' most continuous archaeological sequences, recording cultural and demographic change. The emergence of Herrera culture ∼2,200 BP coincided with a sharp genetic break by ∼2,000 BP, which reflects migration by people descended from admixture ∼4,000 BP between groups with Chibchan- and Amazonian-Andean-related ancestries. Herrera and Muisca Period individuals show north-south genetic substructure paralleling archaeological differentiation.

Article.Title: Convergent genomic evolution of human gut bacteria along an industrialization gradient
Article.Authors: Rühlemann M.; Ma Y.; Szánthó L.; Waschina S.; Moitinho-Silva L.; Mews L.; Faus-Camarena J.; Jebens H.; Costa J.; Juimo V.; Fezeu A.; Agyei A.; Afihene M.; Asibey S.; Awuku Y.; Duah A.; Nartey Y.; Ibrahim F.; Lim Y.; Tan M.; Onyekwere C.; Rusine J.; Mwikarago I.; Baines J.; Franke A.

Leveraging isolate genomes from multiple species, we find that strains from industrialized hosts experience an expansion of proteome size and harbor greater pangenome fluidity, driven by recent HGT events. Gene- and variant-level analyses reveal convergent patterns of lifestyle-specific adaptation in functions that are critical for ecological adaptation, such as the stress response, cell-envelope remodeling, and central metabolism. Our results demonstrate that industrialization drives convergent genome evolution in gut bacteria, providing a framework for understanding the mechanisms of microbial adaptation to rapidly changing human environments.

Article.Title: Industrialization drives convergent microbiome and host physiological shifts in the human metaorganism
Article.Authors: Poyet M.; Rühlemann M.; Schaan A.; Ma Y.; Moitinho-Silva L.; Wacker E.; Jebens H.; Patel L.; Nguyen L.; Zimmer A.; Plichta D.; McDonald D.; Stevens C.; Agyei A.; Afihene M.; Asibey S.; Awuku Y.; Badiane A.; Corzett C.; Deme A.; Dominguez-Rodrigo M.; Duah A.; Fezeu A.; Froment A.; Gibbons S.
Article.Abstract: Understanding how industrialization reshapes the human metaorganism requires integrating microbiome ecology with host physiology across globally diverse populations. Here, we generate multivariate data from the Global Microbiome Conservancy cohort, including gut microbiome, immunoglobulin A (IgA) sequencing, host genotyping, diet, lifestyle, and fecal biomarker profiles, to investigate host-microbiome interactions across gradients of industrialization and geography. We show that industrialization is associated with homogenized microbial compositions, reduced microbial diversity, and lower community stability, independent of host confounders. We further show that industrialization is linked to elevated markers of gut stress, increased IgA secretion, and altered patterns of IgA-bacteria interactions. Finally, we show that microbiome-based disease predictors trained on industrialized populations are uninformative in less industrialized cohorts, highlighting limited cross-population transferability. Together, our results reveal coordinated restructuring of the microbial ecosystem and host physiology and emphasize the need for inclusive, globally representative data to improve translational microbiome applications across diverse human populations.

Article.Title: TECR palmitoylation triggers a necrotic cell death program driving acute liver injury
Article.Authors: Ru X.; Li X.; Wu Z.; Ren X.; Zong Y.; Cui Y.; Li Y.; Ding Z.; Wang X.; Zhang Z.
Article.Abstract: Acute liver injury caused by drug toxicity or immune activation remains a major clinical challenge with limited mechanistic understanding and few effective therapies. Here, we identify a previously unrecognized form of regulated cell death driven by palmitoylation of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-resident enzyme trans-2,3-enoyl-coenzyme A (CoA) reductase (TECR). We show that multi-site palmitoylation of TECR, redundantly catalyzed by the palmitoyl acyltransferases ZDHHC5 and ZDHHC2 and dynamically reversed by the depalmitoylase ABHD10, activates PERK-dependent ER stress signaling to trigger cell death. This cell death pathway is a TECR-dependent, palmitoylation-induced, ER stress-mediated necrotic cell death program (TPNCD). TPNCD contributes to liver injury in mouse models of acetaminophen- and concanavalin A-induced hepatotoxicity and is attenuated by hepatocyte-specific TECR ablation or by pharmacological inhibition of palmitoylation or ER stress signaling. Together, these findings establish TPNCD as a distinct, necrotic cell death pathway underlying acute liver injury and highlight new therapeutic entry points for hepatoprotection.

Article.Title: CRISPR mutagenesis of the MYC locus reveals a druggable ultraconserved RNA element
Article.Authors: Shi P.; Yang F.; FNU T.; Huang W.; Xing L.; Alam S.; Dai W.; Aparicio A.; Kalicki C.; Trehan A.; Murphy M.; Rotlevi E.; Iyer P.; Wang L.; Zaccara S.; Reilly M.; Liao Y.; Zhang C.; Que J.; Wu X.

Steric-blocking antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting this element selectively eliminate diverse MYC-dependent cancer cells and inhibit growth of patient-derived tumor organoids. Article.Title: In Vivo CRISPR Base Editing of ANGPTL3 for Durable Lipid Lowering
Article.Authors: Mizoguchi T.; DeNizio J.; Chadwick A.; Mazzola A.; Brown M.; Mishra S.; Damle M.; Matsumoto Y.; Neang V.; Garrity R.; Mantri M.; Olorife J.; Hsu H.; Peshdary V.; Shabani E.; Ganey J.; Santos R.; Federico A.; Garcia S.; Hao P.; Wu Y.; Glass Z.; Kasiewicz L.; Summers C.; Sanjeev A.
Article.Abstract: Circulating concentrations of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and triglyceride-rich lipoproteins are leading risk factors for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease1. Despite several approved lipid-lowering medications, most patients fail to achieve target lipid levels under the chronic care treatment model2,3. Here, we describe a potential single-course treatment in which an infusion of guide RNA and mRNA encoding a CRISPR adenine base editor-encapsulated within a GalNAc-lipid nanoparticle-leads to durable, liver-selective inactivation of angiopoietin-like 3 (ANGPTL3), a known driver of increased LDL-C and triglyceride concentrations. Analyses in human liver cells in vitro confirmed that the base editor introduces a DNA base-pair change at the target ANGPTL3 locus with no detectable off-target editing at any of approximately 3000 candidate sites or treatment-related structural variants. Targeted ANGPTL3 inactivation in nonhuman primates was well-tolerated and led to a > 90% mean reduction in circulating ANGPTL3 protein, with durability confirmed out to 3 years following a single dose. In mouse and nonhuman primate models of hyperlipidemia, gene inactivation was associated with reductions of approximately 40 to 50% in LDL-C and 50 to 70% in triglycerides. These results provided the scientific foundation for initiation of an ongoing first-in-human clinical trial in patients with refractory hyperlipidemia syndromes.

Article.Title: Opportunistically Detecting Signs of Hypertension on a Consumer Smartwatch
Article.Authors: Di Achille P.; Cai L.; Wu J.; Gao M.; Daryani B.; Wang J.; Khanna U.; Ko H.; Pathak A.; Malhotra M.; Patel S.; Shreibati J.; Juraschek S.; Rudrapatna P.; Thompson M.; Poh M.
Article.Abstract: Hypertension is a silent killer, with over half of affected adults unaware of their condition1,2. This lack of awareness is a major concern, as early intervention is critical for preventing major adverse cardiovascular events3,4. Here we show that applying artificial intelligence (AI) to multimodal waveforms (photoplethysmography and accelerometry) recorded using a widely available consumer smartwatch (AI-PPG-ACC-HTN), without any cuff calibration, can detect hypertension with accuracy levels comparable to traditional cuffed blood pressure (BP) devices in the existing clinical framework. We validated AI-PPG-ACC-HTN in a prospective, multicenter study of 196 diverse participants free from known cardiovascular disease and antihypertensive medication against gold-standard 24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring. Over seven days of real-world monitoring, AI-PPG-ACC-HTN detected hypertension with a sensitivity of 65.8% (95% CI, 54.0%-76.3%), specificity of 90.0% (95% CI, 83.2%-94.7%), and positive predictive value (PPV) of 80.6% (95% CI, 68.6%-89.6%). In comparison, initial office BP screening achieved a sensitivity of 55.3% (95% CI, 43.4%-66.7%), specificity of 90.0% (95% CI, 83.2%-94.7%) and PPV of 77.8% (95% CI, 64.4%-88.0%). These results highlight an opportunity for consumer smartwatches to facilitate population-level opportunistic hypertension screening by prompting at-risk individuals toward clinical assessment and confirmatory diagnosis using established cuff-based methodologies, offering an accessible tool to address this major public health challenge.

Article.Title: Hydrogen Derivatives Enable Cost-Effective Carbon Neutrality in China
Article.Authors: Chen X.; Guo X.; Yang X.; Li J.; McElroy M.
Article.Abstract: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change recommended 1.5°C carbon reduction target, requiring powerful enforcement from major economies. China, the largest CO2 emitter, is facing severe difficulties for both variable renewable accommodation and decarbonization of hard-to-abate sectors. Hydrogen, as a critical green energy carrier bridging renewable to end-users, faces significant obstacles in real-world deployment such as costly transportation, storage and fuel-cell adoption. Affordable and coordinated hydrogen deployment plan to accelerate the carbon-neutral transition remains ambiguous. Here, we present cost-effective carbon-neutral transition pathways for entire energy economy of China emphasizing the significant role of hydrogen and derivatives as green energy carriers, considering high-resolution renewable deployments, hourly power system operations in 29 provincial regions, over 46,000 rail/road/marine/pipeline transfer routing of hydrogen derivatives, process-level fuel adoption strategies in all end-use sectors. Results show that incorporating hydrogen and derivatives can reduce the overall transition cost by $ 10.7 trillion compared with renewable and electrification pathways, achieving negative carbon abatement costs ($-6.15/ton), eliminating external oil import expenses, equivalent to over 50% of China trade surplus (2023 level)1, significantly boosting employment and economic growth. Hydrogen derivative based transition pathway offers a vital direction for affordable and secure decarbonization for China and beyond under volatile international energy markets.

Article.Title: Observation of prethermal dynamical phase transitions and resonant melting
Article.Authors: Darbha S.; Khudorozhkov A.; L. S. Lopes P.; Liu F.; Rrapaj E.; Balewski J.; Hamdan M.; Dolgirev P.; Schuckert A.; Klymko K.; Wang S.; Lukin M.; Camps D.; Kornjača M.
Article.Abstract: The dynamics of isolated quantum systems following a sudden quench has a central role in many areas of material science, high-energy physics and quantum chemistry1-4. Such far-from-equilibrium quantum dynamics-which features complex phenomena with implications for thermalization, non-equilibrium phase transitions and Floquet phase engineering5-8-is challenging to study numerically, in particular, in high-dimensional systems9,10. Here we use a programmable neutral-atom quantum simulator11 to systematically explore quench dynamics in spin models with up to 180 qubits. By initializing the system in a product state and performing quenches across a broad parameter space, we discover several stable, qualitatively distinct dynamical regimes. We trace their robustness to Floquet-like prethermal steady states8 that are stabilized over exponentially long emergent timescales by strong dynamical constraints. We further observe sharp peaks in the dynamical response that are quantitatively explained by the structured melting of prethermalization through resonances. In two dimensions, we uncover a prethermally driven, first-order dynamical phase transition linked to the proliferation of Néel-order defects6,12, and probe it quantitatively using a generalized Clausius-Clapeyron test. Together, these results establish a programmable route to high-energy prethermal phase structure: long-lived dynamical phases, their resonant breakdown and a first-order dynamical phase transition that is not inherited from the equilibrium phase boundaries.

Article.Title: Synergy in viral–bacterial co-infection expedites algal bloom demise
Article.Authors: Kuhlisch C.; Soffer E.; Raina J.; Tadmor G.; Nir-Zadock T.; Barak-Gavish N.; Schleyer G.; Joffe N.; Nussbaum I.; Clerc E.; Stocker R.; Schatz D.; Zeevi D.; Vardi A.
Article.Abstract: Algal bloom demise, often caused by viruses, is a major driver of carbon cycling in the surface ocean1,2. However, although blooms collapse synchronously, fewer than 30% of algal cells are actively infected by viruses3, indicating the involvement of additional mortality agents. Here we quantified tripartite interactions within a synthetic community composed of the abundant coccolithophore Gephyrocapsa huxleyi, bacteria and viruses isolated during a bloom. We found that bacteria significantly enhanced virus-induced algal mortality in G. huxleyi as well as in three other globally widespread microalgae. We quantified this interaction using two new metrics: the synergy index, which measures viral-bacterial interaction strength, and the benefit index, which assesses changes in bacterial fitness. We identified Alteromonas bacteria as drivers of viral-bacterial co-infection, with consistently high synergy index and benefit index. We found that during algal blooms, Alteromonas displayed high chemoattraction towards infected cell extracts, accumulated in aggregates derived from bloom demise, and increased in abundance during oceanic bloom collapse. Viral-bacterial synergy represents a previously unrecognized mortality agent that controls bloom termination, modulating the balance between the carbon-recycling viral shunt and the carbon-exporting viral shuttle pathways, which influence global carbon cycling4-6.

Article.Title: Aggression experience and observation drive shared behavioural and neural changes
Article.Authors: Iravedra-García J.; Guthman E.; Tsin D.; Cherepanova P.; Cuturela L.; Ocasio-Arce E.; Pillow J.; Falkner A.
Article.Abstract: The ability to observe the social behaviour of others and use observed information to bias future action is a fundamental building block of social cognition1-3. Aggression observation activates hypothalamic neurons relevant for aggression control4,5, but whether observation and experience engage common circuit mechanisms that promote a new shared behavioural policy is unclear. Here we develop a strategy to perform large-scale cell-type-specific recordings across subcortical networks for social behaviour generation and learning. We record longitudinally while animals train through direct aggression experience or observation, then probe shared differences in behaviour and neural activity in a novel aggression context. After training, we detect unique signatures of a shared adaptive behavioural strategy that is absent in animals without training. During aggression observation, observed behaviour recruits widespread activation across subcortical networks for behavioural generation and mimics activity evoked by experienced behaviour, and shared neural changes persist into the novel aggression context. Multiregion modelling reveals shared changes to a core aggression network across both experience and observation, including a widespread reduction in inhibition, which we find is necessary for adaptive behavioural change. Together, this demonstrates that experience-like activity during aggression observation can recruit a shared inhibitory plasticity mechanism that biases behaviour toward adaptive proactive behavioural strategies.

Article.Title: Twist-angle-dependent quantum phase diagrams in moiré bilayer MoTe2
Article.Authors: Sun Z.; Xu F.; Li J.; Jiang Y.; Gao J.; Xu C.; Jia T.; Cheng K.; Wang S.; Tian W.; Zhang J.; Watanabe K.; Taniguchi T.; Jia J.; Jiang S.; Zhang Y.; Zhang Y.; Lei S.; Liu X.; Li T.
Article.Abstract: Two-dimensional semiconducting moiré superlattices provide a highly tunable platform for investigating strongly correlated and topological quantum phases1-5. As a prototypical example, twisted bilayer MoTe2 (tMoTe2) has been shown to host fractional topological phases at zero magnetic field6-20. However, their evolution with twist angle and competition with other correlated quantum states remain largely unexplored. Here we report a systematic transport study of twist-angle-dependent phase diagrams in tMoTe2 across a range of 3.79°-5.76°, revealing an evolution from valley-polarized, fractional topological states to valley-degenerate correlated states and superconductivity. At relatively small twist angles, partially filled Chern bands of tMoTe2 host fractional quantum anomalous Hall states following the Jain sequence, together with signatures of an anomalous composite Fermi liquid at moiré hole filling factor νh = 1/2. Increasing twist angle progressively suppresses fractional topological phases and reconstructs the half-filled Chern band into symmetry-breaking integer Chern insulating states. At νh = 1, we observe a transition from robust integer quantum anomalous Hall insulators at small angles to displacement-field-tuned, topologically trivial correlated insulators at larger angles. At twist angles above approximately 5.6°, superconductivity emerges adjacent to the νh = 1 correlated insulator, with a phase diagram closely resembling that recently reported in twisted bilayer WSe2 (refs. 21-24). Our results indicate a unified twist-angle-driven phase evolution linking fractional topology, symmetry breaking, magnetic order and superconductivity, providing new insight into the emergent quantum phenomena in moiré systems.

Article.Title: Comprehensive mapping of essential-gene interactions in M. tuberculosis
Article.Authors: Kresse I.; Sayegh N.; Munsamy-Govender V.; Na A.; Nitz S.; Ozakman Y.; Bosch B.; Gonzalez Behn-Eschenburg S.; Poulton N.; Reddy A.; Wallach J.; Aguilera Olvera R.; Castro A.; Kim H.; Wong A.; Tornow S.; Bueler S.; Law W.; Glickman M.; Rubinstein J.; Schnappinger D.; DeJesus M.; Rock J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Mycobacterium tuberculosis , the causative agent of tuberculosis, remains the world’s deadliest pathogen 1 . Despite intensive study, many of its genes remain uncharacterized, which limits the insight that can be gained into tuberculosis biology and constrains drug development. Genetic interaction (GI) mapping is a powerful strategy to define functional relationships between genes by quantifying how the phenotypic effects of combined perturbations deviate from expectations based on single-gene perturbations 2,3 . Here we develop a dual-sgRNA CRISPR-interference platform that enables high-throughput GI mapping in mycobacteria. We address key technical challenges in library construction and data interpretation by incorporating unique barcodes for each sgRNA pair and implementing a robust statistical pipeline for GI detection. Focusing on essential genes, we generate comprehensive GI maps in the model mycobacterium Mycobacterium smegmatis and the pathogen M. tuberculosis . These maps recapitulate known biology, uncover thousands of previously unrecognized interactions and identify functional connections between essential genes and drug targets. By generating AlphaFold3-based protein–protein interaction predictions 4 for all gene pairs in our GI maps, we show that a subset of GIs is likely to reflect underlying physical associations. Validation of selected GIs confirms both novel biological relationships and opportunities for synergistic targeting. Overall, this work establishes a generalizable framework for dual-gene perturbation and defines the architecture of essential-gene networks in mycobacteria, advancing both our understanding of tuberculosis biology and the rational design of combination therapies.

Article.Title: Cancer-selective gene circuits via intrinsic ribosomal frameshifting
Article.Authors: Wang Q.; Chen A.; Liu Y.; Yu X.; Zhang H.; Yu Y.; Chen P.; Zhang Y.; Chan F.; Gao X.; Mao Y.

Taking advantage of this frameshifting-permissive state in cancer cells, we engineered a frameshifting-activated synthetic therapeutic circuit (FAST) that conditionally expresses the pyroptotic effector gasdermin D. FAST is activated across diverse cancer cell types, inducing potent and selective pyroptosis, while sparing normal tissues from detectable toxicity. Article.Title: An AI-native experimental laboratory for autonomous biomolecular operations
Article.Authors: Wu M.; Wang Z.; Wang J.; Dong Z.; Yang J.; Li Q.; Huang T.; Zhang C.; Song P.; Zhao L.; Li M.; Zuo X.; Wang F.; Fan C.; Chen H.
Article.Abstract: Developing artificial intelligence (AI)-native experimental laboratories for autonomous scientific exploration with minimal human intervention represents a long-standing goal. Although autonomous experimental systems are emerging1-4, especially in chemical and materials science, they remain largely confined to domains with singular objectives, well-defined workflows and simple instrumentation. This limitation may reflect an 'add-on' architecture that uses AI as a task-specific tool rather than providing it with a global understanding of experiments, especially under engineering-oriented circumstances. Here we present AutoDNA, an AI-native autonomous biomolecular engineering laboratory targeting multi-objective experiments across diverse instruments. Through the co-design of models, experiments and instruments, AutoDNA realizes the co-evolution of AI and the automation system within an end-to-end multi-user framework. The system autonomously orchestrates over 20 types of instruments across more than 11,000 steps to execute core nucleic acid operations including synthesis, transcription, amplification and sequencing, while human intervention is limited to hardware maintenance tasks, such as reagent and labware replenishment. Across four representative applications, AutoDNA matched expert-optimized enzymatic DNA synthesis yields, accelerated concurrent protocol execution by 3.2-fold, completed an end-to-end DNA data storage cycle with exact recovery of the original digital content, and identified and validated a clinically detected KRAS G13D mutation. Article.Title: The neural basis of flavour–nutrient learning
Article.Authors: Grove J.; Hakimi A.; Li Q.; Zhang J.; Backes H.; Kuzmanovic B.; Choi J.; Ubadiah V.; Qiu L.; Liu Z.; Small D.; Tittgemeyer M.; Knight Z.

For example, the nutrient content of food is first estimated in the mouth, in the form of flavour, and then it is measured again through slower signals from the gut. How these signals from the mouth and gut are integrated to drive learning is unclear. Here we identify a dopamine (DA) pathway that enables learning about the nutrient content of food. We show that DA neurons in the ventral tegmental area are necessary for associating nutrients with flavours, and that post-ingestive nutrients trigger DA release selectively in a small region of the anterior basolateral amygdala (BLA) but not in canonical DA targets in striatum. This nutrient-triggered DA release occurs preferentially in the left BLA in mice, and this same structure is preferentially activated by post-ingestive nutrients in humans. Article.Authors: Sun Y.; Robles R.; Linker T.; Chen Y.; Cesar D.; Chollet M.; Driver T.; Esposito V.; Gee C.; Guo V.; Ghimire S.; Halavanau A.; Ichii Y.; Inoue I.; Li H.; Nakahara K.; Lutman A.; Ornelas-Skarin C.; Osaka T.; OTool S.; Pasquinilli H.; Reis D.; Sato T.; Song S.; Sudar N.

Here, building on a broadband X-ray split-delay line, we establish metrology of attosecond hard X-ray pulses. Article.Abstract: Abstract Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is highly heritable, and mutations in hundreds of genes have been implicated as individually rare causes of ASD 1–3 . Article.Authors: de Jong G.; Memi F.; Gracia T.; Lazareva O.; Gould O.; Solomou G.; Aivazidis A.; Dave M.; Zhang Q.; Jensen M.; Rifaioglu A.; Barros-Silva J.; Eckert S.; Zhou D.; Wood Y.; Tuck E.; Er S.; Rademaker K.; Petryszak R.; Marshall H.; Roberts K.; Trinh A.; Rai S.; Shaw T.; Oszlanczi A.

Article.Authors: Gao G.; Jiang C.; Wu W.; Kan J.; Guo Y.; Jayakodi M.; An C.; Sun M.; Cheng C.; Feng J.; Wang J.; Liu J.; Li X.; Camara A.; Xu X.; Yang H.; Zeng Y.; Shen H.; Zhou W.; Zhang J.; Stein N.; Mascher M.; Yang P.

Article.Abstract: RNA language models have achieved strong performance across diverse downstream tasks by leveraging large-scale sequence data. Higher-order weaving (≥3 axes) of nonlinear building blocks is expected to produce intriguing architectures and bring new and unforeseen functions to the resulting materials; however, their construction and property investigation remain underexplored. Article.Authors: Wang D.; Goumagias A.; Andreu-Sánchez S.; Peng H.; Ruiz-Moreno A.; Zhernakova D.; Krempel T.; Zhang Y.; Wu J.; Kurilshikov A.; Gacesa R.; Temba G.; Kullaya V.; N/A N/A.; N/A N/A.; Xavier R.; de Mast Q.; Joosten L.; Riksen N.; Rutten J.; Netea M.; Sanna S.; Wijmenga C.; Weersma R.; Zhernakova A.

Article.Abstract: Abstract The vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) ligand and its main receptor VEGFR2 are considered to be essential for endothelial differentiation, proliferation, sprouting and survival 1 . Blood vessels cannot form in growing embryos or tissues when VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling is compromised in all cells 2,3 . The anti-VEGF antibody, which can block angiogenesis in cancer, wound healing or ischaemic diseases, is among the most widely used antibodies in the clinic. These included significant endothelial venousization and upregulation of ligands for VEGFR1 and VEGFR3. VEGFR1 only partially compensated for VEGFR2 loss in capillary ECs, whereas VEGFR3 compensated only in arterial ECs. Loss of the three VEGF receptors did not compromise venous growth. Notably, loss of the master regulator of venous development, NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII), significantly compromised expansion of Vegfr2 KO ECs. Article.Title: Ecological and social cues orchestrate concerted courtship in Drosophila
Article.Authors: Brand P.; Keller K.; Coleman R.; Eghbali N.; Zylka S.; Prieto-Godino L.; Ruta V.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Mating decisions are often attributed to the sensory signalling between prospective sexual partners. Yet these interactions are also shaped by the broader environmental context in which they unfold, to appropriately align sexual arousal with reproductive opportunities 1–6 . Here we show that in Drosophila erecta mating is strictly contingent on the ecological and social environment generated as flies densely aggregate in groups on a food patch. We find that food volatiles directly promote male sexual arousal, triggering individuals to sample and pursue potential mates, giving rise to dynamic interactions across the group. The ensuing visual motion transforms each male’s visual field, which in turn further amplifies his arousal, generating a multisensory feedback loop that coordinately promotes courtship across individuals. D. erecta ’s strict dependence on environmental cues appears latent in related species, such as Drosophila melanogaster , where food odour can promote arousal 7 but is dispensable for vigorous courtship. Comparative circuit analyses show that species-specific thresholds for sexual arousal reflect variation in how olfactory input modulates conserved nodes controlling courtship drive, rendering food volatiles a strict sensory gate only in D. erecta . Together, our findings highlight how environmental cues not directly tied to sexual signalling can profoundly influence reproductive behaviour and reorganize the social landscape to ensure mating occurs in contexts where reproductive opportunities are abundant.

Article.Authors: Dhungana S.; Flament N.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The Great Unconformity marks a globally extensive erosive surface linked to climatic shifts 1 and environmental transitions 2 that preceded the Cambrian explosion of life. The processes proposed to explain the formation of the Great Unconformity include glacial erosion during the Snowball Earth 1,3,4 , rifting and plume activity 5–7 , sea-level fall 8 and mantle-driven dynamic topography 6,9–11 . However, the dynamics of these processes have not been tested. Here we show that continental-scale uplift and subsidence associated with long-wavelength dynamic topography 12 due to mantle convection drove the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity. Our models predict prolonged continental-scale Neoproterozoic uplift and long-term Phanerozoic subsidence for Laurentia, Baltica and North China. This vertical motion scenario is ideal for the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity, which is a first-order surface expression of deep Earth processes. The predicted prolonged continental uplift throughout Cryogenian times would have resulted in marked erosion due to the action of glaciers 13 . The large area of Laurentia and limited deformation at its margins explain why the Great Unconformity is best preserved and documented there. Our models predict cycles of dynamic topography that are broadly reflected in preserved sediment volume across continents 1,14 , and open new avenues for understanding the environments of Cambrian animal diversification.
