Article.Title: Structural basis of ligand recognition and gating in mosquito IRs
Article.Authors: Xu L.; Wang X.; Quan X.; Ferguson S.; Liu D.; Chen J.; Wang S.; Liang S.; Huang G.; Huang K.; Liu F.; Pan X.
Article.Abstract: Ionotropic receptors (IRs) are essential for insect olfaction, enabling the detection of carboxylic acids, amines, moisture, and temperature cues that mediate critical behaviors, including mosquito host-seeking 1,2. However, the structural mechanisms underlying ligand specificity and channel activation in these receptors remain unclear. Here, we report cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures and functional validation of the IR8a-IR75k complex from the malaria mosquito Anopheles stephensi, a carboxylic acid detector, captured in four states: the ligand-free full-length closed form (apo state), the ligand induced full-length open state, and the nonanoic acid (NA)- and octanoic acid (OA)-bound extracellular domains. These structures reveal a dynamic ligand-binding pocket in IR75k, in which specificity is determined by alkyl chain length and carboxylate geometry. Ligand binding triggers closure of IR75k's bilobed ligand binding domain (LBD), and this conformational change propagates through conserved mechanical linkers to the transmembrane domain (TMD), functioning as a molecular lever that dilates the pore via outward displacement of transmembrane helices. This gating mechanism was further corroborated by molecular dynamics simulations and electrophysiology. These insights provide an atomic resolution view of IR mediated host detection in mosquitoes and establish a foundation for the rational design of next generation mosquito control strategies targeting host-seeking behavior.

Article.Title: Catalytic transfer of carbon atoms enables spirofusion of C–C σ-bonds
Article.Authors: Fujimoto H.; Mizutani M.; Imachi K.; Nishioka T.; Ikeda R.; Tobisu M.
Article.Abstract: Spirocyclic frameworks, polycyclic structures in which two rings share a single carbon atom, constitute key structural motifs across diverse areas, including optoelectronic and hole-transporting materials1-3, ligand design for coordination complexes4-6, and numerous natural products7. In a spiro skeleton, the two molecular units adopt an orthogonal arrangement, generating a rigid three-dimensional (3D) architecture. Introducing a single carbon atom to join two components to form the spiro centre therefore represents a direct strategy for constructing such frameworks. Previous carbon-atom-transfer approaches have largely relied on π-bond reactivity, whereas controlled insertion of a carbon atom into C-C σ-bonds remains challenging8-11. Here we report a rhodium-catalysed spiro-carbon-atom insertion reaction that converts biphenylene substrates into spirocyclic structures through sequential C-C bond activation. Using N-isocyanoiminophosphorane (PINC)12-14 as an atomic carbon equivalent, the reaction forms four new C-C bonds at a spiro centre. The transformation enables both homo- and cross-spirofusion of biphenylenes and can be extended to reactions combining σ- and π-bond activation. These results establish a catalytic strategy for constructing structurally complex spirocyclic frameworks through C-C σ-bond activation, with a single carbon atom serving as a central linchpin.

Article.Title: Atomic-scale spin sensing of a 2D d-wave altermagnet via helical tunneling
Article.Authors: Wang Z.; Yu S.; Cheng X.; Xiao X.; Ma W.; Ma Y.; Quan F.; Song H.; Zhang K.; Zhang Y.; Liu W.; Yadav P.; Sheng H.; Wang A.; Shi X.; Wang Z.; Niu Q.; Gao Y.; Xiang B.; Liu J.; Wang Z.; Chen X.
Article.Abstract: Altermagnets simultaneously possess momentum-dependent nonrelativistic spin splitting and zero net magnetization (1-6). Their defining crystalline symmetry connects opposite-spin sublattices in real space and imposes alternating spin polarization on the symmetry-related electronic states in momentum space (1-3). Identifying such an order and its associated spin response therefore calls for atomic-scale spin-sensitive measurements in both real and momentum space, an experimental milestone yet to be achieved. Here we show that the helical edge modes of the higher-order topological insulator α-Bi4Br4 can serve as a spin-selective scanning tunnelling microscopy probe of the two-dimensional d-wave altermagnetic order in the surface layer of KV2Se2O. Atomically registered mapping reveals the spatial relationship between the two V sublattices and a density-wave lattice modulation, as well as real-space patterns consistent with the checkerboard antiferromagnetic order. Field-dependent spectroscopy further finds opposite energy shifts of the unidirectional quasiparticle excitations extending along two orthogonal crystal axes and a predominantly out-of-plane magnetic response. In momentum space, spin-sensitive quasiparticle interference imaging reveals a bias-reversing d-wave anisotropy between the symmetry-paired X and Y valleys. These results provide converging evidence for two-dimensional d-wave altermagnetism on the surface of KV2Se2O and demonstrate helical-edge-mode tunnelling as a route for atomic-scale spin sensing in quantum materials.

Article.Title: Selective, Catalytic Oxidation of Polyethylene Surfaces
Article.Authors: Woroch C.; Klivansky L.; McCarthy D.; Miao H.; Fink Z.; Zuo X.; Guthrie C.; Wang C.; Helms B.; Hartwig J.
Article.Abstract: Polyethylene (PE) accounts for more than a quarter of all plastic produced, owing to its exceptional material properties and scalable production.1 However, pristine PE lacks critical properties, such as adhesion, that are needed for many additional commercial applications.2 Selective post-polymerization functionalization of PE can impart properties that are absent in the pristine polymer, but global functionalization in a uniform medium perturbs bulk properties.3-5 Here, we demonstrate catalytic functionalization of solid PE at a solid-liquid interface. The resulting materials possess enhanced surface properties while maintaining bulk properties, such as melting temperature or tensile strength. The method selectively converts methylene units to ketones with just 0.001 mol% iron catalyst below 80 °C with inexpensive oxidants. PE functionalized at the solid-liquid interface adheres to polar surfaces up to 90-fold more strongly than does pristine PE and up to 4-fold more strongly than does PE functionalized in a uniform medium at a comparable level. We demonstrate that the surface ketones can be modified to enhance adhesive strength further and that the augmented surface properties persist for longer than they do after other unselective functionalizations. Thus, selective C-H bond functionalization at the solid-liquid interface produces materials inaccessible by bulk functionalization methods or by traditional surface oxidations.

Article.Title: Antiviral immunity via telomerase-like reverse transcription in bacteria
Article.Authors: Tang S.; Ramirez J.; He Q.; Rodríguez Mestre M.; Wiegand T.; Zhang D.; Wang M.; Lampe G.; Wang J.; Ma Y.; Jovanovic M.; Pinilla-Redondo R.; Fernández I.; Sternberg S.
Article.Abstract: Defense-associated reverse transcriptases (DRTs) employ diverse and distinctive mechanisms of cDNA synthesis to protect bacteria against viral infection1. However, the functions and mechanisms of many DRTs remain unknown2. Here we identify a new antiviral defense system, DRT10, that associates with a noncoding RNA (ncRNA) to catalyze processive, protein-primed synthesis of tandem-repeat DNA. Reverse transcription is templated by a defined ncRNA region with a characteristic sequence pattern and template boundary elements, both of which are conserved and essential for DNA repeat addition. Cryo-EM reconstructions reveal an unanticipated 2:1 architecture, wherein two RT monomers bind opposite sides of a pseudo-symmetric ncRNA. Biochemical experiments further demonstrate that each RT monomer reverse transcribes the template encoded on its respective side of the ncRNA, but only one generates the long repetitive product, whose template is defined by the distance between two flanking stem-loop anchors. This mode of iterative, boundary-delimited cDNA synthesis exhibits direct parallels to the mechanism of telomeric repeat addition by eukaryotic telomerase, and phylogenetic analyses of RTs across domains of life place telomerase in a monophyletic clade with the DRT family, suggesting a common origin for their DNA polymerization activities. Together with earlier studies of DRT2, DRT3, and DRT93-5, our findings identify a conserved mechanistic logic underlying RNA-templated DNA repeat addition across diverse DRTs, despite vastly different architectural solutions, and expand the repertoire of reverse transcription-based strategies for antiviral immunity in bacteria.

Article.Title: Melting and resistivity of iron at Earth core conditions using pulsed Joule heating
Article.Authors: Geballe Z.; Yang J.; Dobrosavljevic V.; Miozzi F.; Sime N.; Vitale S.; Driscoll P.; van Keken P.; Tappero R.; Liu W.; Chariton S.; Prakapenka V.; Meng Y.; Walter M.
Article.Abstract: The melting temperature and electrical resistivity of iron at high pressure are essential for understanding Earth’s core. Here we use a new high-pressure method – microsecond pulsed Joule heating in diamond anvil cells – to identify melting and measure resistivity of solid and liquid iron. More than 300 reproducible melting measurements indicate a surprisingly shallow melting curve, reaching 6 K/GPa and 4160 ± 80 K at 200 GPa. Extrapolating in pressure and iron alloy composition, and combining with our 76 μ Ω cm measurement of liquid iron’s resistivity, we infer a relatively cold core-mantle boundary (3430 K) with a low adiabatic outer core heat flow (9.8 TW). This suggests thermal convection alone could have powered the geodynamo prior to inner core formation and that today’s lowermost mantle is fully solid.

Article.Title: Equivalence of pseudogap and pairing energy in a cuprate high-temperature superconductor
Article.Authors: Niu J.; Larrazabal M.; Gozlinski T.; Sato Y.; Bastiaans K.; Benschop T.; Ge J.; Blanter Y.; Gu G.; Swart I.; Allan M.
Article.Abstract: The pseudogap stands out in the phase diagram of the cuprate high-temperature superconductors because its origin and relationship to superconductivity remain elusive. The origin of the pseudogap has been debated, with competing hypotheses attributing it to preformed electron pairs or local order, such as charge density waves. We present unambiguous evidence supporting the pairing scenario, using local shot-noise spectroscopy measurements in Bi 2 Sr 2 CaCu 2 O 8+δ . Our data demonstrate that the pseudogap energy coincides with the onset of electron pairing and is spatially heterogeneous with values reaching up to 70 milli–electron volts. Our results exclude a pure local order origin of the pseudogap, link the pseudogap to Cooper pair formation, and suggest that the limiting factor for higher critical temperature in cuprates is phase coherence.

Article.Title: Discovering molecular modulators with nanoswitch screening
Article.Authors: Hansen C.; Lipstein M.; Erlandson S.; Schwalbe T.; Bernier S.; Gmeiner P.; Kruse A.; Wong W.
Article.Abstract: Molecules that modulate protein-protein interactions, including through ternary complex formation, have been established as key therapeutics. Yet they can be challenging to discover, as standard screening approaches often lack throughput or fail to directly assay multibody interactions. We addressed this by combining DNA nanoswitch–based selection of nucleotide-encoded libraries with next-generation sequencing to create FIND (Functional Interaction–based Nanoswitch Discovery), which enables ultrahigh-throughput discovery of compounds that induce or increase protein-protein interactions. We demonstrate FIND by discovering nanobodies that stabilize the interaction between angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 and the receptor-binding domain of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 and by discovering agonists of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor gamma from a DNA-barcoded small-molecule library. By enabling rapid discovery of molecular modulators, FIND could lead to new therapeutics across many conditions.

Article.Title: Echoes of the Anthropocene: Noise pollution as a global threat
Article.Authors: Kunc H.; Schmidt R.
Article.Abstract: Anthropogenic noise is a rapidly expanding global pollutant, but its effects across biological levels from individuals to ecosystems remain unquantified. We conducted phylogenetically controlled meta-analyses of 214 experimental studies on 177 aquatic and terrestrial species with ranges that span six continents. Noise altered at least one physiological, developmental, or behavioral trait in 80% of species studied, with declines in fitness and abundance and disruptions of predator-prey interactions. Effects occurred in every habitat, although response mechanisms varied for some traits and species, creating winners and losers. Only multispecies analyses can reveal such species- and ecosystem-level impacts of anthropogenic stressors. Our results establish noise as a novel selection pressure reshaping ecosystem dynamics and as a pervasive stressor requiring soundscape protection alongside habitat conservation.

Article.Title: Quantum gas microscopy of three-flavor Hubbard systems
Article.Authors: Mongkolkiattichai J.; Liu L.; Dasgupta S.; Hazzard K.; Schauss P.
Article.Abstract: Hubbard systems are paradigmatic realizations of strongly correlated many-body systems. Introducing additional species breaks the SU(2) symmetry of the Hubbard model and leads to a wide variety of new exotic quantum phases. Here, we extended quantum gas microscopy to three-flavor Fermi lattice gases in the Hubbard regime. Relying on site- and flavor-resolved detection, we studied the phase diagram of the three-flavor Hubbard model and found signatures of flavor-selective localization and selective pairing at temperatures down to the tunneling energy scale. Our measurements were then compared with numerical linked-cluster expansion calculations. Further increase of phase space density may enable the observation of a distinct pair Mott phase at half filling and shows a path toward the study of color superfluidity and other aspects of quantum chromodynamics.

Article.Title: Tumor metastasis co-opts liver hematopoiesis to promote immunosuppression
Article.Authors: Pan Q.; Wang X.; Li Y.; Li N.; Han Y.; Zhang G.; Guo J.; Zhang L.; Cui A.; Gu Y.; Lian Y.; Zhang W.; Lin N.; Xu B.; Jin Z.; Zeng X.; Wang L.; Li Y.; Peng J.; Wang X.; Yu Z.; Wang G.; Lu W.; Qin J.
Article.Abstract: Cancer-associated hematopoietic abnormalities contribute to systemic immunosuppression. However, whether tumors can initiate localized extramedullary hematopoiesis to suppress antitumor immunity remains unclear. In this study, we identify a distinct form of hepatic hematopoiesis driven by liver metastasis–associated hematopoietic stem cells (LM-HSCs). Liver metastases establish ectopic periportal hematopoietic niches that recruit bone marrow HSCs through Kupffer cell–dependent C-C motif chemokine receptor 1 (CCR1) signaling. Although LM-HSCs retain self-renewal and multipotency, cAMP response element–binding protein (CREB) activation skews their differentiation toward the myeloid lineage, particularly annexin A1–positive (ANXA1 + ) immature neutrophils. These neutrophils produce glucocorticoids, which activate glucocorticoid receptor signaling in a paracrine manner and induce immune checkpoint receptor expression and functional anergy in CD8 + T and natural killer cells. Collectively, these findings suggest that liver metastases reprograms hepatic hematopoiesis to promote immunosuppression.

Article.Title: Glacial abrupt transitions in ocean circulation were much slower than ice-core records imply
Article.Authors: Dong X.; Zhang X.; Sun Y.; Kathayat G.; Li Y.; Rasmussen S.; Svensson A.; Buizert C.; Sinha A.; Barker S.; Pérez-Mejías C.; Knorr G.; Chen R.; Zhao K.; Du W.; Zhang H.; Li H.; Columbu A.; Tan L.; Zhang Y.; Ning Y.; Werner M.; Wang Y.; Edwards R.; Cheng H.
Article.Abstract: Dansgaard-Oeschger (DO) events during the last ice age are thought to reflect rapid shifts in the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC). Greenland ice cores suggest warming transitions within only a few decades—or even just over 10 years. Using precisely dated speleothem oxygen-isotope records from the Asian monsoon region, we have shown that the same DO warmings unfolded over more than a century. Isotope modeling revealed that Greenland records primarily capture a rapid atmospheric reorganization triggered by the initial sea-ice retreat in the northeastern North Atlantic, whereas the parallel AMOC recovery and hemispheric thermal adjustment proceeded much more slowly. These findings reveal that natural AMOC transitions evolved more slowly than the rapid North Greenland oxygen-isotope shifts would imply, thereby refining our understanding of “abruptness” during DO events.

Article.Title: Targeting hormone conversion through dietary fiber improves polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome
Article.Authors: Qi X.; Chen H.; Nie Q.; Niu H.; Ding Y.; Luo X.; Si M.; Wu S.; Xiong X.; Li M.; Dong B.; Ma H.; Guo C.; Wang Y.; Long X.; Zheng J.; Wang K.; Nie S.; Jiang C.; Pang Y.; Qiao J.
Article.Abstract: Excessive androgens serve as a primary driver for many phenotypic features of polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS). Although dietary fiber has been shown to alleviate PMOS, its effects on androgen concentrations and the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. In a clinical trial, we demonstrated that a dietary fiber combination consisting of inulin, resistant starch, and β-glucan reduces androgen concentrations in patients’ plasma. Mechanistically, dietary fiber increased the abundance of Bacteroides xylanisolven s, which converts androstenedione into a nonandrogenic secondary hormone metabolite we named coproandrosterone, which is further metabolized by gut microbiota into dihydro-coproandrosterone. This metabolic pathway was validated in a mouse model. These findings highlight the potential of dietary fiber to alleviate PMOS by modulating androgen homeostasis through gut microbiota, offering insights for prebiotic and probiotic therapies.

Article.Title: When fat adapts: From physiological remodeling to disease
Article.Authors: Drareni K.; Seale P.
Article.Abstract: Adipose tissue undergoes extensive remodeling to adapt to changing physiological demands. This plasticity encompasses changes in adipocyte metabolism and number, extracellular matrix organization, vascularization, immune composition, and innervation. When coordinated, these processes preserve energy buffering, thermogenesis, endocrine function, and local tissue support. Pathological adipose tissue remodeling drives obesity-related complications and contributes to many diseases involving organ-associated adipose depots throughout the body. In cancer, tumor-associated fat can develop a metabolic and fibroinflammatory niche that promotes tumor growth and invasion, and remodeling of other depots can directly disrupt neighboring tissues. Recent studies have identified mesenchymal, immune, vascular, and adipocyte states that govern adaptive or pathological outcomes. These findings broaden therapeutic goals beyond reducing fat mass toward restoring adipogenesis, substrate turnover, thermogenic capacity, and tissue-niche function.

Article.Title: Direct evidence for psychoactive cannabis use 2800 years ago
Article.Authors: Caspari G.; Sadykov T.; Fomicheva D.; Blochin J.; Armbruster D.; Happel O.; Ryabogina N.; Boxleitner K.; Spengler R.
Article.Abstract: Cannabis is the world’s most-used illicit psychoactive plant, yet direct prehistoric evidence for its consumption is rare. In this study, we present the earliest direct evidence of cannabis use: offerings of plant parts and chemical compounds in ancient human hair recovered from a monumental tomb in Siberia. The findings suggest that the plant was used for its psychoactive qualities across Eurasia, where specific wild populations might have had naturally higher active compound levels. We show that the practice of cannabis consumption dates back at least 2800 years, anchoring debates around contemporary usage and informing discussions on cannabis in medicine, public health, law, and industry.

Article.Title: Seafloor geodesy delineates fast megathrust relocking after the giant 2011 Tohoku earthquake
Article.Authors: Tomita F.; Sun T.; Kido M.; Iinuma T.; Uchida N.; Ohta Y.; Hino R.; He J.; Wang K.
Article.Abstract: How and when the subduction megathrust recovers its locking state after a great earthquake is important to understanding earthquake-cycle physics and future hazards. Here we report the delineation of the relocking process after the 2011 magnitude 9 Tohoku earthquake with 14 years of postseismic seafloor geodetic observations. These data, combined with onshore geodetic observations, analyses of repeating earthquakes, and numerical modeling, reveal how the recovery of locking is interrupted by afterslip on the megathrust and accompanied by stress relaxation in the viscoelastic upper mantle. The results indicate that the megathrust has already arrived at a locking state today similar to that before the earthquake despite the ongoing stress relaxation. The acquired knowledge aids understanding of megathrust earthquake cycles at other subduction zones.

Article.Title: Stacked porous NiTi structure with low cost and ultrahigh fatigue life for elastocaloric cooling
Article.Authors: Su C.; Li Y.; Deng Z.; Zhong S.; Hu J.; Li X.; Li Q.; Sun Q.
Article.Abstract: Elastocaloric cooling (eC) uses shape memory alloys (SMAs) as energy-efficient, eco-friendly refrigerants. However, cost-effectively fabricating SMAs into fatigue-resistant, heat transfer–enhanced structures remains a key obstacle to commercialization of the eC technology. We introduce a “stamping and stacking” (S-S) method for producing porous, fatigue-resistant SMA structures. Honeycomb-like chips are stamped from nitinol (NiTi) thin sheets and then stacked into a layered tubular structure to increase heat exchange surface and at the same time avoid buckling and splitting failures encountered in existing SMA structures. The stacked structure endures >10 8 compression cycles and can deliver high specific cooling power of 3850 watts per kilogram. Our S-S method reduces fabrication costs by one order of magnitude compared with existing approaches, enabling mass production of eC refrigerant structures for commercial deployment.

Article.Title: The first 1000 days: Modeling language learning from individual children’s everyday speech
Article.Authors: Raviv H.; Tsyhanov A.; Gousios K.; Altenhof A.; Wang H.; Chen B.; Raviv O.; Rosenwein T.; Lew-Williams C.; Hasenfratz L.; Hasson U.
Article.Abstract: Children learn to understand and speak from the speech around them, yet how that everyday input shapes learning remains unresolved. Large language models show that language is learnable from data, but their scale and training conditions differ sharply from a child’s natural experience. We trained cognitively feasible, child-specific models on longitudinal home recordings from eight children across their first 1000 days of life. Each model learned incrementally from a single child’s ordered speech input without prior linguistic knowledge, developing phoneme-like and word-form representations that tracked each child’s learning pace. Learning was dependent on dense daily sampling and replay of recent input, indicating that both experience- and memory-related processes are necessary. These findings show that everyday experience contains sufficient structure for language learning and establish child-specific modeling for testing developmental theories.

Article.Title: Obesity management medications: The way forward
Article.Authors: Blüher M.
Article.Abstract: Obesity is now widely recognized as a chronic progressive condition. The altered biological mechanisms that cause obesity frequently require long-term treatment, including pharmacotherapies or bariatric surgery. In recent decades, the pathophysiology of obesity has been understood to an extent that obesity management medication (OMM) discovery could be rationally pursued. Advances in defining the regulation of food intake and energy expenditure by molecular communication from peripheral organs to the brain led to the development of OMMs that appear capable of safely achieving scalable and sustained body weight loss. However, side effects, heterogeneous treatment responses, long-term metabolic adaptations, adherence, and other factors may limit the use of existing OMMs and justify the development of additional medications to improve the health of people living with obesity.

Article.Authors: Ghazi B.; Kamath P.; Kumar R.; Manurangsi P.; Sealfon* A.
Article.Abstract: The 2020 United States Census adopted differential privacy to protect individual confidentiality, adding calibrated noise to summary demographic measurements that are then reconciled into population tables. We developed BlueDown, a postprocessing algorithm that combines techniques from linear regression and constrained optimization while exploiting measurement structure for efficiency. On 2020 Census data, BlueDown reduced the error of groupings by race at the county level by 21 to 36% and of all county-level groupings by 9 to 58%; at the tract level, it reduced error of groupings by housing type by 38 to 61%. These gains came at no cost to confidentiality or computational efficiency and would improve the validity of research relying on this definitive dataset and analyses used to guide the distribution of more than $1.5 trillion in annual federal spending.

Article.Authors: Shadlen K.; Wouters O.
Article.Abstract: ore than 1 billion people worldwide are obese, and roughly 500 million have type 2 diabetes.These conditions are major risk factors for dementia, heart disease, and various cancers.Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, commonly referred to as GLP-1s, have transformed the treatment of both obesity and type 2 diabetes.Yet despite their promise, global use of these therapies remains uneven.Access has largely been concentrated in high-income countries, even though low-and middle-income countries account for more than 80% of the world's population and a substantial share of the global burden of obesity and type 2 diabetes.Generic versions of the popular GLP-1 drug semaglutide became available in a number of countries in 2026, offering opportunities to substantially expand access.The likely emergence of newer GLP-1s with moredesirable attributes, however, may produce a segmented global market that gives rise to familiar tensions over access to newer, patentprotected therapies.Clinical trials have shown that GLP-1s, part of a broader category of incretin-based therapies, support weight loss, improve glycemic control, and reduce the risk of heart disease (1).Other potential uses are under investigation, including for cardiovascular disorders, neurodegeneration, liver disease, and addiction.The first GLP-1 receptor agonist to be approved in the US for both diabetes and weight management was liraglutide.An earlier drug in this class, exenatide, was approved for diabetes only.Semaglutide, marketed by Novo Nordisk for both diabetes and weight management, revolutionized obesity therapy and, in doing so, became one of the most commercially successful medicines in history (2).Newer incretinbased therapies target multiple gut hormones to produce greater metabolic effects.Tirzepatide, a dual GLP-1 and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptor agonist marketed by Eli Lilly, has overtaken semaglutide in prescription volume for both indications in many markets.These medicines are all polypeptides (i.e., amino acid chains) that mimic the natural GLP-1 hormone.In 2026, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved orforglipron, an oral, nonpeptide small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist, for chronic weight management.

Article.Title: Obesity pharmacotherapies and cognition
Article.Authors: Börchers S.; Mazzini G.; Zetterberg H.; Clemmensen C.
Article.Abstract: Pharmacotherapies for obesity and type 2 diabetes are increasingly being evaluated for their effects on cognition and brain health. Evidence from preclinical models, observational cohorts, and clinical trials has intensified interest, but findings remain mixed. A central challenge is to determine whether potential cognitive effects arise from direct actions on neural circuits, indirect consequences of improved cardiometabolic health, or both. This Review examines the evidence across cardiometabolic disease, aging, and Alzheimer’s disease, focusing on glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)–based therapies and combination approaches that engage glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon, and amylin pathways. We assess how receptor pharmacology, brain exposure, metabolic context, and disease stage shape cognitive outcomes and discuss how mechanistic clarity could guide therapies aimed at preserving or improving cognition.

Article.Title: Can artificial intelligence align with Indigenous science?
Article.Authors: Running Horse Collin Y.
Article.Abstract: As the use of generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) increases, alarms are being raised about how the technology could replace human contribution, override human supervision, ignore ethical and technical guardrails, and cause increasingly irreparable harm to the environment. This creates potentially destructive outcomes for life on Earth. From a traditional Indigenous science perspective, such possibilities in themselves would be enough to immediately stop presently configured AI releases. In a Lakota context, science must ensure as little harm as possible is done to life. Therefore, AI as presently configured simply would not qualify to advance further from an ethical and scientific standpoint. Indigenous science asks something fundamentally different than what AI presently seeks to, or can, answer. But that does not mean that future forms of AI can never align with Indigenous science.

Article.Abstract: Ultracold atom platforms enable low temperatures and long free evolution times, which are crucial for fundamental physics tests and atom interferometry. The lowest equivalent temperature reported in such a system is 38 pK with a free expansion time of 2 s, achieved in atom-chip-based magnetic traps in microgravity. Optical dipole trap (ODT) systems offer better optical access and the flexibility to condense both magnetic and non-magnetic atoms, but have not been used to prepare quantum degenerate gases under microgravity conditions. Article.Title: In-cell structures visualize human pre-ribosome assembly in the nucleolus
Article.Authors: Zhao X.; Hayashi Y.; Fung H.; Cuylen-Haering S.; Mahamid J.; Müller C.
Article.Abstract: In eukaryotes, ribosome biogenesis initiates within the nucleolus, a hallmark multilayered compartment of the nucleus. Here, we used cryogenic correlative light and electron tomography to visualize molecular landscapes within HeLa cell nucleoli and obtained in-cell structural snapshots of both ribosomal subunit precursors, the small subunit processome and the pre-60S. Article.Title: Emergence of Chern metal in a moiré Kondo lattice
Article.Authors: Zhao W.; Tao Z.; Zhang Y.; Shen B.; Han Z.; Knüppel P.; Zeng Y.; Xia Z.; Watanabe K.; Taniguchi T.; Shan J.; Mak K.
Article.Abstract: A Chern metal is a two-dimensional metallic state of matter carrying chiral edge states. We report the observation of a Chern metal at the onset of the magnetic Kondo breakdown in a frustrated moiré Kondo lattice--angle-aligned MoTe 2 /WSe 2 bilayers. The state is compressible and is manifested by a nearly quantized Hall resistance and a finite longitudinal resistance arising from a bad metallic bulk. We demonstrate the presence of a chiral edge state by nonlocal transport measurements and current-induced quantum anomalous Hall breakdown. Magnetic circular dichroism measurements further reveal a magnetization plateau for the Chern metal before a metamagnetic transition at the Kondo breakdown. Our results open an opportunity for moiré engineering of exotic quantum phases through the interplay between band topology and Kondo interactions.

Article.Authors: Liu Y.; Saper L.; Bell E.; Ma C.; Li H.; Hu J.; Guan Y.; Melton H.; Cruz-Uribe A.; Yap T.; Tissot F.; Bucholz C.; Ziegler K.; Agee C.
Article.Abstract: Martian meteorites provide a record of the planet’s geological history. However, most are geologically young samples that are not representative of Mars’ surface, which is dominated by ancient rocks. We describe the Martian meteorite Teghaza 001 (Teg 001), a slowly cooled igneous rock that formed at least 4.1 billion years ago. Its composition, mineralogy, and texture are distinct from other Martian meteorites. We determine that Teg 001 is a sample of ancient crust, which formed from a geochemically distinct mantle source with primordial composition. The presence of aqueously altered minerals, combined with bulk and mineral-specific oxygen isotope measurements, indicate that Teg 001 experienced reactions with fluids enriched in 18 O, before ejection into space by an impact.

Article.Authors: James L.; Oudyk K.; Pescaru M.; Wall E.; Chen Y.; Pearse W.; Sakata J.
Article.Abstract: Bird songs are often described as analogs to human speech and songs, but expansive comparisons are necessary to determine analogy and mechanistic substrates. Article.Title: Chiral altermagnon in MnTe
Article.Authors: Jost D.; Regmi R.; Lomeli E.; Sahel-Schackis S.; Scheufele M.; Neuhaus M.; Nickel R.; Yakhou F.; Kummer K.; Brookes N.; Shen L.; Dakovski G.; Ghimire N.; Geprägs S.; Kling M.
Article.Abstract: Altermagnetism has been recognized as a magnetic phase that bridges the properties of ferro- and antiferromagnetism. The momentum-dependent spin splitting observed in these materials reflects their distinctive symmetry characteristics, which also establish the conditions for chiral magnons to emerge. Here we provide direct experimental evidence for a chiral magnon in the altermagnetic candidate manganese telluride (MnTe) revealed by circular-dichroism resonant inelastic x-ray scattering. This mode, which we term chiral altermagnon, exhibits a distinct momentum dependence of its spin polarization consistent with the altermagnetic g -wave symmetry of MnTe. Our polarization-resolved data corroborate the existence of a discrete class of magnetic excitations, demonstrating how altermagnetic order shapes spin dynamics and paving the way for advances in spintronic and quantum technologies.

Article.Title: Rapid longitudinal flights cause time shifts and Sun compass error
Article.Authors: Lewin P.; Wynn J.; Morford J.; Padget O.; Lancaster-Reeves L.; Siddiqi-Davies K.; Bailey H.; Bond S.; Davis M.; Dean B.; Fayet A.; Freeman R.; Gillies N.; Harris S.; Jaggers P.; Kirk H.; Maurice L.; Morgan E.; Nisbet C.; Owen E.; Parker J.; Shoji A.; Syposz M.; Guilford T.
Article.Abstract: Many animals use the Sun compass to guide their movement, sometimes over thousands of kilometers. Consistent use of the Sun compass relies on the endogenous clock to track the Sun’s arc, yet animals traveling east-west experience time shifts, potentially causing mismatches between their internal clock and local time. Using GPS, we reveal that Manx shearwaters ( Puffinus puffinus ) experience such shifts during homing flights, generating predictable errors in Sun compass orientation. Use of the Sun compass persists even when shearwaters have access to compass-independent cues during coast following. Our findings provide a new avenue for chronobiology research in the wild, suggesting that rapid longitudinal movements may affect other processes governed by the endogenous clock and that conserved chronobiological mechanisms impose substantial constraints on navigation.

Article.Title: The global geography of threats to freshwater biodiversity
Article.Authors: Brabant C.; Pollock L.; Geldmann J.; Bendixen M.; Comte L.; Farooq H.; Hébert K.; Lehner B.; Sayer C.; Iversen L.
Article.Abstract: Human activities are eroding biodiversity, especially in freshwater systems. Despite major advances in quantifying species vulnerability and threats, we still lack a crucial understanding of where threats are affecting freshwater species globally. Here, we produced a species-centered spatial assessment of threats, mapping the impact of 45 threats across 21,490 freshwater species of amphibians, fish, mammals, odonates, and reptiles. We found that species in highly developed and water-managed regions are strongly affected by multiple overlapping threats. Although threats vary across taxa and regions, increasing threat probabilities elevate extinction risk and population declines, with freshwater species experiencing greater threat intensity and distinct spatial patterns than terrestrial species. Our findings establish a spatially explicit baseline for targeting the most urgently needed freshwater conservation and management interventions.

Article.Title: Intrinsic gestational timing governs human cerebellar development after preterm birth
Article.Authors: Sanidas G.; Simonti G.; Ghaemmaghami J.; Woyshner K.; Polyviou A.; Vidva R.; Lowe C.; Vij A.; Bittel D.; Triantafyllou M.; Wolff N.; Cardenas R.; Chen H.; Almeida F.; Sudhakar S.; Mankad K.; Koutroulis I.; Pettersen H.; Stein-O’Brien G.; Sidiropoulos D.; Gallo V.; Kratimenos P.
Article.Abstract: Intrinsic programs shape brain maturation; however, which of these programs are perturbed by prematurity as well as the molecular pathways involved remain unknown. The human cerebellum serves as a paradigm of extrauterine development—its accelerated growth and circuit formation align with the third trimester, a period disrupted by preterm delivery. Using multimodal datasets encompassing in vivo neuroimaging and neurodevelopmental outcomes with postmortem spatial-transcriptomic and histopathological profiling, we show that prematurity diverts the cerebellar developmental trajectory. Cerebellar growth and functional outcomes scaled with gestational age, despite modifying perinatal exposures. Spatially resolved developmental programs underlying macroscopic trajectories were marked by incomplete granule cell maturation and impaired Purkinje cell structural refinement, which indicate lineage-specific developmental asynchrony. Thus, prematurity constitutes biologically displaced maturation, in which infants of equivalent postmenstrual age occupy divergent developmental states.

Article.Title: Altermagnetism revealed by polarized neutrons in MnF <sub>2</sub>
Article.Authors: Faure Q.; Bounoua D.; Balédent V.; Gukasov A.; Garlea V.; Ribeiro A.; Rau J.; Petit S.; McClarty P.
Article.Abstract: Altermagnets are compensated magnets with symmetry-enforced spin split bands. Direct spectroscopic evidence for their existence has been reported in several materials. For example, inelastic neutron scattering (INS) has recently been used to witness a splitting of magnon bands in MnTe that is compatible with altermagnetism. Here, we present polarized INS results on MnF 2 showing that it is altermagnetic. Our data reveal a splitting coming from the long-range dipolar coupling. Furthermore, using a domain-biased sample, the data reveal a nonzero chirality in the neutron scattering cross section that reverses the sign between the two magnon modes. It is this feature that clearly demonstrates altermagnetism in MnF 2 . This finding highlights the potential for polarized INS to characterize altermagnets through its sensitivity to fine structure in magnon spectra.

Article.Title: Stimulated protein degradation to promote mitochondrial function and neuronal survival
Article.Authors: Chandrasekhar S.; McMinimy R.; Manford A.; Wehri E.; Gee C.; Miller C.; Bingol B.; Kuriyan J.; Schaletzky J.; Rapé M.
Article.Abstract: Targeted protein degradation is a promising modality to treat cancer or inflammation, but whether it can provide a similar benefit for disorders caused by pervasive protein dysregulation is unclear. We describe stimulated protein degradation (SPD) as a strategy that leverages agonists of stress-responsive E3 ubiquitin ligases to simultaneously eliminate multiple pathogenic factors. Specifically, we show that activators of the reductive stress response E3 CUL2 FEM1B boost degradation of multiple physiological substrates to improve mitochondrial import and electron transport chain assembly. In this manner, CUL2 FEM1B agonists preserve mitochondrial function and neuronal survival in models of neurodegenerative COX deficiency syndrome and Friedreich’s ataxia. By activating E3 ligases that evolved to safeguard cellular integrity, SPD expands the use of compound-induced protein degradation to complex pathologies of high unmet need.

Article.Title: Spatial coordination in the codevelopment of the human urogenital system during organogenesis
Article.Authors: Guo Y.; Cai H.; Li D.; Ren P.; Cui L.; Hao C.; Jiang H.; Zhang Z.; Wang X.; Guo J.
Article.Abstract: The human urogenital system originates from a common embryonic domain, yet the mechanisms guiding its spatiotemporal coordination remain understudied. Here, we combined high-resolution spatial transcriptomics with single-cell multiomics to profile human embryos from Carnegie stages 15 to 23, capturing the codevelopmental dynamics of the urogenital system. We revealed mesonephros- and adrenal primordium–derived signals that promote gonadal specification and enable efficient in vitro generation of cells resembling early gonadal lineages. We also uncovered a possible mesonephric origin of gonadal supporting cells through rete testis or ovarii linking the mesonephros. Finally, we delineate three transcriptionally distinct steroidogenic lineages differing in cholesterol sourcing, cortisol synthesis, and sex hormone production that together orchestrate sex differentiation. These findings deepen our understanding of urogenital system assembly and guide the exploration of coordinated multiorgan development.

Article.Title: A commensally regulated immune rheostat fine-tunes skin barrier fitness
Article.Authors: Gola A.; Srinivas R.; Rodig E.; Schernthanner M.; Abdusselamoglu M.; Tierney M.; Alexander N.; Gonzales K.; Sajjath S.; Soto-Ugaldi L.; Bonny A.; Fuchs E.
Article.Abstract: At the skin’s surface, the epidermis must balance stem cell renewal with barrier maintenance to withstand environmental stress and shield against pathogens. In this study, we identify a microbial-immune-epithelial feedback mechanism that integrates environmental information into stem cell regulation in mice. Specifically, we show that Langerhans cells (LCs), an intraepithelial macrophage population, orchestrate this circuit by producing prostaglandin E 2 , which restrains stem cell proliferation, promotes epidermal differentiation, and maintains barrier integrity during homeostasis. Upon pathway disruption, stem cells become overactivated, hindering terminal differentiation and weakening barrier function. Upstream, LC activity is tuned by the local microbial environment in a rheostat-like fashion, coupling commensal sensing to stem cell dynamics. Our findings provide a general framework for how barrier tissues achieve adaptive homeostasis amid continual external fluctuations.

Article.Title: Genomic erosion across avifauna in a biodiversity hotspot sounds a conservation alarm
Article.Authors: Liu R.; Liu Y.; Wu F.; Yan D.; Dong F.
Article.Abstract: Loss of biodiversity can have a hidden dimension—the cryptic erosion of genetic diversity even in the face of apparent species resilience. We quantified changes in genetic diversity by comparing historical and modern genomes of 62 songbird species from the Gaoligong Mountains, a biodiversity hotspot in southwestern China. We identified genomic loss averaging between 43 and 49%; and, unexpectedly, common species were disproportionately affected. We argue that this loss was driven primarily by habitat fragmentation (and mitigated by dispersal ability) and show that it exceeds prior estimates and conservation policy thresholds. Species identified as having lost diversity continue to be listed as “Least Concern” on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Red List of Threatened Species, exposing a blind spot in extinction risk monitoring. We call for genomic metrics to be rapidly integrated into global conservation frameworks.

Article.Title: Western Pacific double subduction drives Gulf of California rifting
Article.Authors: Gianni G.; He X.; Becker T.; Faccenna C.
Article.Abstract: Continental rifting reflects the balance between tectonic forces and lithospheric strength, yet the mechanisms of breakup remain debated. Rapid rifting of the Gulf of California oblique rift (GOCOR) ~6 million to 8 million years ago is a key example; it may have resulted from the lithosphere responding to external kinematics or acceleration of long-lived extension. The dynamics of either scenario remain incompletely understood. In this study, we highlight that the rapid rifting of the GOCOR coincides with the initiation of Western Pacific double subduction. Using three-dimensional geodynamic models, we show that such subduction reorganization can transmit extensional stresses of ~5 to 15 megapascals across the Pacific plate, loading the GOCOR and the southern San Andreas fault. Subduction reorganization may represent the missing driver for the initiation of rapid GOCOR rifting within a preconditioned lithosphere and may be an overlooked tectonic force behind other rifting events.
Article.OpenAlexKeywords: southern San Andreas fault; lithospheric extension; extensional stress; continental rifting

Article.Title: Whole-body single-cell atlas of an adult vertebrate, Danionella cerebrum
Article.Authors: Atabay K.; Aoude P.; Park C.; Kadobianskyi M.; Paugois O.; Judkewitz B.; Reddien P.
Article.Abstract: A complete cell type transcriptome atlas of a vertebrate could promote understanding of animal cell type composition, organization, and evolution. The miniaturized, transparent, and regenerative teleost Danionella cerebrum brings whole-vertebrate single-cell profiling experiments within reach. We performed region-stratified single-cell RNA sequencing across the adult Danionella body and mapped cell types and gene expression at single-cell resolution using spatial transcriptomics. We delineated spatially distinct neural cell types on the basis of their regional gene expression signatures. The body-wide atlas elucidated cell types harboring adult molecular positional memory, uncovered paedomorphic features, and revealed conserved body-region and appendage-specification programs in adult connective tissue. Comparative analyses revealed conserved neural cell types, and regeneration datasets uncovered expression dynamics during telencephalon regeneration. This whole-vertebrate transcriptome atlas yields a comprehensive resource for myriad questions in biology and neuroscience.

Article.Title: Papaver self-incompatibility is controlled by two multiallelic idiomorphs
Article.Authors: Jin K.; Du Z.; Xiong T.; Leng F.; Liu J.; Zhang M.; Tian B.; Hu J.; Hu H.; Wang W.; Zhao T.; Xue J.; Yang X.; Ye K.; Li C.; Wang X.; Wang X.; Wang X.; Chai L.; Xu Q.; Sun M.; Franklin-Tong V.; Igić B.; Jiao W.; Lin Z.
Article.Abstract: Self-incompatibility (SI) prevents self-fertilization through highly polymorphic genetic recognition at the S locus with multiple alleles. In Papaver rhoeas , the S determinants were previously identified as PrpS and PrsS . However, we found that PrpS-PrsS was absent in many S haplotypes. In this work, we report the identification of an alternative pair of polymorphic S genes, S locus oligopeptide transporter ( SOPT ) and S locus glycine-rich protein ( SGRP ), segregating at the S locus when PrpS-PrsS is absent. SOPT and SGRP display hallmark S determinant features and confer SI when heterologously expressed in Arabidopsis thaliana . Therefore, instead of having allelomorphs with homologous variants, the Papaver SI system is determined by two multiallelic idiomorphs sharing no obvious common ancestry. This discovery of a dual-idiomorph system reveals a distinct genetic basis for polymorphism, with implications for the evolution of allorecognition mechanisms.

Article.Title: Data-driven discovery and rapid, direct synthesis of MXenes
Article.Authors: Shamshirgar A.; Portugal G.; Ershadrad S.; Ivanov R.; Dahlqvist M.; Chabanais F.; Chakraborty S.; Traksmaa R.; Jussila T.; Karppinen M.; Hussainova I.; Heintz F.; Persson P.; Rosen J.
Article.Abstract: MXenes are a rapidly expanding family of two-dimensional transition metal carbides and nitrides, yet scalable synthesis routes remain limited and historical reports suggest a broader, largely unexplored chemical space. We used machine learning–assisted database mining to uncover hidden multilayer MXenes. Screening reveals 33 previously synthesized but unrecognized MXene candidates. Guided by these findings, we synthesized seven multilayer MXenes using a rapid, scalable self-propagating high-temperature method that requires no sustained external heating and completes within minutes. We further realized 11 previously unexplored rare earth–based MXenes (M = praseodymium, neodymium, samarium, gadolinium, terbium, holmium, and thulium). Experiments and modeling suggest semiconducting behavior and diverse magnetic states across this family. Together, these results expand the MXene family and demonstrate a data-driven strategy for accelerating materials discovery through sustainable methods.

Article.Title: The delocalized nature of chemical bonding at a catalytic metal surface
Article.Authors: Nitz F.; Hörandl S.; Pätzold J.; Kandratsenka A.; Kitsopoulos T.; Auerbach D.; Wodtke A.; Borodin D.
Article.Abstract: Adsorbate bonding at metal surfaces requires hybridization of localized molecular orbitals with delocalized electronic bands of the metal; hence, the electronic wave function involved in bonding may extend far beyond the adsorption site. We revealed the consequence of this delocalization by determining the distance over which structural variations of the metal surface influence the molecule-metal bond strength. Velocity-resolved kinetics provided adsorption energies for three molecules bound at atomic steps of platinum (Pt), each exhibiting bond-strength changes of up to 0.2 electron volts as the step-step distance varied over 100 angstroms. We observed molecule-specific behavior reflecting the hybridization of molecule-specific orbitals with symmetry-selected orbital bands of the metal that respond differently to structural modifications of the solid. We discuss implications of these observations for adsorption on Pt nanoparticles.

Article.Title: When AI takes away the thrill of discovery
Article.Authors: Thorp H.
Article.Abstract: “Pure math is being devastated or revolutionized, depending on your point of view.” So said Cornell professor Steven Strogatz after the artificial intelligence (AI) company OpenAI announced in early September a potential solution to the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of the seven Millennium Prize problems that represent the highest goals for mathematical proofs. OpenAI’s solution involved unleashing an army of AI agents at a cost of millions of dollars in computing power, and it also certainly drew on decades of human effort in mathematics before it. Then a few weeks later, OpenAI posted 722 manuscripts describing progress on 372 mathematical problem families, and Google DeepMind published (in Science ) solutions from their own AI math system. These events are potentially exciting for those who long to know the answers to these problems as soon as possible, but they have also sent the world of mathematics reeling, and pose an even bigger question for all fields: Can the satisfaction of understanding ever replace the thrill of discovery?

Article.Title: Noncoding transcription controls the developmental dynamics of long-range gene regulation
Article.Authors: Batut P.; Levine M.
Article.Abstract: The genomic regions regulating gene expression are often themselves transcribed into a variety of noncoding RNAs (ncRNAs). However, the regulatory roles of this noncoding transcription remain largely unknown. By using live imaging, we reveal that the sequential transcription of ncRNAs emanating from distinct regulatory elements underlies gene activation in Drosophila embryos. Single-allele covisualization uncovers that optimal gene activation is achieved by only moderate levels of enhancer activity. Disrupting enhancer-associated ncRNAs causes precocious gene activation, providing evidence that ncRNAs control the timing of gene expression in development. We further show that enhancer transcription can regulate long-range interactions within complex regulatory landscapes. We propose that ncRNAs locally modulate regulatory element activity in cis to shape genome organization and orchestrate the temporal control of gene expression in development.

Article.Title: The Virtual Biotech: A multi-agent AI framework for therapeutic discovery and development
Article.Authors: Zhang H.; Eckmann P.; Miao J.; Mahon A.; Zou J.
Article.Abstract: Drug development requires evidence integration across biological scales and modalities, but relevant tools are fragmented. We introduce the Virtual Biotech, an organization of artificial intelligence (AI) agents modeled on a drug-development company, with agentic divisions spanning target discovery, safety assessment, modality selection, and clinical development. We demonstrate its utility at three drug-development decision points. First, more than 37,000 agents annotated outcomes from 55,984 trials and found that drugs targeting cell type–specific genes were 48% more likely to reach market with 32% fewer adverse events. Second, it integrated multimodal evidence to propose a therapeutic strategy in lung cancer. Third, it analyzed a terminated ulcerative colitis trial and inferred potential mechanisms of failure. These results demonstrate that human-guided multi-agent systems can conduct transparent, multiscale analyses to inform therapeutic-development decisions.

Article.Title: Safeguarding global terrestrial vertebrate species from future sea level rise
Article.Authors: Jiang Z.; Xiao H.; Hanson J.; Zeng Y.; Wilcove D.; Schuerch M.; Kirwan M.; Yan Q.; Chen Y.; Ma L.
Article.Abstract: Sea level rise (SLR) threatens terrestrial biodiversity, yet its spatiotemporal and species-specific impacts remain unclear. Integrating relative SLR projections across five shared socioeconomic pathways (SSPs) with area of habitat (AOH) maps for 34,120 terrestrial vertebrate species, we project that species exposed to SLR will increase from up to 13,680 in 2050 to 15,324 by 2100, including 57 to 63% of birds, 47 to 52% of mammals, 28 to 36% of reptiles, and 20 to 24% of amphibians. In Southeast Asia, inland inundation areas support high richness. Under SSP5-8.5, species facing >10% habitat inundation surge from 18 in 2050 to 109 by 2100, with reptiles and already threatened species overrepresented. Safeguarding SLR refugia—the noninundated habitats for exposed species—is critical, yet more than 96% lie outside protected areas, which means that early international action is required.

Article.Title: Thermodynamic origin of the phonon Hall effect in a honeycomb antiferromagnet
Article.Authors: Meng Q.; Li X.; Liu J.; Zhao L.; Dong C.; Zhu Z.; Li L.; Behnia K.
Article.Abstract: The underlying mechanism of the thermal Hall effect generated by phonons in a variety of insulators is yet to be identified. In this work, we report on a sizable thermal Hall conductivity in nickel phosphorus trisulfide (NiPS 3 ), a van der Waals stack of honeycomb layers with a zigzag antiferromagnetic order. The longitudinal (κ aa ) and the transverse (κ ab ) thermal conductivities peak at the same temperature, and the thermal Hall angle, at this peak, respects a previously identified bound. The amplitude of κ ab is extremely sensitive to the amplitude of magnetization along the b axis but is not correlated with the phonon mean free path, which points to an intrinsic origin.

Article.Title: Electronic bound states in the continuum in a two-dimensional metal
Article.Authors: Thinel M.; Huang X.; Chica D.; Turkel S.; Rossi S.; Koay C.; Li H.; Mihalyi-Koch W.; Samanta B.; Holbrook M.; Devarakonda A.; Nashabeh L.; Georgescu A.; Roy X.; Zhu X.; Pasupathy A.; Queiroz R.
Article.Abstract: Bound states in the continuum (BICs) are quantum states that remain localized despite lying within a continuum of extended, delocalized states. Whereas optical BICs have been realized in photonic systems, achieving electronic bound states embedded in a metallic background remains an ongoing challenge. In this study, we used scanning tunneling microscopy to identify two defect-induced electronic states that remain localized within the metallic continuum of Pd 5 AlI 2 , a two-dimensional van der Waals metal. Our calculations suggest that electron-hopping interference on the decorated checkerboard lattice of Pd 5 AlI 2 gives rise to a (quasi) flat band built from spatially localized eigenstates that are orthogonal to the dispersive continuum. Atomic defects within this frustrated lattice shift the associated flat-band localized states into the metallic continuum, forming robust, symmetry-protected BICs.

Article.Title: Wireless electrocatalytic closed-loop system for drug-free management of diabesity
Article.Authors: Maity D.; Guha Ray P.; Buchmann P.; Charpin-El Hamri G.; Fussenegger M.
Article.Abstract: Lifestyle-related type 2 diabetes and associated obesity (diabesity) affect >2.5 billion people worldwide and impose nearly $3 trillion in annual health care costs. We developed an implantable, wirelessly powered electrocatalytic closed-loop health optimization (ECHO) device containing platinum-decorated gold nanoclusters embedded in graphite felt that enabled selective, electrically tunable oxidation of blood glucose to renally cleared gluconate. In type 2 diabetic mice, wireless, low-power activation (0.75 volts, 10 milliamperes) restored glucose homeostasis within 1 hour, shifted metabolism from glucose to lipid utilization, reduced body weight and triglycerides, and increased circulating free fatty acids and ketone bodies without detectable hypoglycemia or adverse physiological, inflammatory, or behavioral effects during 6 weeks of treatment. Coupling this ECHO device to a commercial continuous glucose monitoring system enabled autonomous, smartphone-controlled, drug-free closed-loop management of experimental diabesity.

Article.Title: BAK and BAX form a multiprotein complex to drive mtDNA efflux and caspase-independent cell death
Article.Authors: Yang S.; Kim H.; Liao G.; Ta N.; Tu H.; Ramani S.; Chen C.; Li Z.; Tanno N.; Hsieh J.; Cheng E.
Article.Abstract: The apoptotic regulators BAX and BAK, once activated, form homo-oligomers to trigger mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP), activating the apoptosome and caspases. We purified a macromolecular complex comprising BAK, BAX, activator BH3-only molecules, voltage-dependent anion channels 1 and 2 (VDAC1 and VDAC2), and prohibitins that released mtDNA from mitoplasts. BAX-BAK activation resulted in VDAC closure, mitochondrial calcium influx, and mtDNA efflux. Loss of VDAC1, VDAC2, or prohibitins prevented BAX-BAK activation–induced mtDNA efflux and caspase-independent cell death without affecting MOMP or mitochondrial inner membrane herniation. These findings support differential regulation of cytochrome c and mtDNA efflux by distinct BAX-BAK complexes.

Article.Title: Intron retention regulates STAT2 function and associates with immunotherapy response in lung cancer
Article.Authors: Englander R.; Brugiolo M.; Devoucoux M.; Wu T.; Kostich M.; Leclair N.; Walawalkar I.; Kang H.; Park S.; Marches F.; Peeples M.; Chen P.; Banchereau J.; Yu P.; Salner A.; Banchereau R.; Palucka K.; Anczuków O.
Article.Abstract: Immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibitors has revolutionized cancer therapy and enabled considerable therapeutic advances for treating various diseases, including lung cancer. Article.Title: Late Holocene reexpansion of the Laurentide Ice Sheet
Article.Authors: Young N.; Miller G.; Raynolds M.; Bueltmann H.; Lehman S.; Raberg J.; Seward K.; Pendleton S.; Andrews J.; Webber P.; Schaefer J.
Article.Abstract: During interglaciations, the Laurentide Ice Sheet (LIS), which is the largest of the Pleistocene ice sheets, retreats to Arctic Canada, where it achieves a minimum configuration. The reexpansion of the LIS following this minimum marks the start of the next glaciation. Here, we show that the last remaining remnant of the most recent LIS, Barnes Ice Cap (Baffin Island, Canada), achieved its minimum interglacial dimensions after ~3.6 thousand years ago, before reexpanding ~2000 years ago, marking the onset of the next glaciation. The new LIS reached maximum dimensions in ~1960 CE, after which anthropogenic summer warming resulted in a negative mass balance, ice margin recession, and the termination of the next glaciation. The demise of the next glaciation, despite the ongoing decline in summer insolation, illustrates the influence of anomalous greenhouse gas forcing on climate.

Article.Title: Ultrarapid decision-making in an avian brain
Article.Authors: Schmidbauer P.; Nieder A.
Article.Abstract: Perceptual decision-making is well studied in mammals, but its operation in other vertebrates remains unclear. We show that carrion crows ( Corvus corone ) make deliberate decisions in a classic visual motion discrimination task with unprecedented speed, reporting choices in approximately 235 milliseconds on average, which is roughly twice as fast as has been observed in monkeys or humans and without sacrificing accuracy. Recordings from the pallial endbrain reveal that direction-selective neurons encode the upcoming choice as early as about 70 milliseconds after stimulus onset and about 170 milliseconds before the response, with ramping activity scaling with sensory evidence and converging at response onset. These findings highlight the extraordinary efficiency of avian decision-making circuitry, possibly shaped by evolutionary pressures for rapid visuomotor control.

Article.Title: Dynamic functionality–enabled fast and selective transport in nanochannels
Article.Authors: Zhang H.; Kang Y.; Feng F.; Hu T.; Xu R.; Yu H.; He K.; Yang Z.; Wang Z.; Lau C.; Low Z.; Gu Q.; Liu J.; Wang H.; Zhang X.
Article.Abstract: Nanochannels capable of fast and selective mass transport are central to applications in energy, resources, biomedicine, and the environment. However, extreme nanoscale confinement, often coupled with rigid channel environments, imposes substantial frictional and adhesive barriers, causing sluggish transport and constrained selectivity. We identified nanochannel dynamics as a key to addressing these challenges by harnessing the intrinsic mobility (e.g., self-rotation) of confined functionalities to enhance molecular transport. Through a combination of experiments and simulations, we demonstrated that such dynamics reshape transport by promoting kinetic energy transfer and enabling more efficient molecular relays, thereby improving separation performance beyond current benchmarks. Our findings highlight the role of nanochannel dynamics in regulating mass transport under confinement and provide a framework for designing advanced nanochannel systems.

Article.Title: Imaging electron-hole asymmetry in the quantum melting of generalized Wigner crystals
Article.Authors: Berger E.; Arumainayagam M.; Dong Z.; Schneider L.; Wang T.; Nichols G.; Kahn S.; Dutta R.; Wang G.; Taniguchi T.; Watanabe K.; Naik M.; Zaletel M.; Wang F.; Crommie M.
Article.Abstract: Two-dimensional moiré materials provide a versatile platform to explore phase transitions in strongly correlated systems. Using scanning tunneling microscopy, we imaged the density-driven melting of generalized Wigner crystals (GWCs) and Mott insulators (MIs) in electron-doped, near-60°–twisted molybdenum diselenide bilayers featuring a triangular moiré superlattice. We observed notable electron-hole asymmetry in GWC melting: Hole-doped GWCs yielded interaction-driven disordered states, whereas electron-doped GWCs melted into delocalized liquid-like states. This asymmetry arose from the broken particle-hole symmetry of the moiré superlattice, which produced electron and hole Fermi pockets with different momentum geometries upon GWC condensation. MI states melted without such asymmetry, consistent with the absence of a symmetry-breaking density modulation. This work provides direct visualization of the emergent phases that appear as GWCs undergo quantum melting transitions.

Article.Title: Visualizing symmetry-broken Chern insulators and their quantum melting
Article.Authors: He M.; Tsui Y.; Peng R.; Watanabe K.; Taniguchi T.; Vafek O.; Yazdani A.
Article.Abstract: In the presence of a magnetic field, electronic states of moiré quantum materials develop a Hofstadter spectrum that provides a distinctive setting for studying the interplay between band topology and strong electron-electron interaction. Our measurements revealed the formation of phases that double, triple, or quadruple the moiré unit cell at fractional filling of the Hofstadter bands as well as states with complex intra–unit cell wave functions. Article.Abstract: The power conversion efficiency (PCE) and stability of flexible perovskite solar modules (PSMs) are less than those of their rigid devices because surface hydroxyls desorption on flexible substrates, which disrupts self-assembled monolayer (SAM) anchoring and perovskite crystallization. Article.Title: The AI debate is missing half the system
Article.Authors: Michelucci P.
Article.Abstract: Last month, leading executives of artificial intelligence (AI) companies warned the United Nations Security Council about the risks of losing human control over this rapidly advancing technology. Their recommendations focused heavily on safeguards, evaluation, and governance of AI models and systems, largely overlooking the risks that arise from the interactions of AI with people and institutions. AI safety needs to be addressed at the level of the human–AI system, not the AI model alone.

Article.Title: Modular van der Waals MOSFETs through layer-by-layer chalcogen substitutions
Article.Authors: Min S.; Cho H.; Lee S.; Choi J.; Kim T.; Choi J.; Park H.; Yoon J.; Mo T.; Nayak C.; Kim G.; Her S.; Lee C.; Kim Y.; Choi S.; Kim C.; Jo M.
Article.Abstract: In two-dimensional transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), the local electrostatic field of the chalcogen p -orbitals dictates the crystal field splitting of the transition metal d -orbitals, stabilizing diverse electronic states from semiconducting and semimetallic to exotic topological phases. On-demand substitution of the lattice chalcogens is therefore an efficient route to tuning TMDC electronic phases. Here, we custom-molded van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures by layer-by-layer vapor-phase chalcogen substitution starting from p -type WSe 2 multilayers into which we locally inscribed insulating WO x , n -type WS 2 , and semimetallic WTe 2 . This spatially precise conversion seamlessly integrated distinct electronic phases, both vertically and laterally, into modular vdW semiconductor heterostructures that are otherwise inaccessible. As a demonstration, we integrated WO x /WSe 2 local gate stacks to build ultrascaled metal oxide–semiconductor field effect transistors (MOSFETs), achieving an unprecedented subthreshold swing at subnanometer equivalent oxide thickness.

Article.Title: To reverse nature loss, change what drives it
Article.Authors: Cooper D.; Díaz S.
Article.Abstract: This week, at the 17th Meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17), delegates from 195 countries and the European Union are gathering in Yerevan, Armenia, for a global review of progress under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, an international set of goals and targets adopted in 2022 to tackle the biodiversity crisis. The urgent question before them is clear: What must change now to halt and reverse nature’s decline and put it on a path to recovery by 2030? COP-17 comes as international cooperation is under increasing strain. Extreme weather is intensifying, ecosystem deterioration is creating new security risks, and geopolitical tensions are rising. Yet nature’s decline does not pause for geopolitical instability—it deepens it. That makes effective multilateralism, with North and South as equal partners, more important, not less.

Article.Title: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics of cellular heterogeneity in Alzheimer disease
Article.Authors: Emerson N.; Vallejo K.; Rahimzadeh N.; Kwang N.; Swarup V.
Article.Abstract: Alzheimer disease (AD) is defined neuropathologically by the presence of amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles, yet these canonical lesions alone cannot account for its clinical, regional and cellular heterogeneity. AD is a multicellular, spatially organized disease shaped by the interactions of neurons, glia and vascular cells within distinct anatomical microenvironments. Single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing have made it possible to dissect the transcriptional signatures of individual cell populations in the AD brain, revealing selective neuronal vulnerability, stage-dependent glial remodelling and widespread disruption of cell-cell communication networks, whereas spatial transcriptomics and multiplexed imaging have anchored these molecular changes to their tissue context. Studies of defined populations, such as people with autosomal-dominant AD or Down syndrome-associated AD, and of the oldest-old cohorts help disentangle the molecular changes that are causal drivers from those that are downstream consequences. Across individuals, AD heterogeneity is further shaped by sex and ancestry, underscoring the need for broader representation of these factors in single-cell and spatial studies. These advances are also reshaping translational pipelines through multi-omic benchmarking of animal models and single-cell-based drug-repurposing strategies. Thus, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics are redefining our understanding of AD heterogeneity and informing precision approaches to treatment.

Article.Title: The nanotubular network as a new dimension of intercellular communication in the nervous system
Article.Authors: Chang M.; Ryu S.; Kwon H.
Article.Abstract: Communication between cells in the nervous system has long been understood to occur through chemical and electrical synapses, and through the release of signalling molecules and extracellular vesicles across the extracellular space. Intercellular nanotubes (NTs) - thin, membranous tubular bridges that physically connect distant cells - represent a structurally distinct route of communication, enabling the direct, targeted transfer of cellular cargoes between selected cells. Once studied almost exclusively in culture, NTs have now been visualized in situ and in vivo throughout the nervous system, including dendritic NTs between neurons, NTs formed by microglia and astrocytes, interpericyte NTs in the retina and NTs between satellite glia and peripheral sensory neurons. Through these connections, cells exchange mitochondria, proteins and their aggregates, and calcium, supporting three emerging roles: homeostatic rescue of stressed cells, pathological propagation of toxic proteins in neurodegeneration and non-synaptic calcium signalling, respectively. NT networks are dynamic and stress-responsive, suggesting that they provide a plastic infrastructure for resource sharing among neurons and glia. Understanding their function will require establishing a standardized definition, achieving rigorous in situ validation and quantification, and developing specific molecular tools to manipulate NTs.

Article.Title: Interneurons and network activity in the cerebral cortex: a developmental dialogue
Article.Authors: Moissidis M.; Marín O.
Article.Abstract: The mammalian cerebral cortex undergoes profound functional changes during early postnatal development. During this period, neurons generate spontaneous electrical activity long before sensory experience, coordinating into distinct patterns of synchronous activity. Traditionally, neuronal activity has been viewed as instructing interneuron development by modulating transcriptional programmes, morphology and connectivity. However, accumulating evidence in rodents reveals that this relationship is bidirectional: cortical interneurons are not merely passive recipients of activity-dependent signals but also active architects of developing network dynamics. They regulate spontaneous activity transitions from gap-junction-mediated synchronous events to large, synaptically driven bursts, and later to sparse firing characteristic of mature circuits. Critically, different interneuron subtypes mature at distinct timelines and orchestrate transitions in network activity. Activity-dependent mechanisms, in turn, regulate interneuron wiring, programmed cell death, diversification and terminal differentiation. This reciprocal dialogue between interneurons and network activity is essential for establishing functional cortical circuits.

Article.Title: The endocannabinoid system and the ageing brain
Article.Authors: Zimmer A.
Article.Abstract: Ageing is accompanied by a progressive decline in homeostatic resilience that increases vulnerability to chronic disease, disability and cognitive impairment. Although unhealthy brain ageing can often be prevented by managing the underlying risk factors, the molecular, cellular and physiological mechanisms that connect risk factors to late-life brain dysfunction remain incompletely understood. This review examines the role of the endocannabinoid system in brain ageing. The endocannabinoid system is a short-range lipid signalling network that helps to maintain neuronal, glial, metabolic and inflammatory homeostasis. Endocannabinoid signalling follows a dynamic lifespan trajectory, with relatively high activity during early adulthood and functional decline during ageing. Genetic or pharmacological disruption of endocannabinoid system activity impairs several processes linked to hallmarks of brain ageing, including neuroinflammatory control, adult neurogenesis, synaptic plasticity, cognitive performance, metabolic regulation and epigenetic stability. Conversely, low-dose Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) treatment can ameliorate several ageing-related brain phenotypes in old animals. However, clinical evidence in older humans remains limited, and the therapeutic potential of cannabinoid-based interventions requires further evaluation.

Article.Title: Integration and annotation of spatial multi-omic data with DIRAC
Article.Authors: Xu C.; Liu S.; Heng Y.; Yang C.; Cao Y.; Gao J.; Wei S.; Jia D.; Liang D.; Ma Y.; Ng S.; Li H.; Zhang X.; Gong Y.; Shen H.; Deng H.; Chen A.; Xu X.; Liao S.; Jiang Q.; Liu B.
Article.Abstract: Spatial multi-omic technologies measure multiple molecular layers within intact tissues. Two central challenges are vertical integration, which combines different molecular modalities, and horizontal integration, which aligns cell types across studies. Here we show domain invariant representation through adaptive calibration (DIRAC), a geometric deep learning model that unifies these tasks in a generalized domain adaptation framework. DIRAC learns task-discriminative features that are insensitive to domain shifts caused by batch effects, omic modalities or study sites, enabling a shared embedding space and automated cell-type annotation through label transfer from reference datasets. Across sequencing-based and imaging-based datasets, DIRAC identified a new microvascular proliferation domain in glioblastoma, corrected cortical-layer annotations in severe Alzheimer's disease, resolved subtle structures in mouse embryos and remained robust to missing data and unseen cell types. We generated mouse spleen and thymus Stereo-CITE-seq data and used DIRAC to reveal thymic T cell migration and splenic immune cell interactions. DIRAC is fast and scales to millions of cells.

Article.Title: Automated identification of individual birds by song enables multi-year recapture from passive acoustic monitoring data
Article.Authors: Lapp S.; Lyon R.; Wilson S.; Rhinehart T.; Czarnecki C.; Chronister L.; Fiss C.; Larkin J.; Bayne E.; Kitzes J.
Article.Abstract: Autonomous sensors and machine learning are transforming ecology by enabling large-scale observation of organisms and ecosystems. However, camera traps, audio recorders and other sensors currently produce species-level detections. Tracking individuals continues to require invasive, high-effort capture-mark-recapture. Here we introduce an automated, general approach that identifies individual animals in passive acoustic recordings based on individually distinctive vocalizations. We train a convolutional neural network to extract salient features from audio recordings using a location-prediction task, then apply dimensionality reduction and clustering on features to achieve song-based individual identification. We identify individuals not included in the training data with 96% accuracy. We apply this approach to track 405 male ovenbirds (Seiurus aurocapilla) from 126 locations across 4 years, then model abundance and apparent survival. We provide open-source code to facilitate applications of our approach to other species. Performing automated individual identification on passive acoustic datasets will support the study of population trajectories and inform proactive ecosystem management to prevent biodiversity loss.

Article.Title: abcFISH enables multiplexed, single-molecule visualization of circular RNA spatial heterogeneity
Article.Authors: Liu Y.; Jiang B.; Liu K.; Yang L.; Chen L.
Article.Abstract: Understanding the subcellular localization of RNAs is critical for their functions, but visualizing circular RNAs (circRNAs) has been hindered by their sequence overlap with linear counterparts. Here we developed amplicon-based circRNA fluorescence in situ hybridization (abcFISH), which uses an optimized rolling-circle amplification strategy targeting back-splicing junction sites for robust, high specificity, single-molecule circRNA imaging. abcFISH enables quantitative, multiplexed imaging in cells and tissues, allowing us to reveal alternative circularization patterns from the single locus, uncover cell-type-specific circRNA expression linked to combinatorial effects of RNA-binding proteins, map distinct spatial distribution patterns of circRNAs in neurons and brain tissues, and show functional colocalization of circRNA Cdr1as and long noncoding RNA Cyrano. We further applied abcFISH to validate therapeutic double-stranded circRNA aptamers, simultaneously visualizing AAV-delivered double-stranded circRNA aptamers and the resulting reduction in astrocyte infiltration around transduced cells. Collectively, abcFISH provides a robust, user-friendly toolkit for deciphering circRNA localization and function in vivo.
