Article.Title: Weakened association between sequential phenological events corresponds to interphase extension
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Gao M.; Zhang Y.; Peñuelas J.; Fu Y.; Wu C.; Xia J.; Hong S.; Piao S.
Article.Abstract: The sequential occurrence of leaf unfolding, flowering, fruiting, foliar senescence and other life-cycle events constitutes a full cycle of plant phenology. Temporal shifts in the seasonal timing of these phenophases have been regarded as key evidence of global environmental change. Most previous studies, however, have focused on the timing of individual phenophases. Little is known about the relationships between changes in timing across sequential phenophases. Here, using in-situ phenological records of major European tree species between 1980 and 2017, we show strong positive associations between consecutive phenophases. In particular, the statistical relationship between the timing of consecutive phenophases is comparable to that of temperature for spring phenological events and substantially exceeds the relationship with climatic factors for late-season phenological events. However, the associations themselves have shifted across years, with a significant decrease in the association between the timing of fruit ripening and autumnal coloration, corresponding to the largest extension of interphase duration. Current process-based phenological models largely overlook associations between consecutive phenological events and their interplay with climate change, potentially leading to biased projections of phenological changes and ecosystem adaptation to future climate change. Seasonal events in temperate deciduous trees, from leaf-out to leaf fall, follow a fixed annual sequence. This study shows that the timing of consecutive events is statistically associated in European trees, but that the association between fruiting and leaf coloration has weakened in some species as the interval between these phases has increased.

Article.Title: B7-H4‒directed antibody-drug conjugate AZD8205 (puxitatug samrotecan) in patients with advanced/metastatic solid tumors: the Phase 1/2a (BLUESTAR), first-in-human study
Article.Authors: Meric-Bernstam F.; Naito Y.; Gaillard S.; Shimoi T.; Chung V.; Davis A.; Proia T.; Wang J.; Dubois V.; Rebelatto M.; McFarlane M.; Kulkarni M.; Upadhyay S.; Tian J.; Miller N.; Luheshi N.; Varga A.; Oh D.; Mileshkin L.
Article.Abstract: B7-H4 is a promising antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) target with high expression in several solid tumors and limited expression in normal tissue. AZD8205 (puxitatug samrotecan [Puxi-Sam]) is a novel B7-H4–directed ADC with a stable cleavable linker and a bystander-capable topoisomerase-1 (TOP1) inhibitor payload. The primary objectives were to evaluate the safety and tolerability of Puxi-Sam (incidence of adverse events [AE], serious AEs and dose-limiting toxicities), and to determine the maximum tolerated dose and/or recommended phase 2 dose of Puxi-Sam. Secondary objectives included characterizing the pharmacokinetics, assessing the antitumor activity (objective response rate [ORR]), and determining the pharmacodynamics of Puxi-Sam. The most common treatment-related adverse events were nausea (51.1%), neutropenia (48.9%) and anemia (38.3%). At 3.2 mg/kg, dose-limiting neutropenia and thrombocytopenia were observed. In patients treated at ≥1.6 mg/kg (predicted efficacious range), partial responses were observed in ovarian, endometrial and breast cancer (ORR 20.5% [9/44]). Translational data indicated selective localization of the TOP1 inhibitor payload to B7-H4–expressing tumor cells and induction of target-dependent DNA damage. In this first-in-human trial, the authors report safety and efficacy outcomes for B7-H4–directed antibody-drug conjugate AZD8205 (puxitatug samrotecan) in patients with heavily pretreated ovarian, endometrial, and breast cancers, and cholangiocarcinoma.

Article.Authors: Kitamura N.; Shinomiya H.; Kawanishi M.; Konishi N.; Ohya K.; Tomita H.; Asano Y.; Kimura C.; Sekiguchi H.; Ozawa M.; Ishihara K.; Kurushima J.; Tanimoto K.; Nomura T.; Hashimoto Y.; N/A N/A.; Hirai S.; Fukuguchi Y.; Aoki N.; Otsuka Y.; Yamagami T.; Takahashi Y.; Hashimoto Y.; Osanai S.; Iwama T.

Agona isolates carrying fosA7.2, with pairwise SNP distances of 13–15 SNPs, suggesting that resistant Salmonella strains are shared between human and food sectors. For Campylobacter, we identified closely related human- and food-derived ST-22 isolates carrying a tetracycline resistance gene and a fluoroquinolone resistance-conferring gyrA mutation, with a pairwise SNP distance of 4 SNPs. These findings highlight potential genetic links of antimicrobial-resistant foodborne bacteria between food and humans. In this study, the authors use nationwide genomic data collected across sectors in Japan to identify closely related antimicrobial-resistant Salmonella and Campylobacter isolates in food and humans, highlighting the value of integrated One Health surveillance.

Complementary pH 5.0 measurements reveal additional mechanistic features and, together, these datasets define the transport cycle in a membrane-embedded context. Supported by molecular dynamics simulations, the results reveal a coordinated, transport cycle-dependent mechanism in which paired catalytic carboxylates act sequentially in substrate binding, proton relay, gate control, and transporter resetting.

Article.Abstract: Biomolecular condensates have so far been studied in terms of their structural, compositional, and functional properties. Article.Title: Canopy nutrient balance predicts autumn senescence across U.S. forests
Article.Authors: Chen H.; Wei Y.; Townsend P.; Kovach K.; Finley A.; Peñuelas J.; Qiu T.
Article.Abstract: Terrestrial ecosystems are changing rapidly under global nutrient enrichment, yet how canopy nutrients balance shapes the seasonal end of photosynthesis, a critical control on ecosystem carbon cycling, remains unclear. Rising anthropogenic nitrogen inputs are shifting many ecosystems towards relative phosphorus limitation, with uncertain consequences for autumn phenology. Here, we combined airborne imaging spectroscopy with remotely sensed phenology to test whether canopy nutrient ratios predict spatial variations in autumn senescence across National Ecological Observatory Network sites in the United States. Higher canopy N:P is consistently associated with earlier senescence in 20 out of 25 sites, whereas higher N:K has opposite effects in 19 sites after controlling for climate, elevation, dominant species, and canopy structure. Growing-season productivity is generally related to later senescence, but only modestly mediates the direct nutrient-phenology associations. These findings add a phenological dimension to the functional impacts of nutrient imbalance on terrestrial ecosystems and demonstrate that nutrients provide predictive power beyond climate alone. Continued nitrogen deposition is expected to increase relative phosphorus limitation, a shift that could be associated with earlier senescence and shorter growing season. Incorporating canopy nutrients into phenological models may therefore improve forecasts of canopy duration and carbon fluxes under ongoing nutrient enrichment.

Article.Title: Video-rate volumetric chemical imaging via mid-infrared photothermal optical diffraction tomography
Article.Authors: Fukushima M.; Toda K.; Sugawara Y.; Kawano S.; Ideguchi T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Label-free vibrational microscopy provides chemically specific access to cellular structures, yet quantitative volumetric imaging of intracellular dynamics remains challenging on subsecond timescales. Here, we demonstrate video-rate mid-infrared photothermal optical diffraction tomography (MIP-ODT) by combining high photothermal sensitivity with rapid angular scanning. The system achieves 19.2 volumes per second, nearly 400 times faster than previous MIP tomography implementations, with a signal-to-noise ratio exceeding 70 and no temporal averaging. We track lipid droplets in living cells and quantify anomalous diffusion from three-dimensional trajectories, revealing heterogeneous intracellular transport behaviors obscured in two-dimensional measurements. Rapid mid-infrared wavenumber sweeping further enables broadband multi-wavenumber volumetric chemical imaging across a 300 cm⁻¹ spectral window within 1 s. These results establish MIP-ODT as a platform for high-speed, label-free volumetric chemical imaging of single cells and quantitative investigation of dynamic intracellular organization.

Article.Title: Towards the real diamond formation conditions: insights and perspective
Article.Authors: Murri M.; Gilio M.; Nestola F.; Duretz T.; Marone F.
Article.Abstract: Pressure and temperature conditions of diamond formation provide valuable insights for reconstructing paleo-geotherms and the deep carbon cycle. These conditions can be determined by investigating mineral inclusions in diamonds using elastic geobarometry, which can be applied to any mineral inclusion in a diamond. However, it assumes purely elastic host-inclusion behaviour throughout exhumation. In reality, almost all mineral inclusions in diamonds are surrounded by cracks. Here, we combine in situ high-temperature micro-Raman spectroscopy with thermo-elastic modelling to evaluate the pressure-release process in one of the most common diamond inclusions, olivine [(Mg,Fe)2SiO4]. Our results indicate that a diamond can sustain pressures of ~2.5 GPa before undergoing minor fracturing, which induces only partial loss of inclusion pressure rather than a complete reset. The estimated pressure loss can lead to an underestimation of up to 2.5 GPa in the entrapment pressure at 1150 °C, a typical temperature for diamond formation. This study shows that olivine in diamond can undergo partial release of pressure during kimberlite eruptions due to fast adiabatic decompression, leading to cracked olivine inclusions and entrapment pressures underestimated by up to 2.5 GPa at 1150 °C

Article.Title: Liquid-metal physical unclonable functions resistant to both physical and digital cloning
Article.Authors: Lee S.; Kim M.; Kim W.; Heo S.; Ahn Y.; Lee J.; Kwon D.; Oh S.; Yoon S.; Dickey M.; Song Y.; Jeong J.
Article.Abstract: Physical unclonable functions (PUFs) leverage device-specific randomness for hardware security, yet their static, persistently accessible responses allow attackers to collect sufficient data for digital cloning. We present a liquid-metal PUF (LM-PUF) that integrates physical unclonability with material-driven resistance to digital attacks. Randomly mixed, visually indistinguishable LM particles form thermally unique microstructures, ensuring physical unclonability. Digital protection arises from two concealment mechanisms: time-limited accessibility restricts meaningful data collection, while decoy obscuration prevents reliable key identification. At equilibrium, the device remains cryptographically silent, but heating through a transient non-equilibrium window reveals thermal patterns convertible to cryptographic keys. Outside the predefined temperature range, misleading thermal patterns conceal the authentic key among decoys. LM-PUF supports scalable patterning, demonstrated in secure labels and QR codes, highlighting its potential for secure supply chains and physical unclonable authentication. Physical unclonable functions (PUFs) secure hardware identity but can be digitally cloned by machine-learning attacks. Here, authors report a liquid-metal PUF whose thermal keys appear only briefly during heating and are hidden among decoys, resisting both physical and digital cloning.

Article.Title: Observation of quantized charge accumulation in a quantum anomalous Hall system
Article.Authors: Li Y.; Chen J.; Wang R.; Zhang Y.; Deng Y.; Xie J.; Kou X.; Liu Y.; Liang T.
Article.Abstract: The quantum anomalous Hall effect in magnetically doped topological insulators exhibits a quantized Hall conductance σxy = e2/h arising from the two-dimensional surface states. While conventional transport probes confirm this quantization, they remain insensitive to the field-induced surface charge accumulation as a direct manifestation of σxy. Here, we experimentally validate an out-of-plane capacitive method that directly detects this quantized charge accumulation in a quantum anomalous Hall system. Using Corbino and simple disk devices, we measure charge accumulation proportional to field variation ΔB, with dissipation characterized by longitudinal conductance σxx and frequency f. A quantitative dissipation model extracts the intrinsic quantized charge density η0 = (e2/h)ΔB, which is confirmed through f- and σxx-dependent measurements. Under ultra-low dissipation (σxx ≈ 10−9 S), we directly resolve the fully quantized charge accumulation. This methodology establishes a direct charge-accumulation probe and provides a pathway toward detecting the topological magnetoelectric effect, a condensed matter manifestation of the four-dimensional quantum Hall effect. The quantum anomalous Hall effect in a magnetically doped topological insulator exhibits a quantized Hall conductance. Here, the authors demonstrate an out-of-plane capacitive method that directly measures field-induced quantized charge accumulation originating from the quantized Hall conductance.

Article.Title: Ultrahigh strength aluminum alloy by green laser additive manufacturing
Article.Authors: Liu T.; Cheng X.; Mikula J.; Ng F.; Xiong L.; Zhao Y.; Laskowski R.; Luan J.; Wu X.; Tan C.
Article.Abstract: Infrared laser additive manufacturing of high-strength 7××× aluminum (Al) alloys is hindered by low absorptivity, high cracking-susceptibility, and insufficient precipitation strengthening. Herein, we investigate a new approach to process high-performance AA7075 by integrating green laser directed energy deposition (L-DED) with nano-TiC embedded composite AA7075 powder. The green laser achieves better energy-material coupling, enabling high-quality deposition at a lower laser power than conventional infrared lasers. The green laser also stabilizes the melt pool, reduces thermal gradients and elemental evaporation, and promotes more uniform grains with lower dislocation density. Heat treatment yields an ultra-high density of nano-scale η′ precipitates and GP zones (~2.13×1016 m−2) in the green laser deposited Al alloy, achieving a tensile yield strength of ~600 MPa, which is higher than forged AA7075 and almost all L-DED-processed Al alloys hitherto reported. This work presents an integrated material-process strategy for additive manufacturing of highly reflective, hot-crack-susceptible alloys using short-wavelength lasers. Cracking and poor laser absorption curbed additive manufacturing of high-strength aluminium alloys. Using a TiC/AA7075 composite powder and a green wavelength laser, researchers produced crack-free aluminum alloy with a yield strength of nearly 600 MPa.

Article.Title: A multilamellar organelle for chemosymbiosis in an aplacophoran mollusc adapted to anoxic cold seep sediment
Article.Authors: Li Y.; Chen C.; Liu X.; Li M.; Yan G.; Zhou H.; Wang H.; Zheng X.; He X.; Liu S.; Qiu J.; Qian P.; Sun J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Symbiosis with chemoautotrophic bacteria has evolved in many animal lineages inhabiting reducing habitats such as hydrothermal vents, allowing these holobionts to thrive in dark biospheres 1 . In certain instances, the symbionts have become intracellular, residing within specialised bacteriocytes 2 . The integration of microbial symbionts with eukaryotic cells vary across known animals; however, no specialised organelle dedicated to chemosynthesis has been identified yet 2 . Here, we report a mode of symbiosis where sulphur-oxidising bacteria cultured within spherical multilamellar compartments (~12 μm) in the cold-seep aplacophoran mollusc Chaetoderma shenloong . This organelle, which we name ‘dracosphera’, is ubiquitous within the hypertrophied and intricately reticulate digestive gland of C. shenloong , which has otherwise lost most of its gut. Given that the symbionts are strictly anaerobic and the host resides in anoxic sediments tens of centimetres below the surface, the dracosphera may serve to minimise oxygen diffusion to the bacteria, akin to mechanisms observed in microbial diazotrophs 3 or termite hindguts 4 , as supported by our genomic and spatial transcriptomic analyses. Hypoxic conditions have been known to induce radical adaptations in meiofauna, exemplified by the acquisition of hydrogenosomes 5 . Our discovery of similarly exceptional adaptations in C. shenloong provides new insights into the evolution of such organelles also in larger animals.

Article.Title: Precise modular engineering of neutral organometallic rectangles from binuclear palladacycles via hierarchical assembly strategy
Article.Authors: Ma Y.; Duan L.; Hou T.; Zhang J.; Sun H.; Ma R.; Tu T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Metallosupramolecular assembly provides a powerful strategy for the precise construction of well-defined architectures with diverse topologies and functionalities. However, the construction of neutral organometallic architectures supported by robust metal-carbon bonds remains underdeveloped, largely because kinetic persistence limits the reversible structural correction required for conventional self-assembly. Herein, we employ binuclear palladacycles as intrinsically neutral and geometrically preorganized building blocks and develop a hierarchical assembly strategy that temporally separates geometric programming, scaffold editing, and topology locking. Through a polymerization-cleavage-assembly process, cyclopalladated polymers are converted into discrete binuclear precursors while retaining their programmed geometrical information. Subsequent trans-effect-directed N -heterocyclic carbene ligation affords a series of size-tunable, kinetically robust, and neutral organometallic rectangles. The resulting architectures are fully characterized by spectroscopic methods and single crystal X-ray diffraction analyses. Moreover, single crystal X-ray diffraction identifies guest-mediated breathing-like geometric deformations in the solid state, driven by exo-wall π-π stacking and charge-transfer interactions with both electron-rich and electron-deficient planar guests. This work establishes a hierarchical construction principle for accessing discrete neutral organometallic architectures by separating geometric programming from the final locking of the topology through strong bond formation, while demonstrating that local geometric adaptation can occur without disrupting the framework connectivity established by Pd-C bonds.

Article.Title: Programmable hydrogel-nanocapsule protein delivery system targeting dense cartilage regeneration for osteoarthritis therapy
Article.Authors: Zhu Q.; Sun W.; Su H.; Wang T.; Yan Y.; Li R.; Chen Y.; Fang J.; Zhang Y.; Zhang J.; Mo R.; Ouyang H.
Article.Abstract: The clinical translation of protein therapeutics for osteoarthritis has been hampered by rapid synovial clearance, poor penetration into cartilage, and insufficient retention under joint loading. In this work, we develop hydro/nano-bFGF, a programmable system that integrates an FGF-loaded nanocapsule (nano-bFGF) with an injectable, cartilage-adhesive hydrogel. Nano-bFGF is generated through interfacial polymerization of monomers with enzyme-cleavable crosslinkers directly on the protein surface, forming a nanoscale shell that preserves bioactivity while enabling pathology-specific disassembly. The hydrogel anchors nano-bFGF to the cartilage surface and undergoes gradual degradation in response to disease-associated enzymatic activity, allowing spatiotemporally programmed release aligned with the joint microenvironment. This spatiotemporally controlled design enhances intra-cartilage transport, prolongs local retention, and maintains growth factor functionality. In human osteoarthritic cartilage explants, nano-bFGF doubles glycosaminoglycan deposition and triples type II collagen expression. In a rat model, hydro/nano-bFGF restores cartilage integrity, preserves subchondral bone architecture, and achieves restoration of cartilage thickness. Owing to its modular design, this strategy is broadly adaptable to diverse protein therapeutics and degenerative joint diseases, offering a generalizable platform for spatiotemporally precise biologic delivery. In osteoarthritis, protein therapeutics show poor joint retention and cartilage penetration. Here, authors develop a programmable two-stage, enzyme-responsive hydrogel-nanocapsule system to deliver a model protein drug and promote cartilage regeneration.

Article.Abstract: Abstract The hydrogenation of carbon dioxide to value-added chemicals is a major challenge. Metal-oxide interfaces and surface structures play fundamental roles and govern the selectivity of this reaction; thus, catalysts must be investigated under relevant reaction conditions to identify structure-activity relationships and engineer more efficient materials. This work aims to elucidate mechanisms of carbon dioxide hydrogenation to methanol and side products by using operando characterization techniques within a pressure range of 1 mbar up to 15 bar. Bifunctional Ag/ZnO and Ag/ZnO:Al 2 O 3 catalysts are studied using multiple spectroscopic techniques combined with online product analysis. During catalyst activation in hydrogen, several restructuring processes of the catalyst occur at different pressures. Under carbon dioxide hydrogenation reaction conditions carbonate, formate and CH x surface intermediates show strong pressure-dependent abundances. Combining thermodynamics with in situ and operando investigations of pressure-dependent structures and intermediates allows assessing carbon dioxide hydrogenation through the pressure gap.

Article.Authors: Liu J.; Schäfer S.; Lehnung S.; Baumann L.; Mühlberg L.; Steiner C.; Schreiber M.; Linder M.; Welsch S.; Liu F.; Bogdanow B.; Krijnse Locker J.; Turoňová B.

The pore is formed by a heteromeric assembly of the viral proteins E8, E6, and L3, which together create a hollow hexameric tube spanning both the core wall and the surface-exposed palisade layer. Within the pore channel, we observe a rod-like density consistent with the viral RNA helicase I8, which may contribute to the release of the newly synthesized viral mRNAs from the core. We further observe a state of the pore lacking the outer and basal rings under transcription conditions. Article.Title: Recruitment of TEX15 by HUSH2 drives repression of multicopy gene families in fertility regulation
Article.Authors: Yang F.; Yoon S.; Jaiswal A.; Kang Z.; Leu N.; Monahan K.; Wang P.
Article.Abstract: Chromatin-associated proteins are key regulators of fertility. While the testis-specific protein TEX15 and a HUSH2 component TASOR2 have established roles in early germ cells and somatic cells respectively, this study identifies their cooperative role during spermiogenesis. Postnatal loss of either TEX15 or TASOR2 in mice causes teratozoospermia without retrotransposon de-repression. Mechanistically, TEX15 complexes with TASOR2 but not its paralogue TASOR in the testis. The resulting TEX15-HUSH2 complex localizes to nuclear foci in round spermatids, particularly at XY chromatin, with TASOR2 acting as the recruiter. TASOR2 and MPP8 preferentially bind to multicopy gene families in round spermatids. Consequently, many of these families—including the X-linked H2al histone-like genes—are upregulated in both TEX15-deficient spermatids and TASOR2-deficient testis. Together, these findings show that the TEX15-HUSH2 complex represses multicopy gene families during spermiogenesis, revealing a molecular mechanism underlying postmeiotic repression of sex chromatin critical for male fertility. In this study, Yang et al showed that the TEX15-HUSH2 complex represses multicopy gene families in haploid spermatids. Their study revealed a molecular mechanism underlying postmeiotic repression of sex chromatin (PMSC) critical for male fertility.

Article.Authors: Lu X.; Wang Z.; Zhu J.; Hang Y.; Lu X.; Sun J.; Cai Y.; Zhao C.
Article.Abstract: Topological light fields, with their robust properties, offer transformative potential across photonics. However, achieving flexible manipulation and practical deployment of topological light fields in hard-to-reach areas remains challenging. To overcome this limitation, we propose an adaptive topological light endoscopic system (ATLES) and pioneer an integrated transceiver design based on a multi-core fiber, enabling minimally invasive detection with topological light field manipulation. Leveraging the ATLES framework, we reconfigure a 10,000-core fiber into a high-resolution modulator for phase, amplitude, and coherence control. This enables the on-demand creation of both coherent and incoherent topological light fields, tailored in their structures, directly from a bare fiber tip of just 350 μm in diameter. We demonstrate the power of this approach by performing highly precise rotational velocity measurements under endoscopic conditions, achieving a relative error below 0.055%. Our work establishes a versatile platform for the implementation of topological photonics in hard-to-reach areas, thereby paving the way for their application in biomedical imaging and optical computing. This study presents a 350 μm-wide lensless fiber endoscope that creates tailored topological light and measures rotation with relative errors below 0.055%, enabling precise optical control and sensing in hard-to-reach spaces.

Article.Authors: Troman L.; Paul B.; Kim J.; Fenno J.; Goetting-Minesky M.; Reynolds E.; Banfield J.; Veith P.; Ghosal D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Spirochetes are spiral-shaped bacteria whose curved periplasmic flagella drive corkscrew-like motility through viscous environments. We show sheath asymmetry imposes differential axial compaction on the FlaB1/2 core, generating convex and concave filament faces and establishing curvature. FlaB sequence and glycosylation differences at sheath–core interfaces correlate with selective incorporation into distinct filament types, supporting a mechanism for regulated filament architecture. Phylogenetic analysis reveals FlaL conservation across spirochete lineages, suggesting modular sheath lattices provide an adaptable mechanism for tuning flagellar mechanics across diverse pathogenic lifestyles.

Article.Title: Genomic surveillance meets clinical practice: rule-based individualized treatment prediction for gonorrhoea using SensiTyper
Article.Authors: Golparian D.; Sánchez-Busó L.; Unemo M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Extensively drug-resistant (XDR) Neisseria gonorrhoeae strains threaten the current empirical gonorrhoea treatment. We designed and analytically validated SensiTyper, a rule-based framework that predicts antimicrobial susceptibility from whole-genome sequencing data and generates susceptibility-guided individualized treatment recommendations. SensiTyper was applied to 13,701 gonococcal genomes from 68 countries in 1928-2024, including cultured isolates and clinical molecular samples, and benchmarked predictions against previous genomic and phenotypic data. Susceptibility predictions for ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin, spectinomycin, and zoliflodacin had 98.9-100% sensitivity and specificity. Azithromycin susceptibility predictions had 92.5% sensitivity and 97.1% specificity, and gepotidacin susceptibility prediction 100% sensitivity, but 0% specificity, illustrating that low-level phenotypic gepotidacin resistance is not caused by the only known resistance determinants (GyrA A92T plus ParC D86N). The SensiTreat module integrates antimicrobial susceptibility profiles into sequential treatment logic, providing susceptibility-guided individualized treatment recommendations while also enabling alternative stewardship strategies prioritizing, e.g., ciprofloxacin. SensiTyper flags XDR isolates for expert follow-up, test-of-cure and comprehensive contact tracing. In conclusion, SensiTyper is a robust and adaptable approach for gonococcal antimicrobial susceptibility prediction, individualized gonorrhoea treatment and antimicrobial stewardship.

Article.Title: Process-dependent shifts in conspecific negative density dependence during boreal forest succession
Article.Authors: Zhu Y.; Chen C.; Chen H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Conspecific negative density dependence (CNDD)—the stronger negative effects of conspecific than heterospecific neighbours on plant demographic performance—is a key process proposed to stabilize forest diversity, yet how it changes during succession remains poorly understood. Using a 25-year spatially explicit dataset from 148 post-fire plots in boreal forests, we show that species richness increases with stand age and that CNDD varies in process- and abundance-dependent ways across recruitment, survival, and growth. Plot-level CNDD shows no significant change with stand age in recruitment or survival, but mean relative effects are generally stronger for recruitment, and CNDD shifts from destabilizing to stabilizing for growth as stands mature. Species-level CNDD is strongly associated with species abundance, with rare species consistently experiencing stronger CNDD in recruitment and growth, whereas common species tend toward neutral or destabilizing effects. For survival, by contrast, CNDD is stronger in common than in rare species. These abundance-related differences remain broadly consistent across stand development, except in recruitment, where CNDD intensifies in rare species but remains consistently weak or near-neutral in common species. This shifting balance of density-dependent pressures highlights succession-driven trade-offs as central to species coexistence and increases in diversity in disturbance-driven forests.

Article.Title: Ligand hardness as a key feature differentiating base- versus noble-metal mechanisms of nickel-catalyzed Suzuki-Miyaura cross-couplings
Article.Authors: Bardhan A.; Eason E.; Herbert C.; Das T.; Cypcar A.; Yang J.; Hirschi J.; Jarvo E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Nickel-catalyzed cross-coupling reactions that engage alkyl electrophiles provide potential routes for synthesis of molecules with high F sp3 . However, development of these reactions remains a challenge since the impact of ligand identity on competing mechanistic pathways is not yet well understood. To address this knowledge gap, we establish structure-reactivity trends across >550 Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling reactions with known mechanistic pathways. We evaluate reaction outcome by ligand features including heteroatom identity, hybridization, bite angle, geometry, and buried volume. The most important determinant of reactivity is heteroatom identity: nitrogen-based ligands support open-shell reactions while phosphorus-based ligands support closed-shell reactions. Here we report that experimental and calculated reduction potentials and charge density analysis correlate with catalytic activity and propose a rationale for these observations based on hard-soft acid-base theory.

Article.Title: Ancestry-specific and multi-ancestry genome-wide association studies of restless legs syndrome
Article.Authors: Akçimen F.; Medeiros M.; Cederberg K.; Khani M.; Roth A.; Nalls M.; Bandres-Ciga S.; Dion P.; Rouleau G.; Mignot E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Restless legs syndrome is a neurological disorder that disrupts sleep and quality of life, but its genetics have mostly been studied in individuals of European ancestry. Here, we perform GWAS of restless legs syndrome using data from individuals of African, Latin American, and European ancestry, followed by a multi-ancestry meta-analysis. We leverage biobank-based cohorts that established RLS diagnosis using validated clinical criteria, allowing for precise phenotypic characterization. We perform ancestry-specific association studies and post-GWAS analyses to prioritize candidate genes. Our analyses reveal ancestry differences in the genetics of restless legs syndrome. At the MEIS1 and BTBD9 loci, lead variants showed lower allele frequencies and did not reach genome-wide significance in African ancestry. We identify ancestry-specific and shared risk loci, including novel associations near GYPC/TEX51 and PRIMA1 in African ancestry and ISX in Latin American ancestry. The European meta-analysis identifies 11 additional loci and replicates 50 previously reported associations. The combined multi-ancestry analysis finds ten new loci. This multi-ancestry study broadens the genetic understanding of restless legs syndrome, and the absence or reduced frequency of key European restless legs syndrome alleles in individuals of African ancestry provides insights into known epidemiological differences.

Article.Title: Performance of artificial intelligence-assisted cytology and high-risk human papillomavirus testing for cervical cancer screening
Article.Authors: Yan Q.; Gong Y.; Zhou D.; Yang R.; Peng K.; Wang J.; Fan Z.; Wang T.; Yao L.; Zhou A.; Ma J.; Yin X.
Article.Abstract: Evidence comparing cervical cancer screening strategies that combine artificial intelligence-assisted liquid-based cytology (AI-LBC) and high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) testing in large-scale populations is limited. This study includes 284,002 women who underwent AI-LBC and HR-HPV genotyping in community-based screening in Wuhan, China. We evaluate the performance of nine hypothesized screening strategies in detecting cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or worse (CIN2+) and their colposcopy referral rates. After correcting for verification bias, HR-HPV testing alone (Strategy 4) demonstrates higher sensitivity (94.93% vs. 83.88%) and a higher Youden’s index (0.864 vs. 0.789) than AI-LBC alone (Strategy 1), but requires a higher referral rate (9.05% vs. 5.49%). Among the triage-based strategies, Strategy 3 (AI-LBC with reflex HR-HPV) achieves a sensitivity of 82.90%, a referral rate of 2.67%, and a Youden’s index of 0.807. HR-HPV genotyping with reflex AI-LBC (Strategy 7) demonstrates a sensitivity of 92.68%, a Youden’s index of 0.899, and a referral rate of 3.34%. Co-testing of AI-LBC and HR-HPV genotyping (Strategy 9) achieves the highest Youden’s index (0.932), with a sensitivity of 96.37% and a referral rate of 3.70%. These findings suggest that AI-LBC performs well as a standalone screening method, triage tool, or a component a co-testing strategy in cervical cancer screening. When HR-HPV genotyping is available, Strategy 7 or Strategy 9 may be considered, depending on the trade-off between detection performance and referral burden. The authors prove AI-assisted cytology effective for cervical cancer screening. When combined with HPV testing, it detects more precancerous lesions and maintains low referral rates.

Article.Title: Interfacial reinforcement relieves mechanical mismatch for stable perovskite photovoltaics
Article.Authors: Li Y.; Zhang Y.; Zhu S.; Fu S.; Sun N.; Zhu X.; Tan Y.; Wang M.; Zhang W.; Li X.; Yang Z.; Chen H.; Li X.; Fang J.
Article.Abstract: Long-term operational durability under realistic day-night cycling remains a critical bottleneck for the commercialization of perovskite solar cells (PSCs). While significant progress has been made in managing thermo-mechanical stress within the perovskite layer, day-night cycling tolerance remains far from real-world applications, as cycling-induced interface degradation at adjacent functional layers has largely been overlooked. Here, we identify a failure mechanism at the C60/atomic layer deposition (ALD)-SnO2 interface in inverted PSCs, where a severe mismatch in mechanical properties leads to substantial internal stress accumulation, readily causing interfacial delamination and accelerating device degradation. To address this, we introduce graphitic carbon nitride (g-C3N4) as a multifunctional buffer layer between C60 and ALD-SnO2. This two-dimensional material acts as a compliant mechanical bridge, effectively alleviating stress and suppressing microcrack formation, while simultaneously facilitating electron transport across the interface. As a result, the target PSCs achieve a remarkable efficiency of 27.05% and exhibit superior robustness. Notably, the devices retain over 90% of their initial efficiency after 1056 h of maximum power point tracking under day-night cycling. Our findings advance the understanding of interfacial failure mechanisms and provide a practical strategy to support the commercialization of durable PSCs. The day-night cycling durability remains a bottleneck for the commercialization of perovskite photovoltaics. Li et al. introduce g-C3N4 as a buffer layer between C60 and SnO2 to alleviate stress and suppress microcrack. The resulting device achieves a power conversion efficiency of 27.05%.

Article.Title: Sequence Display generates large-scale sequence–activity datasets for reprogramming SlugCas9 toward difficult-to-access PAMs
Article.Authors: Cheng L.; Zheng X.; Ding H.; Jiang S.; Hu Y.; Wang C.; Li C.; Tian Z.; Leeuwon R.; Rui J.; Ye H.; Yuan T.; Liu Y.; Yang K.; Zhou B.; Huang X.; Xiao H.
Article.Abstract: Protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) requirements constrain the targeting scope of CRISPR-Cas9 systems and limit genome editing applications that require precise nuclease positioning. Although broad-PAM and near-PAMless Cas9 variants have expanded the editable genome, robust targeting across certain PAM families remains difficult, particularly at NNAN PAMs. Here, we apply Sequence Display to generate multiplexed, large-scale sequence–activity datasets for Staphylococcus lugdunensis Cas9 (SlugCas9) across the NNAN PAM family, including NNAA, NNAT, NNAC and NNAG. These datasets quantitatively resolve how individual and combinatorial mutations reshape nuclease activity across distinct PAM contexts. By integrating Sequence Display-derived datasets with protein language models, we construct fine-grained activity landscapes and identify SlugCas9 variants with enhanced and broadened activity across NNAN PAMs. The resulting variants reprogram PAM recognition beyond the native G-compatible landscape of SlugCas9 and enable improved base editing at selected endogenous NNAN-constrained sites in cultured mammalian cells, including disease-relevant sites in APOC3 and PCSK9. Together, our results establish a strategy for reprogramming PAM preference in compact Cas9 nucleases and highlight Sequence Display as a general platform for evolving genome editors toward specific and difficult-to-access PAM spaces. Compact CRISPR-Cas9 enzymes are easier to deliver but recognize few targets. Here, authors use Sequence Display to generate large-scale SlugCas9 sequence–activity datasets and apply protein language models to engineer variants that recognize difficult NNAN PAMs and edit selected human genomic sites.

Article.Title: Memristive crossbar architecture for programmable and scalable terahertz metasurface
Article.Authors: Guo H.; Chen B.; Wu J.; Li G.; Wang S.; Zhu W.; Huang X.; Feng Y.; Fan K.; Zhang C.; Ma H.; Zhang X.; He Y.; Wang H.; Jin B.; Chen J.; Wu P.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Programmable terahertz (THz) metasurfaces have emerged as a versatile platform for dynamic wavefront control, offering possibilities for high-capacity wireless communication and advanced sensing. Realizing full wavefront control requires scaling to large-format arrays with pixel-level reconfigurability, but this is fundamentally limited by inter-pixel crosstalk and the increasing complexity of electrical interconnections. Here, we present a scalable, pixel-level programmable metasurface addressing architecture inspired by the crossbar architecture of memristor arrays, and implement it in the THz regime. By integrating VO 2 -based snapback selectors, this design effectively suppresses sneak path currents, allowing low-crosstalk addressing of each pixel. A modular row-column tiling scheme facilitates scaling to large arrays while preserving per-pixel programmability. We further demonstrate independent two-dimensional phase modulation and non-volatile THz beam steering. This work provides a theoretical framework and design paradigm for a versatile and scalable photonic platform spanning the THz to optical regimes.

Article.Title: A motion vector sensor-enabled 3D spinal morphology monitoring suit for intelligent scoliosis identification
Article.Authors: Xu L.; Chen G.; Liu H.; Zhao X.; Yao C.; Si H.; Lin M.; Wang Y.; Wang B.; Yin X.; Yuan J.; Qiu G.; Wu Z.; Zhang T.; Liao Q.; Zhang Y.; Wu N.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Early identification of scoliosis is highly significant for timely intervention and efficient management of the disease. However, conventional static screening approaches rely heavily on subjective assessments, resulting in limited diagnostic accuracy and insufficient continuity. Here, we propose a motion vector sensor-enabled 3D spinal morphology monitoring suit for intelligent identification and continuous monitoring of scoliosis. By orderly aligning elastic conductive fibers, highly anisotropic soft meshes are customized and achieve dual responses to motion amplitude and direction. The sensors exhibit a minimal directional resolution of 2° while maintaining a linear response up to 100% strain. The suit integrates motion sensors positioned at symmetrical body locations to quantify 3D spinal motions via precise measurement of skin-surface deformation amplitude and direction. Dynamic scoliosis identification is achieved through machine learning-powered kinematic symmetry evaluation of 3D spinal motions. The system demonstrates accuracies of 100% for scoliosis detection, 97.7% for curvature degree quantification, and 93.37% for curvature location identification, rigorously validated on a multi-center dataset from four hospitals and one school-based screening program. This work provides a radiation-free alternative for scoliosis screening, with potential to facilitate lifelong monitoring and management of the condition.

Article.Title: Intruding delta waves during REM sleep are associated with tau, amyloid, and forgetting in aging
Article.Authors: Desel T.; Walker M.; Brown C.; Chen C.; Chadwick T.; Jagust W.; Sharon O.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep degrades with age, and more severely in Alzheimer’s disease (AD). REM sleep comprises about twenty percent of adult sleep, alternates between phasic and tonic periods, and includes delta waves (1-4 Hz) in two forms: fast sawtooth waves and slower, NREM-like waves, whose expression dynamically varies across REM periods. Yet, the functional relevance of these REM sleep delta waves remains unknown. Here, using two independent cohorts, we show that aging is associated with a shift from fast sawtooth to slow NREM-like delta waves, particularly during phasic REM sleep - a period typically marked by high cortical activation. Beyond chronological age, this shift is associated with amyloid-β and tau burden, suggesting that AD pathology is associated with REM-specific oscillatory patterns. Furthermore, this shift in REM oscillations is linked to impaired overnight memory consolidation, independent of NREM sleep quality. Moreover, variation in APOE alleles, a major genetic risk factor for AD, was independently associated with a reduction in fast sawtooth wave density, thereby linking a genetic predisposition for AD to these specific REM microstructural changes. These findings identify a signature of memory decline in aging and implicate REM sleep as a distinct vulnerable substrate through which AD pathology may impair brain function.

Article.Title: Genomic heterogeneity inflates the performance of variant pathogenicity predictions
Article.Authors: Lu B.; Liu X.; Lin P.; Brandes N.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Recent studies have reported unprecedented accuracy predicting pathogenic variants across the genome, including in noncoding regions, using large deep-learning models trained on vast genomic data. To verify and understand the basis of these reports, we systematically evaluated the prediction accuracy of frontier models over single-nucleotide variants, focusing on general models capable of scoring multiple variant types across coding or noncoding regions. Our evaluations reveal that the performance of genome-wide predictions is severely inflated by mixing variant categories with different baseline prevalences of pathogenic variants. We constructed a benchmark stratified by variant type to identify the best-performing models for each genomic context, determine where reliable predictions remain out of reach, and establish rigorous standards to guide future evaluations.

Article.Title: Equipositioning of chromosomes in the polyploid archaeon Haloferax volcanii by HpaAB
Article.Authors: Premrajka K.; Johnsen U.; Preidel H.; Wienberg J.; Corleis C.; Ortjohann M.; Giacomelli G.; Bramkamp M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Proper genome segregation is essential for cellular survival, yet this process is poorly understood in archaea. Archaea show considerable variability in genome ploidy and organization. Haloferax volcanii DS2 is a polyploid archaeon with a fragmented genome consisting of a main chromosome, three secondary chromosomes and a plasmid. Due to high ploidy, genomic segregation in H. volcanii is typically considered random. However, we identified four two-gene operons encoding ParA-like proteins and uncharacterized partners. Here we characterized HpaA and HpaB, encoded on the secondary chromosome pHV3. HpaA contains conserved ATPase walker motifs and is a ParA protein with a bacterial origin. Mutation of key residues in HpaA alters its localization, while HpaA is necessary for proper HpaB spatial distribution. HpaB forms cytosolic foci and functions as a centromere-binding protein, analogous to bacterial ParB. Deletion of the genes hpaA and hpaB results in severe growth defects when xylose is the sole carbon source, consistent with the location of xylose degradation genes on pHV3. It also reduces the pHV3 to main chromosome ratio. Single-particle tracking suggests that HpaB influences HpaA dynamics. Together, these findings demonstrate an equipositioning of pHV3, likely supporting maintenance in the different cell morphologies observed in H. volcanii .

Article.Title: Host diet may shape bat RNA viromes within geographic and phylogenetic constraints at a global-scale
Article.Authors: Huang Z.; Liu Y.; Wang Z.; Ke C.; Si M.; Geng Y.; Liu Y.; Feng J.; He B.; Jiang T.
Article.Abstract: Bats are key models for studying the ecological mechanisms driving viral community structure, yet the role of diet remains unclear. By integrating 1627 RNA virome libraries from 78 bat species across 13 countries, we recovered 309,546 vOTUs spanning 66 recognized RNA virus families, whereas 82.74% remained unclassified, suggesting extensive viral “dark matter”. Classified viruses were associated with vertebrates, invertebrates, plants and plant-associated fungi, with invertebrate-associated viruses contributing prominently to overall diversity. Viral community composition differed significantly among feeding guilds, with sanguivorous bats exhibiting a specialized viral community structure. However, sampling site and host phylogeny explained substantially more variation than feeding guild, indicating that broad-scale bat virome structure is primarily shaped by geography and host evolutionary history. Analyses restricted to vertebrate-associated viruses further showed that feeding guild was associated with community composition but not viral species diversity. Viral sharing was more strongly structured by sampling site and host phylogenetic distance than by shared diet. Together, these findings indicate that geography and host phylogeny dominate broad-scale viral community structure, whereas diet plays a secondary role by modulating exposure to viruses through predation. This improves our understanding of bat viral assemblages and informs assessments of host–virus associations and spillover risk. By analyzing 1,627 bat RNA viromes from 78 species worldwide, the study shows that geography and host evolution shape bat viral communities more strongly than diet, while feeding ecology plays a secondary role in viral exposure.

Article.Title: IDPForge: deep learning of proteins with global and local regions of disorder
Article.Authors: De Castro S.; Zhang O.; Liu Z.; Forman-Kay J.; Head-Gordon T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Although machine learning has transformed protein structure prediction of folded protein ground states with remarkable accuracy, intrinsically disordered proteins and regions (IDPs/IDRs) are defined by diverse and dynamical structural ensembles that are predicted with low confidence by algorithms such as AlphaFold and RoseTTAFold. We present a machine learning method, IDPForge ( I ntrinsically D isordered P rotein, FO lded and disordered R egion GE nerator), that exploits a transformer protein language diffusion model to create all-atom IDP ensembles and IDR ensembles that maintains the folded domains. IDPForge does not require sequence-specific training, back transformations from coarse-grained representations, nor ensemble reweighting. The created IDP/IDR conformational ensembles show good agreement with both NMR and SAXS solution experimental data, and options for biasing with experimental restraints are available if desired. IDPForge with these diverse capabilities facilitates integrative and structural studies for proteins that contain intrinsic disorder, and is available as an open source resource for general use.

Article.Title: Phylogeny and intraspecific variability dominate nitrogen fixer biomass responses to nitrogen enrichment
Article.Authors: Yao Y.; Han B.; Bodegom P.; Zhong Y.; Dong X.; Niu S.; Li Z.
Article.Abstract: Anthropogenic nitrogen (N) enrichment profoundly influences the growth of N-fixing plants, but the drivers underlying their highly variable biomass responses remain poorly quantified. Through a meta-analysis of 2,110 paired observations across 76 N-fixing plant species from 121 experiments, we demonstrate that N enrichment increases N-fixing plant biomass by 14.2% on average, with responses ranging from −99.4% to 1301.3%. Intraspecific variability (26.9%; i.e., variation among individuals within species) and plant phylogeny (21.1%) represent substantial yet frequently overlooked sources of uncertainty in biomass responses of N-fixing plants to N enrichment, even though environmental conditions (climatic and edaphic factors) and experimental design (N enrichment rate and duration) account for a significant portion of biomass response variation. Intraspecific variability, phylogeny, and experimental design collectively explain a larger proportion of variance in root than in shoot biomass responses, whereas environmental conditions show the opposite trend. These results provide quantitative evidence that phylogeny and intraspecific variability are indispensable for accurately predicting the response of N-fixing plants to global change. Nitrogen enrichment alters the growth of nitrogen-fixing plants, but responses vary widely. This meta-analysis shows that phylogeny and intraspecific variation are major contributors to that variability.

Article.Title: Real-time quantification of skeletal muscle metabolism in healthy men using hyperpolarised [1-¹³C]pyruvate reveals training-dependent adaptation
Article.Authors: Torchi A.; Mallinson J.; Bawden S.; McGing J.; Lobo D.; Cooper A.; Glaser M.; Twyman F.; Awais R.; Årstad E.; Auer D.; Gowland P.; Greenhaff P.; Morris P.; Serres S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Skeletal muscle undergoes rapid and dynamic changes in energy demand during exercise, limiting the physiological relevance of resting-state measurements. Here, we demonstrate the feasibility of combining hyperpolarised ¹³C magnetic resonance spectroscopy (¹³C-MRS) with ³¹P-MRS to non-invasively measure real-time metabolic responses in exercising human skeletal muscle. Sedentary and endurance-trained men perform plantar-flexion exercise inside a magnetic resonance scanner. Dynamic hyperpolarised [1-¹³C]pyruvate spectra from the medial gastrocnemius show that increasing exercise intensity escalates pyruvate-to-lactate conversion relative to mitochondrial pyruvate utilisation. Endurance training is associated with greater bicarbonate labelling, consistent with increased mitochondrial pyruvate utilisation, and reduced lactate production. These metabolic signatures are accompanied by intensity- and training-dependent differences in phosphocreatine degradation and intracellular pH decline measured by ³¹P-MRS. Together, these findings demonstrate the feasibility of combining hyperpolarised ¹³C- and ³¹P-MRS to phenotype skeletal muscle metabolism during exercise, providing a platform for investigating metabolic adaptations in ageing, disease and therapeutic intervention.

Article.Title: Proximity labeling of the Listeria monocytogenes surface reveals pathogen control of a host deubiquitinase
Article.Authors: Woida P.; Smith M.; Lamason R.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Intracellular pathogens must navigate the crowded cellular environment to establish infection. Listeria monocytogenes achieves this by recruiting host factors to its surface to hijack the host actin cytoskeleton for motility, form membrane protrusions, and spread from cell to cell. Although these types of Listeria -host interactions are critical for infection, systematic characterization of this interface has been limited. Here, we implement surface display of the promiscuous biotin ligase split-TurboID to profile host proteins recruited to the surface of L. monocytogenes during intracellular infection. This approach identified the host deubiquitinase CYLD as a protein selectively enriched at the pathogen surface. While CYLD promotes infection by suppressing autophagy and innate immunity in macrophages, how L. monocytogenes recruits and appropriates CYLD function in other cell types has remained unclear. We demonstrate that the E3 ligase RNF213 decorates bacterial poles with M1-linked linear ubiquitin, thereby redirecting CYLD to the bacterial surface. We further show ubiquitin is not sufficient to recruit CYLD but requires the L. monocytogenes secreted effector internalin C (InlC). Despite its presence at the bacterial surface, CYLD does not deubiquitinate bacteria or regulate autophagic bacterial clearance in infected epithelial cells. Instead, CYLD and InlC protect L. monocytogenes from IFN-γ- and RNF213-dependent restriction of cell-to-cell spread. Overall, our work profiling the bacterial surface-host interactome has identified a new mechanism by which InlC spatially reprograms CYLD activity, uncoupling its canonical immune functions to promote cell-to-cell spread in epithelial cells. These findings highlight how L. monocytogenes exploits, a host deubiquitinase, to perform cell-type-specific functions during infection.

Article.Title: A training-free, domain-extensible LLM-based approach for automated extraction of standardized preparation procedures
Article.Authors: Costa D.; Manica M.; Laino T.; Ribeiro M.; Mendes P.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Millions of synthesis procedures have been published, but their meta-analysis (e.g., to identify successful synthesis patterns) is troublesome due to the variety of reporting structures. Mapping unstructured language to a precise sequence of actions requires an understanding of domain-specific jargon, a challenge usually addressed by fine-tuning models on labeled data. Herein, we present a simple, training-free workflow for laboratory action extraction that works across fields. It encodes domain knowledge through explicit action sets and uses powerful, readily available Large Language Models (LLMs). Applied to zeolite synthesis, our approach outperforms existing open-source tools and delivers context-aware results with open, locally runnable LLMs. It also matches the performance of state-of-the-art, field-specific models in their own domains, highlighting the generalization ability of current LLMs. With our methodology and open algorithms, chemists can evaluate actions sets, screen LLMs for their specific needs, and accurately digitize laboratory procedures with minimal effort.

Article.Title: Viral tRNA-like structure hijacks host ribosomes for poly(A)-independent translation
Article.Authors: Lu G.; Wan L.; Chen Y.; Li Y.; Yan Y.; Liu Y.; Wu Z.; Zhang N.; Lin J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Positive-sense RNA viruses often use 3′ tRNA-like structures (TLSs) instead of poly(A) tails to capture the host translation machinery. While TLSs resemble canonical tRNAs and engage host factors, their ability to directly recruit ribosomes has remained unresolved. Here, we present cryo-electron microscopy snapshots of the histidine-accepting TLS (TLS His ) from tobacco mosaic virus bound to the 60 S subunit, the 80 S ribosome, and the 80 S -tRNA i Met initiation complex. Across these states, TLS His is consistently anchored to the L1 stalk of 60 S , even under cycloheximide treatment, yet remains dynamic on the 40 S subunit. Structural analysis shows that TLS His transitions from the E-site to an adjacent Z-site to accommodate initiator tRNA. Functional assays show that TLS His preferentially associates with ribosomal subunits over polysomes and can substitute for a poly(A) tail to promote robust cap-dependent translation. Together, these findings reveal how a viral tRNA mimic hijacks host ribosomes to promote poly(A)-independent translation.

Article.Title: CryoET imaging reveals that mitotic spindles are locally organized by microtubule density and Eg5 activity
Article.Authors: Conway W.; Bobe D.; Zimyanin V.; Fabig G.; de Marco A.; Redemann S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract When eukaryotic cells divide, a mitotic spindle, composed of microtubule filaments interacting with molecular motors, self-assembles and is responsible for aligning and segregating chromosomes to the opposite daughter cells. Recent structural studies revealed that spindles are composed of short microtubules that do not span the full pole-to-chromosome distance. It remains unclear how these short, disconnected microtubules collectively assemble a bipolar spindle. Using cryo-electron tomography to map microtubule polarity in human spindles, we find that microtubules organize with consistent 8 nm wall-to-wall spacing. Spacing scales inversely with local microtubule density, consistent with organization by density-driven steric interactions, analogous to liquid crystal ordering. We find that the Eg5 motor establishes local antiparallel overlap independently of spindle bipolarity, while a balance of Eg5 and dynein regulates microtubule density to maintain spindle architecture. Together, these findings reveal the mesoscale principles by which cells build complex, self-healing cellular architectures from nanoscale building blocks.

Article.Title: Tree shrew more closely recapitulates primate spermatogenesis than the mouse in cross-species single-cell transcriptomic analyses
Article.Authors: Lin H.; Kang W.; Xie L.; Hu S.; Li Y.; Bi R.; Yao Y.; Zheng P.
Article.Abstract: The rapid evolution of spermatogenesis limits the utility of mouse models for studying human spermatogenesis because some genes are absent or divergent in mice. Primate models face practical and ethical constraints, whereas tree shrews are closely related to primates and suitable for laboratory research. Here we integrate histology and single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from human, rhesus macaque, mouse and tree shrew testes to assess the tree shrew as a model of human spermatogenesis. We show that transcriptional landscapes in tree shrew spermatogenic cells, particularly late-stage spermatids, more closely resemble those of primates than mice. Conservation and enrichment analyses identify two core gene modules shared among humans, macaques and tree shrews but distinct in mice. Gene expression trajectories also align between tree shrews and primates, including for genes without murine orthologs. Immunostaining and RNA-FISH support representative expression patterns. These findings define contexts in which tree shrews can complement existing models of human spermatogenesis and male infertility.

Article.Title: Local albumin excess exacerbates Candida albicans-induced inflammasome activation linked with hyperinflammation during vulvovaginal candidiasis
Article.Authors: Austermeier S.; Cheng K.; Dietschmann A.; Vascelli G.; Montaño D.; Hitzler S.; Skurk K.; Fernández-Fernández C.; Saloni S.; Westermann S.; Jaeger M.; Jablonowski N.; Wisgott S.; Elshafee O.; Brachelente C.; de Graaf D.; Próchnicki T.; Latz E.; Wirtz S.; Becker C.; Renga G.; Oikonomou V.; Hube B.; Donders G.; Pekmezovic M.
Article.Abstract: Vulvovaginal candidiasis (VVC) is a mucosal yeast infection, mostly caused by Candida albicans, where symptoms are driven by inflammation. The onset of VVC is instigated by C. albicans pathogenicity, but the underlying causes of disease-driving hyperinflammation remain incompletely resolved. We found that vaginal albumin concentrations are higher in women with recurrent VVC and during experimental VVC in mice. These albumin levels correlated with inflammatory cytokines in vaginal lavages. While the abundance of this serum protein in the vagina can be a hallmark of inflammation-induced vascular permeability, we reveal molecular mechanisms by which albumin can also drive inflammation. Albumin increased NLRP3 inflammasome activation in human macrophages elicited by C. albicans. This was associated with increased resistance of C. albicans to macrophage-mediated clearance in the presence of albumin. Further, albumin increased the expression of fungal secreted aspartic protease 1, which we identified as the effector driving inflammasome activation and IL-1β responses in vitro and in an in vivo VVC model. Moreover, neutrophils also exhibited impaired clearance of C. albicans in the presence of albumin. Collectively, vaginal albumin may not only be a consequence of inflammation of the vaginal mucosa, but also can drive C. albicans-induced hyperinflammatory IL-1β responses that underlie immunopathology in VVC.

Article.Title: Global arable land redistribution toward the tropics and drylands under human settlement expansion
Article.Authors: Gao L.; Lu X.; Anderson W.; Lesk C.; Mazur E.; Stolle F.; Potapov P.; Tubiello F.; Fritz S.; Mao J.; You L.; Ray D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Arable land has been expanding since the advent of agriculture, and now sustains over eight billion people by supplying food, fiber, and fuel. However, the rapid expansion of built-up areas is increasingly displacing arable land across diverse regions, raising concerns about the long-term sustainability of global food systems. Addressing these concerns requires a fundamental understanding of global arable-land dynamics, which remains largely unknown. Using our newly developed high-quality arable-land product—integrated with global settlement layers, Köppen–Geiger climate classifications, and historical land-use reconstructions—we show that competition between arable land and urban systems for favorable climate fundamentally shapes global arable-land dynamics. Globally, urbanization in the Northern Hemisphere is displacing arable land from climatically favorable regions toward more marginal tropical and arid environments. In North America, Europe, and Asia, early co-development of arable land and urbanization has transitioned into intensified urban encroachment, pushing cultivation into adjacent arid zones. By contrast, low-latitude tropical regions continue to expand both systems at the expense of natural ecosystems, driven in part by agricultural investment from Northern Hemisphere countries. This framework not only offers a new perspective for synthesizing existing regional arable-land dynamics but is also closely linked to ongoing dryland greening, tropical deforestation, and groundwater depletion in drylands. Reconciling agricultural production with rapid urban growth is therefore essential to safeguarding sustainable land resources, forest health, water security, and global food security under accelerating demographic pressures.

Article.Title: Framework desymmetrization enables partial pore space partition in metal-organic frameworks
Article.Authors: Zhong X.; Wei M.; Wang J.; Zhang Y.; Jiang X.; Yu J.; Zhao X.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The pore-space-partition (PSP) has been recognized as a powerful strategy for boosting the uptake capacity of small gas molecules and has seen wide application in reticular chemistry. However, the most successful PSP platform—the partitioned- acs (pacs) net—has followed only one pattern since its inception over a decade ago: one partition agent per partition site, with a general formula of [M 3 O( L1 ) 3 ]( L2 ). This fully partitioned architecture occupies all metal sites, eliminating open metal sites (OMSs) and compromising selectivity. Herein, we introduce a partial PSP concept accessed through a framework desymmetrization strategy. By replacing traditional high-symmetry D 2h ligands with lower-symmetry C 2h ligands (e.g., fumaric acid), we introduce structural distortions into the acs network, breaking the uniformity of partition sites and allowing partition agents to occupy only a fraction of available positions. This provides access to a PSP mechanism, namely part-pacs (partially partitioned- acs ), with a general formula of [M 3 O( L1 ) 3 ]( L2 ) 1/3 . The part-pacs structures retain high acetylene capacity while exhibiting significantly enhanced selectivity compared to their fully partitioned analogues. Specifically, part-pacs-fum-tpa achieves C 2 H 2 /CO 2 separation productivity nearly twice that of its full-pacs counterpart (1.92 mol kg −1 vs 0.98 mol kg −1 ).

Article.Title: Aberrant thymic architecture and enhanced interferon signaling in Down syndrome
Article.Authors: Hall T.; Schild A.; Li L.; Sheppard H.; Chasteen H.; Liu Y.; Cotton A.; Mehmood R.; Dezem F.; Hodges J.; Lear M.; Fountain B.; Fan Y.; Gossett J.; Kang G.; Gheorghe G.; Crawford J.; Thomas P.; Feng Y.; Wu G.; Plummer J.; Boston U.; Crispino J.
Article.Abstract: Individuals with Down syndrome (DS) have an elevated risk of autoimmune disease, particularly celiac disease, type 1 diabetes, and autoimmune hypothyroidism. In DS, thymi show characteristic structural and cellular changes, but the connection between these and the propensity to autoimmune disease is still unclear. Here we present a cell atlas from single cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics of age-matched thymi from infants with and without DS, which might contribute to filling this knowledge gap. DS does not significantly alter CD34+ diversity in the thymus; however, the gene expression changes we observe indicate altered differentiative potential in DS CD34+ cells. Although many genes involved in T-cell development and function (including USP16, RUNX1 and ETS2) are located on chromosome 21, several important T cell regulatory genes that are located on other chromosomes also change in DS. In contrast, CD34- DS thymocytes are characterised by maturation defects. CD34+ progenitors and proliferating DP thymocytes are in a functional state of chronic interferon activation. In summary, we identify several notable differences in key functional cellular subsets and pathways within the DS thymus, providing insights into the spatiotemporal dynamics of the thymic environment for this genetic condition. Down syndrome is a complex condition which results in immune alterations, including higher risk of autoimmune diseases. Here the authors show by single cell and spatial transcriptomics that the differentiation of thymic T cell precursors is disturbed in Down syndrome, which might underpin the functional alterations.

Article.Title: Deuteration of arenes in D2O exclusively driven by single-atom Pt sites under visible light
Article.Authors: Xu J.; Wu X.; Cao R.; Zhao D.; Song X.; Chen H.; Li W.; Pan T.; Liew K.; Besenbacher F.; Dai Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Deuterated arenes play crucial roles in medicinal chemistry and materials science (e.g., psychotropic drugs and deuterated OLEDs). However, the desired late-stage deuteration via conventional hydrogen isotope exchange (HIE) methods always demands expensive isotopic reagents (e.g., D2, C6D6, or C2H5OD), metal complex catalysts, or harsh conditions (≥120 oC, 20 bar H2). Here, we report a single-atom photocatalytic strategy for efficient HIE of electron-rich arenes using D2O as the deuterium source. Under visible light irradiation at ambient temperature in an inert atmosphere, a single-atom photocatalyst (Pt1/TiO2) afforded high deuterium incorporation across 54 electron-rich arene substrates. The protocol is mild, sustainable, and scalable: gram-scale synthesis of deuterated arenes (11.98 g, 100 mmol) was successfully realized. Mechanistic studies indicate that the catalytically active sites are primarily Pt–O coordinate bonds, whose light-modulated charge distribution facilitates a possible electrophilic platinization pathway for C–H activation before H/D exchange.

Article.Title: Antimicrobial peptides derived from Nemuri induce ribosomal condensation to inhibit translation
Article.Authors: Nishinami S.; Hasan M.; Niwa T.; Inui T.; Yokoyama T.; Otsuki H.; Ogasawara Y.; Sugai H.; Otobe Y.; Machida M.; Abdelaziz M.; Ageta-Ishihara N.; Sasaki R.; Ishizaki Y.; Iwasaki K.; Fujioka Y.; Ohishi T.; Kajimoto S.; Nakabayashi T.; Tanaka Y.; Yoshitane H.; Kumeta H.; Sehgal A.; Igarashi M.; Noda N.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Antibiotic resistance is a global health threat requiring antimicrobials with alternative modes of action. Growing evidence indicates that bacteria organize key intracellular processes through biomolecular condensates and other forms of spatial organization, yet whether such spatial organization can be exploited as an antimicrobial target remains unclear. Here, we identify intrinsically disordered antimicrobial peptides, generated from the Drosophila sleep-inducing protein Nemuri, that inhibit bacterial growth by targeting ribosomal organization. Mechanistically, these peptides enter bacterial cells without overt membrane disruption and accumulate in ribosome-rich regions, where they bind broadly to RNA and ribosomal surfaces through multivalent interactions. This engagement remodels ribosome-rich regions into condensates with reduced ribosomal mobility, thereby suppressing global protein synthesis and distinguishing these peptides from canonical site-specific ribosome-targeting antibiotics. Furthermore, Nemuri-derived peptides exhibit broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity, including activity against drug-resistant pathogens, with low cytotoxicity toward Drosophila and mammalian cells. Together, our findings identify the organization and material dynamics of bacterial ribosomes as a biophysical vulnerability that can be exploited by antimicrobial peptides, revealing how a naturally evolved metazoan host-defense system turns intracellular organization itself into an antibacterial target.

Article.Title: Widespread selection of antibiotic resistance within hospital sewers
Article.Authors: Gray D.; Nhung N.; Coertze R.; Ekwanzala M.; Waters N.; Järhult J.; Wenzel M.; Åhrén C.; Fick J.; Flach C.; Larsson D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Environmental microbiomes are sources of diverse antibiotic resistance determinants that can be mobilized and transferred to human pathogens under a selection pressure from antibiotics. Hospital sewers contain more antibiotics than most environments and are thus increasingly recognised as potential arenas for resistance evolution. However, it is unknown if resistance selection occurs there and what the drivers are. Here we show selection of antibiotic-resistant bacteria within Swedish hospital sewers. Evidence include; consistent selection of multiple resistances in Escherichia coli exposed to filtered wastewater from ten hospitals, but not to corresponding municipal wastewaters; in-situ enrichment of resistant over sensitive E. coli from wastewater to sewer biofilms at hospitals, but not at municipal sites; and higher resistance in bacteria collected from hospital sewers than from municipal sites as assessed by culturing and metagenomics. Evidence for drivers includes complete rescue of sensitive E. coli by addition of resistance genes to fluoroquinolones and β-lactams, and cellular effects typical for β-lactams. Measured concentrations by liquid-chromatography-tandem-mass-spectrometry compared to selective thresholds identify ciprofloxacin and cefotaxime as principal selective agents. Antibiotic concentrations and use data allow extrapolation of risks beyond Sweden. Given the absence of detectable selection at municipal sites, mitigations of risks in hospital sewers should be prioritized.

Article.Title: Layer-wise Prediction for Interpretation of Hidden Representations in Deep Neural Networks through Evolving Probability Distributions
Article.Authors: Liu Z.; Liu Y.; Li J.; Yu Z.; Yang Z.; Guo Y.; Liu Q.; Wang G.
Article.Abstract: The sequential architecture of DNNs enables accurate predictions by encoding input features, yet their limited interpretability and transparency during forward propagation undermine the credibility of predictions. Therefore, we propose layer-wise prediction for interpretation method (LPI), which involves mapping the representation from each layer to a probability distribution, explaining the hidden-layer prediction process. To ensure interpretation fidelity to DNN mechanisms, we employ a reconstruction strategy to map probability distributions back to hidden layer features while reducing their influence on model prediction. Meanwhile, we define a rank-index metric to quantify the consistency of probability distribution evolution. Furthermore, we show how each hidden layer probability distribution evolves consistently during DNN forward propagation. Experiments on various models show that LPI achieves superior performance in consistency, stability, fidelity and certainty, outperforming AdditionalLayer, SDN, MetaGF, and DFS. Notably, LPI not only enhances deep learning interpretability but also provides valuable insights into reliable and credible model security assessment. Here, the authors introduce a hidden-layer interpretation method that maps intermediate DNN representations to probability distributions and reconstructs features to ensure faithful explanation.

Article.Title: Resolving the Kay–Dunn limit and the speed–endurance dilemma in ferroelectric Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 for DRAM-class sub-volt capacitors
Article.Authors: Park G.; Jo S.; Park S.; Cho Y.; Choi H.; Jeong H.; Kim S.; Lee D.; Jeong M.; Kwon T.; Kim D.; Lee G.; Jeong S.; Kim Y.; Lee S.; Lee Y.; Park J.; Jung C.; Lim H.; Kwon D.; Kim H.; Park M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Ferroelectric hafnium zirconium oxide can increase charge density in scaled capacitors, but its high coercive field limits the low-voltage, high endurance switching required for dynamic random-access memory and embedded ferroelectric memories. Here we show that plasma-engineered (111)-textured TiN electrodes with N-rich, oxidation-resistant surfaces suppress interfacial oxidation and enable robust switching in 5 nm Hf 0.5 Zr 0.5 O 2 capacitors. The devices exhibit saturated hysteresis at 0.6 V, with 2 P r = 31.5 μC cm −2 and E c = 0.62 MV cm −1 , and no hard electrical breakdown through 10 12 bipolar cycles. Their nucleation-limited switching kinetics extrapolate to sub-nanosecond polarisation reversal at DRAM-relevant capacitor areas. At 1.1 V, circuit simulations of a common plate 1T–1 C cell yield short- and long-term stand-by sensing margins of 482 and 201 mV under a 20 fF bit line load. Electrode texture and interface engineering therefore enable low-voltage, high speed switching without compromising endurance, mitigating the practical Kay–Dunn scaling penalty and the speed–endurance dilemma.

Article.Title: Wavelength selective fragmentation of metastable photoresponsive platelets via light irradiation
Article.Authors: Liu L.; Xia T.; O’Reilly R.; Chen S.; Tong Z.
Article.Abstract: Polymer lamellar crystals commonly consisting of folded chains are frequently formed since they are kinetically favorable. Hence, the metastability of polymer crystals can be regulated by crystallization pathways, and the thinner lamellar crystals display a tendency to transform into thicker crystals via lamellar thickening process. Herein, we report that photoresponsive two-dimensional (2D) platelets with low metastability undergo controllable fragmentation upon light irradiation. Mechanistic studies indicate that the metastability within a single platelet particle is heterogeneous across different domains. Light irradiation triggers lamellar thickening preferentially within less stable domains decorated with photoresponsive molecules, leading to site-specific fragmentation. To illustrate the utility of light-stimulated fragmentation, wavelength selective fragmentation of 2D segmented platelets with spatially defined photoresponsive molecules is achieved upon light irradiation, yielding 2D hollow platelet structure. This important feature holds significant promise for advanced applications such as spatially resolved therapeutic delivery systems, thereby broadening the functional scope of 2D nanomaterials. Two-dimensional platelets are typically formed from polymer lamellar crystals, with metastability regulated by crystallization pathways. Here, the authors report photoresponsive platelets with low metastability, which undergo controllable fragmentation on light irradiation.

Article.Title: Increasing prevalence and expanding diversity of tet(X4)-carrying Salmonella in China
Article.Authors: Li W.; Yang T.; Cui Q.; Li B.; Zhan L.; Jiang X.; Yan S.; Liu L.; Qin X.; Liu Z.; Ying L.; Yu B.; Qiao X.; Huo X.; Zhang M.; Chen W.; Lu X.; Guo Y.; Fu M.; Shen Z.
Article.Abstract: The plasmid-mediated tigecycline resistance gene tet(X4) threatens the efficacy of tigecycline. While prevalent in Escherichia coli across diverse ecological niches, its evolutionary trajectory in Salmonella remains underappreciated. Here, we conducted nationwide genomic surveillance of 42403 clinical nontyphoidal Salmonella isolates collected from diarrheal patients in China between 2014 and 2025, of which 102 were tet(X4)-positive. Although the overall prevalence remained low, detection showed a statistically significant upward trend over 2019-2025. Importantly, the newly accrued 2025 data were broadly consistent with short-term forecasts generated by the beta regression model, providing partial support for short-term trend consistency. Genomic analyses showed that tet(X4) remained concentrated in ST34 but was also detected in additional sequence types, including ST469, ST8971, ST11 and one isolate with an unassigned ST, across multiple provinces, indicating broader geographic representation and genetic diversification. Plasmid analyses likewise revealed broader replicon diversity, with the dominant IncHI1A/IncHI1B/IncFIA background accompanied by less frequent IncHI2/IncHI2A, IncI1(Alpha) and IncFIA/IncFIB/IncFIC. Phylogenetic analyses further revealed shared clustering of the dominant plasmid background across host species and bacterial genera, consistent with cross-host and cross-genus circulation. Here, they determine that tet(X4)-carrying Salmonella remains rare in China but is being detected more often and in a wider range of bacterial sequence types and plasmids, supporting continued surveillance.
