Article.Title: Genotype and phenotype analyses of 689 individuals with PCDH19-clustering epilepsy
Article.Authors: Grasso K.; Corbett M.; Scheffer I.; Gecz J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract PCDH19 -clustering epilepsy ( PCDH19- CE) is an infantile-onset neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by clusters of seizures, typically triggered by fever. PCDH19 -CE follows an unusual X-linked inheritance pattern whereby heterozygous females, and males with X-chromosome disomy or pathogenic postzygotic mosaic PCDH19 variants, are affected, while hemizygous males are spared. We aggregate published PCDH19 variants and their corresponding PCDH19 -CE phenotypes to analyse phenotype-genotype correlations. Data extracted from 110 publications identified 689/735 (94%) individuals with PCDH19 variants and the typical PCDH19 -CE phenotype. Three hundred seventy-three unique PCDH19 variants were identified; 195 were not recorded in ClinVar. Seizure onset prior to 12 months of age was associated with more severe intellectual disability (p < 0.001) and the presence of psychiatric morbidity (p = 0.001). There were no phenotypic differences between missense, nonsense, and frameshift variants or between individuals of different geographical backgrounds, which was assessed as a proxy for ancestry. Twenty-nine hemizygous males with constitutive PCDH19 variants did not exhibit the typical PCDH19 -CE phenotype, suggesting that the identification of variants in these individuals likely results from chance or ascertainment bias. The correlation between earlier seizure onset and poorer neurodevelopmental outcomes emphasises a critical window for therapeutic intervention. The lack of phenotypic difference between variant types demonstrates that loss of PCDH19 function underpins PCDH19 -CE. Moreover, the identification of PCDH19 cytoplasmic domain variants in 78 affected individuals challenges the traditional view that PCDH19 -CE is caused primarily by defects in cell-cell adhesion, as variants in this domain are expected to disrupt the nuclear function(s) of PCDH19.

Article.Title: Tryptophan metabolism within the gut–brain axis in depression: mechanisms, association with heterogeneity, and therapeutic opportunities
Article.Authors: Qin Z.; Lei T.; Yi T.; Zhang S.; Tang Y.; Xiang Y.; Zhou Z.; Mei Z.; Qiu F.; Zhang X.
Article.Abstract: Depression is a highly heterogeneous psychiatric disorder, characterized by substantial variability in clinical manifestations, treatment responses, and disease progression, thereby posing significant challenges to precision diagnosis and therapeutic intervention. Accumulating evidence indicates that dysregulated tryptophan metabolism, mediated through dynamic crosstalk with the gut microbiota and the gut-brain axis (GBA), plays a pivotal role in both the pathophysiology and biological heterogeneity of depression. In this review, we delineate the contributions of the three principal tryptophan metabolic pathways-the kynurenine, serotonin, and microbial indole pathways-in modulating neuroimmune signaling, neurotransmitter function, and gut-brain communication. Moreover, we synthesize current evidence demonstrating that microbiota-dependent tryptophan metabolism exhibits distinct profiles across clinical, demographic, immunometabolic, trauma-related, and genetically defined depressive phenotypes, thereby establishing its role as a unifying biological framework underlying depressive heterogeneity. We further provide a critical appraisal of emerging therapeutic strategies targeting microbiota-associated tryptophan metabolism, including pharmacological, nutritional, microbial, and traditional Chinese medicine-based interventions. Future investigations should integrate multi-omics approaches, longitudinal study designs, and mechanistic validation with artificial intelligence to elucidate causal relationships between microbiota-associated tryptophan metabolism and depressive heterogeneity, ultimately facilitating biomarker discovery and the development of precision therapeutics.

Article.Title: Evolutionary neuropharmacology of serotonergic psychedelics: a cross-species perspective on mechanisms, consciousness, and therapeutic potential
Article.Authors: Zhai H.; Wang H.; Wang Y.; Wang X.
Article.Abstract: Serotonergic psychedelics have revitalized psychiatric research by producing rapid and potentially sustained clinical benefits in selected neuropsychiatric conditions. However, the mechanisms linking receptor activation to neural plasticity, altered conscious experience, and clinical improvement remain incompletely understood, while the evolutionary origins of psychedelic signaling and the translational value of animal models continue to be actively debated. In this review, we integrate evolutionary biology, molecular pharmacology, comparative neuroscience, and computational psychiatry into a unified framework for understanding psychedelic action across biological scales. Building upon predictive processing and the Relaxed Beliefs Under Psychedelics (REBUS) framework, we discuss how serotonergic psychedelics transiently reshape hierarchical inference, providing computational principles that can be experimentally investigated across species despite profound differences in neural architecture and subjective experience. Comparative analyses from invertebrates to non-human primates further suggest that conserved receptor pharmacology coexists with species-specific circuit organization, highlighting that animal models should be interpreted as complementary platforms for investigating molecular, cellular, and computational mechanisms rather than direct proxies for human hallucinatory experiences. We further discuss preclinical and emerging translational evidence suggesting that biased receptor signaling and non-hallucinogenic psychoplastogens may partially dissociate plasticity-related therapeutic actions from hallucinogenic effects, providing new opportunities for mechanism-based drug development. By integrating evolutionary biology with molecular psychiatry, this review provides a mechanistic framework linking receptor pharmacology, neural plasticity, circuit computation, and therapeutic outcomes, thereby offering new conceptual and experimental strategies for developing next-generation psychedelic therapeutics.

Article.Title: Multivariate genome-wide association study of post-traumatic stress disorder, alcohol use, and alcohol use disorders
Article.Authors: Barr P.; Bountress K.; Chatzinakos C.; Hart J.; Neale Z.; Sheerin C.; Johnson E.; Atkinson E.; Nievergelt C.; Maihofer A.; Powers A.; Porjesz B.; Agrawal A.; Edenberg H.; Gelernter J.; Koenen K.; N/A N/A.; Nievergelt C.; Maihofer A.; Atkinson E.; Chen C.; Choi K.; Coleman J.; Daskalakis N.; Duncan L.
Article.Abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) commonly co-occurs with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Comorbid PTSD and AUD is associated with poorer outcomes including worse treatment prognosis and significant physical health consequences. Both PTSD and AUD are polygenic in nature and genetically overlap. Previous work showed negative or non-significant associations between PTSD and alcohol consumption but positive genetic associations between PTSD and AUD. This work highlights the need for more nuanced examination of the similarities and distinctions in the associations between PTSD and alcohol consumption versus AUD. We leveraged the latest large-scale GWAS data to perform a multivariate GWAS of alcohol consumption (ALCC), problematic alcohol use (ALCP), and PTSD using GenomicSEM. Partial genetic correlations revealed that ALCP and PTSD were associated with each other (rG = 0.39, p = 4.38 × 10-60) and with other psychiatric problems, medical conditions, and pain, while ALCC was only weakly correlated with PTSD (rG = -0.08, p = 2.03 × 10-4) and uncorrelated with most traits after accounting for its genetic overlap with ALCP and PTSD. We examined associations between GenomicSEM-derived polygenic scores (PGS) and their corresponding phenotypes in participants from the Collaborative Study on the Genetics of Alcoholism (COGA). PGS for ALCC were unrelated to PTSD diagnosis and PGS for PTSD were unrelated to drinks in a typical week. PTSD is more strongly related to alcohol problems, and much of the overlap in PTSD and consumption is accounted for by its overlap with alcohol problems. These results help demonstrate the complex partial overlaps of PTSD, AUD, and alcohol consumption.

Article.Title: Real-world associations of antipsychotic use with clinical outcomes in schizophrenia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
Article.Authors: Yao H.; Peng Z.; Huang Y.; Wu R.
Article.Abstract: To systematically synthesize evidence on the association between antipsychotic medication use and diverse outcomes in individuals with schizophrenia, we searched PubMed, Embase, PsycINFO, and Web of Science from inception to May 1, 2026. Eligible studies were observational studies reporting associations between antipsychotic use and clinical outcomes in individuals with schizophrenia. Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed study quality. Data was synthesized using multilevel random-effects models. Outcomes were categorized into mortality (including all-cause and cause-specific), somatic disorders, and other clinical outcomes. Sixty-eight studies comprising 1,424,455 individuals were included. Among individuals with schizophrenia, antipsychotic use was associated with lower all-cause mortality (pooled estimate, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.54-0.77) and lower relapse risk (pooled estimate, 0.34; 95% CI, 0.12-0.99) compared with nonuse. In contrast, compared with nonuse, antipsychotic use was associated with higher risks of cancer (1.41; 95% CI, 1.17-1.69), fractures (1.35; 95% CI, 1.17-1.56), and lung infections (1.25; 95% CI, 1.04-1.51), whereas evidence for other outcomes was non-significant. Overall, the evidence base was limited, with several pooled estimates derived from a small number of studies. Subgroup analyses suggested variation by region and study design. Antipsychotic use was associated with lower all-cause mortality and relapse risk, alongside increased risks for some adverse outcomes such as fractures and lung infections. These findings should be interpreted cautiously, as residual confounding and bias may influence the observed associations and preclude causal interpretation. Further studies using rigorous designs are needed to clarify outcome-specific associations.

Article.Title: HINT1 in ventral hippocampal GABAergic neurons mediates depressive-like behaviors
Article.Authors: Li S.; Liu D.; Zhang H.; Wen R.; Hu H.; Xv J.; Cheng D.; Dang Y.
Article.Abstract: Depression is a complex psychiatric disorder with multifaceted etiologies, and its underlying molecular mechanisms are incompletely elucidated. Although histidine trimeric nucleotide-binding protein 1 (HINT1) has been implicated in major depressive disorders (MDD), its precise role and regulatory mechanism remain unclear. This study investigated the role of HINT1 in depression-associated phenotypes. In mice subjected to chronic social defeat stress (CSDS), stress-susceptible individuals exhibited significant upregulation of HINT1 in the hippocampus and medial prefrontal cortex. Targeted overexpression of HINT1 in ventral hippocampus (vHip) demonstrated that HINT1 directly induced depressive-like behaviors, whereas its knockdown exerted a robust antidepressant-like effect. Pharmacological inhibition of HINT1 with the selective inhibitor Tryptamine guanosine carbamate (TpGc) in vHip also reversed behavioral deficits and normalized neuronal activity in the CSDS-exposed mice. Cell-type-specific analyses demonstrated that HINT1 overexpression in vHip GABAergic neurons, including somatostatin-positive (SST+) and parvalbumin-positive (PV+) subtypes, exacerbated depressive-like phenotypes and disrupted neuronal activity. Proteomics analysis identified that HINT1 overexpression in the vHip significantly upregulated the small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) E3 ligases chromobox 4 (CBX4). Further overexpression of CBX4 in the GABAergic neurons of vHip induced depressive-like behaviors. Mechanistically, HINT1 interacted with and inhibited the phosphorylation of protein kinase C-β1 (PKCβ1), suppressing its downstream MEK1/2-ERK1/2 signaling and thereby increasing CBX4 levels. CBX4 promoted the SUMOylation of the glutamate N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor subunit 2 A (GluN2A) and affected its phosphorylation and trafficking. These findings demonstrated HINT1 as a key regulator of GABAergic signaling in vHip and highlighted its therapeutic potential for depression.

Article.Title: Genome-wide analysis identifies pleiotropic genes shared between severe mental disorders and biomarkers of cellular aging
Article.Authors: Pisanu C.; Nishioka M.; Manchia M.; Squassina A.; Kato T.
Article.Abstract: Severe mental disorders such as bipolar disorder (BD), major depressive disorder (MDD) and schizophrenia (SZ) are characterized by reduced life expectancy, premature mortality and alterations of aging biomarkers, leading to hypothesize that they might be associated with accelerated cellular aging. We quantified the genetic overlap between severe mental disorders and a comprehensive set of aging biomarkers including multivariate longevity and healthy aging (mvAge), brain age gap (BAG), leucocyte telomere length (gLTL), mitochondrial DNA copy number and epigenetic age acceleration (gEAA) using cutting-edge methods, and evaluated their functional enrichment and suitability as drug targets. All disorders were negatively correlated with mvAge. Further, MDD correlated negatively with gLTL and positively with gEAA. We identified several pleiotropic variants, with nine genes (AC068490.2, ASIC2, CNNM2, FURIN, GPM6A, HS6ST3, RP5-1043L13.1, SORCS3 and SP4) containing variants shared between aging biomarkers and all disorders. Functional analyses with summary-data-based Mendelian randomization showed that increased expression of the druggable gene CRHR1 in the prefrontal cortex was associated with increased risk of MDD and BAG measures. Our findings suggest that shared heritability might contribute to reduced longevity and healthy aging in severe mental disorders and identify pleiotropic genes involved in synaptic function and metabolic processes related to micronutrients such as folate and magnesium.

Article.Title: The non-inflammatory effect of neuronal NLRP3 on spatial memory after traumatic brain injury
Article.Authors: Tan S.; Xie Q.; Zhang J.; Li P.; Ning Y.; Yang N.; Wang B.; Peng Y.; Chen X.; Gao R.; Li C.; Du H.; Zhou Y.; Zhao Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The NLRP3 inflammasome has emerged as a critical regulator in neuroinflammatory responses to various brain insults from traumatic, ischemic and neurodegenerative conditions, an effect almost exclusively attributed to microglial NLRP3. Here, we demonstrated that in the absence of changes in inflammatory factors IL-18, IL-1β and TNF-α, neuronal Nlrp3 knockout in hippocampus (nNlrp3 -/- ) improved long-term spatial memory performance, with increased synaptic proteins levels and enhanced amplitude of long-term potentiation at 4 weeks after traumatic brain injury (TBI), compared to wildtype littermates. We further identified that NLRP3 structurally and functionally directly interacted with the R1 subunit of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NR1) in hippocampus after TBI. Accordingly, pharmacological inhibition of NLRP3 by MCC950 rescued the decrease in the NMDAR-gated calcium influx by LPS-stimulated hippocampal neurons while selective Nlrp3 knockout in hippocampal neurons partially reversed the decreased phosphorylation level of NR1 after TBI. Collectively, this study provides the first evidence that neuronal NLRP3 constitutes a non-inflammatory response to control synaptic plasticity and cognitive function via NR1-dependent non-inflammatory mechanism in TBI and thus broadens the central role of NLRP3 in neuronal adaptive mechanisms to include both microglial NLRP3-inflammation arm and the neuronal NLRP3-synaptic plasticity arm.

Article.Title: Multimodal associations between posterior hippocampus glutamate metabolism, visual cortex connectivity, and intrusive trauma reexperiencing symptoms
Article.Authors: Clancy K.; Chen X.; Song X.; Song T.; Zhou S.; Akman E.; Ostrand C.; Ren B.; Du F.; Rosso I.
Article.Abstract: Hippocampal dysfunction is implicated in posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), particularly intrusive reexperiencing symptoms, and may be mediated by glutamatergic excitotoxicity. Markers of glutamate dysfunction (higher glutamate to N-acetyl aspartate levels; Glu/NAA) in the hippocampus (HPC) have been linked to reexperiencing symptoms. However, the HPC demonstrates heterogeneity along its anterior-posterior axis, with different functional connectivity patterns and PTSD symptom associations, motivating investigations into glutamate metabolism in anterior and posterior HPC subregions (a/pHPC). PTSD symptoms were assessed with the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale for DSM-5. Reexperiencing symptom severity was associated with greater Glu/NAA in the pHPC, but not aHPC. pHPC Glu/NAA was further linked to stronger functional connectivity between the pHPC and visual cortex (VC), which in turn correlated with more severe reexperiencing symptoms. This strengthened pHPC-VC connectivity explained the shared variance between pHPC Glu/NAA and reexperiencing severity, suggesting dysregulated glutamate metabolism in the pHPC may contribute to reexperiencing symptoms through functional connectivity with the VC. These findings replicate prior work linking HPC Glu/NAA to trauma reexperiencing symptoms and provide novel evidence of this association in the pHPC, but not aHPC, which is mediated by its functional connectivity with the VC. This multimodal investigation supports translational models of glutamatergic dysfunction in trauma-related disorders and highlights new targets for pharmacological and neuromodulatory interventions.

Article.Title: Breast carcinoma amplified sequence 2 rescues adult hippocampal neurogenesis and cognitive deficits in Alzheimer’s disease via regulating BDNF/TrkB signaling
Article.Authors: Ma H.; Liu C.; Liu W.; Liu J.; Hou Y.; Song Q.; Wang Y.; Wang P.
Article.Abstract: Adult hippocampal neurogenesis (AHN) occurs throughout lifespan of humans and rodents and is correlated with memory performance and cognitive plasticity. In Alzheimer's disease (AD), AHN is impeded, while the molecular basis behind this impairment remains to be elucidated. Here we identified Breast carcinoma amplified sequence 2 (BCAS2), a core component of the CDC5L/Prp19 spliceosome complex, regulating AHN in AD. Using Bcas2 conditional knockout mice, AD mouse model APP/PS1 mice, established mouse primary adult neural stem cells and single cell sequencing, we demonstrate that BCAS2 replacement in adult mouse hippocampus promotes NSC activation and differentiation to neuron, restore AHN and relevant memory deficits through BDNF/TrkB signaling. Our findings corroborate the significance of AHN in AD and reveal the possible therapeutic potential of targeting BCAS2 in neurodegeneration.

Article.Title: Two distinct projection pathways converge onto the same BLA neurons to contribute to fear memory retrieval
Article.Authors: Yang H.; Xia T.; Kuang S.; Fu Y.; Cao Z.; Wen Y.; Yuan Y.; Chu C.; Guo X.; Yang L.; Sheng H.; Lei C.; Cui D.; Shao D.; Cai Z.; Lai B.; Chen M.; Zheng P.
Article.Abstract: Studying the neural circuits that mediate context-induced fear memory retrieval is of importance to develop new therapeutic approaches to prevent post-traumatic stress disorder relapse. The basolateral amygdala (BLA) is crucial for context-induced retrieval of fear memory. Previous studies indicate that projection neurons from the ventral hippocampus CA1 (vCA1) to the BLA (vCA1-BLA neurons) mediate context-induced retrieval of fear memory. However, it remains unclear whether other projection neurons to the BLA are involved in context-induced retrieval of fear memory and how they interact with vCA1-BLA neurons. Our findings indicate that the postrhinal cortex (POR) to the BLA (POR-BLA) neurons are also involved in context-induced retrieval of fear memory. These neurons innervate the same BLA neurons as vCA1-BLA neurons and participate in fear memory retrieval. These results suggest that two different projection neurons of POR-BLA and vCA1-BLA innervate on the same BLA neurons and POR-BLA neurons and vCA1-BLA neuron contribute to fear memory retrieval. These findings provide new insights into the neural mechanisms underlying fear memory retrieval.

Article.Title: Shared cortical morphometry and molecular signatures across depression and physical diseases
Article.Authors: Jiang C.; Zhou H.; Yuan Y.; Xu W.; Zhou Y.; Sun T.; You L.; Chen S.; Yin Y.; Yue Y.; Liu X.; Sun G.; Zhang Y.; Tan J.; Shi R.; Xu X.; Xu Z.; Zhou Z.; Guo W.; Jiang W.; Yuan Y.
Article.Abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is highly comorbid with physical diseases, suggesting shared neurobiological mechanisms. However, the common structural and molecular substrates underlying this comorbidity remain poorly understood. We analyzed multimodal MRI data from 577 patients (MDD, asthma, fibromyalgia, gastroesophageal reflux disease, type 2 diabetes) and 275 healthy controls, constructed individual morphometric similarity networks (MSN) to identify shared cortical alterations, and applied principal component analysis with multiscale molecular annotation (transcriptomic, cell-type, neurotransmitter, and cognitive mapping) to characterize underlying mechanisms. All patient groups exhibited regional MSN abnormalities. A shared MSN pattern emerged, featuring increased similarity in visual and somatomotor regions and decreased similarity in ventral attention, limbic, and default mode networks, and was replicated in independent cohorts. This pattern was significantly associated with spatial gene expression enriched for synaptic signaling, membrane potential regulation, and neuronal architecture, with predominant expression in excitatory/inhibitory neurons and astrocytes. It further mapped onto specific neurotransmitter systems, with exploratory cognitive decoding suggesting possible relevance to emotion and social cognition. Related genes overlapped with known risk loci for Alzheimer's disease and bipolar disorder. These findings identify a robust across diseases cortical MSN phenotype linked to convergent molecular and neurochemical correlates, offering a framework for studying shared vulnerability and transdiagnostic mechanisms across depression and physical diseases.

Article.Title: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) combined with antidepressant pharmacotherapy for depression: state-dependent mechanisms, clinical evidence, and translational challenges
Article.Authors: Deng J.; Shao Y.; Jiang L.; Wu B.; Roberts N.; Wang Q.; Jia Z.
Article.Abstract: Depression is a highly prevalent and debilitating mental disorder. Pharmacotherapy remains the primary treatment modality; however, its efficacy is often limited by a delayed onset of action, suboptimal response in some patients, and a high risk of recurrence. Treatment-resistant depression, characterized by poor response to conventional therapies, poses a major clinical challenge and highlights the need for improved treatment strategies. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), a noninvasive neuromodulation technique, has shown promise for depression, particularly when combined with antidepressant pharmacotherapy. Advances in neuroimaging, neurochemistry, and network neuroscience have clarified how high-frequency rTMS may modulate cortical excitability, monoaminergic transmission, synaptic plasticity, and distributed brain networks. Clinical evidence suggests that combined treatment may accelerate early improvement, increase response and remission, and reduce relapse risk; however, these benefits are heterogeneous across patients and symptom domains and should be interpreted in light of expectancy effects and limitations of sham blinding. Neuroimaging studies have identified treatment-associated functional and structural changes, including hippocampal volume changes, but the causal links among molecular signaling, circuit reorganization, structural findings, and symptom improvement remain unresolved. The interaction between rTMS and antidepressants should therefore not be viewed as uniformly additive or synergistic, but as a state-dependent process shaped by medication class, stimulation protocol and timing, cortical excitability, metaplasticity, and individual neurobiological context. This review integrates mechanistic, neuroimaging, and clinical evidence and discusses how biomarker-, state-, and symptom-informed targeting, optimized treatment sequencing, and pragmatic implementation strategies could improve the precision and accessibility of combined treatment for depression.

Article.Title: A microglial basis for fragile X syndrome via impairment of FMRP-regulated lysosomal function
Article.Authors: Li H.; Choi J.; Huang E.; Xu B.
Article.Abstract: Silencing of the FMRP-encoding FMR1 gene results in fragile X syndrome (FXS), the most common inheritable intellectual disability and autism. FMRP regulates various neuronal functions but clinical trials targeting neurons have failed, suggesting unrecognized disease mechanisms. We find that mice with selective Fmr1 deletion in microglia exhibit audiogenic seizures (AGS) and parvalbumin (PV) neuron loss, recapitulating two key phenotypes observed in FXS (Fmr1-/y) mice. By combining snRNA-Seq and RNA immunoprecipitation, we identify several lysosomal mRNAs as FMRP binding targets. FMRP promotes lysosomal protein expression and its deficiency disrupts lysosomal function in microglia. Notably, FMRP depletion reduces Grn-encoded secretory progranulin and increases PV neuron apoptosis in immature brains. PV neuron density is decreased similarly in Grn+/-, Fmr1-/y, and Grn+/-;Fmr1-/y mice, and progranulin overexpression rescues AGS and PV neuron loss in Fmr1-/y mice. Thus, our study identifies microglia and progranulin as critical regulators of FXS pathogenesis and potential targets for FXS therapy.

Article.Title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: transition to psychotic disorders
Article.Authors: Thapar A.; Dennison C.; Kandeğer A.; Owen M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract It is well recognized that Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is associated with heightened risk for common psychiatric disorders; early identification and treatment of ADHD may help reduce some of this risk. However, the substantially increased risk of bipolar disorder, psychosis, and schizophrenia (hereafter psychotic disorders) is often overlooked (odds ratios 4.7–8.9). Given how common ADHD is, there is growing pressure for greater involvement of primary care services, especially for less complex forms of ADHD. However, those at highest risk for transition to a psychotic disorder need to be prioritised for secondary care follow up. Currently it is unknown how to stratify ADHD according to risk or indeed why only some develop a psychotic disorder. This perspective examines key hypotheses that may explain why transition occurs only in a subset of individuals. One hypothesis is that features suggestive of ADHD may represent early manifestations of psychotic disorders, although direct support for this is limited. The potential role of ADHD treatment is also considered; current data indicate that therapeutic use of methylphenidate is not associated with increased risk of psychotic disorders, while uncertainty remains for amphetamines. The possible mediating roles of ADHD-evoked environmental exposures are discussed, but evidence for mediation is lacking. We also consider the evidence that ADHD and psychotic disorders result from shared underlying neurodevelopmental processes. We highlight key clinical implications for screening and monitoring individuals with ADHD for psychotic disorders and consider what factors may help in weighting risk. Finally, we identify important evidence gaps for future research.

Article.Title: The role of white matter microstructure in the association between childhood maltreatment and adult post-traumatic symptoms
Article.Authors: Berger L.; Rojczyk P.; Seitz-Holland J.; Zhang F.; Pankatz L.; Sollmann N.; Kaufmann E.; Carrington H.; Puri T.; Coleman M.; Pasternak O.; Bouix S.; Rathi Y.; Cetin-Karayumak S.; O’Donnell L.; Falkai P.; George M.; McAllister T.; Zafonte R.; Stein M.; Shenton M.; Koerte I.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Childhood maltreatment (CM) is a risk factor for adult post-traumatic symptoms and white matter (WM) alterations. It remains unknown how WM microstructure is affected alongside two common military conditions, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). Data from 299 participants (53% male, 35.69 ± 12.23 years of age) of the Injury and Traumatic Stress (INTRuST) clinical consortium was analyzed. The study included 56 individuals with PTSD (41 with comorbid mTBI), 107 with mTBI, and 136 controls (no PTSD and/or mTBI). CM was assessed using the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (CTQ). Multiple regression models examined associations between CM severity and WM diffusion. Moderation analyses assessed the effect of PTSD and/or mTBI on these associations. Mediation analyses examined how WM diffusion affects the associations between CM and both PTSD and post-concussive symptom severity. Greater CM severity was associated with lower MD and AD, independent of PTSD and/or mTBI. WM diffusion, particularly in the corpus callosum and the superior longitudinal fasciculus, mediated the associations between CM severity and both PTSD (MD b ab = 0.022, AD b ab = 0.019-0.034) and post-concussive symptoms (MD b ab = 0.028-0.040, AD b ab = 0.032-0.047). Findings suggest that WM alterations are more strongly associated with CM itself than with either PTSD and/or mTBI. Mediating effects in regions critical for sensory integration highlight the role of WM microstructure as a neurobiological pathway through which CM might predispose to post-traumatic symptoms.

Article.Title: Zebrafish behavioral phenomics reveals functional subtypes of autism risk genes
Article.Authors: Stuntzner-Gibson K.; Zhang P.; He B.; Diaz L.; Geng Y.
Article.Abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a highly heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition caused by many genetic mutations, each conferring modest individual risk. Despite its genetic complexity and clinical burden, no effective treatments targeting core symptoms are available. Although ASD is diagnosed as a single disorder, accumulating evidence suggests that it comprises biologically distinct subtypes, yet how genetic risk maps onto phenotypic substructure remains poorly defined. Here, we apply zebrafish behavioral phenomics to systematically link ASD risk genes to functional behavioral subtypes in vivo. Using an unsupervised deep learning-based behavioral profiling platform, ZeChat, we characterized the behavioral repertoires of zebrafish mutants for 11 high-confidence ASD risk genes. ZeChat analysis revealed distinct behavioral phenotypes for each mutant that was classified into three behavioral subtypes (Clusters 1-3) via hierarchical clustering of their behavioral fingerprints. By integrating mutant phenotypes with a large neuroactive drug phenomics database, we identified subtype-specific correlations with serotonergic, dopaminergic, and opioid receptor-modulating compounds. Using an orthogonal social preference assay, Fishbook, we further demonstrate subtype-specific pharmacological rescue of social deficits, including selective rescue of the Cluster 3 mutants arid1b, adnp, grin2b, pten, and the Cluster 2 mutants pogz and shank3, by μ-opioid receptor antagonists. Together, these results demonstrate a scalable in vivo framework for behavioral phenomics-driven classification of ASD risk genes into functional subtypes and discovery of targeted rescue strategies.

Article.Title: Hypothalamus-driven brain health through metabolic flexibility
Article.Authors: Horvath T.; Romanov R.; Matarese G.; Cota D.
Article.Abstract: Organismal physiology depends on continuous, non-hierarchical communication among cells, tissues, and organs. We argue that this communication rests on metabolic flexibility-the capacity of cells and tissues to adapt substrate use to changing energetic demands-and that the hypothalamus serves as the central hub coordinating this flexibility across the body. Using hypothalamic agouti-related protein (AgRP) and pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons as a model, we show these melanocortin neurons do more than regulate hunger and satiety: by integrating metabolic, hormonal, and immune signals, they shape reward, learning, executive function, and social behavior, while imposing coordinated metabolic states on peripheral tissues. When this flexibility is lost, as with aging or overnutrition, body-brain communication becomes rigid, driving cognitive decline, chronic inflammation, and neurodegenerative disease. We propose that signals from the body are not peripheral modifiers of brain function but fundamental determinants of it, with direct implications for hypothalamus-centered strategies to preserve brain health across the lifespan.

Article.Title: Redox-dependent remodeling of mitochondrial nucleoids contributes to bioenergetic decline during neuronal aging
Article.Authors: Cheng X.; Gao Y.; Chan C.; Xie Y.; Dai Y.; Xiong G.; Sathler A.; Roney J.; Li S.; Li Y.; Wu L.; Sheng Z.
Article.Abstract: Why mitochondria progressively fail in aging neurons remains a fundamental question in neurobiology. Although bioenergetic decline and oxidative stress are hallmarks of aging, whether redox signaling remodels mitochondrial nucleoids (mt-nucleoids) to impair neuronal bioenergetics remains unclear. Using aged mouse neurons and human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons, we demonstrate that redox-driven mt-nucleoid remodeling underlies reduced mtDNA transcript abundance and bioenergetic decline. Combining minimal photon fluxes (MINFLUX) nanoscopy with single-molecule transcription mapping, we identify distinct mt-nucleoid architectures governed by mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM)-mediated mtDNA compaction. Aging-associated oxidative stress drives mt-nucleoid remodeling from compact, transcriptionally active structures toward decompacted forms with reduced mtDNA transcript abundance and impaired mitochondrial ATP production. This remodeling involves species-specific TFAM redox mechanisms: cysteine oxidation promotes human TFAM polymerization, whereas methionine oxidation weakens mouse TFAM-mtDNA interactions. Notably, expressing an oxidation-resistant TFAM variant restores mt-nucleoid organization, mtDNA transcript abundance, and ATP production in aged neurons, identifying mt-nucleoid architecture as a potential target for preserving neuronal bioenergetics during aging.

Article.Authors: Bodart-Santos V.; Ravula A.; You Y.; Abdullah M.; Ruan Z.; Ellison J.; Radhakishun S.; Basu Ray N.; Melvin B.; Kurti A.; Liang Z.; Sakai Y.; O’Brien D.; Nguyen S.; Shaffer S.; Fiddes L.; Butovsky O.; Springer W.; Ikezu S.; Ikezu T.

Microglia-specific, but not astrocyte-specific, deletion of P2rx7 suppresses tau propagation. P2RX7 increases EV loading of tau and of mitochondrial proteins and DNA, which activate cytosolic DNA sensing and interferon signaling in recipient microglia. Tau-containing microglial EVs disrupt neuronal endolysosomal integrity and facilitate endosomal tau escape and phosphorylation. Thus, P2RX7 regulates the FRM branch point, driving inflammatory microglial transition and EV-mediated spread of tau and toxic mitochondrial molecules and highlighting the P2RX7-EV axis as a therapeutic target in AD.

Article.Title: Opposing excitatory and inhibitory synaptic pathologies drive ZC4H2-associated intellectual disability
Article.Authors: Ma P.; Wan L.; Li Y.; Bu Y.; Li D.; Zhao S.; Zhang H.; Zhao S.; Yuan K.; Ding Y.; Li M.; Tao W.; Zhu J.; Tang A.; Bai G.; Mao B.; Sheng N.
Article.Abstract: Understanding genotype-phenotype correlations is critical for precision medicine, yet patients carrying mutations in the same gene are often classified under one disorder and treated alike, despite potentially opposite responses to therapy. ZC4H2-associated rare disorder (ZARD) is an X-linked neurodevelopmental condition caused by diverse mutations across ZC4H2. Here, we show that distinct ZC4H2 mutations drive intellectual disability through opposing synaptic mechanisms. The gain-of-function mutation ZC4H2L66H enhances GABAA receptor (GABAAR) degradation, impairing inhibitory synaptic transmission and plasticity. By contrast, the loss-of-function mutation ZC4H2R213W increases AMPA receptor (AMPAR) stability and dysregulates excitatory synaptic activity. Despite these diametrically opposed synaptic pathologies, ZC4H2L66H/y and ZC4H2R213W/y knockin mice exhibit comparable cognitive deficits. Importantly, muscimol, a GABAAR agonist, specifically rescues deficits in ZC4H2L66H/y mice, whereas the AMPAR antagonist perampanel rescues ZC4H2R213W/y mice. These findings demonstrate that opposing synaptic etiologies can underlie a single genetic disorder and highlight pathomechanism-based stratification for targeted therapeutic strategies.

Article.Title: Oxygen fugacity, temperature, and pressure of Siberian eclogitic diamonds: Implications for the Archaean convecting mantle redox state
Article.Authors: Marras G.; Mikhailenko D.; McCammon C.; Aulbach S.; Lu Y.; Tao R.; Logvinova A.; Zedgenizov D.; Stagno V.
Article.Abstract: Kimberlite-borne eclogite xenoliths ultimately derive from ancient subducted oceanic crust. Some specimens still record the chemical and redox conditions of their igneous protoliths, allowing a view into contemporaneous convecting mantle sources. However, accurate reconstructions are limited because eclogites have been exposed to metasomatism in the subcontinental mantle for billions of years. Here, we investigated garnet and clinopyroxene inclusions, both touching and nontouching pairs, in 19 eclogitic diamonds from the Siberian craton, hence shielded from post-entrapment overprint. Inclusion compositions indicate average sampling depths of 180 to 280 km, temperatures of 1030° to 1540°C (±60°C), and redox conditions, for most of the samples, oxidized enough for diamonds to have originated from water(carbonate)-rich fluids. The reconstructed bulk composition points to basaltic oceanic crust formed from an Archaean convecting mantle region that was more oxygen-depleted than today, providing compelling evidence of redox heterogeneities in the source rocks of ancient oceanic crust.

Article.Authors: DiPrete B.; Perez-Saez J.; Wohl S.; Matteson N.; Kim S.; Azman A.; Lessler J.
Article.Abstract: Much remains unknown about cholera transmission dynamics in Africa. These units can be grouped into two major transmission clusters, one in Western Africa and bordering countries and one spanning the Central, Eastern, and Southern regions. Simulation studies show that these clusters can be used to assess the risk of international spread of introduced cholera strains and identify heterogeneities in the speed of international spread based on outbreak location. Article.Authors: Trokhimovskiy A.; Mège D.; Korablev O.; Olsen K.; Fedorova A.; Taysum B.; Tesson P.; Luginin M.; Montmessin F.; Vlasov P.; Grigoriev A.; Alday J.; Belyaev D.; Ignatiev N.; Patrakeev A.; Kokonkov N.; Ivanov Y.; Gurgurewicz J.; Pommerol A.; Cremonese G.; Thomas N.

While sulfur dioxide, so far undetected, could testify to ongoing eruptive activity, evidence of active magma chambers may be better identified by seepage of halogen gases, such as hydrogen chloride (HCl). Observations by Atmospheric Chemistry Suite led to the widespread observations of HCl at part-per-billion levels in the atmosphere of Mars during the warm perihelion period, attributed to aerosol-atmospheric sources. We also identify fresh and narrow (<1 meter) fissures in this area, which we interpret to be potential HCl pathways rooted into magmatic bodies at depth. Our results are best explained by ongoing igneous processes in the Martian interior.

Article.Authors: Kumari K.; Pérez-Núñez I.; Noguera Castells A.; Pluvinet R.; Peula C.; Patthey A.; Khan G.; Pajdzik K.; Román Á.; Dassi E.; He C.; Lundin E.; Esteller M.; Celià-Terrassa T.; Aguilo F.

Knockdown and rescue studies further reveal that DNMT1 primarily mediates METTL3-dependent regulation of cell migration, whereas the antiproliferative effects of METTL3 suppression are likely driven by additional downstream targets. Collectively, these findings identify the m 6 A-METTL3-DNMT1 axis as a mechanistic link between RNA and DNA methylation pathways and a potential therapeutic vulnerability in HGSOC.

Article.Title: Stony coral symbioses show variable responses to future ocean conditions
Article.Authors: de Souza M.; Bruce J.; Cros A.; Jury C.; Drury C.; Toonen R.
Article.Abstract: Coral reefs support over a quarter of marine species and nearly a billion people worldwide but are also among the ecosystems most threatened by anthropogenic impacts. There is long-standing debate about whether coral symbioses will be disrupted or respond adaptively under future ocean conditions. Using a factorial 2.5-year future-ocean mesocosm experiment across eight coral species representing the major coral lineages, we tracked symbiont community shifts within replicate fragments from the same individual coral. Some corals exhibited stochastic divergence, whereas others showed deterministic shifts in symbiont community composition. Heat stress generally reduced symbiont diversity and promoted predictable restructuring, consistent with deterministic adaptation to moderate thermal stress but stochastic accumulation of diversity under extreme conditions. We propose that adaptive and stochastic responses represent endpoints along a continuum of host-orchestrated symbiont sorting. This study bridges coral reef ecology with broader host-microbiome theory, offering an integrated perspective on how symbiotic systems may respond to environmental change.

Article.Title: A functional connectome identifies vulnerability to cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s disease progression
Article.Authors: Zhao K.; Xie H.; Fonzo G.; Carlisle N.; Jacobs T.; Osorio R.; Church A.; Lin F.; Zhang Y.; N/A N/A.
Article.Abstract: Identifying the neurobiological basis of cognitive vulnerability is essential for preventing Alzheimer’s disease (AD). We derived the Alzheimer’s Resilience-Vulnerability Connectome (ARC) by contrasting SuperAgers (SA), an extreme phenotype of preserved late-life memory, with AD using resting-state fMRI. ARC distinguished SA from AD in a discovery cohort ( N = 290; AUC = 0.85) and replicated independently ( N = 143), involving prefrontal, temporal, and insular networks and associating with brain age. Applied to cognitively unimpaired adults (discovery: N = 818; replication: N = 497), ARC-based subtyping revealed SA-like and AD-like subgroups with comparable baseline cognition but divergent longitudinal trajectories. AD-like individuals exhibited faster cognitive decline, greater amyloid-β accumulation, and higher AD conversion risk. Exploratory GWAS nominated CLYBL and FRMD6 as candidate novel loci associated with the subtype difference. These findings suggest that ARC captures a continuous connectomic dimension of cognitive aging spanning SA, cognitively typical aging, and AD, highlighting the potential of functional connectomic variation for early risk stratification in AD.

Article.Title: Local translational program at the muscle-tendon junction endows domain identity in muscle syncytia
Article.Authors: El Khazen N.; de Carvalho Neves J.; Franke V.; Smith C.; Mankhong S.; Jauliac E.; Yedigaryan L.; Lefebvre E.; Akalin A.; Maire P.; Kim M.
Article.Abstract: How cells establish specialized subdomains is a fundamental question in cell and tissue biology. Skeletal muscle fibers, among the largest cells in the body, are multinucleated and form distinct regions such as the neuromuscular and myotendinous junctions (MTJs), the latter forming a critical interface between muscle and tendon that transmits contractile force. While transcriptional heterogeneity among myonuclei has been described, whether local translation contributes to domain identity remains unknown, largely due to the lack of tools for domain-specific manipulation. Here, we introduce MTJ-AAV, a viral system that enables selective genetic targeting of MTJ myonuclei. This approach allowed MTJ-specific ribosome tagging and revealed extensive translational regulation underlying MTJ biology and its remodeling during exercise. Untranslated regions of these transcripts were sufficient to control regionalized translation. Notably, the Krüpper-like factor–family transcription factors emerged as translationally up-regulated targets at the MTJ, where they drive local gene expression. Our findings establish local translation as a key layer of subcellular specialization and provide a versatile toolkit for dissecting spatial molecular regulation within muscle syncytia.

Article.Title: Clinically derived micro- and nanoplastic uptake drives spatiotemporally confined metabolic stress revealed by bond-selective imaging
Article.Authors: Li J.; Liu N.; Zhang D.; Lee H.
Article.Abstract: Although microplastics and nanoplastics (MPs/NPs) are pervasive environmental contaminants, our understanding of cellular toxicity remains incomplete, as adverse effects are often attributed to long-term intracellular accumulation, while the spatiotemporal onset of cellular damage remains poorly defined. Here, we use chemical bond–selective stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy and cell models that decouple continuous exposure from intracellular retention to directly visualize clinically derived MP/NP-cell interactions. Cellular stress occurs primarily during MP/NP exposure, accompanied by alterations in lipid droplet (LD) composition. In contrast, following extracellular removal, intracellularly retained MP/NP become largely inert, with recovery of lipid metabolism and cellular functions. Lipidomics identifies arachidonic acid (AA) as a key dysregulated metabolite, and SRS imaging further reveals transient, spatially confined AA enrichment in MP/NP–proximal LDs during uptake. Phospholipid coating of MP/NP attenuates LD alterations and cytotoxicity while preserving particle internalization, establishing uptake-driven metabolic stress, rather than long-term intracellular retention, as a primary source of MP/NP–induced damage.

Article.Title: Persistent bistability of Nordic Seas overflow waters over 800,000 years
Article.Authors: Stevenard N.; Govin A.; Kissel C.; Swingedouw D.; Toucanne S.; Bouttes N.
Article.Abstract: The stability of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a major uncertainty in projections of future climate. However, direct evidence for AMOC tipping behavior on orbital timescales remains scarce. Here, we reconstruct the strength of Iceland-Scotland Overflow Water, a key lower branch of the deep Atlantic circulation, over the past 800,000 years by combining 12 current-speed records from North Atlantic sediment cores with a data-driven hybrid model. The resulting reconstruction reveals persistent alternation between weak (glacial) and strong (interglacial) circulation modes, pervasive millennial-scale variability within both regimes, and systematic asymmetry between weak-to-strong recoveries and strong-to-weak collapses. Threshold and phase-space analyses show that regime shifts occur within a narrow window of atmospheric carbon dioxide and sea level and often follow hysteresis-like loops. Although bistability persists throughout the last 800,000 years, its sensitivity and timing evolve through time. These findings provide long-term, high-resolution, data-driven constraints on the bistability of Nordic Seas overflow waters and its implications for AMOC resilience in a warming world.

Article.Title: On-going retinal neuronal degeneration despite clinical stability in glaucoma
Article.Authors: Raghavendra A.; Elbash K.; Diaz M.; Saeedi O.; Liu Z.; Hammer D.
Article.Abstract: Glaucoma, a leading cause of irreversible blindness, involves progressive retinal ganglion cell loss. Early detection of this neurodegeneration is critical, yet current clinical methods often identify disease only after substantial damage has occurred. This preliminary study used high-resolution adaptive optics–optical coherence tomography (AO-OCT) to track individual retinal ganglion cells in patients and healthy volunteers over 3 to 5 years. Results revealed higher neurodegeneration in glaucoma compared to normal aging. We observed 4.16 to 6.86% annual decrease in cell density in glaucoma, far exceeding the 0.27% cell loss rate observed in the healthy volunteer group. Critically, AO-OCT detected progression significantly earlier, identifying cell loss 0.74 years before conventional OCT and 1.49 years before visual field testing. These findings demonstrate AO-OCT as a more sensitive tool capable of monitoring glaucomatous damage with superior precision, potentially representing a major advancement over current clinical imaging.

Article.Title: Oxygen-mediated projection microstereolithography for sub–100-μm zirconia dental veneers
Article.Authors: Shen Y.; Wang X.; Yang C.; Jiang Y.; Wang F.; Pan Z.; Li J.; Fang N.; Sun Y.
Article.Abstract: High-resolution vat photopolymerization of ceramics is constrained by light scattering, which broadens cured features, and by shallow penetration, which limits interlayer bonding. This trade-off is particularly damaging for microscale structures such as no-preparation dental veneers. We introduce an oxygen-mediated projection microstereolithography strategy in which an oxygen-permeable release film creates an interfacial inhibition field in high-solid–loading zirconia slurry. Rather than uniformly reducing curing, oxygen preferentially filters low-dose scattered light at pattern edges while preserving curing in the projected core. This anisotropic inhibition reshapes the accuracy-depth trade-off, enabling optimized multilayer printing of thin-wall zirconia. The process enabled reproducible fabrication of ∼80-micrometer zirconia veneers with high trueness, improved marginal adaptation, and handling-related strength comparable to substantially thicker milled veneers. The approach provides the potential for minimally invasive dental restoration and a general strategy for high-resolution additive manufacturing of strongly scattering ceramic suspensions.

Article.Title: BCLAF1 links RNA splicing to ATF4-dependent metabolic adaptation in acute myeloid leukemia
Article.Authors: López-Hernández L.; Crowley S.; Cea-Sánchez S.; de Arellano R.; Krishnan N.; Toolan-Kerr P.; White L.; Ignoti D.; Soto-Hidalgo E.; Gustincich S.; González-Prieto R.; Pandolfini L.; Barbieri I.; Altea-Manzano P.; Magee J.; Ferraro F.; Taylor S.; Bednarski J.; Millán-Zambrano G.
Article.Abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is driven by genetic alterations and non-mutational mechanisms that disrupt normal hematopoiesis and support leukemic cell survival. While the mutational landscape of AML is well characterized, the non-genetic processes sustaining leukemic maintenance remain less understood. Using human AML cells and murine models, we identify BCL2-associated transcription factor 1 (BCLAF1) as a key regulator of leukemic progression through control of mRNA processing. BCLAF1 physically associates with core spliceosome components and regulates alternative splicing programs in leukemic cells. Mechanistically, BCLAF1 is required for productive splicing of activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4) mRNA, thereby sustaining ATF4 protein levels and downstream metabolic gene expression programs. Loss of BCLAF1 reduces ATF4 levels, leading to impaired de novo amino acid biosynthesis and increased sensitivity to venetoclax. Together, these findings uncover a previously unrecognized mechanism linking RNA splicing control to metabolic adaptation in AML, identifying BCLAF1 as a potential therapeutic vulnerability.

Article.Title: Hoxa10 governs lifelong skeletal stem cell maintenance and bone repair
Article.Authors: Leclerc K.; Sambon M.; Weng R.; Suhardi V.; Ramsukh M.; Phadke R.; Pack G.; Rytel M.; Zhong J.; Schaffler B.; Butron S.; Morgani S.; Leucht P.
Article.Abstract: Skeletal stem and progenitor cells (SSPCs) sustain bone homeostasis and regeneration throughout life, yet the transcriptional programs that preserve their identity remain poorly defined. Here we identify the distal Hox gene Hoxa10 as a cell-autonomous regulator of skeletal stem cell maintenance. Using inducible genetic deletion, lineage tracing, single-cell transcriptomics, and injury models, we show that loss of Hoxa10 leads to progressive depletion of SSPCs, impaired bone regeneration, and defective matrix organization. Mechanistically, Hoxa10 maintains the undifferentiated state of skeletal stem cells by restraining premature osteogenic, adipogenic, and chondrogenic commitment, while promoting collagen III production and collagen fiber alignment within regenerative niches. Hoxa10 -dependent regulation of extracellular matrix composition is restricted to primitive progenitors and is uncoupled from osteoblast differentiation. Notably, transient depletion of distal Hox genes in primary human SSPCs recapitulates the murine defects in proliferation, self-renewal, and differentiation restraint. Together, these findings define a conserved Hox-dependent program that preserves skeletal stem cell identity and regenerative competence, revealing how developmental transcription factors are repurposed to sustain the adult skeleton across the life span.

Article.Title: Ultrasound neural interface enabling acute spinal cord monitoring and blood flow modulation
Article.Authors: Kerensky M.; Krishnan S.; Liang R.; Kempski Leadingham K.; Quiroz V.; Punnoose J.; Smit C.; Routkevitch D.; Kumar A.; Davidar A.; Steger L.; Weber-Levine C.; Jiang K.; Bhimreddy M.; Bauer S.; Lopez A.; Kramer P.; Robinson K.; Menta A.; Ghaith A.; Hersh A.; Abramson H.; Mohammadabadi A.; Theodore J.; Zmily O.
Article.Abstract: The days following decompression surgery for acute spinal cord injury (SCI) are a critical period for postoperative monitoring. After wound closure, clinicians lack on-demand access to local spinal cord morphology and hemodynamics, and care therefore remains guided largely by systemic surrogates rather than direct postoperative insight into the injured cord. We present the Multimodal Ultrasound System for Injury Care (MUSIC), a temporary epidural ultrasound neural interface placed during standard decompression surgery to enable postoperative brightness-mode imaging, Doppler-derived hemodynamic monitoring, and future device-integrated ultrasound actuation. Across simulations, benchtop, human cadaveric, and porcine studies, MUSIC enabled on-demand visualization of cord structure, hematoma tracking, detection and longitudinal tracking of localized Doppler flow signatures attributable to the sulcal artery region, and, in healthy pigs, proof-of-concept focused ultrasound modulation of blood-flow velocity. MUSIC establishes a temporary postoperative acoustic interface that provides spinal cord information to inform monitoring, future management, and localized intervention strategies after SCI.

Article.Title: Common transcriptional changes in the brain during hibernation and Alzheimer’s disease
Article.Authors: Largo-Barrientos P.; Praschberger R.; León-Espinosa G.; Bultynck P.; Mallopoulou A.; Machado J.; Poovathingal S.; Davie K.; Verstreken P.
Article.Abstract: Hibernation demands rapid brain adaptations, involving cycles of reduced metabolic rate during torpor, followed by brief periods of arousal. Previous studies show hibernation induces a drastic increase in Tau hyperphosphorylation, but a mechanistic connection to disease remains unclear. Using single-nucleus RNA sequencing on hippocampi of golden hamsters, we unveil large transcriptional shifts across the hibernation cycle in all cell types, especially glia. Common transcriptional changes in mitochondrial and ribosomal genes are observed in all different cell types. In addition, hibernation triggers an inflammatory-like response in microglia that in part resembles cell states observed in Alzheimer’s disease, but here in the absence of Aβ-accumulation and neurodegeneration. These findings reveal brain transformations that might help preserve vital functions under extreme conditions and they suggest that early cellular changes in AD may be a natural adaptive process.

Article.Title: Genetic dissection of cell type–specific congenital heart disease variants reveals ETS1 control of vascular smooth muscle cell fate
Article.Authors: Li X.; Fu M.; Jia S.; Wu Z.; Pang L.; Xiong K.; Wang Y.; Li W.; He A.; Ai S.
Article.Abstract: Numerous congenital heart disease (CHD) risk variants lie in cis-regulatory elements, yet the impact of variants in repressed and bivalent chromatin on cell type–specific heart development is unclear. Here, we generated a single-cell multiomic atlas of human cardiac differentiation by jointly profiling H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H3K4me3, and transcriptomes in individual cells, classifying cis-regulatory elements into six chromatin states, enabling prioritization of 610 CHD-associated noncoding variants enriched in lineage- and state-specific regulatory elements, including repressive and bivalent regions. CRISPR knockin of selected variants perturbed nearby gene expression and impaired cardiac differentiation. Dissection of a Polycomb-marked variant near ETS1 (ETS proto-oncogene 1) revealed local H3K27me3 loss, H3K27ac gain, and ETS1 up-regulation, which redirects differentiation toward second-heart-field progenitors with epithelial characteristics at early stages and, ultimately, highly migratory ETS1 + vascular smooth muscle cells. Together, our work establishes a single-cell chromatin-state framework for interpreting noncoding CHD risk variants and uncovers an ETS1-driven program linking Polycomb-deregulated noncoding variation to aberrant vascular smooth muscle fate commitment during human cardiogenesis.

Article.Title: Unveiling the underlying spin mechanism in quasi-2D perovskite spin-polarized lasing
Article.Authors: Li Q.; Hu Z.; Zhou H.; Liu Z.; Huang S.; Wang H.; Zhan Z.; Nie B.; Zhang Z.; Luo J.; Leng Y.; Du J.
Article.Abstract: Spin-polarized lasers hold great potential in integrated photonic devices for secure communication, optical interconnections, and advanced optical devices, offering excellent properties superior to those of conventional lasers. Quasi-two-dimensional (quasi-2D) perovskites are promising candidates for spin-polarized lasers, because their potential structural inversion asymmetry will result in strong spin-orbit coupling (SOC) facilitating spin injection and hence spin splitting of electronic bands. However, strong SOC involves a trade-off between spin injection and spin lifetimes. How to prolong spin lifetimes in the lasing regime while maintaining the optical gain make it challenging to sustain spin polarization for lasing. Here, we unveil the underlying spin mechanism and successfully realize quasi-2D perovskite spin-polarized lasing by suppressing fast spin relaxation through triplet exciton regulation using organic cations of phenylethylammonium (PEA) and 1-naphthylmethylamine (NMA). We identify the Bir-Aronov-Pikus (BAP) mechanism is the dominant spin relaxation mechanism preventing the achievement of spin-polarized lasing in quasi-2D perovskites. By modulating the reverse intersystem crossing of triplet excitons, the D’yakonov-Perel’ (DP) mechanism becomes to play a key role and results in a new-emerged prolonged spin lifetime of 35.4 ps at 77 K, which is ∼5 times that of the BAP-induced one. Consequently, spin-polarized lasing is realized below 200 K, and the threshold is 30.2% lower than that for linearly polarized excitation. This work underscores the potential of PEA-based quasi-2D perovskites in spin-polarized lasing and contributes to the rapid advancements in perovskite spintronic devices.

Article.Title: Self-charged toothbrush facilitates tooth healthcare maintenance
Article.Authors: Lu Y.; Song J.; Chi X.; Li W.; Wu L.; Guo Y.; Cui Q.; Zheng X.; Bai Y.; Heng B.; Han X.; Zhang X.; Deng X.
Article.Abstract: Toothbrushes have undergone no substantive improvements beyond their mechanical function for about 1118 years to date. Conventional toothbrushes often fail to establish an antibacterial environment on the tooth surface, allowing bacteria to recover and recolonize. Here, we developed an innovative self-charged toothbrush that integrates daily tooth brushing with piezoelectric functionality, synergizing both optimal mechanical properties and stable electrical activity. The self-charged toothbrushes can generate reactive oxygen species to disrupt bacterial membrane integrity and diminish bacterial adhesion by combining static antibacterial inhibition through surface potential with dynamic piezoelectric stimulation. Clinical evaluation revealed that the localized piezoelectric stimulation of self-charged toothbrushes can mitigate plaque formation and gingival inflammation. Mechanistic studies further revealed that the self-charged toothbrushes induced oxidative damage to the oral pathogenic bacterial membranes, thereby impairing the ATP-binding cassette transporter pathway. Hence, this study developed a concept of piezoelectric PVDF toothbrushes that combine physical cleaning with sustained antibacterial effect, thus highlighting the potential of self-charged materials in advancing oral healthcare.

Article.Title: Thermalization of quantum light induced by classical nonlinear wave dynamics
Article.Authors: Chahrour F.; Özdemir Ş.; Busch K.; El-Ganainy R.; Perez-Leija A.
Article.Abstract: Thermalization of isolated quantum systems is an intriguing phenomenon at the forefront of contemporary physics. In this work, we demonstrate that nonlinear multimode optical platforms can be harnessed to induce effective quantum interactions between photons. Through numerical experiments, we reveal the thermalization of quantum light, specifically single- and two-photon states, propagating alongside classical light within multimode nonlinear optical systems. This thermalization is clearly manifested by the emergence of Rayleigh-Jeans and Boltzmann statistical distributions. Beyond providing a deeper understanding of how classical nonlinearities can be used to investigate quantum many-body dynamics, our findings enable the exploration of a broader range of complex quantum phenomena, including aspects of quantum phase transitions, within readily accessible classical optical settings.

Article.Title: N 6-methyladenosine–dependent ARv7 translation couples lactate metabolism with enzalutamide resistance in prostate cancer
Article.Authors: Zhang M.; Cheng B.; Jia M.; Li X.; Huang Y.; Li B.; Wang X.; Shao J.; Deng Q.; Yu W.; Li M.; Yang Z.; Liang C.; Li T.; Dai R.; Wang R.
Article.Abstract: Enzalutamide (Enz)–resistant prostate cancer (PCa) is a lethal disease that affects a broad population of elderly men. Experimental and clinical evidence has demonstrated that androgen receptor variant 7 (ARv7) plays a critical role in Enz-resistant (EnzR) PCa by functioning as a constitutively active transcription factor driving disease progression. However, the predictive value of the ARv7 transcript has not been fully recognized due to its low frequency in castration-resistant PCa. In this study, we identified ARv7 mRNA as an N 6-methyladenosine (m 6 A)–modified transcript. Enz treatment increases METTL3-dependent m 6 A methylation of ARv7 mRNA at the A1177 site, which is subsequently recognized by the reader protein YTHDC2, leading to enhanced translation efficiency of ARv7. Furthermore, EnzR PCa exhibited elevated lactate metabolism, which regulated AR transcription through promoter-mediated epigenetic modifications at H3K9 and H3K14. Reactivated AR exhibited enhanced phase separation to transcriptionally up-regulate YTHDC2 expression. In vivo experiments demonstrated that targeting the METTL3-YTHDC2-ARv7 axis represents a promising therapeutic strategy to suppress EnzR PCa progression. Moreover, the METTL3 inhibitor STM2457 synergized with Enz to inhibit tumor growth without observable toxicity. Collectively, our findings suggest that the clinical utility of ARv7 may need to be reconsidered in light of its m 6 A-dependent translational regulation.

Article.Title: Toxic mercury, aquatic ecosystem collapse, and the ancient Lowland Maya
Article.Authors: Waters M.; Wooten S.; Abrook A.; Brenner M.; Curtis J.; Langdon P.; Medina-Gonzalez R.; Paradeisis-Stathis S.; Vachula R.
Article.Abstract: Environmental impacts endured by the Lowland Maya during the Classic Period (250 to 920 CE) included droughts, deforestation, and soil erosion. Recent studies on mercury (Hg) pollution and cyanotoxins suggest that degraded water quality was also a stressor for the Pre-Columbian Maya. Hg in the Maya region is related to use of both elemental mercury and mineral cinnabar (HgS), the latter used as a red pigment. Questions, however, remain concerning the toxicity of Hg or the consequences of prehistoric Hg exposure on ecosystem and human health. Here, we show that Classic Period Hg concentrations in sediment cores from two lakes on the Yucatán Peninsula exceeded modern sediment Hg toxicity thresholds by orders of magnitude for centuries during ancient Maya occupation. Sediments also have evidence of aquatic food web collapse (algae, bacteria, cyanobacteria, ostracods, snails, and nonbiting midges), coincident with the time of high Hg concentrations, confirming that Hg toxicity was an additional environmental stressor for Classic Maya populations.

Article.Title: A disynaptic trigeminal circuit for the transformation and integration of oral chemesthesis in male mice
Article.Authors: Liu F.; Cui K.; Mao J.; Wang H.; Li B.; Guo L.; Zhang N.; Li Y.; Ruan S.; Pei W.; Hao Z.; Zhang Q.; Chai G.; Liu C.; Zhang C.; Wang J.; Zhang S.; Li L.; Zhang Y.; Xie J.
Article.Abstract: Chemesthesis, encompassing oral sensations such as spiciness and coolness, is an important yet incompletely understood component of mammalian chemical sensing. Unlike taste or olfaction, these sensations are conveyed primarily through trigeminal pathways; however, how modality-specific peripheral signals are processed and transformed along central ascending pathways remains poorly understood. Herein, we delineate the structural and functional organization of an ascending trigeminal-brainstem-parabrachial circuit that mediates oral chemesthetic processing in male mice. Using viral tracing, in vivo calcium imaging, and chemogenetic and optogenetic manipulations, we identify a genetically defined disynaptic glutamatergic pathway (trigeminal ganglion → spinal trigeminal nucleus caudalis → lateral parabrachial nucleus) that is both necessary and sufficient for capsaicin- and menthol-evoked defensive behaviors. Although peripheral TRPV1 + and TRPM8 + neurons retain a degree of modality bias, we observe substantial convergence of spicy and cooling signals within the spinal trigeminal nucleus, followed by sustained and synchronized population activity in vglut2 + neurons of the external lateral parabrachial nucleus. This hierarchical transformation from peripheral segregation to central integration reveals the organizational principle by which distinct chemesthetic modalities are progressively integrated along a trigeminal-mediated ascending pathway, providing a circuit-level framework for understanding how chemical stimuli are processed and coordinated to drive defensive behaviors.

Article.Title: Independent origin of genomic imprinting in placental fish
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Campbell P.; Kingsley A.; Reynoso Y.; Kang Y.; Huang C.; Werren J.; Reznick D.; Wang X.
Article.Abstract: Genomic imprinting results in biased expression of one parental allele. Such non-Mendelian expression occurs in angiosperms and placental mammals, which share having an active paternal genome during maternal offspring provisioning. It is hypothesized that imprinting modulates conflict between maternal control of resource allocation and paternal control of resource acquisition. If true, then imprinting should evolve in any organism that evolves a placenta. Here, we demonstrate genomic imprinting in a placental poeciliid fish, Poeciliopsis prolifica . Using transcriptomes from reciprocal crosses between two inbred strains, we identified 84 protein-coding genes with robust evidence of imprinting in P. prolifica placenta. These include the teleost ortholog of mammalian imprinted gene, grb10 , and a pair of adjacent genes, dpp4 and gcga , with opposing effects on glucose metabolism that are oppositely imprinted in a fashion that potentially resolves parental conflict. Significantly elevated allelic DNA methylation on the promoters of two focal imprinted genes suggests epigenetic mechanisms of imprinting similar to those in mammals. We also discovered the convergent recruitment of a gene network associated with nutrient transport in mammals. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of genomic imprinting in a non-mammalian vertebrate and supports the potential role of imprinting in resolving parental conflict.

Article.Title: Cytoplasmic crowding drives intracellular viscoelastic increase during epithelial maturation
Article.Authors: Arkowitz G.; Destrian O.; Aggoun A.; Fardin M.; Berto P.; Tessier G.; Mège R.; Berret J.; Ladoux B.
Article.Abstract: The cytoplasm is a crowded, active medium whose mechanical properties underpin essential cellular functions, yet how intracellular rheology adapts during tissue maturation remains unclear. Here, we examine the evolution of cytoplasmic viscoelasticity in Madin-Darby canine kidney epithelial monolayers as cell density increases. Using magnetic rotational spectroscopy, an active microrheology technique, we quantify zero-shear viscosity and elastic modulus throughout monolayer maturation. We uncover a substantial enhancement of intracellular viscoelasticity correlated with increasing cell density and a concomitant rise in cellular dry mass concentration. Hyperosmotic perturbations on subconfluent monolayers reproduce this effect, confirming cytoplasmic crowding as a driver of rheological changes. Notably, intracellular viscoelasticity scales linearly with dry mass concentration, suggesting a direct coupling between internal mechanics and cytoplasmic concentration during epithelial maturation. These findings establish a link between tissue-level organization and intracellular mechanics, highlighting cytoplasmic crowding as a regulator of epithelial homeostasis and providing a framework to connect rheology with tissue behavior.

Article.Abstract: Ultrasound-modulated electroencephalography (USMEEG) has become a vital tool in neuroscience because it integrates millimeter-level spatial resolution with millisecond-level temporal resolution. Article.Title: Pink noise in dyads’ semantic similarity trajectories predicts conversation enjoyment
Article.Authors: O’Nell K.; Sanchez K.; Finn E.
Article.Abstract: Conversation is a core component of human social life. Many influential theories treat conversation as a linear system, i.e., the sum of its parts. We propose an alternate account that considers the multiscale organization of semantic similarity over the course of a conversation, as indexed by pink noise. Our records show that cryospheric expansion was followed by large, precessionally paced variations in sea-surface salinity and a marked regional increase in biological productivity. Article.Title: Revisiting the additionality and durability of carbon uptake in large-scale ocean iron fertilization
Article.Authors: Noh K.; Liu X.; Stock C.; McGillicuddy D.; Dunne J.
Article.Abstract: Climate stabilization pathways limiting global warming to 1.5° to 2°C require rapid emission reductions alongside additional carbon dioxide removal (CDR) of ∼2 to 3 PgC year −1 . This uptake nearly matches the additional carbon uptake from global fertilization. In other iron-limited regions, fertilization-induced uptake is largely offset (70 to 100%) by anomalous outgassing in nonfertilized regions. After terminating OIF following 30 years of fertilization, the ocean retains ∼50% of the additional carbon in the SSO, whereas retention is negligible elsewhere. These results identify the SSO as the most favorable region for durable carbon removal through large-scale OIF, particularly in terms of additionality and durability, although its carbon uptake is smaller than earlier estimates. Article.Title: Electron competition in azobenzene programs infection-adaptive antibacterial therapy
Article.Authors: Hu Y.; Li J.; Wang G.; Wang X.; Zhu Z.; Rao J.
Article.Abstract: Conventional stimulus-responsive antibacterial systems generally operate through binary trigger–activation mechanisms, making them poorly suited to evolving infection microenvironments and thereby contributing to persistent infection and resistance development. Oxygen acts as a competing electron acceptor within the reductive reaction network, partitioning electron transfer between azo reduction and oxygen consumption. Article.Authors: Devienne J.; Liu Z.; Jiang C.; Tosca N.; Ginnis T.; Sasselov D.; Harrison R.; Ozturk S.

Article.Title: Adaptive dual-programming magnetic soft robot with lifelike behavior
Article.Authors: Ye Y.; Xu C.; Wang S.; Li W.; Wu R.; Wu H.; Xia N.; Yang T.; Song S.; Zhang L.; Dong Y.; Li B.
Article.Abstract: Magnetic soft robots with embodied intelligence of multimodal motions, environmental perception, and functional decoupling depend on ingenious material arrangement and programmable morphing information introduction. While some efforts have been made, achieving lifelike behaviors for soft robots in system-level strategy remains a notable challenge. Here, we present dual-programming hydrogel-based soft robots (DHSRs) that couple magnetic and anisotropic programming through the spatial arrangement of patterned magnetic skeletons into responsive and structural hydrogel bodies. These DHSRs exhibit programmable exquisite and multicurved structures in three-dimensional (3D) space, environment-adaptive deformation behaviors proved by switching from random jumping on land to regular swimming in water of a fish-like soft robot, and further locomotion-function decoupling capabilities of region-selective cargo delivery in an integrated “locomotion-perception-action” workflow. Our strategy in biomedical potential is exemplified by a ring-like pH-responsive DHSR for gastric ulcer therapy, which integrates multimodal locomotion (rolling, tumbling, and rotating), adaptive matching, and microneedle-mediated penetration. By collaborating with a capsule endoscopy system, we explore the possibility of a wireless and painless diagnostic-therapeutic platform in a pig model. This strategy endows the robot with perception and multitask execution capabilities, highlighting a promising route for the intelligent evolution of soft robots across diverse application domains.

Article.Title: Age reshapes selection on melanoma driver mutations
Article.Authors: Liu Y.; Mandell J.; Rajaei M.; Brash D.; Alfaro-Murillo J.; Townsend J.
Article.Abstract: Aging is a major risk factor for melanoma. However, it is unclear whether aging fuels tumor evolution by altering mutation rates, changing the microenvironmentally induced selection on drivers, or both. We analyzed 5472 melanomas, estimating how selection on individual variants changes with patient age while accounting for differing neutral mutation rates. Neutral mutation rates increased only modestly with age; ultraviolet damage remained predominant, but endogenous processes increasingly contributed to older tumors. In contrast, selection on major drivers was strongly age dependent: The advantage of BRAF V600E declined precipitously with age, whereas NRAS Q61 mutations gained advantage. TERT promoter mutations became more frequent, yet less advantageous. Aging therefore reshapes melanoma evolution primarily by altering selection, motivating age-conscious evaluation of clinical biomarkers and therapies.

Article.Title: Measuring mixed-state topological invariant in open photonic quantum walk
Article.Authors: Wang Q.; Xu X.; Han Y.; Li C.; Guo G.
Article.Abstract: Pure-state manifestations of geometric phase are well established and have found applications across essentially all branches of physics, yet their generalization to mixed-state regimes remains largely unexplored experimentally. The Uhlmann geometric phase offers a natural extension of pure-state paradigms and can exhibit a topological character. However, observation of this invariant is impeded by the incompatibility between Uhlmann parallel transport and Hamiltonian dynamics, as well as the difficulty of preparing topologically nontrivial mixed states. To address this challenge, we report an experimentally accessible protocol for directly measuring the mixed-state topological invariant. By engineering controlled nonunitary dynamics in a photonic quantum walk, we prepare topologically nontrivial mixed states from a trivial initial state. Then, by machine learning the full density matrix in momentum space, we directly extract the quantized geometric phase of the nontrivial mixed states. Furthermore, we observe that this transition of the quantized mixed-state topological invariant from a trivial to a nontrivial value is closely associated with the emergence of a topological kink structure. These results highlight a geometric phase framework that naturally extends to open quantum systems both in and out of thermal equilibrium.

Article.Title: A full-hardware edge detection system based on a highly robust dual random number generator
Article.Authors: Xu J.; Wang J.; Liu W.; Zhang J.; Chen J.; Yan X.
Article.Abstract: Conventional edge computing hardware at autonomous driving terminals is limited by chip area and power efficiency for complex image data. Recently, researchers have used memristors to construct dedicated hardware systems, achieving advancements in multiple image processing fields such as pattern recognition and edge detection. However, a full-hardware image processing system with anti-interference, low power, and high real-time performance remains challenging. Here, we fabricated a volatile Ag/AlO x /n-Si memristor with exceptional stability and low power. High-resolution electron microscopy visualized Ag conductive filament formation. Integrating two memristors with a logic circuit, we designed a low-power edge detection unit using dual random number hardware computation. Its energy consumption is 92.3% lower than traditional logic circuits, with strong anti-interference. To validate practical use, we constructed a 32-channel parallel full-hardware system with 64 devices, achieving 31.25 frames per second and excellent edge detection. The system exhibits excellent scalability, stability, and anti-interference, offering great potential for edge vision hardware in autonomous driving, safety monitoring, and surgical assistance.
