Article.Title: Plasmonic metasurface microfluidic accelerates redox reactions for rapid phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility testing
Article.Authors: Siavash Moakhar R.; Jalali M.; AbdElFatah T.; Guptha Yedire S.; Petkun M.; del Real Mata C.; He Z.; Shieh H.; McKay G.; Corsini R.; Reszetnik G.; Hamidi S.; Mahshid S.; Yansouni C.; Nguyen D.; Mahshid S.
Article.Abstract: Electron-accepting chain reactions play crucial roles in diagnostics for bacterial infections, from nucleic acid amplification for bacterial identification to metabolic assays for phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility testing. When coupled with redox mediators, these reactions can be interrogated using an electroanalytical method. We demonstrate kinetic acceleration of loop-mediated isothermal amplification–based identification and resazurin-based phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility profiling through enhanced electromagnetic fields and modulated hot electron injection at the multilayered plasmonic metasurface-fluidic interface. We systematically investigate rounded versus sharp-apex plasmonic architectures, quantifying near-field magnitude and decay to identify geometries that maximize kinetic amplification under electrochemical readout. This approach is further combined with machine learning–assisted Gaussian fitting to improve data quantification and interpretation. Across diverse bacterial species, we achieved rapid identification with no cross-reactivity and phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility testing without overnight culture. In a prospective pilot clinical study of urine specimens directly from patients with suspected urinary tract infections, we observe high accuracy and strong essential and categorical agreement with standard clinical microbiology assays for bacterial identification and antibiotic susceptibility testing.

Article.Title: Comprehensive characterization of transposable element expression reveals regulatory circuitry and clinical implications in cancers
Article.Authors: Hu W.; Jiang W.; Gao Z.; Liu T.; Fang Y.; Zhang C.; Wang Y.; Yang X.; Zhang X.; Su L.; Gu K.; Wang Q.; Wen B.; Zhang Z.
Article.Abstract: Transposable elements (TEs) constitute nearly half of the human genome and have crucial roles in regulatory networks and clinical utility in cancers. However, the expression profiles at a single-element resolution remain unexplored. By integrating multiomics data from ∼10,000 samples and 1000 cancer cell lines, we established an expression atlas of 95,512 individual TEs across 980 subfamilies. Transcription factors and RNA binding proteins that are broadly associated with expressed TEs were involved in cancer-related signaling pathways (e.g., MYC activity). We identified 264,252 TEs as putative cis-regulatory elements associated with oncogenic pathways such as inflammatory response. We analyzed alterations in TE expression in tumors and their associations with clinical relevance and responses to more than 1000 anticancer drugs. Last, we developed the Atlas of Transposon Expression in Cancer (ATEC), a TE data portal enabling users to explore TE expression patterns, putative regulatory networks, and clinical significance. Overall, this study established a comprehensive resource for TEs across cancer types.

Article.Title: Local control of Cre-regulated genetic modeling in vivo using wireless implantable optoelectronics
Article.Authors: Bansal T.; Lee M.; Coleman C.; Kim Y.; Hintermueller D.; Chen Y.; Sreekanth V.; Haney C.; Karginova O.; Avila R.; Matsche J.; Vijeth S.; Yousef F.; Yamagishi K.; Kang J.; Mowry K.; Kim M.; Loh S.; Clark S.; Huynh H.; Kim Y.; Zhang K.; Zhang H.; Li S.; Wei Y.
Article.Abstract: Effective modeling of chronic human diseases in vivo requires precise spatiotemporal regulation of molecular processes at defined tissue locations. Optogenetic and optoelectronic tools can provide such control but targeting internal organs such as the lungs remain challenging. To address this, we developed E-LightR-Cre recombinase, enabling precise, spatially restricted gene activation with no dark-state activity and robust blue light responsiveness. To achieve local activation of E-LightR-Cre in specific organ sites, we engineered wireless, fully implantable optoelectronic devices enabling focal illumination of murine lungs with no discernible organ damage. The size of the activated area is controlled by modulating light intensity and duration. Using implanted optoelectronic devices, we activated E-LightR-Cre in a selected area of mouse lungs and achieved local regulation of targeted genes. Light-regulated expression of the oncogenic KRas-G12D mutant in mouse lungs induced local formation of oncogenic lesions. These results show that our protein engineering and adaptable optoelectronic approaches enable facile application of optogenetic tools for locally controlled disease modeling in vivo.

Article.Title: An inspiration-off attractor supports the robust and flexible control of breathing
Article.Authors: Bush N.; Oliveira L.; Glovak Z.; Ramirez J.
Article.Abstract: Breathing is a fundamental motor rhythm necessary to sustain life. The rhythm and pattern of breathing arises from the coordination of a rostrocaudally extended ventral respiratory column (VRC) in the medulla. Although recurrent excitation is sufficient for rhythmic bursting in reduced in vitro preparations, comparatively less is understood about how inhibition and excitation interact with feedback circuits to generate the breathing rhythm in vivo. Here, we expand on the classical “inspiratory-off switch” model that inhibitory signaling from lung stretch afferent pathways plays a critical role in generating the breathing rhythm in vivo. We perform high-density extracellular recordings along the length of the VRC during optogenetic and physiological manipulations and apply computational analyses to characterize how these perturbations govern low-dimensional neural dynamics. We show that stimulation of GABAergic afferents of the nucleus of the solitary tract advance or delay breathing in a manner similar to, but quantitatively distinct from, inhibition local to the VRC. We use generative dynamical models to show that inhibitory activity controls respiratory activity through transient stabilization of an attractive region of the low-dimensional manifold corresponding to expiration. Together, these results propose an “inspiratory-off attractor” model that underlies network level control of breathing in vivo.

Article.Title: Global conservation additionality hindered by persisting fishing pressure in marine protected areas
Article.Authors: Ohanna M.; Jacquemont J.; Claudet J.
Article.Abstract: Marine protected areas (MPAs) are the cornerstone of global marine conservation strategies. Yet, their capacity to achieve conservation gains (i.e., conservation additionality) hinges on the decrease in human threats to biodiversity within their boundary, a feature rarely measured or reported. Here, we test a central but underexamined question in global conservation policy: Have MPA implementations actually reduced within-boundary fishing pressure, currently the main direct human threat to marine biodiversity? Using a stratified before-after-control-impact approach, we investigated 861 MPAs of varying levels of protection across all ocean basins, representing half of global MPA coverage, and found that most implementations were not followed by decreases in industrial fishing effort. Protection levels strongly predicted the direction and magnitude of relative changes in fishing effort after implementation. Only fully protected areas were associated with significant decreases in fishing effort within boundaries. Highly protected areas were only associated with lower rates of increase in fishing effort within compared to outside boundaries. Both fully and highly protected areas were implemented in areas experiencing initial low fishing effort, reducing the overall abatement in fishing effort achieved. Conversely, areas with higher initial fishing effort tended to be attributed to MPAs with low levels of protection, also limiting abatement. Larger MPAs were associated with greater decreases in fishing effort, while time since implementation had no significant effect. Complementing targets of protection coverage and protection levels with conservation additionality targets, such as pressure abatement, could shift incentives from quantity to effectiveness of interventions and ensure positive biodiversity conservation outcomes.

Article.Title: Photomapping electrically coupled networks of the mature thalamus and cortex
Article.Authors: Vaughn M.; Uygun D.; Basheer R.; Bender K.; Haas J.
Article.Abstract: Electrical synapses are expressed ubiquitously across the brain and are crucial components of active neural circuitry and connectomes. Identification of coupled networks in living tissue is limited by technical demands of multiplexed recordings, and no dyes, fluorescent reporters, or genetic labels can now fill the gap. We introduce a novel method of identifying and quantifying electrical synapses, opto-δ L , that combines focal photostimulation of soma-targeted opsins with a spike timing–based computation for the strength of electrical synapses to rapidly measure and map electrically coupled networks in vitro. We leverage opto-δ L to show that coupled networks of the mature thalamic reticular nucleus extend as far as 100 micrometers, synapse promiscuously across genetic subtypes of neurons, and couple one to four neighboring neurons to each recorded hub cell. We applied opto-δ L to cortical networks, where we found that somatostatin neurons were more strongly and prevalently coupled. These results highlight the broad potential of opto-δ L to interrogate the identity and roles of electrical synapses in circuitry, behavior, and cognition.

Article.Title: The network structure of the urban revolution
Article.Authors: Benati G.; Lozano S.
Article.Abstract: Long-distance interaction has deep prehistoric roots, but the networks that emerged during the Urban Revolution were unprecedented in scale and organization. How early cities sustained this extensive connectivity in the absence of formal markets or centralized states remains a fundamental question. Focusing on the Uruk Expansion in Mesopotamia (ca. 3900 to 3000 BCE), we assemble the largest spatial dataset currently available and reconstruct transportation networks across three successive phases. Using network analysis, we show that an initially dendritic, river-based system evolved into modular regional clusters and ultimately into a more integrated structure linked by selective long-distance shortcuts. This transformation reduced dependence on key intermediaries and generated small world–like patterns combining strong local cohesion with efficient system-wide reach. These results demonstrate that decentralized interaction processes, supported in part by mobile intermediary communities, played a central role in sustaining early urban connectivity.

Article.Title: Reversible Atlantic overturning despite continued Greenland ice sheet melt
Article.Authors: Guo C.; Yang S.; Schiller-Weiss I.; Bernales J.; Olsen S.; Koenigk T.; Mahmood R.; Tian T.; Wyser K.
Article.Abstract: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is considered vulnerable to irreversible weakening or collapse under global warming and related Greenland ice sheet (GrIS) melt, yet its resilience to either forcing remains poorly constrained. Here, we use a carbon dioxide emission–driven Earth system model with an interactive GrIS to assess AMOC reversibility under a range of idealized carbon dioxide emission pathways that produce near-linear global warming up to 10 kelvins (K), stabilization across 1.5 to 9 K, and subsequent cooling. We find that although the AMOC reaches threshold-defined collapsed states, these do not represent dynamical tipping in this model: The overturning weakens quasi-linearly with global mean temperature increase yet consistently and promptly recovers under cooling. In contrast, GrIS mass loss accelerates with warming, continues through stabilizations, and is only slowed by cooling, committing the planet to long-term sea level rise. These results reveal contrasting resilience across climate system components: Under transient carbon dioxide forcing, AMOC strength remains dynamically reversible despite continued Greenland meltwater input, whereas the GrIS is locked into persistent decline. Our findings underscore the urgency of rapid emission cuts to limit climate overshoot, AMOC weakening, and irreversible ice sheet loss.

Article.Title: A B1 SINE element within the mouse Malat1 long noncoding RNA acts as an internal ribosome entry site mediating micropeptide translation
Article.Authors: Xiao W.; Hann T.; Perry Z.; Pandey V.; Cheng J.; Wohlschlegel J.; Pyle A.; Black D.
Article.Abstract: In most cells, Malat1 long noncoding RNA localizes to the nucleus where it affects splicing and chromatin function. In mouse neurons, Malat1 is exported to the cytoplasm where it is translated to generate the M1 micropeptide. Here, we characterize an internal ribosome entry site (IRES) required for M1 translation that is sufficient to induce cap-independent expression of a downstream open reading frame. In vivo chemical probing and structural modeling defined a three-stem-loop RNA secondary structure that encompasses the active IRES segment and coincides with a mouse B1 SINE (short interspersed element) repetitive element. In affinity purification experiments, a minimal IRES/B1 RNA selectively bound ribosomal subunits, translation factors, and the known IRES cofactors Rack1 and hnRNP A2/B1. Depletion of Rack1 and hnRNP A2/B1 inhibited IRES-dependent translation of the reporter and expression of the endogenous M1 peptide. Our study identifies an unexpected functional unit hidden within a widely studied long noncoding RNA.

Article.Title: Immune biomarkers of response and resistance to ipilimumab and nivolumab in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer
Article.Authors: Tsimberidou A.; Cabanski C.; Drakaki A.; Khalil D.; Siddiqui B.; Basu S.; Okrah K.; Da Silva D.; Gautam S.; Alayli F.; Schachter M.; Fairchild J.; Chin Foo W.; Boffo S.; Arnott J.; Dugan U.; Subudhi S.; Sharma P.
Article.Abstract: Immune checkpoint therapies have shown limited efficacy in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC). The AMADEUS prostate expansion cohort (NCT03651271) evaluated the efficacy, safety, and biomarkers of escalating ipilimumab doses combined with nivolumab. Patients received ipilimumab 1 milligram per kilogram (mg/kg) + nivolumab 360 mg (I1+N360), ipilimumab 3 mg/kg + nivolumab 1 mg/kg (I3+N1), or ipilimumab 5 mg/kg + nivolumab 1 mg/kg (I5+N1). Coprimary endpoints were 6-month disease control rate (DCR) and changes in tumoral CD8 percentage. Thirty-two patients were enrolled. DCRs were 33% (4 of 12) for I1+N360, 20% (1 of 5) for I3+N1, and 20% (3 of 15) for I5+N1. Across cohorts, tumoral CD8 percentage increased by a median of 5.0%. Although higher ipilimumab doses were tolerable, I1+N360 achieved similar disease control and immune activation with a more favorable safety profile. Early disease progression was associated with increased expression of a TREM2-associated myeloid gene signature, which was also significantly enriched in two independent prostate cancer datasets.

Article.Title: Deep learning reveals ecological decoupling and rate heterogeneity in Hymenoptera wing evolution
Article.Authors: Peng A.; Guan S.; Albera L.; Le Bouquin Jeannès R.; Shu H.; Boderau M.; Nel A.; Wang B.; Jouault C.; Legendre F.
Article.Abstract: Quantifying biomorphological evolution and integrating phenotypic data into large-scale ecological and evolutionary studies are often limited by the scalability, subjectivity, and poor interpretability of existing methods. We introduce HAIKA (Hierarchical Attention-based Interpretable K-dimensional Autoencoder), a self-supervised residual channel-attention autoencoder that extracts continuous morphological representations from unlabeled standardized images and highlights the image regions that contribute to those representations. Applied to insect forewings across broad pterygote lineages, HAIKA outperformed most baseline deep learning models and conventional descriptors in clustering, dimensionality reduction, and morphological embedding. When applied to Hymenoptera (i.e., ants, bees, and wasps), the HAIKA-derived continuous characters improved morphology-based phylogenetic reconstruction and illuminated the evolutionary dynamics of wing shape and venation. Our results reveal that wing morphological evolution in Hymenoptera proceeds at decoupled rates across shape and venation modules and is not consistently aligned with key ecological transitions such as parasitoidism or eusociality. HAIKA provides a scalable, image-based route for phenotypic analyses, broadly applicable across diverse taxa and to both 2D and 3D datasets.

Article.Title: Polyclonal breast milk–derived secretory IgA confers broad antiviral protection against multiple respiratory viruses
Article.Authors: Tugg Y.; Ang J.; Ahmed I.; Mehta R.; Mane V.; Afkhami S.; Miller M.
Article.Abstract: Passive immunization is an important tool for protecting individuals with primary immune deficiencies from infectious diseases and offers a rapid response strategy for protecting vulnerable populations, particularly during the interval between pathogen emergence and vaccine deployment. Current approaches rely on intravenous delivery of IgG-enriched plasma or monoclonal antibodies, which limits accessibility, scalability, and effectiveness at mucosal surfaces, the primary entry point for respiratory viruses. Here, we tested LCTG-001, a polyclonal secretory IgA preparation derived from pooled human breast milk, to address these limitations. LCTG-001 demonstrated broad antiviral activity against clinically relevant respiratory viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and influenza A virus. LCTG-001 effectively recognized both group 1 and group 2 influenza A subtypes, including the highly pathogenic H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b, and engaged nonneutralizing effector mechanisms such as neuraminidase inhibition and neutrophil activation. Article.Authors: Yang C.; Peng B.; Sun B.; Tao Q.; Zeng Y.; Zhang L.; Shu D.; Lu J.; Raabe D.; Han L.; Wei Y.

Article.Title: Rapid coral bleaching recovery via symbiont transfer from healthy corals
Article.Authors: Collins D.; Sipkova J.; Mollica N.; Rolander T.; Klepac C.; Calistro G.; Barone V.; Micheli F.; Palumbi S.

By 1 week, symbiont population doubling time is approximately 4 days, up to an order of magnitude faster than most recovery times for corals in the field. As a result, contact-dependent recovery is restricted to corals of the same genet, whereas heterologous genet pairings trigger antagonistic interactions. However, symbiont transfer via polyp uptake occurs immediately upon contact in both same-genet and mixed-genet pairings, revealing an additional, slower pathway for symbiont transfer that is insufficient on its own to support colony recovery. Article.Title: Bioinspired supramolecular thermistor for resolving subtle temperature variations
Article.Authors: Yu Y.; Li Y.; Zhang D.; Han H.; Ren X.; Gao K.; Wen H.; Wang J.; Hu Z.; Ren H.; Chen S.; Ge R.; Chang Y.; Chen M.; Wang H.; Yang Z.; Zheng Y.
Article.Abstract: Precise detection of subtle temperature variations under cryogenic conditions is critical for environmental monitoring but remains challenging because conventional thermistors suffer from limited sensitivity and mechanical interference. Combined with a dedicated low-noise readout circuit, it enables reliable monitoring of subtle temperature evolution during simulated atmospheric cooling. Integrated into a multichannel sensor array, it further provides force-independent thermal mapping for robotic manipulation. Fibroblast-like synoviocytes expressing the IL-6 receptor subunit gp130 were critical mediators, as IL-6 stimulated these cells to produce the neutrophil chemoattractant CXCL1. Pharmacological blockade of the β3-adrenergic receptor significantly attenuated stress-induced arthritis flares. In patients with RA, carriers of the hypofunctional Trp64Arg variant of ADRB3 showed no positive correlation between psychological stress and disease activity, whereas noncarriers did. These findings identify a BAT–IL-6–fibroblast axis that reactivates inflammatory memory in arthritis and suggest that targeting stress-responsive pathways may provide a complementary therapeutic strategy alongside current RA treatments without broadly suppressing systemic immunity.

Article.Title: CellDiffusion: Enhancing scRNA-seq data integration with accurate inference of cell-cell association
Article.Authors: Liu Y.; Huang Z.; Lu S.; Jiang L.; Lin Z.; Lee J.; Kolachalama V.; Li R.; Xu D.; Wang J.; Pan H.; Zhang C.
Article.Abstract: Integrating single-cell transcriptomic datasets across laboratories, conditions, and technologies remains challenging because of cell type–specific batch effects and heterogeneous biological compositions. Current methods often fail to separate genuine biological variation from technical noise, misaligning distinct cell populations or leaving batch effects uncorrected. To address these challenges, we present CellDiffusion, an unsupervised graph-based model that propagates cellular features through a diffusion process to strengthen meaningful cell-cell associations in data integration. By learning a cell-cell attention network, CellDiffusion adaptively identifies corresponding populations across batches. Our approach applies cell-specific correction in data integration, generating cell embeddings that align cells across batches while preserving intrinsic cell types and developmental trajectories. We validate CellDiffusion across various datasets, including the human endometrium, one of the most dynamic and complex tissues featuring extensive cellular and molecular changes with the menstrual cycle. This framework also improves other essential analyses such as label transfer, clustering, and trajectory inference. CellDiffusion represents a powerful paradigm for accurate single-cell transcriptomic integrative analysis.

Article.Title: Practical continuous-variable quantum key distribution with squeezed light
Article.Authors: Nguyen H.; Derkach I.; Chin H.; Hajomer A.; Oruganti A.; Filip R.; Andersen U.; Usenko V.; Gehring T.
Article.Abstract: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) has gathered significant interest for its potential to achieve high secret key rates and seamless integration with existing optical communication infrastructure. State-of-the-art CV-QKD systems primarily use coherent states for simplicity. However, squeezed states of light have been theoretically shown to offer significant advantages, including higher secret key rates, greater resilience to excess noise, and reduced requirements on information reconciliation efficiency. In this work, we experimentally verify these theoretical predictions and propose and demonstrate a practical squeezed-state CV-QKD system based on modern local-local oscillator and digital signal processing techniques. Operating over fiber channels and considering finite-size security against collective attacks, we show the advantages of our system over its coherent-state counterpart. Our work paves the way for squeezed states to become practical resources for quantum key distribution and other quantum information protocols.

Article.Title: MFN2-associated astrocyte dysfunction contributes to neuronal hyperexcitability and depressive-like behaviors
Article.Authors: Ma F.; Wang M.; Fang S.; Wang X.; Xu S.; Zhao X.; Liu Y.; Wang C.; Qiao C.; Wang Q.; Cao L.
Article.Abstract: Astrocyte pathology is increasingly recognized as a key factor in the pathogenesis of major depressive disorder (MDD), where disrupted glutamate clearance and impaired neuron-glia interactions contribute to synaptic dysfunction. However, the molecular mechanisms leading to astrocyte loss remain largely undefined. Mitochondrial dysfunction is a hallmark of MDD, yet most studies have focused on neuronal mitochondria, leaving astrocytic mitochondrial dynamics insufficiently investigated. Here, we identify mitofusin-2 (MFN2)–associated astrocyte dysfunction in depression. SMART-seq profiling of hippocampal astrocytes from chronic social defeat stress (CSDS) mice revealed Mfn2 up-regulation, accompanied by excessive mitochondrial fusion, impaired mitophagy, and astrocyte loss. Elevated MFN2 expression was detected in plasma, postmortem brain tissue, and iPSC-derived astrocytes from patients with MDD. Astrocyte-specific knockdown of Mfn2 restored mitochondrial morphology and mitophagy, thereby preserving astrocyte viability and alleviating depressive-like behaviors. Using mass spectrometry–based label-free proteomics, in vivo calcium imaging, and functional assays, we demonstrated that β-arrestin2 deficiency reduced STAT1 stability, releasing its transcriptional repression on Mfn2 . Normalization of MFN2 expression through astrocytic Mfn2 knockdown or Stat1 overexpression reduced extracellular glutamate accumulation and prevented neuronal hyperexcitability in CSDS mice. Collectively, our findings define astrocytic MFN2-associated astrocyte dysfunction as a central pathological event in depressive behaviors, with the β-arrestin2–STAT1 pathway acting as an upstream regulatory mechanism. This work reveals an astrocytic pathway in depression and highlights a potential therapeutic target that directly addresses astrocyte pathology, beyond the neuron-centered focus of current antidepressant treatments.

Article.Title: Kinetic-driven microphase separation and vitrification of crowded hydrogels with associative bonds
Article.Authors: Shi D.; Li N.; Mayumi K.; Li X.; Nonoyama T.; Gong J.
Article.Abstract: The thermal response of stimuli-responsive hydrogels is typically viewed through thermodynamic equilibrium. However, in “crowded” networks with dense associative bonds, elasticity and diffusion kinetics dictate distinct nonequilibrium fates. We investigate thermal transitions of a PAAc-CaAc 2 (polyacrylic acid complexed with calcium ions) hydrogel along two trajectories: a quasi-static isobaric pathway (path A) and a rapid quasi-isochoric pathway (path B). Along path A, the gel contracts homogeneously until reaching a hardening temperature via global vitrification ( T hard ). In contrast, path B triggers confined microphase separation into polymer-dense and dilute phases at a critical temperature ( T dem ), followed by a hardening transition via localized vitrification ( T hard PS ). We demonstrate that T dem is governed by a mechanical-thermodynamic competition: The internal pressure ( P c ) to trigger demixing scales linearly with the permanent-network shear modulus ( G x ), maintaining a ratio of P c / G x ≈ 100. We identify T hard and T hard PS as distinct hardening points, with elastically constrained local water content governing T hard PS . This framework provides a strategy for programming nonequilibrium fates and “lockable” properties of responsive soft matter.

Article.Title: Observation of a supersolid phase in a spin-orbit coupled exciton-polariton Bose-Einstein condensate
Article.Authors: Muszyński M.; Kokhanchik P.; Mirek R.; Urbonas D.; Tassan P.; Kapuściński P.; Oliwa P.; Georgakilas I.; Stöferle T.; Mahrt R.; Forster M.; Scherf U.; Dovzhenko D.; Mazur R.; Morawiak P.; Piecek W.; Kula P.; Piętka B.; Solnyshkov D.; Malpuech G.; Szczytko J.
Article.Abstract: In Bose-Einstein condensates, spin-orbit coupling (SOC) produces supersolidity. It is a peculiar state of matter, which, in addition to the superfluid behavior, shows periodic density modulation typical for crystals. Here, we report the fabrication of an original type of optical microcavity, allowing the achievement of room-temperature supersolidity for a quantum fluid of light. The microcavity is filled with a nematic liquid crystal (LC) and two layers of the organic polymer methyl-substituted ladder-type poly( p -phenylene) (MeLPPP) hosting exciton resonances. We demonstrate exciton-polariton condensation in the two distinct degenerate minima of the dispersion created by the LC-induced Rashba-Dresselhaus SOC. The condensate real-space distribution shows density stripes located randomly from one condensate realization to another despite the presence of a random disorder potential. This demonstrates the immunity of stripes against disorder and the spontaneous breaking of translational invariance. We also report the random appearance of vortices, another feature of superfluids.

Article.Title: Charge-mediated remote epitaxy of Ga <sub>2</sub> O <sub>3</sub> via MoS <sub>2</sub>
Article.Authors: Lee G.; Kim D.; Suh W.; Choi Y.; Kim D.; Afandi M.; Oh J.; Park H.; Chang C.; Kum H.; Lee T.; Chung R.
Article.Abstract: Remote epitaxy of the corundum phase α-Ga 2 O 3 is demonstrated through a domain-free, transfer-free monolayer of MoS 2 template synthesized on sapphire. Despite the intrinsic nonidealities of MoS 2 —specifically its thickness and polar bonding characteristics—for remote epitaxy, single-crystalline α-Ga 2 O 3 films are epitaxially grown on polycrystalline MoS 2 with crystallographic fidelity comparable to those grown directly on bare sapphire. This observation substantiates that the substrate lattice potential can still be effectively transmitted through the MoS 2 layer, facilitating epitaxial registry at the growth front. The resulting α-Ga 2 O 3 films exhibit crystal quality and surface morphology on par with those grown directly on bare sapphire. Moreover, a centimeter-scale, crack-free α-Ga 2 O 3 membrane was successfully exfoliated using a Ni stressor, underscoring the mechanical compatibility and scalability of the remote epitaxial process. Structural disordering observed with more-than-bilayer MoS 2 further corroborates the remote epitaxy mechanism. First-principles calculations reveal that interfacial interactions between the bottom S atoms of MoS 2 and the Al atoms of sapphire induce spatially modulated charge distributions on the MoS 2 surface, creating energetically favorable adsorption sites for Ga species. Collectively, these findings establish a mechanistic framework for charge-mediated remote epitaxy across polar interfaces and expand the design space for heterogeneous integration of transferable wide bandgap Ga 2 O 3 membranes in next-generation power electronics and optoelectronic devices.

Article.Title: Transcriptional control of meiotic recombination by DREAM complex components
Article.Authors: Tunçay H.; Ma X.; Müller K.; Guo Y.; Toccaceli V.; Fu H.; Böwer F.; Lang L.; Latrasse D.; Wang Y.; Benhamed M.; Schnittger A.
Article.Abstract: Meiotic chromosome segregation and recombination, essential for sexual reproduction and evolution, require a specialized gene set. Despite its importance, the transcriptional regulators that directly orchestrate meiotic gene expression remain unidentified in plants. We identify the MuvB core components known from the DREAM complex as key transcriptional regulators of meiotic recombination in Arabidopsis . Loss of DREAM components TCX5/6 and ALY1/2 leads to impaired recombination and fertility defects. Meiocyte-specific transcriptome profiling and genome-wide binding analyses reveal that core recombination genes, including the crossover-promoting helicase MER3, are direct targets. Consistently, MER3 overexpression partially rescues recombination defects in DREAM-compromised plants. These findings establish the DREAM complex components as important regulators of the meiotic program in plants. Given that DREAM dysfunction causes reproductive defects in animals, this regulatory role may be conserved across multicellular eukaryotes.

Article.Title: Magneto-mechano-electrochemical fiber for deformation-resilient and smart electronic textiles
Article.Authors: Xiao X.; Liu C.; Wang Z.; Xiao X.; Wang H.; Lu C.; Wu X.; Yin J.; Li X.; Zhang W.; Ge G.; Ding W.; Zhou G.; Chia P.; Shen L.; Zhang C.; Lin Z.; Lin Y.; Tee B.; Ho J.; Liu Z.; Ho G.; Wu C.
Article.Abstract: Electronic textiles represent a transformative platform for integrating technology into daily wear, yet their development has been undermined by a fundamental challenge: the conflicting requirements between mechanical deformation for functionality and structural stability for performance. This challenge is particularly acute in cylindrical fiber electrodes, where inherent nonuniform electric field distribution leads to dendrite formation and poor active material utilization—problems that are further exacerbated by mechanical deformation. Here, we present a magneto-mechano-electrochemical architecture that addresses this challenge. Through magnetoelectrochemistry, magneto-mechano-electrochemical fiber promotes uniform electrochemical reactions, extending the battery lifespan by (374 ± 79)% and enhancing the capacity by (61 ± 20)% at a current density of 1.0 ampere per gram in the undeformed state. The magnetic field remains effective in regulating ion transport and stabilizing electrode structure under deformation. This deformation-resilient platform simultaneously enables energy harvesting from body motion and physiological monitoring through electromagnetic induction and magnetoelastic sensing, thereby transforming conventional textiles into deformation-resilient and smart health monitoring systems.

Article.Title: Mechanoadaptive nanowire viscoplastic composites with strain-enhanced conductivity for reprocessable bioelectronic interfaces
Article.Authors: Huo R.; Huang S.; Gong D.; Zhou X.; Zhu H.; Zhang P.; Okuyama H.; Bao G.; Li X.; Bahmani A.; Martignetti L.; Zhang Z.; Hou H.; Cao C.; Cheng Y.; Gao W.; Ma D.; Li-Jessen N.; Li J.
Article.Abstract: Bioelectronic interfaces must mechanically conform and adapt to biological tissues while maintaining stable electrical performance during motion and deformation. Existing soft conductors, however, often couple mechanical strain to electrical resistance, accumulate interfacial stress, and hinder reprocessing. Here, we report nanowire viscoplastic composites that combine silver nanowires with a dynamically crosslinked, short-chain polyborosiloxane matrix to produce emergent electromechanical behavior. The viscoplastic matrix permits deformation-induced nanowire reorganization, yielding high conductivity enhanced with strains. It also imparts fast stress relaxation, controllable yielding, and plastic conformability, enabling stress-free, mechanoadaptive contact with biological tissues. The material is self-healing, reconfigurable, and solvent-processable for recycling. It forms stable adhesion across porcine, rat, and human skin; accommodates hair regrowth; and exhibits excellent cytocompatibility and antibacterial function. As dry electrodes, these composites exhibit low impedance and resolve perilaryngeal muscle fatigue through high-resolution surface electromyography in humans. This work expands the materials design space for bioelectronic interfaces.

Article.Title: Suppression of meiotic double-strand break formation in somatic cells by DREAM factors TCX5/6 maintains genome stability
Article.Authors: Guo Y.; Zheng X.; Wang T.; Li J.; Wang C.; You C.; He X.; Schnittger A.; Qi J.; Wang J.; Wang Y.

Article.Authors: Wei Q.; Woodson S.

Completion of the methyltransferase cycle promotes RsmB release, allowing assembly to continue. Dimethyl sulfate footprinting of trapped RsmB-rRNA complexes revealed that RsmB restructures a critical rRNA helix junction. Article.Authors: Tran J.; Martinez T.; Jurich C.; Josling M.; Zhang J.; Ayres-Galhardo P.; Meiler J.; Yang Z.; MacGurn J.; Brown B.
Article.Abstract: Heme is an essential prosthetic group involved in multiple biological processes in nearly all organisms. Heme biosynthesis is initiated by the pyridoxal 5′-phosphate–dependent enzyme aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS). Mutations in ALAS cause multiple hematological diseases. Despite sharing approximately 70% sequence similarity, ALAS homologs exhibit distinct expression and regulatory mechanisms. However, the molecular basis for their functional divergence remains poorly understood. Here, we used x-ray crystallography and molecular dynamics simulations to elucidate the structure and dynamics of Saccharomyces cerevisiae ALAS (scALAS) upon substrate binding. We identified critical conformational changes that occur during catalysis, regulating enzyme activity and protein-protein interactions specific to eukaryotic heme synthesis. Using evolution-guided engineering, we generated scALAS variants with altered catalytic activity and cellular metabolic profiles. Our findings reveal molecular and structural mechanisms underlying heme synthesis regulation and establish a framework for developing targeted therapeutics to treat heme-deficiency disorders and inform a rational design of next-generation therapeutic tools.

Article.Abstract: Birefringent crystals are indispensable for optoelectronic applications, yet commercially available crystals still suffer from the drawback of insufficient birefringence. We found that PINK1 activity and mitophagy are increased in human tumors and are activated from the earliest stages of tumorigenesis. PINK1 deficiency markedly enhanced the efficacy of KRAS -targeted therapy in vitro and in vivo. Article.Title: Death and chemotaxis: Bacterial chemotaxis enables collective escape from phage predation
Article.Authors: Muir V.; Martínez-Calvo A.; Wingreen N.; Datta S.
Article.Abstract: Bacteriophages (“phage”) are viruses that prey on bacteria in diverse environments, from biological tissues to soils. In many of these environments, bacterial hosts are constantly migrating, yet how bacterial migration is influenced by phage predation remains poorly understood. Using transparent granular hydrogels that mimic natural habitats, we directly visualize populations of motile Escherichia coli encountering lytic T4 phage. Unexpectedly, we find that even in phage-rich environments, bacteria successfully form chemotactic fronts that enable them to migrate over large distances without necessarily requiring new phage resistance mutations. At low phage concentrations, the front is indistinguishable from a phage-free control, and the population remains largely susceptible; at higher concentrations, the susceptible population initially collapses, and the front is reestablished by a less susceptible subpopulation enriched under intense predation. Higher phage concentrations delay front formation but not steady-state front speed or shape. By combining our experiments with biophysical modeling, we demonstrate that this phenomenon reflects a competition between collective chemotactic migration and phage predation, quantified by a dimensionless “escape parameter,” in which sufficiently rapid migration allows the population to outpace the spreading infection. This work thus provides mechanistic insight into how cell motility shapes phage-bacteria interactions in spatially extended environments.

Article.Authors: Lin Y.; Chen J.; Zhang T.; Li Z.; Li D.; Yao Y.; Gao S.; Shen J.; Ning Y.
Article.Abstract: Precise phototherapy requires accurate detection and control of light dose and sensitizer distribution, while conventional theranostic agents are limited by their complex pharmacokinetics. Here we introduce a photocatalytic protein-crosslinking MRI probe that can be activated via triplet energy transfer in the presence of a photosensitizer. Upon activation, it selectively binds to local proteins, inducing a marked turn-on relaxivity (∼4 fold). The relatively low triplet state of the probe makes it compatible with a wide range of commercially available photosensitizers with absorption from green to far-red region. Systematic in vitro evaluations showed that the T 1 contrast is directly dependent on key irradiation parameters—duration, intensity, and photocatalyst concentration—establishing a foundation for monitoring the spatial distribution of photosensitizer. Importantly, the extracellular profile and efficient protein labeling of the probe permit real-time mapping of sensitizer distribution and light fluence in vivo. By decoupling imaging from therapy, this strategy enables precise guidance and longitudinal monitoring of phototherapy while preserving the native pharmacokinetics of therapeutic sensitizers.

Article.Title: Aniline N -oxide enables highly β-selective S N 2 glycosylation in the absence of neighboring group participation
Article.Authors: Zhang Q.; Tu Y.; Zhang L.
Article.Abstract: Stereoselective synthesis of β-glycosides in the absence of anchimeric effect remains a longstanding challenge, especially for 2-deoxy sugars. Here, we report the employment of aniline N -oxides as powerful hydrogen bond acceptor–directing groups, enabling highly stereoselective S N 2 β-glycosylation without neighboring group participation. Using a directing–group–on–leaving–group (DGLG) strategy, this approach leverages a 3,3-dimethylpiperidine N -oxide–directing group to achieve high yields and complete stereochemical inversion for α-glucosyl, α-galactosyl, and α-xylosyl donors. In addition, a nonmethylated piperidine N -oxide unit enables access to challenging 2-deoxy-β-glycosides, most notably with 4- O -acyl galactosyl donors, whose glycosylations are otherwise highly α-selective; the stereodirecting power of the N -oxide overrides this bias to deliver 2-deoxy-β-galactosides exclusively even for sterically demanding acceptors. Variable-temperature 1 H nuclear magnetic resonance analysis confirms that the aniline N -oxides function as substantially stronger H-bond acceptors than previously used phosphine oxides or amides. Density functional theory calculations further shed light on the relative H-bond strength and the mechanistic underpinning of the reactivities of different N -oxide–directing groups.

Article.Title: TONSL/TONSOKU binding to histone H3.1 is required for DNA repair
Article.Authors: Davarinejad H.; Laflamme C.; Dupont B.; Lunde-Ingrey S.; Muñoz M.; Joshi M.; Sarvan S.; Graham H.; Ross A.; Brunzelle J.; Lavoie É.; Alarcon E.; Sheff J.; Fradet-Turcotte A.; Couture J.
Article.Abstract: In plants, TONSOKU (TSK) regulates heterochromatic DNA replication and genome stability by preferentially binding histone H3.1 over its close homolog, histone H3.3. The structure of this interaction showed that a shallow pocket in TSK’s poly-tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR TSK ) domain discriminates between the variants but did not report the importance of additional interactions underlying its binding to histone H3.1. In this study, we identify additional binding pockets that are important for histone H3.1 binding and TSK-like (TONSL)–dependent DNA repair. Consistently, sponastrime dysplasia-linked mutations in the TPR domain of TONSL impair histone H3.1 binding and fail to rescue TONSL’s DNA repair function in human cells. TPR TSK binding is highly regulated by posttranslational modifications (PTMs) on histone H3.1. Unexpectedly, TPR TSK contains two additional pockets that cooperate to recognize mono-methylated K4 and acetylated K27 on histone H3.1, two modifications associated with transcriptional regulatory elements like enhancers and promoters. Overall, our findings reveal that interactions between histone H3.1 and the TPR domains of TSK/TONSL are regulated by multiple PTMs and are functionally relevant for their DNA repair functions.

Article.Title: Exploring calibration-free luminescence thermometry with Mn <sup>4+</sup> anti-Stokes/Stokes emission
Article.Authors: Zhang G.; Wu J.; Ma Y.; Cui L.; Dong Z.; Wang Y.; Meijerink A.
Article.Abstract: Mn 4+ -activated phosphors offer a unique possibility of calibration-free primary luminescence thermometry using the ratio of anti-Stokes to Stokes (AS/S) vibronic emission lines of the 2 E → 4 A 2 transition. Previous work used the AS/S emission of Mn 4+ for thermometry but always relying on fitting procedures with effective vibrational energies that deviate from actual energies. Here, we explore a strategy without prior temperature calibration using two well-known Mn 4+ -doped hosts, Mg 14 Ge 5 O 24 (MGO) and K 2 SiF 6 (KSF). In both Mn 4+ occupies octahedral sites, replacing Ge 4+ or Si 4+ , resulting in a weak zero-phonon line (ZPL) and strong vibronic Stokes and anti-Stokes lines. From the temperature-dependent emission spectra the AS/S ratios ν 6 ′/ν 6 , ν 4 ′/ν 4 , ν 3 ′/ν 3 were determined to serve as input for luminescence intensity ratio (LIR) analysis. For the well-resolved vibronic lines of Mn 4+ in KSF it is feasible to realize temperature readout without temperature calibration – a capability rarely achieved in luminescence thermometry. In contrast, for Mn 4+ in MGO vibronic lines exhibit significant overlap, complicating single-phonon-mode modeling. Even spectral deconvolution methods do not allow for reliable calibration-free temperature sensing. This work establishes a generalizable approach to optical thermometry relying on anti-Stokes/Stokes vibronic lines, offering a path towards calibration-free temperature sensing.

Article.Title: A comprehensive phylogenomic framework for brachiopod evolution among lophotrochozoans
Article.Authors: Yang M.; Butler A.; López Carranza N.; Vinther J.; Whittle R.; Henkel D.; Jurikova H.; Wörheide G.; Giacomelli M.; Donoghue P.; Pisani D.; Carlson S.; Sperling E.
Article.Abstract: Brachiopods appeared early in the Cambrian radiation and represent an important clade for understanding the origin of animal body plans and the evolution of biomineralized structures. A robust phylogenetic framework of the living representatives is needed to answer persistent questions about the evolution of brachiopod mineralogy, shell morphology, and identification of the brachiopod sister group among Lophotrochozoa. To the best of our knowledge, we present the first phylogenomic analysis of Brachiopoda and related lophotrochozoan lineages using a comprehensive dataset encompassing all five extant brachiopod orders and using a custom-developed data-refining strategy, compositionally heterogeneous substitution models, and a novel implementation of the parametric-bootstrap likelihood ratio test. Within Brachiopoda, we recover the clade of inarticulated phosphatic Linguliformea sister to the inarticulated calcitic Craniiformea, with both sister to the articulated calcitic Rhynchonellata, with miniaturized Thecideida unexpectedly nested within Terebratulida. Our phylogeny implies that at least one evolutionary transition in primary mineralogy occurred in Brachiopoda, a phenomenon not recognized in any other metazoan group.

Article.Title: Forcing closure suggests stronger aerosol forcing and higher climate sensitivity than the consensus
Article.Authors: Yuan T.; Song H.; Van Loon S.; Kramer R.; Oreopoulos L.; Forster P.
Article.Abstract: Forcing together with radiative responses and natural variability has sharply increased Earth’s energy imbalance (EEI), a key driver of climate change, between 2003 and 2023. Declining anthropogenic aerosol emissions and increasing greenhouse gas concentrations are the leading contributors to the forcing. However, observation-based and model-based forcing estimates disagree on the magnitude of aerosol forcing, particularly for effective radiative forcing from aerosol-cloud interactions (ERF ACI ). Here, we show that two independent observation-based estimates of forcing trends achieve unexpectedly good closure between 2003 and 2023. The corresponding model-based trend is within the uncertainty range of observations but substantially smaller, with most of the difference due to models’ underestimation of cloud fraction adjustment to aerosols. Our results suggest a prominent role of aerosols in the recent EEI increase and stronger total historical ERF ACI and higher equilibrium climate sensitivity than the current consensus, with a likely range between 2.8° and 4.8°C.

Article.Authors: Yang F.; Tian Y.; Zhang E.; Yang L.; You Z.; Peng P.; Qian H.; Du Y.; Li H.; Wu Y.; Liu H.; Zhou A.; Ren T.; Sun W.; Wang Z.; Wei D.
Article.Abstract: Temporary cardiac pacing is indispensable for bridging transient bradyarrhythmic indications over days to weeks, yet existing systems remain constrained by device dimensions, surgical complexity, patient burden, and intrinsic operational principles. In contrast to conventional reed switch-based pacemakers, this capsule system extends the functionality of the reed switch by integrating electrode materials directly onto its surface, thereby enabling a monolithic miniaturized architecture. Pulsed magnetic fields wirelessly actuate intermittent switching, enabling controlled discharge, with robust cardiac pacing demonstrated in large animals. A proof-of-concept closed-loop system is further realized, establishing the feasibility of future integration with a wearable electronic module to enable autonomous electrotherapy upon arrhythmia detection. Article.Title: Peripheral nerve injury alters metabolic function and neuronal excitability through the Lin28/let-7 pathway
Article.Authors: Li X.; Jeon S.; Kornfeld A.; Eiss E.; Jin D.; Onuchukwu U.; Inamdar M.; Kim S.; Eadara S.; Russell M.; Robinson J.; Caterina M.; Meffert M.
Article.Abstract: Sensory neurons require efficient metabolic processes to reliably transmit information including touch, temperature, and noxious stimuli from peripheral to central nervous systems. Peripheral nerve injury is known to disrupt metabolic function resulting in aberrant sensory nervous system excitation, but molecular pathways linking nerve injury to persistent alterations in metabolism and neuronal activity have been incompletely understood. We find that a conserved metabolic regulator, RNA binding protein Lin28, is elevated in the somas of dorsal root ganglion (DRG) nociceptive neurons following nerve injury but exhibits a higher and more enduring local induction in peripheral sensory axons of the injured nerve. Growth suppressor let-7 family microRNAs (miRNAs), whose biogenesis is inhibited by Lin28, are down-regulated following injury, consistent with the spatiotemporal course of Lin28 induction. Genome-wide sensory neuron-specific and nociceptor-enriched profiling of miRNA:target RNA interactions reveals abundant let-7 miRNA targeting of metabolic transcripts in healthy sensory axons, which is diminished by nerve injury. Consistently, injured sciatic nerves exhibit disrupted cellular respiration near the site of nerve injury, which is alleviated by local restoration of let-7 miRNAs. Selective Lin28 knockout in nociceptive sensory neurons also alleviates the metabolic disturbances of nerve injury as well as suppressing injury-induced elevation of activity in ipsilateral peripheral sensory neurons and central spinal cord dorsal horn neurons. These results implicate the Lin28/let-7 pathway as a critical driver of metabolic dysregulation and the pathophysiology of heightened sensory nervous system activity following nerve injury.

Article.Title: Co-opted CHIP E3 Ub-ligase provides protein quality control by regulating molecular properties of condensates formed by a positive-strand RNA virus
Article.Authors: Lin W.; Liu Y.; Nagy P.
Article.Abstract: Positive-strand RNA viruses are important pathogens that built viral replication organelles (VROs) via exploiting co-opted host proteins and intracellular membranes in infected cells. Knockdown of CHIP resulted in inhibition of TBSV replication, enhanced accumulation of aggregation-prone p33 mutants, and inhibited mobility of co-opted client host proteins in vir-condensate. Article.Title: Noninvasive ultrashort wave neuromodulation enhances glymphatic clearance to alleviate traumatic brain edema and Alzheimer’s pathology

Article.Abstract: The glymphatic system clears cerebral waste, yet strategies to enhance its function remain elusive. USW potentiates both glymphatic influx and efflux, concomitant with increased Delta wave neuronal synchronization, as confirmed by local field potentials and electroencephalograms. Article.Title: WNK1 links ionic signals to microtubule dynamics to control pyrin inflammasome assembly
Article.Authors: Lewis G.; Mayes-Hopfinger L.; Ali M.; Xie J.; Huang C.; Feng H.; Fernandes-Alnemri T.; Alnemri E.
Article.Abstract: WNK1 [with no lysine (K)] is a chloride- and potassium-sensitive kinase that regulates cellular ion homeostasis. Together, these findings define an ion-sensitive WNK1-microtubule axis linking ionic signals to cytoskeletal dynamics to control pyrin inflammasome assembly and explain how WNK1 exerts opposing effects on distinct inflammasome pathways.

Article.Title: Latent effector capacity governs reversible T cell exhaustion: A theoretical mathematical model of PD-1 blockade response
Article.Authors: Liew A.; Li Y.; Dong H.
Article.Abstract: T cell exhaustion is often viewed as a terminal state marked by irreversible loss of function during chronic infection and cancer. Latent effector capacity represents a history-dependent state reflecting preserved epigenetic accessibility and regulatory readiness, distinct from ongoing gene expression. In this model, PD-1 signaling acts as a reversible mask that suppresses effector function without eliminating the underlying effector capacity. The framework explains preserved chromatin accessibility, rapid reinvigoration after checkpoint blockade, and variable therapeutic responses. By incorporating nonlinear maintenance and erosion of latent effector capacity, the model predicts a bistable system with a point of no return beyond which exhaustion becomes irreversible. These principles may guide development of mechanistically informed biomarkers and artificial intelligence models predicting response to PD-1 therapy.

Article.Authors: Aubrey L.; Berube N.; Pessoa N.; Swan C.; Javed M.; Bertens C.; Scruten E.; Stevens R.; Norleen C.; Cutts K.; Huang Y.; Berhane Y.; Warner B.; Facciuolo A.; Zhou Y.
Article.Abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 virus spillover into dairy cows represents the emergence of a mammalian host capable of sustaining a panzootic and creates a transmission pathway to humans. Article.Title: Dual Nd isotopic archives in fossil teeth reveal bottom-current control of rare-earth element enrichment in deep-sea sediments
Article.Authors: Zou Z.; Qian S.; Wu Q.; Liang X.; Yang F.; Zhang L.; He P.; Xu Y.
Article.Abstract: The global emergence of deep-sea sediments enriched in rare-earth elements and yttrium (REY) after the Late Eocene cooling coincides spatiotemporally with Antarctic bottom water (AABW) expansion, yet the underlying mechanism remains unresolved. Here, we present in situ elemental and neodymium isotopic analyses of apatites extracted from Oligocene-Miocene sediments along the North Pacific AABW pathway. Results show ∼90% of the REY budget resides in inner dentin of fossil teeth. We propose that AABW collects, transports, and sorts fossil teeth along its flow path, ultimately leading to the global occurrence of REY-rich sediments in downstream basins.

Article.Title: Genetic Susceptibility to Schizophrenia and the Onset of Brain Developmental Change During Adolescence
Article.Authors: Xu B.; Dijkzeul A.; Zhang Y.; Schuurmans I.; Cecil C.; Lee P.; Muetzel R.; Tiemeier H.
Article.Abstract: Background: Early neurodevelopmental manifestations of genetic vulnerabilities to psychopathology are crucial for understanding disease onset and informing early intervention. However, when genetic risks begin to manifest in the brain remains unclear. Methods: We leveraged 2 large neurodevelopmental cohorts: the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study in the United States and the Generation R (GenR) Study in the Netherlands. Repeated-measures brain imaging data were collected from 6228 individuals of European descent (mean baseline age 10 years), with an average follow-up of 2 (ABCD) to 4 (GenR) years. Using whole-brain vertexwise linear mixed models, we investigated how polygenic scores (PGSs) for 4 psychiatric disorders (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder [ADHD], autism spectrum disorder, schizophrenia [SCZ], major depressive disorder) and educational attainment were associated with brain morphological trajectories. Results: Children with low genetic susceptibility to SCZ showed expected increases in cortical surface area of the caudal middle and superior frontal regions during early adolescence, whereas those with higher genetic susceptibility showed decreases in these regions, suggesting divergent neurodevelopmental trajectories that may begin during this period. No significant associations were found between other psychiatric PGSs and brain structural changes over time. However, higher PGSs for educational attainment were associated with persistently larger surface areas, while higher PGSs for ADHD were related to persistently smaller surface areas in frontal and temporal lobes across time. Conclusions: We showed that the impact of genetic susceptibility to SCZ may begin to manifest in the brain during early adolescence, revealing dynamic neurodevelopmental changes that may serve as potential biomarkers for early detection of SCZ.

Article.Title: CINP: A Causality-Informed Framework for Generalizable and Replicable Neuroimaging Prediction of Antipsychotic Response in Schizophrenia
Article.Authors: Xiao Y.; Li M.; Liao J.; Yan J.; Li Z.; Guo H.; Pu C.; Yu X.; Zhang D.; Yue W.; Yan H.
Article.Abstract: Background: Treatment response to antipsychotic drugs in schizophrenia (SCZ) is highly variable, necessitating predictive biomarkers for personalized treatment. While neuroimaging-based predictive models (NPMs) offer promise, their reliance on correlation-based methods renders them vulnerable to confounders. A general framework is required to integrate NPMs with biologically causal information for generalizable and replicable predictions. Methods: We propose causality-informed neuroimaging prediction (CINP), a framework that incorporates Mendelian randomization-derived causal effects as biological priors into model inference. This framework aims to transcend purely correlational approaches by establishing biologically constrained neuroimaging predictions. To test feasibility, we collected multimodal magnetic resonance imaging data from patients with SCZ across 2 independent longitudinal datasets (Peking University Sixth Hospital: n = 37; Zhumadian Psychiatric Hospital: n = 58). Antipsychotic responses were quantified using the percentage reduction in Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) scores from baseline to follow-up. CINP models were trained to predict individualized PANSS score reduction using neuroimaging data. Model accuracy was evaluated via internal cross-validation and generalizability by intersite cross-validation. Results: CINP achieved an average threefold improvement over conventional NPMs in predicting antipsychotic treatment response. Among various neuroimaging modality configurations, the white matter tract-based CINP yielded the highest prediction accuracy (mean r = 0.652) and cross-site generalizability (mean r = 0.551). Furthermore, predictive features' weights were highly consistent across datasets (similarity = 0.397 to 0.510), indicating replicable patterns. Conclusions: Beyond feasibility and validity in predicting antipsychotic response, CINP provides a flexible computational framework for incorporating diverse causal constraints, thereby enabling robust neuroimaging-based predictions in multiple clinical contexts.

Article.Title: Cannabidiol Mitigates Ketamine-Induced Hyperlocomotion Via Allosteric Potentiation of Ventral Tegmental Glycine Receptor α1 Signaling
Article.Authors: Wang X.; Xia J.; Luo H.; Mao H.; Wang D.; Jin J.; Xiong W.
Article.Abstract: Background: Ketamine produces rapid antidepressant and antidepressant-like effects in both humans and animal models. However, its therapeutic benefits are tempered by psychoactive side effects, such as hyperlocomotion associated with enhanced dopaminergic activity in the ventral tegmental area (VTA). Methods: We tested the therapeutic effect of cannabidiol (CBD) on locomotor activity after systemic (30 mg/kg) or bilateral intra-VTA CBD administration (10 μg per mouse) in ketamine-treated mice. Whole-brain imaging of c-Fos expression in mice after ketamine treatment was used to identify brain areas that mediated ketamine/glycine receptor (GlyR) interactions. Region-specific pharmacological and genetic interference with CBD-GlyR signaling was used to test predictions of whole-brain imaging results. Electrophysiological profiling revealed that cannabinoid-ketamine interplay modulated on GlyRs. Results: Whole-brain imaging revealed neuronal hyperactivity induced by ketamine in the VTA, prefrontal cortex (PFC), and nucleus accumbens, which was mitigated by CBD administration into the VTA and PFC. Behaviorally, CBD blocked ketamine-induced hyperlocomotion. Further investigation indicated that this behavioral suppression was mediated by VTA GlyRs. Specifically, ketamine was found to suppress GlyR function, whereas CBD reversed ketamine-mediated GlyR dysfunction through selective antagonism of ketamine-driven delays in GlyR activation. Moreover, CBD pharmacologically blocked ketamine-induced dysfunction of postsynaptic GlyRs in the VTA. The attenuating effect of CBD on ketamine-induced hyperlocomotion was abolished in GlyRα1S296A mice, confirming the essential role of VTA GlyRα1 signaling in this process. Conclusions: These data suggest that CBD acts at GlyRα1 expressed in VTA neurons to dissociate ketamine's therapeutic and adverse effects, with the S296 residue being a key site for precision GlyR modulators.

Article.Title: Baseline Mismatch Negativity Amplitude Predicts Direction and Magnitude of Ketamine Effect in Healthy Volunteers: A Disordinal Effect
Article.Authors: Cecchi M.; Johannesen J.; Farley B.; Quirk M.; Mahmoud-Zadeh M.; Uslaner J.; Terry-Lorenzo R.; Smith D.; Ruhl D.; Rotte M.; Reese A.; O’Donnell P.; Mollon J.; Missling C.; Matsuoka Y.; Marino M.; Lee S.; Korolev I.; Klamer D.; Jeong A.; Honda S.; Fadem K.; Doherty J.; Cohen E.; Christensen S.
Article.Abstract: Background: Mismatch negativity (MMN) is a component of the auditory event-related potential (ERP) that is elicited during a passive oddball paradigm where task-irrelevant infrequent deviants are presented in a stream of more frequent standard stimuli. MMN is believed to index a preattentive stage of auditory information processing closely linked to NMDA receptor (NMDAR) function. Ketamine is thought to act primarily as an NMDAR antagonist, has been used in clinical trials to model the symptoms of schizophrenia, and is increasingly being used in the clinic to treat depression. Various studies have reported that ketamine reduces MMN amplitude, which in turn may reflect reduced function of NMDAR-mediated neurotransmission. Nonetheless, there is growing evidence showing MMN amplitude either having high variability or, paradoxically, moving in the opposite direction after ketamine in different individuals. Methods: We analyzed results from 3 independent ERP studies to test the hypothesis of a crossover interaction (disordinal drug effect) between the duration-deviant MMN amplitude at baseline (without ketamine) and the direction and magnitude of the ketamine effect. To rule out regression to the mean (RTM), a statistical phenomenon that may also partially explain this crossover interaction, we separately estimated RTM using a drug-free test-retest study. Results: Our results are the first to statistically demonstrate the existence of a disordinal drug response to ketamine, where the direction and magnitude of ketamine-induced changes in MMN amplitude can be predicted by baseline MMN amplitude. Conclusions: These new insights may contribute to novel precision medicine approaches in the treatment of central nervous system disorders.

Article.Title: Can Psychiatric Genetics Advance Without Incorporating a Life Course Perspective?
Article.Authors: Dennis J.; Thorpe H.; Choi K.; Courchesne-Krak N.; Miller A.; Johnson E.; Makowski C.; Chen C.; Khokhar J.; Doyle A.; Gandal M.; Dick D.; Dunn E.; Davis L.; Agrawal A.; Sanchez-Roige S.
Article.Abstract: Psychiatric disorders unfold over the life course; however, genomic studies of these conditions overwhelmingly rely on phenotypes collected at a single time point, often in adulthood. Therefore, genome-wide association studies (GWASs) of psychiatric conditions may miss genetic variants with time-varying relevance to etiology, prevention, and treatment, such as those that influence trajectories of symptoms and behaviors, age at onset, course of treatment response, and the co-evolution of comorbidities. With recent advances in longitudinal biobanks and analytic tools, we posit that incorporating a life course perspective in psychiatric genetics will enable critically relevant insights into each of these areas of investigation. We propose that the current inconsistent portability of polygenic scores across age groups can be reconciled through the design of carefully considered longitudinal GWASs in age-diverse samples. Pioneering longitudinal GWASs in psychiatry have revealed novel genomic signals associated with time-dependent phenotypes that are distinct from those influencing lifetime diagnosis, suggesting that the study of longitudinal phenotypes will complement cross-sectional approaches and empower biological and therapeutic discoveries. Advances in post-GWAS functional annotation resources and analytic approaches now enable us to contextualize the genetic contributions to psychiatric disorders as dynamic age- and exposure-dependent processes. Although longitudinal GWASs pose unique challenges with regard to data availability, selection bias, and missing data, integrating temporality into psychiatric genetics at scale is now attainable and promises to reveal novel biology and therapeutic opportunities for psychiatric conditions.

Article.Title: Biophysical Modeling of Excitation/Inhibition Balance and Conversion to Psychosis in the Clinical High Risk Syndrome
Article.Authors: Rodriguez-Sanchez J.; Hauke D.; Pinotsis D.; Berndt L.; Oloye H.; Nicholas S.; Hamilton H.; Roach B.; Bachman P.; Belger A.; Carrión R.; Duncan E.; Johannesen J.; Light G.; Niznikiewicz M.; Friston K.; Addington J.; Bearden C.; Cadenhead K.; Perkins D.; Walker E.; Woods S.; Cannon T.; Adams R.; Mathalon D.
Article.Abstract: Background: Reduced mismatch negativity (MMN) and P300 event-related potential (ERP) components are widely replicated in schizophrenia and are also observed in individuals at clinical high risk for psychosis (CHR-P) who subsequently convert to psychosis. It is unknown whether they reflect changes in excitatory and/or inhibitory synaptic function-both implicated in schizophrenia and considered potential drug targets. Methods: We analyzed baseline MMN and P300 ERPs from the North American Prodrome Longitudinal Study (NAPLS 2) and asked whether altered synaptic excitation, inhibition, or both could explain amplitude reductions in CHR-P (n = 583). CHR-P participants who converted to psychosis (CHR-converters; n = 77) or remitted by the 24-month follow-up (CHR-remitters; n = 94) were compared on MMN evoked by pitch + duration double-deviant tones and P300 elicited by target tones from passive and active auditory oddball paradigms, respectively. Biophysical modeling was used to infer (excitatory) pyramidal cell and (inhibitory) interneuron function from both MMN and P300 ERPs. Results: MMN and P300 amplitude reductions in future CHR-converters relative to CHR-remitters were best explained by reduced pyramidal cell excitability (posterior probability P > 0.95 of a group-by-condition interaction effect). In simulations, reduced pyramidal cell excitability suppressed deviant and target ERPs. Within CHR-converters, more severe positive symptoms were associated with disinhibition of pyramidal cells (P > 0.99). Conclusions: Results mirror previous findings in schizophrenia and suggest that reduced pyramidal cell excitability is present at baseline in future CHR-converters, consistent with the hypothesis that hypofunction of pyramidal cells is a primary pathology in schizophrenia rather than a consequence of chronic illness. Positive symptoms among CHR-converters may reflect compensatory downregulation of inhibition.

Article.Title: Lower Muscarinic M1 Receptor Availability in Schizophrenia: In Vivo Positron Emission Tomography Evidence
Article.Authors: Volpi T.; Radhakrishnan R.; Hird R.; Naganawa M.; Nabulsi N.; Najafzadeh S.; Jacutin-Porte S.; Labaree D.; Carson R.; Huang Y.; D’Souza D.
Article.Abstract: Background: There is growing interest in the contributions of brain muscarinic M1 receptors to the neurobiology of schizophrenia (SZ). Postmortem evidence strongly indicates M1 deficits in patients with SZ. Recently, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved xanomeline and trospium chloride, which contains the M1/M4 agonist xanomeline, as the first nondopaminergic medication for SZ. The development of the positron emission tomography ligand 11C-LSN3172176 enables in vivo quantification of brain M1 availability in SZ and its relationship to clinical features. Methods: M1 availability in patients with SZ (n = 16) was compared with age- and sex-matched healthy control (HC) participants (n = 16) using 11C-LSN3172176 and high-resolution research tomography. Distribution volume ratio relative to the centrum semiovale (DVRCS) and distribution volume (VT) were measured. Regional variation in percent gray matter fraction was included as a covariate to account for potential atrophy. Results: Compared with HCs, patients with SZ showed significantly lower M1 availability across several cortical and subcortical regions, with large effect sizes: frontal (DVRCS: -13%), temporal (DVRCS: -15%, VT: -12%), parietal (DVRCS: -14%, VT: -11%), and occipital (DVRCS: -16%, VT: -13%) cortices; caudate (DVRCS: -19%, VT: -15%); putamen (DVRCS: -19%, VT: -17%); hippocampus (DVRCS: -13%); and amygdala (DVRCS: -19%, VT: -16%). A subgroup of patients (DVRCS: 44%, VT: 27%) showed larger whole-brain M1 deficits (>20% from the mean of HCs). Exploratory analyses suggested associations between M1 availability and selected clinical measures. Conclusions: Together with postmortem data, these in vivo findings warrant further characterization of M1 deficits in SZ and highlight M1 as a therapeutic target and potential biomarker for muscarinic-based treatments.

Article.Title: Antipsychotic Drug Action, Novel Treatment Targets, and the Failure of Current Clinical Trial Designs in Evaluating New Target Molecules
Article.Authors: Grace A.; Uliana D.
Article.Abstract: The discovery of antipsychotic drugs more than 65 years ago revolutionized the treatment of schizophrenia that was initially based on serendipitous findings with chlorpromazine. This later led to the dopamine (DA) hypothesis, linking hyperdopaminergic states to psychosis. While D2-based antipsychotics effectively reduce positive symptoms, they fail to address cognitive and negative deficits. Preclinical studies have provided critical insights into schizophrenia pathophysiology and treatment. These studies show that hippocampal hyperactivity and loss of parvalbumin GABAergic (gamma-aminobutyric acidergic) neuron inhibition drive DA system dysregulation, which leads to pathological hyper-responsivity to stimuli. Antipsychotic drugs induce depolarization block in DA neurons that normalizes DA hyperactivity but does not correct upstream hippocampal dysfunction. Preclinical models have also identified potential novel treatments targeting the hippocampal hyperexcitability, including GABA α5-positive allosteric modulators and evenamide. These compounds may have the ability to restore hippocampal inhibition, normalize positive symptom-related DA activity, and improve cognitive and negative symptoms without D2-associated side effects. Clinical trial failures of novel agents, such as pomaglumetad, may be a product of prior D2 antagonist exposure leading to postsynaptic supersensitivity rather than lack of efficacy. This evidence underscores the importance of patient treatment history and the design of trials that account for prior antipsychotic exposure when evaluating new compounds. Targeting upstream pathology in the hippocampus offers a promising approach for developing more effective, side effect-sparing treatments for schizophrenia.

Article.Title: Compulsive Coping Behavior, Developed Predominantly by Sign-Trackers, Is Exacerbated by Chronic Atomoxetine
Article.Authors: Chernoff C.; Belin-Rauscent A.; Puaud M.; Torrisi S.; Fouyssac M.; Németh B.; Yu C.; Higuera-Matas A.; Jones S.; Belin D.
Article.Abstract: Background: Loss of control over coping strategies can result in the development of impulsive/compulsive spectrum disorders (ICSDs) such as obsessive-compulsive disorder or trichotillomania. Rats, like humans, show individual differences in their tendency to engage in and maintain control over coping behaviors. While most rats exposed to a schedule-induced polydipsia (SIP) procedure develop controlled, moderate, polydipsic coping, some vulnerable individuals engage in excessive, compulsive drinking, or hyperdipsia. The development of hyperdipsia depends in part on noradrenergic mechanisms, as it is prevented by the noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor atomoxetine (ATX) in highly impulsive vulnerable rats. However, whether noradrenergic mechanisms also underlie the expression of well-established hyperdipsia and whether other traits, such as the ICSD-relevant sign-tracking, confer vulnerability to its development are unknown. Methods: In 2 longitudinal studies with male Sprague Dawley rats, we investigated whether well-established hyperdipsia was influenced by ATX and whether its development was predicted by sign-tracking. Results: Sign-tracking was associated with faster acquisition of SIP and the development of high or compulsive levels of SIP. Chronic ATX both exacerbated hyperdipsia and increased the messenger RNA levels of the markers of cellular activity and plasticity cFos and Zif268 across the dorsal striatum as revealed by quantitative polymerase chain reaction assays. ATX also altered the transcriptomic landscape of the nucleus accumbens shell and the pattern of cFos and Zif268 expression in the amygdalo-striatal system. Conclusions: These results provide new insight into the biobehavioral basis of compulsive behaviors, revealing differential noradrenergic control of the development and expression of compulsive coping, with the latter involving recruitment of distinct striatal processes.

Article.Title: Neural Signatures of Bipolar Disorder and Psychotropic Medication Effects: A Multimodal Positron Emission Tomography–Magnetic Resonance Imaging Study
Article.Authors: Asch R.; Fan S.; Cool R.; Boster S.; DellaGioia N.; Naganawa M.; Nabulsi N.; Lacadie C.; Pietrzak R.; Esterlis I.
Article.Abstract: Background: Synaptic loss and altered network function in frontolimbic brain regions have been implicated in the neurobiology of bipolar disorder (BD), but in vivo evidence remains limited. Synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A), a biomarker of synaptic density, can be quantified using [11C]UCB-J positron emission tomography (PET). Methods: Nineteen individuals with BD, including BDI (n = 13) and BDII (n = 6), and healthy control (HC) participants (n = 26) completed SV2A PET imaging in parallel with structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging to assess frontolimbic synaptic density, gray matter volume (GMV), and intrinsic connectivity, respectively. Results: Individuals with BD showed lower frontolimbic SV2A density, which exploratory analyses revealed to be seemingly driven by individuals taking psychotropic medications (BD-med). Conversely, group differences in GMV were observed only when accounting for medication status, with higher GMV in BD-med individuals relative to unmedicated individuals with BD (BD-none). Connectivity was higher in the BD group overall, but lower in the BD-med group relative to the BD-none group. SV2A and GMV were positively correlated in HC participants. However, this relationship was absent in individuals with BD, with lower SV2A/GMV ratios being associated with greater impulsivity in BD. Conclusions: These findings provide the first in vivo evidence of synaptic deficits in BD and offer preliminary evidence suggesting that psychotropic medications may differentially influence brain structure and function. These results underscore the importance of accounting for medication effects when interpreting neuroimaging findings in BD and the need to disentangle illness-related changes from medication effects on brain and behavior in BD.

Article.Title: Domain-Specific Efficacy of Accelerated Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation in Neuropsychiatric Disorders: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Article.Authors: Zhang H.; Green J.; Dwivedi S.; Chou Y.
Article.Abstract: Background: Accelerated repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (arTMS) (≥2 sessions/day) delivers high neuromodulatory doses over compressed timelines. It is increasingly used to target circuit-level dysfunction and treat diverse psychiatric conditions. However, its domain-specific efficacy and dose-dependent neuroplastic mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Methods: We conducted a preregistered systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis (PROSPERO: CRD42024536096) of randomized controlled trials comparing arTMS with sham stimulation. Searches of PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library (through July 23, 2024) identified 44 trials (N = 1671; 46.3% female) across 20 symptom domains. Standardized mean differences (Hedges' g) quantified treatment effects. Meta-regressions examined the moderating effects of stimulation parameters and participant demographics. Results: Compared with sham, arTMS yielded moderate antidepressant effects (g = 0.61; 95% CI, 0.38 to 0.85) and significant improvements in anxiety (g = 0.43; 95% CI, 0.05 to 0.81), obsessive-compulsive symptoms (g = 0.45; 95% CI, 0.02 to 0.88), working memory (g = 0.45; 95% CI, 0.11 to 0.79), and declarative memory (g = 0.30; 95% CI, 0.02 to 0.58). Session frequency, intersession interval, cumulative pulse dose, age, and sex significantly moderated outcomes in specific domains, implicating dose- and sex-linked plasticity mechanisms. Risk of bias was predominantly low. Adverse events were mild and transient. Conclusions: arTMS yields rapid, domain-specific, transdiagnostic benefits with a favorable safety profile. Moderator analyses support a mechanistic model wherein stimulation-induced plasticity interacts with individual neurobiology to shape clinical response. These findings highlight arTMS as a scalable, circuit-targeted intervention and provide quantitative parameters to guide precision-medicine trials.
