Article.Title: A novel TARGET for anti-CD20 antibody therapy in multiple sclerosis
Article.Authors: Freeman S.; Liblau R.
Article.Abstract: This scientific commentary refers to ‘Multimodal discovery of a pathogenic B cell-dependent T cell state in multiple sclerosis’ by Farooq et al. (https://doi.org/10.1093/brain/awag303). Monoclonal antibodies that target and deplete CD20-expressing cells—predominantly B cells—are among the most effective disease-modifying therapies for relapsing multiple sclerosis (MS).1 Despite their striking clinical efficacy, however, their mechanisms of action remain incompletely defined. Conceptually, two non-mutually exclusive modalities can be envisioned (Fig. 1): Direct effects, mediated by elimination of directly pathogenic CD20-expressing cells, such as pro-inflammatory or Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-harbouring B cells3 and subsets of pro-inflammatory CD20dim T cells.4 Indirect effects, arising from removal of a critical node in the immunopathogenic cascade of MS, such as memory B cells. This may induce secondary changes in the frequency, phenotype or function of pathogenic immune subsets—including autoreactive or EBV-specific T cells5,6—and/or promote regulatory mechanisms involving anti-inflammatory myeloid cells, gut mucosa-derived IgA-producing B cells and regulatory CD4+ T cells.7,8 Mechanisms of action of anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies in multiple sclerosis. Systemic administration of anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies depletes blood-accessible lymphocytes expressing CD20 at the cell surface—namely, B cells and a quantitatively minor subset of T cells expressing low levels of CD20, referred to as CD20dim T cells. The beneficial effects of anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies in multiple sclerosis are thought to result from a combination of direct and indirect mechanisms. The direct effects (left) may reflect the depletion of pro-inflammatory B cells, of the small fraction of EBV-infected B cells, and/or of potentially pathogenic CD20dim T cells, all capable of promoting CNS inflammation. The indirect effects (right) may result from the depletion of B cells, particularly memory B cells, that present autoantigens or EBV-derived peptides to pathogenic CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, thereby promoting their activation. B cells may also support the activation or differentiation of inflammatory myeloid cells and, through mechanisms that remain incompletely understood, suppress regulatory immune pathways. The study by Farooq and co-workers2 identifies an additional indirect mechanism (not shown): depletion of circulating T cells with a distinctive molecular signature suggestive of cytotoxic and inflammatory potential, as well as the capacity to migrate to and persist within the CNS. Created in BioRender. Astier, A. (2026) https://BioRender.com/o15u1j7. Clarifying the precise mechanisms of action of these highly effective therapies extends well beyond conceptual interest. It has direct implications for monitoring people with MS treated with anti-CD20 antibodies and provides a unique window into the immune pathways that drive relapsing MS. In this context, the study by Farooq and colleagues2 in this issue of Brain offers important new insights by identifying a single-cell transcriptomic and proteomic signature that delineates an activated effector T-cell population with a propensity to home to and reside in non-lymphoid tissues, and that is reduced in peripheral blood several months after initiation of ocrelizumab in people with MS. The authors used cellular indexing of transcriptomes and epitopes by sequencing (CITE-seq), combined with refined machine-learning models, to profile peripheral blood mononuclear cells at single-cell resolution in a cohort of 14 treatment-naïve people with MS. Samples were obtained before treatment and at multiple time points following ocrelizumab initiation.2 Although the cohort is small, the longitudinal design and depth of single-cell profiling provide high resolution information on immune trajectories within individuals. By comparing pretreatment samples with early (2 weeks) and late (6 to 18 months) post-treatment time points, the authors quantified enrichment or depletion of specific cell states over time. As expected, the dominant change was depletion of naïve and memory B cells (but not antibody-secreting cells) at early and, to a lesser extent, late time points. Strengthening previous data, the gene program associated with transitional and naïve B cells was the only B-cell program enriched at the late post-treatment time point. The most novel and compelling observation was the marked depletion of T-cell programs associated with (i) cytotoxicity and inflammatory cytokine production; (ii) T helper 1-like characteristics linked to tissue homing and residency; and (iii) T-cell activation signalling. Together, these programs define T cells with the capacity to enter inflamed CNS tissue, persist locally, and mediate tissue damage. By integrating these three transcriptomic programs, the authors defined a molecular signature that they term ‘TARGET’. Importantly, this TARGET signature—shared by subsets of memory CD8+ and CD4+ T cells, as well as innate-like T cells (γδ T cells and MAIT cells)—was depleted only at later time points after ocrelizumab initiation. Because B cells are depleted within 2 weeks of ocrelizumab initiation, whereas the TARGET T-cell signature declines only after many months, the T-cell changes are likely downstream consequences of B-cell loss rather than direct effects of the drug. In addition, the authors show that this B cell-dependent T-cell signature is enriched in the blood of people with MS with higher relapse activity, implicating this T-cell program in MS pathogenicity. To test this hypothesis further, they leveraged published single-cell RNA sequencing datasets of paired peripheral blood and CSF samples and demonstrated a striking enrichment of the TARGET signature in memory T cells from the CSF of people with MS, but not controls, relative to blood. The TARGET signature was also enriched in T cells from lesion rims and in normal-appearing white matter from progressive MS compared with healthy white matter. These T cells are hypothesized to represent tissue-resident T cells that fuel smouldering inflammation in progressive MS (F Masson et al., in press). Finally, reanalysis of blood transcriptomic data from a small cohort of nine people with MS revealed accumulation of the TARGET T-cell signature following initiation of treatment with natalizumab, a monoclonal antibody that blocks anti-α4 integrin. Collectively, these findings provide converging evidence that the newly identified peripheral T-cell TARGET signature, which is B-cell dependent, is associated with pathogenic potential. They also suggest overlapping effects of ocrelizumab and natalizumab on TARGET T cells in people with MS, albeit through different mechanisms: anti-CD20 therapy is associated with depletion of circulating T cells expressing the TARGET signature, whereas natalizumab prevents the migration of these cells into the CNS, leading to their retention in the blood. These findings raise several important mechanistic and translational questions: How does ocrelizumab-induced B-cell depletion lead to the depletion of blood T cells expressing the TARGET signature? Potential mechanisms include T-cell death, cell state transition, or redistribution from blood into tissues. What is the relative contribution of the various T-cell subsets expressing the TARGET signature—namely CD8+ T cells, CD4+ T cells, γδ T cells and MAIT cells—to MS pathogenicity, and what are their antigen specificities? Could some TARGET-signature T cells be specific for EBV antigens? Depletion of EBV-harbouring memory B cells by ocrelizumab may remove the antigenic ‘fuel’ for potentially pathogenic T cells, resulting in reduced recruitment to the CNS or diminished cross-reactive T-cell responses.6,9 How can these data be translated into predictive biomarkers and monitoring tools for anti-CD20-treated people with MS? For example, can the TARGET signature or components thereof stratify risk of relapse, track treatment response or guide therapy switching? Could the TARGET signature, or a reduced gene panel derived from it, be implemented in a blood-based assay to predict relapse risk or treatment response during anti-CD20 therapy? These questions define new research avenues that may refine our understanding of MS immunopathogenesis and optimize the use of B-cell–targeted therapies in clinical practice. Article.Title: Neuronavigated dual-target transcranial magnetic stimulation for schizophrenia negative symptoms
Article.Authors: Wei Y.; Wang J.; Tang X.; Qian Z.; Xu L.; Cui H.; Song Y.; Zhu H.; Ju M.; Long B.; Zhai W.; Zeng L.; Jiao X.; Lan X.; Wei X.; Tang Y.; Wang J.; Zhang T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Negative symptoms in schizophrenia severely impair function and quality of life, yet respond poorly to current therapies. This multicenter, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial aimed to investigate the efficacy of neuronavigated dual-target repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) over the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (rDLPFC) and cerebellum for improving negative symptoms in early-stage psychosis (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04853485). Participants with first-episode schizophrenia or clinical high-risk for psychosis were enrolled from Shanghai Mental Health Center and Suzhou Guangji Hospital. Participants were randomly assigned to either a real or sham group under MRI-guided neuronavigation, targeting rDLPFC with 1Hz at 100% motor threshold(MT), cerebellar with intermittent theta burst stimulation(iTBS) at 120% MT for 20 consecutive days. Clinical assessments were conducted at baseline(T0), 10-session(T1), 20-session(T2) and one month after the intervention(T3). Cognition and MRI were evaluated at T0 and T2. The primary outcome was change of negative subscale score of the Positive and Negative Symptoms Scale(PANSS), while secondary outcomes included alterations in other PANSS subscale scores and fronto-cerebellar circuit functional connectivity. In total, 75 participants were included in the intention-to-treat analysis (36 active, 39 sham). The pre-specified primary linear mixed-effects analysis revealed a non-significant group-by-time interaction for PANSS negative subscale scores (F(3,174.6)=1.45, p=0.230). At the 4-week endpoint (T2), the nominal unadjusted between-group p-value was 0.049; after Sidak correction for multiple comparisons, the adjusted mean difference was −2.48 points (95% CI −4.99 to 0.03, adjusted p=0.150, Cohen’s d=−0.51). Descriptive uncorrected t-tests indicated greater negative-symptom reductions in the active group at T1 and T2, and the 4-week negative-symptom response rate (≥50% reduction) was higher under real rTMS (χ2=9.5, p=0.002). A significant group-by-time interaction was observed for PANSS positive subscale scores (F(3,172.0)=3.26, p=0.023). Both groups exhibited substantial within-group symptom improvement. Resting-state fMRI demonstrated group-by-time interactions within cerebello-temporal, parahippocampal, caudate, and parietal networks (FWE-corrected p<0.05), and negative-symptom change correlated with cerebello-caudate connectivity (r=0.33, p=0.026). These findings suggest neuronavigated dual-target rTMS over rDLPFC and cerebellum may be associated with numerical improvements in negative symptoms in early-stage psychosis.

Article.Title: Extracellular vesicle α-synuclein topology reveals disease-associated conformers in brain and blood
Article.Authors: Dutta S.; Atashgaran A.; Sahoo A.; Chatzimichail S.; Kapanidis A.; Tofaris G.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Parkinson’s disease (PD), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), and multiple system atrophy (MSA) are unified by pathological α-synuclein (αSyn) aggregation, yet diverge in terms of the cellular distribution of pathology and clinical phenotype. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) have emerged as potential mediators or biomarkers of αSyn pathology, but whether their molecular constituents in the brain reflect disease-specific processes or conformations remains unknown. Here, we combined EV isolation, electrochemiluminescence, quantitative mass spectrometry and nanoscale single-vesicle imaging by direct stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (dSTORM) to map the topology, epitope exposure and cellular origin of αSyn in EVs isolated from post-mortem PD, DLB, MSA, and healthy control (HC) brains and assessed the tractability of these molecular signatures in blood. Proteomics and immunoblotting of EV lysates isolated from human brains confirmed that they were highly purified and derived from neurons and glial cell subtypes. Across diseases, αSyn association with EVs exhibited distinct patterns: In PD and DLB, both total αSyn levels normalised to CD81 and the percentage of neuronal (L1CAM+) EVs with aggregated αSyn as detected by aggregate-preferring antibodies, were increased, whereas in MSA, aggregated αSyn was detected primarily in neuronal and to a lesser extent glial EV subpopulations without an increase in total EV-associated αSyn. Further epitope mapping by dSTORM identified a distinct αSyn conformational arrangement, as detected by antibodies against an epitope spanning αSyn residues 34–45, that was enriched on the surface of L1CAM+ EVs in MSA compared to PD. This N-terminal immunoreactive conformer was tractable in serum and enriched on the surface of L1CAM+ EVs from MSA compared to PD patients or controls. Collectively, our findings suggest that the epitope accessibility and topology of EV-associated αSyn proteoforms, rather than their abundance alone, discriminate synucleinopathy subtypes, offering a framework for a blood-based conformational stratification of these disorders.

Article.Title: Biallelic variants in PIKFYVE cause a hypomyelinating leukodystrophy with endolysosomal dysfunction
Article.Authors: Averdunk L.; Groß M.; Hamacher A.; Donkervoort S.; Herebian D.; Mohammad S.; Knaus A.; Seibt A.; Schaper J.; Sticht H.; Bryen S.; Bergmann A.; Langener M.; De Simone L.; Markshausen A.; Lenk G.; Ghosh S.; Sandaradura S.; Guthoff T.; Leventer R.; Orbach R.; Rius R.; Morton N.; Gilmour K.; Mayatepek E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The PIKfyve-FIG4-VAC14 lipid kinase complex generates phosphoinositide PI(3,5)P2. Pathogenic variants in VAC14 and FIG4 cause neurodevelopmental disorders and PIKFYVE has been linked to autosomal dominant fleck corneal dystrophy. We searched for the underlyging, genetic cause of a neurodevelopmental disorder in five affected individuals from three families using exome- or genome sequencing. Cranial MRI images and clinical phenotypes were analyzed. Size, number and acidity of cellular vacuoles were investigated in patient-derived fibroblasts from family 1 using LysoSensor acidophilic probes. Levels of PI(3,5)P2 were quantified in patient-derived fibroblasts from family 1 using high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Pikfyve-mutant zebrafish larvae were injected with wildtype-mRNA or mutant mRNA harboring the PIKFYVE missense variant identified in family 3. Pikfyve-mutant zebrafish larvae were treated with metformin, bafilomycin A1, or rapamycin. We identified biallelic PIKFYVE variants in five affected individuals with hypomyelinating leukodystrophy, brain hyperintensities of inferior olives, thalami, long tracts, and optic nerves. Clinically, they presented with intellectual disability, spasticity, muscular weakness, and nystagmus. Additional features included feeding difficulties, auditory dysfunction, insulin resistance, microcephaly, peripheral neuropathy, and mild creatine kinase elevations. We detected four distinct PIKFYVE variants: three loss-of-function variants (family 1 & 2), and one p.Arg1156Pro missense variant (family 3). The pathogenicity of the p.Arg1156Pro variant was confirmed by phenotypic rescue of pikfyve-mutant zebrafish larvae injected with wildtype-mRNA but not with p.Arg1156Pro mRNA. Consistent with the role of PIKfyve in maintaining endolysosomal homeostasis, patient-derived fibroblasts of family 1 accumulated enlarged, hyperacidic vacuoles and showed a reduced PI(3,5)P2 production upon hyperosmotic stimulation. Exposing pikfyve-mutant zebrafisch larvae to the mTORC1 inhibitor and TRPML1 activator rapamycin attenuated cellular vacuolization, highlighting potential therapeutic approaches. Our findings establish PIKFYVE deficiency as a novel cause of hypomyelinating leukodystrophy and endolysosomal dysfunction.

Article.Title: Target engagement and efficacy in disease-modifying trials of synuclein-related disorders
Article.Authors: Artusi C.; Gallo S.; Galli S.; Rinaldi D.; Tinazzi M.; Rascol O.; Espay A.; Fabbri M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Disease-modifying trials in Parkinson’s disease (PD), multiple system atrophy (MSA), and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) increasingly incorporate fluid and imaging biomarkers to demonstrate target engagement, de-risk subsequent phases of drug development and provide mechanistic evidence of biological activity. Whether biomarker modulation predicts clinical benefit remains unclear. We conducted a PRISMA-compliant review of phase II and III disease-modifying trials (2020-2025) that included at least one biomarker intended to assess target engagement. Twenty-six trials met inclusion criteria (PD=19, MSA=4, DLB=3; n=2,195 participants). Target engagement was reported in 14 of 19 PD trials (12 phase II/2 phase III), 1 of 4 MSA trials, and 2 of 3 DLB trials (all phase II). Concordance between target engagement and clinical improvement was uncommon, as only 8/26 studies (7 phase II/1 phase III) demonstrated both target engagement and statistically significant clinical benefit, and just two of these (both phase II, one in PD and one in MSA) were rigorously controlled with low or moderate risk of bias. Nine trials showed target engagement without clinical benefit, whereas two reported clinical improvement without measurable target engagement. Baseline biomarker-guided patient selection was uncommon and rarely aligned with the compound’s mechanism of action. Patient-reported outcomes were widely used but rarely improved. Across recent disease-modifying trials in PD, DLB, and MSA, target engagement was frequently demonstrated, yet clinical benefit rarely followed. These findings question the predictive value of currently used target-engagement biomarkers and highlight the need to biologically align trial populations with the mechanisms targeted by experimental molecular interventions.

Article.Title: The genetic landscape of myotonic dystrophy type 1: insights from nearly one million genomes
Article.Authors: Rahman R.; Futema M.; Behr E.; Matthews E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Myotonic Dystrophy type 1 (DM1) is a multisystem disorder caused by CTG repeat expansions in the dystrophia myotonica protein kinase (DMPK) gene. Current prevalence estimates of 1 in 3,000-8,000 have traditionally relied on clinically ascertained and geographically restricted cohorts, underestimating population burden and failing to capture ancestry diversity. Using large-scale whole-genome sequencing (WGS) datasets, we aimed to identify DMPK repeat expansions across nearly one million participants, define their ancestry-specific distribution, and evaluate associated clinical phenotypes, with particular focus on cardiac manifestations and early-onset cataracts. We analysed WGS participants from three cohorts: Genomics England (n = 80,110), UK Biobank (n = 490,086), and the All of Us Research Program (n = 414,830). DMPK repeat lengths were estimated using ExpansionHunter. Alleles were classified as Normal (≤37 repeats), Intermediate (38-49 repeats), or Pathogenic (≥50 repeats). Genetic ancestry was assigned using cohort-specific methods. Linked health record data assessed cardiac phenotypes in UK Biobank and early-onset cataracts in Genomics England and UK Biobank. Across all cohorts (n = 985,026), pathogenic DMPK repeat expansions were identified in 645 individuals (0.07%; ∼1 in 1,527), a prevalence two-to-five times higher than previous estimates. Most expansions occurred in those of European ancestry, although expansions were detected across all groups, including up to 1 in 6,693 African and Asian ancestry. In UK Biobank, individuals with a pathogenic expansion had increased odds of any cardiac diagnosis (odds ratio [OR]: 2.06, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.58–2.67; p = 5.8×108) and greater cardiac diagnostic burden (risk ratio 2.46, CI: 1.92–3.15; p = 1.6×10−13). Conduction abnormalities—particularly atrioventricular and left bundle-branch block, atrial fibrillation, and flutter—showed the strongest association with expansion status (OR: 4.86, CI: 3.38–6.79; p = 2.7×10−18). No sex differences were observed among those with a DMPK expansion, although male sex was independently associated with conduction disease in the overall population. Approximately one-in-ten individuals with pathogenic expansions had a cataract diagnosis before age 55. Most individuals with an expansion had no prior DM1 diagnosis, highlighting the value of systematic genetic testing in these phenotypes to improve diagnosis, shorten the diagnostic interval, and mitigate harm. By integrating WGS data from nearly one million individuals, this study refines understanding of the population distribution and clinical consequences of DMPK repeat expansions, revealing a reservoir of undiagnosed and potentially untreated multisystemic disease. These findings support routine inclusion of DMPK analysis within specified cardiac and ophthalmic diagnostic pathways to enable earlier detection.

Article.Title: Bayesian knockoff filter for controlling false discovery rate
Article.Authors: Gu J.; Yin G.; Liu J.
Article.Abstract: In many scientific fields, researchers are interested in discovering features with substantial effects on the response from a large number of candidate features while controlling the proportion of false discoveries. By incorporating the knockoff procedure in a Bayesian framework, we develop the Bayesian knockoff filter (BKF) for selecting important features. The BKF is built upon a tight upper bound for the posterior probability of the null hypothesis, which is derived under the Bayesian “flip-sign” property implied by our procedure. In contrast to the standard knockoff methods in the frequentist paradigm, we allow the knockoff variables to be generated in every iteration of the Markov chain Monte Carlo procedure, which removes the unwanted variability of the single-knockoff generation (knockoff is typically generated only once before the model fitting). Compared with multi-knockoffs, the BKF is more principled and natural in incorporating side information through prior distributions under a fully Bayesian framework. We further develop an e-value BKF approach to theoretically guarantee the frequentist false discovery rate (FDR) control. Numerical experiments on both synthetic and real data demonstrate the advantages of the BKF over existing knockoff methods and Bayesian variable selection approaches, i.e., the BKF possesses comparable power, yields a lower FDR and more stable selection sets.

Article.Title: Predicting key viral mutations from within-host deep sequencing data
Article.Authors: Su S.; Tang Y.; Li Q.; Cao L.; Zhang Y.; Lou J.; Zheng H.; Liu C.; Sun Y.; Li J.; Zhang Z.; Zee B.; Cheung P.; Chen Z.; Chan R.; Wu W.; Yu J.; Yen H.; Gu H.; Man Poon L.; Hui D.; Hiscox J.; Mok C.; Wang M.
Article.Abstract: Rapid SARS-CoV-2 evolution drives continuous epidemic waves, harming vaccine protection and exerting heavy burden to population health. Predicting virus evolution holds the key for current and future medical countermeasures against infectious diseases by allowing well-matching vaccines and timely epidemic response. However, due to its high genetic diversity, fast transmissibility and evolutionary rate, accurate and timely prediction of SARS-CoV-2 evolution remains a challenge. To address this, we developed a computational framework, Beth-2, to predict key mutations of SARS-CoV-2 through analyzing within-host viral genome deep sequencing data. We leveraged the early fitness signals of variants exhibited within-host and their fitness pattern between-host to infer the emerging mutations with fitness potential. In retrospective data validation, 98.6% of the key SARS-CoV-2 mutations on receptor binding domain could be detected by our model with a median lead time of 9 mo before they reached predominance at population level. Among the 26 prospectively predicted mutations, 69% of them exhibited significantly enhanced transmissibility and five showed significant immune escape from plasma of subjects who received COVID-19 mRNA vaccine collected 6 mo after the prediction time. The mutations predicted by Beth-2 that are functionally enhanced include F456L, the defining mutation of multiple current circulating lineages, including KP.3, NB.1.8.1, and XFG. The model captures mutations of high fitness potential under the natural immune environment of host and is applicable to other pathogens. The framework can be implemented along with the existing genome surveillance network and offers an efficient and effective instrument for vaccine preparation and epidemic response.

Article.Title: Methionine restriction inhibits EZH2-mediated GSDMD methylation to promote pyroptosis in prostate cancer
Article.Authors: Liu S.; Ming D.; Xu Y.; Li B.; Shi M.; Xi S.; Cui J.; Yang J.; Xiong X.; He S.; Wang S.; Wang D.; Zhang J.; Weng H.; Zeng X.; Yuan S.
Article.Abstract: EZH2 is frequently overexpressed in solid tumors, yet the clinical efficacy of its inhibitors remains limited, highlighting an urgent need to elucidate their cytotoxic mechanisms. Here, we identify EZH2 as a posttranslational suppressor of pyroptosis through direct methylation of GSDMD. We revealed that EZH2 inhibition triggered GSDMD-dependent pyroptosis in prostate cancer cells. Clinical specimens showed an inverse correlation between EZH2 levels and cleaved GSDMD (GSDMD N-terminal, GSDMD-N) levels, reinforcing its role as a negative regulator of GSDMD activation. Mechanistically, EZH2 methylated GSDMD at lysine 168, thereby blocking caspase-1-mediated cleavage and suppressing its activation. Notably, methionine deprivation overcame this blockade and combined with the EZH2 inhibitor GSK126 to enhance pyroptosis and suppress tumor growth in vivo. These findings establish the methionine–EZH2–GSDMD axis as an epigenetic-metabolic hub controlling pyroptosis via posttranslational regulation, providing a mechanistic rationale for co-targeting methionine metabolism and EZH2 in prostate cancer therapy.

Article.Title: Diffusion in a d -dimensional rough potential
Article.Authors: Jeffries J.; Mendoza Reyes E.; Abdeljawad F.; Daw M.; Martinez E.
Article.Abstract: The prediction of diffusion in solids is necessary to understand the microstructure evolution in materials out of equilibrium. Although one can reasonably predict diffusive transport coefficients using atomistic methods, these approaches can be very computationally expensive. In this work, we develop an analytical model for the diffusivity in a noisy solid solution in an arbitrary number of dimensions ( d ) using a mean first passage time analysis. We observe that roughness always decreases the diffusivity, aligning with sluggish diffusion theories in concentrated alloys, finding that an increase in diffusivity induced by alloying elements must be due to a decrease in the average activation energy, not to the noise. These analytical results are then compared with kinetic Monte Carlo simulations, which are in good quantitative agreement with the simulation data for d ≤ 5, and excellent quantitative agreement for d ≤ 3. This generalization to arbitrary dimensions has been elusive to the community since Zwanzig [R. Zwanzig, Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 85 , 2029–2030 (1988)] published his seminal work on one-dimensional systems.

Article.Title: Gastruloids reveal alternative morphogenetic routes for body-axis elongation with distinct cytoskeletal dependencies
Article.Authors: Serrano Nájera G.; Delahaye A.; Steventon B.
Article.Abstract: Morphogenesis requires cells to integrate genetic and environmental information to pattern and shape tissues. Recent studies in vivo and in vitro have shown how alterations in environmental cues can induce alternative morphogenetic programs. However, what determines which morphogenetic strategy cells deploy in different environments remains unknown. Using gastruloids, a model for mammalian posterior body-axis elongation where environmental cues can be controlled in vitro, we show that substrate availability determines which force-generation strategy cells employ to build the body axis. In free-floating conditions, gastruloids self-assemble a single posterior body axis, presumably through cell–cell interactions. When plated on laminin, gastruloids acquire a flat morphology, break symmetry multiple times, and produce several independently elongating cell streams with anterior–posterior polarity through collective cell migration. On laminin, formin activity and focal adhesion-mediated traction are required for tissue elongation, yet both are functionally dispensable in free-floating conditions. Transcriptomic analysis shows that formin inhibition blocks elongation on laminin without any detectable transcriptional changes, indicating that these cytoskeletal components play primarily a mechanical role that is only required when cells engage a substrate. Furthermore, laminin biases cells toward posterior migratory fates while preserving similar Hox expression. Together, these results show that mammalian body-axis elongation can proceed through different morphogenetic modes that engage distinct mechanical effectors depending on substrate availability. These findings have implications for understanding how evolution explores morphological diversity and how tissue engineering might achieve desired forms through precise environmental control.

Article.Title: Evolutionary dynamics of collective behavior across the tree of ray-finned fishes
Article.Authors: Love J.; Nayak A.; Grassick A.; Kong L.; Henry E.; Gil M.; Fahimipour A.; Pennell M.; Hein A.
Article.Abstract: Trait evolution and lineage diversification are thought to be driven by selection on the phenotypes of individuals. However, many important phenotypes are only manifested when individuals interact. Collective behavior is one such phenotype. During collective behavior, interactions among individuals lead to emergent group-level phenotypes that can govern individual fitness. Yet, whether collective behaviors exhibit similar patterns of trait evolution to individual traits and whether these group phenotypes have influenced macroevolutionary diversification is unknown. In ray-finned fishes, the most species-rich of all vertebrate classes, many species exhibit striking displays of collective behavior in the form of collective movement. Here, we use state-of-the-art machine learning methods for text and image analysis to quantify collective movement phenotypes for 2,839 Actinopterygian fishes, comprising nearly 10% of all extant species. We find that collective movement is highly evolutionarily stable in some clades and extremely labile in others, exhibiting over 300 evolutionary transitions. Consistent with theoretical predictions, collective movement is associated with more patchy diets and higher predation pressure. Finally, we find that the evolution of collective movement coincides with an increase in net macroevolutionary diversification rate. Our analyses reveal that collective behavior is deeply intertwined with ecological and evolutionary dynamics across a vast phylogenetic scale, unlocking questions about the evolution of collective phenotypes and their role in shaping the diversity of life on Earth.

Article.Title: Coupling of structural preordering and density fluctuation: A unified picture of nucleation in metallic glasses
Article.Authors: Xu T.; Wang X.; Cao Q.; Ding S.; Liu S.; Yang K.; Zhang D.; Yang Y.; Jiang J.
Article.Abstract: Crystallization is ubiquitous in nature and technology, occurring in pharmaceuticals, biomacromolecules, polymers, metallurgy and glass formation. Yet how crystallization proceeds, particularly at its earliest stage, remains elusive. Studies on glass-forming liquids increasingly suggest that crystallization initiates in structurally preordered regions, with density fluctuations playing a secondary role, a view widely generalized from hard-sphere colloids. Here we show, across disordered metallic systems from pure elements and intermetallic compounds to glass-forming alloys, that density fluctuations and structural preordering emerge simultaneously during nucleation. This coupling reflects local atomic rearrangements in which free-volume reduction, denser packing, and bond-orientational order develop together. Our findings provide a physical basis for a unified nucleation framework for disordered materials.

Article.Title: Respiratory phase orchestrates human olfactory cortical dynamics
Article.Authors: Hathaway A.; Coleman T.
Article.Abstract: Olfaction is fundamental to perception, memory, and emotion, yet the neural basis of human odor processing remains poorly understood. We demonstrate that odor-evoked brain activity is organized by respiratory phase—not absolute time—revealing that natural breathing structures olfactory cortical dynamics. Using simultaneous nasal respiration and electroencephalography recordings in 17 participants, we delivered naturalistic odors (peppermint, oregano, and grapefruit) synchronized to individual breathing cycles. Odor presentation elicited respiratory phase-locked event-related spectral perturbations (RPL-ERSPs) in frontal and temporal regions, emerging during the first breath after stimulus onset. The most discriminative neural signatures were theta-band activity during inhalation and alpha-band activity during exhalation, patterns that were obscured in traditional time-locked analyses due to natural variability in breath duration. Leave-one-subject-out cross-validation of RPL-ERSPs achieved reliable odor detection (peppermint: AUC = 0.79; oregano: AUC = 0.67; grapefruit: AUC = 0.62), establishing that phase-locked features generalize across individuals. To connect neural responses to perceptual experience without relying on odor naming-which can be disproportionately impaired in some populations-we quantified odor recognition using free-response descriptions scored with a semantic-similarity approach. Behavioral recognition strength paralleled the neural decoding hierarchy across odors, establishing the perceptual validity of RPL-ERSPs. RPL-ERSPs revealed rapid habituation, with decoding performance declining over repeated presentations, due to selective degradation of the most informative phase-locked features. These findings establish respiratory rhythm as a temporal scaffold for human olfactory cortical processing, positioning RPL-ERSPs as a sensitive, task-free approach for assessing olfactory function. We provide an open-source, respiration-synchronized olfactometer design to enable replication and adoption.

Article.Title: Simply aging
Article.Authors: Gladyshev V.
Article.Abstract: Biological aging is complex and resists any single mechanistic narrative. This article develops a conceptual framework for aging biology through a series of brief statements on central topics in the field, with the goal of discussing aging simply, directly and accessibly. The organizing principle is that aging is a default outcome of living: because biological processes are inherently imperfect, deleterious changes (the deleteriome) accumulate over time and progressively erode functional reserve. The deleteriome provides a unifying framework for molecular damage, regulatory drift, maladaptive remodeling, and system-level failure, without reducing aging to individual genes, pathways, compartments, hallmarks, or pathologies. Evolution does not program aging; it shapes maintenance and renewal systems that oppose this trajectory with limited fidelity and unavoidable trade-offs. Aging begins during development, following an early embryonic phase of rejuvenation. Modern biomarkers make biological age imperfectly but increasingly measurable. Biological age is heterogeneous across cells, organs, and systems, modifiable by interventions and environment, and in some contexts partially reversible or resettable, although aging itself is irreversible. This model links first principles of aging to measurement, intervention, and longer-term strategies, with the goal of clarifying how substantial longevity gains might be achieved, both within and beyond existing species-level constraints.

Article.Title: Mussels possess distinct vanadium and iron storage systems for fabricating metal-reinforced adhesive fibers
Article.Authors: Jee S.; Singh N.; Merino G.; Babych M.; Tappero R.; Harrington M.
Article.Abstract: Mussels fashion a protein-based fibrous adhesive holdfast known as a byssus to tether themselves in marine habitats against crashing waves. The capacity of mussels to anchor securely is dependent on load-bearing protein-metal cross-links mediated by 3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine (DOPA) residues coordinated to metal ions, which significantly enhance byssus mechanical properties (e.g., adhesive strength, abrasion resistance, toughness, self-healing capacity). However, the natural metal incorporation process during byssus formation remains poorly understood—a knowledge gap that limits the decades-old field of mussel-inspired materials from fulfilling its potential. Here, we investigate the natural byssus biofabrication system, the mussel foot, focusing specifically on iron and vanadium storage using a multilength scale ensemble of spectroscopic methods. Confocal Raman spectroscopy, synchrotron µ-X-ray fluorescence and µ-X-ray absorption spectroscopy, and scanning transmission electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy studies indicate that these two metals occupy separate coordination environments: vanadium storage is DOPA-based, while iron is stored in ferritin-like structures. Lacking precedence, these findings indicate that mussels evolved a catechol-based metal storage system to specifically acquire and store what is typically considered a trace metal ion in biology, which they employ subsequently to mechanically reinforce protein-based glues and coatings produced by the mussel. Beyond the biological implications, these findings have potential to transform the field of mussel-inspired materials.

Article.Title: Intuitive knowledge of object acoustics enables perceptual separation of physical variables from impact sounds
Article.Authors: Agarwal V.; Traer J.; Schwartz J.; McDermott J.
Article.Abstract: Upon hearing objects collide, humans can estimate physical attributes such as material and mass. Although the physics of sound generation is well established, the inverse problem that listeners solve—of inferring physical parameters from sound—remains poorly understood. Classical accounts posit the use of acoustic cues that correlate with physical variables but do not explain how humans might distinguish multiple concurrent physical causes. To study this problem, we measured impulse responses from hundreds of everyday objects, extracted their resonances, and used statistics of the resonances to build a probabilistic generative model of impact sounds. We then used the model to synthesize and manipulate stimuli for experiments measuring judgments of physical variables. Humans accurately judged object properties from collision sounds. However, when both of the colliding objects varied, performance was impaired if the distribution of object resonances deviated from those measured in real-world objects. The results suggest that humans have internalized the statistical regularities of real-world object acoustics, and use this knowledge to separate the acoustic contributions of the distinct objects in the world that give rise to sounds.

Article.Title: Majorana edge reconstruction and the ν = 5/2 non-Abelian thermal Hall puzzle
Article.Authors: Lotrič T.; Wang T.; Zaletel M.; Simon S.; Parameswaran S.
Article.Abstract: Pioneering thermal transport measurements on two-dimensional electron gases in high magnetic fields have demonstrated that the quantized Hall state at filling factor ν = 5/2 has a thermal Hall conductance κ quantized in half-integer multiples of κ 0 = π 2 k B 2 T / 3 h . Half-integer κ / κ 0 is a signature of neutral Majorana edge modes, in turn linked to the presence of non-Abelian anyon excitations in the bulk. However, the experimentally observed value of κ corresponds to the “PH-Pfaffian” state, in tension with numerical studies which instead favor either the Pfaffian or the AntiPfaffian. A variety of mechanisms have been invoked to explain this discrepancy, but have been either ruled out by further experiments or else involve fine-tuning. Building on density-matrix-renormalization group studies of physically realistic edges and analytic calculations of edge structure, we propose an alternative resolution of this puzzle involving an “edge reconstruction” solely involving the neutral Majorana sector of the theory. Such a Majorana edge reconstruction can “screen” a Pfaffian or AntiPfaffian bulk, so that transport signatures become indistinguishable from those of the PH-Pfaffian. We argue that this physically natural scenario is consistent with experiment.

Article.Authors: Chaudhary V.; Du Y.; Mishra B.; Ah Kioon M.; Ahuja P.; Ivashkiv L.; Truchetet M.; Spiera R.; Lakin K.; Gordon J.; Barrat F.
Article.Abstract: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a severe autoimmune connective tissue disease characterized by immune dysregulation and progressive fibrosis of the skin and internal organs, resulting in substantial organ dysfunction and increased mortality. Fibrosis is driven in part by infiltration of immune cells, including monocytes that become activated within fibrotic tissue. However, how the mechanical properties of fibrotic skin regulate their function remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that increased stiffness activates human monocytes through mechanosensing. Further, monocytes from patients with SSc displayed altered transcriptional trajectories and an exaggerated inflammatory response to high stiffness, accompanied by reduced expression of wound healing and antifibrotic programs. Article.Title: Polarized twin walls in a halide perovskite
Article.Authors: Li W.; Yuan Q.; Johnston M.; Etheridge J.
Article.Abstract: Halide perovskites have emerged as promising materials for next-generation photovoltaics, laser sources, and X-ray detectors. There is intense debate as to whether some photoactive halide perovskites exhibit ferroelectric behavior and whether it might be possible to utilize the bulk photovoltaic effect to enhance the performance of halide perovskite solar cells. Remarkably, despite CsPbI 3 being centrosymmetric and nonpolar, we observe directly that Pb atoms shift at {110} twin walls driving a local ferroelectric-like polarization. These polar twin walls form an intrinsic array of nanoscale interfaces, spaced ~30 to 50 nm apart, embedded within the nonpolar perovskite lattice. In contrast, {112} twin walls do not show a polar displacement of Pb but strongly suppress octahedral tilt and off-center Cs atom displacements, revealing a different untapped structural degree of freedom. These findings reveal previously hidden nanoscale polarization in halide perovskite semiconductors, opening opportunities for enhanced conductivity and photovoltaic behavior through domain wall engineering.

Article.Title: Intermittent gas–liquid rearrangement controls the mixing of gases in porous media
Article.Authors: Jackson S.; Ellman S.; Kalyoncu G.; Borgne T.; Bultreys T.
Article.Abstract: Gas mixing in porous media governs important environmental and industrial applications in which multiple gas components share the available pore space with liquid water, simultaneously undergoing gas mixing and gas–liquid redistribution. Currently, this process is represented by macroscopic models that ignore pore scale dynamics. We demonstrate that this is not generally valid, and can lead to large errors in the mixing rate. We use 4D X-ray imaging to investigate nitrogen injection into a porous sandstone saturated with krypton and water, jointly imaging the gas mixture composition evolution and multiphase flow of gas and water. In contrast to the smooth, continuous representation of the conventional advection–diffusion model, our results show that gas mixing evolves through a sequence of distinct regimes controlled by gas connectivity. Initially, immiscible gas–water displacement generates gas composition variance as the different gases occupy neighboring pores separated by water. As gas connectivity increases, intermittent gas–liquid interfacial rearrangements rapidly connect regions of contrasting gas composition, driving a fast decay in composition variance. Once connectivity stabilizes, mixing is controlled by a confined diffusion process within the quasi-static gas network. At later times, further mixing is driven slowly by multicomponent Ostwald ripening, whereby trapped gas ganglia exchange solutes through the surrounding liquid phase. These findings provide insights into gas mixing in porous media, suggesting concepts for upscaling the role of pore scale multiphase flow in gas mixing in the subsurface.

Article.Title: Trust as a hidden driver of epidemic-relevant behavior: Institution- and behavior-specific associations across 20 national survey waves
Article.Authors: Zapf A.; Dewey G.; Ognyanova K.; Baum M.; Hanage W.; Lipsitch M.; Uslu A.; Druckman J.; Perlis R.; Lazer D.; Santillana M.
Article.Abstract: Compartmental models of infectious disease transmission make assumptions about human behaviors. Specifically, they parameterize interactions across population groups, assumed to have distinct epidemiologically relevant behavioral patterns, primarily through contact matrices stratified by demographic variables such as age, gender, or socioeconomic status. Although such demographic characteristics are readily measurable, they may inadequately capture the social and psychological forces that govern protective behaviors. Drawing on 20 waves of a national survey conducted throughout the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States, we show that institutional trust—particularly trust in public health agencies, physicians, and hospitals—is a dominant predictor of protective behavior adoption. For mask wearing during periods of strongest pandemic activity, institutional trust explains more behavioral difference across population groups than age, income, education, and partisan affiliation combined. In unadjusted analyses, the difference in protective behavior adoption between individuals with the highest and lowest trust in the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) was four- to six-fold larger than the corresponding differences by age, income, or education, and exceeded the difference between Democratic and Republican respondents. This association was institutionally specific (the relationship attenuates for trust in banks), and behaviorally specific (trust in the CDC is associated with protective behaviors but not visiting a doctor). The latter suggests that trust modifies voluntary compliance with public health recommendations rather than healthcare access or use. These findings identify institutional trust as a candidate stratifying variable for models of behavior-coupled transmission dynamics, and as a measurable target for public health surveillance.

Article.Title: Normalized Raman imaging for studies of tissue physiology of the kidney
Article.Authors: Trim W.; Oh S.; Diakova M.; Petrova K.; Ichimura T.; Takakura A.; Karmakar R.; Nørrelykke S.; Peshkin L.; Bonventre J.; Kirschner M.

Article.Title: USP46 restrains K63-linked polyubiquitination–dependent aggregation and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in lupus nephritis
Article.Authors: Sun Y.; Liu L.; Jiang M.; Wan L.; Ke Y.; Liang J.; Xu D.; Yang K.; Lin J.; Cao H.
Article.Abstract: The activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome necessitates its aggregation within the dispersed trans-Golgi network (dTGN) and subsequent transport from the dTGN to the microtubule organizing center (MTOC), a process facilitated by HDAC6. However, the regulatory mechanisms governing the formation of NLRP3 aggregates remain insufficiently understood. In this study, we demonstrate that proteasome impairment induces polyubiquitination and aggregation of NLRP3 at the MTOC. We demonstrate ubiquitin-specific protease 46 (USP46) as a key factor that recognizes NLRP3 as a substrate and restricts nondegradative K63-linked polyubiquitination at lysine residue K930, thereby preventing excessive aggregation, transport to the MTOC, and inflammasome activation. Furthermore, myeloid-specific knockout of USP46 exacerbates renal injury and inflammation in both lipopolysaccharide-induced-induced endotoxic shock and pristane-induced lupus nephritis models. Our findings provide insights into the regulatory mechanisms underlying the aggresomal activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome.

Article.Title: An aggregation-prone region in talin controls talin self-interactions and regulates integrin adhesion complex dynamics
Article.Authors: Ball N.; Turkki P.; Guo Y.; Tanvir M.; Le S.; Chin J.; Baker K.; Luo J.; Atherton P.; Brown N.; Hytönen V.; Yan J.; Goult B.
Article.Abstract: Talin is a mechanosensitive scaffold that couples integrins to the actin cytoskeleton and coordinates signaling at integrin adhesion complexes. A second integrin-binding site (IBS2) has been proposed within the R11–R12 region of the talin rod, although the molecular basis of this interaction has remained unclear. Here, we show that talin R11 contains a cryptic aggregation-prone region (APR) embedded within Helix50. Mechanical unfolding of R11 exposes this motif, enabling high-affinity talin–talin interactions and force-dependent self-association. The isolated APR forms amyloid-like fibers in vitro, and APR-disrupting gatekeeper mutations suppress fiber formation, talin self-association, and cellular recruitment. We therefore designate this motif Aggregation-Prone Region 1 (APR1). Mitochondrial-targeting experiments demonstrate that APR1-dependent recruitment occurs in cells independently of focal adhesions and integrins. APR1 overlaps the vinculin-binding site in Helix50, and vinculin disrupts preexisting talin assemblies, revealing a mechano-chaperone function for vinculin. Disruption of APR1-mediated self-association does not impair adhesion formation but instead generates larger, more talin-rich adhesions with altered assembly dynamics and signaling properties, indicating a role for APR1 in regulating adhesion remodeling. Together, these findings identify force-dependent talin self-association as a mechanism in mechanotransduction and suggest that the region previously designated IBS2 functions primarily as an aggregation-prone regulatory element.

Article.Title: Maize genetic diversity is largely unstructured by human ethnolinguistic diversity in its center of origin
Article.Authors: Snodgrass S.; Li F.; Mambakkam S.; Medina-Muñoz S.; Sparreo L.; Menon M.; Perez C.; Kalsi N.; Ghosh A.; Schuster S.; Kim H.; Moreno-Estrada A.; Runcie D.; Coop G.; Ross-Ibarra J.
Article.Abstract: Population structure and environmental features often capture major axes of genetic variation in many species. Yet the impacts of human activity often remain unquantified. For domesticated species that rely on human activity for survival and dispersal, human movements and cultural differences may play key roles patterning genetic diversity. Maize is a staple crop of enormous cultural importance to indigenous peoples of the Americas, but cannot survive or disperse without farmers. Using publicly available genotyping and passport data from approximately 2,000 traditional maize varieties, more than 500 whole genome sequences of humans from Mexico, and indigenous linguistic maps, we quantify anthropogenic effects on maize genetic diversity in the Americas. Maize shows very little overall structure, highlighting the effectiveness of indigenous farmers in moving and mixing maize populations. While principal components of maize diversity show meaningful correlations to human genetic diversity, our linear modeling suggests little additional impact of human population structure beyond shared geography. Though differences in maize diversity are often patterned by language locally, we find only weak genome-wide effects at larger spatial scales. Despite the relatively weak global signal of anthropogenic effects, linguistic Genome-wide association, outlier F ST analyses, and selection scans identified loci associated with specific languages. Leveraging landscape-level sequencing data, we highlight how anthropogenic factors have shaped patterns of maize genetic diversity across Mesoamerica.

Article.Title: Dynamic virulence decomposition disentangles host and pathogen contributions over the course of infection
Article.Authors: Franz M.; Bonneaud C.
Article.Abstract: Decomposing virulence into host and pathogen effects is key to understanding how virulence is generated during infection, and how host and pathogen contributions evolve over time. Conventional virulence decomposition is, however, not designed to quantify how these contributions vary throughout an infection. Building on conventional virulence decomposition, we developed a dynamic framework that integrates disease space analysis to quantify these changing contributions. We applied this framework to existing data from house finches ( Haemorhous mexicanus ) experimentally infected with the emerging bacterial pathogen, Mycoplasma gallisepticum , examining two biologically meaningful infection phases: an early phase dominated by innate immune responses and a later phase in which the adaptive immune response is fully activated. Our analyses revealed that virulence components evolved differently across infection phases, with pathogen exploitation, per-parasite-pathogenicity (PPP), and host resistance each exhibiting distinct trajectories. These findings corroborated several known evolutionary patterns, while also revealing the evolution of increased PPP in this system. In contrast, the apparent evolution of host tolerance inferred from aggregated peak measurements was not supported by phase-specific analyses, demonstrating that aggregated and phase-specific measures can provide different mechanistic insights into virulence. By linking conventional virulence decomposition with disease space analysis, our dynamic virulence decomposition framework provides a general approach for quantifying how host and pathogen processes shape virulence over the course of infection.

Article.Title: A DPY19L2/FAM209-associated protein–Arp complex–CAPZA3 scaffold is essential for perinuclear theca assembly and fertilization
Article.Authors: Ruan T.; Shen G.; Zhuo L.; Zhang Y.; Wang X.; Tian E.; Tian Y.; Tang X.; Chen D.; Jiang C.; Yang X.; Ma J.; Zhao S.; Zhao C.; Cui X.; Jiang X.; Yang Y.; Wang Y.; Shen Y.
Article.Abstract: Fertilization is a fundamental biological process that enables the fusion of a spermatozoon with an oocyte to initiate embryonic development. However, the underlying mechanisms leading to fertilization failure remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrated that the actin-related protein (Arp) family members ACTRT2 and ACTRT3 are essential for fertilization in both humans and mice, whereas ACTL10 is dispensable for fertility and the human-specific ACTL8 may play a role in early spermatogenesis. Ultrastructural and immunofluorescence analyses revealed that, during spermatogenesis, ACTRT2 or ACTRT3 deficiency disrupts the assembly of subacrosomal layer of the perinuclear theca (SAL-PT), leading to acrosome detachment and subsequent manchette abnormalities, which in turn impairs the formation of the postacrosomal sheath of the PT. These structural defects were accompanied by reduced abundance of the candidate sperm-borne oocyte-activating factors PAWP and PLCζ. Moreover, knockout of Actrt2 or Actrt3 severely impaired spermatozoa’s ability to penetrate the zona pellucida during in vitro fertilization. Mechanistically, ACTRT2, ACTRT3, ACTL7A, ACTL7B, and ACTL9 form a testis-enriched Arp complex in the SAL-PT and maintain the stability of one another. This complex interacts with the PT protein CAPZA3, which subsequently binds and stabilizes PLCζ. Additionally, the Arp complex interacts with DPY19L2/FAM209-associated proteins to mediate acrosome anchoring to the nuclear envelope. Therefore, these findings established a sequential DPY19L2/FAM209-associated protein–Arp complex–CAPZA3 scaffold extending from the nuclear envelope to the acrosome that is indispensable for fertilization. Collectively, we defined a previously unidentified structural and molecular framework for fertilization and provided insights into the diagnosis and treatment of fertilization failure.

Article.Title: Comprehensive classification of HCN1 variants linked to neurodevelopmental disorders with and without epilepsy
Article.Authors: Castelli R.; Marini C.; Porro A.; Castellini A.; Fontana G.; Saponaro A.; Cavalleri G.; Rizzi S.; Fusco C.; Parida A.; Caswell R.; Sherlaw-Sturrock C.; Pruna D.; Reid C.; Bleakley L.; Howell K.; E. Scheffer I.; Cuddapah V.; Zeidler S.; Pavlidis E.; Pal D.; Szczałuba K.; Mirzaa G.; Couque N.; Capri Y.
Article.Abstract: Hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated 1 (HCN1) channels mediate the cationic I h current, a fundamental regulator of neuronal excitability and synaptic integration, and are predominantly expressed in the cortex and hippocampus. Although HCN1 variants have been increasingly identified in patients with epilepsy, from milder forms to developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEE), genotype–phenotype correlations remain poorly defined. Here, we used patch-clamp electrophysiology and confocal imaging in HEK293 cells to functionally characterize 43 HCN1 variants identified in patients with neurodevelopmental disorders, with or without epilepsy. Based on biophysical properties, we established a classification system comprising four distinct functional classes: I) low or no current; II) hyperpolarizing shift in voltage dependence; III) depolarizing shift in voltage dependence; and IV) generation of an instantaneous current. The molecular basis for this classification was further interpreted using available cryo-EM structures of HCN1. Integration with clinical data from 50 patients revealed a striking correlation between functional class and clinical presentation. Loss-of-function variants prevailed among individuals with milder phenotypes or without epilepsy, with the latter distinctively clustering within the channel selectivity filter. In contrast, gain-of-function and mixed variants were predominantly associated with DEE. Finally, we demonstrate that allosteric modulators, including peptides NB6 and TRIP8b nano and the small molecule J&J12e, effectively normalize channel function across three of the four classes in vitro. These findings establish a biophysical framework for interpreting HCN1 variants, demonstrating that the direction of channel dysfunction is a major determinant of epilepsy risk and severity, and providing a conceptual foundation for future class-based precision medicine approaches.

Article.Title: Intrinsically motivated humans and agents in open-world exploration
Article.Authors: Lidayan A.; Du Y.; Kosoy E.; Rufova M.; Abbeel P.; Gopnik A.
Article.Abstract: What drives exploration? Understanding the intrinsic motivation to explore is a long-standing challenge in both cognitive science and AI. In this study, we directly compare adults, children aged 8 to 12 y, and AI agents exploring a complex, open-ended environment called Crafter ( 1 ). We study how three common information-theoretic intrinsic objectives—entropy, information gain, and empowerment—relate to their behavior. We find that all three are positively correlated with human exploration progress for both children and adults, although entropy and empowerment are more strongly related to exploration progress in children than information gain. Furthermore, across agents and humans we observe that entropy initially increases rapidly, then plateaus, while empowerment increases continuously, suggesting that in early exploration they look for novel states, while in advanced exploration they look for states they can control. Finally, we find preliminary evidence that private speech about goals may aid exploration in children. Our data are available at https://github.com/alyd/humans_in_crafter_data .

Article.Title: Lead impairs long-term memory by disrupting mitochondrial redox homeostasis in Drosophila
Article.Authors: Hsu C.; Lu T.; Yang Y.; Chen C.; Chiu Y.; Yang J.; Wu Z.; Cheng W.; Wu J.; Shiu C.; Chuang S.; Feng K.; Lin H.; Yang J.; Chiang A.
Article.Abstract: Lead (Pb) exposure remains a major environmental risk factor for cognitive dysfunction, yet the cellular mechanisms underlying Pb-induced memory impairment are poorly understood. Here, we show that both developmental and adult-onset Pb exposure selectively disrupts protein-synthesis-dependent long-term memory (LTM) in Drosophila melanogaster while sparing other memory forms. Using a mitochondria-targeted redox biosensor (mito-roGFP2-Orp1), we found that Pb elevates mitochondrial oxidative stress and disrupts redox homeostasis in cholinergic neurons and in dorsal-anterior-lateral (DAL) neurons, a critical locus for LTM consolidation. Pb-induced redox imbalance suppresses training-induced de novo protein synthesis in DAL neurons, thereby impairing memory consolidation. Antioxidant treatment with epigallocatechin gallate restores mitochondrial redox balance and rescues LTM by reinstating activity-dependent protein synthesis in DAL neurons. These findings identify mitochondrial redox dysregulation as a key mechanism linking environmental Pb exposure to impaired memory consolidation. Our results further establish a genetically tractable platform for dissecting neurotoxic mechanisms and for evaluating antioxidant-based strategies to mitigate Pb-induced cognitive dysfunction.

Article.Title: A tetravalent bispecific protein enables targeted degradation of VCAM-1 and VEGFR for treatment of choroidal neovascularization
Article.Authors: Zhang J.; Du M.; Ge L.; Cao Y.; Jiang J.; Yin X.; Chen G.; Wang Q.
Article.Abstract: Wet age-related macular degeneration (AMD), a leading cause of irreversible vision loss, is driven by pathological choroidal neovascularization (CNV). Although anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapies remain the clinical standard, their utility is constrained by incomplete responses in nearly 50% of patients and off-target risks—such as geographic atrophy—stemming from non-specific VEGF blockade. Here, we identify a robust correlation between vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM-1) and VEGF/VEGF receptor (VEGFR) expression in aqueous humor from AMD patients and in murine CNV models. Thus, we engineered a tetravalent bispecific protein, RHV, by functionalizing an L-rhamnulose-1-phosphate aldolase scaffold with peptides that selectively bind VCAM-1 and the VEGFR on neovessels. The tetravalent design confers high apparent affinity, enhancing pathological endothelial targeting while sparing healthy retinal vasculature. RHV induces concurrent internalization and lysosomal degradation of both VCAM-1 and VEGFR via a head-to-tail binding mode, leading to sustained inhibition of the VEGF/VEGFR, PI3K/AKT and Apelin/APJ signaling pathways. In murine CNV models, a single intravitreal injection of RHV exhibits superior ocular retention and lesion penetration, achieving therapeutic efficacy comparable to aflibercept [a ligand-trap fusion protein for VEGF-A, VEGF-B and placental growth factor (PIGF)] at one-quarter of the molar dose. This dual-receptor degradation-based strategy represents a targeted and durable approach for treating ocular neovascularization.

Article.Title: Entropic tightening of knots in granular chains under vibration
Article.Authors: Qiu Q.; Zheng Y.; Yang J.; Hua P.; Han Y.; Dai L.
Article.Abstract: Knots are common in long chains, from DNA and proteins to everyday strings, yet direct observation of knot dynamics is difficult. Using granular chains on vibrating platforms, we directly visualize knot dynamics and find that knot cores spontaneously tighten, a behavior observed across different knot types. We quantitatively explain spontaneous knot tightening using knot-tube theory: segments confined within the knot core experience entropic loss and tend to escape the core to gain conformational entropy. Although driven granular chains are not in thermodynamic equilibrium, their steady-state knot-size statistics are approximately captured by equilibrium statistical mechanics and Monte Carlo simulations. Analyses of state-transition probabilities and time-reversal asymmetry suggest a weak violation of detailed balance when the granular dynamics are projected onto the knot-size coordinate. Finally, we discuss the possible relevance of knot tightening to topoisomerase-mediated DNA unknotting.

Article.Title: Municipal sludge disposal emerges as a major, hidden, and rapidly growing atmospheric mercury source
Article.Authors: Cai X.; Yang M.; Liu M.; Ma S.; Qiu X.; Zhang Q.; Wang X.
Article.Abstract: Wastewater treatment greatly reduces mercury pollution in aquatic ecosystems but does not eliminate it. Here, we identify municipal sludge disposal as a major, long-overlooked atmospheric mercury source. In China, sludge disposal emitted 42 - 10 + 18 Mg in 2024, exceeding 10% of national anthropogenic emissions and ranking third after cement production and nonferrous metal smelting. These emissions have increased by nearly a thousandfold since the 1970s and are concentrated in densely populated urban areas, driven by the rapid expansion of sludge incineration, codisposal, and composting. Our findings reveal a cross-media pollution transfer embedded in sustainability transitions and call for sludge disposal to be incorporated into UNEP mercury budget and Minamata Convention assessments.

Article.Title: The purinergic receptor P2Y <sub>13</sub> controls the activation and mode of division of adult ventricular–subventricular zone neural stem cells
Article.Authors: Paniagua-Herranz L.; Serrano-López J.; Llorente-Sáez C.; Pérez-Sanz M.; de Agustín-Durán D.; Duart-Abadia P.; Domingo-Muelas A.; Vincelle-Nieto Á.; Bragado P.; Manzano-Franco D.; Arribas-Blázquez M.; Gallego L.; Garcia-Mora A.; Olivos-Oré L.; Gascón S.; Gutierrez-Uzquiza Á.; Berninger B.; Pérez-Sen R.; Delicado E.; Gómez-Villafuertes R.; Reyes-Palomares A.; Artalejo A.; Fariñas I.; Ortega F.
Article.Abstract: The ventricular–subventricular zone (V-SVZ) is the most active germinal area in the mammalian brain and it continues to generate newborn neurons throughout life. This area harbors a population of neural stem cells (NSCs) that exist in different states of activation: quiescent NSCs, primed NSCs, and activated NSCs. There are currently few specific markers to effectively discern each state. Likewise, the molecular signals that control the transition from quiescence to activation remain largely unexplored, and the factors that controls whether dividing NSCs differentiate or self-renew are poorly understood. Here, we present evidence that the metabotropic P2Y 13 purinergic receptor plays a critical role in regulating adult neurogenesis. We found that P2Y 13 is specifically expressed in NSCs within the adult V-SVZ and that its levels can be used to distinguish quiescent from activated NSCs. P2Y 13 signaling promotes NSC activation, enhancing lineage progression as opposed to their self-renewal. Conversely, pharmacological blockade or genetic silencing of P2Y 13 receptors favors NSC quiescence. Thus, we consider the metabotropic P2Y 13 purinergic receptor a pivotal modulator of NSC dynamics.

Article.Title: Patterns of implicit and explicit attitudes V: Increases in bias from 2021 to 2025
Article.Authors: Charlesworth T.; Doyle M.; Banaji M.
Article.Abstract: Between 2007 and 2020, implicit and explicit intergroup attitudes declined in bias steadily and were forecasted to continue toward attitude neutrality. But, since 2020, 5 y of new data (2021–2025) from 2.8 million U.S. respondents reveal that past trends have stalled or, in some cases, even reversed. The largest reversals in bias emerged for sexuality, transgender, race, and skin-tone bias which increased by 12 to 22% on implicit measures and by 24% to more than tripling on explicit measures. Age, disability, and body weight bias also increased, but at relatively slower rates. Breakpoint analyses showed that implicit attitudes were early indicators of change, reversing trend ~1 y earlier than explicit reports. For most topics, reversals were widespread across demographic groups and even extended to an international sample of 274,884 non-U.S. respondents. However, younger respondents (<20-y-old)—who had previously shown the largest decreases in bias—now showed the largest increases in bias; these trends also interacted with politics and gender (e.g., young conservative men were the most likely to increase). Exploratory analyses ruled out various single-cause explanations. Instead, we suggest that the best explanation is that 2020–2021 marked a turning point in the sociopolitical climate, whereby co-occurring existential threats from the COVID-19 pandemic, amplified economic insecurity, political sectarianism, and online toxicity prompted increases in intergroup bias. These data underscore how large populations of individual-level attitudes are continually shaped and altered by macro, societal-level events.

Article.Title: Multifunctional multiphysics metamaterials via decomposition-based multiobjective optimization design
Article.Authors: Chen Z.; Yin S.; Zhu Z.; Liu Y.; Yang J.; Ritchie R.; Mai Y.
Article.Abstract: Metamaterials offer unprecedented control over physical fields through their microstructure, but current design methods cannot meet the demands of scenarios involving active sources, multiphysics field coupling, and multifunctional requirements. Moreover, existing approaches are generally developed for specific functions, making it difficult to integrate different functionalities and select the functional priorities within a single structure. To overcome these limitations, this study presents a systematic inverse design framework for multifunctional multiphysics metamaterials via multiobjective optimization. To uniformly explore the Pareto front, which clearly exhibits trade-offs among functionalities and facilitates the selection of functional priorities, we employ dynamic normalization into the decomposition-based multiobjective evolutionary algorithm. A robust anisotropic unit-cell database is constructed and used for generating metamaterials with optimized microstructures for multifunctionality. Three complex cases are studied that can simultaneously achieve mechanical cloaking plus stress minimization, thermal cloaking plus stress minimization, and direct current cloaking plus thermal stress minimization. Furthermore, the proposed framework is employed in potential engineering problems, for example, to realize mechanical cloaking by embedding functional components in structural materials, while minimizing the surrounding stress on functional components for mechanical protection when the assembled structures are compressed, thereby decoupling the interaction between functional and structural components. This systematic framework expands the capabilities of metamaterials in complex multiphysics coupling, offering a robust blueprint for future intelligent, structurally and functionally integrated systems.

Article.Title: Amphipathic helices repurpose a Patched/NPC1-like cholesterol transporter to function at Plasmodium –erythrocyte membrane contact sites
Article.Authors: Ray A.; Istvan E.; Goldberg D.; Garten M.
Article.Abstract: The interface between the malaria parasite Plasmodium spp. and its host erythrocyte critically mediates nutrient uptake, lipid exchange, and protein export required for parasite replication and thus pathogenesis. Approximately half of this interface consists of narrow membrane contact sites, a region defined by only 3 to 4 nm of aqueous space between the parasite plasma membrane and the parasitophorous vacuole membrane. Despite its extent, the region remains largely uncharacterized and inaccessible, not least due to its narrowness. The sole identified resident is the Plasmodium falciparum Niemann-Pick Type C1-Related protein, PfNCR1, an essential Patched/NPC1-like cholesterol transporter, suggesting this conserved transporter family has evolved an unconventional adaptation for localizing to membrane contact sites that can reveal a mechanism to access the region. Here, using live-cell microscopy and assessment of cholesterol homeostasis, we identify a helix–linker–helix (HLH) domain as the necessary modification for efficient PfNCR1 localization. We find that correct localization is required for the parasite to maintain low cholesterol levels, connecting targeting to function. Using a glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchored fluorescent reporter as a minimal membrane-associated protein, we show that the HLH domain is sufficient to drive localization to the narrow membrane contact site region. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that targeting depends on the physicochemical character of the targeting domain rather than a specific primary sequence, identifying amphipathicity as a determining property of the HLH domain. Taken together, we propose physicochemical partitioning as a fundamental principle for protein targeting at the Plasmodium –erythrocyte interface, and for driving direct functional interactions of a Patched/NPC1-like protein with a second membrane.

Article.Title: Progressive shifts in soil respiration response to long-term nitrogen enrichment across global forests and grasslands
Article.Authors: Xing A.; Zhao M.; Liu S.; D. Broadbent A.; Du E.; Shen H.; Fang J.
Article.Abstract: Soil stores the largest pool of actively cycling carbon (C) on land, and its dynamics under global changes are critical for projecting climate feedbacks. Global nitrogen (N) deposition has more than doubled since the 1860s; however, the temporal dynamics of soil C emissions under prolonged N deposition are poorly understood. Here, using a global time-series dataset compiled from 38 long-term experiments in forests and grasslands, we find that the response of soil respiration (Rs) to N addition systematically shifts from a transient increase persisting for approximately 2 y to a sustained suppression over time (mean effect = −6%; 95% CI = [−10%, −3%]). Rs in forests and grasslands followed consistent nonlinear trajectories, characterized by a rapid initial decline in the magnitude of the response, which progressively leveled off. Notably, suppression of Rs emerged when cumulative N inputs exceeded a threshold of ~100 kg N ha −1 . Consequently, the suppression was both stronger and occurred more rapidly under high-level N additions (>50 kg N ha −1 y −1 ). These temporal dynamics were associated with N-induced soil acidification and related changes in microbial properties. Overall, these findings indicate that accurate prediction of land–atmosphere C fluxes under global change requires models to capture the reported temporal dynamics.

Article.Title: Codfishes survived essential gene loss by functionally co-opting freshwater ovulatory pathways to marine egg hydration
Article.Authors: Rey-Alfonso Á.; Yilmaz O.; Chauvigné F.; Finn R.; Cerdà J.
Article.Abstract: Adaptive evolution associated with dispensable gene loss is widespread in the animal kingdom. However, loss of genes essential for embryonic survival and the mechanisms that evolved to bypass negative selection and extinction are less well known. Here, we show that all Gadiformes, an ecologically dominant order of codfishes, lost the aqp1ab -type genes that are essential for the formation of hydrated pelagic eggs and embryonic survival of marine teleosts in oceanic environments. Despite such gene loss, codfishes produce some of the most highly hydrated pelagic eggs of all marine teleosts. To resolve this apparent paradox, we initially confirmed that the mechanisms of osmotic drive are conserved with other pelagic-egg-producing marine teleosts, and then conducted comparative transcript analyses of aquaporin water channels in distantly-related freshwater and marine teleosts. This uncovered Aqp4-type channels that have been chromosomally linked to the Aqp1-type channels in jawed vertebrate genomes for >450 million years as the primary candidates. Using immunolocalization, functional assays, and inhibition experiments with zebrafish and Atlantic cod as model organisms, we show that short isoforms of Aqp4 are required for egg ovulation in more ancestral lineages of freshwater teleosts and were recruited to the oocyte hydration pathway of codfishes. By contrast, the oldest and most modern lineages of marine teleosts producing pelagic eggs still utilize the aqp1ab genes for egg hydration. Our data thus reveal that codfishes survived essential gene loss by functionally co-opting freshwater ovulatory pathways to marine egg hydration.

Article.Title: Modified Newtonian Dynamics and galaxy clusters
Article.Authors: Combes F.
Article.Abstract: First proposed by Milgrom in 1983 as an alternative to the standard Cold Dark Matter (CDM) paradigm, Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) has gained renewed momentum in light of persistent nondetections of exotic dark matter particles and growing tensions facing CDM on galactic scales. While MOND perfectly reproduces galactic rotation curves, it encounters notable challenges in explaining the equilibrium of galaxy clusters. Although it reduces the overall dark matter budget in these massive systems, an unidentified mass component remains required. This paper investigates the hypothesis that this missing mass is baryonic: composed of nonradiating ordinary matter such as stellar remnants, gas too diffuse to initiate star formation, or compact, ultra-dense clouds of cold molecular gas with low volume filling factors. Using a sample of 106 clusters mapped in X-rays, emitted by the hot intracluster medium composing most of the visible mass, we derive first the total mass within the Newtonian dynamics, assuming hydrostatic equilibrium and spherical symmetry. Then, with the modified Poisson equation, we reconstruct the spatial distribution of the invisible missing matter within the MOND framework. In the sample, the relaxed systems harboring cooling flows, known as cool-core clusters, have the highest peaks of dark missing mass. Its density profile reveals a pronounced central concentration bounded by a steep truncation immediately beyond a core radius of 20 to 30 kpc, confirming previous studies. MOND reduces the necessary dynamical mass by a factor of 4 to 10. The residual missing mass is proportional to the total gas mass, being roughly twice lower.
