Here, we report cryo-EM structures of human full-length multidomain UGGT1. Monomeric UGGT1 structures reveal two conformational states corresponding to “open” and “closed” architectures. Three-dimensional variability and molecular dynamics simulations suggest the existence of intermediate conformations, leading to a model in which a continuum of structural transitions underlies UGGT1 function. Notably, in the open state, the EM-maps reveal at the top of the U-shaped protein a density that bridges the sensory TRXL2 and the glucosyltransferase catalytic domains, consistent with substrate association. This observation supports a mode of binding that places the substrate near the catalytic domain. A dimeric form of UGGT1 was observed in which the glycoprotein substrate binding sites are occluded, suggesting that dimerization may regulate UGGT1 activity. To better understand the spatial relationship between the site of misfolding and that of UGGT-mediated N-glycan reglucosylation, we identified N-glycosylation sites on endogenous glycoprotein substrates by glycoproteomics. No consensus sequence was found flanking modified sites, indicating that substrate recognition relies on mechanisms beyond primary sequence. Mutations in the UGGT1 gene cause a novel congenital disorder of glycosylation characterized by developmental delay and intellectual disability, and the human UGGT1 structure helps explain how disease-associated missense and deletion variants disrupt function. Together, our data provide insight into the relationship between UGGT1 structure and function, integrating enzyme conformational states with client glycoprotein interaction and processing.

Article.Title: Deep mutational scanning of the GPCR rhodopsin reveals pleiotropic mutational effects and their roles in modulating receptor signaling
Article.Authors: Chen S.; Liu J.; Chang B.
Article.Abstract: Biophysical pleiotropy, the phenomenon in which a mutation affects multiple protein properties, underlies many genetic diseases and shapes protein evolution, yet remains poorly understood, limiting synthetic biology and therapeutic development. Although extensively studied in soluble proteins, little is known about how pleiotropic effects shaped the evolution of receptor protein functions. Here, we developed a cell-based assay designed to assess pleiotropic effects in G protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs), the largest receptor class in eukaryotes. Because our assay allows for multiple GPCR molecular phenotypes (basal activity, ligand-dependent signaling, and cellular receptor abundance) to be simultaneously assessed, we applied it to study rhodopsin, a visual GPCR that evolved for high phototransduction capabilities by maximizing light-driven responses while minimizing noise. To investigate this, we integrated our assay with deep mutational scanning to test the impacts of ~2,000 single-residue substitutions in rhodopsin across all three molecular phenotypes (~6,000 measurements). By analyzing these data in the context of rhodopsin’s protein structures, we found complex pleiotropic effects that act asymmetrically to impose joint constraints, restricting mutational tolerance in rhodopsin’s retinal binding pocket and G protein interaction interface. A dose–response analysis of rhodopsin signaling revealed that these pleiotropic constraints arise from the dual functions of its chromophore, which acts as an agonist upon light-driven isomerization but also an inverse agonist in darkness. Because these constraints reflect mechanistically driven limitations in the evolution of receptor signaling, these findings reveal a role for biophysical pleiotropy in shaping the signaling capabilities of receptor proteins.

Article.Title: Where intention goes, responsibility flows: Grounding AI accountability in the machine learning paradigm
Article.Authors: Hilbert M.
Article.Abstract: An opening salvo of lawsuits in US courts has begun holding AI companies accountable through independent doctrinal routes: Product liability and agency law cut as swords, while the shields of Section 230 immunity and First Amendment doctrine begin to crack. This Perspective points out that these converging paths share a unifying principle, built on the very engineering architecture of machine learning (ML) itself. Every ML system, across all variants, is constituted by a human-specified objective function before learning begins. Training data, deployment context, user interaction, and postdeployment oversight add further layers of deliberate human intention traceable to identifiable actors. AI output is therefore not the expression of a single speaker but a composite of layered human intents. It takes a village to raise an AI, and everyone in that village bears a duty of care. This transforms AI accountability from a philosophical puzzle into a tractable legal inquiry: Trace the chain of intentional design decisions across the ML pipeline, grade each actor’s responsibility by their intent’s specificity and foreseeability, and apportion liability accordingly, following the standard three doctrine-neutral questions (attribution, causation, apportionment). Sufficient for most cases, four gaps remain: who owes what share when many hands build one system, proving fault inside an opaque model, harms that surface only after deployment, and remedies that match the technology’s pace. Targeted reforms drawing on environmental, vaccine, and financial regulatory precedents can close these gaps without requiring new legal categories, AI speech rights, AI legal personhood, or defining AI consciousness.

Article.Title: Ddx3x deficiency in mice impairs corticofugal motor circuits and causes motor deficits that are attenuated by early-life exercise
Article.Authors: Dierdorff L.; El Khaldi I.; Garcia-Forn M.; Wang W.; Lukin J.; Smith C.; Mossa A.; Wu Z.; De Rubeis S.
Article.Abstract: The X-linked RNA helicase DDX3X is a high-risk gene for autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability primarily in females. Individuals with pathogenic variants in DDX3X have pervasive and often severe motor manifestations. Using mouse models, we studied the circuits underlying the motor phenotypes associated with Ddx3x deficiency and examined the feasibility of an early intervention to ameliorate motor trajectories. We show that Ddx3x controls both the development and later plasticity of motor circuits connecting the motor cortex with the pontine nuclei. Ddx3x haploinsufficiency during development affects the dendritic arborization of corticopontine neurons. Juvenile-onset Ddx3x loss in corticopontine neurons is sufficient to induce adult motor impairments overlapping with those caused by chemogenetic disruption of corticopontine circuits. Further, Ddx3x mutant mice engage corticopontine circuits in skilled motor tasks in a sex-dependent manner. Last, Ddx3x haploinsufficient female mice undergoing a juvenile motor intervention show long-lasting specific benefits in their adult motor function. Together, these findings establish Ddx3x as an essential regulator of corticopontine neuron development and function and provide an early motor intervention to ameliorate motor outcomes in a mouse model of DDX3X haploinsufficiency.

Article.Title: Crowding limits relative bacterial surface accumulation with density-induced effective heating
Article.Authors: Liu Y.; He R.; Wei D.; Li L.; Yang M.; Yuan J.; Peng Y.
Article.Abstract: The accumulation of microswimmers near walls has been studied for decades. While hydrodynamics and single-cell kinematics are well-explored, the role of cell-cell interactions remains understudied. However, in realistic, crowded environments such as the human gut, these interactions can be just as crucial. Here, we demonstrate that they actively weaken bacterial surface accumulation. Analysis of entrapped cell tracks reveals that crowding enhances orientational fluctuations, which increase the effective rotational diffusion and facilitate wall escape. A minimal model shows that this collective effect is equivalent to raising the system’s effective temperature with density.

Article.Title: Potential energy landscape networks of confined vortex matter
Article.Authors: Ma X.; Li W.; Ray D.; Toroczkai Z.; Jankó B.
Article.Abstract: Advances in nanoscale patterning of superconducting films [Y. L. Wang et al ., Nat. Nanotechnol. 13 , 560–565 (2018)] and the availability of submicron-sized superconducting single crystals with controlled geometry allow for the investigation of superconducting vortex matter under extreme confinement [A. K. Geim et al ., Nature 390 , 259–262 (1997)]. It has been observed in these systems that the interplay between sample geometry and vortex number results in the emergence of so-called “magic number” configurations which show unusually high stability against thermal fluctuations. However, a detailed, comprehensive theoretical study of the ground state and metastable states of confined vortex matter has not yet been developed. Here we show that the intricate properties of a system of vortices under extreme confinement can be characterized in detail by mapping the potential energy landscape of the system onto a network [J. P. K. Doye, Phys. Rev. Lett. 88 , 238701 (2002)] with nodes corresponding to local potential energy minima and edges to transition states between local minima. We apply these techniques to systems featuring repelling particles/vortices confined in small containers of various geometric shapes. We demonstrate that the ground state almost always belongs to a subset of system states within the deepest network core. We find that the emergence of magic number configurations in the ground state results in a drastic decrease in the complexity of the entire network. We use large-scale molecular dynamics simulations to study the size dependence of melting in different configurations. We find that as confinement effects increase, magic number configurations transition to states with lower symmetry.

Article.Title: Intrinsic function of leptin receptor–regulated endothelial PD-L1
Article.Authors: Cheung Y.; Yeung H.; He C.; Zhang Q.; Chook C.; Tse G.; Liao Y.; Wong W.
Article.Abstract: Programmed cell death ligand-1 (PD-L1) is an immune checkpoint protein expressed in vascular endothelial cells (ECs). In contrast to cancer, our understanding of endothelial PD-L1 in relation to metabolic syndromes and its vascular complications is less studied. For example, its regulation and intrinsic function remain unclear. Here, we showed that endothelial PD-L1 is regulated by leptin receptor signaling in male mice. In particular, endothelial PD-L1 expression is affected by leptin resistance. A lack of leptin receptors leads to PD-L1 downregulation in vascular ECs via posttranslational degradation. To understand the fundamental roles of endothelial PD-L1, RNA interference and selective knockout are employed in human endothelium and animals, respectively. Silencing or deleting endothelial PD-L1 expression delays cell cycle progression and proliferation due to rat sarcoma (RAS)/mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) inactivation. In obesity, endothelial PD-L1 deficiency impairs the EC turnover and worsens the vascular function. Overall, we provide an insight into how endothelial PD-L1 contributes to vascular homeostasis, suggesting its pathophysiological importance in maintaining cellular turnover.

Article.Title: The efficiency of information gain by natural selection
Article.Authors: McGee R.; Kosterlitz O.; Kaznatcheev A.; Kerr B.; Bergstrom C.
Article.Abstract: Natural selection enriches populations for genotypes that are well adapted to their environments, accumulating information about the selective conditions in the process. Therefore, selection can be viewed as a learning process through which populations acquire information about the environment. Motoo Kimura derived a relationship between the amount of information gained by selection and a measure of the inefficiency of the selective process, known as substitution load [M. Kimura, Genet. Res. 2, 127–140 (1961)]. Due to the gradual nature of selection and the ongoing mismatch of types to the environment, a lineage that is still acquiring information has lower mean fitness than a lineage that already has it. While this has been an influential insight, we find that Kimura’s model is inconsistent with selection experiments involving Escherichia coli . To address limitations in this model and develop a more robust measure for the efficiency of selection, we turn to computational learning theory. We show that the learning-theoretic concept of regret quantifies the inefficiency of selection as a learning process in terms of relative lineage fitness. We establish bounds on the efficiency of information gain in general settings, including frequency-dependent selection and arbitrary environmental change. We experimentally validate these bounds and demonstrate that our extended theory recovers Kimura’s fundamental insight. Finally, we show that selection is an asymptotically optimal algorithm for the basic problem faced by evolving populations and that it acquires information more efficiently than comparable processes in complex environments.

Article.Title: Direct atomic-scale observation reveals rare earth element fractionation at mineral–water interfaces
Article.Authors: Ran L.; Wang G.; Zhu J.; Ling B.; Xu J.; Zhang X.; Liang X.; Yang Y.; Wei J.; He H.
Article.Abstract: Clay minerals, ubiquitous across diverse geological systems, exert fundamental controls on critical geochemical processes, particularly through their adsorptive interactions with economically vital elements such as heavy rare earth elements (HREEs). The adsorption of HREEs onto clay surfaces is not only the key process that enriches these critical resources but also a potential archive for dating significant weathering events. However, the atomic-scale mechanisms governing the preferential adsorption and fractionation of rare earth elements (REEs) at mineral–water interfaces have remained poorly constrained. Here, employing in situ atomic-scale imaging via high-resolution atomic force microscopy, we systematically investigate the adsorption behaviors of light and heavy REEs (La, Y, Yb) onto key crystallographic planes—Si-basal, Al-basal, and edge terminations—of representative clay minerals (kaolinite, illite, mica) under environmentally relevant conditions (pH 4.8 to 6.4). We directly visualize and quantitatively reveal that Si-basal planes selectively enrich HREEs with pH-enhanced adsorption capacity, whereas Al-basal planes exhibit negligible REE adsorption below pH 5.8 but preferential HREE adsorption at pH 6.4. Integrating synchrotron X-ray absorption spectroscopy, we identify the adsorption mechanism of REE on Si-basal and Al-basal/edge planes as outer-sphere complexation and inner-sphere binding, respectively. Furthermore, we quantify the contributions of distinct planes via surface complexation modeling, revealing Si-dominated to Al- and edge-controlled adsorption with elevating pH. These atomic-scale findings not only resolve long-standing debates about clay mineral-mediated REE fractionation but also redefine fundamental paradigms of surface reactivity at silicate mineral–water interfaces, offering insights into the cycling and metallogeny of other critical metals in aqueous and sedimentary environments.

Article.Title: Computation and sampling for Schubert specializations
Article.Authors: Anderson D.; Panova G.; Petrov L.
Article.Abstract: We study a problem at the interface of enumerative algebraic geometry, algebraic combinatorics, and the statistical mechanics of vertex models with long-range interactions. We develop methods to explore the values S w ( 1 , … , 1 ) of Schubert polynomials (called principal specializations), which count reduced bumpless pipe dreams (RBPDs) with boundary permutation w ∈ S n . We exhibit counterexamples to the conjecture of Merzon and Smirnov that S w ( 1 n ) is maximized on layered permutations; the smallest such example we find is at n = 17. Despite the counterexamples, we present bounds that support a refined conjecture that the maximum of S w ( 1 n ) over all w ∈ S n grows at the same asymptotic rate as the maximum over layered permutations (found by Morales, Pak, and Panova). We implement and benchmark four recurrences for Schubert specializations: the descent formula of Macdonald, the transition formula of Lascoux–Schützenberger, the cotransition formula of Knutson, and the formula of Billey, Jockusch, and Stanley. We also explore typical random permutations drawn with probability proportional to S w ( 1 n ) , equivalently from uniformly random RBPDs. Our simulations reveal a permuton-like limit analogous to the Grothendieck setting studied by Morales, Panova, Petrov, and Yeliussizov. For sampling, we show that the standard monotone Coupling From The Past framework does not apply to RBPDs, leaving exact uniform sampling open. To bypass this, we develop an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler augmented with macroscopic “droop” updates that preserve connectivity and accelerate mixing. Our publicly available fast implementations reach n = 20 for exact computation of S w ( 1 n ) and n = 100 for Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling using a chain whose stationary distribution is uniform on RBPDs (run on a cluster).

Article.Title: Elucidating molecular regulatory rules of nanoparticle biological identity via standardized deep proteomics
Article.Authors: Jiang C.; Huang H.; Gao R.; Du Y.; Jin B.; Li W.; Wang M.; Dai Y.; Liu Y.
Article.Abstract: The biological identity of nanoparticles is often redefined upon exposure to physiological fluids through the formation of a protein corona (PC), However, the molecular rules linking synthetic design to biological fate remain elusive owing to the fragmented and inconsistent proteomics data. Here, leveraging a standardized deep proteomic database of 42 diverse nanomaterials, we reveal the general molecular selection rules that govern the PC formation. We demonstrate that the PC is not a product of random adsorption but is shaped by strict property-dependent recruitment. First, surface charge regulates cellular uptake, with anionic nanoparticles specifically recruiting adhesion proteins to promote Itgav-mediated endocytosis, thus forming a causal charge-corona-receptor chain. Second, PEGylation engineers immune evasion by selectively depleting specific complement and coagulation factors, rather than merely preventing protein adsorption. Third, nanoparticle geometry imposes structural constraints and selects proteins based on specific physicochemical features such as lysine content. Beyond mechanistic insights, we show that material-specific PCs can rebalance the serum proteome and enable the detection of low-abundance disease biomarkers. This work shifts the paradigm from empirical description toward rule-based prediction and provides a foundational framework for rationally engineering nanomedicines with predictable and programmable biological identities.

Article.Title: A sulfotyrosine motif in the human TrkB extracellular domain is required for activation by the agonist antibody ZEB85
Article.Authors: Briggs D.; Duffy R.; Ateaque S.; Maslen S.; Nagaraj H.; Barde Y.; DiStefano P.; Lindsay R.; Armstrong P.; Peach C.; McDonald N.
Article.Abstract: The brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)-tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB) signaling axis is a key effector of synaptic plasticity and neuroprotection. While TrkB activation is a major target to prevent neural dysfunction, stimulation with exogenous BDNF administration has not proven tractable given the unfavorable physiochemical properties of BDNF. In addition, BDNF also activates a cell death pathway by binding to the neurotrophin receptor p75. The TrkB agonist antibody ZEB85 provides an alternative route to the selective activation of TrkB. To understand the ZEB85 mechanism of action, we mapped the binding site for ZEB85 to the TrkB extracellular juxtamembrane domain and found a sulfotyrosine modification at residue 400 crucial for ZEB85 interaction and activation of TrkB signaling. We determined the structures of ZEB85 and BDNF bound to their respective binding sites on human TrkB suggesting independent sites for each ligand, despite prior evidence of direct competition. Using structure-guided BDNF- and ZEB85-binding deficient TrkB mutants, we assessed their ability to sequester ligands from full-length TrkB in cultured human neurons. We found that the BDNF binding site extends into the juxtamembrane domain of TrkB but does not require the sulfotyrosine 400 to activate TrkB. Together with biophysical analysis and AlphaFold modeling, these results explain how BDNF can displace ZEB85 from TrkB through an overlapping epitope. Our findings reveal unique features of TrkB, not present in the related neurotrophin receptors TrkA and TrkC and suggest future directions to explore the role of sulfotyrosine in TrkB signaling.

Article.Title: A chemomechanical bifurcation landscape unifies sustained growth, length homeostasis, and regenerative collapse in axons
Article.Authors: Zhang H.; Huang W.; Xu S.; Genin G.; Peng X.; Feng X.
Article.Abstract: Axonal growth machinery is largely shared across neurons, but axons exhibit strikingly different fates depending on developmental and environmental context: sustained elongation in peripheral neurons under permissive conditions, length homeostasis in cortical neurons after target innervation, and pathological collapse into dystrophic endbulbs in injured adult central nervous system (CNS) axons. These divergent outcomes have resisted explanation by length-sensing and biomechanical models that treat long-range transport and local force generation as separate problems. We unify these phenomena through a mechanochemical model that couples bidirectional motor transport and intracellular signaling to growth-cone balance of axonal tension, actomyosin contraction, and adhesion within a single feedback loop: The lengthening axon uses its own growing transport delay to establish self-limiting mechanical feedback, as the accumulating delay reshapes signaling waveforms to progressively elevate myosin contractility against actin-driven protrusion. Two physical parameters, the transport delay and the signaling feedback strength, organize axon fate into a unified state-space landscape spanning sustained growth, length homeostasis, and pathological collapse. Reduced feedback strength weakens this self-limiting mechanical feedback by simultaneously enhancing protrusion and suppressing contractility, providing a mechanistic interpretation of axon lengthening under partial reduction of retrograde transport. Bistability in the inhibitory regime explains why mature CNS tracts persist where nascent sprouts collapse, recasting regenerative failure as a state-dependent gate rather than a capacity limit. The framework predicts that partial rather than complete inhibition of retrograde transport could shift collapsed axons across the bifurcation into a growth-permissive regime, identifying a class of interventions complementary to existing capacity-restoration strategies for nerve injury.

Article.Title: Global bee bioregions mirror those of other taxa despite a uniquely bimodal latitudinal diversity gradient
Article.Authors: Laborieux L.; Heinrich L.; Januario M.; Sanders N.; Vasconcelos T.; Swain A.
Article.Abstract: Bioregionalization, the partitioning of the globe into areas of biotic similarity, is one of nature’s most striking patterns, and highly congruent boundaries have been identified across plants, tetrapods, ants, and butterflies. However, these taxa also share a unimodal latitudinal diversity gradient (LDG), raising the question of whether bioregionalization and the LDG are mechanistically coupled or instead arise from largely independent processes acting on different timescales. Bees (Hymenoptera: Anthophila) provide a natural test, their diversity peaking at mid-latitudes rather than in the tropics. Using range estimates for 3,370 species and a phylogenetic beta-diversity framework, we recover 21 bee bioregions nested within at least six major realms (Australasia, Indomalaya-Oceania, Nearctic, Neotropics, Palearctic, and Sub-Sahara) that closely align with those of other taxa despite bees’ atypical diversity gradient. We propose that bioregionalization and species richness are decoupled because they arise from distinct processes: the former reflects historical dispersal and evolutionary history, the latter local diversification, extinction, and environmental filtering. Our analysis provides a global biogeographic framework for future bee research and highlights the processes shaping the world‘s major biogeographic boundaries.

Article.Title: A symbiogenic merger enabled by oxygen initiated the evolution of eukaryotes
Article.Authors: Speijer D.
Article.Abstract: Recently, extensive genetic information about archaeal hosts at the basis of eukaryogenesis has come to light. Characterization of these first eukaryotic common ancestor (FECA) related organisms allows improved understanding of the enigmatic FECA to last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA) transition. However, these gene-centered discoveries have the unfortunate side effect of entrenching erroneous ideas about early eukaryotic evolution. This is apparent in the two-Domain vision of life, with eukaryotes seen as specialized Asgard archaea, while underestimating the contribution of the endosymbiont to eukaryogenesis. Establishment of the alpha-proteobacterium as the future mitochondrion is treated as one of many such endosymbiotic occurrences, ignoring its unique evolutionary position. I will marshal evidence for symbiogenic mechanisms involved in the FECA to LECA transition, with a key role for the endosymbiont’s electron transport chain and its acceptor molecular oxygen, especially in the incarnation of reactive oxygen species occurring in the host cytoplasm. We should overcome overestimating gene determinism, while not sufficiently allowing for effects of biological hierarchies, emergent properties, and chance. Many eukaryotic properties are best understood by envisaging the crucial uptake of the future mitochondrion as a merger instead of an acquisition. This merger is characterized by a new kind of elaborate cellular entity emerging as a result of rapid coevolution, replacing a scenario in which already complex pre-eukaryotes acquired endosymbionts, accompanied by important, but limited, changes. Successful mergers are rare because they are intrinsically more difficult, but synergistically open up completely new areas of possibilities, as illustrated by incredible eukaryotic success.

Article.Title: The ABCD hypothesis
Article.Authors: Chan W.
Article.Abstract: If α and β are cardinals, then the cardinal exponentiation α β is the set of all functions from α into β . The ABCD hypothesis is the statement that for all infinite cardinals α ≤ β and γ ≤ δ , | α β | ≤ | γ δ | if and only if α ≤ γ and β ≤ δ . The Axiom of Determinacy, AD, states that every two-player infinite game on ω has a winning strategy for one of the two players. Let Θ be the supremum of the ordinals onto which R surjects. This paper will show that if AD holds and V = L ( R ) , then the ABCD hypothesis holds below Θ .

Article.Title: Hydration at the base of the mantle transition zone by ancient subductions in Asia
Article.Authors: Liu J.; Wang W.; Xiao W.; Mao Z.; Zhao Y.; Wu Z.
Article.Abstract: Whether and how the subduction processes result in water enrichment at the base of the mantle transition zone (MTZ) remain elusive. The major orogenic belts of the Asian continent, including the Central Asian, Tethyan, and Alpine–Himalayan belts, which record extensive subduction processes, offer an ideal target to address the hydration of the MTZ and its relationship with subduction. Here, we map water content at the MTZ base by combining mineral physics constraints on hydrous pyrolite and global seismic observations of velocity structure and 660-km discontinuity topography. Our results indicate an average global water content of approximately 0.14 wt%, with pronounced hydration anomalies in parts of Asia. Linking these anomalies with reconstructions of past subduction events since 410 Ma reveals extensive water delivery to the MTZ, particularly beneath parts of the Mongol–Okhotsk suture zone, the Central Asian Orogenic Belt, and the Tethyan orogenic domain, where water content exceeds 0.5 wt%. These results connect ancient subduction history to present-day mantle hydration, offering insights into Earth’s deep water cycle.

Article.Title: Complexity functions of infinite sequences
Article.Authors: Greenfeld B.; Leemann P.; Moreira C.; Zelmanov E.
Article.Abstract: We address the inverse problem for complexity functions of infinite words, which asks which functions can occur as complexity functions of infinite words. We survey our recent advances on this problem and several of its ramifications. We describe an asymptotic solution to the inverse problem, realizing every function satisfying two necessary conditions as the complexity function of an infinite word up to asymptotic equivalence. We then turn to phenomena beyond asymptotic equivalence, presenting constructions of infinite words with seemingly contradictory behavior of the discrete derivatives of their complexity functions. These lead to a solution of a 1995 problem of Cassaigne and to applications in symbolic dynamics, including the question of convergence of Rauzy graphs, as well as to the growth and asymptotic invariants of algebraic structures.

Article.Title: Defining and measuring proximity to criticality based on univariate time series
Article.Authors: Sooter J.; Fontenele A.; Barreiro A.; Ly C.; Hengen K.; Shew W.
Article.Abstract: Diverse social, engineered, and biological systems are made up of multiple interacting dynamical components; to work properly, certain components must be carefully regulated so that their dynamics avoid instability. However, many desirable properties, like optimized computation and control, emerge close to the tipping point between stability and instability, i.e., near criticality. Claims that such dynamical systems operate near criticality have been controversial because it is difficult to assess proximity to criticality when control parameters are unknown, hard to manipulate experimentally, and fluctuating in response to changing environmental or internal conditions. Moreover, observations of system dynamics are often limited to time series measurements of one or a few components. Here we develop a temporal renormalization group theory for defining criticality for univariate time series models and an information theoretic definition of proximity to criticality that is independent of model parameterization. We apply this theory to order-n autoregressive models resulting in a data-analytic strategy for time-resolved estimates of proximity to criticality based on measured univariate time series. After benchmarking our approach on diverse ground-truth cases, we apply it to recordings of spiking activity in the mammalian brain. Our estimate of proximity to criticality predicts behavior and suggests that brain dynamics shift closer to criticality during wakefulness and shift away during deep sleep.

Article.Title: Functional redundancy between atypical CDKs reveals a vulnerability in hepatocellular carcinoma
Article.Authors: Martínez-Alonso D.; Nogueira E.; López-Sainz L.; Pérez A.; Villarroya-Beltri C.; Garcia-Diaz A.; Bonel-Pérez G.; El Bakkali A.; Wakahashi S.; Sánchez-Belmonte A.; García-Cao I.; Castillo-Sanchez J.; González-Martínez J.; Megias D.; Sánchez J.; Geley S.; Muñoz J.; Ortega S.; Ferguson F.; Gray N.; Shields D.; Lujambio A.; de Cárcer G.; Malumbres M.
Article.Abstract: The atypical cyclin-dependent kinase subfamily (CDK14–18) encompasses five related proteins with unclear function, and for which individual depletion has not demonstrated sustained therapeutic relevance. We report here that CDK16 and CDK18 compensate each other and liver cancer cells are sensitive to the concomitant inactivation of both kinases, resulting in persistent defects in DNA repair and subsequent cell death. Article.Title: Isotopic evidence of dissolved organic nitrogen production and consumption in ocean surface waters
Article.Authors: Ryu Y.; Marconi D.; Liang Z.; Knapp A.; Fripiat F.; Fawcett S.; Rafter P.; Oleynik S.; Martínez-García A.; Haug G.; Sigman D.
Article.Abstract: Unlike dissolved inorganic nitrogen, which is scarce in much of the tropical, subtropical, and temperate surface ocean, dissolved organic nitrogen (DON) has significant concentrations and gradients. Net local DON production or consumption appears to dominate the observed spatial variation in the DON-to-subsurface nitrate δ 15 N difference. For example, N 2 fixation tends to lower the δ 15 N of surface DON relative to subsurface nitrate mostly through encouraging DON accumulation rather than by the specific δ 15 N of the nitrogen introduced by N 2 fixation. Unique conditions appear to apply in the equatorial Atlantic, where despite high productivity, a local minimum in DON concentration and a slight elevation in DON δ 15 N suggest net DON degradation. Article.Title: Environmental RNA improves detection and surveillance of schistosomiasis transmission
Article.Authors: Mercier C.; Douchet P.; Pouzol D.; Allienne J.; Caldeira R.; Mourão M.; Gomes Lima M.; Montresor L.; Blanchet S.; Loot G.; Rey O.

Article.Title: Rapid green leaf volatile sensing allows intact plants to release induced volatiles earlier than wounded emitters
Article.Authors: Cofer T.; Hu L.; Glauser G.; Erb M.

Article.Authors: Diga R.; Amit T.; Mueller B.; Genin A.; Carlson C.; Yahel G.

These results challenge the prevailing assumption that POM is the exclusive food source for these organisms. TFIIH categorically dissociates before Spt4/5 arrives, with a clear interval in between when neither factor is present. Therefore, Spt4/5 binding is not required to dissociate TFIIH from RNA polymerase II.

Article.Title: TEDEdb: A multicohort analysis and resource for transposable element differential expression in cancer
Article.Authors: Calendo G.; Chaunzwa M.; Dehzangi I.; Madzo J.; Issa J.
Article.Abstract: The human genome consists of nearly 50% repetitive DNA, referred to for decades as “junk DNA.” These repetitive sequences, usually under the strict control of epigenetic silencing, can become aberrantly expressed in cancer. Some of these expressed sequences, e.g., transposable elements (TEs), can induce innate immune responses when derepressed following treatment with epigenetic therapies. As a result, epigenetic therapy has been suggested to augment cancer therapies. TEs are traditionally ignored in most RNA-seq studies and their expression is often excluded from publicly available data sources. Thus, the vast amount of publicly available RNA-seq data is an untapped resource for exploring the role of TE expression in cancer and cancer treatment. Here, we present a uniform reanalysis of over 7,000 RNA-seq samples, encompassing more than 2,000 differential expression experiments across 220 cancer cell lines and 700 drug treatments. We observed that TE expression is more prone to batch effects than gene expression alone, necessitating the use of meta-analysis techniques to probe the dataset for global trends. We confirm that DNMTi and HDACis are powerful inducers of TE expression. We also show that nonepigenetic compounds such as cyclin-dependent kinase and topoisomerase inhibitors can also induce robust up-regulation of TE-derived repetitive DNA elements and confirm that this induction is consistent with transcriptional signatures of viral mimicry response. We made all data available through a publicly available database called the Transposable Element Differential Expression Database, or TEDEdb, and created an interactive web application for its exploration located at https://dataexplorer.coriell.org/TEDEdb/

Article.Title: Scaling laws link conserved gene-abundance distributions to adaptive expression in diatom communities worldwide
Article.Authors: Pigani E.; Simoens K.; Bernardi D.; Campese L.; Iudicone D.; Azaele S.; Suweis S.
Article.Abstract: Marine microbes sustain Earth’s major biogeochemical cycles, yet how they maintain stable ecosystem functions across diverse environments remains unclear. We analyzed metagenomic and metatranscriptomic data from diatom communities sampled during the Tara Oceans global expedition. While gene abundance distributions remain statistically similar across sample, gene expression varies systematically across geographical locations, a global pattern we show reflects predictable scaling laws. Global distributions, scaling relationships, and variability among sampling stations are captured by a stochastic model linking gene abundance dynamics to gene expression. While colder waters are associated with higher transcriptional activity and warmer regions show more selective gene usage, we find that transcript abundance increases nonlinearly with transcript richness. This general scaling is captured by our model and suggests that diatom communities balance high expression of core genes with specific functional diversity. These scaling relationships hold consistently across ocean basins, with temperature, used as an effective large-scale environmental descriptor whose signature cannot be fully disentangled from spatial structure, sufficing to predict transcriptional patterns from genetic composition. Our findings reveal how the stability of gene-abundance structure in diatom ecosystems coexists with transcriptional variability, enabling flexible functional responses.

Article.Title: Cooperative nature of residue interactions in biomolecular condensates
Article.Authors: Chen L.; Wu X.; Hu G.; Zeng X.; Li J.
Article.Abstract: Cooperativity of residue interactions is prevalent in proteins and plays an essential role in protein folding. However, whether cooperativity exists in intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and their assembled biomolecular condensates remains elusive. Here, we reveal the presence of residue interaction cooperativity in various IDP condensates using atomistic molecular dynamics simulations. In all these condensates, cooperative residue interactions manifest as packing between finite residue motifs (3 to 5 residues) with lifetimes three orders of magnitude longer than residue contacts. Notably, these higher-order interactions (HOIs) exhibit a significant nonadditive free energy, which originates from a local low-dielectric environment. The underlying sequence patterns like “Y-X-Q”, “D-X-R”, and “S-Y-X” are identified. Furthermore, HOIs dominate the cohesive energy of IDPs and condensates can be treated as HOI-crosslinked networks. This model can successfully reproduce experimental results of condensate physical properties, including saturation concentration, viscoelasticity, and interfacial tension.

Article.Title: Orexin and pupillary modulation for hunger control
Article.Authors: Kosar S.; Bracey E.; Grujic N.; Du Y.; Peleg-Raibstein D.; Burdakov D.
Article.Abstract: Fasting-based interventions improve metabolic health and are also explored as adjuncts in other clinical settings, but hunger remains a barrier to adherence. Fasting activates AgRP/NPY neurons (ANs), a hunger-promoting population whose inhibition reduces eating in hungry animals. Here we identify hypocretin/orexin neurons (HONs), classically associated with arousal, as rapid suppressors of AN activity. HON ablation increased AN population activity, whereas HON optostimulation rapidly suppressed it. Combined recordings of AN activity and pupil size—a direct arousal metric not previously linked to AN dynamics—revealed that HONs contributed to pupil dilation-associated AN suppression. In fasted mice, sensory stimulation rapidly recruited this pupil-HON pathway, and suppressed AN activity and eating. These findings reveal an arousal–hunger pathway through which self-initiated pupil dilations, or dilations driven by salient environmental events, interrupt fasting-induced hunger signals. They also suggest a framework for noninvasive, sensory-, and pupillometry-guided approaches to hunger control during fasting.

Article.Title: The lncRNA-encoded micropeptide ANCHOR promotes lateral root growth and drought tolerance in rice
Article.Authors: He R.; Jiang J.; Yuan C.; Cao X.; Peng K.; Zhang N.; Luo L.; Fang C.; Zhang Z.; Niu X.; Li W.; Mo W.; Liao Y.; Liu Q.; Zhang Y.; Lian J.; Cheng Y.; Chen Y.
Article.Abstract: Lateral roots (LRs) are important components of plant root systems, determining the robustness of root system architecture and influencing water uptake efficiency. Enhancing the phenotypic plasticity of LRs is key to improving crop production under fluctuating environmental conditions. In this study, we identified ANCHOR, a micropeptide encoded by a long noncoding RNA that is predominantly expressed in LR primordia and plumules. Overexpression of ANCHOR resulted in significantly longer and wider LRs, thereby altering root system architecture and enhancing drought tolerance; knockouts of ANCHOR produced the opposite phenotypes. Mechanistically, ANCHOR localized to plastids and directly interacted with the lysine biosynthetic enzyme LL-diaminopimelate aminotransferase 1 (LL-DAPAT). Our results indicate that ANCHOR functions as a “molecular glue” that enhances DAPAT dimerization. Through its influence on lysine metabolism, ANCHOR raises the levels of the auxin biosynthetic precursor tryptophan, thereby affecting auxin homeostasis. These findings show that lncRNA-derived micropeptides, like their precursor RNAs, can function as fine-tuning regulators. This function of micropeptides, together with their small molecular size, may make them suitable for application as bioeffectors to stimulate root growth and improve plant tolerance to abiotic stress without side effects for plants.

Article.Title: piRNA loss unleashes episodic transposition bursts
Article.Authors: Chen P.; Xu P.; Waseem H.; McCormick J.; Pan K.; Aravin A.; Clark A.; Feschotte C.
Article.Abstract: In Metazoa, transposon expression is suppressed by the piRNA pathway, and disruption of this pathway leads to rampant transposon expression. However, it remains unclear whether increased transposon expression results in actual transposition, and if so, which and how frequently transposons mobilize upon piRNA loss. Here, we developed a framework to track transposon copy accumulation across generations on a single set of nonrecombining haploid genome in the Drosophila male germline, with or without the piRNA biogenesis factor HP1D/Rhino. Single-fly Nanopore DNA sequencing revealed that multiple transposon families mobilized after 10 to 45 generations of piRNA loss. Among them, the most prolific across all replicates was copia , producing dozens of new insertions that were distributed across chromosome arms. With genomic DNA collected at every generation, we validated and dated each copia insertion, revealing episodic bursts of transposition that deviated strongly from a Poisson process. Using phylogenetic analysis, we further showed that multiple copia loci—both autonomous and nonautonomous copies—can mobilize. Interestingly, two additional transposon families, mdg3 and invader3 , also mobilized episodically, but with distinct timing and magnitude, highlighting the stochastic nature of transposition bursts. Because we did not observe a single transposition event for these elements in controls, our results provide direct evidence that the piRNA pathway tightly suppresses germline transposition. More importantly, our findings argue that disruption of the piRNA pathway does not simply elevate transposition rates, but it instead unleashes punctuated and stochastic bursts of transposon movement that may radically reshape the timing and magnitude of mutational input during evolution.

Article.Title: Quantifying ancient architecture: Stone-level machine learning reveals architectural variation and settlement growth at Shivta
Article.Authors: Uziel E.; Avni G.; Feinman G.; Bar-Oz G.; Jaffe Y.
Article.Abstract: Built environments provide durable evidence for how ancient settlements were organized, expanded, and transformed over time. Yet quantitative approaches to documenting architectural variability are generally labor-intensive, limited to individual structures, or dependent on aggregate volumetric estimates. We present a scalable, machine-learning-based framework that shifts the unit of analysis to the individual building stone and combines two complementary datasets: low-altitude drone imagery of surface remains and close-range photographs of standing walls. Applied to the Late Antique settlement of Shivta in the Negev Desert, the method automatically digitized approximately 235,000 surface stones and 12,000 stones in 604 walls, quantifying stone size, shape regularity, and masonry arrangement across walls, households, insulae, and the settlement as a whole. Higher masonry scores cluster around churches and parts of the settlement boundary, while the spatial distribution of masonry variation reveals a previously unidentified earlier boundary and provides evidence for outward expansion from a southern core. Combined with architectural sequencing, these patterns indicate the use of larger and more regularly shaped stones during Shivta’s principal phase of growth. The framework combines analytical flexibility with demonstrated robustness, supporting broader application across diverse stone-built archaeological contexts while complementing architectural energetics and enabling settlement-wide and cross-site comparisons of construction practices and settlement change.

Article.Title: Profile of Barbara Sherwood Lollar

Article.Abstract: In a laboratory nearly 2.4 kilometers under the Canadian Shield, geochemist Barbara Sherwood Lollar has tracked the sustained release of enough hydrogen gas from Earth’s crust to produce 4.7 million kilowatt-hours of energy per year. Article.Title: Septin binding restricts Shigella growth and triggers intracellular tolerance
Article.Authors: Özbaykal Güler G.; Zhang C.; Brokatzky D.; Das R.; Wheeler R.; Boneca I.; Cortes T.; Manley S.; Mostowy S.
Article.Abstract: Pathogen survival relies on their ability to adapt to changing environments, yet how intracellular bacteria tolerate cell-autonomous immunity remains unclear. RNA-sequencing reveals that septin binding to Shigella upregulates type III secretion system (T3SS) effectors and triggers a stress response. Article.Title: Intraventricular clindamycin enhances interstitial brain fluid drainage and the blood–brain barrier after a traumatic brain injury
Article.Authors: Ashby L.; Crowe M.; Chakravarty D.; Medam S.; Frampton G.; Das A.; Hormuth D.; Yankeelov T.; Wang V.; Noble-Haeusslein L.; Umlauf B.
Article.Abstract: Despite advances in the acute clinical management of severe traumatic brain injuries (TBIs), treating injury-derived secondary pathogenesis remains challenging. Consistent with these data, a novel objective recognition test revealed an improvement in recognition memory in brain-injured mice treated with clindamycin. These collective findings reveal a counterintuitive finding that I.C.V. clindamycin enhances drainage of toxins from the brain while simultaneously restoring the BBB, potentially providing a new solution for alleviating secondary pathogenesis in brain-injured patients.

Article.Title: Holocene millennial climate variability influenced by tropical–Antarctic ocean–atmosphere interactions
Article.Authors: Zhou P.; Shi Z.; An Z.; Cai W.; Braconnot P.; Zhang Q.
Article.Abstract: A prominent unstable feature, millennial-scale climate oscillation (MCO), punctuated the Holocene. Solar activity and deep ocean variability are generally regarded as the origin of the MCO, yet the dynamics remain debated. Using a Holocene transient simulation with the EC-Earth climate model (8 to 0 ka BP), together with a global compilation of 304 temperature reconstructions, here we identify a robust ~1,350-y oscillatory mode that characterizes Holocene climate variability and is self-sustained and crucially influenced by tropical–Antarctic ocean–atmosphere interactions. Within each cycle, Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW) strengthening evolves with the developing warming and an El Niño-like tropical sea surface temperature (SST) response, accompanied by anticyclonic circulation anomalies over the high-latitude Southern Ocean. Northward cold advection of the associated enhanced westerly winds off the Antarctic coast overcomes the effect of sea ice retreat to promote AABW formation, ocean stratification, and warming. Positive feedbacks including sea ice-albedo, tropical air–sea interaction, and SST-AABW magnify surface warming till AABW reaches its peak. Thereafter, reduced brine rejection from sea-ice retreat weakens AABW, counteracts the warming, and commences a switch to its cooling phase. The dominant periodicity, consistent with that inferred from proxy reconstructions, is confirmed by complementary climate simulations. These results provide an alternative physical mechanism for Holocene millennial-scale climate variability. Under future anthropogenic warming, a positive phase of the oscillation may heighten the positive feedbacks, thereby increasing the risk of rapid climate transformation.

Article.Abstract: Somatostatin secretion from pancreatic δ cells inhibits nearby α- and β cells and tunes the body’s glycemic set-point. Here, we compared the function of isolated δ cells of cadaveric nondiabetic and type-2 diabetic donors by single cell total internal reflection microscopy, electrophysiology, and secretion measurements. Elevated glucose stimulated exocytosis of somatostatin, which was further amplified by glucagon, exendin-4, or forskolin, independent of diabetic status. gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) enhanced exocytosis and electrical activity, while insulin had no detectable effect. Adrenaline and somatostatin strongly inhibited δ cell activity, leading to autocrine feedback inhibition of somatostatin exocytosis. In type-2 diabetes, δ cell inhibition by somatostatin and adrenaline was impaired, together with a marked reduction in somatostatin receptor (SSTR2) surface expression. The data suggest that selective loss of inhibitory control of δ cells may dysregulate intraislet somatostatin signaling in type-2 diabetes.

Article.Title: Revised estimates of types and duration of long COVID symptoms based on claims records from 245 million US patients
Article.Authors: Nilforoshan H.; Reisler J.; Jahanparast E.; Moor M.; Goodman S.; Wager S.; Leskovec J.
Article.Abstract: COVID-19 has been reported to cause multisystem effects lasting years [Z. Al-Aly, E. Topol, Science 383, 830–832 (2024)]. These findings are primarily based on cohort studies comparing test-positive COVID-19 patients to controls without known COVID-19 infection, tested or untested [M. Cai, Y. Xie, E. J. Topol, Z. Al-Aly, Nat. Med. 30, 1564–1573 (2024)]. However, such comparisons can be biased by the reasons people were tested. Using 14.4 billion insurance claims from 244.7 million US patients, we find that most long-term effects attributed to COVID-19 by unrestricted control designs likely reflect bias due to selective testing of individuals with non-COVID conditions, causing long-term effects of those conditions to be misattributed to COVID-19. We removed this bias by analyzing only tested individuals, comparing test-positive to test-negative patients. Across 614 clinical outcomes followed over 2 y, the test-based design resulted in 83.5% fewer symptoms being attributable to COVID-19 between 30 to 119 d after infection (43 attributable symptoms vs. 262 for the unrestricted control design), a 98.2% reduction at 120 to 359 d (5 vs. 286), and a 100% reduction at 360 to 719 d (0 vs. 369). The unrestricted control design also attributed unrelated outcomes (e.g., firearm injuries) to COVID-19 at a high rate, whereas the testing-based design did not. The test-based control design may modestly underestimate some effects. This study does not indicate that symptoms beyond one year are not genuine but that their attributability to COVID-19 is uncertain.

Article.Title: Neuromodulation-inspired gated associative memory networks: Extended memory retrieval and emergent multistability
Article.Authors: Goto D.; Lopez Rios H.; Scholz M.; Vaikuntanathan S.
Article.Abstract: Classical autoassociative memory models have been central to understanding emergent computations in recurrent neural circuits across diverse biological contexts. However, they typically neglect neuromodulatory agents that are known to strongly shape memory capacity and stability. Here we introduce a minimal, biophysically motivated associative memory network in which neuromodulator-like signals are modeled by a self-adaptive, activity-dependent gating mechanism. Using many-body simulations and dynamical mean-field theory, we show that such gating fundamentally reorganizes the attractor structure: the network bypasses the classical spin-glass transition, maintaining robust, high-overlap retrieval far beyond the standard critical capacity. Mechanistically, when the gates act as fully open or fully closed switches, the gate stabilizes transient “ghost” remnants of stored patterns even far above the Hopfield limit, converting a single memory fixed-point attractor into a cluster of fixed points. The retrieved state is set by the initial overlap rather than quantized to the stored pattern. This graded dependence may be exploited for input-driven computation with persistent activity. These results establish that neuromodulation-like gating alone—without modifying synaptic weights or introducing explicit higher-order couplings—can dramatically expand memory capacity, eliminate catastrophic breakdown, and reshape a discrete attractor landscape into a rich continuum, suggesting a general and biologically accessible route to enhanced computational capabilities in neural circuits and neuromorphic architectures.

Article.Abstract: Progression to chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection entails loss of HCV-specific CD4+ T cell help, emergence of viral variants that escape recognition by CD8+ T cells and neutralizing antibodies, and exhaustion of CD8+ T cells targeting remaining intact epitopes. However, in some chronically infected women, a surprising postpartum viral load decline has been linked to resurgent functional HCV-specific CD4+ helper T cells. A minority of women even spontaneously clear long-standing chronic infection postpartum. Plasma from controllers also demonstrated a postpartum increase in neutralization of multiple HCV strains. Article.Title: Viral metagenomics reveals heterogeneity in mammalian virus hosting, sharing, and spillover
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Qu G.; Huang Z.; Zhang X.; Li H.; Wei X.; Hu L.; Xu S.; Becker D.; Wei F.; Xu Y.
Article.Abstract: Zoonotic viruses originating from mammals pose a persistent threat to global health. While rodents and bats are often considered “special reservoirs,” it is debated if spillover risk is driven by specific taxa or merely reflects mammalian species richness. However, most tests have focused on published host–virus association datasets, which can reflect systematic biases in host and virus sampling effort. To address this limitation, we analyzed a comprehensive repository of 4,685 metagenomic datasets, minimizing bias toward any one viral taxon and spanning 296 species across 14 mammalian orders. We characterized the global mammalian virome and found substantial heterogeneity in the capacity of different mammalian orders to harbor and share human-associated viruses. Counter to conventional wisdom, carnivores exhibited significantly higher propensities to carry human-associated viruses, with bats ranked lower in this metric of zoonotic risk. Network analyses of viral sharing further revealed higher cross-order virus sharing among specific mammalian orders (e.g., carnivores and artiodactyls). Phylogenetic comparative analyses revealed that host life-history traits (e.g., longevity) and anthropogenic factors (e.g., urban land use) were key ecological drivers of both virus richness and transmission centrality. Our study provides a data-driven framework that challenges prevailing narratives of zoonotic risk and offers a refined strategy for prioritizing surveillance and mitigating emerging zoonotic threats.

Article.Title: Encoding metal coordination pathways and nuclearity by molecular knotting
Article.Authors: Chi G.; Li B.; Feng H.; Zhang Z.; Wang H.; Li X.; Zhang L.
Article.Abstract: Precise control over the nuclearity and spatial organization of metal ions is a central objective in coordination chemistry. Direct metalation affords Mn(II) 5 -, Fe(II) 5 -, Co(II) 5 -, and Cd(II) 5 -knots through a dinuclear intermediate and an unusual 2-to-5 metal nuclearity progression, even though these metals do not template knot formation. Crystallization of a Mn(II) 2 -intermediate reveals partial demetalation but retains a Mn(II) center displaying a “3 + 3” coordination mode, whereas all Fe(II) ions in the fully metalated Fe(II) 5 -knot adopt a “3 + 2” binding geometry. Together with computational simulations, these observations support a stepwise metalation mechanism in which the dinuclear “3 + 3” coordination environment evolves into the “3 + 2” motif of the pentanuclear knot. Although the Ni(II) 5 - knot cannot be obtained by direct metalation because of slow incorporation, it forms readily via transmetalation from a Zn(II) 5 -knot. Circular dichroism measurements show that chiral expression is dictated by the overall ligand arrangement rather than the identity of the metal ions. Article.Title: Mechanically driven grain refinement in Mo by nanoindentation pop-ins: A case of transient instability
Article.Authors: Li F.; Mostafa A.; Kauffmann Y.; Abdolrahim N.; Rabkin E.
Article.Abstract: During load-controlled nanoindentation of pristine metals, the homogeneous dislocation nucleation manifests as a sudden displacement burst, or pop-in, associated with shear stresses approaching the theoretical strength, massive dislocation nucleation, and rapid yet uncontrolled indenter penetration. Using single-crystal Mo with different surface orientations, we demonstrate pop-in-induced nucleation of new, highly misoriented grains at room temperature. Displacement-controlled atomistic simulations reproduce both twin- and dislocation-mediated grain nucleation within an individual grain when a preexisting grain boundary blocks dislocation glide. However, in the absence of such a grain boundary, nucleated dislocations glide into the surrounding crystal and fail to form new grains. Continued indentation beyond pop-in mechanically erases newly formed grains, as confirmed in both experiments and simulations, explaining why this phenomenon was not detected in previous studies. Together, the observed nucleation and subsequent erasure of the grains establish the nanoindentation pop-in as a simple, widely accessible platform for qualitatively probing transient microstructural evolution in defect-scarce metals.

Specifically, at high specific growth rates, the protein mass fraction (PMF) from certain compartments, (e.g., nucleus) is consistently reduced, coinciding with the increasing protein resource demand from ribosomes. Meanwhile, nutrient limitation may induce resource recycling by upregulating protein resources within specific compartments (e.g., vacuole) to sustain stress adaptation. Importantly, our integrative analysis indicates that PMF from a few subcellular compartments (e.g., nucleus and ribosomes) can accurately predict yeast physiological parameters (e.g., specific growth rate, oxygen uptake rate), and a limited protein set (≥ 23) could be used to capture the variation in resource allocation across seven major subcellular compartments. Furthermore, our comparative analysis between Crabtree-positive and Crabtree-negative species across conditions illustrates that subcellular resource allocation could be shaped by multiple factors and the two species differ markedly in their robustness to environmental perturbations. In summary, the high-quality quantitative proteomic dataset for yeast species offers an unprecedented opportunity for understanding the general principles underlying subcellular resource allocation, laying foundations for precision engineering of cell factories in synthetic biology.

Specifically, we found +OPN4 RGCs to show functional rhabdomeric and ciliary motifs of phototransduction as we previously found in ipRGCs. +OPN4 αRGCs (the largest RGCs in the retina) exhibited light-triggered fast (via TRPC signaling) and slow (via cAMP signaling) response components, whereas +OPN4 non-αRGC responses comprised predominantly just a fast component. Genetic ablation of TRPC channels (TRPC6/7) or group II adenylyl cyclase (AC2/4/7) to abolish the fast or the slow response component, respectively, largely attenuated the axonal regeneration of +OPN4 αRGCs in the optic-nerve-crush model. At the same time, administration of cell-permeant cAMP not only rescued the AC2/4/7-knock-out phenotype in +OPN4 αRGCs but also potentiated axonal regeneration in some +OPN4 non-αRGCs, thus, possibly overcoming the potential subtype-specific barrier to axonal regeneration. Our results reveal an important role of joint TRPC- and cAMP-signaling in +OPN4 RGC axonal regeneration.

Article.Title: Capture and reduction of singlet oxygen via an anthracene-based framework for stable Li-O <sub>2</sub> batteries
Article.Authors: Jiang Z.; Zhao Zhao N/A.; Gao L.; Ma Y.; Liu K.; An J.; Huang Y.; Chen Z.; Tian X.; Li F.
Article.Abstract: Given the increasing global energy demand and rapid advancement of low-carbon technologies, Li-O 2 batteries have attracted considerable attention owing to their exceptionally high theoretical energy density, offering great promise for advanced energy systems. However, the formation of harmful singlet oxygen ( 1 O 2 ) in both discharge and charge processes induces parasitic reactions that deteriorate round-trip efficiency and cycling stability. Herein, an anthracene-based covalent-organic framework (AntCOF) is introduced as a highly effective catalyst for the 1 O 2 reduction reaction (SORR) in Li-O 2 batteries. The conjugated porous framework selectively captures electrophilic 1 O 2 , enabling effective charge transfer from AntCOF to the empty π* orbital of 1 O 2 and promoting SORR in subsequent discharge processes. This mechanism suppresses 1 O 2 diffusion and mitigates associated side reactions, leading to reduced overpotentials and improved cycling performance when coupled with a RuO 2 catalyst. This work may enlighten further investigations into 1 O 2 -related chemistry across a broad range of oxygen-redox electrochemical systems.

Article.Title: Synchronous end-Permian mass extinction zenith in marine and low–middle latitude terrestrial North China
Article.Authors: Lu H.; Huang B.; Li M.; Zhao Q.; Li X.; Liao Y.; Pei Z.; Xue Y.; Parés J.; Zhang H.; Jiang Q.
Article.Abstract: The end-Permian mass extinction was the most severe biotic crisis of the Phanerozoic, yet temporal synchrony between marine and terrestrial extinctions remains debated due to correlation uncertainties. Here, we present an integrated magnetostratigraphic, cyclostratigraphic, and carbon-isotope and mercury (Hg) chemostratigraphic record from the fluvial Upper Shihhotse, Sunjiagou, and Liujiagou formations at the Sigou section, North China. We identify 14 magnetozones spanning the late Changhsingian to late Olenekian, constrained by a floating timescale based on gamma-ray cyclostratigraphy and subsequently anchored through magnetostratigraphic correlation. Our chronostratigraphy reveals a Hg peak at 252.4 Ma, aligning with the main eruptive phase of the Siberian Traps Large Igneous Province, while the carbon isotope excursion onset (252.1 Ma) and minimum (252.0 Ma) are synchronous with the Meishan Global Stratotype Section and Point. Furthermore, the Induan–Olenekian boundary is positioned below magnetozone SG4n, constraining the Induan Stage duration to 1.6 to 1.8 My. These findings establish a high-resolution chronostratigraphic framework for the Permian–Triassic boundary in North China, supporting a synchronous extinction zenith across marine and low–middle latitude terrestrial ecosystems, with latitudinal diachroneity relative to high-latitude and tropical landmasses.

Article.Title: Predicting birth weights in West Africa using subseasonal to seasonal climate and socioeconomic variables shows potential for an early warning system
Article.Authors: Shukla S.; Davenport F.
Article.Abstract: Past research has shown a negative impact of climate extremes on child birth weight (BW), which is modulated by household socioeconomic and individual maternal conditions as well as the timing and degree of exposure. This study tests the potential of predicting BW using subseasonal to seasonal (S2S) climate predictors and socioeconomic indicators to support early warning systems for BW. Three sets of predictors were tested: a) a suite of biological and socioeconomic indicators from the Demographic and Health Survey (DHS), b) S2S climate predictors, and c) a combination of climate predictors and selected socioeconomic indicators. The most accurate models incorporated the full set of DHS variables [predictors set (a)], with within-country (models trained and tested on the same country) predictive errors ranging from 13.5 to 17% for Burkina Faso and 20 to 25% for Mali. Cross-country (models trained on one country and tested on others) errors varied from 14 to 21% in Burkina Faso to 20 to 26% in Senegal. Models using only climate predictors [predictors set (b)] showed comparable skill to those using the full set of DHS indicators, with a relative error difference of 1 to 5%. The predictive skill was highest for children born with the most in-utero exposure to the lean season (months between planting and harvest). The results of this study have important implications for the prospect of implementing child BW early warning systems in data-sparse regions, based solely on climate predictors or based on selected socioeconomic indicators with climate predictors, to support malnutrition surveillance, to improve antenatal/maternal nutrition, policy formulation, and mitigation decisions.

Article.Title: Humid-heat shifts conceptions and increases pregnancy termination risks in Nigeria
Article.Authors: Brooks N.; Tuholske C.; McMahon K.; Andam K.
Article.Abstract: Climate change is increasing the occurrence of dangerous heat events globally with immediate health consequences, particularly in the Global South. In this paper, we spatially integrate Demographic and Healt 9 h surveys with a high-resolution, blended remotely sensed and station-derived dataset of humid-heat events spanning 1983–2016 to examine the effect of humid-heat exposure on fertility in Nigeria, one of the largest and most climate-vulnerable countries in the world. We use discrete-time models to examine the relationship between humid-heat exposure and conception probability and linear probability models to examine the relationship between humid-heat exposure and pregnancy termination (spontaneous and induced). We find that a 1 ° C increase in the current maximum wet bulb globe temperature decreases conceptions (0.2 conceptions per 1,000 woman-months, 95% CI: 0.03 to 0.4), but exposure to hotter temperatures 1 to 2 mo prior increases conception probability. Exposure to hot-humid temperatures during pregnancy increases probability of pregnancy termination (1.73 terminations per 100 pregnancies, 95% CI: 0.7 to 2.7). The net effect is an increase in births, but the timing may be shifted. Subgroup analyses reveal that effects of humid-heat on conception were larger for women residing in rural areas or in northern districts, or who are Muslim or have lower educational attainment, while the association between humid-heat and pregnancy termination was larger for women in southern areas, older women, and Christian women. Differences in how humid-heat affects populations may exacerbate existing inequalities. Overall, our analysis contributes to a better understanding of how humid-heat exposure affects fertility and reproductive health among women in the Global South.

Article.Title: Heterogeneous impacts of temperature extremes on climate attitudes and Green voting
Article.Authors: Bassetto J.; Hoffmann R.; Muttarak R.; Peisker J.; Stanig P.
Article.Abstract: In the past decade, the public in Europe has become more concerned about climate change and expresses stronger proenvironmental policy preferences. Based on data from the European Social Survey (2012–2022, 25 countries), we show that the increased exposure to temperature extremes has contributed to the observed changes in climate change attitudes and electoral support for environmentalist policy platforms. For each additional degree of excess temperature experienced during warm spells measured over the previous 12 mo, we find that the probabilities of being worried about climate change, of feeling responsible for climate change, and of voting for Green parties and Green coalitions increase by 4.0 [CI95: 2.5, 5.5], 2.5 [CI95: 1.1, 3.9], and 2.8 [CI95: 0.9, 3.7] percentage points respectively. We also document significant heterogeneity across individuals, based on gender and education, particularly between highly educated women and low-educated men. While the latter group consistently exhibits the lowest proenvironmental attitudes and voting, it is this group that shows the strongest increases when exposed to temperature extremes, converging toward the levels of their more educated counterparts. Further regional heterogeneity analyses reveal that the effects of warm temperature extremes are smaller in less prosperous or economically disadvantaged regions, as well as in regions with greenhouse gas emission levels above the median. The findings suggest a nuanced interplay between individual factors and contextual influences in shaping climate attitudes of European citizens and their motivations or reservations toward greater climate action.

Article.Title: Decoding climate anomalies—From scientifically sound to societally relevant
Article.Authors: Brown M.; Tarnavsky E.; Enenkel M.
Article.Abstract: As climate impacts worsen, decision-makers, researchers, and public sector institutions increasingly need reliable, relevant, and appropriate information about emerging weather and climate anomalies. However, with the ever-expanding choice of datasets based on ground observations, satellite data, and models, it is critical to not only use the best dataset for a specific decision-making need but to avoid misinforming and even derailing decision-making due to dataset selection. The main objective of this perspective is to illustrate the importance of understanding datasets used to translate climate data into actionable knowledge, supporting the next generation of science- and data-driven climate risk management instruments, projects, and global initiatives. Through the lens of three use cases, we illustrate what data quality means for different applications, the implications of choosing, aggregating, and combining different climate datasets, and the potential consequences of dataset and baseline choice on decision-making. Choosing different datasets often leads to trade-offs that decision-makers need to be aware of, for instance, between the spatial resolution of a dataset and length of the data record. Here, we discuss the implications of selecting the appropriate time step, resolution, and dataset and provide examples of how these choices affect the identification of societally relevant anomalies.

Article.Title: Propagating shocks and transitions across networked food systems: Insights from multiplayer microeconomic modeling
Article.Authors: Zaitchik B.; Siddiqui S.; Simane B.; Zhang Y.; Sankaranarayanan S.; Bakker C.; Witkin S.
Article.Abstract: Accelerating global change is affecting coupled natural ecosystems and human activities in every part of the world. The local and regional expressions of these changes are a product of interacting and networked systems such that a shock, trend or development transition in one region, ecosystem, or sector can propagate impacts to other regions, ecosystems, and sectors. Informed adaptation and development strategies require an understanding of how signals propagate through these coupled systems and regions. Here, we synthesize findings from our work in Ethiopia and Mali, where we developed and applied a modeling system designed to capture cross-sector dynamics of networked food, water, and energy systems at subnational scale. We approach the problem using a multiplayer microeconomic model that accounts for diverse objectives through chains of food production, distribution, and consumption that connect resource regions to market regions. This paper draws lessons from three case studies in Ethiopia and one in Mali that are designed to examine impacts of a subnational climate shock (drought), a centralized national policy decision (export restrictions in response to food shortage), a distributed development strategy (solar-powered groundwater irrigation), and an external intervention (food aid). In each case, we consider how an initial signal propagates through the country via markets, infrastructure, and interactions between economic actors. An understanding of this propagation can inform strategies for food security in a changing climate.

Article.Title: Populations, exposures and outcomes: How social media data is poised to advance climate-demography research
Article.Authors: Mikal J.; Chancellor S.; Grace K.; Rajamani S.
Article.Abstract: As the natural environment continues to change, there is a shared sense among researchers, policymakers, and health practitioners that we need to better understand the impacts of those changes on health and health behaviors for individuals and populations. “Big” social media data, including large datasets from platforms like X (formerly Twitter), Reddit, Facebook, TikTok, and YouTube, provide access to previously hard-to-reach populations. These data are posed to revolutionize the data landscape in climate change research; however, there are limitations and ethical concerns with data from these platforms, such as ethical questions, biases, noise, and a distinct underrepresentation of marginalized groups. These issues could hamper the adoption of social media data in research on climate change and health. In this commentary, we propose leveraging and augmenting a “human-in-the-loop” approach that uses humans in data extraction, quality assurances, and model testing to ensure data quality and overcome known limitations of social media data. Using examples from health data, we propose new horizons in climate change health research made possible with qualitative research methods.

Article.Title: Equity dimensions of future vulnerabilities to climate hazards: Long-term spatial population projections for New York City consistent with Shared Socioeconomic Pathways
Article.Authors: Balk D.; Tipaldo J.; Jiang L.; Zoraghein H.
Article.Abstract: Projections of future population are important for a myriad of reasons. Large cities, states, and countries routinely produce near- and mid-range population projections. In the context of climate change, the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP) framework is used at global and national scales to project long-term population to inform future emissions scenarios and understand future climate-related exposures and impacts. Much less consideration has been given to long-term projections at smaller scales, even though climate impacts are place based and cities now host most of the world’s population. Cities and their metropolitan regions are complex, heterogeneous in terms of population, environmental, and built features. Thus, using global or national-scale approaches overlooks important aspects of urban futures. Cities are diverse, fluid population centers home to migrants, with employment opportunities yet substantial inequality. These quintessential city-centric features are ignored in global/national-scale population projection methods, including long-term ones consistent with the SSPs. Leveraging state-level SSP-based projections, here we extend that approach for New York City, currently home to 8.8 million persons. Combining multistate and multiregional demographic projection and spatial downscaling models, we project county-level population by racial/ethnic groups and age–sex to 2100 and downscale to 100 m. Such projections allow for an equity lens to inform assessments of future vulnerabilities to climate hazards. Four of the five SSPs project that the population of New York City will be smaller and much older at the end of the century, though these futures are dependent on demographic assumptions about fertility and especially migration.

Article.Title: Spontaneous replication fork collapse regulates telomere length homeostasis in wild-type yeast
Article.Authors: Paschini M.; Gillespie A.; Reyes C.; McCoy C.; Lewis K.; Glustrom L.; Sharpee T.; Wuttke D.; Lundblad V.

We show here that this second substrate, created by spontaneous replication fork collapse in wild-type budding yeast, is elongated by telomerase at a much higher frequency than fully replicated chromosome termini. Furthermore, as much as ~200 nucleotides can be added in a single cell division to newly collapsed forks, indicating that replication fork collapse and the subsequent response by telomerase is a major determinant of telomere length homeostasis. This challenges a long-standing model which posits a length-sensing mechanism that assesses individual telomeres to determine whether yeast chromosome ends are in “telomerase-extendible” versus “telomerase-non-extendible” states. We propose that these two states are instead structurally and temporally distinct substrates for telomerase, generated by two different processes (fork collapse versus completion of DNA replication). We also show that fork collapse at telomeres is kept in check by a telomere-dedicated Cdc13/Stn1/Ten1 complex in collaboration with the canonical RPA complex, indicating that these two complexes stabilize single-stranded DNA exposed at the replication fork. However, eukaryotic genomes contain billions of low-affinity DNA sequences to which TFs associate with a sequence-dependent binding energy. In this model, nucleotide–TF interfaces collectively switch between two states, weak binding and strong nucleotide-specific binding, and the states of neighboring interfaces are coupled with J ∼ 2 k B T . We find that this statistical mechanics model parameterized by our in vitro measurements captures Klf4 binding patterns on an individual long DNA molecule stretched in the optical tweezer, and is predictive for Klf4 occupancy across the entire human genome without additional fit parameters.

Article.Title: Sources and sinks: Geoclimatic dynamics shaped the assembly of endemic fauna in the world’s Third Pole
Article.Authors: Jiang D.; Li M.; Ren J.; Li R.; Lyu Z.; Klaus S.; Jia R.; Xue T.; Li J.
Article.Abstract: The Qinghai–Tibet Plateau (QTP), a biodiversity hotspot shaped by tectonic and climatic forces, has seen significant progress in understanding its floristic origins.
