Article.Title: Hyperdivergent haplotypes control melanic camouflage in a polymorphic moth
Article.Authors: Livraghi L.; Cassily J.; Brayer M.; Carter A.; Alqassar J.; Sim S.; Geib S.; Hanly J.; Martin A.
Article.Abstract: A majority of moths use melanic pigmentation to blend into the visual environment, and some species display genetically controlled color polymorphisms that provide tractable systems for dissecting the genetic basis of camouflage. Here, we leveraged the natural polymorphism of Anticarsia gemmatalis moths to map a major-effect gene that controls melanic variation and study its developmental roles using expression and loss-of-function assays. Genome-wide association mapping identifies the ivory:mir-193 non-coding RNA locus as a major locus of melanic variation, with highly divergent haplotypes differentiating the Light and Dark morphs. Second, the expression of ivory:mir-193 prefigures the melanic coloration of each morph and suggests that cis-regulatory variation at this locus determines the difference in adult pattern. Finally, CRISPR disruption of the ivory promoter and mir-193 hairpin region each abolishes melanic scale pigmentation, demonstrating that this lnc-pri-miRNA module is required for dark-scale differentiation. These findings corroborate the emerging role of ivory:mir-193 as a key factor in the development of melanic patterning and highlight its unique propensity to repeatedly drive phenotypic variation of adaptive potential in butterflies and moths.

Article.Title: A female-specific RWP-RK transcription factor controls gamete differentiation and underlies anisogamy in the macroalga Bryopsis
Article.Authors: Ochiai K.; Goshima G.
Article.Abstract: Anisogamy-the production of male and female gametes of unequal size-and maternal organelle inheritance have evolved repeatedly across diverse eukaryotic lineages despite extensive diversification in sex-determination mechanisms. Yet the genetic and cellular mechanisms underlying gamete dimorphism remain poorly understood. Coenocytic green macroalgae of the order Bryopsidales, which lack complex reproductive organs, provide an attractive system for studying gamete differentiation. However, the absence of genomic resources has prevented the identification of sex-specific chromosomal regions and sex-limited genes in this group. Here, by assembling a de novo genome of a male Bryopsis strain and comparing it with available female genomes, we identified sex-determining regions and sex-limited genes. RNAi screening of these genes identified BrRWP1, a female-limited gene encoding an RWP-RK domain-containing transcription factor related to the volvocine master male-determining factor MID. BrRWP1 knockdown reduced female gamete size and shifted multiple female traits toward male-like characteristics, including chloroplast and nuclear size, swimming behavior, and organelle DNA retention. Gametogenesis imaging revealed that BrRWP1 is required to maintain the female-specific patterns of chloroplast and nuclear division before cellularization, suggesting a potential mechanism linking organelle division to gamete size determination. Despite these pronounced phenotypic changes, BrRWP1 knockdown gametes were not fully masculinized and exhibited fertilization defects, indicating that additional factors contribute to sexual differentiation. Together, our findings identify a female-linked regulator of gamete differentiation and anisogamy in a green macroalga and highlight the independent evolutionary rewiring of RWP-RK transcription factors to control sexual dimorphism across green plant lineages.

Article.Title: Serotonin signaling in the central nervous system is required for correct spine morphogenesis in zebrafish
Article.Authors: Messa G.; Wyart C.
Article.Abstract: Although adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) affects over 1% of children and teenagers worldwide, its causes are not fully understood. While defects in serotonergic system have been associated with certain familial cases of AIS, the underlying causes remain elusive. Over the last decade, zebrafish have emerged as a valuable model to study the mechanisms driving deformations of the spine by uncovering roles for cilia, sensory feedback, and the Reissner fiber (RF). In tryptophan hydroxylase 2 (tph2) mutant zebrafish, we demonstrate that serotonin (5HT) depletion causes progressive 3D spinal misalignment mimicking human AIS. Mutant larvae develop normally up to 21 days post-fertilization (dpf) when spine curvatures emerge. As in AIS, deformities of zebrafish tph2 mutant worsen with age both in sagittal and coronal planes, without vertebral malformations. Remarkably, the RF is intact, yet 5HT is absent from the spinal cord. Intraspinal serotonergic neurons are gradually depleted up to scoliosis onset, together with supraspinal projections from the inferior raphe, eliminating all sources of 5HT to the spinal cord by 21 dpf. Our findings indicate that spinal 5HT signaling plays an essential role for proper spine alignment during post-embryonic morphogenesis.

Article.Title: Non-triazole agricultural fungicides indirectly select for triazole resistance in the human pathogen Aspergillus fumigatus
Article.Authors: Kortenbosch H.; Kanellopoulos S.; Timmermanns L.; Reyes Marquez F.; Zwaan B.; Auxier B.; Snelders E.
Article.Abstract: Agricultural intensification relies on chemical fungicides to manage crop disease,1,2 driving the evolution of resistance in plant pathogens.3 Fungicides persist in the environment, allowing activity beyond their intended targets, affecting downstream ecosystems and agricultural practices. The saprophytic and ubiquitous fungus Aspergillus fumigatus is an important human pathogen causing severe invasive fungal disease.4 Selection by agricultural triazoles, or demethylase inhibitors (DMIs), has led to cross-resistance to clinical triazoles, as both target the cyp51A gene.5,6 In the Netherlands,7,8 most triazole resistance arises from two cyp51A haplotypes, TR34 and TR46.9,10 Genomic surveys show that these resistance alleles often co-occur with resistance alleles to non-DMI fungicides, including quinone outside inhibitors (QoIs) and succinate dehydrogenase inhibitors (SDHIs).11 We hypothesize that agricultural environments with non-DMI fungicides can indirectly select for triazole resistance. Using grass mesocosms to compete A. fumigatus isolates, we found that low concentrations of DMI, SDHI, and QoI fungicides, comparable to agricultural residues, independently increased the proportions of triazole-resistant alleles. Resistance alleles for each class are not intrinsically cross-resistant, indicating that their co-occurrences result from linked resistance alleles. Consistent to these findings, environmental samples from heaps with only non-DMI fungicides contained high phenotypic triazole resistance (>20%). This work provides experimental and field evidence that triazole and non-DMI resistance can increase in parallel, consistent with genomic hitchhiking. We thus predict that novel resistance alleles are likely selected in isolates that have already accumulated resistance alleles to other fungicide classes. Therefore, managing selection and spread of environmental triazole resistance will require consideration of all fungicide classes.

Article.Title: Directional evolution of parasitoid strategies and contingent host shifts shape the radiation of Darwin wasps (Ichneumonidae)
Article.Authors: Santos B.; Bossert S.; Kolasa J.; Broad G.; Bennett A.; Fernandes D.; Klopfstein S.; Rousse P.; Wahl D.; Brady S.
Article.Abstract: Evolutionary change is not always reversible: some traits evolve repeatedly in one direction but rarely in the other, forming evolutionary "ratchets" that constrain future trajectories. Parasitoid wasps provide a powerful system to test this idea because their modes of host exploitation range from relatively simple strategies to highly integrated developmental interactions with living hosts. Here, we investigate the evolution of parasitoid strategies and host use across Darwin wasps (Ichneumonidae), the most diverse parasitoid family, using a phylogenomic dataset comprising 697 species and all ichneumonid subfamilies. Our results reveal that the evolution of parasitoid strategies is strikingly asymmetric: transitions from idiobiosis (permanent host paralysis) to koinobiosis (in which hosts continue development after oviposition) and from ectoparasitoidism to endoparasitoidism occurred repeatedly, whereas reversals were virtually absent. In contrast, host associations were dynamic but contingent on parasitoid strategy: moths and butterflies (Lepidoptera) were inferred as the ancestral hosts, but repeated host shifts subsequently occurred across nearly all holometabolous insect orders despite strong phylogenetic conservatism within major lineages. However, this flexibility was strongly asymmetric, with host-taxon shifts occurring predominantly in idiobiont lineages and becoming much rarer after transitions to koinobiosis. These results show that macroevolutionary dynamics can differ sharply among interacting traits, with directional evolutionary ratchets reshaping not only individual trait trajectories but also the ecological options available to diversifying lineages.

Article.Title: Sex- and frequency-dependent acute pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic effects of smoked cannabis: a randomized controlled trial
Article.Authors: Lake S.; Pabon E.; Baglot S.; Eversole A.; Murray C.; Hampilos K.; Fong T.; Middlekauff H.; Haney M.; Evans S.; Tran A.; Torrens A.; Piomelli D.; Cooper Z.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Cannabis use is rising among women. Studies suggest females are more sensitive to the intoxicating and misuse-related effects of delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). While preclinical studies point to sex-specific development of tolerance, this has not been translated to humans. In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study, 44 participants (22 F) smoked three cannabis strengths (0% [~0 mg] THC, 4% [~20 mg] THC, 10% [~60 mg] THC), provided blood for plasma analysis, and completed subjective mood and drug effects assessments and a self-administration task. Outcomes were analyzed by cannabis strength, sex, and use frequency ( > 4 vs. ≤4 days/week; balanced across sex). Relative to placebo, active cannabis strengths increased subjective effects and plasma THC and metabolites ( p s < 0.05). Exploratory follow-up of interactions (cannabis strength*frequency p < 0.10) showed the frequent-use group exhibiting significant increases from placebo in misuse-related ratings (“Like”, “Take again”) and self-administering more cannabis than the occasional-use group ( p s < 0.05), and this was not modified by sex. Ratings of “High”, Sedation/impairment, Dysphoric arousal, and “Bad effect” were higher at active strengths for occasional-use males relative to sex- and/or frequency-matched counterparts ( p s < 0.05; via exploratory follow-up for “High” and Sedation/impairment). THC and metabolites tended to be highest in frequent-use males. These findings contrast with previous evidence of greater cannabis sensitivity among females and point toward future investigation into sex-dependent exposure thresholds for tolerance development/escalation. Sex and frequency of use are both implicated in cannabis use disorder risk, and consideration of their interaction is critical in characterizing the acute effects of, and tolerance to, cannabis.

Article.Title: Testing neurobiological models of reward/incentive sensitization in the continuation of alcohol use disorder (AUD) symptoms in young adults with AUD: A four-year longitudinal study
Article.Authors: King A.; Nordgren R.; Cao D.; Wellendorf C.; Fridberg D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Alcohol use disorder (AUD) remains an urgent public health problem. Alcohol response phenotype may be an important factor underlying vulnerability to and progression of AUD. This study examined the prospective association between acute alcohol responses and continued or remitted AUD over time in young adults with AUD. This sample was N = 101 AUD participants (M age =27.1 ± 4.0 SD yrs) comprising the third cohort of the Chicago Social Drinking Project. They completed two beverage challenge laboratory sessions (0.8 g/kg fixed-dose alcohol vs . placebo) and four years of follow-up to ascertain future AUD symptoms, drinking behaviors, and consequences. Retention was high with an overall 99.2% follow-up rate. Analyses identified three AUD trajectory subgroups over follow-up including a high AUD trajectory subgroup ( n = 37), a medium AUD trajectory subgroup ( n = 48), and a low AUD trajectory subgroup ( n = 16). Generalized estimating equations showed that greater sensitivity to alcohol’s pleasurable effects, including stimulation and hedonic and motivational reward (liking and wanting, respectively) predicted more AUD symptoms over follow-up ( p s<0.001) and were positively associated with AUD trajectory subgroups. However, sedation, heart rate, and cortisol response to alcohol were not significantly associated with AUD trajectory subgroups. In sum, greater alcohol stimulation, liking, and wanting prospectively predicted the continuation and increasing severity of AUD over a four-year period. The findings challenge theoretical models emphasizing reward deficit and global tolerance in addiction and support the role of positive reinforcement, indexed by sensitivity to alcohol’s pleasurable effects, as an important factor in AUD persistence. Article.Title: A living systematic review, meta-analysis, and open data resource of trials of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD
Article.Authors: Sevchik B.; Singleton S.; Lahey A.; Cuijpers P.; Harrer M.; Jones M.; Nayak S.; Strain E.; Vandekar S.; Yaden D.; Dworkin R.; Scott J.; Satterthwaite T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract 3,4-Methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) has emerged as a potential treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). However, rapidly changing evidence in a fast-moving field can be challenging to integrate. Here, we present a living systematic review and open-data meta-analytic resource on MDMA treatment for PTSD. In this initial release, 6 randomized controlled trials comprising 286 participants are included in the database. All six studies included in the review to date are sponsored by the Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies (MAPS). Our primary model uses inverse-variance random-effects meta-analysis of standardized mean differences on primary outcomes of PTSD. Compared to control conditions, MDMA-assisted therapy (MDMA-AT) showed a greater reduction in PTSD symptoms (Hedges’ g = −0.71). Meta-regressions on dosing variables were explored. Treatment with MDMA-AT as compared to placebo also resulted in higher response (risk ratio [ RR ] = 1.35) and remission ( RR = 2.25) rates. Most studies included in the database had a low risk of bias according to Cochrane guidelines, though these fail to capture pertinent challenges in the field such as expectancy, functional unblinding, potential issues with study conduct, and safety. The current findings were assigned an overall low certainty rating using the GRADE approach. Together, this systematic review and meta-analysis suggests that MDMA-AT results in short-term decreases in PTSD symptoms across studies to date. This living systematic review, meta-analysis, database, and online dashboard ( sypres.io ) will continue to be updated as evidence emerges, providing a valuable, open, and transparent resource for researchers in a rapidly evolving field.

Article.Title: Sperm phospholipase C signaling via PLCζ1 and PLCδ4 is essential for Ca2+ oscillations and fertility in mice
Article.Authors: Gupta N.; Zhang L.; Akizawa H.; Gervasi M.; Tourzani D.; Visconti P.; Romarowski A.; Buffone M.; Cui W.; Fissore R.
Article.Abstract: Fertilization-induced calcium (Ca 2+ ) oscillations are essential for egg activation and embryonic development in mammals. The sperm-specific phospholipase C isoform, PLCζ1, is the primary trigger of these oscillations. Functional and clinical studies have linked mutations or reduced expression of PLCζ1 to male infertility. However, whether PLCζ1 alone accounts for Ca 2+ release at fertilization in all mammals remains uncertain. Male mice lacking Plcζ1 exhibit subfertility and reduced litter sizes; their sperm induce delayed, low-frequency Ca 2+ oscillations, indicating a compensatory mechanism. Notably, mouse sperm express high levels of PLCδ4, essential for completing the acrosome reaction (AR). In Plcζ1 -null sperm, PLCδ4 is upregulated and retained post-AR. These observations suggest a secondary functional role for PLCδ4. Using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing, we generated Plcδ4 knockout (KO) mice. Plcδ4 -null sperm trigger attenuated, delayed Ca 2+ oscillations and significantly reduced fertilization rates, indicating that PLCδ4 contributes to but does not independently drive Ca 2+ signaling. We therefore generated a Double Knockout (DKO) mouse line lacking both sperm-enriched PLCs. DKO males were sterile, with sperm failing to induce Ca 2+ oscillations, and the isolated residual Ca 2+ rise was insufficient to activate eggs. These findings reveal that PLCζ1, the primary oscillator, and PLCδ4, a compensatory factor, work cooperatively within a complex, multi-component PLC system that ensures robust fertilization. This work reveals molecular specialization among mammals in initiating the fertilization Ca 2+ signals. It has implications for understanding male infertility, improving assisted reproductive technologies, and developing contraceptive strategies.

Article.Title: Phylogenetic evidence that migratory behavior increases ungulate extinction rates
Article.Authors: Abraham J.; O’Brien K.; Upham N.; Jesmer B.; Bibi F.; Faith J.
Article.Abstract: Widespread instances of migratory collapse have been documented within the past several decades, indicating that migration may be a fragile strategy in the Anthropocene. Yet the fragility of migration as a strategy for navigating seasonally variable resource availability may extend deeper into evolutionary time. We used phylogenetic imputation to infer the migratory habits of 51 ungulate species that went extinct during the late Quaternary and evaluated whether migration enhances extinction rates on macroevolutionary timescales. We found that ~80% (41 of 51) of recently extinct species were migratory, whereas only 46% (95 of 207) of extant ungulates are migratory. Furthermore, Hidden State Speciation and Extinction modeling indicated that migratory species likely experienced higher speciation and extinction rates compared to nonmigratory species, resulting in elevated lineage turnover for migratory ungulates, though diversification parameter estimates depended strongly upon whether extinct species were included in analyses. The extinctions of these ungulates led to negligible declines in global ungulate functional richness (0.8%) but more substantial declines (2.7%) across Africa. Altogether, our findings indicate that migration has complex macroevolutionary consequences, enhancing both speciation and extinction rates, which may render migration an evolutionarily fragile strategy, particularly as increasingly widespread and intensive anthropogenic activity cause gradients of resource availability to become severed ( e.g ., via human infrastructure) and more unpredictable ( e.g ., via climate change).

Article.Title: Can the exposome help solve the alcohol and cancer mystery?
Article.Authors: Vasiliou V.; Stem A.; Thompson D.
Article.Abstract: Alcohol consumption is a preventable driver of many cancers, yet a central biological question remains unresolved: by what mechanisms does ethanol promote malignancy? We propose that alcohol in the context of the exposome (i.e., the network of chemical, biological, and social determinants that interact with ethanol across the life span) provides a unifying framework for understanding alcohol-related carcinogenesis. Viewed through the lens of the exposome, alcohol is not only as a direct carcinogen but also as a systemic amplifier of environmental risk acting across multiple levels of biological organization, from molecular damage to whole-body physiology. This reframing has important implications for mechanistic research, precision prevention, and public-health policy.

Article.Title: Two parallel lateral hypothalamic GABAergic projections differentially modulate pain and anxiety in mice
Article.Authors: Sun Y.; Peng Y.; Zhang X.; Yin C.; Xiao C.; Chen J.; Zhou C.
Article.Abstract: The lateral hypothalamus (LH) is fundamentally involved in motivated behaviors, yet the precise functional segregation of its GABAergic projections in modulating pain and its affective dimensions remains poorly understood. Here, using male and female mice, we revealed that LH GABAergic neurons sent parallel projections to two pivotal pain and affect processing centers: the lateral parabrachial nucleus (LPB) and the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus (PVT). In vivo fiber photometry revealed that LH GABAergic terminals in both the PVT and LPB are robustly activated by noxious, aversive, and rewarding stimuli, indicating their roles in encoding salient and affective information. Critically, we uncovered a remarkable functional segregation of these LH GABAergic pathways. Optogenetic activation of the LH-PVT projection exerted anxiogenic effects without altering pain sensitivity in both naïve and neuropathic pain mice; whereas optogenetic inhibition of this pathway exerted significant analgesic and anxiolytic effects specifically in neuropathic pain, highlighting a context-dependent modulation of pain and affect. In contrast, optogenetic activation of the LH-LPB projection induced contralateral pronociception without impacting affective behaviors, conversely, inhibition of this pathway significantly elevated contralateral pain thresholds in both physiological and neuropathic pain conditions. We also demonstrated that stimulation of the LH-LPB projection acted via a disinhibitory mechanism involving local LPB GABAergic interneurons to enhance activity of LPB glutamatergic neurons. Collectively, our findings delineate two parallel and functionally segregated LH GABAergic output pathways that differentially control distinct aspects of pain experience, thereby offering novel circuit-specific targets for the treatment of chronic pain and its debilitating emotional comorbidities.

Article.Title: Saccadic suppression enhances saliency of ecologically relevant stimuli in the zebrafish optic tectum
Article.Authors: Soto G.; Thomas C.; Funk L.; Hladnik T.; Dehmelt F.; Hafed Z.; Arrenberg A.
Article.Abstract: Saccadic suppression, a reduction in visual sensitivity around the time of rapid eye movements, is well-documented in primate psychophysics, but its mechanisms and functions remain debated. Here, we use zebrafish to trace the origins of saccadic suppression, and we demonstrate how saccadic suppression selectively enhances the visual salience of ecologically relevant stimuli. Saccadic suppression thus contributes to more than just compensation for rapid saccade-induced image shifts. We first established a behavioral correlate of saccadic suppression in larval zebrafish escape behavior. Then, using electrophysiology, we show that retinal ganglion cells jumpstart saccadic suppression in a spatial frequency-dependent manner. Calcium imaging, combined with 360° visual stimulation and behavioral tracking, revealed that motor signals enhance peri-saccadic suppression strength in the optic tectum, where suppression lasts for more than 3,000 ms. Notably, saccadic suppression is much weaker and more short-lived for stimuli related to hunting or escape behavior than for behaviorally less relevant global flashes. This unequal attenuation effectively increases the salience of the ecologically relevant stimuli in the optic tectum after saccades. Our results demonstrate that saccadic suppression integrates visual and motor signals to optimize sensory processing within neural constraints, and they provide insights into evolutionarily conserved visual strategies.

Article.Title: Infant presence and mother-infant conflict predict fetal loss in wild mandrills
Article.Authors: Smit N.; Roura-Torres B.; Delaunay A.; Baniel A.; Huchard E.; Charpentier M.
Article.Abstract: Female fitness depends on reproductive pace and offspring survival, both of which are determined by the ability to balance resource allocation between current and future reproduction. Using 11 years of data on 356 pregnancies (52 of which resulted in fetal loss) from 117 wild female mandrills, we show that females who conceive while still caring for a young infant experience a greater probability of fetal loss as well as increased mother-infant behavioral conflict in the form of maternal rejection. In addition, females whose infants throw more tantrums show a greater probability of fetal loss, consistent with observations from other species where living offspring can interfere in parental reproduction. Finally, females who lose a fetus show greater subsequent reproductive success (produce more surviving infants and show shorter inter-birth intervals) than females who give birth but their infants die soon after birth. These findings suggest that fetal loss may represent an adaptive physiological response to the energetic constraints imposed by overlapping gestation and maternal care, potentially limiting the fitness costs associated with short inter-birth intervals and concurrent investment in multiple dependent offspring.

Article.Title: A deep genetic structure phylogenomically frames the closest algal relatives of land plants
Article.Authors: Bierenbroodspot M.; Kunz C.; Goldbecker E.; Lorenz M.; Irisarri I.; Pröschold T.; Darienko T.; de Vries J.
Article.Abstract: Discerning the nature of the last common ancestor of land plants (embryophytes) and algae allows to retrace the adaptations that ushered in the conquest of land by plants. For this, the closest streptophyte algal relatives of embryophytes hold key information. Albeit initially coming as a surprise due to their plain body plans, all major phylogenomic efforts have concluded that the Zygnematophyceae are the algal sisters to land plants. The Zygnematophyceae are the streptophyte algal class with the greatest species richness and while we now have ample genome information on a few select members of zygnematophytes, our understanding of the genomic divergence as well as genetic potential for key traits is limited by a lack of phylodiverse data that accounts for this diversity and integrates it into a phylogenomic framework. We here sequenced 43 new transcriptome datasets for the Zygnematophyceae and built a phylogenomic tree based on a total of 104 zygnematophyceaen transcriptomes and 2243 loci. We recover a deep genetic structure for the Zygnematophyceae: Despite the deep split between Spirogyrales and their unicellular sister group Desmidiales, most Spirogyrales emerged after pronounced genetic divergence, accommodating the attainment of multicellularity and divergent traits such as unique cell and plastid division. Overall, our data capture signatures of massive ancient radiations that could only be revealed thanks to a phylodiverse sampling. Recognizing the deep genetic divergences and a vast evolutionary history of the Zygnematophyceae are key to illuminate the nature of the algal progenitors of land plants.

Article.Title: A split nozzle and two-protein chain-like fibers define the tail architecture of Pseudomonas aeruginosa podophage A1002
Article.Authors: Pang H.; Chen Y.; Peng Z.; Xiao H.; Chen W.; Li X.; Chen P.; Zheng J.; Liu H.
Article.Abstract: Phage therapy offers unique advantages against antibiotic-resistant bacteria. However, high-resolution structural studies of phages targeting Pseudomonas aeruginosa —a top-seven global pathogen—particularly podophages, remain severely limited, directly impeding structure-based development of novel antimicrobials. In this study, we utilize cryo-EM to resolve the high-resolution intact structure of mature phage A1002, a podophage infecting carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa . Based on density maps combined with AlphaFold3 predictions, we identified 11 structural protein components from the head to the tail. Phage A1002 exhibits a distinctly elongated tail morphology distinct from other reported podophages. Notably, the A1002 nozzle employs a distinct assembly strategy, featuring the unique nozzle-rope protein and nozzle-base protein, which may have evolved through modular evolution and horizontal gene transfer. Furthermore, the nozzle-rope protein provides 11 adsorption sites for fiber dimers, and these dimers are assembled from two proteins, giving rise to two types of dimers: dimers 1–7 correspond to fiber I (gp40), and dimers 8–11 correspond to fiber II (gp41). The nozzle-rope protein and these dimers combine to form a chain-like fiber. The tail tube comprises a double-layered, elongated tube structure that functions to simultaneously increase tail length and provide docking sites for six chain-like fibers. These distinctive structural features provide the molecular basis for A1002’s broad-spectrum infection of drug-resistant P. aeruginosa and offer a novel molecular blueprint for rational design of structure-guided phage therapeutics.

Article.Title: The human hippocampus supports auditory coding and multisensory integration
Article.Authors: Raccah O.; Agarwal A.; Zhu Y.; Turk-Browne N.
Article.Abstract: The hippocampus receives convergent input from multiple sensory systems, yet in humans it has been studied almost exclusively through vision. Here we examine how the hippocampus contributes to sensory processing beyond the visual modality and to the multisensory integration of visual information with these other modalities. Participants were exposed to multiple repetitions of short naturalistic movie clips, each presented in four formats: auditory-only, visual-only, congruent audiovisual, and incongruent audiovisual (audio and video from different movies). Using high-resolution fMRI, we measured univariate activation and multivariate representations across the longitudinal axis and subfields of the human hippocampus. Whereas univariate analyses detected only visual responses across hippocampal subregions, with no activation for auditory stimuli and no benefit of congruent stimuli, multivariate analyses revealed robust representations of both auditory and visual scenes. The posterior hippocampus showed enhanced pattern similarity for congruent stimuli relative to unisensory stimuli, especially in the left hemisphere, demonstrating multisensory facilitation. The anterior hippocampus showed crossmodal decoding between auditory and visual versions of the same clip, driven by the right hemisphere, suggesting a more abstract representation. Finally, whole-brain searchlight analyses revealed parallel effects in cortical regions known to support multisensory integration. These findings advance understanding of auditory and multisensory coding in the human hippocampus, revealing specialization and lateralization along its longitudinal axis.

Article.Title: An open-source eye-tracking system adaptable to diverse terrestrial vertebrates reveals state-dependent visual acquisition in lizards
Article.Authors: Leberstein N.; Remenick T.; Becker M.; Shein-Idelson M.
Article.Abstract: Gaze shifts are fundamental to visual exploration and processing, yet empirical knowledge is largely confined to a small number of model species, limiting our understanding of general principles of visual acquisition across animals. Here, we introduce a versatile, low-cost, and open-source framework design for eye-tracking in small, freely moving animals. Leveraging photogrammetry, 3D modeling, and 3D-printing, we produce headmounts adaptable to diverse head-eye geometries, as we demonstrate for lizards, turtles, and mice. Detailed recordings in Pogona vitticeps, a laterally eyed ectotherm with a high-acuity retina, reveal a rich oculomotor repertoire with kinematics closely resembling the saccadic main sequence in primates. We found both movement-coupled large binocular saccades, which exhibited a strong axial bias as well as small, isotropic, and monocular saccades suggesting a capacity for visual exploration of local details. Visual acquisition strategies were strongly tied to behavioral states with periods of active sampling (3–5 Hz saccades) separated by periods of ocular stillness lasting many seconds and suggesting a visual acquisition strategy distinct from those commonly described in endothermic model species. Furthermore, active states were correlated with pupil constriction in contrast to mammals and similarly to birds. Our results demonstrate the utility of our experimental approach for understanding visual acquisition across terrestrial vertebrates. Such a multi-perspective view on natural visual acquisition across species will be essential for developing a generalized understanding of vision, its ecological functions, and its evolutionary trajectory.

Article.Title: LEM-3/ANKLE1 nuclease prevents the formation of abnormal syncytium to safeguard neuronal differentiation
Article.Authors: Deng S.; Zheng C.
Article.Abstract: In animal development, cells exit the cell cycle after a final round of cell division to differentiate into specialized cell types. However, the impact of failed cytokinesis on the fate specification of postmitotic cells, especially neurons, remains poorly understood. We analyzed the Caenorhabditis elegans mutants lacking the midbody-tethered endonuclease LEM-3/ANKLE1, which resolves chromatin bridges during cytokinesis. Using genetic analysis, fluorescence microscopy, and RNA visualization, we found that unresolved DNA bridges lead to the formation of stable intercellular bridges, creating binucleate syncytia between touch receptor neurons and sister cells, which allows thorough cytoplasmic mixing despite independent nuclear transcription. In some cases, the cytoplasmic linkage between sister cells also led to the suppression of neuronal fates and prevention of apoptotic fates. Thus, LEM-3 prevents syncytium formation to ensure proper cellular differentiation.

Article.Title: Emotion knowledge is structured in a grid-like coordinate system in the human ventromedial prefrontal cortex
Article.Authors: Ma Y.; Kragel P.
Article.Abstract: Human emotional experiences vary widely in everyday life, yet they are systematically organized within a continuous affective space defined by valence and arousal. Although this circumplex organization has shaped decades of research, its neural implementation remains unclear. Here, we asked whether abstract emotion concepts are encoded using grid-like coordinate principles in the human brain. During fMRI, participants tracked trajectories through affective space conveyed through morphs of facial expressions and sequences of phrases. We found that ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) encoded affective space with robust hexadirectional modulation characteristic of grid-like coding. This coordinate representation generalized across stimulus modalities, indicating abstraction beyond perceptual features. The grid-like signal reflected a metric organization of emotion concepts independent of overt behavior, whereas distance-related signals in vmPFC predicted trial-by-trial affective judgements. Together, these findings suggest that emotion knowledge is structured by a grid-like coordinate system in the human brain that can support predictive inference and flexible decision-making.

Article.Title: Fungal suppression by bacterial metabolite-activated human intestinal γδT-cells is disrupted in Crohn’s disease
Article.Authors: Mathew L.; Carlson S.; Savage M.; Pardieu C.; O’Brien M.; Crawley E.; Harrow P.; Kaune A.; Devlin E.; Priest E.; Crescente M.; Martinod K.; Boot J.; Ngan S.; Gasparetto M.; Kok K.; Lindsay J.; Richardson J.; Naglik J.; Stagg A.; Eberl M.; Sze S.; Munro C.; McCarthy N.
Article.Abstract: Gut symbionts condition mucosal immunity to resist infection by enteropathogens, but the specific microbes and mechanisms involved differ significantly between host species. In higher primates, bacterial metabolite HMB-PP is sensed by a specialized population of Vγ9Vδ2+T-cells, which we now report can potently suppress growth of endogenous fungi in human intestinal organ cultures. In healthy intestine, HMB-PP-stimulated Vδ2+ T-cells restricted outgrowth of keystone fungus Candida albicans via a mechanism that required IL-22. In Crohn’s disease (CD), Vδ2+ T-cells were poorly responsive to HMB-PP and permitted outgrowth of C. albicans strains that formed toxin-producing filaments, triggered neutrophil extracellular traps, and induced macrophage IL-1β release ex vivo . Genomic and proteomic analysis of the Candida isolates suggested increased tissue adhesion of CD-derived strains, which rapidly invaded the gut barrier in an ‘intestine-on-a-chip’ model. These data reveal that bacterial activation of Vδ2+ T-cells suppresses fungal pathobionts in human gut via an IL-22-dependent mechanism that is dysregulated in CD.

Article.Title: CFL1-dependency of discrete cell behaviours driving mouse spinal zippering
Article.Authors: Marshall A.; Krstevski A.; Crosswell H.; Shah R.; Maniou E.; Greene N.; Copp A.; Galea G.
Article.Abstract: Epithelial fusion is critical for formation of many embryonic tissues. The developing mammalian spinal cord fuses by zippering, through cell behaviours dependent on F-actin turnover. We propose a caudal-to-rostral sequence of surface ectoderm cell behaviours which drive zippering progression in mice, and test the requirement for the F-actin severing protein CFL1 in this process. Key zipper-advancing behaviours are: (i) constriction of supracellular actomyosin cables; (ii) extension of filopodial/lamellipodial protrusions at periodic intervals; (iii) constriction of leading-edge cell borders bringing together protrusions which establish ‘pioneering’ contacts across the midline; (iv) cell-cell and v. cell-ECM adhesion remodelling; (vi) zipper advancement through cell partner exchange. In wild-type embryos, CFL1 is enriched at the leading edge of surface ectoderm cells adjacent to the zippering point and localised within some protrusions. Conditional Cfl1 deletion in the surface ectoderm produces denser F-actin stress fibres, makes filopodial protrusions excessively stable, diminishes their exploratory movements which may establish nascent contacts, and impairs junctional constriction of cells at the point of fusion. Zippering speed is reduced ~30% in conditional Cfl1 -deleted embryos and ~30% develop spina bifida. We therefore propose that impaired filopodial dynamicity and junctional constriction limits the sequence of behaviours driving spinal zippering, predisposing to spina bifida.

Article.Title: Resistance mutation supply modulates the benefit of CRISPR immunity against virulent phages in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Article.Authors: Wright R.; Lovell S.; Richmond A.; Harrison C.; Ashworth E.; Kadioglu A.; Fothergill J.; Friman V.; Westra E.; Brockhurst M.
Article.Abstract: Only a fraction of bacterial genomes encode CRISPR-Cas systems, but the selective causes of this variation are unexplained. How naturally virulent bacteriophages (phages) select for CRISPR immunity has rarely been tested experimentally. Here, we show against a panel of genetically and functionally diverse virulent phages that CRISPR immunity was not universally beneficial to Pseudomonas aeruginosa , and its fitness effect varied strongly between phages in predictable ways. In addition to mechanisms known to alter the effectiveness of CRISPR immunity, such as encoding a matching spacer or a protective nuclear shell, we show that the fitness effect of CRISPR immunity negatively associated with the probability of evolving receptor-based resistance to the phage via spontaneous mutation. The supply of resistance mutations differed strongly between very closely related lipopolysaccharide-binding phages and was associated with variation at the C-terminus of the tail fibre protein altering residues involved in hydrogen bonding and the predicted binding site. Our results show that CRISPR immunity is more beneficial against virulent phages that are harder to evolve resistance to via receptor mutations, suggesting that virulent phage community composition and diversity will be important drivers of the prevalence of CRISPR immunity.

Article.Title: Transient feedforward communication between somatosensory and premotor cortex supports goal-directed behavior
Article.Authors: Ranjbar-Slamloo Y.; Kamigaki T.
Article.Abstract: Goal-directed behavior requires sensory information to be transformed into motor commands, yet the precise temporal structure of communication between sensory and motor cortices during this process remains poorly understood. By simultaneously recording spiking activity from primary somatosensory cortex (S1) and secondary motor cortex (M2) in mice performing a tactile delayed go/no-go task, we identified a brief, stimulus-triggered communication window that predicted behavioral success. Time-shifted canonical correlation analysis revealed a sharp, feedforward surge in S1 → M2 coupling peaking at a short latency, as expected for a potentially direct transmission pathway. This transient interaction conveyed stimulus-selective information such that the S1 → M2 communication subspace aligned with stimulus-coding axes in both regions. In contrast, M2 → S1 feedback interactions were weaker and delayed. Brief optogenetic suppression of S1 reduced both M2 stimulus selectivity and behavioral discriminability, consistent with a functional role of the transient S1 → M2 coupling. These findings demonstrate that sensorimotor transformation is supported not by sustained linear coupling along the stimulus- or choice- axis, but by a short-lived and highly selective feedforward communication channel that rapidly transmits reliable sensory representations into motor-planning circuits.

Article.Title: Full-length genomes evolve in parallel in a long-term evolution experiment with phage φX174
Article.Authors: Bons E.; Chabas H.; MacDonald H.; Escalera Ledermann A.; Ösze S.; Dunstan J.; Ochsner N.; Angst D.; Bonhoeffer S.; Regoes R.
Article.Abstract: The study of evolution in organisms with high mutation rates requires detailed data on the genomic composition of the population. Here we report on an innovative use of high-throughput sequencing technology combined with rapid experimental evolution that allowed us to follow the genetic diversification of four independent bacteriophage populations for 412 generations in extraordinary detail. One of our goals was to assess phylodynamic methods that use genetic information to infer key parameters of the population history. Because phylodynamic methods assume neutral evolution, we did not actively impose any selection pressures in our evolution experiment (in addition to those inherent in the bacterial cell environment). Tracing over 80′000 bacteriophage genomes, representing 884 distinct genotypes, we find that the patterns of viral diversification result in largely non-congruent genotype distributions, but also document multiple instances of parallel evolution. Unlike previous observations of parallelism in viral evolution, we do not just see the parallel evolution of mutations at single sites, but on the level of full-length genomes. Computer simulations that recapitulate our experiments in great detail show that this degree of parallelism is inconsistent with neutral evolution. We further show that the observed extent of parallel evolution biases phylodynamic analysis of migration rates, and wrongly estimates significant migration between the independent evolution lines. Our approach is applicable to many other viruses and paves the way to advanced population genetic investigations that aim to shed light on phenomena that relate to genetic linkage across the genome.

Article.Title: Viral disease outcomes are indistinguishable between experimentally infected bats and rodents
Article.Authors: Farrell M.; Tucker S.; Mollentze N.; Streicker D.
Article.Abstract: A common explanation for bats being a conspicuous source of zoonotic viruses is their purported ability to coexist with viruses without suffering overt disease. Widespread acceptance of the idea that bats have unusual antiviral traits has catalyzed the discovery of unique features of bat immune systems which may have translational value as broad-spectrum antivirals, particularly if they evolved as a byproduct of bats’ unique life history rather than through conventional co-evolutionary processes. Surprisingly, whether bats compared to other host groups suffer less disease from co-evolved viruses or from viruses generally has not been formally assessed. Here, synthesizing 86 years of experimental infections, involving 54 viruses, 85 host species, and over 5,600 animals, we document disease in bats following inoculation by taxonomically diverse viruses, including ones that are relatively benign in humans. The occurrence of overt disease, the likelihood of mortality, and the severity of disease in bats were indistinguishable from those experienced by rodents, another group associated with many zoonotic viruses. These patterns were consistent when considering only bat-associated viruses inoculated into bats and rodent-associated viruses inoculated into rodents and among inoculations which lacked shared co-evolutionary history. Instead, disease outcomes following infection were shaped by experimental design, viral host range, and evolutionary context. Unexceptional disease in bats from novel or co-evolved infections suggests that order-level host life history traits such as flight have inconsistent consequences for antiviral immunity and highlights the need to evaluate the functional properties of putatively unique features of bat immunity in vivo. While these results do not exclude the possibility of developing broader-acting or more potent antivirals from bat immune systems or diminish the potential value of mechanistic insights into bat immunity, they suggest that bat immune systems were shaped by conventional co-evolutionary processes rather than through unique circumstances that endow exceptional antiviral defenses.

Article.Title: fruitless is essential for male Aedes aegypti mosquito attraction to female flight sounds
Article.Authors: Loh Y.; Thornton A.; Loh W.; Lee T.; Chen W.; Xu Y.; Yap J.; Tsuchiya Y.; Eberl D.; Su M.; Kamikouchi A.
Article.Abstract: Male mosquitoes locate females through strong and innate attraction to female flight sounds, the basis of mating in the world’s deadliest animal. In contrast, females do not show any sound attraction behaviors. Despite being documented for almost a century, the molecular underpinnings of these behavioral dimorphisms remain unknown. Here, we found that by disrupting the male-specific isoform of fruitless (referred to as fruM ) in Aedes aegypti , fruM mutant males show complete abolition of sound attraction behaviors, resulting in failure of mutant males to locate females for mating. We identified strong fruitless expression in control male ears, with the loss of FruM severely disrupting mutant male ability to amplify female flight sounds. fruM mutant male ears also propagate frequency-specific, sound-evoked electrical signals at about one-sixth the magnitude of control males, significantly reducing the amount of auditory information relayed to the brain. fruitless thus plays a significant role in determining proper male peripheral hearing function underlying mating. Transcriptomic analyses of mosquito ears identified essential hearing genes under the transcriptional influence of FruM via direct or indirect actions, thus shaping male-specific hearing cellular machineries that support male attraction to female flight sounds. Our work demonstrates that FruM commands male-specific hearing behaviors involved in mating by directly controlling the earliest stages of auditory organ performance, sound amplification and acoustic signal detection. Our findings show that FruM is essential for male-specific reproductive behaviors in mosquitoes.

Article.Title: Pollinator abundance shapes sexual selection in an angiosperm
Article.Authors: Barbot E.; Dufaÿ M.; Janicke T.; Lapeyre B.; Orcel D.; Rousset F.; Tonnabel J.
Article.Abstract: Sexual selection is a central force in evolutionary biology that has been shown to shape phenotypes and population dynamics in animals. While this selective force is increasingly recognized in flowering plants, theory predicts that anisogamy generates sex differences in the fitness benefits of acquiring additional mates—a pattern well supported in animals but with limited tests in plants. Plant studies rely solely on genetic parentage analyses to estimate mate numbers, thereby conflating performance in accessing mates with success in gamete fertilization. Pollinators add an ecological layer, as their behavior and abundance can influence competition for access to mates and their gametes. Here, we disentangle consecutive episodes of sexual selection in the hermaphroditic plant Brassica rapa by combining direct observations of Bombus terrestris movements with genetic paternity analyses in experimental populations, thus providing independent estimates of the observational number of mates acquired and realized fertilization success. Our approach identifies pollen competition for ovules as the primary arena for sexual selection in B. rapa . Competition for access to mates constitutes a secondary force and was found to be stronger in the male compared to the female sex function, as predicted by classic theory. Experimentally reduced pollinator abundance modulated the balance between pre- and post-pollination sexual selection, increasing the opportunity for selection on mate acquisition. Ignoring pollinator movements led to biased estimates of pre-pollination sexual selection. Our findings demonstrate that sexual selection in plants unfolds across multiple, sequential episodes shaped by ecological context.

Article.Title: Tolerance measured at one developmental stage mispredicts climate resilience in an animal with a complex life cycle
Article.Authors: Song H.; Shi T.; Yang M.; Liu X.; Li Z.; Shi P.; Wu Y.; Allam B.; Jeffs A.; Skelton B.; Zhang T.
Article.Abstract: Forecasts of whether marine species can evolve fast enough to survive climate change rely largely on single-stage tolerance assays, tacitly assuming that tolerance measured at one developmental stage reflects adaptive capacity across the organism’s life cycle. We test this assumption in a common marine bivalve ( Mercenaria mercenaria ) and find that it fails in sign, not degree: larval and post-metamorphic tolerance to end-century ocean acidification are strongly negatively correlated ( r = −0.53, 95% CI [−0.69, −0.33]) across family-level, pedigree-conditioned and animal model estimates, with pervasive rank reversals among the top performers of each stage. A multivariate analysis of the among-family covariance matrix G shows why: under acidification, 57% of the among-family variance collapses onto a single dominant axis that loads positively on every larval trait and negatively on every post-metamorphic trait, whereas under ambient conditions the same families show no cross-stage covariance at all. Acidification therefore does not merely depress performance—it reorganizes the genetic architecture into a cross-stage conflict. Under ramping RCP 8.5 forcing this conflict geometry dictates the direction—not merely the magnitude—of adaptation: only balanced multi-stage selection preserves family diversity, whereas single-stage selection systematically erodes the opposite axis. In complex life cycles, resilience is a geometric property of ontogeny that forecasts cannot compress into a single-stage without inverting the sign of the answer.

Article.Title: High-resolution paleobiome reconstructions highlight ecological and historical dynamics underpinning global terrestrial vertebrate diversity
Article.Authors: Skeels A.; Rogger J.; Cardillo M.; Farnsworth A.; Lunt D.; Karger D.
Article.Abstract: Past climate change has repeatedly reshaped Earth’s biomes, yet how their expansion and contraction influence biodiversity patterns through time remains unclear. Competing hypotheses propose that either historical biome area has a strong influence on diversity, or that biodiversity responds rapidly to environmental change, such that present-day biome area and energy are sufficient to explain diversity patterns. Progress in testing these ideas has been limited by sparse and inconsistent proxy data and the coarse resolution of existing paleoclimate models. Here, we reconstructed global biome histories for the Cenozoic (66–0 Ma) by downscaling five different paleoclimate simulations. Estimates of change in biome area through time were generally consistent among alternative climate models and with the empirical proxy record. Accounting for variation among models, we found that present-day area and energy were consistently better predictors of vertebrate diversity than historical measures. These findings suggest biodiversity tracks the ecological limits set by shifting biomes, leaving sparse legacy of past dynamics. Our results highlight the importance of integrating multiple paleoclimate reconstructions when assessing the historical drivers of biodiversity.

Article.Title: A cortical semantic map integrates fractions and integers in the human brain
Article.Authors: Valério D.; Debray S.; Karami A.; Cauté M.; Gravel N.; Dehaene S.
Article.Abstract: How does the human brain represent the meaning of abstract symbols? Some theories postulate the existence of semantic spaces where concepts occupy positions that reflect their conceptual relationships. In the number domain, psychological evidence suggests that integers are represented along a mental number line which, with education, integrates higher-level number concepts such as fractions. To test this hypothesis, we recorded whole-brain 7T fMRI responses to integer and fraction symbols during an active magnitude comparison task designed to engage magnitude processing. Consistent with predictions, we found both behavioral and neural numerical distance effects. Activation vectors in intraparietal, inferior temporal, prefrontal, hippocampal, and parahippocampal cortices formed a two-dimensional semantic space organized by numerical magnitude and domain (fractions versus integers). Gaussian fits revealed a topographic map of numerical preferences in the anterior inferior parietal cortex, common to both domains. Our results suggest that, when educated adults engage in an explicit magnitude comparison task, their brain can construct an ordered representation that integrates fractions and integers, with a topographic organization in the anterior IPS/IPL.

Article.Title: Host–virus interactions dominate fitness and conceal additive genetic variation
Article.Authors: Belyi A.; Du Y.; Wilson A.; Longdon B.; Jiggins F.
Article.Abstract: Host–parasite coevolution is expected to generate strong selection for resistance and infectivity that has the potential to erode genetic variation. Despite this, natural populations often retain extensive genetic variation in these traits. Genotype-by-genotype interactions on fitness can generate negative frequency-dependent selection, which helps maintain this variation by preventing any host or pathogen genotype from retaining a permanent advantage. Because these interactions place genetic variance in the interaction term rather than in additive differences among hosts or pathogens, that variance is masked from directional selection and can remain ‘cryptic’. Here we combine coevolutionary modelling with large‑scale experimental infection assays to quantify how host-pathogen interactions structure fitness variance in a vertically transmitted virus system, Drosophila melanogaster and sigma virus. Simulations show that coevolution typically erodes additive genetic variance in host and pathogen fitness, concentrating variance in host-virus interaction terms. Consistent with these predictions, experiments spanning 90 host-virus genotype combinations reveal that transmission, viral load, and virulence are overwhelmingly governed by host-virus genetic interactions rather than host or virus main effects. As a result, neither host resistance alleles nor viral genotypes confer consistently higher fitness across genetic backgrounds. Interactions tend to be sex‑specific, further limiting heritable fitness variation. Our results demonstrate that coevolution can substantially mask heritable genetic variation from directional selection by rendering fitness context-dependent. This extensive cryptic genetic variation may be revealed either when ecological or evolutionary conditions shift, or when the process of coevolution itself alters the direction of selection. This demonstrates the need to account for genotype-specific interactions when forecasting evolutionary responses.

Article.Title: A macrophage-targeted TIMD4 Peptide-Nanoparticle attenuates colitis symptoms and monocyte recruitment in a mouse model
Article.Authors: Liu H.; Wang Y.; Yu R.; Liu K.; Zheng D.; Wang B.; Chang Y.; Liu B.; Yue X.; Wu Z.; Li C.; Liang X.; Ma C.; Liu G.; Li J.; Xu L.; Gao L.
Article.Abstract: Macrophages play a pivotal role in the pathogenesis of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). T-cell immunoglobulin and mucin domain-containing molecule 4 (TIMD4) is involved in the regulation of tissue-resident macrophages. TIMD4 expression is elevated in colonic tissues from patients with ulcerative colitis (UC) and mice with dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis, but its role in IBD pathogenesis remains unclear. In this study, we found that Timd4 deficiency aggravated DSS-induced colitis, accompanied by increased infiltration of monocytes into the colonic tissues. Treatment with a CCR2 antagonist attenuated colonic inflammation and reduced monocyte infiltration into colonic tissues in Timd4 KO mice. Mechanistically, in vitro studies revealed that TIMD4 stabilized the LKB1-STRAD-MO25 complex via its intracellular domain, thereby activating the AMPK pathway and suppressing NF-κB-dependent chemokine production in macrophages. Based on these findings, we designed a TIMD4-derived peptide and developed a macrophage-targeted nanoparticle system (T4 (365–378) ‑NPs). Treatment with T4 (365–378) -NPs reduced P65 phosphorylation and attenuated DSS-induced colitis in mice. Treatment with either T4 (365–378) -NPs or the CCR2 antagonist attenuated DSS-induced colitis, and no statistically significant differences in the assessed outcomes were detected between the two groups. Administration of T4 (365–378) -NPs before DSS exposure also attenuated subsequent colitis. Furthermore, combining the T4 (365–378) ‑NPs with anti-α4β7 or anti-TNF-α antibodies produced greater improvements than either monotherapy in the DSS-induced colitis model. Article.Title: Non-adaptive evolutionary forces predominantly shape nucleotide composition near human transcription start sites
Article.Authors: Qiu Y.; Hebraud E.; Pouyet F.; Palazzo A.
Article.Abstract: In the human genome, mutation rates vary along genes, yet how their fine-scale structure contributes to gene evolution has remained largely unexplored. Here, we map inherited mutations at single-nucleotide resolution and uncover a striking hypermutation peak at transcription start sites (TSSs) of human protein-coding genes. This pattern is observed both in population polymorphisms and in de novo mutations from parent-offspring trios, and is dependent on transcriptional activity in testes. We also find similar hypermutation peaks at TSSs used to produce long noncoding RNAs and at intergenic RNA Polymerase II pause sites. In addition, we identify distinct mutational signatures at exon-intron boundaries and in introns. By comparing the current nucleotide content to predicted equilibrium levels, inferred from mutation and fixation rates, and by analyzing derived ancestral frequency spectrums, we detect signals that are compatible with a low level of ongoing background GC-biased gene conversion (gBGC) throughout the region and ancestral elevated gBGC activity that is centered right downstream from the TSS. Using a forward-in-time simulation algorithm, we show that the current nucleotide composition surrounding the TSS of protein-coding genes is best explained by local mutation biases coupled to ongoing and ancestral patterns of gene conversions. Our simulations allow us to infer several features of these gBGC events. Overall, these findings indicate that the nucleotide composition around TSSs is largely shaped by non-adaptive forces, particularly mutation bias and gBGC.

Article.Title: Oxidative signaling thresholds shape vulnerability in the central and peripheral nervous systems
Article.Authors: Wakatsuki S.; Araki T.
Article.Abstract: Neurodegeneration is frequently associated with oxidative stress, yet the mechanisms that convert reactive oxygen species (ROS) into irreversible degenerative signals remain incompletely understood. Neurons in the central and peripheral nervous systems often differ in their responses to injury, but these differences cannot be reduced to a simple contrast between weak and strong antioxidant capacity. This Essay proposes that neuronal vulnerability is shaped by multilayered signaling thresholds comprising ROS production, antioxidant and thiol buffering, redox-sensitive signal detection, molecular gating, and commitment to degeneration, survival, or repair. This framework may help explain selective neuronal vulnerability in neurodegenerative diseases and identify intervention points downstream of global ROS suppression.

Article.Title: A systematic fluorescently tagged protein toolkit for dissecting apical extracellular matrix patterning in C. elegans
Article.Authors: Ragle J.; Pooranachithra M.; Ashley G.; Cadena E.; Blank B.; Kang K.; Chen C.; Bhowmick A.; Mercado S.; Wells T.; Clancy J.; Chisholm A.; Ward J.
Article.Abstract: Barrier epithelia are shielded from the external environment by their apical extracellular matrices (aECMs). The molecular complexity of aECMs has challenged understanding of their organization in vivo. We developed efficient pipelines for modular protein tagging and rapid fluorophore swapping. Most tagged collagens were functional and exhibited exquisitely specific patterning across stages, cell types, and matrix substructures. We define multiple reference markers for key substructures including the little-understood cortical layer, as well as the helical crossed fiber arrays that function as a hydrostatic skeleton to maintain organismal shape. We further tagged 30 members of key aECM protein classes including proteases, protease inhibitors, and lipid transporters. Article.Title: Interindividual vocal tract diversity influences the phonetic diversification of spoken languages
Article.Authors: Moran S.; Danner T.; Ponce de León M.; Zollikofer C.
Article.Abstract: Human vocal tracts, like other physical traits, exhibit extensive interindividual variation. However, little is known about how this variation translates into phonetic diversity between speakers, and ultimately, across languages. Here we develop a biocultural model of phonetic evolution, analogous to Russell Lande’s model of multivariate phenotypic evolution. We show that individual vocal tract morphologies and associated articulatory strategies leave consistent acoustic signatures, resulting in a characteristic pattern of phonetic variation within speaker groups that correlates with the pattern observed between groups. Recalling a central tenet of evolutionary biology—that within-group variation feeds between-group diversification—our findings suggest that phonologically similar vowel systems can attain phonetically diverse realizations according to a neutral-like evolutionary process. Our model serves as a null hypothesis for disentangling the biological versus cultural mechanisms underlying phonetic diversification, where deviations from the neutral expectation may indicate culturally mediated language change.

Article.Title: Bridging energy and proteome allocation models allows prediction of the resource cost of traits across environments
Article.Authors: Meghrazi M.; Otto S.
Article.Abstract: Many traits divert resources from reproduction and are costly due to the physiological trade-offs organisms face. These traits might require the allocation of different resources, e.g., energy expenditure or production of macromolecules, and it is unclear how their costs can be compared given their different units. Moreover, the effect of environmental conditions and genetic background on the cost of traits is not well understood. Two different frameworks have been proposed to quantify the resource costs of traits, focusing on either energy allocation or proteome allocation. These frameworks implicitly assume energy provisioning or protein production limits growth, respectively, but the connection between the two limitations has been underexplored. To better connect these frameworks, we develop a framework that considers limitations in energy provisioning and macromolecule biosynthesis simultaneously to quantify and compare the cost of traits that require different resources. Using this model, we explore how environmental quality and genetic background affect the cost of traits. Notably, our model predicts that increasing food quality increases the cost of traits that require the production of new structures, while decreasing the cost of traits requiring energy expenditure. Moreover, our model makes novel predictions about the effect of degradation, recycling, and energetic demands for maintenance on the relationship between the macromolecular composition of the cells and growth rate (also known as bacterial growth laws).

Article.Title: Eye movements reflect capacity-dependent organization of working memory
Article.Authors: Huang Q.; Doeller C.
Article.Abstract: Human cognition is capacity-limited, requiring strategies to actively structure information. Eye movements offer a natural mechanism for sequential sampling, but whether such sequences reflect memory organization is unknown. We developed a working-memory task where color-frequency pairings created a latent ordinal structure to optimally reduce memory load. Across two experiments, gaze patterns spontaneously aligned with this structure. Participants sampled items following this sequence during encoding and revisited them during maintenance. Critically, the expression of this structure depended on cognitive demand. In a 3-item task, high performers showed robust sequential sampling during encoding, whereas lower performers compensated with replay-like revisitation during maintenance. Under higher demand (4 items), encoding-based organization was disrupted, and structured revisitation emerged primarily during maintenance. These findings suggest that eye movements provide an overt expression of an internally generated organizational process that flexibly adapts to cognitive demands, revealing a behavioral analogue to neural replay when encoding resources are strained.

Article.Title: PrimeStack editors enable efficient and site-specific integration of large multigene cargos in plants
Article.Authors: Sánchez E.; Sedeek K.; Butt H.; Mahfouz M.
Article.Abstract: Precise, site-specific integration of large DNA sequences into plant genomes is a long-standing goal of crop biotechnology and synthetic biology, yet remains constrained by random insertion, inefficient homologous recombination, and gene targeting. Optimized prime editors first install attP landing sites with high fidelity and heritability followed by Bxb1-mediated recombination that generates irreversible integration of genetic information. PrimeStack enabled targeted large-cargo integration in regenerated rice plants with efficiencies of up to 45%, as determined by junction-specific PCR analyses. No obvious morphological differences from WT plants were observed at 5 weeks after transfer to soil under the evaluated conditions. We validate its utility by achieving targeted insertion of a carotenoid cassette at an experimentally confirmed genomic safe harbor. PrimeStack delivers a modular, site-specific gene stacking platform that enables predictable, multigene trait pyramiding and pathway construction at GSH, thereby accelerating the development of improved and resilient crop varieties, as well as scalable plant-based biomanufacturing and a powerful chassis for synthetic biology.

Article.Title: An inositol receptor Itr4 coordinates carbon catabolite regulation and virulence in Cryptococcus neoformans
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Tancer R.; Wear M.; Jackson K.; Zhang Y.; Li K.; Wang J.; Gao Y.; Nielsen K.; Casadevall A.; Xue C.
Article.Abstract: Nutrient sensing and utilization are critical for microbes to adapt to their environment and evade predators. The encapsuled yeast Cryptococcus neoformans has a unique ability to sense and utilize the sugar inositol as both a signaling molecule and as a carbon source. This trait is advantageous not only in the natural environment but also to promote its pathogenesis, including invasion of the central nervous system. Itr4 binds inositol and regulates the function of other ITR s and its loss leads to a significant decrease in inositol uptake activity, resulting in a lack of mating, reduced capsule size, reduced blood–brain barrier (BBB) penetration, and virulence attenuation. Mutagenesis analysis of Itr4 protein identified an essential N-terminal tail and two amino acids, Q388 and Q389, as sites of functional importance. The ITR4 Q388A, Q389A allele showed a dominant phenotype with increased inositol uptake, enlarged capsule and significantly attenuated virulence. Article.Title: The Cryptococcus neoformans titanide is a pathogenic cell type that arises from typical yeast cells in response to host conditions
Article.Authors: Potton A.; Kalinina I.; Brown G.; Makarova M.; Catania S.; Corzo-Leon D.; Ballou E.
Article.Abstract: Fungal morphogenesis is a major driver of disease outcome. One such cell type is the small, oval, titanide (2–4 µm). This poorly understood cell type is prevalent in lung histology as well as host-relevant in vitro conditions. In conditions that generate cellular heterogeneity, titanides comprise 4%–10% of cells 24 hours post-induction and by 72 hours are the dominant cell type. Despite their prevalence and the significance of cryptococcal morphogenesis for virulence, key questions pertaining to their origin, fate, and underlying biology remain unstudied. Using TEM, SEM, and fluorescence microscopy we demonstrate that titanides display distinct morphological features; they possess thin cell walls, single birth scars, and capsules, with reduced Pathogen-Associated Molecular Pattern exposure and altered distribution. These features distinguish titanides from previously described C. neoformans ‘small cells’ such as in vivo seed cells (6 µm, high cell-wall mannan content) and micro cells (round, <1 μm, with thick cell walls) among others. Using microfluidics, we reveal that titanides arise from yeast-like ‘typical’ mothers, highlighting the morphological plasticity of typical cells in host-relevant conditions. Upon birth, titanides have compact nuclei and do not immediately proliferate, but transfer to fresh media results in rapid swelling and cell division. Consistent with this, titanides are more resistant to some cell wall/membrane stressors and are an effective infectious propagule in a murine model. Together, these findings establish a definition and essential characterisation of the titanide cell type and provide new insight into a key player in C. neoformans cell biology and pathogenesis.

Article.Title: Recombination shapes the dynamics of selective constraint in global populations of human gut bacteria
Article.Authors: Liu Z.; Good B.
Article.Abstract: The ratio of nonsynonymous to synonymous substitutions (dN/dS) encodes important information about the selection pressures acting on protein-coding genes. In bacterial populations, dN/dS often declines with the sequence divergence between strains, but the mechanisms responsible for this broad empirical trend are still debated. Existing models have primarily focused on de novo mutations, overlooking the older genetic variants that are continually introduced through horizontal gene transfer and recombination. Here we introduce a phenomenological model of dN/dS in recombining populations of bacteria, which allows us to disentangle the effects of recombination among pairs of closely related strains. We find that clonally inherited regions of the genome exhibit consistently higher dN/dS ratios, and that the accumulation of recombined segments can quantitatively explain the majority of the decline in dN/dS. We use these observations to re-examine models of purifying selection and adaptive reversion in human gut bacteria, and uncover evidence for widespread weak selection at a large fraction of protein-coding sites. Our findings show that horizontal gene transfer can be an important factor in shaping genome-wide patterns of selective constraint, and raise new questions about the effectiveness of natural selection in complex bacterial populations.

These findings reveal a ubiquitin-dependent mechanism that restricts morphogen-induced gene expression and ensures timely developmental progression.

Article.Title: Pharmacological blockade of p65 palmitoylation modulates NF-κB transcriptional activity
Article.Authors: Zhang J.; Hu L.; Sun L.; Che J.; Yates J.; Park J.; Wu X.
Article.Abstract: Nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) regulates inflammation and immunity and is frequently dysregulated in autoimmune diseases, inflammatory disorders, and cancers. Cytokines and pathogens activate NF-κB transcription factors, and nutrients and metabolites, including fatty acids, also modulate its activation, though the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we report that RelA (p65), a major component of the NF-κB transcription complex, is autopalmitoylated at cysteine 197 and 206. Palmitoylation of p65 enhances its nuclear localization and p65-p50 complex formation, thereby increasing NF-κB transcriptional activities. We further show that licochalcone D, a small-molecule anti-inflammatory compound, directly inhibits RelA/p65 autopalmitoylation, suggesting it may act through an additional mechanism. These results indicate that fatty acid metabolism can directly regulate NF-κB activity through p65 palmitoylation and suggest that targeting p65 autopalmitoylation may be a therapeutic strategy for diseases with dysregulated NF-κB signaling.

Article.Title: BATF condensation drives gastric cancer metastasis via chromatin association and transcriptional regulation
Article.Authors: Feng T.; Deng Z.; Deng K.; Zhang L.; Yang L.; Lu Y.; Chen H.; Kerr D.; Yao X.; Yang J.; Jiang H.
Article.Abstract: While liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) is understood to be relevant with various types of cancers, the relationship between LLPS and gastric cancer (GC) remains ambiguous. In this study, we demonstrate that the basic leucine zipper ATF-like transcription factor (BATF) shows increased DNA-binding activity and expression in GC tissues and cell lines, based on assay for transposase-accessible chromatin sequencing (ATAC-seq) and RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analyses. Article.Title: Optogenetic reduction of theta oscillations induces remapping of time cells without memory impairment
Article.Authors: Yong H.; Chang H.; Brandon M.
Article.Abstract: In a delayed alternation spatial working memory task, hippocampal time cells fire during specific moments of the delay period to form a sequential representation of the entire delay interval. The causal relationship between these sequences and working memory remains unclear. Similarly, hippocampal theta oscillations are thought to support working memory, primarily through the generation of time cell sequences. To causally examine these relationships, we optogenetically silence the medial septal GABAergic theta-generating circuit during the delay portion of a delayed spatial alternation task. With hippocampal theta oscillations substantially reduced, many time cells exhibit remapping, and new time cells are recruited. Despite partial remapping of time cell sequences, behavioral performance remains intact and trajectory-specific coding is preserved, suggesting that task-relevant information remains available under theta disruption.

Article.Authors: Ge P.; Rashid F.; Gaarthuis L.; Cajili M.; Tan M.; Pang B.; Schnetz K.; Dame R.
Article.Abstract: Escherichia coli is highly sensitive to acid and osmotic stress but adapts by modulating the expression of stress-responsive genes. Nucleoid-associated proteins (NAPs) play key roles in DNA organization and sensing environmental changes. H-NS may alter local chromatin structure to modulate the expression of such genes in response to environmental stress. The H-NS homolog suppressor of td phenotype A (StpA) co-regulates several target genes, but its role is poorly defined. Article.Abstract: Neuronal activity causes topoisomerase IIβ (TOP2B) to form DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) within the promoters of early response genes (ERGs), such as Fos and Npas4. Article.Authors: Webber C.; van der Spek S.; Cruz A.; Puri S.; Shao Y.; Zhang C.; Aw J.; Papadimitriou G.; Roberts R.; Jiang K.; Tran T.; Zhang L.; Taylor A.; Wang Z.; Tobunluepop K.; Ellini M.; Porter J.; Sotiropoulos I.; Emili A.; Silva J.; Li H.; Wolozin B.

Article.Authors: Li S.; Hong Y.; Deng S.; Wu X.; Jia Z.; Liu Y.; Liu Y.; Wu G.; Chen Y.; Wu A.; Gao X.; Chen Z.
Article.Abstract: Dysregulated mRNA translation is a critical driver of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) progression. Article.Authors: Lou L.; Feng H.; Zhang X.; Wang H.; Fan Y.; Tao Y.; Zhang Z.; Lin C.; Sun Y.; Zhang L.
Article.Abstract: Lenvatinib is a first-line therapy for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), yet resistance remains a major clinical challenge. Article.Authors: Zhang C.; Li F.; Gao M.; Ma J.; Wang S.; Xiao B.; Zhong B.; Zhang J.
Article.Abstract: Metabolic enzymes are increasingly recognized for "moonlighting" functions beyond their primary metabolic roles. Article.Abstract: AKT hyperactivation is a hallmark of many human cancers and contributes to poor clinical outcomes, yet the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood.
