Article.Title: Baseline microbial ecology encodes probiotic responsiveness through distinct metabolic and network configurations
Article.Authors: Li J.; Özkurt A.; Baertschi I.; Wang J.; Aeschlimann L.; Goepfert C.; Misselwitz B.; Sokollik C.; Yilmaz B.
Article.Abstract: Probiotic efficacy in inflammatory bowel disease varies widely between individuals, and the sources of that variability remain poorly understood. D-lactate is a microbiota-derived metabolite that accumulates during intestinal inflammation and is associated with epithelial barrier dysfunction, which motivated our use of a consortium selected to contribute none of it. Here we show that its benefit is not an intrinsic property of the administered strains but is determined by the pre-existing ecological state of the recipient microbiome. Across three independent mouse resources, preventive administration reduced disease severity and histopathological damage only where baseline communities carried higher diversity and more complex co-occurrence architecture; in those animals the consortium preserved community structure and metabolic output, restoring disease-disrupted metabolites, and selectively raising butyrate and propionate. Sustained exogenous D-lactate did not abolish protection, placing D-lactate as a tractable readout of ecological restoration rather than its effector. Responsiveness is encoded in the baseline microbiota and predictable before intervention, establishing probiotic efficacy as a stratifiable property of the host microbiome.

Article.Title: RAStoERK: A reference interaction atlas for insights into signaling and disease
Article.Authors: Vucak G.; Didusch S.; Cannizzaro L.; Santiago A.; Hartl M.; Menche J.; Baccarini M.
Article.Abstract: The RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK pathway has been extensively studied for its roles in physiology and disease, yet a systems-level view of its interplay with the broader cellular context is lacking, limiting insight into paralog-specific roles, mutation-driven rewiring, and cross-pathway integration. To address this, we simultaneously mapped the interactomes of all pathway components and their activating and inactivating mutations, identifying 2,500 high-confidence interactors, 88% of which previously unreported, and generating a high-confidence, comprehensive reference map of the pathway in resting and activated states. The pathway behaves like a "molecular organism" that connects to other signaling complexes, operates from distinct subcellular sites, and integrates into networks relevant to physiology and disease. Dataset exploration uncovers paralog- and mutation-specific interaction signatures and pathway-level crosstalk, including previously unknown connections to mRNA metabolism and WNT signaling. The interactomes available at RAStoERK.univie.ac.at provide a foundational community resource for unbiased discovery, targeted mechanistic studies, and potential therapeutic exploration.

Article.Title: Mechanisms of vesicular monoamine transporter 2 modulation by amphetamines and lobeline
Article.Authors: Wu D.; Liu C.; Wang H.; Chi C.; Wang Y.; Zhang W.; Wang X.; Jiang D.
Article.Abstract: Amphetamine-type stimulants (ATSs) disrupt the brain monoaminergic system and strongly stimulate motivation, movement, and addiction. Vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2) plays a vital role in monoaminergic neurotransmission by sequestering monoamines in presynaptic vesicles. How ATS binds to and regulates VMAT2 remains elusive. Here, we report the cryo-EM structures of human VMAT2 in complex with four ATSs (AMPH, METH, MDMA, and MDA) and the inhibitor lobeline, revealing the molecular mechanisms underlying ATS recognition and modulation. ATSs mimic monoamines and occupy the substrate-binding site of VMAT2, indicating that ATSs function as substrates and thus redistribute the vesicular monoamine pools to the cytosolic pools. Lobeline adopts an unexpected dual-binding mode and locks VMAT2 in a lumen-facing conformation, inhibiting monoamine and ATS uptake. Our dopamine release assay revealed that lobeline regulates AMPH-induced dopamine release by modulating both VMAT2 and DAT. This study provides important mechanistic insights into VMAT2 modulation by amphetamines and lobeline.

Article.Title: Embryonic reprogramming drives anaplastic transformation in thyroid carcinoma
Article.Authors: Kawaura R.; Unome A.; Tomita H.; Ishihara H.; Kuroki M.; Komura S.; Kato K.; Takashima S.; Nishio N.; Shigeyama M.; Hirata T.; Ishii R.; Kimura S.; Tsunekawa S.; Akiyama H.; Hara A.; Yamada Y.; Ogawa T.; Shibata H.
Article.Abstract: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) is a highly aggressive malignancy that often arises through anaplastic transformation of papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC). Although genetic drivers such as BRAF and TP53 mutations are implicated, the mechanisms underlying this transition remain poorly understood. Here, we show that human ATC loses thyroid differentiation and acquires pluripotency-associated features, accompanied by MAPK pathway activation. Guided by parallels with induced pluripotent stem cell reprogramming, we develop an in vivo reprogramming mouse model. Forced expression of Oct3/4, Sox2, Klf4, and c-Myc (OSKM) induces anaplastic transformation of Braf-mutant thyroid epithelium even without Trp53 mutation, yielding an ATC-like phenotype that shares molecular and histological features with human ATC. A conventional Braf/Trp53-mutant model shows similar features. Reintroduction of NKX2-1 into human and murine ATC cells partially reverses embryonic reprogramming, suppresses proliferation and induces redifferentiation toward a PTC-like phenotype. Embryonic reprogramming is a central driver of anaplastic transformation and supports redifferentiation strategies.

Article.Title: SIR2-mediated filament assembly activates the NLR-like protein Avs5 for bacterial antiviral defense
Article.Authors: Wang C.; Xie J.; Shen Z.; Ehrmann J.; Yu C.; Fang M.; Wu H.; Fu T.
Article.Abstract: Like mammalian nucleotide-binding and oligomerization domain receptors (NLRs), bacterial NLR-like proteins mediate antiviral defense. Avs5, a representative of a large family of short bacterial NLR-like proteins, contains an N-terminal SIR2 effector, a central nucleotide-binding domain (NBD), and a C-terminal sensor domain. Whereas canonical inflammasome NLRs use NBD oligomerization to nucleate effector-domain filaments, Avs5 forms SIR2-mediated filaments that couple receptor assembly to NADase activation. In the resting state, ATP-bound Avs5 is monomeric and subsequently forms a SIR2-mediated dimer that likely represents an intermediate in a stepwise activation pathway. Upon activation, ATP-dependent conformational remodeling of the NBD promotes conversion of these dimers into active filaments. Structure-guided mutagenesis, biochemical assays, and functional analyses show that filament assembly is required for efficient NAD+ hydrolysis and antiphage defense. These findings reveal an effector-driven activation mechanism and extend the principles by which NLR proteins couple higher-order assembly to immune defense across domains of life.

Article.Title: Role of Leu and Val synthesis in sensing mitochondrial nutrient and energy availability
Article.Authors: Phan J.; Gay L.; Dokládal L.; De Virgilio C.; Salcedo L.; Tha S.; Wandvik C.; Babst M.
Article.Abstract: How cells integrate nutrient availability to coordinate metabolism and growth remains poorly understood. Here, we identify branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) synthesis as a metabolic sensing system linking mitochondrial activity to translational and transcriptional control. Yeast limits Leu and Val import and instead relies on their synthesis, allowing BCAA production to reflect mitochondrial anabolic capacity. Reduced Val synthesis activates Gcn2, whereas reduced Leu synthesis inhibits TORC1, together decreasing translation efficiency and restricting growth. This response lowers levels of the transcriptional repressor Mig1, suppressing the Warburg/Crabtree effect and promoting alternative carbon source utilization. Remarkably, pharmacological inhibition of Leu/Val synthesis induces this metabolic reprogramming even in nutrient-rich medium, indicating that mitochondrial BCAA synthesis can partially override other nutrient-sensing pathways. Thus, BCAA synthesis couples mitochondrial anabolic capacity to Gcn2 and TORC1 activity and, through translational control of transcription factor abundance, shapes cellular metabolism.

Article.Title: Single-cell multi-omics reveals archetypal regulatory programs shared across T cell subsets
Article.Authors: Walker S.; van der Veeken J.; Rudensky A.; Pritykin Y.
Article.Abstract: T cells differentiate into functionally distinct subsets in response to pathogens, yet essential immune functions such as self-renewal, expansion, cytokine production, and cytotoxicity are common to multiple subsets and therefore must be programmed via shared regulatory mechanisms. To uncover these "archetypal" epigenomic programs, we integrated a single-cell multiomic (scATAC+RNA-seq) dataset of CD4 and CD8 T cells responding to acute and chronic viral infection with a comprehensive bulk ATAC-seq compendium. Our analysis reveals a modular architecture governing T cell identity, implicating distinct transcription factors in reusing regulatory programs across subsets and lineages. Notably, translationally important progenitor CD8 T cells, critical for sustained immunity and present in both acute and chronic infection, exhibit a composite regulatory state, combining a CD8 exhaustion program with a follicular helper CD4 T cell program. In sum, this resource and generalizable computational framework will aid the mechanistic dissection of adaptive immunity and immunotherapy design.

Article.Title: CCN1-mediated stress signaling underlies intrinsic cardiomyocyte dysfunction in spinal muscular atrophy
Article.Authors: Zeng W.; Liu W.; Caudal A.; Liu L.; Kong X.; Zhu W.; Kim H.; Lee A.; Alamana C.; Melesio J.; Cao X.; Howell K.; Chen K.; Pang P.; Day J.; Wu J.
Article.Abstract: Cardiac involvement in spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is increasingly recognized, but its cellular basis remains poorly defined. Using patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CMs) and engineered heart tissues (EHTs), we identify reduced survival motor neuron (SMN) expression, mitochondrial respiratory defects, and impaired contractility in SMA. Transcriptomic analyses reveal cellular communication network factor 1 (CCN1) as a top upregulated gene in SMA iPSC-CMs, consistent with its enrichment in cardiomyocytes across cardiomyopathies. Exogenous CCN1 exacerbates contractile dysfunction in SMA iPSC-CMs. Proteomic profiling reveals sustained p38/mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling activation, synergistically amplified by CCN1 and TNFα, thereby linking stress signaling to cardiac dysfunction in SMA. Therapeutic intervention with tanshinone IIA suppresses CCN1 expression, attenuates p38 activation, and improves contractile function. Notably, combining tanshinone IIA with risdiplam produces additive benefits in mitochondrial and contractile performance. Together, these findings identify a CCN1-mediated mechanism underlying SMA cardiac dysfunction and support combination strategies integrating SMN-dependent and independent therapies.

Article.Title: Early mitophagy defects and impaired mitochondrial energy metabolism drive target organ damage progression: Lessons from the Fabry heart
Article.Authors: Gambardella J.; Fiordelisi A.; Cerasuolo F.; Buonaiuto A.; Avvisato R.; Viti A.; Sommella E.; Campiglia P.; D’Argenio V.; Prevete N.; Pezone A.; D’Apice S.; Altobelli G.; Varzideh F.; Pande S.; Paolillo R.; Perrino C.; Riccio E.; Pisani A.; Bianco A.; Sadoshima J.; Spinelli L.; Santulli G.; Sorriento D.; Iaccarino G.
Article.Abstract: Increasing evidence supports a pathogenic role for impaired energy metabolism in organ damage. Genetic diseases provide opportunities to investigate these mechanisms, as exemplified by Fabry disease (FD), caused by an α-galactosidase A (GLA) deficiency and globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) accumulation, with cardiomyopathy as the leading cause of death. Beyond Gb3 storage, impaired energy metabolism may contribute to cardiomyopathy. Here, we demonstrate mitochondrial dysfunction in FD heart and its therapeutic targeting. Using a humanized FD mouse model (R301Q-Tg/GLA knockout), embryonic fibroblasts, and neonatal and adult cardiomyocytes, we found impaired mitophagy and mitochondrial respiration, increased reactive oxygen species, and a vicious cycle aggravating lysosomal dysfunction. These defects progressed with age, causing accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria, energetic failure, apoptosis, cardiac hypertrophy, and diastolic dysfunction. L-arginine, promoting NO/PGC-1α-dependent mitochondrial rescue, prevented cardiac abnormalities. Our findings identify mitochondrial dysfunction as a key driver of FD cardiomyopathy and reveal the lysosome-mitochondria axis as a targetable pathway in FD and beyond.

Article.Title: Heterogeneous contributions of APOBEC3 deaminases to substitution and indel mutagenesis in lung adenocarcinoma
Article.Authors: Striepen J.; Culibrk L.; Dananberg A.; Rozowsky J.; Petljak M.; Maciejowski J.
Article.Abstract: APOBEC3 cytosine deaminases are major sources of cancer mutations. In lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), APOBEC3 activity drives tumor evolution and therapy resistance, nominating these enzymes as therapeutic targets. Although APOBEC3A drives most APOBEC3-associated mutational signature burden across cancers, the relative contributions of individual paralogs in LUAD remain unclear. Here, we define the roles of endogenously misregulated APOBEC3 deaminases using CRISPR-Cas9 knockouts and whole-genome sequencing of 197 long-term propagated single-cell clones. APOBEC3 mutagenesis falls into three patterns, driven predominantly by APOBEC3A, by both APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B, or minimal despite detectable enzyme expression. Commonly used surrogate measures, including mRNA and protein levels and in vitro deaminase activity, do not predict these contributions. We also provide the first causal evidence that endogenous APOBEC3A generates the indel signature InD9a, linking it to uracil excision following cytosine deamination. These heterogeneous contributions highlight the need for biomarkers that resolve individual APOBEC3 activities to guide therapeutic targeting.

Article.Title: The compositional encoding of hand-eye coordinated movements for single neurons in the posterior parietal cortex
Article.Authors: Mynhier N.; Gamez J.; Moorse K.; Pejsa K.; Bari A.; Murray R.; Andersen R.
Article.Abstract: Human posterior parietal cortex (PPC) is known to play a role in hand-eye (H-E) coordination, yet the underlying encoding mechanisms remain uncertain. We recorded 412 single neurons across 11 sessions from motor cortex (MC; n = 251) and PPC (n = 161) in a single human participant performing an H-E coordinated center-out task. While MC neurons showed negligible modulation by eye movements, 79% of PPC neurons had neural representations that were additively separable into independent hand- and eye-movement tuning curves. Due to this separability, representations could be separated and additively recomposed while maintaining structural similarity. Consequently, compositional decoders trained solely on single-effector movements could match the performance of decoders trained on coordinated H-E movements (hand: 66% vs. 69%; eye: 34% vs. 36%). These results show that, during simple center-out tasks, MC hand-movement codes are unaffected by eye movements and that compositionality can be used to modularly decode H-E coordinated movements in PPC.

Article.Title: Mesothelin-induced lysosomal biogenesis sustains neutrophil longevity to drive brain metastasis
Article.Authors: Chen X.; Dong C.; Wang Y.; Yun T.; Wang L.; Chen R.; Shen Y.; Tang C.; Xie Y.; Zeng K.; Yang Y.; Han Z.; Bu J.; Li S.; Zhou A.
Article.Abstract: Tumor-associated neutrophil (TAN) enrichment is a defining feature and driving force of brain metastases (BrMs), a leading cause of death in solid tumors. Yet, the mechanisms governing TAN enrichment in BrM remains undefined. Specifically, sMSLN binds to toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) on neutrophil to activate the JAK2-STAT3 pathway. This activation promotes lysosomal biogenesis and function, reducing cellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) and inhibiting neutrophil apoptosis. Neutrophil depletion or TLR4-STAT3 blockade abrogates sMSLN-induced BrM progression. Targeting MSLN with Anetumab effectively reduces TAN enrichment, and combining this with TLR4 inhibition synergistically suppresses lung cancer BrM. Our findings establish a critical role for tumor cell-derived sMSLN in sustaining neutrophil longevity and driving BrM, highlighting the sMSLN-TLR4 axis as a promising therapeutic target for brain metastatic tumors.

Article.Authors: Pastor A.; Shirsathe S.; Vidal-Freire S.; Ferressini-Gerpe N.; Guito J.; Somavarapu R.; Patiño-Galindo J.; Giannetti E.; Tagliavia M.; Pan H.; Worwa G.; García-Sastre A.; Towner J.; Johnson J.; Kuhn J.; Sanchez-Lockhart M.; Palacios G.
Article.Abstract: Bats tolerate viruses that cause severe disease in humans. Article.Title: Neuroprotectant development from small molecule inhibitors of CHOP/ATF4 expression
Article.Authors: Li M.; Yan X.; Yang H.; Liu L.; Feng X.; Bian F.; Huang H.; Dalal R.; Solow-Cordero D.; Schow S.; Liu D.; Hu Y.
Article.Abstract: Glaucoma is a neurodegenerative disease that is in urgent need of neuroprotective therapies. We previously revealed the critical role of neuronal endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress induced by optic nerve injury in glaucomatous neurodegeneration. Article.Title: Sleep-dependent DNA methylation remodeling in basolateral amygdala fear engrams
Article.Authors: Chen X.; Ruan F.; Rodriguez A.; Pan R.; Wang R.; Jin M.; Zhou L.; Yi K.; Liu H.; Zhou W.; Peng Y.; Liu X.
Article.Abstract: How sleep consolidates fear memories at the molecular level within individual engram neurons is unknown. Article.Title: Stress hyperglycemia impairs FOXK2-dependent macrophage cardiac repair after myocardial infarction
Article.Authors: Lv H.; Liu Z.; Feng S.; Liu W.; Guo Y.; Bao K.; Shen X.; Li Y.; Zhou X.; Ai D.; Yang Q.; Zhang Y.; Li J.
Article.Abstract: Stress hyperglycemia (SHG) predicts poor outcomes after myocardial infarction (MI), but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we identify FOXK2 as a key regulator of macrophage-mediated cardiac repair. Article.Abstract: Loss of cardiomyocytes drives cardiac remodeling and ultimately leads to heart failure, highlighting the need to promote cardiac regeneration. Mechanistically, clusterin activated NF-κB via proteasome-dependent IκBα degradation through direct binding with IκBα. Furthermore, the liver was identified as the major source of exercise-induced circulating clusterin; hepatocyte-specific Clu knockdown abolished the stimulatory effect of exercise plasma on cardiac regeneration. Article.Title: Arbitrium crosstalk enables shared signaling among phages
Article.Authors: Lomeli-Ortega C.; Balcázar J.
Article.Abstract: The arbitrium system has transformed our understanding of phage biology by demonstrating that temperate phages communicate through extracellular peptides to coordinate lysis-lysogeny decisions. Initially considered a highly specific signaling pathway restricted to individual phage lineages, arbitrium communication has now been shown to extend beyond lineage boundaries in some phage systems. Recent studies have shown that non-cognate arbitrium peptides can interact with heterologous receptors, providing evidence of inter-phage crosstalk. Here, we synthesize current knowledge of the molecular basis of arbitrium signaling, the structural determinants of peptide-receptor specificity, and the potential ecological and evolutionary consequences of inter-phage communication. We suggest that arbitrium crosstalk may shape phage ecology by mediating competitive and potentially cooperative interactions within shared signaling environments. We also discuss its potential uses in engineered phage systems, synthetic biology, and microbiome engineering. Collectively, the available evidence broadens the concept of viral communication beyond lineage-specific signaling, while the ecological significance and practical applications of arbitrium crosstalk remain to be established.

Article.Authors: Wang B.; Kuo Y.; Dasdemir E.; Xiao W.; Rebboah E.; Tang G.; Wang W.; Abbas H.

Article.Title: Programmed bacterial lysis in vivo alters host immune responses and microbial pathogenesis
Article.Authors: Lembke M.; Simmons D.; Robins W.; Toska J.; Meader B.; Mekalanos J.
Article.Abstract: Vibrio cholerae injects toxic type VI secretion system (T6SS) effectors to lyse sensitive intestinal commensals, but how this bacterial antagonism enhances mucosal host immune responses and its pathogenicity remains unknown. To mimic T6SS-mediated killing, we engineered V. cholerae lysis strains by using CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) to knockdown essential genes in peptidoglycan biogenesis or lipopolysaccharide (LPS) transport. Our results indicate that controlled bacterial lysis in vivo leads to divergent mucosal immune responses that directly modulate colonization and pathogenicity of a bystander, non-lysing V. cholerae ΔT6SS strain. Mass spectrometric analysis of the lysis debris revealed proinflammatory muropeptides correlating with these changes. We confirmed that oral co-administration of a synthetic peptidoglycan-derived metabolite with a V. cholerae ΔT6SS mutant, but not the wild type, shows dramatic enhancement of disease symptoms. These findings show that intestinal exposure to discrete bacterial cell wall metabolites can differentially modulate host innate immune responses and consequently bacterial pathogenesis.

Article.Title: A single-cell atlas of pediatric undifferentiated recurrent fever reveals candidate immune regulators
Article.Authors: Jung S.; Wiedemuth R.; Martinez Perez A.; Wannige C.; Strauss T.; Körholz J.; Pietzsch L.; Thieme S.; Morbach H.; Schuetz C.; del Sol A.
Article.Abstract: Children with periodic fever syndromes not attributable to infections, rheumatic disorders, malignancies, or known monogenic autoinflammatory conditions are classified as "syndrome of undifferentiated recurrent fever" (SURF). To date, treatment remains empirical, often resulting in only a partial response, underscoring the unmet clinical need for new therapeutic strategies. To advance the molecular understanding of SURF, we generated a large-scale single-cell RNA-seq immune atlas of 29 SURF patients with more than 200,000 cells. Comparison of patients with three healthy cohorts revealed large-scale metabolic shifts together with a distinct cytokine signature already observable during afebrile periods. This indicates that afebrile SURF cannot be considered a less inflammatory resting state but rather as a distinct homeostatic state. Furthermore, our analysis suggests an NAMPT-mediated autocrine feedback loop connecting the metabolic dysregulations with the pro-inflammatory phenotype in monocytes. This study offers insights into the SURF immunopathology and generates testable hypotheses to guide future therapies.

Article.Title: Intermittent fasting enhances muscle regeneration via an EDA2R-NIK-myomixer axis
Article.Authors: Arabaci D.; Sucuoglu M.; Gokoglan F.; Agca S.; Kizilyer A.; Gurel Z.; Uslucan C.; Serit I.; Kir S.
Article.Abstract: Skeletal muscle exhibits a remarkable regenerative capacity that relies on adult stem cells known as satellite cells (SCs), which differentiate into myogenic progenitors to drive muscle repair. How varying energy availability alters myogenesis, however, remains unknown. Here, we demonstrate that intermittent fasting (IF) in mice upregulates a myogenic gene program, including Myomixer, a muscle-specific fusogen that facilitates the merging of progenitor cells into myofibers. IF enhances the regeneration of injured muscles by expanding the SC population and promoting the proliferation and fusion of myogenic progenitors. These effects are absent in an SC-depletion model. We show that fasting-induced EDA2R-NIK signaling increases Myomixer expression and fusion in myoblasts. Notably, mice lacking EDA2R or NIK fail to respond to the myogenic effects of IF. Furthermore, our data suggest that mice with Duchenne muscular dystrophy also benefit from an IF regimen. Therefore, IF-induced regeneration holds potential for aiding recovery from muscle damage.

Article.Title: eHLAstic reveals an extended canonical and non-canonical HLA-E immunopeptidome in human cancers
Article.Authors: Liao H.; Quastel M.; Shepherd C.; Nicastri A.; Kok L.; van Hateren A.; Palmer S.; Yang Q.; Dzhoneva A.; Peeters B.; Marrer-Berger E.; van Heesch S.; Gillespie G.; Ternette N.
Article.Abstract: HLA-E is a non-classical MHC class I molecule with restricted polymorphism, offering a putative path to broadly applicable off-the-shelf therapies. Yet, the wider HLA-E peptide repertoire remains poorly defined and is largely assumed restricted to signal peptide-derived sequences. We developed eHLAstic, a dedicated HLA-E-binding predictor, that improved the precision of HLA-E ligand discovery almost 3-fold compared with existing approaches. Using eHLAstic and orthogonal biochemical validation, we report 30 previously unrecognized canonical and non-canonical HLA-E-associated peptides, including six cancer-restricted ligands detected in acute lymphoblastic and myeloid leukemia but not healthy blood or bone marrow cells. Most identified ligands were shared across individuals with diverse HLA backgrounds and were detected across hematological and solid cancers. All but one non-canonical ligands were detected exclusively in cancer-associated samples and not in healthy tissues. These findings redefine the HLA-E ligandome and uncover canonical and non-canonical HLA-E ligands with potential for immune recognition and therapeutic targeting.

Article.Title: Clearing perivascular light chain-derived amyloid to counteract aging-associated decline in liver regeneration
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Yang Y.; He G.; Ren Y.; Wang Y.; Zheng Q.; Li J.; Qing J.
Article.Abstract: Aging impairs organ regeneration, with insufficient angiogenesis as a key contributor. Here, we show that the endothelial immunoproteasome subunit PSMB8 is upregulated in aged mouse livers after partial hepatectomy. Endothelial PSMB8 deletion or PR-957 inhibition promotes angiogenesis and rescues liver regeneration. diGly proteomics identifies TAZ (transcriptional co-activator with PDZ-binding motif) as a ubiquitin-dependent immunoproteasome substrate, and TAZ activation restores aged liver regeneration. Aging triggers the infiltration of CD38+IGLC1+ IgM B cells and aberrant perivascular light chain-derived amyloid deposition in the liver. Recombinant light chain-derived amyloid fibrils directly induce PSMB8 expression in vitro. Anselamimab-mediated light chain-derived amyloid clearance mitigates immunoproteasome overactivation and restores regeneration. Single-cell RNA sequencing confirms that anselamimab reverses aging-induced endothelial marker loss and inflammatory gene upregulation. Our findings establish a pathway linking perivascular light chain-derived amyloid deposition to regenerative decline via endothelial immunoproteasome activation, suggesting amyloid clearance as a promising therapeutic strategy for aging-associated decline in liver regeneration.

Article.Title: 5-Azacytidine incorporation into mRNAs disrupts translation and induces ribosome collisions
Article.Authors: Roberson A.; Marks J.; Pitts R.; Tamilselvam B.; Britt G.; Grieb B.; Tansey W.; Meydan S.
Article.Abstract: 5-Azacytidine (5-AzaC) is a cytidine analog chemotherapeutic widely used to treat myeloid malignancies. Although its activity is primarily attributed to DNA hypomethylation, the majority of 5-AzaC is incorporated into RNA, where its functional consequences are less understood. Here, we show that 5-AzaC treatment of cells leads to inhibition of protein synthesis. Ribo-seq, Disome-seq, and RNA-seq in treated cells exhibit a time-dependent C-to-G conversion in mRNAs. These conversion events are enriched within footprint positions corresponding to the A-site of monosomes or stalled leading ribosomes in a disome complex. Footprints are accumulated at sites with C-rich codons in the A-site, with particular emphasis on the second codon position. Consistent with disome-mediated signaling, 5-AzaC activates ZAK- and GCN2-dependent stress responses. Furthermore, loss of the ribosome-associated quality control factor, ZNF598, sensitizes cells to 5-AzaC. These findings suggest that translation disruption represents an additional layer of 5-AzaC's mechanism of action, alongside its known DNA-mediated effects.

Article.Title: Hyperosmotic stress induces rewiring of 3D chromatin interactions
Article.Authors: Flores J.; Perreault A.; Drum Z.; Xu C.; Alonso D.; Rashid T.; Burgess J.; Fox G.; Petros G.; Wu Y.; Quiroga-Barber I.; Kim H.; Sahasrabudhe I.; Lee Y.; Black E.; Li Y.; Demmerle J.; Strahl B.; Dowen J.; Wang G.; Cai D.; Phanstiel D.
Article.Abstract: Cells continually face environmental stressors that challenge homeostasis, yet how three-dimensional (3D) chromatin structure contributes to these stress responses remains unclear under hyperosmotic conditions. To investigate this, we map 3D chromatin structure, its molecular drivers, and transcriptional outcomes during sorbitol-induced hyperosmotic stress. Within 1 hour of sorbitol treatment, pre-existing loops and domains collapse, while several hundred de novo sorbitol-induced loops emerge. These loops are punctate, longer-range, and transient. 3D chromatin structure largely returns to baseline conditions by 24 hours. Loop reorganization is consistent across cell types and hyperosmotic stimuli. Sorbitol-induced loops require cohesin but not CTCF, and anchors are enriched at active promoters harboring GC-rich transcription factor motifs. Genes at these anchors show delayed activation following loop formation, consistent with loops acting upstream of transcription. Together, hyperosmotic stress triggers rapid, reversible, CTCF-independent chromatin reorganization that correlates with transcriptional adaptation.

Article.Title: Plagl2 reprograms adult mouse retinal Müller glia for proliferation and injury-enhanced neurogenic competence
Article.Authors: Masaki T.; Watanabe M.; Mandai M.; Kihara M.; Abe T.; Kageyama R.
Article.Abstract: Müller glia (MG) in the adult mammalian retina have long been recognized as a potential endogenous source for the regeneration of lost retinal neurons. However, existing MG reprogramming strategies yield an incomplete regenerative response by favoring either proliferation or neurogenic differentiation. Here, we show that the zinc-finger transcription factor gene Plagl2, previously shown to reactivate quiescent neural stem cells, is sufficient to reprogram adult mouse MG into a progenitor-like state with coupled proliferative and neurogenic competence. Using histology, time-lapse imaging, and single-cell transcriptomics, we find that Plagl2 drives regulated rounds of MG cell cycle re-entry, while N-methyl-D-aspartate-induced retinal injury further promotes the acquisition of neurogenic competence biased toward inner nuclear layer neuronal identities. These findings indicate that Plagl2 regulates mammalian MG reprogramming, and supports a broader approach to tissue regeneration through the adaptation of reprogramming modules across distinct cell types.

Article.Title: Temporal shifts in post-asthmatic immune responses define tumor outcomes via strain-specific monocyte reprogramming
Article.Authors: Wang X.; Chen C.; Wan Y.; Dang B.; Liu X.; Gao Q.; Zhang J.; Cheng S.
Article.Abstract: Epidemiological evidence linking asthma to lung cancer risk remains contradictory, presenting asthma as either a risk factor or a protective condition. We hypothesize that this heterogeneity stems from the temporal dynamics of inflammatory response and host genetic background. Using ovalbumin (OVA)-induced asthma models, we identify a temporal shift in immune effectors driving post-asthmatic tumorigenesis. During acute airway inflammation, eosinophil infiltration accelerates tumor growth across mouse strains. Following resolution, however, tumorigenic outcomes in recovery diverge along genetic lines. Prior asthma reshapes chromatin landscapes of bone marrow myeloid progenitors, establishing innate immune memory that differentially programs monocytes across strains. In C57BL/6 mice, trained monocytes adopt oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), acquiring a suppressive, tissue-remodeling phenotype that promotes tumor progression. Conversely, BALB/c-trained monocytes utilize glycolysis to maintain a pro-phagocytic state, enabling tumor clearance. These findings delineate a biphasic mechanism wherein temporal shifts in post-asthmatic immune responses define tumor outcomes via strain-specific monocyte metabolic reprogramming.

Article.Title: Single-cell and spatial characterization of the human pancreas in cystic fibrosis
Article.Authors: Mummey H.; Corban S.; Lucero J.; Melton R.; Pittigher M.; Johnston V.; Deutsch G.; D’Antonio-Chronowska A.; Wang A.; Hull-Meichle R.; Gaulton K.
Article.Abstract: Cystic fibrosis (CF) causes severely damaged pancreatic morphology and cystic fibrosis-related diabetes (CFRD), but the cellular drivers of CFRD in the pancreas are not understood. Here, we perform single-cell and spatial profiling of 2.04 M cells from 23 non-disease or CF pancreas donors. A high-mucin ductal sub-type had relatively preserved abundance and genomic profiles but altered localization in CF. Changes in inflammatory and fibrotic pathways were driven by crosstalk between immune and pro-fibrotic cells in specific niches. Beta cells had extensive changes in CF, including increased stress responses and evidence for compensatory secretion, that were distinct from those in type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Islets localized near large adipose tissue and collagen in CF had reduced beta cells linked to signaling from adipocytes, macrophages, stellate cells, and high-mucin ductal cells. Overall, our results highlight pancreatic microenvironments of beta cell dysfunction in CF and offer in-roads to preserving beta cells in CFRD.

Article.Title: IDO1 methylation by EZH2 confers resistance to its targeted therapy in colorectal cancer through tryptophan-kynurenine metabolic rewiring
Article.Authors: Tang Y.; Huang Z.; Jia Y.; Guo Y.; Cao X.; Jin R.; Yin Q.; Song J.; Chen H.; Zhang X.; Zhou X.; Cheng R.; Yang J.; Guo Z.; Bu P.; Xue L.
Article.Abstract: Deciphering cancer metabolic reprogramming mechanisms can identify new targets to potentiate EZH2 inhibitor efficacy. EZH2 blockade remodeled CRC cell metabolism by upregulating IDO1 protein and hyperactivating the tryptophan-kynurenine pathway. Both genetic and pharmacological inhibition of IDO1 suppressed tumor growth and rescued EZH2 inhibitor resistance in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, EZH2 directly binds and methylates IDO1. Methylation of IDO1 facilitates IDO1 ubiquitination and subsequent degradation. Accordingly, EZH2 inhibition stabilizes IDO1, augments tryptophan-kynurenine metabolic flux, and ultimately confers therapeutic resistance. In summary, our study identifies IDO1 as a non-histone substrate of EZH2 methyltransferase activity and validates that disrupting IDO1-mediated tryptophan metabolism is a viable strategy to overcome EZH2 targeted therapy resistance in cancers.

Article.Title: ApoE-dependent lipid handling by median eminence microglia supports myelin remodeling and metabolic function
Article.Authors: McGrath E.; Folick A.; Morrissette L.; Brown Mayfield S.; Kim H.; Weng L.; Pham V.; Pillutla S.; Choi M.; Tomaka C.; Mechelke A.; Cheang R.; Bolus W.; Schwendeman A.; Ntranos V.; Koliwad S.; Valdearcos M.
Article.Abstract: Microglia regulate hypothalamic control of systemic metabolism, but the mechanisms underlying their contribution remain unclear. Here, we identify apolipoprotein E (ApoE)-associated microglial transcriptional states enriched in the median eminence (ME), a brain region involved in sensing peripheral cues and metabolic regulation. These transcriptional states are characterized by programs related to lipid handling, interferon-associated responses, and cellular stress. Consumption of a Western diet (WD) increased microglial lipid accumulation and altered myelin remodeling within the ME, while expression of the human APOE4 isoform exacerbated these changes. Deletion of Apoe altered microglial responses to nutritional stress, supporting a role for ApoE in microglial lipid handling. Finally, activation of liver X receptor using synthetic high-density lipoprotein (sHDL) nanoparticles enhanced microglial lipid-handling programs, improved hypothalamic leptin responsiveness, reduced food intake, and limited weight gain in WD-fed mice. Together, these findings identify ApoE-dependent lipid handling as a key component of adaptive microglial responses to metabolic stress.

Article.Title: A bivalent chromatin reader-WOX5 module maintains root stem cell niche in Arabidopsis
Article.Authors: Zhang L.; Qian S.; Zhong X.
Article.Abstract: Root stem cell niche maintenance requires precise control of quiescent center (QC) and columella stem cell (CSC) activity, yet how chromatin regulators interface with key transcription factors remains poorly understood. Here, we identify the bivalent chromatin reader EARLY BOLTING IN SHORT DAYS (EBS) as an essential regulator of root stem cell maintenance in Arabidopsis. A strong ebs-1 mutant shows CSC differentiation and QC activation, and EBS function requires its histone mark-recognizing BAH and PHD domains and a C-terminal SUMO-interacting motif. EBS physically interacts with the QC master regulator WUSCHEL-RELATED HOMEOBOX 5 (WOX5) and, together with WOX5, activates WOX5 transcription by promoting EBS enrichment at the WOX5 promoter. Consistently, wox5-1 is epistatic to ebs-1, and WOX5 overexpression rescues the ebs-1 stem cell defects. Together, this work uncovers a chromatin-based positive autoregulatory loop that integrates histone-state recognition and transcriptional feedback, providing a framework for epigenetic control of stem cell fate in plants.

Article.Title: Theta-based organization of information in the frontal cortex
Article.Authors: Broschard M.; Brincat S.; Loonis R.; Miller E.
Article.Abstract: Theta (4-10 Hz) oscillations seem to coordinate activity across long-range distances. It is less clear how theta coordinates activity more locally within frontal subareas. We examined activity in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC), ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (vlPFC), and frontal eye fields (FEFs) as non-human primates categorized dot patterns. We characterized how theta coordinates activity within frontal cortex. First, theta phase selectively couples to behaviorally relevant information in spiking. Second, theta influences move in a posterior direction during choices (i.e., dlPFC/vlPFC to FEF) and after correct outcomes (i.e., dlPFC to FEF), but not after errors. Instead, anterior-direction (i.e., FEF to vlPFC) theta influences are stronger after errors. Third, theta participates in behaviorally associated nested cross-frequency interactions. Theta couples to beta (15-30 Hz) oscillations during choices and after errors, whereas beta couples to gamma (40-90 Hz) oscillations after correct outcomes. Our results position theta as a critical mechanism that flexibly and dynamically coordinates activity in frontal cortex.

Article.Title: A shared multi-feature population code for sensory reliability across mouse visual cortex
Article.Authors: Edwards E.; Lipton M.; Sereno A.; Dadarlat M.
Article.Abstract: Successful behavior depends on evaluating both what is present in the environment and how reliable that information is. Yet how neural populations represent reliability, and whether this representation is shared across cortical areas, remains unknown. Using two-photon calcium imaging of over 150,000 neurons in mouse visual cortices during presentations of coherent motion stimuli, we find that sensory reliability is encoded through coordinated changes in response amplitude, selectivity, and signal-to-noise ratio. These coherence-dependent response patterns are not fully accounted for by stimulus-based normalization models; rather, they track the distribution of motion energy across directions, while remaining relatively invariant to total motion energy. This multi-feature code is expressed at the single-neuron and population levels and is consistent across visual areas, suggesting a shared encoding scheme rather than area-specific computations. Together, these findings support a common population code for stimulus reliability across visual cortices.

Article.Title: Self-amplifying RNA vaccines encoding chimeric and mosaic hemagglutinins confer immunity against phylogenetically diverse influenza A viruses
Article.Authors: Abbad A.; Yellin T.; Carreño J.; McPartlan J.; Talukder P.; Puente-Massaguer E.; González-Domínguez I.; Scherm M.; Bielak D.; Lerman B.; Mandl C.; Chahal J.; Krammer F.
Article.Abstract: Seasonal influenza vaccines require annual reformulation due to antigenic drift and provide suboptimal protection. Here, we evaluate self-amplifying mRNA (samRNA) vaccines encoding chimeric (cHA) and mosaic (mHA) hemagglutinins representing influenza A virus HA phylogenetic groups 1 and 2. Following prime-boost immunization, group 1 cHA vaccines (cH8/1-cH5/1) elicit broad cross-reactive antibodies and confer complete protection against diverse H1N1 strains covering decades of antigenic drift. Group 2 vaccines (cH4/3-cH15/3 and mH10/3-mH14/3) provide comparable breadth against multiple H3N2 strains and heterosubtypic H7N9 challenge, with cHA samRNA showing superior cross-group protection. Protection is associated with Fc-mediated effector functions and CD4+ T cell responses, with minimal hemagglutination inhibition and neutralizing titers. Passive serum transfer confirms antibody-mediated protection independent of cellular immunity. Protective immunity is maintained at doses as low as 0.4 μg, demonstrating the dose-sparing advantage of the samRNA platform. These results support samRNA-delivered cHA and mHA antigens as promising candidates for broadly protective influenza vaccines.

Article.Title: Chronotherapy leveraging dietary context overcomes circadian rhythm influence on cancer cell response to PPAR antagonists
Article.Authors: Bruno P.; Özkan K.; Renoult O.; Giolito M.; Ibanez S.; Srhir S.; Guilbaud C.; Laloux F.; Leclercq I.; Bouzin C.; Serafimov K.; Dessy C.; Aubert L.; Feron O.
Article.Abstract: Circadian physiology coordinates systemic and cellular metabolism through a light-entrained central clock and metabolically synchronized peripheral clocks. Whether feeding-fasting cycles or tumor-intrinsic clocks primarily set tumor metabolic state is unclear. Here, we profiled colorectal cancer (CRC) responses to PPAR antagonists across 2D and 3D CRC models and tumor-bearing mice. In standard high-glucose, low-fat medium, Bmal1 oscillations and daily variation in PPAR antagonist sensitivity were apparent in CRC cells. By contrast, nutrient-defined media that recapitulate feeding and nighttime fasting abolished time-dependent variability and unified drug responses across models. Still, the fed state selectively sensitized spheroids and patient-derived organoids to PPAR-γ antagonism. In mice, dosing PPAR-γ antagonist in the fed state prolonged survival and reduced hepatotoxicity. The use of Bmal-1-silenced CRC cells validated that feeding-fasting rhythms, not tumor-intrinsic clocks, govern CRC sensitivity to PPAR antagonists. Our study also supports the predictive capacity of nutrient-alternating 3D tumor models, enabling metabolism-targeted anticancer treatment evaluation.

Article.Title: Succinate promotes multiple myeloma cell proliferation through TCA cycle oxidation
Article.Authors: Gudgeon N.; Fulton-Ward T.; Stavrou V.; Haslam A.; McIlroy G.; Giles H.; Pratt G.; Dimeloe S.
Article.Abstract: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell malignancy that develops within the bone marrow. The bone marrow metabolome is altered in myeloma, with implications for malignant cell growth. Here, the impact of elevated bone marrow levels of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle metabolite, succinate, was interrogated. Succinate was found to promote proliferation of several myeloma cell lines. This was linked to its uptake and oxidation in the TCA cycle, as indicated by increased ATP-coupled mitochondrial respiration and incorporation of succinate-derived carbons into downstream TCA cycle intermediates, which also occurs in primary myeloma cells. Succinate-driven proliferation was dependent upon mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and abrogated by ATP synthase inhibition. Furthermore, interrogation of large-scale transcriptomic data identified that elevated expression of a mitochondrial succinate transporter associates with accelerated disease progression in myeloma, indicating this mechanism may promote plasma cell growth in vivo and highlighting a target for therapeutic intervention.

Article.Title: TNF- and IL-1-induced inflammation are enhanced through cooperative interactions between Nrf2 and NF-κB

Article.Abstract: Reactive oxygen species are typically elevated at inflammatory sites due to influx of large numbers of neutrophils and other myeloid cells that produce oxygen free radicals as microbicidal agents. Here we show that the redox-responsive transcription factor, Nrf2, can act as an enhancer of TNF- and IL-1-initiated inflammation. Silencing or deletion of the Nrf2 antagonist, Keap1, led to robustly enhanced TNF- or IL-1-driven inflammatory cytokine production. Conversely, suppression of Nrf2 activation blunted inflammation in the same contexts. Mechanistically, Nrf2 enhanced inflammation through cooperative interactions with p65 RelA at NFκB-regulated promoters. These observations reveal a direct link between the Keap1/Nrf2 reactive oxygen-sensing pathway and TNF- or IL-1-initiated inflammation and suggest that Nrf2 can act as a rheostat for NFκB-dependent inflammatory outputs.

Article.Abstract: Pangenomes are reshaping gene-family analysis by shifting from single-genome views to pangene families, yet many studies still rely on orthogroups as proxies, overlooking crucial allele- and locus-level diversity. Compared with single-genome analyses, pangenome-level family membership increases by 59-264%, and many families show pangene accumulation curves that remain far from saturation, indicating that substantial allelic diversity is still uncharacterized even when 320 rice genomes are included. We further quantify family behavior along three complementary dimensions and reveal extensive remodeling of membership and copy-number allocation that is largely invisible when only total family size is considered. Article.Authors: Li X.; Han T.; Chen L.; Suresh M.; Rahimov F.; Gao C.; Wang J.; Ma R.; Stender J.; Katlinski K.

CD86 is functionally required for TolDC-mediated suppression of T cell proliferation and cytokine secretion, supporting its use as a surrogate marker of tolerogenic potential. Article.Title: Cell-type specific and nanoscale control of hippocampal presynaptic homeostatic plasticity

Article.Abstract: The lifelong continuity of neuronal function rests upon the perdurance of neurons, synapses and neural circuits that are sustained, in part, by homeostatic signaling. Currently, the implementation of homeostatic signaling within complex brain circuitry remains poorly defined. Given the tremendous diversity of cell and synapse types, is homeostatic plasticity deployed in a cell-type specific manner and, if so, what are the rules? Here, we report that presynaptic homeostatic plasticity (PHP) is achieved in a target neuron-specific manner. PHP is robust at synapses that contact parvalbumin-positive (PV+) and absent at somatostatin-positive (SST+) interneurons. Furthermore, PHP can be differentially induced at adjacent synapses that are present within single axonal boutons, separated by hundreds of nanometers. These highly localized effects are eliminated in the absence of Sema3A signaling, a homeostatic signaling molecule. Our data suggest a model where PHP is repressed throughout axons that contact SST+ interneurons and locally de-repressed with nanoscale precision.

Here, we show that the receptor-like kinase FERONIA and its co-receptor LORELEI-LIKE GPI-ANCHORED PROTEIN1 (LLG1) are required for a large portion of high-humidity-associated Arabidopsis transcriptomic changes, including CNGC2, CAMTA-regulated genes, and cell wall remodeling genes, and for high-humidity-induced leaf hyponasty. High humidity triggers petiole-localized Ca2+ waves that precede hyponastic leaf movement. The petiole-localized Ca2+ signals were also significantly altered in the fer-4 mutant. Article.Title: Proteolytic dissection of eIF4G reveals that closed-loop mRNP formation is dispensable for bulk translation in mammalian cells
Article.Authors: Johnston R.; Brekker M.; Khalil N.; Goldstein M.; Aldrich A.; Grimins A.; Gritli S.; Marintchev A.; Blower M.; Saeed M.; Lyons S.
Article.Abstract: The "closed-loop" mRNP, in which the 5' cap and 3' poly(A) tail are bridged by eIF4E-eIF4G-PABP interactions, has been proposed to drive efficient translation. Direct rigorous tests of this model in mammalian cells have remained elusive. Using auxin-inducible degrons to acutely deplete eIF4G1, we find that global translation is only partially reduced and recovers without restoration of eIF4G1 levels. We identify eIF4G3 as an underappreciated contributor to basal translation that buffers translational output upon eIF4G1 loss. eIF4G1 mutants reveal that PABP binding by eIF4G1 is dispensable for bulk protein synthesis. Further, PABP depletion has no immediate effect on protein synthesis but instead destabilizes poly(A) mRNA. In contrast, the N-terminal enteroviral cleavage product (2A-cpN) is a potent, dominant translational repressor that requires both PABP- and eIF4E-binding domains for inhibition. These findings suggest that the eIF4G-PABP closed-loop architecture is not required for productive initiation but may be actively co-opted for translational silencing.

Article.Title: The neuropathic chameleon: we are hot on the scent
Article.Authors: Kersebaum D.; Forstenpointner J.; Sachau J.; Hüllemann P.; Baron R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract A common chronic pain condition, neuropathic pain arises from a lesion or disease affecting the somatosensory or neural tissue and is characterized by a combination of negative (eg, numbness) and positive (eg, burning pain) sensory symptoms that significantly affect the quality of life. Common comorbidities such as depression and sleep disruption contribute to a substantial disease burden, which is further exacerbated by the apparent lack of effective therapeutic options. Current treatment options frequently achieve only partial, insufficient pain relief or may be completely ineffective in a considerable number of patients. The development of new drugs has thus far achieved moderate success, with many clinical trials failing to meet their primary endpoints; thus, a substantial unmet clinical need persists. One reason for this therapeutic deadlock is the considerable heterogeneity of neuropathic pain, driven by diverse pathophysiological mechanisms that vary between patients regardless of the underlying disease etiology. Accordingly, reclassification efforts follow a mechanism-based approach that reflects pathophysiological pain generators rather than disease etiology. Although diagnosis remains anchored in lesion- or disease-based criteria and structured clinical assessment, treatment development increasingly benefits from mechanism-informed phenotyping. A priori stratification based on individual mechanisms may help identify treatment responders, but implementation requires surrogate markers, as no biomarkers for pain mechanisms currently exist. In this article, we discuss candidate predictive markers and surrogate markers, focusing on sensory symptoms and signs assessed through patient-reported outcome measures and sensory testing, and their integration into future clinical trials.

Article.Title: Trustworthiness in pain research is essential. Developing and implementing the ENTRUST-PE framework
Article.Authors: O'Connell N.; Belton J.; Cashin A.; Eccleston C.; Ferraro M.; Keefe F.; Knaggs R.; Norris E.; Pogatzki-Zahn E.; Palermo T.; Pickering G.; Rice A.; Segelcke D.; Sharma S.; Smart K.; Soliman N.; Toelle T.; Stewart G.; Vollert J.; Wainwright E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Trustworthy pain research is essential for developing a deeper understanding of the phenomena, how it is experienced, its many impacts and how it might be reduced, prevented or managed to improve the lives of those who live with pain. Recognising multiple critical challenges that undermine trust in health research, an international, interdisciplinary network was convened to create an integrated framework for enhancing the trustworthiness of research in pain. The ENTRUST-PE framework was launched in 2024 with a call to action, proposing that trustworthiness in pain research is multidimensional and underpinned by 7 Core Values: Integrity and Governance; Equity, Diversity and Inclusivity; Patient and Public Involvement and Engagement; Methodological Rigour; Openness and Transparency; Balanced Communication and Data Authenticity. The framework includes specific recommendations for a range of interest holders and resources to support those recommendations. In this paper, we summarise the framework, reflect on the response to the framework from the pain research community, consider challenges and opportunities in the evolving research landscape and suggest how we might move towards deeper implementation to enhance the trustworthiness of pain research.

Article.Title: Exercise therapy for chronic pain: an updated perspective on mesocorticolimbic system function
Article.Authors: Senba E.; Minami K.; Habata S.; Kami T.; Kouda K.; Tajima F.; Kami K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Patients with chronic pain often experience behavioral issues linked to pain, depression, and other emotional disorders. These problems stem from dysfunction in the mesocorticolimbic system, and exercise offers a safe, accessible, and effective alternative. It not only reduces pain but also activates multiple neural pathways, helping restore normal function. First, in the periphery, exercise promotes the release of myokines, which are essential for the body-brain connection and influence neural activity. IGF-1, released from muscles during exercise, can cross the blood-brain barrier and affect the brain. IGF-1 specifically targets orexin neurons in the hypothalamus, which then stimulate dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area, triggering the reward system. Second, exercise can reshape neural circuits and restore mesocorticolimbic function, reducing chronic pain and related issues. We showed that exercise activates neurons in the basal nucleus of the amygdala that project to the nucleus accumbens, supporting patients' goal-directed behavior. Moreover, inhibiting GABAergic neurons in the central nucleus of the amygdala decreases freezing behavior. Third, chronic pain often leads to depression, mainly due to reduced activity of serotonin (5-HT) neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus, which impairs the brain’s reward system. Exercise boosts activity of 5-HT neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus. Furthermore, exercise can modify gene expression through epigenetic mechanisms, leading to long-lasting improvements in brain function and behavior. Overall, exercise can restore brain function, helping individuals overcome chronic pain and lead healthier lives. These findings support exercise therapy as a key component of chronic pain management and suggest mesocorticolimbic mechanisms underlying its effects.

Article.Title: Under pressure: lessons from and beyond entrapment neuropathies
Article.Authors: Schmid A.; Chang P.; Camerone E.; Sierra-Silvestre E.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Entrapment neuropathies are the most prevalent focal neuropathic pain conditions globally and impose a substantial individual and socioeconomic burden. Traditionally conceptualised as purely mechanical compression syndromes, this view is increasingly challenged by converging evidence from human tissue analyses, advanced neuroimaging, and deep clinical phenotyping. Entrapment neuropathies are now recognised as biologically dynamic disorders shaped to different extents by microvascular compromise, demyelination, axonal degeneration, immune dysregulation, neuroinflammation, central nervous system adaptations, and psychosocial influences. Varying combinations and dominance of biopsychosocial processes give rise to marked clinical heterogeneity even within the same diagnostic label. This mechanistic diversity helps explain common diagnostic discordances, including extraterritorial symptom spread, normal electrodiagnostic findings despite clinical symptoms indicative of entrapment neuropathies, and imaging–clinical presentation mismatch. It also challenges one-size-fits-all treatment approaches, which have largely failed in entrapment neuropathies. Uniquely, entrapment neuropathies provide a natural human model of focal nerve injury in the context of neuropathic pain. Surgical decompression allows integration of tissue-level biology with precise clinical phenotypes and offers time-locked insights into recovery. Lessons derived from this model extend beyond entrapment neuropathies and can inform broader understanding of neuropathic and nerve-related musculoskeletal pain conditions. Here, we synthesise contemporary mechanistic insights, examine how biological heterogeneity translates into distinct clinical phenotypes, and discuss potential implications for mechanism-informed management.

Article.Title: Brain sites involved in endogenous analgesia
Article.Authors: Henderson L.; Crawford L.; Kang J.; Keay K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Pain modulation is a fundamental survival mechanism that prioritises, shapes, and suppresses nociceptive inputs to optimise behaviour. Although acute pain signals potential or actual tissue damage, sustained pain can impair essential behaviours, necessitating modulatory circuits that dynamically regulate nociception according to context and motivational state. These systems are deeply conserved, embedded within primitive spinal and brainstem structures, and capable of powerful modulation independent of cortical input, although higher regions such as the prefrontal cortex can influence their function. Decades of work have sought to identify these core modulatory circuits to advance basic understanding and develop strategies for clinically meaningful hypoalgesia. More recently, dysfunction within these circuits has been implicated in chronic pain, driving efforts to characterise how their organisation and function change during persistent pain states. Although most mechanistic insights come from animal studies, human neuroimaging, particularly since the advent of functional magnetic resonance imaging, has begun to map their location and engagement during pain modulation. Early work focused on forebrain regions due to the limited spatial resolution of standard MRI, but ultra-high-field functional magnetic resonance imaging now enables mm 3 -scale investigation of brainstem nuclei. This review synthesises evidence from animal and human studies to outline the best-characterised modulatory pathway, consisting of projections from the midbrain periaqueductal gray to the rostral ventromedial medulla and onward to the dorsal horn/spinal trigeminal nucleus, and highlights recent work detailing its organization.

Article.Title: Advances in research on combination therapy for the management of pain
Article.Authors: Gilron I.; Peterson C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Pharmacotherapy remains an important component of multidisciplinary, multimodal pain treatment. Based on a well-established understanding of multiple concurrent mechanisms of nociceptive transmission and modulation, the demonstrated potential for synergistic interactions of drug combinations seen in preclinical studies supports the hypothesis of superior analgesia, and possibly also, fewer side-effects as compared with monotherapy. Likely related to this hypothesis and rationale, real-world evidence shows that approximately half of all patients with chronic pain, and even more with acute pain, concurrently receive 2 or more drugs from different mechanistic classes. To date, many dozens of randomized controlled trials have evaluated various analgesic combinations for the treatment of postoperative, neuropathic, back, arthritis, fibromyalgia, pelvic, and cancer-related pain conditions. Despite this growing area of research, most analgesic drug combinations are currently administered without rigorous evidence, thus exposing patients to the added cost or risk of some combinations that are not necessarily superior to monotherapy. As such, we propose future efforts to more efficiently exploit the potential benefits of combination therapy including: (1) expansion and coordination of translational collaborations to prioritize the most beneficial and clinically relevant combinations; (2) ensuring that preclinical combination studies evaluate multiple drug dosages and multiple relevant adverse effects; (3) ensuring that clinical trials include comparisons with each and every monotherapy component of the combination; (4) conducting further real-world studies of clinically beneficial combinations to ensure safety and efficacy in broader clinical settings; and (5) the application of these principles also to the evaluation of nonpharmacological treatment combinations.

Article.Title: Molecular histochemical analysis of neuroplasticity-related gene expression in pain pathway
Article.Authors: Noguchi K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract I am deeply honored to receive the 2026 John Bonica Prize for distinguished lifetime achievement in the basic science of pain. Reflecting on 40 years of research, this review paper will summarize my key findings to date. For the past four decades, my research has focused on elucidating the molecular mechanisms of pain using animal models. By integrating morphological techniques with molecular biology, behavioral analysis, and electrophysiological recordings, I have sought to clarify how pain signals are modulated and sustained under chronic pain conditions. Since the early stages of my career, I have been particularly interested in the diverse molecular dynamics within pain pathways and their functional significance. This long-term research has been driven by the conviction that a detailed analysis of gene expression changes within pain pathways—particularly those associated with neuroplasticity—is essential to understanding the mechanisms underlying intractable pain. This review provides a comprehensive overview of our investigation into the molecular and cellular mechanisms of chronic pain, focusing on gene expression analyses related mainly to dorsal root ganglion and spinal cord plasticity, alongside historically significant contributions from the global pain research community. Finally, I will also discuss recent methodological advances and their applications, as well as the challenges and future directions facing basic pain research.

Article.Title: Prediction and prevention of pain after surgery
Article.Authors: Pogatzki-Zahn E.; Pradier B.; Segelcke D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Postoperative pain is common and has substantial clinical consequences for patients, their families, and society. Acute pain is not the only problem: a meaningful subset of patients develops chronic postsurgical pain, which is associated with considerable functional and psychosocial burden. Because established chronic postsurgical pain is difficult to treat, prevention is a key clinical objective, but it depends on the early identification of vulnerable patients and timely mechanism-informed interventions. This review examines mechanisms of postsurgical pain, as well as the prediction and prevention of unfavorable outcomes, from a translational perspective that integrates clinical evidence with mechanistic insights from preclinical models. After briefly summarizing recent developments, we outline current challenges and argue that progress requires alignment of outcome constructs across species, rigorous selection and reporting of experimental models, and identification of shared intermediate phenotypes linking mechanisms to patient trajectories. We then summarize the perioperative risk architecture underlying the transition from acute to chronic postsurgical pain, focusing on bio-psycho-social patient-related and surgical factors. Because current risk assessment tools do not yet provide sufficiently precise, reliable, and generalizable prediction, we discuss emerging evidence, including biological signatures that may refine prediction and risk stratification. We further argue that risk emerges dynamically through interactions across pre-, intra- and postsurgical phases. Building on this multi-stage, interactive framework, we propose a strategy integrating bio-psycho-social factors into clinically relevant prognostic models. Finally, we outline how this may not only help identify patients at risk, but also support mechanism-based, personalized prevention in vulnerable patients.

Article.Title: Chloride dysregulation: the next target for chronic pain therapeutics
Article.Authors: De Koninck Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Chronic pain affects a substantial fraction of the population, yet pharmacological management remains deeply inadequate. This failure likely reflects the focus on developing analgesics suppressing normal nociceptive signalling rather than correcting the pathological substrates distinguishing chronic from acute pain. Here we review how the identification of injury-induced downregulation of the potassium-chloride cotransporter KCC2 in spinal dorsal horn neurons represents a landmark. It first provided a mechanistic, long-term substrate for spinal inhibitory failure. This form of disinhibition had the potential to explain several cardinal symptoms of neuropathic pain; not just hyperalgesia, through spinal hyperexcitability, and tactile allodynia, through cross-talk between sensory modalities, but also spontaneous pain, through enabling spontaneous bursts of activity in spinal nociceptive output to emerge. A second landmark is that chloride dysregulation as a substrate of disinhibition yields non-linear, non-intuitive predictions of neural circuit behaviours that shed light on several features of chronic pain and its therapeutic challenges. One is paradoxical pro-excitatory actions of tapping into normally endogenous inhibitory neurotransmission, potentially explaining failures of benzodiazepines analgesia and of conditional pain modulation. Others include degradation of sensory processing, possibly explaining diffuse pain, and leaky plasticity, predisposing to catastrophic sensitization. In turn, mechanisms regulating KCC2 itself emerge as substrates of chronification, as well as substrates of opioid-induced maladaptive paradoxical hyperalgesia. Finally, divergent yet convergent signaling cascades underlying KCC2-downregulation reveal a form of pathway degeneracy across sexes with lessons for therapeutics. All-in-all, these findings position KCC2 as a key novel target, not just for analgesia, but also for disease modification.

Article.Title: An integrative view of human nociceptor diversity: from microneurography to molecular identity
Article.Authors: Lampert A.; Tigerholm J.; Stiehl T.; Kurth I.; Haag N.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Neuropathic pain arises from dysfunction of the peripheral or central nervous system and affects up to 10% of the population worldwide. Aberrant activity in injured sensory nerve fibers, particularly spontaneous firing and altered conduction properties of nociceptors, is tightly linked to pain, yet its molecular underpinnings in humans have long remained elusive. Over recent years, major technological advances have transformed both functional and molecular analyses of sensory neurons. High-resolution single-cell and spatial transcriptomics have produced detailed atlases of sensory neuron diversity, while traditional electrophysiological approaches such as patch-clamp and microneurography have provided unparalleled insight into nerve fiber properties. Despite their individual strengths, molecular and functional classifications of sensory neurons have largely evolved in parallel. This review focuses on emerging strategies that bridge these approaches to achieve an integrated, mechanistic understanding of neuropathic pain. We discuss how microneurography-defined biophysical hallmarks, such as activity-dependent slowing, recovery cycle signatures, and following frequency, can be transferred into in vitro patch-clamp paradigms, enabling direct functional comparison with dissociated human and large-animal sensory neurons. The incorporation of Patch-seq approaches has further enabled the assignment of molecular identity to functionally defined nociceptor subtypes, exemplified by the characterization of the mechano-insensitive “sleeping” nociceptors. Finally, we highlight how multimodal datasets combining electrophysiology, transcriptomics, and computational modeling provide new opportunities to unravel the ion channel mechanisms, particularly sodium channel subtypes, that shape pathological firing states. By directly linking human nerve fiber function to molecular programs, this integrative framework paves the way toward stratified, mechanism-based therapies for neuropathic pain.

Article.Title: Toward precision pediatric pain care: integrating mechanistic science, real-world measurement, and patient partnership
Article.Authors: Simons L.; Aghaeepour N.; Cashman C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Pediatric pain science is at an inflection point. Advances in neuroscience, behavioral science, digital health technologies, and patient engagement are rapidly expanding how chronic pain in youth can be understood, measured, and treated. Yet despite these advances, many children and adolescents continue to experience persistent pain-related disability and limited access to effective care, reflecting a gap between scientific discovery and real-world clinical practice. In this perspective, we propose the BRIDGE framework (Biobehavioral Research Integrated with Digital Monitoring and Guided Engagement) as a model for advancing pediatric pain research and care. Mechanistic science is increasingly identifying neural, behavioral, and contextual processes that contribute to pain persistence and recovery, creating opportunities to target modifiable mechanisms underlying pain-related disability. At the same time, digital health technologies including wearable sensors and ecological momentary assessment enable continuous measurement of activity, physiology, and patient-reported experiences in daily life, offering new insights into the dynamic nature of pain and the potential to develop digital biomarkers of risk, recovery, and treatment response. Central to this framework is meaningful partnership with youth and families, ensuring that innovations in measurement and intervention remain aligned with patient priorities and lived experience. Integrating these domains can support precision behavioral interventions, adaptive treatment strategies, and scalable models of care that expand access to evidence-based pediatric pain treatment.

Article.Title: Spontaneous neuropathic pain
Article.Authors: Zeng X.; Woolf C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Spontaneous pain is a highly prevalent and disabling consequence of neuropathic disorders, yet it remains mechanistically underdefined and therapeutically underserved. Historically, preclinical animal models and clinical trials have been overwhelmingly biased toward stimulus-evoked hypersensitivity, relegating spontaneous pain to a secondary manifestation. Emerging evidence now challenges this view. Converging data from pharmacology, neural recordings, and systems-level causal manipulations indicate that spontaneous and stimulus-evoked pain arise from substantially dissociable molecular, cellular, and circuit substrates. Injured-fiber–derived ectopic activity within specific sensory neuron subtypes serves as a dominant peripheral generator of spontaneous pain, whereas cellularly distinct, intact spared-fiber pathways mediate stimulus-evoked hypersensitivity. At spinal and supraspinal levels, spontaneous pain preferentially engages affective–salience networks during pain chronification and may ultimately become stabilized within higher-order circuitry—while remaining dynamically coupled to afferent input. This mechanistic delineation carries critical translational implications. Current diagnostic and treatment guidelines rarely differentiate symptom domains, and most therapies have been validated primarily using stimulus-evoked or overall pain intensity endpoints—potentially contributing to a mechanism–therapy mismatch and variable efficacy. We argue that spontaneous neuropathic pain should be defined as a separate symptom domain rather than considered as a spontaneous manifestation of evoked pain mechanisms. This recognition demands longitudinal, biomarker-informed phenotyping to capture its persistent and fluctuating nature, and thereby enable robust mechanistic dissection at peripheral, spinal, and cortical nodes. Reframing spontaneous neuropathic pain along these lines will provide a foundation for precision therapeutics that target defined cell types, specific molecular drivers, and maladaptive network states—enabling mechanism-based, symptom-aligned treatments.

Article.Title: Advancing equitable pain care worldwide requires progress in low- and middle-income settings: priorities for practice, research, and policy
Article.Authors: Sharma S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Equitable, high-value pain care remains out of reach for many populations worldwide, particularly for people living in low- and middle-income countries and cultural minority groups in high-income settings. Despite carrying a disproportionate burden of chronic pain, these populations remain underrepresented in high-quality pain research, underserved by existing health systems, and constrained by social, political, environmental, and commercial determinants of health. The lack of locally generated evidence forces clinicians and policymakers to rely on externally produced research that may not translate to local cultural, linguistic, or health-system contexts. This invited viewpoint synthesizes key contributors to pain inequity—including limited prioritization of chronic pain in low- and middle-income countries, underdeveloped rehabilitation capacity, poor access to essential treatments, commercial exploitation, and misalignment between culturally shaped pain beliefs and Western-derived assessment and treatment models. I highlight opportunities to strengthen equity in clinical care through improved education of health professionals and the public, culturally and linguistically responsive assessment, and contextually adapted self-management and treatment strategies. Equitable research requires standardized collection of sociodemographic variables, deliberate inclusion of underrepresented groups, and global partnerships that avoid colonizing practices. I propose principles for fair and impactful North–South collaborations focused on co-creation of research agendas, shared leadership, sustainable capacity building, and transparent governance. Advancing equitable global pain care and research will require collective action from clinicians, researchers, institutions, policymakers, journals, funders, and communities. A coordinated shift toward culturally grounded, contextually adaptable, and ethically collaborative approaches is essential to meaningfully reduce global pain disparities and ensure all individuals benefit from scientific progress.

Article.Title: Life course trajectories of musculoskeletal pain
Article.Authors: Ahacic K.; Raices Cruz I.; Kåreholt I.; Bartels S.; Oksanen A.; Wicksell R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract A life course perspective can help identify critical periods and high-risk groups for musculoskeletal pain. However, how musculoskeletal pain develops over the adult life course and the extent to which this development varies among individuals remain largely unexplored. This Swedish population-representative survey followed a sample of 6328 individuals over 7 waves and 42 years, from ages 15 to 101 years, including about 25,000 observations. Reported musculoskeletal pain in the joints, back, or shoulders over the past year was categorized as follows: no pain (0), light pain in 1 to 3 sites (1), severe pain in one site (2), and severe pain in 2 to 3 sites (3). Age-related pain trajectories were identified through a sex-stratified latent class growth analysis. For both women and men, 2 distinct trajectories emerged. In the high-risk group, pain increased consistently throughout working age before declining postretirement. In the other group, pain levels were generally low, surpassing light pain only after retirement age. Although the trajectory patterns were similar for women and men, the high-risk group was twice as large among women (20%) as among men (9%). The general increase in pain towards the end of the life course likely reflects normal ageing processes, including disease onset and frailty, while the trajectory of the high-risk group may indicate the cumulative effect of risk factors associated with working life. Average trends across the entire sample mask the unique experience of this high-risk group and obscure the distinct effects of ageing on the development of musculoskeletal pain.
