Article.Title: Flippability of Escherichia coli membrane proteins under lipid stress reveals a new job for old genes
Article.Authors: Sawasato K.; Bogdanov M.
Article.Abstract: Normally, the “flip-flop” motion is reserved for small lipid molecules which move from one leaflet of the membrane to the other, and even that process is very slow without the aid of specific enzymes. Unexpectedly, we recently found that despite a prohibitively high energy barrier, Escherichia coli cardiolipin (CL) synthase A (ClsA) flips its large catalytic domain across the inner (cytoplasmic) membrane (IM) when cells were fully or partially depleted of phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) and that this was necessary to support cell viability. Here, we demonstrated that production of the non-native phospholipid phosphatidylcholine (PC) in PE-depleted cells prevents ClsA flipping and halts cell growth, a phenotype rescued by constitutively inverted ClsA. Surprisingly, properly oriented lactose permease (LacY) acts as a multicopy suppressor, rescuing the growth defect in the -PE+PC cells. These data indicate that neutral PC regulates the membrane topology of ClsA and LacY, and subsequently the appearance of CL to the periplasmic leaflet required for viability. Therefore, ClsA and potentially LacY may achieve varied roles from the same amino acid sequence through an unusual flip-flopping mechanism. This fruitful “repurposing” of genetic material highlights the remarkable adaptability of living organisms and their membranes. Altering E. coli lipids disrupts growth, but controlled membrane protein flipping simulates natural selection and resemonstrates that membrane proteins can re-evolve under the selective pressure of an altered lipid bilayer.

Article.Title: The representation of order and randomness in the auditory cortex
Article.Authors: Bashari S.; Jankowski M.; Nelken I.
Article.Abstract: Perception fundamentally relies on the brain’s ability to extract structure from its sensory environment. The auditory cortex possesses significant sensitivity to statistical regularities in tone sequences. To examine this phenomenon at the single-neuron level, we used multitone sequences and recorded responses from the auditory cortex of awake adult female Sprague Dawley rats. Tones were presented in periodic sequences with a fixed, repeated cycle; in a fully random condition; or in an intermediate condition in which cycles were maintained, but tones were randomly permuted within each cycle (random cycle condition). Units showed a continuum of preferences between order-preferring neurons and randomness-preferring neurons. Unexpectedly, we found sensitivity to the position of sounds in the cycle (‘phase modulation’). The strongest and most consistent phase modulations were in the responses to the random cycle condition. Finally, we show how such phase sensitivity may emerge from a simple, biologically plausible computation. Neurons in the auditory cortex exhibit a continuum of preferences from order to randomness, and show sensitivity to the position of tones in abstract repeating patterns.

Article.Title: VASP cooperates with zyxin to organize mechanically competent adhesions
Article.Authors: Chung W.; Boujemaa-Paterski R.; Winograd-Katz S.; Eibauer M.; Geiger B.; Medalia O.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Focal adhesions (FAs) are dynamic macromolecular assemblies that anchor the actin cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix via integrin receptors, thereby regulating cell morphology and migration. Here, we show that the vasodilator-stimulated phosphoprotein (VASP) cooperates with the mechanosensitive scaffold protein zyxin to maintain FA during maturation under actomyosin-generated tension. Using sequential CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing and cryo-electron tomography, we resolved the in situ nanoarchitecture of the FA-stress fiber interface. We establish that tropomyosin decorates the dorsal aspect of adhesion-associated stress fibers independently of VASP and zyxin. VASP and zyxin are required for the assembly of dense, aligned actin bundles with uniform polarity, oriented with their barbed ends toward the cell edge. Live-cell imaging and quantitative analyses of cells confined on micropatterns reveal that VASP and zyxin cooperate to preserve the mechanical coupling between FAs and the actin cytoskeleton under contractile load. Our findings establish that VASP and zyxin perform distinct yet complementary functions to organize FA-associated actin into mechanically competent force-transmitting units.

Article.Title: BUB signaling in cancer and molecular insights into targeted therapies
Article.Authors: Baweja B.; Saini C.; Vats P.; Soni R.; Jangir K.; Patidar P.; Kumar A.; Nema R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The Spindle Assembly Checkpoint (SAC) is vital for proper chromosome segregation during cell division and for maintaining genomic integrity; its disruption can cause aneuploidy and tumors. The BUB gene family ensures SAC fidelity by regulating kinetochore–microtubule attachments and mitotic progression. Dysregulation leads to chromosomal instability (CIN), contributing to cancer progression, heterogeneity, metastasis, and therapy resistance. Beyond mitosis, BUB proteins influence DNA repair, chromatin remodeling, transcription, and immune responses. They interact with cell cycle and genome stability pathways, impacting cancer prognosis and therapy response. Research is ongoing to validate BUB proteins as biomarkers and develop inhibitors, possibly combined with immunotherapies or DNA-damaging agents for resistant tumors. This review summarizes their functions, highlighting their potential in personalized cancer treatment.

Article.Title: A circRNA-microRNA-Pdcd1 axis drives microglial activation and retinal ganglion cell degeneration
Article.Authors: Sun L.; Ke X.; Yu J.; Wei J.; Gu J.; Zhou W.; Cen Y.; Huang J.; Zhang X.; Zhang J.; Zhang S.; Liu X.; Ji Y.; Yan W.; Pan S.; Zhou M.; Wu W.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Retinal ganglion cell (RGC) degeneration is the primary cause of vision loss, driven by the complicated effects of intrinsic neuronal damage and neuroinflammation. However, current single-target therapies fail to address these dual pathological challenges. CircRNAs, functioning through ceRNA networks, represent a multi-target intervention due to their stability. Here we show that, using whole‑transcriptome sequencing of optic nerve crush (ONC), we bioinformatically predicted nine candidate ceRNA networks. Among these, the network centered on circAgtpbp1 was significantly up-regulated post-injury, independent of its host gene. Mechanistically, circAgtpbp1 functions as a ceRNA by sequestering miR-3098-3p, thereby de-repressing the translation of PD-1 ( Pdcd1 ). In the ONC model, this upregulation of PD-1 protein amplifies microglial activation, creating a pathogenic non-cell-autonomous inflammatory amplification loop that drives RGC degeneration. Our findings not only uncover a novel circRNA-mediated mechanism in neurodegeneration but also identify the circAgtpbp1-miR-3098-3p-Pdcd1-microglia axis as a promising therapeutic target for neuroprotective interventions.

Article.Title: Towards a comprehensive landscape and mechanism understanding of virus-disease associations
Article.Authors: Wu Y.; You R.; Feng Y.; Lu S.; Chen S.; Fu P.; Zhu Z.; Lu C.; Zhang Z.; Xu L.; Li H.; Wang X.; Wang X.; Huang Q.; Liu X.; Xu Z.; Dong G.; Li S.; Hu X.; Xiang Z.; Hu Y.; Mao L.; Miao Z.; Meng X.; Peng Y.
Article.Abstract: Viruses are linked to human diseases through complex molecular mechanisms, yet a comprehensive investigation of virus-disease associations and their molecular basis remains lacking. We curated 3,555 high-confidence virus-disease associations involving 267 viruses and 954 diseases through text-mining over 28 million PubMed abstracts followed by rigorous manual verification, establishing the most comprehensive resource in this field to date. We then developed AVD, a user-friendly online database to store, visualize, and analyze these associations and their molecular mechanisms. Our analysis revealed that virus-disease association patterns are significantly influenced by viral taxonomy, phenotype, and key biological traits such as transmissibility, transmission routes, and tissue tropism. Molecular analysis identified a core set of bridging genes involved in the majority of virus-disease associations. Notably, these bridging genes were extensively involved in viral infections and diseases, and exhibit distinct characteristics, including a high proportion of secreted proteins, elevated expression across human tissues, and high centrality in the human protein-protein interaction network. Furthermore, we developed a machine-learning model capable of accurately predicting virus-disease associations. Collectively, this study provides a valuable data resource and analytical framework for studying virus-disease relationships and offers novel insights into their molecular mechanisms. In this manuscript the authors analyze viral-disease associations and identified that virus-disease associations are significantly influenced by viral taxonomic, phenotype, and their biological traits. Genes that may mediate the viral-disease associations are also discovered. A database called AVD (Association of Virus and human Diseases) is also constructed to facilitate the storage and convenient analysis of the associations.

Article.Title: Metabolic characteristics and evolutionary history of the nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterial endosymbionts of pennate diatoms
Article.Authors: Cheung S.; Cornejo-Castillo F.; Bianchini G.; Coale T.; Vieyra-Mexicano C.; Sánchez-Baracaldo P.; Zehr J.; Turk-Kubo K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria are important sources of bioavailable nitrogen on Earth. Some nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria are endosymbionts of algae, and recently one of them, UCYN-A2, was shown to be an early-stage organelle (nitroplast) of haptophytes. These biological associations are important models for studying co-evolution and organellogenesis. Endosymbioses between Rhopalodiaceae diatoms and nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria (spheroid bodies, SBs) are widespread in marine and freshwater ecosystems, but their adaptation and evolution remain unclear. We found that the genomes and metabolic characteristics of marine and freshwater SBs are remarkably similar. Purifying selection pressures dominated SB diversification both within marine and freshwater habitats and across habitat boundaries. The metabolic characteristics and genome reduction of SBs are substantially different from UCYN-A, suggesting different evolutionary journeys for the endosymbionts influenced by different hosts. We estimated that the marine SBs diversified ~185 Mya (95% highest posterior density (HPD): 340-88 Mya), which was within a prolonged oligotrophic period in the ocean, during which UCYN-A also diversified. The freshwater SBs diversified from the marine SBs ~137 Mya (95% HPD: 258-66 Mya) and further diversified ~80 Mya (95% HPD: 157-31 Mya), when sea level was increasing. Our study reveals the genetic and metabolic underpinnings characterizing the nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterial endosymbionts of Rhopalodiaceae diatoms.

Article.Title: Conserved Core but Divergent Biochemical Features of RAS-MAPK Signalling in C. elegans
Article.Authors: Bernal Astrain G.; Strakhova R.; Amro J.; Banerjee R.; Teszner E.; Decorso I.; Reiner D.; Smith M.
Article.Abstract: Genetic studies in Caenorhabditis elegans have established core principles of RAS-MAPK signalling. These nematodes encode three RAS proteins: LET-60/KRAS is essential for vulval induction, while RAS-1 and RAS-2 are orthologs of RRAS/RRAS2 and MRAS, respectively, but remain biologically and biochemically uncharacterized. We here present a comprehensive biochemical analysis of all three C. elegans RAS proteins, defining nucleotide cycling and effector interactions. We show that conserved RAS scaffolds are tuned by sequence variation to balance signalling with developmental fidelity. LET-60 has significantly impaired nucleotide exchange and changing its sequence to match human KRAS induces a protruding vulva phenotype in vivo. RAS-1 rapidly exchanges GDP-to-GTP, whereas RAS-2 remains consistently GDP-bound. LET-60 engages the RAF ortholog LIN-45 through a divergent interface, and RAS-1 unexpectedly drives SOC-2:RAS:PP1C holophosphatase assembly in a nucleotide-independent manner. Our findings reveal both conserved and distinctive biochemical features underlying RAS signalling and suggest species-specific tuning of this key proliferation pathway.

Article.Title: Age-related shift towards feedforward motor control under uncertainty
Article.Authors: Kreter N.; Sager C.; Barany D.; Dundon N.; Marneweck M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Humans perform movements in the face of uncertainty on a daily basis. To accomplish these tasks without error, young adults frequently rely on feedback-mediated motor strategies that allow them to update their movement as certainty evolves. However, it remains unclear how aging impacts the ability to plan and execute movement under uncertain conditions. To investigate how aging affects the ability to plan actions under uncertainty, we designed a “go-before-you-know” (GBYK) reaching task in which we varied certainty by changing the probability that a reach target would be correct. Fifteen healthy young adults and fifteen older adults completed this task while undergoing fMRI. Behaviorally, young adults employed a strategy consistent with feedback-mediated control, biasing their reach trajectories toward the more likely target when uncertainty was low, and intermediate to potential targets when uncertainty was high. Older adults employed a different approach, characterized by a pronounced rightward bias, particularly under high uncertainty, suggesting a shift toward feedforward control. Neuroimaging results mirrored these behavioral patterns, revealing that young adults encoded task certainty and reach direction in sensorimotor regions more strongly than older adults. Overall, these findings suggest that aging diminishes the ability to flexibly encode task-related uncertainty, resulting in a shift towards feedforward control strategies.

Article.Title: Distinct genetic perturbations at the endogenous Atf4 locus uncouple polyadenylation loss from transcriptional readthrough
Article.Authors: Zhang Z.; Wu T.; Chen Z.; Chen D.; Ye M.; Chen J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Transcription termination by RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) is coupled to co-transcriptional cleavage and polyadenylation directed by the canonical AAUAAA polyadenylation signal (PAS). However, the in vivo requirement of the canonical PAS for termination fidelity remains unclear. Here, we dissect PAS-dependent termination at the endogenous Atf4 locus using complementary mouse models. A previously characterized Atf4 ΔCDS + ΔPAS allele deleting exons 2-3 induces strong transcriptional readthrough, producing an Atf4 – Cacna1i fusion transcript that suppresses Rps19bp1 and causes severe cardiac defects. To isolate PAS function, we generated an Atf4 ΔCDS allele retaining the PAS and an Atf4 ΔPAS allele preserving the coding sequence but deleting the PAS. The ΔCDS allele produces modest readthrough, whereas ΔPAS does not produce detectable downstream readthrough. Instead, PAS loss permits utilization of a cryptic intragenic polyadenylation site within exon 3, generating a prematurely terminated transcript. These findings demonstrate that PAS loss does not necessarily cause transcriptional readthrough in vivo and can instead promote alternative polyadenylation at an endogenous mammalian locus.

Article.Title: Towards a unified biology of vertebrate number sense
Article.Authors: Zanon M.; Messina A.; Butterworth B.; Vallortigara G.; Brennan C.; Torres-Pérez J.; Miletto-Petrazzini M.
Article.Abstract: Number sense, the ability to estimate and compare numerical quantities, emerges early in development and is widespread across species. Despite decades of work on behavioural and neural correlates of numerosity, the genetic and mechanistic foundations remain poorly integrated. We propose a review and perspective that brings together evidence from vertebrates. Our unique focus relies on how genetic variation, brain lateralisation, and neural circuit organisation across development shape number cognition. We highlight zebrafish (Danio rerio) and chicks (Gallus gallus) as complementary comparative models that can uncover conserved principles and novel mechanisms, opening new avenues for studying the biological bases of numerical cognition and its disorders from the very early developmental stages.

Article.Title: Spi1 and Usp7 aggravate diabetic encephalopathy through regulating Ddx3x
Article.Authors: Zhao N.; Chen L.; Qin L.; Liu T.; Han G.
Article.Abstract: DEAD-box helicase 3 X-linked (DDX3X) can interact with NOD-like receptor protein 3 (NLRP3) to drive inflammasome activation. Nonetheless, the role of DDX3X on NLRP3 inflammasome activation in diabetic encephalopathy remains unidentified. Here, Ddx3x knockdown alleviates microglial NLRP3 activation, which reverses the increased permeability and decreased tight junction proteins induced by conditioned medium of lipopolysaccharide-stimulated microglia (LPS-CM) in bEnd.3 endothelial cells, and overturns LPS-CM-elicited apoptosis promotion in HT22 neurons. In male type 2 diabetes db/db mice, Ddx3x silencing mitigates microglial activation, blood-brain barrier disruption, neuronal apoptosis and cognitive impairment. Spi-1 proto-oncogene (SPI1) transcriptionally activates Ddx3x ; Additionally, ubiquitin-specific protease (USP)7 reduces DDX3X ubiquitination to increase its protein stability. Silencing Spi1 / Usp7 exerts beneficial effects in vitro and in vivo, which are neutralized when overexpressing Ddx3x . In conclusion, Spi1 / Usp7 knockdown downregulates DDX3X to inhibit microglial NLRP3 activation, alleviating BBB dysfunction and neuronal loss to ameliorate diabetic encephalopathy, which suggests prospective targets for diabetic encephalopathy.

Article.Title: Evolutionary transitions in social organization and the relationship between climate and queen number in ant societies
Article.Authors: De Gasperin O.; Silvestro D.; Helanterä H.; LeBoeuf A.; Downing P.; Chapuisat M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract In about one fourth of ant species, multiple queens reproduce within the same colony (‘polygyny’), reducing relatedness and potentially fuelling evolutionary conflicts among colony members. Polygyny is more common at higher altitudes / latitudes in several species, suggesting that cold climates favour multiple queens. We tested this prediction with phylogenetic analyses comparing 263 ant species and modelled the evolutionary pathways between alternative social structures. Queen number was phylogenetically labile, with bidirectional transitions between single and multi-queen species passing through socially polymorphic species (with both types of colonies). Contrary to our predictions, polygyny was not more common at higher latitudes or altitudes. Socially polymorphic species tended to occur in environments with more uniform precipitation throughout the year, and queen number increased towards the tropics. We discuss how multiple queening may be favoured in warm climates due to competitive advantages of faster colony growth and higher genetic diversity. We also call for more studies in tropical regions, as most studies were performed in the northern hemisphere.

Article.Title: CircAbcc1-encoded ABCC1-677aa modulates DLX1 to suppress ferroptosis in chronic cerebral ischemia
Article.Authors: Yang J.; Yu Y.; Fan J.; Hong K.; Zhang N.; Zheng J.
Article.Abstract: Cerebral ischemia leads to progressive neurological dysfunction due to restricted blood perfusion in the brain. While circular RNAs are known to regulate pathological processes, their ability to encode functional proteins during ischemic injury remains unclear. Here, we show that the circular RNA circAbcc1 suppresses ferroptosis in mouse and cellular models of chronic cerebral ischemia‘. We found that circAbcc1 translates into a functional protein, ABCC1-677aa. This protein actively interacts with and phosphorylates the transcription factor DLX1, triggering its export from the nucleus to the cytoplasm. This translocation prevents DLX1 from transcriptionally repressing the crucial anti-ferroptotic genes, Gpx4 and Fsp1. The subsequent upregulation of Gpx4 and Fsp1 limits lipid peroxidation and iron accumulation, successfully protecting brain neurons from ferroptosis. These findings elucidate a regulatory mechanism driven by a circular RNA-encoded protein and identify the circAbcc1-DLX1 axis as a potential therapeutic target for cerebral ischemic injury. A circular RNA, circAbcc1, protects neurons from ferroptosis during chronic cerebral ischemia by encoding the protein ABCC1-677aa. This protein relieves repression of anti-ferroptotic genes, reducing neuronal damage and highlighting the circAbcc1-DLX1 pathway as a therapeutic target.

Article.Title: Uncoupling of seagrass host selection and succession for microbial guilds in meadow chronosequence
Article.Authors: Maithani P.; Sim C.; Srinivas S.; Kwek Z.; Case R.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Succession is an ecosystem building process in which a habitat and its community interact predictably by increasing diversity, habitat engineering, and ultimately reaching a climax community, where other ecological processes influence its dynamic. Key to succession is the establishment of primary producing habitat forming species, which drives niche differentiation leading to increasing diversity. Here, we use the primary colonizing and habitat forming seagrass, Halophila ovalis , to demonstrate that it drives bacterial succession in a meadow ecosystem, and its microbiome, both rhizoplane and phylloplane, are under host selection. Many of the characteristics attributed to plants for habitat modification are microbial processes such as nitrogen fixation and sulfide detoxification and succession is often extrapolated to such processes. To determine if succession (increasing diversity) or selection (reducing diversity) drives changes in diversity (16S rRNA gene) or habitat modifying processes ( nifH , soxB , aprA , dsrA ), molecular analysis was performed along chronosequences (as a proxy for succession) of seagrass patches. Bacterial communities were sampled within the meadow ecosystem and the microbiomes of H. ovalis (both rhizoplane and phylloplane). Genes involved in biogeochemical cycling are differentially impacted within the microbiome and meadow sediments, with only nifH under succession. All genes from all niches sampled for community analysis are under directional community trajectories, despite being subjected to distinct ecological processes, signifying that many ecological processes, including succession and host association, drive community assemblage.

Article.Title: Selective inhibition of IL-6 trans-signalling reveals distinct mechanisms of human classic and trans-signalling receptor-complex formation
Article.Authors: Rieneck E.; Haak J.; Asgarov K.; Pallandre J.; Wundrack N.; Ettich J.; Miri N.; Floss D.; Scheller J.; Garbers C.; Clark A.; Wijdenes J.; Schaper F.; Dittrich A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The cytokine interleukin-6 orchestrates inflammation through two distinct pathways of receptor activation: anti-inflammatory classic signalling via membrane-bound interleukin-6 receptor and pro-inflammatory trans-signalling via soluble interleukin-6 receptor. Current interleukin-6-targeted therapies block both pathways, thereby disrupting essential homeostatic functions initiated by classic signalling. We here show a high-affinity, human-specific antibody that selectively inhibits interleukin-6 trans-signalling. This antibody maintains classic signalling-induced expression of hepatic acute phase genes while completely blocking trans-signalling-induced activation of endothelial cells. By targeting the domain D2 of membrane-bound and soluble human interleukin-6 receptor, the antibody selectively prevents formation of the trans-signalling receptor complex without interfering with ligand binding. This selective blockade demonstrates that human interleukin-6 classic and trans-signalling proceed through distinct receptor assemblies. Our findings describe mechanistic insight into interleukin-6 receptor assembly and provide a strategy to suppress inflammatory interleukin-6 activity while preserving regenerative and anti-inflammatory signalling, thus offering both conceptual and potential therapeutic advances in the targeted modulation of cytokine signalling networks.

Article.Title: NEDD1 stabilization regulated by hUTP14a and FBW7γ axis safeguards mitotic cell fate homeostasis
Article.Authors: Su Y.; Jiang Y.; Sun X.; Zhang C.; Zhao Z.; Li L.; Du X.
Article.Abstract: Accurate spindle formation is vital for mitotic progression and genomic DNA segregation, with γ-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC) mediating microtubule nucleation, and NEDD1 serving as its essential recruitment/anchoring adaptor. However, the mechanisms underlying the regulation of NEDD1 remain largely elusive. Here, we identify a pathway that controls NEDD1 stability during mitosis. hUTP14a relocates to the perichromosomal region at mitotic onset; its depletion causes mitotic catastrophe, impaired chromosomal congression, and reduced γ-tubulin recruitment around chromosomes. Mass spectrometry identifies NEDD1 as a critical hUTP14a-interacting partner during mitosis. hUTP14a protects NEDD1 from ubiquitin-mediated degradation. UbiBrowser 2.0 database prediction and validation experiments identify FBW7γ as an E3 ligase to promote NEDD1 K323 ubiquitination-mediated degradation, while hUTP14a facilitates FBW7γ degradation in a leucine-rich repeat (LRR)-dependent manner. The hUTP14a depletion-induced mitotic catastrophe is reversed by ectopic Flag-NEDD1-K323R but not wild-type Flag-NEDD1. Thus, NEDD1 is stabilized via hUTP14a-mediated FBW7γ degradation to safeguard mitotic cell fate.

Article.Title: Engineering T cell-selective chemokine inhibitors through network-level directed evolution
Article.Authors: Payne M.; Durães F.; Clark C.; Wilde E.; Karuppanan K.; Chandra S.; Brennan P.; Hodson D.; Smagurauskaite G.; Bhattacharya S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Immune-mediated inflammatory diseases (IMIDs) are sustained by chemokine-driven recruitment of effector T cells. Although direct suppression of T cell function can be effective, systemic immunosuppression and infection risk limit clinical utility. Targeting chemokine networks offers an alternative strategy, yet chemokine redundancy has hindered the development of clinically effective inhibitors. Tick evasins overcome chemokine redundancy by binding multiple chemokines. Here we show that network-level directed evolution of class B evasin-derived peptides generates T cell-selective chemokine inhibitors. In contrast to analogous class A-derived peptides, these preferentially bind and inhibit chemokines that drive T cell migration. Structural modelling of chemokine:peptide complexes and structure-guided mutagenesis suggest that evasin-derived peptides sterically occlude receptor-binding surfaces and that class B-derived peptides exhibit a more compact organisation of key interaction hotspots than a previously characterised class A-derived peptide. Together, these findings suggest that anti-chemokine peptide specificity can be engineered through scaffold choice and network-level directed evolution.

Article.Title: KCNQ1 disruption alters human neuronal development through mitochondrial and insulin signalling pathways
Article.Authors: Schall D.; Güler B.; Alibrahim S.; Hasan M.; Ahmad N.; Widomska J.; Acuna C.; Sullivan M.; Röth R.; Liu C.; Blaier L.; Vincze K.; Burau K.; Macri S.; Mauceri D.; Luzarowski M.; Apáti Á.; Réthelyi J.; Poelmans G.; Rappold G.; Franke B.; Glennon J.; Berkel S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract KCNQ1 encodes a voltage-gated potassium channel implicated in peripheral and neurological disorders, but its role in human neurodevelopment remains unclear. We generated KCNQ1 knockout (KO) human induced pluripotent stem cells and differentiated them into neural stem cells (NSCs) and cortical neurons. KCNQ1 -deficient NSCs show impaired neurite outgrowth, linked to reduced cell adhesion and disrupted neural cell adhesion molecule signalling, a phenotype reproduced by pharmacological KCNQ1 inhibition. Multi-omics and follow-up analyses reveal mitochondrial dysfunction, including reduced mitochondrial copy number and ATP synthase expression. KO cells also show impaired insulin signalling, with diminished insulin receptor gene expression and altered RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT pathways. In differentiated neuronal cultures, KCNQ1 loss decreases synaptic activity and maintains an immature transcriptional profile. Together, these findings identify a role for KCNQ1 in regulating cell adhesion, mitochondrial function, insulin signalling, and neuronal maturation, expanding our understanding of processes that may contribute to neurological manifestations associated with KCNQ1 -related disorders.

Article.Title: Divergent processing strategies for auditory sequence recognition in humans and zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata)
Article.Authors: Ning Z.; Li J.; ten Cate C.; Honing H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Deriving sequential information from complex sounds is a challenge for auditory systems, yet it remains unclear whether humans and nonhuman species integrate multidimensional cues or prioritize a single dimension when processing multidimensional input. We investigated how humans and zebra finches ( Taeniopygia guttata ) process concurrent acoustic cues using an identical behavioural paradigm with complex-tone sequences. By presenting probe stimuli that selectively preserved or disrupted either pitch or formant trajectory, we quantified these processing strategies. We show that zebra finches employ an additive integration strategy, treating pitch and formant trajectories as complementary components of a unified auditory pattern. In contrast, humans exhibit a dominant reliance on pitch. Experience further modulates this bias, with trained human listeners recruiting secondary cues to preserve learned relational structure when pitch is unreliable. These findings imply a cross-species divergence in auditory representation, suggesting that auditory processing is shaped by an interplay of species-specific priorities and experience-dependent functional substitution.

Article.Title: Functional specialization and dynamical interaction in human amygdala subregions support fearful-expression processing
Article.Authors: Cao D.; Cui J.; Yan X.; Zhang X.; Dang Y.; Zhao H.; Li J.; Zhang J.; Zhang Y.
Article.Abstract: Fearful-expression processing supports adaptive responses to potential threats, requiring both rapid threat evaluation and face-related information processing. However, how human amygdala subregions contribute to these complementary processes remains unclear. Here we record intracranial electroencephalography from twelve patients with epilepsy during an emotional face-matching task, sampling 58 amygdala contacts with balanced hemispheric distributions. Condition-specific analyses reveal separable theta/alpha dynamics between the lateral and medial amygdala within fearful-face and neutral-face matching conditions, but not shape matching. Between-condition contrasts further reveal earlier lateral amygdala engagement and stronger lateral-to-medial directional interactions for fearful-face versus neutral-face matching, whereas later medial engagement and stronger medial-to-lateral interactions emerge for neutral-face versus shape matching. Control analyses preserve the main neural effects. In a separate cohort of seven patients, intracranial stimulation produces dissociable behavioral effects, with lateral stimulation impairing fear matching and medial stimulation facilitating neutral-face matching. Together, these findings reveal a condition-dependent functional differentiation within the human amygdala during fearful-expression processing.

Article.Title: Frequency-specific oscillations track parallel processing of linguistic structural and lexical-semantic information from perception to decision
Article.Authors: Fu Y.; Xu Z.; Yao Q.; Mu Y.; Jiang Y.
Article.Abstract: The ability to perceive linguistic features is essential for language comprehension, yet how our brains dynamically recognize, integrate and process distinct linguistic features is still controversial. Here, we employ magnetoencephalography to examine the spatiotemporal organization of two word-level dimensions: syllabic structural and lexical-semantic regularities using a novel auditory linguistic task with an orthogonal design. During the recognition of linguistic features, we identify time-dependent and frequency-specific oscillations in temporal-frontal, para-hippocampal, parietal areas, supporting neural dynamics spanning from linguistic to memory and decision-making processing. Decoding linguistic features in timeseries reveals parallel activities of structure and lexical semantics through distinct neural networks, which beyond the language network extending from auditory cortex to language–sensorimotor hubs. By linking behavior to neural responses, we uncover the frontal-parietal network associated with individual differences in response to dual-feature violations. Overall, our findings reveal the concurrent availability of structural and lexical-semantic representation and characterize task-specific choice tendency under dual-feature conflict.

Article.Title: Time-locked activities of resting-state networks that transiently occur in human resting-state brain activities
Article.Authors: Takeda Y.; Hiroe N.; Yamashita O.
Article.Abstract: Spontaneous brain activities at rest are organized into resting-state networks, such as the default mode network. While the default mode network is assumed to interact with other networks to integrate distributed information, its fine-scale temporal dynamics remain unclear. Here, we demonstrate how the default mode network interacts with other networks at millisecond-scale temporal resolution. Using a large dataset of resting-state magnetoencephalography and our recently proposed method, we estimated the spatiotemporal patterns that recur in resting-state brain activity and then examined the interactions across the resting-state networks in these patterns. In the alpha/beta band component of the spatiotemporal patterns, the default mode network and the visual/sensorimotor network alternately appear with a lag of about 24/13 ms, corresponding to about π /2 rad in the alpha/beta oscillation. These alternating and orthogonal activities of the resting-state networks may reflect the brain’s strategy to achieve both the integration and separation of visual and sensorimotor information via the default mode network. Furthermore, we reveal how these activities consecutively move between the default mode network and the visual/sensorimotor network in tens of milliseconds. They move in different ways depending on their direction, suggesting that distinct mechanisms generate the movements in different directions.

Article.Title: MUFASA: a continuous-time stochastic framework for realistic fluorescence microscopy simulation
Article.Authors: Omezzine W.; Schaub S.; Blanc-Féraud L.; Calatroni L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract We present MUFASA (Multi-Protocol Unified Fluorescence-based Advanced Simulation Algorithm), a physically grounded, continuous-time simulator for super-resolution fluorescence microscopy. By modeling fluorophore dynamics using continuous-time Markov chains, MUFASA’s simulation features yield realistic photon emission behavior across both Single Molecule Localization Microscopy (SMLM) and fluorescence fluctuation-based (FF-SRM) protocols—independently of frame duration and sampling. The framework supports both individual emitters and structure-level simulations, incorporating photophysical transitions, photobleaching, and camera properties. To quantitatively validate simulations with real data, we introduce a novel validation metric based on the 1-Wasserstein distance between simulated and experimental photon-count distributions. In addition to simulation, another functionality estimates key photophysical parameters (e.g., molar extinction coefficient) and to suggest optimal light-source power ranges from fluctuation data. An intuitive Python-based graphical interface enables real-time parameter tuning, visualization, and TIFF export. Designed for biologists, physicists, microscopists, and numerical imaging engineers, MUFASA offers a practical platform for microscopy experiment design, hypothesis testing and the generation of realistic training data for data-driven microscopy methods across modalities.

Article.Title: Machine learning analysis of cilia driven particle transport distinguishes primary ciliary dyskinesia from normal cilia
Article.Authors: Hadas N.; Xu H.; Neupane S.; Twan W.; Elgamal A.; Lunel A.; Mahjoub M.; Horani A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) is a genetic condition causing dysmotile cilia and abnormal mucociliary clearance. Despite advances in understanding disease pathogenesis, diagnosis remains challenging. Here, we show that machine learning analysis of cilia-driven particle transport can objectively detect primary ciliary dyskinesia-related dysfunction. Using high-speed video microscopy, we captured fluorescent microsphere movement on cultured multiciliated cells from 14 individuals with primary ciliary dyskinesia and 10 healthy donors (602 videos). We developed CiliaTracks, an open-source computational framework that extracts measures of micropsphere movement, visualizes transport patterns, and classifies cilia-propelled particle transport. Quantitative and visual analyses reveal distinct motility profiles between PCD and non-primary ciliary dyskinesia and normal recordings. Classical machine learning models and a convolutional neural network classify recordings with 95-97% accuracy and differentiate affected from normal samples. Machine learning provides an objective, accurate framework for characterizing ciliary dysfunction, offering potential as a diagnostic tool for primary ciliary dyskinesia.

Article.Title: Balancing energy efficiency and functional demand via bimodal coupling optimization in biological rhythms
Article.Authors: Zhang J.; Han J.; Xie L.
Article.Abstract: Biological rhythms are governed by intricate interactions among oscillatory subsystems, yet how they balance functional demands and energy efficiency remains unclear. We present a bimodal coupling optimization strategy where physiological systems alternate between synchronized (energy-saving) and desynchronized (function-priority) coupling modes. Using the water-filling principle developed in communications engineering, we derive necessary optimality conditions showing that energy-efficiency (oxygen uptake per cardiac work) maximization requires synchronized heart rate(HR)-respiration oscillations. Then, system modeling confirms task/stress-induced oxygen demands enhance oxygen uptake at the cost of desynchronization and reduced efficiency. Experiments reveal a 70.36% decrease in HR-respiration synchronization during arithmetic versus relaxation, enabling 4.43% higher oxygen uptake but with 11.38% lower energy efficiency. This bimodal coupling optimization strategy is also evident in pancreatic islets, with their insulin/glucagon oscillator alternating between in-phase (energy-saving) and anti-phase (rapid glucose reduction) coupling. This framework, integrating engineering and life sciences, reveals a universal regulatory principle for biological oscillatory systems. Integrating optimization theory, physiological modeling and experiments, this study reveals a bimodal coupling strategy in which biological rhythms switch between synchronized energysaving and desynchronized function-priority modes.

Article.Title: Self-regulated emergence of heavy-tailed weight distributions in evolving complex network architectures
Article.Authors: Li J.; van Leeuwen C.; Bauer R.; Rentzeperis I.
Article.Abstract: The nervous system continuously adjusts connection strengths and reorganizes its structure to form and maintain complex connectivity patterns with heavy-tailed weight distributions. We propose a parsimonious model in which structural and synaptic plasticity are driven by common diffusion dynamics. Synaptic plasticity alone generates heavy-tailed weight distributions, but only when activity spreading remains predominantly local. However, when combined with structural plasticity through adaptive rewiring, the model also generates these distributions with more extensive activity flow. Furthermore, adaptive rewiring produces complex network structures with convergent-divergent circuits. These circuits contain motifs that are pervasive in nervous systems and are responsible for context-sensitive signal propagation and enhanced signal-to-noise ratios. Our model robustly reproduces these results across diverse dynamical regimes while capturing key connectivity features of both C. elegans and mouse brain networks. These findings suggest that the underlying principles are shared across species of varying complexity. We develop a diffusion-based model of evolving neural networks with adaptive weight adjustment and rewiring. Compared with weight adjustment alone, adding adaptive rewiring generates heavy-tailed weights over broader activity regimes.

Article.Title: Persistent impairment of spatial hearing and neural binaural interaction after “temporary” noise-induced hearing loss
Article.Authors: Mackey C.; Mondul J.; Conner A.; Peacock J.; Benson M.; Hackett T.; Tollin D.; Ramachandran R.
Article.Abstract: Many people have trouble understanding speech in noisy environments despite normal audiometric thresholds, a condition referred to as "hidden hearing loss." A leading hypothesis attributes this deficit to inner hair cell synaptic pathology (cochlear synaptopathy), which can persist after recovery from noise-induced temporary elevation of audiometric thresholds. This pathology impairs the temporally precise sound encoding necessary for spatial hearing, but direct evidence in primates, human or nonhuman, is lacking. Here, we show that a single noise exposure, producing only a temporary threshold elevation, induced long-lasting alterations in synaptic morphology, without synapse loss, resulting in persistent spatial hearing deficits for up to 11 months post-exposure in nonhuman primates of both sexes. These perceptual deficits were accompanied by a reduction in a neurophysiological measure of binaural processing - the binaural interaction component (BIC) of the auditory brainstem response (ABR). Both behavioral and neural deficits persisted despite full recovery of audiometric thresholds. Together, these findings provide the first evidence in primates that noise exposure disrupts spatial hearing and binaural neural circuit function without loss of hair cells or synapses. Because spatial hearing tests and the ABR/BIC are clinically accessible, this work also establishes translational biomarkers for early neural dysfunction underlying hidden hearing loss.

Article.Title: Cellular and spatial context of genetic convergence between insomnia liability and DTI ALPS perivascular diffusivity
Article.Authors: Shen J.; Shen Y.; Yu G.; Pang L.; Xiao C.
Article.Abstract: Sleep has been linked to brain waste clearance and glymphatic/perivascular transport, yet whether insomnia shares genetic architecture with perivascular diffusivity remains unclear. Polygenic enrichment, conjunctional false discovery rate, and Bayesian colocalization analyses support shared statistical signals in this region, which contains the MAPT inversion locus. Transcriptome-wide, gene-level fine-mapping, and summary-data Mendelian randomization analyses prioritize HEXIM1, ACBD4, EFTUD2, and MAPT. Tissue, cell-type, spatial transcriptomic, and sleep-perturbation analyses place these candidates in neuronal, glial, immune, vascular, and perivascular contexts, with effects varying by brain region and imaging phenotype. Together, these findings support localized genetic convergence rather than a genome-wide shared architecture and provide biological context for future studies of perivascular imaging phenotypes and neurodegeneration-related processes. Insomnia and MRI-derived perivascular diffusivity show little genome-wide genetic correlation but converge locally at 17q21.31, highlighting HEXIM1, ACBD4, EFTUD2 and MAPT.

Article.Title: Non‑monotonic reorganization of cortical neuron firing despite ongoing delta‑dominated activity
Article.Authors: Ge D.; Qin S.; Huang Z.; Chen L.; Liu Y.
Article.Abstract: Delta - dominated activity is a hallmark of anesthesia and non‑REM sleep, yet how neuronal firing evolves across these rhythms remains unclear. Here, by tracking cortical neuron firing in the ketamine‑xylazine model, we find that across continuing delta - dominated activity, population firing rates progress through successive epochs of excitation, suppression, and re - emergence. Concurrently, fine‑scale spike timing and burst dynamics exhibit non - monotonic modulation, revealing continuous reorganization beneath the ongoing delta-dominated oscillation. At the transition to theta - dominated activity, a restructuring of temporal patterning without a significant shift in the firing - rate distribution suggests that temporal structure, rather than firing rate, defines this transition. These population - level dynamics were firing - rate - dependent: high‑firing - rate neurons were more tightly modulated, whereas low‑firing-rate neurons exhibited more heterogeneous changes. Neither ketamine nor xylazine alone recapitulates these dynamics, suggesting their combined action creates a uniquely dynamic architecture. These findings reveal a continuous, firing - rate - dependent reorganization of single-neuron activity during ongoing delta-dominated states.

Article.Title: Linking centromere stretch to SAC signaling in mammalian oocytes with insights from modified kinetochore model
Article.Authors: Yun Y.; Lane S.; Guo Z.; Zheng Z.; Cai W.; Holt J.; Jones K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) monitors kinetochore-microtubule interactions to ensure accurate chromosome segregation. In mitosis, investigation of its silencing at anaphase centers on whether attachment or tension is the key signal, while in meiosis for mammalian oocytes it remains unclear whether centromere stretching contributes to SAC deactivation, because in this reductional division sister chromatids co-segregate during meiosis I. While previous studies have linked bivalent tension to SAC control in oocytes, this measurement cannot be directly equated with mitotic chromatin stretching. Here, by tagging the N-terminus of NDC80/HEC1, we developed a mouse oocyte model that features stable microtubule attachments, yet exhibits persistent SAC signaling at metaphase I. Our comprehensive analysis reveals a strong correlation between centromere stretching and SAC signaling. Furthermore, high-resolution live imaging demonstrates that these modified kinetochores impair their oscillatory movements, a process vital for error correction, while chromosome congression remains largely unaffected. Collectively, our data suggest that stable microtubule attachment alone is insufficient to silence SAC in mammalian oocytes; instead, centromere stretching may serve as a critical signal to deactivate the checkpoint. These findings underscore the adaptability of core cell-cycle surveillance pathways.

Article.Authors: Harrison M.; Flood T.; Reglinski M.; McNeil M.; Dorfmueller H.; Wren B.; Passmore I.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Production of glycoconjugate vaccines has long relied upon chemical methods which are highly complex and expensive, resulting in vaccines that are not widely affordable. Heterologous bioconjugation methods, such as Protein-Glycan Coupling Technology (PGCT), have emerged as a path to significantly cheaper manufacture using safe host organisms, such as Escherichia coli , for recombinant glycoconjugate expression. PGCT glycoconjugate synthesis components are typically encoded across three plasmids and require the addition of exogenous chemical inducers for gene expression. In this study, we utilise modular DNA assembly to generate a single constitutive plasmid for biosynthesis of a Streptococcus pyogenes rhamnose polysaccharide glycoconjugate vaccine. This approach resulted in a greater than seven-fold glycoconjugate yield as well as simplified cell culture conditions compared to the traditional three plasmid inducible system. Importantly, given the modular nature of this method, this innovation could be applied to the manufacture of glycoconjugate vaccines against a range of pathogens.

Article.Title: Suppression of follistatin by spontaneous seizures dysregulates neurogenesis in a model of Alzheimer’s disease neuropathology
Article.Authors: Furuta Y.; Wang J.; Fu C.; Silva-Pérez M.; Al Faisal M.; Church C.; Hiniker A.; Rissman R.; Lee M.; Yu W.; Chin J.

We identify c-Fos, whose expression is suppressed by the seizure-induced transcription factor ∆FosB, as a transcriptional activator of Fst . Lastly, ablation of Fst dysregulates neurogenesis dynamics in wild-type mice, whereas FST treatment normalizes dynamics in AD mice. These findings reveal a previously unidentified activity-dependent mechanism in which the expression of FST controls neurogenesis dynamics.

Notably, a splice-switching antisense oligonucleotide successfully restored normal STMN2 splicing and function, demonstrating that directly correcting splicing defects can rescue motor neurons. Article.Title: Progressive Lineage Restriction of Bergmann Glia‐Like Progenitors During Postnatal Cerebellar Development
Article.Authors: Adachi T.; Suyama K.; Ito S.; Isogai E.; Sone M.; Hoshino M.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Bergmann glia‐like progenitors (BGLPs) are transient progenitors in the postnatal cerebellum, but how their lineage potential changes during development remains incompletely understood. Our previous electroporation‐based study suggested that P0 BGLPs possess broader lineage potential than P6 BGLPs. Here, we performed recombination‐based lineage tracing by cerebellar surface application of tamoxifen to Ai9/+; Glast CreERT2/+ mice and temporally analyzed the progeny of BGLPs labeled at P0, P3, P6, and P8. We found that BGLPs undergo progressive lineage restriction during postnatal development. P0 BGLPs gave rise to Bergmann glial cells (BGs), inner granule cell layer astrocytes (IGL astrocytes), white matter astrocytes (WM astrocytes), and molecular layer inhibitory neurons (ML‐INs), confirming our previous electroporation‐based findings. In contrast, P3 BGLPs generated BGs, IGL astrocytes, and WM astrocytes, whereas P6 BGLPs generated BGs and IGL astrocytes, and P8 BGLPs generated predominantly BGs. Thus, BGLP lineage output was progressively restricted from four progeny categories at P0 to a predominantly BG‐restricted output by P8, suggesting that BGLPs dynamically adjust their cellular output during postnatal cerebellar maturation. Additional temporal analyses were consistent with a stepwise pathway from P0 BGLPs to ML‐INs, in which astrocyte‐like progenitors (AsLPs) appear first among BGLP descendants, some of which may subsequently transition into committed inhibitory neuron progenitors (INPs) that give rise to ML‐INs. These findings identify postnatal BGLPs as a useful in vivo model for studying progressive lineage restriction and stage‐specific cellular supply during cerebellar development.

Article.Title: A Glial Interplay Regulates Junctional Architecture at the Blood–Brain Barrier of Drosophila
Article.Authors: Contreras E.; Naffin E.; Collins‐Ramírez M.; Surina N.; Rothermel M.; Salazar‐Tirado J.; Schirmeier S.; Klämbt C.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Neurons require a tightly controlled ion and metabolite homeostasis, which is maintained by an effective blood–brain barrier (BBB). Since the integrity of the BBB is essential for brain function, its maintenance during development represents a significant challenge. The Drosophila BBB is formed by two glial layers. Subperineurial glia (SPG) establish pleated septate junctions (pSJs) to generate the primary diffusion barrier. Abutting the SPG lies the mitotically active perineurial glia (PG). Only a small number of PG cells are specified during embryogenesis. The FGF8‐like signal Pyramus presented by the SPG subsequently triggers proliferation of the PG, which ultimately covers the entire nervous system. To investigate the role of PG in the development and physiology of the BBB, we genetically ablated them. In these animals, glucose influx into SPG is unchanged following acute glucose perfusion. However, adult PG‐ablated flies show increased sensitivity to glucose‐only diet, indicating that while baseline carbohydrate transport can be maintained in the absence of most PG, the system fails under metabolic stress. SPG morphology and pSJ organization are largely preserved during larval stages upon PG ablation. In contrast, in PG‐ablated pupae, moody expression is impaired in SPG and pSJs progressively split, producing ectopic junctional strands. Together, these results reveal the necessity of PG for the maturation and function of SPG, as well as the mutual interdependence between the two BBB glial layers.

Article.Title: Amygdala Oligodendrocyte <scp>MDH1</scp> Dysregulation and Mitochondrial Dysfunction in High Urea‐Induced Anxiety‐Like Behavior
Article.Authors: Hu J.; Zhang M.; Jiang S.; Bi H.; Tu B.; Zhang S.; Wan G.; Wang Q.; Liu Y.; Leng J.; Chen X.; Li J.; Chen D.; Li G.; Gui J.; Huang B.; Ran J.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT The high incidence and mortality rates of anxiety disorders in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) have drawn attention. Prior studies identified urea as an independent risk factor for mental disorders in CKD. While urea accumulation is known to impair synaptic plasticity, its effects on glial cells remain unclear. How urea influences oligodendrocyte lineage differentiation may represent a critical node in neuron–glia interactions. Previous studies have shown that OL‐lineage cells may be underrepresented in scRNA‐seq datasets. We selected amygdala tissue from wild‐type and high‐urea (UT‐B − / − ) mice and performed single‐nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA‐seq), behavioral tests, and cellular experiments to delineate the impact of urea on oligodendrocyte lineage dynamics. In UT‐B − / − mice, the relative abundance of oligodendrocyte subpopulations enriched for mitochondrial transcripts decreased, suggesting vulnerability to urea toxicity. Dlat and MDH1, genes associated with TCA cycle‐related metabolism, were downregulated alongside alterations in mitochondrial and oxidative phosphorylation‐related transcriptional programs. Urea dose‐dependently decreased MDH1 expression, mitochondrial membrane potential, and intracellular ATP content in MO3.13 cells. Regulatory analyses linked MDH1 to energy metabolism and neurodegenerative pathways. Trajectory reconstruction suggested altered differentiation‐ and myelination‐related transcriptional programs in mitochondria‐related oligodendrocytes (MitOLs). The cytoplasmic concentration and fate of oxaloacetic acid (OAA) are regulated by the reversible catalysis of MDH1. OAA supplementation partially restored amygdalar MDH1 expression and alleviated anxiety‐like behaviors in UT‐B − / − mice, while improving mitochondrial bioenergetics in urea‐exposed MO3.13 cells. These findings support a candidate metabolic–glial model linking elevated urea, MDH1 dysregulation, oligodendrocyte bioenergetic dysfunction, and anxiety‐like behavior, with potential relevance to CKD‐associated anxiety.

Article.Title: Brain PDGFR β + Cells Exhibit Diverse Reactive Phenotypes After Stroke Without Requiring KLF4
Article.Authors: Manrique‐Castano D.; ElAli A.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT The pathobiology of ischemic stroke is associated with the activation of brain platelet‐derived growth factor receptor (PDGFR) β + perivascular cells. While Krüppel‐like factor (KLF)4 is a well‐established mediator of peripheral PDGFR β + cell activation, its role in brain PDGFR β + cells remains elusive. Herein, we aimed to characterize the spatiotemporal reactivity of brain PDGFR β + cells, while assessing KLF4 contribution upon experimental ischemic stroke using transgenic mice that enable tracking PDGFR β + cells or conditionally depleting KLF4 in PDGFR β + cells. Moving beyond the qualitative descriptors, we sought to develop point pattern analysis (PPA) and topological data analysis (TDA) workflows to generate robust and reusable mathematical models to assess spatial cell responses and tissue scar topological changes. First, we report the emergence of phenotypically distinct reactive parenchymal PDGFR β + cells, which cannot be causally and exclusively linked, as it is currently proposed, to local cell proliferation or adjacent vascular detachment. Furthermore, we show that KLF4 is barely expressed in brain PDGFR β + cells under normal conditions and that it is only marginally induced in reactive PDGFR β + cells at the injured brain. Notably, the conditional attenuation of KLF4 expression specifically in reactive PDGFR β + cells does not alter spatial cellular distribution nor scar organization. This suggests that, in contrast to peripheral PDGFR β + cells upon ischemic insults, KLF4 is not a main regulator of the reactivity of brain cells in response to ischemic stroke. Ultimately, our findings supported by open‐source spatiotemporal models indicate that the reactivity of brain PDGFR β + perivascular cells is highly heterogeneous and fundamentally distinct from peripheral PDGFR β + cells.

Article.Title: sox17 Mutagenesis Reveals Compounding Effects ofMaternal and Zygotic Contribution on Microglia Abundance
Article.Authors: Spring C.; Dennen J.; Gan D.; Li J.; Smith C.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Embryonic development is shaped by maternal and zygotic factors but how the interplay between these factors contributes to phenotypic variability and impacts specific populations of brain cells, and subsequently neurodevelopment, remains largely unknown. Here, we reveal a double hit phenomenon that impacts microglia and microglia precursors during development. Using zebrafish, we identified a mutation in sry‐related HMG box gene‐17 (sox17) that exhibits a maternal effect phenotype presenting as a reduction of microglia in the brain and precursors in the yolk sac. We demonstrate that microglia deficits are exacerbated in homozygous offspring from homozygous parents compared to homozygous offspring from heterozygous parents, suggesting a compounding effect of maternal and zygotic sox17 mutation on microglia abundance. We observe that sox17 is expressed in microglia and yolk sac precursors and is maternally contributed. Injections of sox17 RNA during embryogenesis are sufficient to rescue microglia and yolk sac cell abundance. To identify additional genes interacting with sox17 , we perform a genetic screen using CRISPR mutagenesis and identify f11r.1, gas6 , and mpp1 as microglia regulators, which we demonstrate are expressed in zebrafish microglia. Transcriptional and mutant analyses with these genes suggest sox17 positively regulates mpp1 transcription. These results demonstrate that microglia are susceptible to additive effects of maternal and zygotic sox17 mutation, and that offspring greatly differ in their susceptibility to microglia deficits depending on the mother's genotype. Our findings highlight that both the maternal and offspring genotype should be considered when examining neurodevelopmental disorders that could arise from microglia dysfunction.

Article.Title: Disruption of Lactate Metabolism in the Peripheral Nervous System Leads to Motor‐Selective Deficits
Article.Authors: Bloom A.; Tendulkar S.; Hackett A.; Strickland A.; Sato‐Yamada Y.; Yuan L.; Dong W.; Ippolito J.; Schmidt R.; Sasaki Y.; DiAntonio A.; Milbrandt J.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Schwann cells (SCs) myelinate and provide trophic support to axons in the peripheral nervous system (PNS). Disrupted SC metabolism can lead to demyelination and axon degeneration, cardinal deficits in peripheral neuropathy. The lactate shuttle hypothesis proposes that glycolytic support cells supply lactate to axons to sustain their high metabolic demands. This transfer requires lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) to interconvert lactate and pyruvate in both SCs and neurons. To test the importance of lactate metabolism in the PNS, we selectively knocked out both LDHA and LDHB in ChAT‐positive neurons, including motor neurons (MNs), Nav1.8‐lineage sensory neurons (SNs), or SCs. Interestingly, motor axons and their synapses progressively degenerate when LDH is deleted from either MNs or SCs, but defects in Nav1.8‐lineage sensory axons and their terminals are not observed when LDH is excised from either SNs or SCs. Deletion of LDH in SCs leads to decreased ATP in peripheral nerves despite marked accumulation of pyruvate and glycolytic intermediates, consistent with energetic deficits due to failed conversion of pyruvate to lactate. Cholinergic neuron‐specific gene expression using ribosome affinity profiling (RiboTag) identified a strong response to metabolic compromise by activating axon‐injury stress programs in LDH‐deficient neurons. Finally, blocking axon degeneration in LDH‐deficient mice by SARM1 deletion preserves axon morphology without ameliorating behavioral and electrophysiological defects, demonstrating functional decline of lactate‐deprived axons that remain physically intact. These results show a differential requirement for SC‐derived lactate by motor vs. sensory axons, suggesting that lactate availability could influence the course of motor neuron diseases.

Article.Title: Astrocytic <scp>EAAT</scp> ‐2 Upregulation Supports Neuro‐Axonal Homeostasis in Chronic Inflammatory <scp>CNS</scp> Lesions
Article.Authors: Reukauf L.; Margineanu A.; Muinjonov B.; Chen J.; Cui Y.; Rosiewicz K.; Radbruch H.; Munro I.; Alisch M.; Siffrin V.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Neuronal loss in multiple sclerosis (MS) is a key factor in the progression of disability. Axonal degeneration within MS lesions is central to progressive MS pathology, yet its mechanisms are not fully understood. Excess extracellular l‐glutamate (GLUT) is neurotoxic due to overstimulation of GLUT receptors. Excitotoxicity, driven by GLUT, is a suspected contributor to several central nervous system (CNS) diseases. Astrocytic glutamate transporters EAAT‐1 and EAAT‐2 play crucial roles in managing extracellular GLUT, yet their role in chronic MS remains underexplored. Using the animal model experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) and advanced microscopy in live anesthetized mice, we examined GLUT‐mediated neurotoxicity and protective mechanisms in chronic CNS lesions. By employing genetically encoded fluorescent biosensors, we visualized extracellular GLUT levels and axonal Ca 2+ dynamics within the live mouse brain during EAE. In acute EAE, extracellular GLUT levels were high, while in chronic lesions, normalized GLUT levels together with sustained EAAT‐2 upregulation were consistent with a protective astrocytic response. EAAT‐2 inhibition in chronic lesions led to higher intra‐axonal Ca 2+ levels and morphological changes consistent with neuroaxonal injury, indicating that EAAT‐2 upregulation may counter excitotoxicity and support neuroprotection. Post‐mortem MS brain tissue analysis provided complementary evidence, showing elevated EAAT‐1 and EAAT‐2 expression in chronic MS lesions with expression patterns varying according to lesion type and cellularity. This study highlights astrocytic mechanisms that may contribute to neuroaxonal protection in MS tissue and suggests targeting GLUT transporters as a promising strategy to limit neurodegeneration in progressive MS.

Article.Title: Single‐Cell Integration of Mouse Models of Autism Reveals Conserved Transcriptomic Signatures of Excitatory‐Inhibitory Imbalance and Glial Dysfunction
Article.Authors: Nani J.; Duque V.; Muotri A.; Mecawi A.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT The etiological heterogeneity of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) complicates identifying core molecular mechanisms. We systematically integrated scRNA‐seq data from 11 diverse genetic and environmental mouse ( Mus musculus ) models, encompassing > 300,000 cells across multiple brain regions and developmental stages. Using advanced computational harmonization (RPCA), we identified robust convergent transcriptomic signatures that transcend model‐specific variability. Our findings reveal widespread alterations in neuronal communication pathways, specifically increased excitatory‐inhibitory signaling involving PTN, SLIT, and PTPR pathways. Furthermore, cell–cell communication analysis via NicheNet prioritized ligand‐receptor pairs associated with altered circuit excitability, offering a predictive blueprint of dysregulated intercellular crosstalk. Crucially, we identified significant glial involvement characterized by astrocyte function inhibition, marked by Aqp4 and Kcnj10 downregulation related to impaired water/potassium homeostasis and mature oligodendrocyte metabolic dysregulation through Olig family upregulation and enhanced oxidative phosphorylation. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) significantly overlapped with SFARI‐listed high‐confidence risk genes, particularly within excitatory neuronal subtypes. Comparison with human postmortem single‐nucleus data from the prefrontal and parietal cortices demonstrated conserved signatures related to impaired synaptic protein synthesis (GRIN2B, CAMK2A) and oligodendrocyte‐mediated neurodevelopmental deficits (NRXN, DLGAP). This study confirms that E/I imbalance and glial dysfunction are universal cellular pathologies in ASD, providing a robust, large‐scale reference for identifying novel therapeutic targets with single‐cell resolution.

Article.Title: A Müller Glia‐Retinal Pigment Epithelium Apical Network Surrounding Cone Outer Segments in Fish and Mouse
Article.Authors: Sharkova M.; Housset M.; Boudreau S.; Dworkind C.; Amidian S.; Cayouette M.; Hocking J.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Homeostasis of the vertebrate retina critically depends on two non‐neuronal cell populations, Müller glia and the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Their opposing apical surfaces delineate the subretinal space, a specialized extracellular compartment housing the light‐detecting outer segments of photoreceptors. Although the individual interactions between these supporting cells and photoreceptors have been extensively characterized, Müller glia and the RPE have long been presumed to remain physically separate in the healthy retina. Here, we challenge this assumption and present a revised model of the subretinal space architecture based on detailed FIB‐SEM and confocal microscopy imaging of the zebrafish and mouse outer retina. We demonstrate that both Müller glia and the RPE extend long apical processes that not only contact one another but also collectively ensheath cone outer segments, forming a previously unrecognized tripartite interface. These contact regions are highly elaborated in fish and, while comparatively sparser, are still present in mouse. Developmentally, the growth and interdigitation of Müller glial and RPE apical processes follow the emergence of the outer segment in both species and, in mouse, coincides with the onset of visual function. Although glial–RPE interactions are enriched at cone‐associated sites, their presence is not strictly dependent on cone localization in either species, suggesting they represent a fundamental feature of the vertebrate subretinal space. Together, these findings revise our understanding of the subretinal space cytoarchitecture and reveal a previously unappreciated structural interaction between Müller glia, RPE, and photoreceptors that is conserved across vertebrate species.

Article.Title: <scp>CD47</scp> – <scp>SIRPα</scp> Axis as a Target for Neuroprotection
Article.Authors: Gómez‐López A.; Manich G.; Penas C.; Pampalona J.; Villacampa N.; Almolda B.; Viennois E.; Rojas S.; González B.; Castellano B.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Microglial “Off” signaling is crucial for maintaining microglia in a homeostatic state through the interaction of “Off” neuronal ligands with their corresponding microglial receptors. Dysregulation of “Off” signaling has been reported in both acute and chronic neuroinflammation; however, the influence of inflammatory mediators on this pathway remains underexplored. Here, we investigated whether chronic IL‐6 or IL‐10 overexpression modulates microglia–neuron “Off” signaling after FNA, thereby accounting for the previously observed differences in facial motoneuron (FMN) survival and microglial reactivity in transgenic mouse models (GFAP‐IL6Tg and GFAP‐IL10Tg). To this end, we examined the expression of the neuronal “Off” ligands CD200, CX3CL1, CD47, and CD22, as well as their corresponding microglial “Off” receptors CD200R, CX3CR1, SIRP‐α, and CD45 in non‐lesioned and axotomized GFAP‐IL6Tg, GFAP‐IL10Tg, and WT mice across multiple time points. Our analyses revealed the dynamic regulation of “Off” signaling in both neurons and microglia during microgliosis and FMN phagocytosis and showed temporally restricted strain‐specific differences in CD47 expression across genotypes. Chronic IL‐6 overproduction promoted a more phagocytic microglial phenotype, defined by downregulation of SIRPα and CX3CR1 alongside upregulated CD45 in the microglial population. In contrast, chronic IL‐10 overproduction did not alter the expression of microglial “Off” receptors but induced an IL‐10 dependent accelerated upregulation of neuronal CD47. Our findings highlight the CD47‐SIRPα axis as a key regulator of FMN death via microglial phagocytosis and emphasize IL‐10's neuroprotective potential role through enhanced neuronal CD47 signaling. Overall, this work positions the CD47‐SIRPα axis as a potential therapeutic target to mitigate neuroinflammation‐induced neuronal loss.

Article.Title: Microglial Labeling in Mouse Spinal Cord Injury: A Review of Timing, Efficacy, and Specificity
Article.Authors: Colbert R.; Di Stefano J.; Dooley D.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI) is a complex and disabling condition with no curative therapy currently available. The mechanical damage of the primary injury phase is followed and exacerbated by a secondary injury phase, characterized by the release of free radicals and pro‐inflammatory cytokines that lead to chronic inflammation. Microglia, as the resident immune cells of the central nervous system, play a critical role in orchestrating this inflammatory response. Studying their dynamics after SCI not only deepens our understanding of injury pathology but also advances the development of microglia‐targeted immunotherapies. However, trauma‐induced transcriptional and phenotypic changes mean that markers used to identify homeostatic microglia may be unreliable when applied to their reactive counterparts. Another major challenge lies within discriminating resident microglia from infiltrating monocyte‐derived macrophages (MDM), which permeate the blood‐spinal cord barrier (BSCB) after injury. In this review, we examine three key variables for selecting appropriate strategies for labeling microglia in mice: (i) time (in relation to injury); (ii) efficacy (within the chosen murine SCI model); and (iii) specificity (to microglia). We discuss the transcriptional landscape of murine microglia pre‐injury and its alteration post‐injury, evaluate the strengths and limitations of commonly used markers, and highlight emerging tools and approaches for studying microglia in preclinical murine SCI research.

Article.Title: Ifi27l2a Facilitates the Recruitment of Pathogenic T Cells by Retinal Microglia in the Initiation Phase of Experimental Autoimmune Uveoretinitis
Article.Authors: Gao W.; Wu P.; Xie K.; Zhou P.; Jin B.; Zhu H.; Li F.; Wang Y.; Lei B.; Jin X.; Du L.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT The mechanisms by which pathogenic T cells enter the immune‐privileged retina at the onset of uveitis remain unclear. To identify regulatory targets that promote retinal inflammation, we established an experimental autoimmune uveoretinitis (EAU) model by immunizing C57BL/6J mice with IRBP 651–670 and dynamically evaluated retinal inflammation after induction; fundus lesions were prominent, with the first 14 days representing the initiation phase, Days 14–28 the amplification phase, Days 28–35 the peak phase, and Days 35–42 the regression phase. We characterized retinal cellular alterations from the pre‐inflammatory stage to the peak stage using single‐cell transcriptomic analysis, and found that retinal immune cells changed in parallel with EAU severity, while immune‐cell interactions were strongest on Day 14, especially between microglia and T cells through multiple chemokine‐related pathways. We then identified key cell populations and candidate targets through integrated analyses and functional validation, and Ifi27l2a emerged as a core gene associated with inflammatory and immune responses in retinal microglia on Day 14. In vitro knockdown of Ifi27l2a in LPS‐activated BV‐2 cells reduced inflammatory mediator production and abolished Th1/Th17 induction. In vivo targeting of Ifi27l2a attenuated EAU severity and restored the balance of T‐cell subsets. These findings indicate that microglia are highly activated before retinal inflammation becomes prominent and that Ifi27l2a regulates this early pathogenic process.

Article.Title: Neuronal Overexpression of Glycogen Synthase Kinase‐3β Accelerates Age‐Related Glial, Vascular, and Inflammatory Remodeling of the Murine Dentate Gyrus
Article.Authors: Prádanos‐Senén A.; Rodríguez‐Moreno C.; Llorens‐Martín M.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Adult hippocampal neurogenesis (AHN)—the lifelong generation of new neurons in the dentate gyrus (DG)—depends on the integrity of the subgranular zone (SGZ) neurogenic niche, which comprises astrocytes, microglia, oligodendroglial cells, and a dense vascular network. Although AHN declines during aging and is impaired in Alzheimer's disease (AD), the cell‐type‐specific alterations within the DG underlying this decline remain poorly characterized. Given the critical role of glycogen synthase kinase‐3β (GSK‐3β) in AD pathogenesis and AHN regulation, we studied how the overexpression of this kinase in dentate granule cells (DGCs) remodels the cellular and vascular composition of the DG throughout life. Using a layer‐resolved approach (SGZ vs. granule cell layer (GCL)) and mice of distinct ages (4–30 months), we quantified glial densities, cellular contacts, vascular architecture, and cytokine profiles in wild‐type (WT) and GSK‐3β‐overexpressing (GSK‐3β‐OE) mice. In the former, aging was associated with a layer‐specific reorganization, characterized by progressive astrocyte loss in the SGZ, midlife increases in GCL microglia, a reduction in oligodendroglial progenitors, and enhanced SGZ vascularization. GSK‐3β overexpression accelerated age‐related changes, triggering premature SGZ astrocyte depletion by 4 months, broader disruption featuring reduced SGZ microglial and mature oligodendrocyte densities accompanied by increased microglial morphological complexity, vascular restructuring, and a shift toward a pro‐inflammatory environment. Therefore, neuronal GSK‐3β overexpression promoted a non‐cell‐autonomous reorganization of the DG, consistent with premature remodeling of the neurogenic niche. These results provide mechanistic insights into AHN failure in AD and point to the modulation of GSK‐3β activity as a strategy to preserve DG integrity.

Article.Title: Red Fluorescent Labeling of Myelin by Membrane‐Targeted <scp>tdTomato</scp> in Transgenic Mouse Lines
Article.Authors: Reinert A.; Winkler U.; Goebbels S.; Komarek L.; Möbius W.; Zanker H.; Schoknecht K.; Bornschein G.; Schmidt H.; Fledrich R.; Stassart R.; Hirrlinger P.; Nave K.; Werner H.; Saab A.; Hirrlinger J.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Myelin is a highly complex membranous structure wrapped around axons by oligodendrocytes or Schwann cells in the central and peripheral nervous system, respectively. Fluorescent labeling is widely used to study the structure and dynamics of myelin. Combining structural with functional imaging requires labeling of myelin with red fluorescence, as many functional sensors, including Ca 2+ indicators and genetically encoded metabolite sensors, fluoresce in the green spectral range. However, in vivo tools enabling red fluorescent labeling of myelinating cells and their myelin sheaths remain limited. Here, we generated a set of seven transgenic mouse lines expressing a membrane‐targeted variant of the red fluorescent protein tdTomato in myelinating oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells throughout the nervous system. In summary, our work provides a set of novel mouse lines with myelin labeled by red fluorescence, which are compatible with diverse imaging modalities in the green spectral range enabling integrated structural and functional imaging.

Article.Title: Schwann Cell‐Specific <scp>ATG7</scp> ‐Dependent Autophagy Protects Myelin in a Mouse Model of Krabbe Disease
Article.Authors: Dhimal N.; Sidharth A.; Zhang J.; Rudra T.; Hurley E.; Paez P.; Sim F.; Shin D.; Feltri M.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Krabbe disease (KD) is a lysosomal storage disorder characterized by severe peripheral demyelination caused by mutations in galactosylceramidase (GALC), leading to the accumulation of galactosylceramide and psychosine. Although psychosine toxicity is central to KD pathology, additional mechanisms likely contribute to myelin dysfunction. Because Schwann cells (SCs) play a critical role in myelin maintenance, and GALC deficiency disrupts lysosomal function, we hypothesized that autophagy is altered in SCs during KD progression. Using a SC‐specific Galc conditional knockout ( Galc SC cKO) mouse model, we identified early changes in autophagy‐related protein levels and increased autophagosome abundance during the pre‐symptomatic phase, prior to detectable myelin abnormalities. To assess whether autophagy contributes to disease progression, we selectively deleted Atg7 , an essential regulator of canonical autophagy, in SCs. Atg7 deletion alone did not affect myelin or behavior, but its loss in Galc SC cKO mice markedly worsened disease severity. Atg7‐Galc SC cKO mice exhibited significantly thinner myelin and pronounced deficits in motor performance and nerve conduction, accompanied by altered steady‐state levels of autophagy‐associated proteins and functional decline. Notably, Atg7 deletion in Galc SC cKO mice did not further increase macrophage abundance, suggesting that the worsened myelin phenotype occurs without additional macrophage recruitment at this stage. Together, these findings demonstrate that autophagy‐associated changes occur early in KD and ATG7‐dependent pathways play a protective role during disease progression. Modulating ATG7‐dependent pathways may therefore warrant further investigation as a strategy to support myelin maintenance in KD and related lysosomal disorders.
