Article.Title: Myelin Maintenance and Addition Regulate Synaptic Plasticity in the Adult Mouse Cortex
Article.Authors: Pepper R.; Makowiecki K.; Pitman K.; Ricci R.; Nicoli A.; Nguyen P.; Blizzard C.; Emery B.; Cullen C.; Young K.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Myelin has the capacity to affect synapse number or plasticity across the lifespan. We report that disrupting oligodendrocyte (OL) and myelin maintenance from P57 ( Plp‐CreER T2 :: Myrf fl/fl mice) induces myelin loss and impairs action potential conduction and gross motor performance. By studying sparsely labeled layer V pyramidal neurons in the primary motor cortex of P57 + 60 mice, we determined that apical and basal dendritic spine densities were normal; however, more were large, stable mushroom spines that generated larger amplitude miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents. When we instead prevented OL and myelin addition from P57 ( Pdgfrα‐CreER:: Myrf fl/fl mice), action potential conduction velocity, gross motor performance, and spine densities were normal; however, basal dendritic spine morphology was changed. Without adult myelination, the basal dendrites of P57 + 60 mice retained the morphological characteristics of dendrites in P57 + 0 mice, which have a higher proportion of thin, plastic spines. These data indicate that existing myelin imposes limits on the proportion of spines that become mushroom spines, allowing neurons to remain plastic, while adult myelination is required for spine stabilization within the basal but not apical dendritic compartment. These data show that myelin regulates synaptic plasticity within the motor circuit and offer a potential mechanism by which myelination can influence motor skill learning and/or recall.

Article.Title: Plasma SPARC Concentrations in Patients with Subsequent Shunt-Dependent Hydrocephalus After Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
Article.Authors: Hakozaki K.; Nakajima H.; Kitano Y.; Nishikawa H.; Kawakita F.; Yasuda R.; Suzuki H.; N/A N/A.
Article.Abstract: Shunt-dependent hydrocephalus (SDHC) is a delayed complication of aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), and meningeal fibrotic remodeling may contribute to its development. Secreted protein acidic and rich in cysteine (SPARC) regulates collagen processing and extracellular matrix organization. We examined whether serial plasma SPARC concentrations were associated with subsequent SDHC development. We retrospectively analyzed prospectively collected data from 186 patients with aneurysmal SAH enrolled in a multicenter registry. Plasma SPARC was measured at days 1–3, 4–6, 7–9, and 10–12 and analyzed using log-scale linear mixed-effects models. SDHC developed in 54 patients (29.0%). Model-estimated SPARC concentrations increased across periods in both SDHC and no-SDHC groups without a significant SDHC-by-period interaction, whereas all the SDHC/no-SDHC geometric mean ratios were below 1. The clearest difference occurred at days 4–6 and remained significant after adjustment for age, admission World Federation of Neurological Surgeons grade V, modified Fisher grade 4, and acute hydrocephalus (geometric mean ratio, 0.73; 95% confidence interval, 0.57–0.93; Holm-adjusted p = 0.040). In a post hoc exploratory multivariable analysis, each 10 ng/mL increase in SPARC at days 4–6 was associated with lower odds of subsequent SDHC development (adjusted odds ratio, 0.91; 95% confidence interval, 0.84–0.98; p = 0.011). Lower plasma SPARC concentrations, particularly at days 4–6, were associated with subsequent SDHC development.

Article.Title: Immunotherapy: Examining Strategies to Address Cancer Complexity
Article.Authors: Povo-Retana A.; Ruiz-Navarro J.; Fernández-Frías L.; Alvarez-Lucena C.; Landauro-Vera R.; Izquierdo M.; Boscá L.
Article.Abstract: Understanding the interplay between immune and stromal cells in the tumor microenvironment is essential for developing effective cancer therapies and preventing relapses. In this review, starting with the basics of tumor immunology and a historical review from cancer chemotherapy to current immunotherapy, in the context of precision medicine, we focus on immunotherapies based on genetically modified macrophages, and chimeric T-cell antigen receptor (CAR), highlighting the similarities and differences between TCR-endogenous signaling and CART-dependent signaling at the immune synapse, presenting all the generations that have been developed briefly, followed by NK cell-dependent CAR therapeutic approaches where a comparison is established, analyzing their respective advantages and drawbacks. Targeting the tumor-immune microenvironment has become central to cancer treatment, with combinatorial therapies applied and assessed as a feasible strategy for this complex group of diverse pathologies. In this context, modulating the immune synapse, rewiring immune cell metabolism, and developing genetically engineered immune cells have emerged as promising approaches that open novel avenues for treating and managing cancer patients. This review offers a holistic, historical view of state-of-the-art molecular approaches, along with insights into future perspectives and current limitations of the technologies supporting immunotherapy in molecular oncology.

Article.Title: Blood Cell Intracellular pH Dynamics and Metabolic Biomarkers Under Simulated Postmortem Interval Conditions: An Exploratory Pilot In Vitro Study
Article.Authors: Ndunduma P.; Cordeiro C.; Faria S.; Criado M.; Coimbra S.; Monteiro M.
Article.Abstract: Intracellular pH (pHi) may provide complementary information on postmortem cellular metabolism and homeostasis, but its temporal behavior remains poorly understood. This pilot in vitro study evaluated temporal changes in platelet pHi and pHi in a mixed non-platelet blood-cell population (predominantly erythrocytes and leukocytes), together with plasma glucose, lactate, and ammonia during a simulated postmortem interval (PMI). Venous blood from eight healthy volunteers was maintained at 24 ± 3 °C and analyzed at 0, 3, 6, and 24 h. Intracellular pH was assessed by BCECF-AM flow cytometry, and metabolites were quantified enzymatically. Platelet and non-platelet-cell pHi remained stable during the first 3 h, decreased significantly at 6 h, and increased toward baseline values at 24 h. Glucose concentrations decreased over time, lactate increased progressively, and ammonia increased significantly only at 24 h. Lactate was associated with pHi in both blood-cell populations. Intracellular pH exhibited a biphasic temporal pattern and distinct relationships with metabolic biomarkers during the simulated PMI. An exploratory mixed-effects model incorporating non-platelet-cell pHi, lactate, and glucose explained a substantial proportion of temporal variability (marginal R2 = 0.907) and yielded a leave-one-donor-out cross-validation RMSE of 0.4998 on the log-transformed time scale. These findings support further investigation of multi-marker approaches for PMI estimation.

Article.Title: Hemostasis and Beyond: The Diverse Functions of Protein S in Controlling Coagulation, Inflammation, and Cancer
Article.Authors: Mehrpour-Karmakan N.; Jauquet M.; Wood J.
Article.Abstract: Protein S (ProS) is a vitamin K-dependent glycoprotein that was first described as an anticoagulant cofactor for activated protein C (APC). Since its initial discovery, studies of ProS have revealed an array of functions, spanning coagulation and inflammation, including in the context of cancer. ProS is now known to inhibit all three coagulation complexes—through interactions with APC, tissue factor pathway inhibitor, and activated factor IX—and to have its anticoagulant activity modulated by multiple other plasma proteins. Beyond hemostasis, ProS also participates in complement regulation, through its interaction with complement component C4b-binding protein, and regulates inflammatory cell phenotype and function, through Tyro3 and Mer-Tyrosine Kinase, receptors which mediate efferocytosis, inflammatory resolution, and tissue repair. Emerging evidence further implicates ProS in cancer biology, where its effects are context-dependent and may either support or suppress tumor progression. In this review, we highlight these many functions of ProS and discuss their mechanistic commonalities. Collectively, these functions position ProS as a central regulatory node, with critical roles in physiology and disease.

Article.Title: Germline HLA and KIR Variation and Disease Control After Immune Checkpoint Blockade in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: Exposure Definition Shapes the Signal
Article.Authors: González-Hernández A.; Ríos A.; Onieva J.; Cantero A.; Rivero-Aguilar M.; Paz-López G.; Rueda-Domínguez A.; Garrido-Barros M.; Martínez-Gálvez B.; Pérez-Ruiz E.; Benítez J.; Barragán I.; Oliver J.
Article.Abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) benefit only a minority of patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Whether germline human leukocyte antigen (HLA) or killer cell immunoglobulin-like receptor (KIR) variation identifies them is unclear, partly because studies define HLA exposures differently. We asked whether allele groups, supertypes and evolutionary divergence associate with disease control. In 122 ICI-treated patients, HLA and KIR typed from germline exomes were tested in 448 pre-specified exposure-endpoint combinations; the primary endpoint was progression or death at 3 months (99 evaluable patients; 31 events). No test survived correction across the screen (lowest n = 0.299). Nominally, HLA-A*02 carriers had higher odds of early failure (odds ratio 4.00, 95% CI 1.64 to 10.07), whereas none of the 12 HLA-B*14 carriers failed (0.07, 0.0006 to 0.58), yet the B27 supertype containing B*14 was null. In 297 public SU2C-MARK patients, B*14 was not supported; A*02 was inconclusive for time to event and not reproduced at a 90-day landmark. HLA-DQA1 divergence at 12 months was hypothesis-generating (within-family n = 0.004). Exome typing resolved HLA allele groups (99.1%) but not KIR (19.0% ambiguous). How an HLA exposure is defined determines whether a signal is visible; only large effects were detectable; replication is required.

Article.Title: Myelin Changes in H-ABC Tubulinopathy Revealed by Nile Red Hyperspectral Imaging
Article.Authors: Jaramillo-Restrepo C.; Piazza V.; Eguibar J.; Cortes C.; Hernandez V.
Article.Abstract: Hypomyelination with atrophy of the basal ganglia and cerebellum (H-ABC) is a recently described tubulinopathy caused by mutations in the tubulin beta-4a isotype. It is a severe disorder characterized by progressive myelin loss and neurological impairment. The taiep rat, a spontaneous TUBB4A mutant, is a model for investigating the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying this disease. Homozygous taiep rats exhibit hallmark features of H-ABC, including early-onset hypomyelination, progressive demyelination, and microtubule accumulation in oligodendrocytes, whereas heterozygous animals appear to maintain normal myelin structure using conventional techniques. We combined hyperspectral imaging (HSI) and Nile Red (NR) staining to differentiate homozygous taiep and wild-type animals and determine whether subtle myelin alterations could be detected in heterozygous rats. Remarkably, heterozygous animals also showed changes in the Nile Red emission profile, with fluorescence shifted toward longer wavelengths compared with controls, uncovering previously unrecognized modifications in the myelin microenvironment. Using spectral phasor analysis, these alterations were localized and quantified without model assumptions, demonstrating the sensitivity of this approach for detecting subtle pathological changes. Together, our findings contribute to the characterization of myelin-associated spectral changes in this tubulinopathy and support the use of spectral microscopy to distinguish alterations in myelin properties, with potential applications in the study of other white matter disorders.

Article.Title: pH-Dependent Developmental and Behavioral Toxicity of Diethanolamine in Zebrafish (Danio rerio)
Article.Authors: Jablonski C.; Pereira F.; Oliveira J.; Bandeira L.; Pereira T.; Oliveira G.; Kist L.; Silva V.; Monteiro W.; Lautert-Dutra W.; Seferin M.; Ligabue R.; Bogo M.
Article.Abstract: Amine-based compounds are used in petroleum and gas processing for CO2 capture and gas sweetening. Diethanolamine (DEA), a water-soluble alkaline compound, can alter exposure-medium physicochemical properties. Its industrial use and potential release into aquatic environments highlight the need to characterize its aquatic toxicity. However, data on DEA developmental toxicity remains limited, particularly regarding the distinction between intrinsic chemical toxicity and pH-mediated effects. This study investigated the developmental and behavioral toxicity of DEA in zebrafish (Danio rerio) under pH-adjusted and unadjusted exposure conditions to examine the contribution of exposure-medium pH to the observed effects. Acute toxicity assays determined the median lethal concentration (LC50), followed by sublethal assessments of spontaneous tail coiling, heart rate, morphology, and larval locomotor activity. Under pH-adjusted conditions, heart rate increased, indicating a sublethal effect on cardiac function. In contrast, unadjusted exposures caused a concentration-dependent increase in medium pH associated with adverse effects on survival, development, and behavior, despite no morphological abnormalities. For statistical analyses, individual measurements were averaged within each vessel, and vessel-level means were used to assess concentration–response relationships and estimate concentration–response trend rates. Responses differed between DEA-Adj and DEA-Unadj under their respective testing conditions, highlighting the importance of considering exposure-medium pH when assessing alkaline chemical toxicity. pH alterations caused by chemical releases may also contribute to adverse effects in aquatic organisms and should be considered when evaluating the environmental implications of DEA contamination.

Article.Title: Long-Term Effects of Isoflurane Anesthesia and Surgery: Sex-Associated Neurological Dysfunction and Alterations in Circulating Extracellular Vesicles
Article.Authors: Li Y.; Park R.; Krishnamachary B.; Lee H.; Lei Z.; Li H.; Wu J.
Article.Abstract: Volatile anesthetics and surgery can trigger neuroinflammation and neurological dysfunction, but their long-term effects remain poorly understood. Young adult male and female C57BL/6 mice underwent 4 h of 2% isoflurane anesthesia combined with laparotomy (Iso/OP) or sham treatment. At 12 weeks, olfactory and cognitive functions were assessed, followed by RNA sequencing of olfactory bulbs and hippocampi and plasma extracellular vesicle (EV) profiling. EV-associated inflammatory bioactivity was evaluated by hippocampal injection into naïve male mice. Iso/OP induced olfactory deficits at 12 weeks, with greater impairment in females. Female mice also exhibited deficits in spatial working memory and associative learning, whereas males showed relatively preserved cognitive function. Transcriptomic analyses revealed sex-dependent alterations in pathways related to synaptic function, neurodevelopment, extracellular matrix remodeling, stress responses, and chemotaxis. Iso/OP reduced circulating EV abundance, particularly among 40–100 nm particles, and altered EV proteomic profiles. Exploratory analyses of pooled hippocampal tissues revealed distinct cytokine and chemokine profiles following injection of plasma EVs from the four donor groups. Collectively, these findings demonstrate sex-dependent neurological and molecular alterations persisting 12 weeks after Iso/OP, accompanied by changes in circulating EVs. The exploratory EV transfer findings warrant further investigation into the potential contribution of circulating EVs to brain inflammatory responses.

Article.Title: E3 Ligase TRIM21 Deficiency-Driven GAS2L3 Accumulation Facilitates Oncogenic Progression in Breast Cancer
Article.Authors: Li P.; Zhao C.; Ren Y.; Wei Y.; Zhang N.; Xin L.; Sun Y.; Yang J.; He J.; Liu X.; Gao X.
Article.Abstract: GAS2L3, a member of the growth arrest-specific 2 protein family, is abnormally upregulated in multiple human cancers, implying its potential oncogenic role. However, the mechanisms underlying its stabilization and accumulation during breast cancer progression remain unclear. This study aimed to clarify the regulatory mechanism and oncogenic role of GAS2L3 in breast cancer. We analyzed the expression and prognostic value of GAS2L3 and its related signaling pathways using public breast cancer databases, and conducted functional assays to assess the malignant phenotypes of breast cancer cells. Mass spectrometry and co-immunoprecipitation were performed to identify and verify TRIM21 as a binding partner of GAS2L3. Ubiquitination and cycloheximide chase assays confirmed that TRIM21 facilitates the ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of GAS2L3, while immunohistochemical staining of clinical specimens and mouse tissues verified their negative correlation. Rescue experiments further validated this regulatory axis. High GAS2L3 expression predicted poor prognosis and promoted breast cancer cell proliferation, migration, and invasion. Loss of TRIM21-mediated GAS2L3 degradation results in aberrant GAS2L3 accumulation, and the TRIM21–GAS2L3 axis drives breast cancer malignant progression, providing potential prognostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets for breast cancer.

Article.Title: Magnetic Nanoparticles in Precision Cancer Therapy: From Synthesis and Biological Interactions to Clinical Translation
Article.Authors: Wang J.; Xu S.; Hosseinikhah S.; Zhang W.; Zhang X.; Sacchetti A.
Article.Abstract: Cancer treatment increasingly relies on integrated therapeutic approaches, particularly for solid tumors that remain difficult to eradicate using a single modality. Magnetic nanoparticles (MNPs) have emerged as versatile therapeutic platforms owing to their magnetic responsiveness and tunable physicochemical properties. Advances in synthesis methods enable precise control over MNP size, morphology, composition, and surface chemistry, shaping their biological behavior across multiple scales. At the cellular level, these properties regulate nanoparticle uptake, intracellular trafficking, and subcellular interactions. At the tissue and systemic levels, administration route, vascular transport, magnetic targeting, and ligand-mediated recognition influence biodistribution, tumor accumulation, and cellular selectivity. Material composition and surface functionalization further determine responsiveness to external or endogenous stimuli and mediate therapeutic effects, including heat generation, controlled drug release, catalytic activity, and reactive oxygen species production. These features allow MNP-based systems to support localized hyperthermia, drug delivery, catalytic therapies, and embolization-based interventions, making them attractive for treating deep-seated and inoperable tumors. However, heterogeneous tumor delivery, variable activation efficiency, off-target toxicity, and long-term safety concerns remain major barriers to clinical translation. Overall, this review summarizes recent advances and current limitations in MNP-based cancer therapy, providing a multiscale perspective that links material design, biological interactions, systemic delivery, therapeutic activation, and translational challenges.

Article.Title: Adjunctive Resveratrol or Omeprazole in Patients with Non-Transfusion-Dependent Thalassemia with Iron Overload: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial
Article.Authors: Chopetgool T.; Chai-adisaksopha C.; Rattarittamrong E.; Norasetthada L.; Rattanathammethee T.; Hantrakool S.; Piriyakhuntorn P.; Punnachat T.; Hantrakun N.; Srichairatanakool S.; Koonyosying P.; Srichairatanakool S.; Tantiworawit A.
Article.Abstract: Increased gastrointestinal iron absorption contributes substantially to iron overload in non-transfusion-dependent thalassemia (NTDT) patients. Resveratrol (RVT) and omeprazole (OMP) may reduce intestinal iron absorption and potentially complement iron chelation therapy. This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial evaluated the efficacy and safety of adjunctive RVT or OMP in adults with NTDT receiving stable iron chelation therapy. The primary outcome was the change in serum ferritin; secondary outcomes influenced serum iron (SI), transferrin saturation (TS), erythroferrone (ERFE), hepcidin, fetal hemoglobin (HbF), and safety. Participants with serum ferritin ≥ 300 ng/mL were randomized (1:1:1) to receive RVT 250 mg, OMP 20 mg, or the placebo (PLA) twice daily for 6 months. Thirty participants were randomized (RVT, n = 10; OMP, n = 11; PLA, n = 9), with a baseline median serum ferritin value of 629 ng/mL, interquartile range (IQR) 484–975. Serum ferritin decreased numerically over 6 months in the RVT and OMP groups relative to PLA; however, no significant treatment × time interactions or adjusted between-group differences in changes from the baseline were observed. Although significant within-group changes were observed for selected iron-regulatory biomarkers, including hepcidin, ERFE, and TS, these were not accompanied by significant treatment × time interactions and did not demonstrate differential treatment effects. Both interventions were generally well tolerated, and no serious adverse events were reported. In this underpowered trial, neither adjunctive RVT nor OMP demonstrated statistically significant treatment-specific effects on serum ferritin or other iron-related outcomes when compared with the placebo. The observed numerical trends warrant evaluation in larger, adequately powered trials. Trial Registration: ISRCTN73258526.

Article.Title: Paper-Mulberry-Silage-Enhanced Lipid Metabolism and Milk Polyunsaturated Fatty Acid Concentration in Dairy Cows: A Multi-Omics Study
Article.Authors: Yang S.; Tang W.; Wang Y.; Yang H.; Wang W.; Cao Z.; Wang W.; Li S.; Bai Y.; Hao Y.
Article.Abstract: Developing alternative forages that modify milk fatty acid composition is important for improving milk nutritional quality and diversifying feed resources in dairy production. Previous studies have demonstrated the potential of paper mulberry (PM, Broussonetia papyrifera) silage to partially replace conventional roughages and influence antioxidant status and milk fatty acid composition. However, its effects on milk polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) and the associated ruminal microbial and metabolic mechanisms remain insufficiently characterized. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of feeding PM silage on the concentration of polyunsaturated fatty acids in milk, the structure of the rumen microbial community, and lipid metabolic functions, as well as to analyze the associations between rumen microbial and metabolic profiles and the fatty acid composition of milk. Thirty lactating Holstein cows were randomly assigned to control and PM groups, with 15 cows per group. The PM group received diets containing 9% PM silage for the first 28 days and 18% for the subsequent 28 days on a dry matter basis. Rumen fluid, plasma, and milk were collected on day 56 for integrated analyses combining fatty acid profiling, ruminal fermentation measurements, 16S rRNA gene sequencing, metagenomics, and metabolomics. Milk PUFA concentration was significantly higher in the PM group than in controls, with no significant differences in dry matter intake or milk yield. PM feeding also altered ruminal microbial community composition and lipid-metabolism-related functional gene abundances, accompanied by increased glycerophosphocholine and glycerophosphoethanolamine levels. Integrated analyses linked these changes to fatty acid profiles in rumen fluid, plasma, and milk, supporting ruminal lipid remodeling as a candidate mechanism underlying the increase in milk PUFA concentrations. These findings provide evidence for the microbial and metabolic basis of the effects of PM silage on milk fatty acid composition and inform its development as a functional forage and the optimization of dairy cow feeding strategies.

Article.Title: dTAG-Mediated Protein Degradation Dissects Nanog Function During ESC Differentiation
Article.Authors: Vasilin V.; Zinovyeva A.; Gordeev M.; Petrenko E.; Tsimokha A.; Aksenov N.; Tomilin A.; Bakhmet E.
Article.Abstract: Protein degradation systems, such as auxin-inducible degron (AID) and dTAG-mediated degradation, have become essential tools in molecular biology. Their primary advantage lies in the rapid and efficient elimination of proteins, which facilitates the study of short-term molecular perturbations. However, these techniques remain underutilized for investigating protein function during the dynamic process of embryonic stem cell (ESC) differentiation. Here, we employed these methods to unveil the role of Nanog during definitive endoderm specification. We demonstrate that dTAG-inducible degradation is significantly more efficient than the AID system for Nanog elimination. Using this approach, we show that Nanog is a context-dependent regulator; while it maintains pluripotency in undifferentiated ESCs, it promotes definitive endoderm maturation during spontaneous differentiation. Our results highlight the advantages of targeted protein degradation for studying developmental transitions and provide new insights into the multifaceted functions of Nanog.

Article.Title: Integrating Chronophysiological and Bioinformatic Perspectives on Nesfatin-1, Circadian Feeding Rhythms, and Cortisol Regulation
Article.Authors: Juliana N.; Abu I.; Azmani S.; Das S.; Abdul Hamid N.; Azzeri A.; Jaafar M.; Maluin S.; Elias M.
Article.Abstract: Nesfatin-1, a peptide derived from nucleobindin-2, regulates feeding, stress, and sleep–wake processes. To date, the available information suggests that nesfatin-1 is involved in stress regulation and colocalises with substances that influence cortisol, but the circadian interplay between nesfatin-1 and cortisol remains poorly defined. This review integrates biological timing, tissue-specific actions of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis, and circadian misalignment, and is supported by in silico protein-association analysis. A structured database search retained relevant studies published from January 2006 to March 2026; heterogeneity necessitated narrative synthesis. Rodent experiments support effects of central NUCB2/nesfatin-1 on feeding and HPA-axis activation. Murine corticotroph experiments report increased POMC abundance, whereas an H295R human adrenocortical carcinoma-cell study reports reduced cortisol content and stimulated release. These findings concern different experimental systems and do not demonstrate coordinated central–adrenal regulation in vivo. The network analysis identified NPY and POMC as prominent nodes within the predefined candidate network, with enrichment of feeding- and HPA-axis-related pathways. Given the biologically targeted selection of input genes, these findings are interpreted as hypothesis-generating associations rather than independent confirmation of a regulatory mechanism. Within the literature examined in this review, direct evidence characterising the 24 h temporal profile of nesfatin-1 in humans, its phase relationship with cortisol, and potential alterations during circadian misalignment was not identified. This apparent evidence gap warrants further investigation through controlled, time-resolved human studies.

Article.Title: SRC-2 Regulates Brain Endothelial and Neuronal Metabolism in a Mouse Model of Neurodegeneration
Article.Authors: Srivastava R.; Singh P.; Jonsson E.; Saleem I.; Desales C.; Lonard D.
Article.Abstract: Cerebrovascular dysfunction and impaired brain energy metabolism are increasingly recognized as important contributors to neurodegenerative diseases, but their molecular regulators remain poorly understood. Here, we examined the roles of steroid receptor coactivator-2 (SRC-2/NCOA2) in the cerebrovascular and metabolic changes associated with neurodegeneration using ps19 mice as a model. In our study, we found a significant decrease in cortical SRC-2 expression in ps19 mice compared with wild-type (WT) controls, with no changes in SRC-1 and SRC-3 levels between the two groups. ps19 mice showed reduced cortical endothelial and blood–brain barrier-associated markers (CD31, occludin, claudin-5, total eNOS (endothelial nitric oxide synthase), and eNOS Ser1177) and increased eNOS Thr495 phosphorylation. HIF-1α, GLUT2, and GLUT4 were also reduced in ps19 mice, whereas GLUT1 and GLUT3 were unchanged between the groups. To examine the role of SRC-2, we used siRNA to reduce its expression in brain endothelial cells and primary neurons. In brain endothelial cells, SRC-2 knockdown reduced the expression of endothelial and BBB-associated markers, including CD31 and occludin, as well as GLUT3, while increasing inhibitory eNOS Thr495 phosphorylation and GLUT4 expression. In brain endothelial cells, SRC-2 knockdown significantly reduced the extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) and NAD+/NADH ratio. Knockdown of SRC-2 in primary neurons (from WT and ps19 mice) significantly reduced the oxygen consumption rate (OCR), while the NAD+/NADH ratio remained unchanged. These findings identify SRC-2 as a regulator of endothelial and neuronal metabolism and support further investigation of SRC-2-dependent pathways as potential therapeutic targets in neurodegenerative diseases.

Article.Title: Angiotensin II-Induced Cardiac Fibrosis: Genomic and Molecular Drivers, Emerging Biomarkers and Therapeutic Perspectives
Article.Authors: Martínez-Rodríguez N.; Campos-González J.; López-Camarillo C.; Medina-Contreras O.
Article.Abstract: Chronically elevated angiotensin II (Ang II) drives adverse cardiac remodelling, converting a reparative response into progressive interstitial and perivascular fibrosis that stiffens the ventricle and precedes overt heart failure. Acting through the angiotensin II type 1 receptor, Ang II generates reactive oxygen species, recruits and polarises immune cells and activates resident fibroblasts, converging on transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β)-dependent and mechanotransductive programmes that drive myofibroblast differentiation and excessive extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition. The magnitude of this response varies between patients: germline variation in renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) genes, loci for heart failure and imaging-defined fibrosis, epigenomic reprogramming of the fibroblast, non-coding RNA networks and metabolic rewiring of collagen-producing cells all modulate the transition from compensated hypertrophy to fibrotic failure. This review integrates these genomic, epigenomic, transcriptomic and metabolomic layers with the signalling architecture of Ang II-induced fibrosis, and reviews the circulating biomarkers—collagen turnover peptides, matricellular and immune mediators, non-coding RNAs and cell-free DNA methylation signatures—that could detect fibrotic activity before remodelling becomes irreversible. We then consider why fibrosis regression under RAAS blockade appears heterogeneous, which emerging targets are mechanistically credible, and how genotype–biomarker–imaging phenotyping could enrich antifibrotic trials. Priorities for ancestrally diverse cohorts and standardised biomarker methodology are identified.

Article.Title: Maternal FNDC5 and ADIPOQ Genetic Variants as Potential Modulators of Susceptibility to Spontaneous Preterm Birth
Article.Authors: Kadivnik M.; Zlatunić P.; Drinić M.; Hercog R.; Kralik K.; Wagner J.
Article.Abstract: Preterm birth (PTB) is a complex and heterogeneous pregnancy outcome in which maternal metabolic and endocrine pathways may contribute to susceptibility to preterm delivery. This study investigated whether two maternal genetic variants involved in metabolic signaling, ADIPOQ rs266729 and FNDC5 rs1746661, are associated with preterm birth (PTB) in a Croatian population. This case–control study included 401 women: 200 with PTB and 201 with term delivery. Maternal genomic DNA was isolated from peripheral blood, and both variants were genotyped using TaqMan-based real-time PCR. Genotype and allele distributions, inheritance models, allelic combinations, logistic regression, and gene–gene interaction were analyzed. Neither variant was significantly associated with overall PTB, and no significant gene–gene interaction was observed (p = 0.18). In early PTB, only a borderline, non-significant tendency toward a higher ADIPOQ rs266729 G allele frequency was found (39% vs. 27%; OR 1.74, 95% CI 0.99–3.04; p = 0.05), which was not supported by genotype, inheritance-model, or regression analyses. The G–T allelic combination was more frequent in early PTB (13.6% vs. 4.6%; p = 0.03) but not after Benjamini–Hochberg correction (adjusted p = 0.09). No significant association between the investigated variants and PTB was demonstrated. The borderline findings in early PTB are hypothesis-generating and require replication in larger cohorts.

Article.Title: Detection of Antagonistic Interactions Between Cannabidiol and Temozolomide in Various Neuroblastoma and Glioblastoma Cell Lines in the MTT Assay by Means of Synergy Finder 3.0 Software and Log-Probit Isobolographic Analysis
Article.Authors: Załuska-Ogryzek K.; Wróblewska-Łuczka P.; Góralczyk A.; Łuszczki J.
Article.Abstract: Despite progress in experimental neuro-oncology and advances in the treatment of brain cancers, glioblastoma multiforme is still the most aggressive primary brain tumor in adults. Cannabinoid-based add-on therapy is likely to be a treatment option for glioblastoma patients who have failed surgical excision and treatment with temozolomide (a classic chemotherapeutic drug). Cannabidiol is one of the naturally occurring compounds isolated from Cannabis, which displays the anti-cancer and anti-viability effects in several glioblastoma cell lines. In the MTT assay, the anti-viability effects of combined treatment with cannabidiol and temozolomide were assessed in two neuroblastoma (CHP-134, KELLY) and four glioblastoma (SF295, U-87MG, T98G, and C6) cell lines. The interactions between cannabidiol and temozolomide from the MTT assay were characterized by means of two independent methods: a classic log-probit isobolographic analysis and a Synergy Finder 3.0 web-application allowing automatic evaluation of interactions in five pharmacodynamic models, including the zero interaction potency (ZIP), Bliss, Loewe, highest single agent (HAS) and Bliss–Loewe consensus models. The impact of cannabidiol on several apoptotic-related proteins (p21, p18, cyclin D1, Bax, Bcl-2) and the cannabinoid CB1 receptor expressed on the glioblastoma SF295 and U-87MG cells was examined with the Western blot technique. Both cell migration and cell–cell interaction after treatment with cannabidiol, temozolomide and their combination were assessed in a wound healing assay. The log-probit isobolographic analysis of interactions revealed that cannabidiol combined with temozolomide exerted antagonistic interactions only in two neuroblastoma cell lines, CHP-134 and KELLY. In contrast, the combination of cannabidiol with temozolomide in all the glioblastoma cells, SF295, U-87MG, T98 and C6, produced (in the classic isobolography) additive interactions with a tendency toward antagonism in the MTT assay. With Synergy Finder 3.0 in the Bliss–Loewe model, the interactions between cannabidiol and temozolomide were antagonistic in all the tested cell lines (except for CHP-134) with synergy score values ranging from −19.64 (for T98G) to −15.07 (for U-87MG). Only the interaction between cannabidiol and temozolomide in the CHP-134 cell line was additive in the Bliss–Loewe model with a synergy score value of 0.95. This comparative study indicates that the combination of cannabidiol with temozolomide should not be recommended and used clinically because of antagonistic interactions reported in the MTT assay. The Bliss–Loewe consensus model can be recommended as a model of choice when screening and evaluating the types of interactions in in vitro studies using the Synergy Finder 3.0 free online available web-application.

Article.Title: The Fibrinolytic System of the Chacma Baboon (Papio ursinus): Implications for Non-Human Primate Haemostatic Disease Models
Article.Authors: Joubert J.; Meiring M.; Janse Van Rensburg W.
Article.Abstract: Baboon models are useful for investigating haemostatic disorders and potential novel treatments. The fibrinolytic system is an integral component of these models and an important potential therapeutic target. We investigated the fibrinolytic system of the Chacma baboon (Papio ursinus), including the effects of sex and ABO blood group. Tissue-type plasminogen activator (tPA), plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1), plasminogen, plasmin-α2-antiplasmin (PAP) complexes, thrombin activatable fibrinolysis inhibitor (TAFI), α2-antiplasmin, fibrinogen levels, and clot lysis times of 40 adult Chacma baboons were assessed. Plasminogen activation using escalating concentrations of streptokinase vs. alteplase was determined and compared with normal human plasma. The results were compared between O and non-O ABO blood groups, and between males and females. PAP complexes and fibrinogen were mostly within the human reference interval, while tPA, PAI-1 and α2-antiplasmin tended towards the lower limit. Plasminogen and TAFI were virtually undetectable with the human ELISA kits used. Alteplase was a potent plasminogen activator compared with streptokinase (p < 0.0001), resulting in brisker clot lysis in baboon than in human plasma (10.8 vs. 13.4 min). Blood group O baboons had higher fibrinogen levels (p = 0.0355), while males had lower fibrinogen (p = 0.0134) but higher PAP complex concentrations (p = 0.0188). Except for plasminogen and TAFI, the Chacma baboon fibrinolytic system appears broadly similar to its human counterpart. Streptokinase does not meaningfully activate Chacma baboon fibrinolysis, but alteplase elicits greater plasminogen activation than in humans. These findings, as well as sex- and ABO-blood-group-related differences in fibrinogen, should be considered when designing future pre-clinical drug testing experiments in this species.

Article.Title: Personalized Geriatric Pharmacotherapy: Pharmacogenomics, Polypharmacy, and Age-Related Pharmacokinetic and Pharmacodynamic Changes
Article.Authors: Buianova A.; Mironenko I.; Arbatskiy M.; Churov A.
Article.Abstract: Aging induces profound physiological changes that alter drug disposition and response, narrowing therapeutic windows and increasing susceptibility to adverse drug reactions (ADRs). This review synthesizes current evidence on age-related pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic changes, with a focus on pharmacogenomic determinants of drug response in older adults. Progressive decline in renal function and hepatic metabolic capacity and alterations in body composition collectively necessitate age-appropriate dose adjustments. Polypharmacy, prevalent in community-dwelling and hospitalized older adults, compounds these challenges through drug–drug and drug–drug–gene interactions. Pharmacogenomic testing—particularly for CYP2D6, CYP2C19, CYP2C9, and SLCO1B1—offers a promising strategy with which to personalize therapy, while deprescribing frameworks provide practical approaches to mitigating medication-related risks. This review provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the mechanistic basis of altered drug response in older adults and proposes actionable strategies for optimizing pharmacotherapy in this vulnerable population. Throughout, pharmacogenomic claims are graded across four levels: biological plausibility, measured pharmacokinetic effect, pharmacogenetic actionability, and demonstrated clinical utility. Furthermore, selected gene–drug examples are explicitly identified as either geriatric-specific evidence or extrapolations from general adult pharmacogenomics, clarifying which findings are truly modified by the aging process.

Article.Title: Mitochondrial DNA Abnormalities in Idiopathic Inflammatory Myopathies: Innate Immune Signaling and Therapeutic Prospects
Article.Authors: Wang G.; Wang Y.; Wang X.; McCullagh K.; Liu A.
Article.Abstract: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) encodes essential components of oxidative phosphorylation and can stimulate innate immunity when released from mitochondria. Its genetic and immunological functions provide a rationale for investigating mtDNA abnormalities in idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIMs), where muscle dysfunction and inflammation coexist. Large-scale deletions and depletion have been documented in inclusion body myositis and polymyositis with mitochondrial pathology, while dermatomyositis studies reveal regional depletion and oxidative modifications in distinct biological compartments. These findings raise the possibility that mtDNA abnormalities contribute to both impaired mitochondrial function and inflammatory signaling. This review integrates subtype-specific findings with mechanistic studies of mtDNA release, DNA sensing, and inflammasome activation in IIM-related and non-IIM systems. It evaluates the evidence for mtDNA-based biomarkers and therapies targeting mitochondrial injury or downstream inflammation. The reported clinical benefits do not establish mtDNA-specific therapeutic effects. Defining how mitochondrial genome abnormalities and inflammatory signaling interact within each subtype is a priority for biomarker validation and therapeutic research.

Article.Title: Endophytic Bacteria as Modulators of Fragrance Biosynthesis in Plants: Mechanisms and Prospects
Article.Authors: Srivastava P.; Verma S.; Israr J.; Misra S.; Kumar M.; Paul D.
Article.Abstract: Plant fragrance is the blend of volatile terpenoids, phenylpropanoids/benzenoids, fatty acid derivatives, and nitrogen- or sulfur-containing compounds released from flowers, leaves, and fruit. It drives pollination and defence and accounts for much of the economic value of aromatic, medicinal, and ornamental crops. However, it shifts with genotype, developmental stage, tissue type, and stress, and a large share of it still comes from wild-harvested plants. Endophytic bacteria are the microorganisms that colonize internal plant tissues without causing apparent disease symptoms, may modulate these specialized metabolic pathways. Only a limited number of studies have directly investigated these interactions. In contrast, a substantially larger body of research has demonstrated the roles of endophytic bacteria in promoting plant growth and enhancing plant tolerance to environmental stresses. However, direct evidence establishing links between bacterial endophytes, specific genes within volatile-biosynthetic pathways, and the volatile compounds actually released by plants remains limited. The current review summarizes the current evidence on the regulation of major plant volatile biosynthetic routes by endophytic bacteria, including the MVA and MEP pathways for terpenoids, the shikimate-derived phenylpropanoid/benzenoid pathway, as well as the lipoxygenase pathway leading to green-leaf volatile production. The suggested mechanisms are generally grouped into several inter-related categories, such as microbial elicitation and pattern recognition, phytohormonal reprogramming, nutrient and precursor acquisition, modulation of carbon flux through the MVA/MEP and phenylpropanoid pathways, redox regulation and stress priming, and bacterial volatile-mediated signalling. More speculative mechanisms are discussed separately, such as microbial biotransformation, direct microbial biosynthesis of plant volatiles, and horizontal gene transfer. Evidence from culinary and essential oil herbs, medicinal plants, ornamental flowers, and fruit crops is evaluated using an evidence hierarchy that distinguishes phenotypic associations from experimentally validated causal mechanisms. Establishing a robust gene-to-metabolite causal framework will require targeted approaches, including gnotobiotic inoculation, volatilomic profiling, and stable-isotope tracing.

Article.Title: miR1919–MCD1 Regulation of Debneyol Biosynthesis in Nicotiana: Enzyme Organisation, Catalytic Evidence and the Limits of Substrate Channelling
Article.Authors: Labudda M.
Article.Abstract: Debneyol biosynthesis in Nicotiana is regulated by the microRNA 1919 (miR1919)–miR1919-targeted cell death factor 1 (MCD1) module, but the mechanisms linking enzyme association to defence-metabolite output remain incompletely resolved. Although MCD1-dependent protein association and catalytic effects have been demonstrated, direct preferential transfer of 5-epi-aristolochene (5-EA) has not. This critical narrative review addresses this evidential gap by distinguishing biochemical pathway reconstruction, protein-interaction assays, enzyme kinetics, transcript responses, metabolite profiles and infection phenotypes, and compares their inferential scope with independent plant metabolic systems. Farnesyl diphosphate is converted via 5-EA and its epoxide to debneyol. In yeast microsomes, MCD1 increased the reported maximum reaction velocity of 5-EA epoxidase (EAE) from 18.07 to 30.24 nM s−1, whereas a separate coupled-enzyme assay produced approximately threefold more epoxide. Plant experiments also revealed altered debneyol-to-capsidiol ratios, transcript abundance and infection responses. The novel contribution of this review is a structured appraisal of what each experimental approach establishes and where competing explanations remain unresolved. Direct substrate channelling, transcription-independent branch selection and specific allosteric mechanisms remain unresolved; controlled intermediate-tracing, quantitative interaction and enzyme-abundance studies are needed to discriminate among them.

Article.Title: Diclofenac Removal by Actinobacterial Strains and Ecotoxicological Responses
Article.Authors: Gonzalez Holc V.; Small M.; Arnau G.; Lautru S.; Pernodet J.; Aparicio J.; Polti M.
Article.Abstract: Diclofenac (DCF) is a widely detected pharmaceutical whose persistence and biologically active transformation products raise environmental concern. This study evaluated DCF tolerance and removal by actinobacterial strains and integrated chemical performance with plant- and earthworm-based ecotoxicological responses. Phenotypic screening at 1, 5, and 10 g L−1 DCF revealed strain- and concentration-dependent responses in growth, sporulation, and pigment production, with Streptomyces sp. E5N50 and Streptomyces sp. Z2 selected for further study. In liquid assays, after 5 days of incubation, only low biomass production was observed when 50 mg L−1 DCF was supplied without glucose, relative to glucose-containing controls. E5N50 showed modest DCF removal (approximately 23–26%), while Z2 achieved 90.8% in glucose-supplemented medium and about 70% when glucose and ammonium were supplied. A seven-day time-course study with Streptomyces sp. Z2 showed that DCF removal continued after biomass had reached its maximum, suggesting that the process was not exclusively growth-associated. Ecotoxicological responses were organism- and endpoint-dependent. The glucose + DCF + Z2 treatment, associated with the highest DCF removal, significantly increased tomato radicle elongation, whereas glucose + ammonium + DCF + Z2 produced the most favorable Eisenia fetida response, with significantly reduced body-mass loss and increased coelomocyte abundance despite the lower DCF removal removalobserved in this treatment. Overall, Z2 exhibited potential for DCF removal under defined laboratory liquid-culture conditions, and the combined chemical and biological assessment highlighted that parent-compound removal and ecotoxicological improvement provide complementary measures of remediation performance.

Article.Authors: Alanazi A.; Bilel H.; Asran A.; Ahmed S.; Al Zbedy A.; Nassar A.
Article.Abstract: Recycling of food waste and animal by-products in order to produce valuable bioorganic products has been playing an important role in the green chemistry field. The GBAE showed potent antioxidant activity since it was capable of completely neutralizing (100%) DPPH radicals at a concentration of 100 mg/mL. Moreover, the hemolytic activity of GBAE was studied and found to be very low (<1% with human erythrocytes), indicating its weak in vitro hemotoxicity. When oxidative stress was generated via lead acetate (0.625 ppm), GBAE provided a considerable protective effect, leading to 65.0%, 67.5%, and 73.7% hemolysis reduction at concentrations of 200, 400, and 800 mg/mL, respectively. Additionally, preliminary in vitro findings suggested that GBAE exhibited fibrinolytic potential and anticoagulant activities. GBAE showed dose-dependent thrombolytic and anticoagulant activity, with a significant increase in the percentage of clot lysis and coagulation time up to 36 min, compared with 13 min in the negative control.

Article.Title: Silica–Lignin Composites—Insight into Physicochemical Properties and Adsorption Mechanisms
Article.Authors: Blachnio M.; Zienkiewicz-Strzalka M.; Juchniewicz Z.; Sternik D.; Derylo-Marczewska A.
Article.Abstract: Two silica–lignin composites with varying biopolymer content were synthesized using the sol–gel method as effective adsorbents for the removal of organic dyes from aqueous solutions. XPS and XRD analysis confirmed the effective modification of the silica surface with lignin. Increasing the lignin content in the composite altered its physicochemical properties. Textural analysis revealed a decrease in the porosity of the composites with increasing the amount of biopolymer incorporated into the silica. Thermal analysis with the identification of gaseous thermal destruction products allowed for the determination of the thermal stability of the composites. Dye adsorption experiments, including equilibrium and kinetic measurements, allowed the determination of adsorption capacity, adsorption rate and adsorption mechanisms. FTIR mapping enabled the identification of differences in the interactions of selected dyes with the synthesized composites and revealed preferential adsorption on surface areas of the adsorbents rich in lignin or silica. The obtained results confirmed the potential of silica–lignin materials in environmental applications as cheap and biodegradable adsorbents.

Article.Title: Psychobiotics and Trace Elements in Neurodegenerative Diseases: From Independent Modulators to Potential Interactions Within the Microbiota–Gut–Brain Axis—Narrative Review
Article.Authors: Sokólska W.; Orywal K.
Article.Abstract: The microbiota–gut–brain axis represents an important bidirectional communication network linking the gastrointestinal tract and the central nervous system and may contribute to processes involved in neurodegeneration. Increasing attention has been directed toward psychobiotics as potential modulators of the microbiota–gut–brain axis, while accumulating evidence also indicates that disturbed trace-element homeostasis may contribute to the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases. This review summarizes current evidence on the roles of psychobiotics and trace elements and examines their potential interplay within the microbiota–gut–brain axis. The review discusses bidirectional interactions between the gut microbiota and trace elements, the potential effects of psychobiotic interventions on trace-element homeostasis, and the possible implications of these interactions for neurodegenerative processes. Taken together, current findings indicate that the gut microbiota, psychobiotics, and trace elements may constitute an interconnected system influencing intestinal and systemic homeostasis as well as biological processes relevant to nervous system function. However, direct evidence demonstrating the clinical relevance of interactions between these components remains limited. Moreover, available evidence is largely based on experimental studies, while clinical findings remain scarce and heterogeneous. Further characterization of this interplay may improve our understanding of mechanisms underlying neurodegeneration and provide a basis for the development of more targeted and personalized approaches to supporting neurological health.

Article.Title: Longitudinal Peripheral Immunophenotyping and Rituximab Response in Primary Membranous Nephropathy: A Prospective Cohort Study
Article.Authors: Georgopoulos C.; Dova L.; Stamellou E.; Duni A.; Vartholomatos G.; Liapis G.; Patsiogiannis V.; Siomou E.; Milionis H.; Dounousi E.
Article.Abstract: Rituximab (RTX) is a first-line option for primary membranous nephropathy (pMN), but many patients fail to respond for reasons that conventional markers only partially explain. By month three, responders showed deeper B-cell depletion, higher CD4+CD25+FoxP3+ T cells, fewer intermediate monocytes and a lower SIRI. On multivariate analysis, month-3 depletion of total CD3−CD19+ B cells below 0.5% (odds ratio 5.8, 95% confidence interval 1.1–31.1) was associated with remission, and each 0.1-unit increase in month-3 SIRI (odds ratio 0.44, 95% confidence interval 0.22–0.91) with lower odds of remission. In a hypothesis-generating analysis, a model combining both had an apparent area under the curve of 0.87. Longitudinal immunophenotyping identifies candidate biomarkers of RTX response in pMN that require multicenter validation.

Article.Authors: Kordas B.; Juranek J.

IF and ketogenic diet identified 6569 and 999 genes, respectively, in diabetic mice. Their effects showed modest agreement (Pearson r = 0.205), with 447 genes significant in both experiments, including 359 with matching directions. They shared 59 pathways with a matching direction at a fixed intergene correlation of 0.01; these overlaps were not supported when correlations were estimated from the data. IF responses in diabetic and APP/PS1 hippocampus agreed poorly (r = −0.056). No human genes met a per-contrast false discovery rate < 0.05. Thirteen diabetic genes showed significant opposition of disease and IF effects; neither primary fasting experiment demonstrated contraction toward controls. The results support limited agreement between the diabetic dietary experiments and little agreement in IF responses across the examined disease contexts. They do not establish transcriptomic restoration.

Article.Title: Identification of a DNA Damage Response-Related Prognostic Signature and Functional Validation of SMC3 in Glioma
Article.Authors: Ma J.; Zhang C.; Zhang J.; Zhong C.
Article.Abstract: DNA damage response (DDR) deficiencies are linked to tumorigenesis and progression. However, the association of DDR with prognosis and therapeutic response in glioma has not been fully illustrated. TCGA and CGGA databases were used to acquire RNA-seq and clinical data about gliomas. LASSO-Cox regression was introduced to establish a DDR-based risk signature. The single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) algorithm was used to estimate immune infiltrates. The performance of the signature and nomogram in predicting survival was evaluated using ROC curves. Connectivity Map (CMap) analysis was used to nominate candidate compounds, and pRRophetic was used to predict drug sensitivity. Through LASSO-Cox regression, we developed a prognostic risk score based on five DDR-related genes (GADD45G, HDAC1, RRM2, SMC3, and WEE1). Higher risk scores were associated with shorter overall survival and remained significant in multivariable Cox analyses. A prognostic nomogram achieved 1-, 3-, and 5-year AUCs of 0.901, 0.936, and 0.903 in TCGA and 0.776, 0.816, and 0.802 in CGGA, respectively. High-risk tumors showed enrichment of TNFα signaling via NFκB and IL6/JAK/STAT3 gene sets, together with differences in inferred immune cell-associated features and immune checkpoint gene expression. Computational drug sensitivity analyses associated higher risk scores with lower predicted IC50 values for GSK269962A, pazopanib, rapamycin, and NVP-BEZ235, providing hypotheses for subsequent experimental validation. SMC3 overexpression inhibited glioma cell proliferation and migration in vitro. The DDR-related signature showed prognostic value and associations with immune-related transcriptional features in glioma, with in vitro evidence suggesting a functional role for SMC3.

Article.Title: Trichostatin A-Induced H3K9ac Hyperacetylation Selectively Enriches Promoters in Adipogenic Human Periodontal Ligament Stem Cells
Article.Authors: Montero-Del-Toro J.; Serralta-Interian A.; Lamas M.; Valle-García D.; Torres-Romero J.; Rodas-Junco B.
Article.Abstract: Adipogenesis is regulated by histone modifications associated with chromatin accessibility. These modifications include histone H3 lysine 9 acetylation (H3K9ac), a mark linked to transcriptional activation. Its dynamics are governed by histone acetyltransferases and histone deacetylases (HDACs). Although trichostatin A (TSA) induces global hyperacetylation, its association with the differential enrichment of H3K9ac at regulatory elements during adipogenesis in human cells remains unclear. Therefore, this study characterized the genomic distribution of TSA-induced H3K9ac enrichment in human periodontal ligament stem cells (hPDLSCs). To this end, hPDLSCs underwent adipogenic differentiation for 14 days following TSA pretreatment (100 nM, 72 h). Cell morphology, lipid droplet radius, and the nuclear distribution of H3K9ac and H3K9me2 were evaluated by immunofluorescence, while the genomic distribution of H3K9ac was assessed by ChIP-seq. Statistical significance was assessed using an unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-test (p < 0.05) and MACS3 peak calling (q = 0.001). TSA reduced the lipid droplet radius by 1.69-fold and increased the nuclear H3K9ac signal by 10.17-fold, while reducing H3K9me2 signal by 1.38-fold. Furthermore, 752 promoters exhibited greater H3K9ac enrichment under TSA treatment compared with 364 in the control, including genes associated with adipogenesis, such as PPARGC1B and AGPAT2, and chromatin remodeling genes SETD5 and KDM2A. Overall, these findings indicate that TSA alters the adipogenic phenotype and increases H3K9ac enrichment at promoters associated with metabolic and chromatin remodeling programs.

Article.Title: Detection of Anti-Platelet Factor 4 Antibodies in Acute and Chronic Thromboembolic Disease—A Pilot Study
Article.Authors: Trunk A.; Wesche J.; Jacobi S.; Bruch-Oms M.; Metzler D.; Herrmann E.; Thiele T.; Lindhoff-Last E.
Article.Abstract: Heterogeneous antibodies directed against platelet factor 4 (PF4-Abs) are associated with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) and vaccine-induced immune thrombocytopenia and thrombosis (VITT). Emerging evidence suggests that these antibodies may also occur in other thromboembolic diseases. In this pilot study, we assessed the prevalence of PF4-Abs in patients with acute thromboembolism and in patients with thromboembolic antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), a chronic autoimmune thrombophilia. Forty patients with acute thromboembolism and 43 patients with APS were included. Both heparin-dependent and heparin-independent PF4-Abs were evaluated using multiple assay platforms, including a prototype chemiluminescence assay for heparin-independent PF4-Abs, an anti-PF4/polyanion IgG chemiluminescence assay, a latex agglutination assay detecting anti-PF4/polyanion IgG/IgM/IgA antibodies, an anti-PF4/heparin IgG ELISA, and functional platelet activation tests. Across the different assays, positivity in at least one assay was observed in 27.5% (11/40) of patients with acute thromboembolism and 27.9% (12/43) of patients with APS. In most antibody-positive patients, no recent heparin exposure was documented. Functional platelet activation was predominantly absent, arguing against a classical HIT- or VITT-like mechanism. Overall, these results demonstrate assay-dependent PF4-Ab positivity in a substantial proportion of patients with acute and chronic thromboembolic conditions. Their clinical and pathogenic relevance remains unclear and warrants further investigation.

Article.Title: Upregulated SMURF1 and miR-520d-5p in Basal Cell Carcinoma: Possible Implications for TGF-β/SMAD Signalling
Article.Authors: Kasap Ş.; Çelik S.; Özdemir Ç.; Aydın M.; Edgünlü T.
Article.Abstract: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common type of skin cancer. SMAD-specific E3 ubiquitin protein ligase 1 (SMURF1), a protein involved in regulating the transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) signalling pathway, and miR-520d-5p may play a role in the development and progression of BCC. In this study, we investigated the potential roles of SMURF1 and miR-520d-5p, known to affect cancer pathogenesis, in the pathogenesis of BCC. We included 30 BCC tissues and 30 noncancerous skin tissues in the study. Gene expression levels were determined by quantitative polymerase chain reaction qPCR. We performed in silico analyses to identify possible genes and signalling pathways associated with BCC. SMURF1 and miR-520d-5p showed significantly increased expression in BCC tissues compared to controls (p = 0.029 and p = 0.011, respectively). According to in silico analyses, SMURF1 and miR-520d-5p are predicted to be involved in the TGF-β signalling pathway. miR-520d-5p is predicted to regulate multiple target genes in the TGF-β signalling pathway, which requires experimental validation. Our findings indicate that SMURF1 and miR-520d-5p are upregulated in BCC and may be associated with BCC pathogenesis. Both molecules are upregulated in BCC tissues and are implicated in the regulation of the TGF-β signalling pathway. According to in silico analysis, SMURF1, SMAD2, SMAD4, TGFBR1, SMAD7, SMURF2, RUNX2, MAPK1, and TGFB3 are key genes involved in the TGF-β signalling pathway, which may be relevant to BCC pathogenesis.

Article.Title: The Effects of the Medium’s pH Value on the Efficiency of the Enzymatic Transglycosylation Catalyzed by Escherichia coli Purine Nucleoside Phosphorylase and Lactobacillus leichmanii Nucleoside Deoxyribosyltransferase Type II
Article.Authors: Alexeev C.; Konkina M.; Oskolsky I.; Platov D.; Drenichev M.
Article.Abstract: The effect of the reaction medium pH value on the rate and yield of enzymatic transglycosylation catalyzed by Escherichia coli purine nucleoside phosphorylase (EcPNP) and Lactobacillus leichmanii type II nucleoside deoxyribosyltransferase (LlNDTII) was investigated. In the presence of EcPNP at pH 5.5, a significant reduction in the inosine formation rate was observed, compared with that of adenosine. A substituent at the purine O6 position neutralizes the negative effect of the 6-oxo group on the reaction rate. A substituent at the purine N6 position has virtually no effect on the transglycosylation rate. In reactions catalyzed by LlNDTII, the rate of nucleoside formation from 4-oxopyrimidines was higher at pH 5.5, but the yield decreased by approximately 10% compared with that at pH 7.0; an unusual dependence of the yield of the target nucleoside on the enzyme concentration used was also revealed.

Article.Title: Recent Advances in Neuronal-like Differentiation of Mesenchymal Stem/Stromal Cells
Article.Authors: Romano I.; D’angeli F.; Maugeri G.; Musumeci G.; Tamburino S.; Lombardo G.; Giuffrida R.; Mannino G.; Lo Furno D.
Article.Abstract: Mesenchymal stem/stromal cells (MSCs) have been widely investigated in recent decades because of their multipotent differentiation abilities. In fact, MSCs are able to differentiate not only into mesodermal cell lines (adipocytes, chondrocytes, osteocytes), but also into neuronal and glial cells. MSCs can be derived from different sources, such as bone marrow, adipose tissue, peripheral blood and various neonatal birth-associated tissues. They are suitable candidate in cell-based approaches for both autologous and heterologous transplantation in the field of regenerative medicine. Unlike other types of stem cells, MSCs raise no ethical issues and feature low risks of tumorigenesis after transplantation into humans or animals. In addition, they may exert beneficial effects due to their paracrine actions which help tissue recovery. Numerous studies describe effects obtained following MSC treatments in a variety of human pathologies, including nervous system diseases. The nervous tissue is characterized by very limited recovery properties, likely because of a scarce presence of stem cell niches, which are confined to the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus and the subventricular zone of the lateral ventricles. These niches cannot be able to counteract the neuronal loss after damage or degenerative events. Many efforts have been made to obtain functional neuronal differentiated MSCs to be used for transplantation. However, evidence of complete neuronal maturation and functional integration of neuronal-like MSCs remains limited, and clinical studies have used undifferentiated MSCs rather than neuronal-like cell populations. In this review, we mainly focus on various differentiation protocols that have been adopted for in vitro studies, taking also into account the underlying pathways involved.

Article.Title: Effects of Repetitive Compressive Loading on the Expression of Autophagy-Related Factors, Autophagy Capacity and Cellular Activity in Human Subchondral Bone Osteoblasts
Article.Authors: Iwata H.; Sato S.; Somemura S.; Takemoto M.; Takahashi-Suzuki Y.; Sugishita Y.; Fujiya H.; Haraguchi N.; Yudoh K.
Article.Abstract: Bone metabolism is known to change in response to mechanical stress. In osteoarthritis (OA), the subchondral bone as well as the articular cartilage layer is damaged by mechanical stress, which adversely affects the mechanical environment and homeostatic balance of the entire joint, leading to the onset of OA. However, the impact of mechanical stress on osteoblasts in the subchondral bone, especially their defense mechanism against stress, remains unclear. We focused on the mechanical stress response capacity of subchondral bone osteoblasts, which, like chondrocytes in the cartilage layer, are routinely exposed to repetitive mechanical stress. The purpose of this study was to determine whether repetitive mechanical force (at a physiologic level of cyclic compressive loading) affects the expression of factors regulating autophagy, autophagy capacity and cellular activity in subchondral osteoblasts. Three-dimensional cultured tissue was generated from human subchondral bone osteoblasts using a collagen sponge scaffold. Repetitive compressive loading was applied to the 3D cell culture constructs. After mechanical loading on 3D cell–collagen sponge constructs, we comparatively analyzed the expression of autophagy-related factors (ATG5, Beclin-1, Parkin) in human osteoblasts. Levels of osteoblast differentiation activity (alkaline phosphatase) were also analyzed, and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was used to detect autophagy processes with or without the repetitive compressive loading. In both premature and mature osteoblasts, repetitive compressive loading decreased expression of the autophagy-related factors ATG5, Beclin-1 and Parkin in comparison with the non-loading group, suggesting that repetitive compressive loading may induce downregulation of mitophagy as well as cellular autophagy in subchondral osteoblasts. TEM analysis indicated that, in both premature and mature osteoblasts of the non-loading group, autophagy processes were progressing. In contrast, repetitive loading decreased the number of autophagosomes and autolysosomes in mature and premature osteoblasts. Our results demonstrated that repetitive mechanical loading resulted in a reduction in cellular autophagy and mitophagy in both premature and mature osteoblasts, while also inducing osteoblast differentiation. While mechanical stress promotes osteoblast differentiation, it also alters autophagy, a cellular defense mechanism, suggesting that under conditions of sustained repetitive loading, alterations in the autophagy response—which is essential for maintaining intracellular homeostasis—occur alongside the adaptive bone-forming response, potentially affecting osteoblast function in the long term. Our data demonstrate that reductions in both mitophagy and cellular autophagy in response to repetitive mechanical stress, even at a physiologic level, may lead to accumulation of defective mitochondria and abnormal cellular proteins in the cells, thus reducing osteoblast activity and affecting the homeostasis of subchondral bone tissue, and ultimately contributing to OA progression.

Article.Title: Hypoxia-Associated Glycolytic–Lipogenic Reprogramming and Impaired Antigen Presentation in SPP1+ Tumor-Associated Macrophages in Ovarian Cancer
Article.Authors: Zuo X.; Huang S.; Li Y.; Wang Z.; Xue H.; Min J.; Hong L.; Li S.
Article.Abstract: Ovarian cancer has an immunosuppressive microenvironment in which SPP1+ tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) are linked to poor prognosis and immune evasion, yet their molecular features and metabolic mechanisms remain unclear. We therefore set out to determine whether SPP1 marks a discrete TAM subpopulation or a functional state in treatment-naïve high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC), to define the transcriptional and metabolic program that accompanies it, and to test whether local hypoxia is associated with it. Tumor-derived, treatment-naïve samples from three single-cell datasets (one lesion per patient; 47 patients) yielded 385,504 cells; Seurat v5 and Harmony were used for clustering, annotation, and batch correction. SPP1+/SPP1− macrophages were compared by differential expression, GO/KEGG/GSEA, metabolic scoring, and transcription factor inference, and the definition was retested with within-sample SPP1-high versus SPP1-low comparisons and with MSigDB Hallmark gene sets scored by two independent algorithms. Validation used Visium spatial transcriptomics (GSE263920), TCGA-OV (n = 429), CD8+ T cell exhaustion analysis, CellChat and a syngeneic ID8 model. Of 64,067 macrophages (16.62%), 82.0% were SPP1+; upregulated genes were enriched in glycolysis, monocyte migration and tissue remodeling, whereas MHC class II and neutrophil-related genes were downregulated. At the sample level, glycolysis, fatty acid synthesis and glutaminolysis scores were elevated and the cholesterol synthesis score was reduced, with no evidence of suppressed fatty acid oxidation or oxidative phosphorylation; HIF1A ranked 4th and NR1H3 3rd among 271 transcription factors. All 8 spatial sections showed positive hypoxia–SPP1 correlations, and hotspots showed elevated glycolysis, EMT, immunosuppression and macrophage scores. No robust association was found between SPP1+ TAM infiltration and CD8+ T cell exhaustion (p = 0.315). MDK–LRP1/SDC1 was the major macrophage-directed input. Immunofluorescence showed SPP1 immunoreactivity in a subset of CD68+ macrophages within HIF1α-rich areas of ID8 tumors, without CD8+PD-1+ T cell aggregation. SPP1+ TAMs therefore correspond to a hypoxic functional state with HIF1A activation, a glycolytic–lipogenic transcriptional program, reduced cholesterol synthesis gene expression and a reduced MHC class II program; protein-level and functional validation, and direct tests of HIF1A dependency, remain necessary.

Article.Title: The Molecular Mechanisms of Cold Tolerance in Brassica napus
Article.Authors: Luo W.; Zhou Y.; Shen J.; Xu L.; Du X.; Sheng F.; Geng R.; Cai G.
Article.Abstract: Brassica napus is a crucial oilseed crop in China, meeting approximately 55% of the country’s demand for vegetable oils. However, throughout its growth cycle, it frequently encounters low-temperature stress. As a key environmental factor constraining the stability of Brassica napus L. yield and quality, cold damage makes research into the cold tolerance mechanisms of Brassica napus L. highly significant for the breeding of cold-tolerant varieties. This paper focuses on the issue of low-temperature stress in Brassica napus L., synthesizing recent relevant research findings. It first clarifies the phenotypic effects of low-temperature stress on Brassica napus L. at different growth stages. Concurrently, low temperatures disrupt the integrity of the Brassica napus cell membrane and inhibit photosynthesis, in response, plants can mitigate oxidative damage by activating antioxidant enzyme systems, such as superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase (CAT). Based on the above, the current research progress in mining cold-tolerant germplasm resources in China and identifying cold tolerance genes in Brassica napus L. is further summarized as follows. This paper provides a theoretical reference for an in-depth analysis of the cold tolerance mechanisms in Brassica napus L. and for accelerating the breeding of cold-tolerant varieties. Future efforts should focus on the functional validation of key genes within cold tolerance pathways and the application of multi-gene pyramiding breeding technologies to break through the bottleneck in controlling cold damage in Brassica napus L.

Article.Title: Comparative Study on Coffee and Spent Coffee Grounds of Arabica and Robusta Varieties of Ugandan Origin: Bioactive Properties of Extracts as Circular Resources
Article.Authors: Dinu M.; Dumitru A.; Brezoiu A.; Isopencu G.; Iancu P.
Article.Abstract: Coffee consumption is increasing yearly, and so is the quantity of spent coffee grounds, a by-product that still contains bioactive compounds. The goal of this work is to evaluate the lipid fractions (LFs) and polyphenolic fractions (PFs) from roasted coffee grounds (RCG; two varieties of Ugandan origin: Arabica and Robusta) and from the corresponding spent coffee grounds (SCG) extracted with solvents of opposite polarities. A qualitative and quantitative analysis of the extracts was performed using GC-FID, 1H-NMR, Folin–Ciocalteu, HPLC-PDA, DPPH and antibacterial activity methods. A high-quality LF, coffee oil (91.82 g triacylglycerides/100 g LF, 49.85 mol% saturated fatty acids and 50.15 mol% unsaturated fatty acid chains, 8.98 mg GAE/g LF, 20.91% DPPH inhibition), with high extraction yield (10.34 g/100 g SCG), can be recovered from SCG of the Ugandan Arabica variety. In addition, SCG of both Ugandan Arabica and Robusta varieties are promising resources for the recovery of high-quality PF (12.30 and 7.85 mg GAE/g PF, 0.684 and 0.837 mg/g PF chlorogenic acids, 85.17% and 73.95% DPPH inhibition) with good extraction yields (9.35 and 5.63 g/100 g SCG) and with antimicrobial activities that remain after the coffee brewing step. These results highlight SCG of Ugandan origin as a promising resource of bioactive compounds for further valorization.

Article.Title: Antimicrobial Resistance and Infectious Complications in Cancer Immunotherapy: CAR-T Cells, Bispecific Antibodies and Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors
Article.Authors: Lasagna A.; Andreoni M.; Silvestris N.; Pedrazzoli P.
Article.Abstract: Cancer immunotherapies, including chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapies, bispecific antibodies (BsAbs), and immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), have improved outcomes across hematologic and solid malignancies. Infection risk remains heterogeneous and depends on treatment platform, target antigen, lymphodepletion, immune reconstitution, concomitant immunosuppression, and supportive care. This narrative review synthesizes clinical trials, observational studies, and guidance identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, reference screening, and a targeted literature update through October 2026. It focuses on infection incidence, microbiological spectrum, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), multidrug-resistant (MDR) colonization and infection, antimicrobial exposure, prevention, and stewardship. Severe infections can be frequent with BCMA-directed BsAbs: the MagnetisMM-3 study reported grade 3–4 infections in 39.8% of elranatamab-treated patients, while a pooled global teclistamab cohort reported grade 3–4 infections in 55.3%; these estimates are study-specific and are influenced in part by COVID-19. Direct AMR evidence is concentrated in CAR-T and broader cellular-therapy cohorts, while comparable data for BsAbs and ICIs remain limited. Associations between broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure, microbiome disruption, and CAR-T outcomes are clinically important but remain vulnerable to confounding. Prevention should integrate immune status, prior microbiology, antimicrobial exposure, and local resistance patterns rather than infer resistance risk from treatment platform alone. Prospective studies using harmonized outcomes are needed to improve individualized infection prevention and antimicrobial stewardship.

Article.Title: Tryptophan and Its Selected Metabolites Modulate Melanoma-Cell Biology: A Preliminary In Vitro Study
Article.Authors: Michalak-Stoma A.; Walczak K.; Kowal M.; Sawa-Wejksza K.; Chojnacki M.; Lemieszek M.; Stoma F.; Krasowska D.
Article.Abstract: Tryptophan (TRP) and its metabolites are involved in numerous physiological and pathological processes within the skin. They may influence melanoma biology, but their role remains insufficiently understood. This study investigated the effects of TRP, anthranilic acid (AA), and cinnabarinic acid (CBA) in melanoma cells in vitro and their potential interaction with the B-Raf proto-oncogene, serine/threonine kinase (BRAF) inhibitor vemurafenib. A375, G361, and SK-MEL-3 melanoma cell lines and a THP-1-derived macrophage model were used. Cell proliferation and metabolic activity were assessed using the 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) assay, migration using a scratch assay, and cell-cycle distribution by flow cytometry. Western blotting was used to analyze selected signaling proteins. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) and nitric oxide (NO) production were evaluated. Bioinformatic analyses investigated associations between BRAF and genes related to tryptophan metabolism and the kynurenine pathway. All compounds showed dose-dependent antiproliferative effects, with prolonged exposure increasing efficacy. TRP and AA increased G0/G1 cell-cycle arrest, whereas CBA increased the G2/M population. TRP also reduced A375 cell migration. All three compounds enhanced the antiproliferative effect of vemurafenib, with CBA showing the strongest effect (approximately 20%). Western blot analysis indicated modulation of p21 expression and ERK1/2 phosphorylation, suggesting implications for cell cycle and stress signaling pathways. Moreover, conditioned medium from A375 cells exposed to tested compounds affected cell viability, ROS, and NO production in THP-1-derived macrophages. TRP and its metabolites may be considered potential supportive agents for melanoma BRAF-targeted therapy. However, further in vivo studies are needed to clarify their therapeutic value and to elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms.
