Article.Title: Human Organoids in Radiation Research: Modeling Tissue Injury, Regeneration and Therapeutic Response
Article.Authors: Hao X.; Li Z.; Wang S.
Article.Abstract: Radiation therapy is a cornerstone in the treatment of abdominal, pelvic, thoracic, head and neck and central nervous system malignancies. However, irradiation inevitably damages adjacent normal tissues, leading to radiation-induced enteritis, lung injury, cardiac injury, salivary gland dysfunction and brain injury, which compromise both quality of life and treatment outcomes. Traditional two-dimensional cell cultures and animal models have significant limitations in mimicking human tissue radiation responses: the former lacks three-dimensional architecture and cell–cell interactions, while the latter exhibits species-specific differences. In recent years, three-dimensional organoid technology has rapidly emerged as a powerful platform in radiation biology and radiation oncology. In particular, organoids derived from patient tissues or induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) offer key advantages, including self-organization capacity and near-physiological tissue structure and function, which have greatly advanced in-depth research in the radiation field. This review comprehensively summarizes applications of human organoids in radiation injury and regeneration research across the brain, heart, lung, esophagus, salivary gland, intestine, muscle, thyroid, hematopoietic system, and tumors. Animal-derived and organotypic models are included only as comparative or supporting mechanistic evidence and are explicitly identified as such. We focus on advances in modeling radiation injury, elucidating regenerative mechanisms, screening radioprotective and radiosensitizing agents and predicting patient responses to chemoradiation. Current limitations and future directions are discussed collectively at the end.

Article.Authors: Normile C.; Irnaten M.; Cappa O.; Zhernovkov V.; O’Callaghan J.; Moran B.; Culligan E.; Feris S.; Curry S.; Clark A.; Simpson D.; O’Brien C.
Article.Abstract: The molecular mechanisms that underlie the extracellular matrix (ECM) remodelling of the human lamina cribrosa (LC) in glaucoma remain obscure. This is the first study to characterise human glaucomatous LC cells using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq). Pathway enrichment analysis was performed using Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA), and transcription factor (TF) motif enrichment was evaluated using i-cisTarget. Validation was performed using quantitative PCR, Western blotting, immunohistochemistry, and immunofluorescence. LC cells were treated with ISRIB and 4-PBA. Pharmacologic treatment with ISRIB or 4-PBA reduced expression of stress-response and ECM genes, while ISRIB attenuated the increased cellular metabolic activity observed in glaucomatous LC cells. Article.Title: Effects of BL Exposure on Circadian Rhythms and Rhythm-Related Disorders
Article.Authors: Wang X.; Pei X.; Ge C.; Chen J.; Xu J.; Wu J.; Lu H.; Xu L.; Weng H.; Chen X.; Deng L.; Xu H.
Article.Abstract: Circadian rhythms represent a core physiological mechanism sustaining human physiological homeostasis and normal bodily function. Environmental light serves as a primary exogenous zeitgeber for circadian regulation. Among visible light spectral components, BL (BL) exerts a critical modulatory influence on the circadian system, with dual implications for physiological regulation and clinical intervention: excessive or inappropriately timed exposure may lead to circadian disruption, whereas appropriately timed BL interventions show potential to improve circadian alignment in selected populations. Accumulated evidence indicates that circadian disruption is associated with sleep disorders, mood disturbances, neurodegenerative disorders, as well as metabolic and immune dysfunction, and may have bidirectional relationships with disease progression. Nevertheless, most existing studies concentrate on circadian modulation by broad-spectrum light. Few efforts have synthesized the molecular mechanisms, potential disease-related pathways, and targeted intervention frameworks of BL-associated circadian disruption, and the translational potential of BL’s bidirectional effects remains under-summarized, forming a prominent research gap. To fill this gap, this narrative review centers on the “BL-circadian rhythm-disease” regulatory axis. It outlines biological pathways in which circadian disruption may be implicated in multiple neurodegenerative disorders, highlights the circadian-modulating properties of BL, describes evidence linking inappropriate BL exposure to circadian disruption and disease onset or progression, and compiles clinical findings on BL-based interventions and their potential benefits for circadian function and selected disease-related symptoms. However, much of the evidence derives from observational studies and animal experiments, and a causal pathway linking BL exposure to disease through circadian disruption has not been definitively established. This review discusses the potential adverse and beneficial effects of BL in circadian disruption-related pathologies, addresses current research limitations, and offers theoretical references and fresh insights for mechanistic investigations, clinical research, and translational development of BL-targeted interventions.

Article.Title: Prospective Proteomic Associations with Incident Type 2 Diabetes and Responses to Metabolic Stress in Women with and Without Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome
Article.Authors: Darwish R.; Sathyapalan T.; Dempsey L.; Abdalla M.; Butler A.; Atkin S.
Article.Abstract: Women with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) have heterogeneous metabolic risk. We investigated whether targeted circulating proteins were associated with incident type 2 diabetes (T2D) and whether the retained proteins responded to experimentally induced lipid stress. In Cohort 1, 231 women with (n = 135) or without (n = 96) PMOS had T2D outcome data, of whom 25 developed T2D during a median follow-up of 12.7 years (range 10.2–15.1); 221 women (20 incident cases) had complete covariate data for adjusted analyses. Of 44 available proteins, 27 were prespecified from prior literature; following Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment, eight biomarkers (Adiponectin (ADIPOQ), Endocan (ESM1), Mast/stem cell growth factor receptor-Kit (KIT), Chordin Like 1 (CHRDL1), Cell Adhesion Molecule L1 Like (CHL1), Cathepsin V (CTSV), L1 Cell Adhesion Molecule (L1CAM) and Delta Like Canonical Notch Ligand 4 (DLL4)) had a statistically significant association with T2D in univariate models. However, following adjustment for group, body mass index (BMI) and age, only ADIPOQ remained statistically significant. In Firth penalised logistic regression adjusted for PMOS status, age and BMI, each 1 SD higher ADIPOQ was associated with lower odds of incident T2D (OR 0.12; 95% CI 0.04–0.31); the association persisted when events were restricted to a common 10-year follow-up horizon, after adjustment for baseline fasting glucose, and after excluding women with baseline fasting glucose ≥ 7.0 mmol/L. Adding ADIPOQ to PMOS status, age and BMI increased the bootstrap optimism-corrected AUC from 0.74 to 0.87. In an independent experimental cohort (PMOS, n = 11; controls, n = 9, with SOMAscan data), ADIPOQ, neural cell adhesion molecule L1-like protein (CHL1), mast/stem cell growth factor receptor-Kit (KIT), chordin-like protein 1 (CHRDL1) and neural cell adhesion molecule L1 (L1CAM) were measured at 0, 180 and 300 min of 5 h saline and Intralipid infusions and analysed using linear mixed-effects models. Relative to saline, Intralipid lowered L1CAM, CHL1 and KIT at 180 min (differences in change from baseline −0.33, −0.30 and −0.25 log2 units; FDR-adjusted p ≤ 0.029), with no evidence that responses differed between women with PMOS and controls, and no lipid-specific change in ADIPOQ was detected; only the L1CAM response persisted after excluding turbid or haemolysed samples. Lower adiponectin was the only protein independently associated with incident T2D, whereas L1CAM, and less robustly CHL1 and KIT, responded to acute lipid exposure. The small number of events, differential outcome ascertainment between groups, absence of external validation and the exploratory experimental cohort preclude claims of clinical prediction. These findings support further evaluation of prognostic and stress-responsive protein phenotypes in larger, independently validated cohorts.

Article.Title: High Temperature Triggers Systemic Necrosis and Reveals PRSV as the Primary Cause of “‘Mazi’ Watermelon”
Article.Authors: Zang Y.; Liu L.; Dou P.; Liang Z.; Geng Y.; Shi J.; Hou B.; Kang B.
Article.Abstract: Huaping County, Lijiang City, Yunnan Province, is a key production area for early-season winter watermelons. In recent years, watermelon fruits in this region have exhibited abnormal symptoms, such as protrusions and necrotic lesions on the surface, which has significantly reduced their commercial value; such fruits are known locally as “’Mazi’ watermelon”. Field symptoms included leaf mosaic, necrosis, malformation, and stem cracking, as well as epidermal protrusions and clustered necrosis. To identify the causal agents, typical diseased samples were collected from Xinzhuang Village, Huaping County, in April 2026. Systematic pathogen identification was conducted using tissue isolation, plate coating, and small RNA-seq techniques to detect fungal, bacterial, and viral pathogens. No pathogenic fungi or bacteria were isolated; however, small RNA sequencing identified the presence of papaya ringspot virus (PRSV) and zucchini tigré mosaic virus (ZTMV) in diseased plants. RT-PCR further confirmed mixed infection of PRSV and ZTMV in one sample and PRSV alone in another. Artificial inoculation experiments demonstrated that both viruses could induce mosaic and malformation symptoms in watermelon leaves, but disease manifestation was temperature-dependent. PRSV caused systemic necrosis under high temperatures (>28 °C), while ZTMV triggered mild necrosis at low temperatures (<25 °C). In greenhouse trials (22~35 °C), PRSV-inoculated plants developed stem cracking, fruit protrusions, and necrotic lesions, matching field “Mazi watermelon” symptoms. In conclusion, PRSV has been identified as the primary pathogen responsible for the “Mazi watermelon” symptoms in Huaping, and high temperature is a critical environmental factor that triggers systemic necrosis and severe fruit symptoms.

Article.Title: Pregnancy as a Stress Test for β-Cell Autoimmunity: The Autoimmune Phenotype of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus
Article.Authors: Yanachkova V.; Shivarov V.; Kostadinov N.; Kirovakov Z.; Yordanov A.
Article.Abstract: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is increasingly recognized as a heterogeneous metabolic disorder comprising pathophysiological phenotypes that differ in their underlying mechanisms, clinical presentation and long-term outcomes. While pregnancy-induced insulin resistance remains the predominant pathogenic mechanism, a subset of women develops hyperglycemia largely because of reduced pancreatic β-cell reserve accompanied by islet autoimmunity. This autoimmune phenotype links gestational diabetes with autoimmune diabetes, but its boundaries and clinical significance remain incompletely defined. We aimed to review current knowledge of the autoimmune phenotype of GDM, with focus on immune pathophysiological mechanisms, biomarkers, clinical characteristics and implications for precision medicine, and to distinguish findings demonstrated directly in GDM from mechanisms extrapolated from type 1 diabetes (T1D). This narrative review was based on a structured PubMed/MEDLINE search from database inception through the end of October 2026, supplemented by targeted searches, manual screening of reference lists, and relevant clinical guidelines and consensus documents. Evidence obtained directly in women with GDM was considered alongside selected mechanistic literature from T1D and adult autoimmune diabetes. In some women with GDM, islet autoantibodies are associated with impaired β-cell function and an increased risk of autoimmune diabetes after delivery. The cellular mechanisms underlying these associations remain insufficiently studied in GDM. Pregnancy may act as a physiological metabolic stress test that exposes previously compensated β-cell dysfunction associated with islet autoimmunity, although its influence on the underlying autoimmune process remains uncertain. Islet autoantibodies are enriched among women with GDM, but their frequency varies widely between populations and assays and is lower after delivery than during pregnancy. The number and persistence of antibodies, particularly when combined with reduced endogenous insulin secretion, carry considerably more prognostic weight than a single positive result. Cellular immune mechanisms are well characterized in T1D but remain largely unvalidated in GDM. Recognition of the autoimmune phenotype extends the concept of GDM beyond a purely glucose-based classification. It is best viewed as a spectrum ranging from isolated seropositivity to pregnancy-unmasked autoimmune diabetes rather than as a uniform independent entity. A phenotype-oriented approach combining clinical features, autoantibody profiles and measures of β-cell function may facilitate earlier recognition of women at risk and more individualized follow-up, but universal autoantibody screening and antibody-specific treatment are not currently supported.

Article.Title: Single-Cell Transcriptomic Analysis of Rat Urethral Tissue Following Simulated Childbirth Injury and Microenergy Acoustic Pulse Therapy
Article.Authors: Lin G.; Zhao L.; Xing E.; Bai T.; Li H.; Tang Y.; Cao T.; Wang G.; Tang Y.; Lue T.
Article.Abstract: Microenergy acoustic pulse (MAP) therapy has been associated with functional and structural improvement after childbirth-related urethral injury, but its multicellular effects remain incompletely defined. We explored treatment- and injury-associated differences in the urethral microenvironment using single-cell RNA sequencing. Eight female Sprague–Dawley rats were assigned to sham, vaginal balloon dilation plus ovariectomy (VBDO), VBDO plus beta-aminopropionitrile (BAPN), or VBDO plus BAPN and MAP (MAP) groups, with one 24-week-old and one 48-week-old rat per group. Urethral tissues were analyzed for cell composition, differential gene expression, Gene Ontology enrichment, stem/progenitor features, senescence-associated secretory phenotype activity, and CellChat-inferred intercellular communication. A balanced single-cell dataset comprising 23,128 cells was used for downstream comparative analyses and resolved 19 annotated cell-type/state categories. Across the injury- and age-associated experimental conditions, epithelial, vascular, stromal, immune, and muscle compartments showed distinct transcriptional patterns, whereas MAP-treated samples showed a distinct cellular distribution; a separate histological cohort showed higher urethral muscle content. MAP-treated samples also showed differences in CellChat-inferred signaling activity in selected extracellular-matrix, adhesion, vascular, developmental, and neural/neuromuscular pathways, including fibronectin 1 (FN1), collagen (COLLAGEN), angiopoietin (ANGPT), vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), Wingless/Integrated (WNT), Notch (NOTCH), reelin (RELN), Slit guidance ligand (SLIT), neural cell adhesion molecule (NCAM), and neurexin (NRXN). Exploratory enrichment analysis identified treatment-associated differences in translation, oxidative metabolism, stress adaptation, synaptic-organization processes, progenitor-associated transcriptional states, and senescence-related programs. The treatment-split marker manifold approximation and projection (UMAPs) are descriptive and do not provide evidence of increased muscle-cell number; the reported difference in muscle-associated staining content derives from a separate animal-level histological analysis. Overall, the findings are descriptive and hypothesis-generating and require validation in independently replicated cohorts.

Article.Title: Gut Microbiota as a Potential Modulator of Response to Biologic and Small-Molecule Therapies in Inflammatory Bowel Disease
Article.Authors: Margul K.; Krawczyk A.
Article.Abstract: The therapeutic landscape of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) has expanded substantially with the development of biologic and small-molecule therapies. Nevertheless, many patients fail to respond to these treatments or experience a secondary loss of response. The mechanisms underlying treatment failure remain incompletely understood. Given the ability of gut microorganisms to modify therapeutic compounds, sustain pro-inflammatory immune activation, alter intestinal barrier function and produce bioactive metabolites, the gut microbiota may represent an important modulator of therapeutic response. To summarize current evidence on the role of the gut microbiota in response to biologic and small-molecule therapies in IBD, with particular emphasis on potential mechanisms of drug–microbiota interactions and their implications for treatment response and non-response. Accumulating evidence suggests that the gut microbiota may influence therapeutic efficacy through direct modification of drugs and indirect effects mediated by host immunity, intestinal barrier function and microbial metabolites. Microbial signatures associated with response to individual biologic therapies have been identified, although findings remain heterogeneous. Emerging evidence also indicates that non-bacterial components of the gut ecosystem may contribute to treatment response. The gut microbiota represents a biologically plausible modulator of therapeutic response in IBD. Integration of microbiome data with host genetic and immunological features may help identify biomarkers capable of predicting response to individual therapeutic agents.

Article.Title: Restoring Bioenergetics in the Traumatized Eye: The Emergence of Mitochondrial Implantation as a Treatment for Acute Ocular Injury
Article.Authors: Peveri E.; Beiner D.; Huang A.; Ma J.; Asthana A.; Atala A.; Orlando G.; Zhang Y.
Article.Abstract: Acute ocular injuries—such as chemical burns, ischemic insults, and mechanical trauma—frequently lead to irreversible vision loss by triggering rapid intracellular adenosine triphosphate (ATP) depletion, mitochondrial calcium overload, severe oxidative stress, and profound mitochondrial dysfunction. Current clinical management primarily focuses on suppressing inflammation and preventing secondary infection, but it fails to address the underlying bioenergetic collapse that drives cellular degeneration. While stem cell and extracellular vesicle therapies have been widely investigated, direct mitochondrial transplantation has recently emerged as a novel strategy for metabolic rescue. This review evaluates the therapeutic potential of exogenously administered mitochondria to mitigate mitochondrial dysfunction and acute trauma in the eye. Emerging preclinical studies demonstrate that transplanted mitochondria can be internalized by selected ocular cell types, conferring short-term cytoprotection, preserving retinal ganglion cell viability, and accelerating corneal epithelial repair. However, robust evidence regarding long-term mitochondrial integration, functional fusion, durable metabolic rescue, and clinical efficacy remains limited. Despite critical challenges in delivery, stability, and dosing, mitochondrial transplantation represents a promising frontier in regenerative ophthalmology that directly targets bioenergetic failure to preserve vision.

Article.Title: Molecular Modeling of Isoniazid Encapsulation by β-Cyclodextrin for Drug Delivery: Molecular Dynamics, Interaction Energies, and DFT Insights
Article.Authors: Rady A.; Sidhom P.; Khanam S.; Abd El-Rahman M.; Mohamed L.; Sayed S.; Shoeib T.; Ibrahim M.
Article.Abstract: β-cyclodextrin (β-CD) plays a crucial role in advanced drug delivery processes, with potential applications in drug protection and release modulation. Therefore, the encapsulation potential of β-CD towards isoniazid (ISO) was herein comprehensively examined by performing molecular dynamics (MD) simulation with density functional theory (DFT) calculations. From an energetic perspective, the encapsulation process within the ISO⋯β-CD complex was energetically preferable, as evidenced by the negative interaction energy (Eint) values of configurations A–E. Compared to the other configurations, configuration A exhibited the most favorable Eint, reaching −41.66 kcal/mol. From FMO and TDOS analyses, a reduction in energy gap values was observed following the encapsulation process, indicating a change in the electronic structure of the ISO⋯β-CD complex. The effect of water on the encapsulation process within the ISO⋯β-CD complex was investigated. Furthermore, the potential release of ISO from β-CD was qualitatively assessed using simplified recovery-time estimates. Moreover, ISO adsorption over the β-CD surface was examined using the same approaches as the encapsulation model; however, it was energetically less favorable, with Eint values reaching only −18.42 kcal/mol. Overall, the MD-enhanced DFT results underscored the potential of β-CD as a candidate platform for ISO drug encapsulation; however, experimental validation is required to establish loading efficiency, release behavior, bioavailability, and toxicity.

Article.Title: Modulatory Effects of the Er,Cr:YSGG—Diode Laser Combination Irradiation on Human Osteoblasts—Might Be Relevant for Periapical Bone Regeneration?
Article.Authors: Ripszky A.; Kably I.; Neculau C.; Voicu Balasea B.; Melis I.; Bancu S.; Cernega A.; Radulescu R.; Pituru S.
Article.Abstract: This in vitro study evaluated how Er,Cr:YSGG irradiation at three energy levels (1, 3, and 6 J/cm2), 810 nm diode irradiation, and their combinations can influence human osteoblast viability and osteogenic activity. Cell viability and membrane integrity were preserved across all protocols (MTT p = 0.325; LDH p = 0.057; both n.s.), and live-cell imaging showed osteoblast morphology and proliferation. Diode irradiation significantly increased ALP activity versus control (12.96 vs. 5.40 IU/L; p = 0.011), confirming a biostimulatory osteogenic effect, whereas Er,Cr:YSGG at 6 J/cm2 almost completely suppressed ALP activity (0.42 IU/L; p < 0.001 vs. diode). Both Er,Cr:YSGG 3 J + diode and 6 J + diode combinations significantly attenuated the diode-induced ALP increase and NO elevation in a dose-dependent manner. No protocol was cytotoxic. The 810 nm diode laser was the most osteogenically favorable condition, whereas higher-energy Er,Cr:YSGG irradiation suppressed ALP activity and, when combined with the diode, attenuated its osteogenic effect.

Article.Title: From Thermosensing to Reproduction: Plant Responses to Elevated Temperature
Article.Authors: He F.; Chen W.; Wu J.; Fang C.; Li S.; Wang L.
Article.Abstract: High temperatures threaten plant productivity and survival worldwide. Plants respond to warming across their life cycle, but the effects of elevated temperature depend on its intensity, duration, and rate of change, and the developmental and environmental context in which it is experienced. Here, we synthesize current knowledge of temperature sensing and developmental responses from seed germination through plant architectural acclimation, floral transition, and reproduction. We distinguish thermomorphogenesis under moderately elevated ambient temperatures from heat-stress responses that protect cellular and developmental integrity under more severe conditions, while emphasizing their mechanistic overlap. Across these stages, we highlight how temperature responses are shaped by organ identity, species, genotype, and photoperiod, and discuss the trade-offs that must be resolved to translate developmental plasticity into heat-resilient crop production.

Article.Title: New Advances and Current Trends in Bioavailability of Coffee and Coffee By-Product Constituents and Their Metabolites: A Review
Article.Authors: Nemzer B.; Al-Taher F.; Abshiru N.; de Mejia E.
Article.Abstract: Coffee is one of the most widely consumed beverages worldwide, yet understanding how its bioactive compounds are absorbed and exert health effects remains incomplete. The objective and scope of this review is to critically summarize current advances in coffee bioavailability research, identify major limitations, and highlight emerging research trends. Recent research has advanced in three core areas. First, genetic stratification has moved the field beyond one-size-fits-all approaches by genotyping for key polymorphisms to explain inter-individual variability. Second, advanced metabolomics, including targeted and untargeted LC-MS/MS and multi-omics integration, has provided comprehensive views of phenolic absorption and bioavailability. Third, rigorous intervention designs, including randomized crossover trials and large prospective cohorts with detailed exposure assessment, have improved causal inference. Despite these advances, major limitations persist. Many studies lack sufficient statistical power to detect gene-treatment interactions. The clinical relevance of discovered metabolites is often not established. Observational cohorts remain susceptible to residual confounding, and the field lacks a standardized food matrix for cross-study comparisons. Key strategies to improve the bioavailability of coffee and its by-products were proposed, including novel delivery systems for coffee phytochemicals, human clinical trials involving encapsulated coffee bioactive compounds, and exploring coffee by-products as novel bioactive sources.

Article.Title: ADAM-10 Is Involved in Osteoblast Mineralization and Rheumatoid Arthritis-Associated Bone Destruction
Article.Authors: Nakamura H.; Kojima H.; Maeda K.; Sakurai K.; Tanioka T.; Ishii S.; Wakabayashi K.; Hosonuma M.; Azetsu Y.; Iyoda M.; Takami M.; Isozaki T.
Article.Abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA), a chronic autoimmune condition, causes irreversible bone destruction. A disintegrin and metalloprotease 10 (ADAM-10) has been implicated in inflammatory processes in RA. We investigated the potential role of ADAM-10 in osteoblast mineralization and RA-associated bone destruction. Serum ADAM-10 levels in RA patients were measured by ELISA, and ADAM-10 expression in osteoblasts was assessed by Western blotting. Collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) mice were treated intraperitoneally with the ADAM-10 inhibitor GI254023X (100 mg/kg) for three weeks. Arthritis and bone destruction were evaluated by macroscopic, immunohistochemical, histological, and micro-CT analyses. The effects of ADAM-10 inhibition on primary osteoblast mineralization were also assessed by Alizarin Red S staining. Serum ADAM-10 levels in patients with RA tended to be higher at Stage III of the Steinbrocker classification. In CIA mice, ADAM-10 inhibition attenuated weight loss, paw swelling, and arthritis scores and suppressed bone destruction. ADAM-10 inhibition also significantly reduced Rankl expression in knee joints. Furthermore, the inhibition reversed the suppression of primary osteoblast mineralization induced by TNF-α. Pharmacological inhibition of ADAM-10 attenuated experimental arthritis and bone destruction and improved osteoblast mineralization, suggesting that ADAM-10 may contribute to inflammatory bone destruction in RA.

Article.Title: FOXM1 Targets TRIM59 to Activate Wnt/β-Catenin in Tumor Stemness and Hepatoblastoma Metastasis
Article.Authors: Yan H.; Liu W.; Jia W.; Huang J.; Xu W.; Fu Z.; Zheng B.; Yu H.; Chen X.; Gao Y.; Tian D.
Article.Abstract: Hepatoblastoma is the most common liver malignancy in children. Approximately 20% of patients present metastasis at diagnosis and have a dismal prognosis. However, the molecular mechanisms and targeted therapeutic strategies remain limited. Integrated analysis of GSE151347, GSE133039, GSE131329 and GSE75271 datasets, incorporating the mRNA expression-based stemness index, weighted gene co-expression network analysis, ChEA3 and TRRUST databases, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and differential expression analysis, identified forkhead box protein M1 (FOXM1) as a key transcription factor significantly correlated with metastatic hepatoblastoma and poor clinical outcomes. The CUT&Tag sequencing revealed that FOXM1 occupied the tripartite motif containing 59 (TRIM59) promoter, and dual-luciferase reporter assays confirmed that FOXM1 transcriptionally activated TRIM59. Furthermore, FOXM1 gain- and loss-of-function were accompanied by changes in axis inhibition protein 1 (AXIN1) protein levels, β-catenin levels, and β-catenin nuclear translocation, potentially contributing to the regulation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling. Finally, TRIM59 knockdown successfully rescued FOXM1-driven malignant phenotypes. This study identifies a novel FOXM1/TRIM59/Wnt signaling axis that drives hepatoblastoma metastasis, highlighting FOXM1 and TRIM59 as promising therapeutic targets for high-risk patients.

Article.Title: Genetic Associations with Type 2 Diabetes Differ According to Metabolic Contexts Defined by Insulin Resistance and Visceral Adiposity
Article.Authors: Shine B.; Hong K.; Choi J.; Kim B.; Kwon Y.; Jeong I.
Article.Abstract: Stratifying populations based on indicators of insulin resistance and visceral adiposity may help identify genetic associations with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) that vary across metabolic environments. This study aimed to investigate metabolic context-dependent genetic associations with T2DM using the metabolic score for insulin resistance (METS-IR) and visceral fat (METS-VF). A total of 70,583 and 70,513 participants were eligible for METS-IR and METS-VF stratification, respectively. After excluding participants with missing diabetes status, the final case–control samples comprised 40,970 and 40,944 participants, respectively. Genome-wide association studies of prevalent T2DM were conducted within metabolic tertiles, with additional evaluation of lead variants in the intermediate tertile (T2). Logistic regression under an additive genetic model was performed, followed by genotype × metabolic stratum interaction analyses and Cochran’s Q heterogeneity tests. Twelve notable loci were identified, showing both shared and varying association patterns across metabolic strata. CDKAL1 showed robust associations across metabolic strata, with progressively attenuated effect sizes from T1 to T3 and significant interaction results under both METS-VF and METS-IR stratifications. PAX4, CPEB3, and HHEX also demonstrated stronger associations in metabolically favorable groups, supported by nominally significant interaction and heterogeneity tests. CDKN2A/B showed associations across metabolic strata, with evidence of differences in genetic effects. KCNQ1 exhibited broadly consistent associations, although evidence of interaction varied by metabolic index. CNNM2, HNF1B, HNF4A, SLC30A8, and DNAJC5B–TRIM55 displayed subgroup-dependent patterns of statistical significance, which did not uniformly correspond to significant interaction effects. ALDH2 showed distinct association patterns across metabolic strata and between men and women. These findings suggest that genetic associations with T2DM may vary according to metabolic context, although subgroup-specific genome-wide significance does not necessarily establish differential genetic effects. Formal interaction and heterogeneity analyses provide additional evidence for metabolic effect modification at selected loci, suggesting that metabolic stratification may help characterize variation in genetic associations with T2DM in the Korean population.

Article.Abstract: For the first time, new natural chlorin derivatives containing tetrahydropyridine and thioimide exocycles have been synthesized. Article.Title: Dihydromyricetin Ameliorates Exercise-Induced Acute Hepatic Dysfunction and Inflammation in Association with the Restoration of the Th17/Treg Balance in Mice
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Yue J.; Zhang Q.; Yi L.
Article.Abstract: Exercise induces acute hepatic dysfunction and inflammation, a condition with currently limited treatment modalities. Dihydromyricetin (DHM) may protect the liver, but its role in exercise-related hepatic dysfunction and inflammation remains to be elucidated. In this work, we investigated whether DHM intervention is associated with the restoration of the T helper 17 (Th17)/regulatory T (Treg) balance in these exercise-induced hepatic disorders.Exhaustive treadmill running was performed on male C57BL/6 mice (8 weeks old, 20–22 g) to establish a mouse model of acute hepatic dysfunction and inflammation. Mice were then administered DHM (400 mg/kg/day by oral gavage for 6 consecutive days, concurrently with the exercise protocol), DHM + recombinant interleukin-17A (IL-17A) (rIL-17A; 100 ng/day, i.p., on Days 1–4 of the exercise protocol), or DHM + anti-CD25 monoclonal antibody (aCD25 mAb; 400 µg, i.p., on the second day of acclimatization and the third day of the exercise protocol). After acute exercise, livers were harvested for histopathological analysis, protein expression profiling, and immune cell population analysis. Acute exercise induced histological changes in the liver with infiltration of inflammatory cells, elevated serum aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT), and increased hepatic Th17 cells and the Th17/Treg ratio, without significantly altering Treg cells, compared with the non-exercise group. Administration of rIL-17A or aCD25 mAb blunted the protective effect of DHM. Our results suggest that DHM administration may serve as a potential protective strategy against exercise-induced transient hepatic dysfunction and inflammation, in association with the restoration of the Th17/Treg balance in mice.

Article.Title: Compartment-Specific Amino Acid Dysregulation in Depression: Integrating Non-Targeted Metabolomics with Brain Barrier Biology
Article.Authors: Perić I.; Stanisavljević Ilić A.; Đorđević N.; Todorović Vukotić N.
Article.Abstract: The introduction of metabolomics into depression research, together with advances in bioinformatics, has substantially expanded our understanding of molecular alterations associated with this disorder. However, the rapid growth of metabolomic studies, combined with variability in analytical workflows, biological matrices, and experimental models, presents major challenges for data interpretation and cross-study integration. In this article, we systematically summarized reported metabolite alterations in human and animal studies using a combined natural language processing (NLP)-based text-mining and vote-counting approach. To our knowledge, this is one of the first studies to apply NLP-based abstract mining to depression-related metabolomics literature across multiple biological compartments. Text-mining analysis of publications retrieved from PubMed and Scopus identified proteinogenic amino acids as the most consistently reported class of altered metabolites across peripheral and central matrices, followed by lipids and other metabolic categories. Vote-counting analysis of non-targeted metabolomics studies revealed relatively consistent decreases in circulating large neutral and branched-chain amino acids, with Leu, Met, Trp, Tyr, and Val representing the most consistently overlapping alterations across human and animal studies. Finally, these findings were discussed in the context of brain barrier transport systems, considering altered metabolite exchange across the blood–brain interfaces as one of several possible explanations for the compartment-specific amino acid alterations observed in depression.

Article.Title: Preclinical Study on Novel Treatment Regimen for Elderly Patients with Drug-Sensitive Pulmonary Tuberculosis
Article.Authors: Zhou J.; Wang B.; Zhang Y.; Wang J.; Sun W.; Liu X.; Ding X.; Fan L.
Article.Abstract: Treatment for elderly patients with pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) is challenging due to poor efficacy and tolerance. The aim of this study is to preliminarily screen candidate regimens for elderly patients with drug-sensitive PTB. Candidate regimens were initially screened using the artificial-intelligence-enabled phenotypic response surface (AI-PRS) platform and in vitro experiments. The hepatorenal cytotoxicity of drug combinations was assessed with HEK293T and THLE-2 cells. In the in vivo validation stage, aged mice with airway Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) infection received the novel regimens by oral gavage for 4 weeks, while isoniazid (H)/rifampicin (R)/ethambutol (E)/pyrazinamide (Z) served as the standard regimen control. Hepatorenal function was monitored during the treatment to assess drug safety, and pathological HE staining was also performed to evaluate liver and kidney damage. Bacterial loads in the lungs and spleens were evaluated using colony-forming unit (CFU) assays. After three rounds of AI-PRS analysis and MIC screening in vitro, three optimized treatment regimens were identified including delamanid (Dlm)/bedaquiline (Bdq)/pretomanid (Pa) combined with rifapentine (Rpt), pasiniazid (PAS-H) and levofloxacin (Lfx). After validation with an experiment on aged mice, the Bdq-containing regimen resulted in the mildest pulmonary inflammation and the lowest bacterial loads in lungs and spleens. The bacterial burden was similar between Bdq- and Dlm-containing regimens, which presented stronger bactericidal activity over the HREZ regimen. Regarding drug safety evaluation, the Bdq-containing regimen showed no marked hepatotoxicity and nephrotoxicity in our preclinical models, while other regimens showed variable abnormalities in serum biochemical indices. The Bdq/Lfx/PAS-H/Rpt regimen presented high efficacy and more favorable safety in aged mice compared with the standard regimen, considered as a promising preclinical candidate for elderly patients with drug-sensitive TB and deserving of further clinical trials for evaluation.

Article.Title: Restoration of the Inner Blood–Retinal Barrier in Diabetic Retinopathy Through Norrin-FZD4 Signaling
Article.Authors: González-González L.; Antonetti D.
Article.Abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a leading cause of irreversible vision loss in the working-age population and is characterized by the disruption of the blood–retinal barrier (BRB) integrity and increased vascular permeability. Elevated vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) contributes to BRB dysfunction in DR. Current therapies for DR, including anti-VEGF agents, have provided significant clinical benefits; however, not all patients respond optimally, highlighting the need for new therapeutic approaches. Norrin, an endogenous cytokine essential for blood–retinal barrier development and maintenance, has emerged as a potential therapeutic target for restoring barrier function in retinal vascular disease. In this review, we summarize the evidence supporting norrin signaling as a mechanism for restoring BRB properties following VEGF-induced barrier disruption and in DR, as well as its role in preserving visual function. We also discuss the development of engineered FZD4 agonists designed to mimic or enhance norrin signaling, providing a therapeutic strategy to activate this pathway independently of endogenous norrin. Article.Title: Genome-Wide Identification of Serine carboxypeptidase-like (SCPL) Genes in Rice and Their Expression in Response to Rhizoctonia solani
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Feng S.; Chen C.; Xue J.; Zhang S.; He T.; Guo G.; Zhou L.; Liu C.; Chen Z.

The segmentally duplicated gene pair OsSCPL4 was significantly upregulated in both genotypes, whereas OsSCPL25 was significantly upregulated in YSBR1 but did not reach significance in LE. This study provides an updated genomic framework for the SCPL gene family in rice and suggests potential roles for OsSCPL4 and OsSCPL25 in rice responses to R. solani, laying a foundation for further functional studies.

Article.Authors: Sample K.; Venkatappa M.; Koo Y.; Foulks Z.; Ng V.; Shaffer M.; Lietsch M.; Adamcakova-Dodd A.; Thorne P.; McCommis K.; Sannaningaiah D.; Robertson R.; Exil V.

VT exposure appeared to cause direct adverse health outcomes leading to increased expression of liver lipogenic genes, such as Scd1, Fasn, Srebp1c, and estrogen receptors. Maternal liver lipid equilibrium was disrupted upon VT exposure. Vaping either VT or MT significantly reduced mitochondrial oxidative function in the livers of pregnant mice but not in those of non-pregnant mice. Article.Title: Photoimmunotherapy Meets Systemic Immunotherapy: Molecular Mechanisms, Microenvironmental Remodeling, and Combinatorial Paradigms in Solid Tumors
Article.Authors: Russano F.; Callegarin F.; Brugnolo D.; Rastrelli M.; Caminiti R.; Sciacca G.; Scafuri D.; Mazza M.; Del Fiore P.; Dall’Olmo L.; Mocellin S.
Article.Abstract: Photodynamic therapy (PDT) remains constrained by physical barriers, including strict oxygen dependence, acute hypoxia exacerbation, and limited light penetration depth. While conventional photodynamic therapy (PDT) is strictly oxygen-dependent and limited by light scattering, Near-Infrared Photoimmunotherapy (NIR-PIT) overcomes microenvironmental hypoxia through targeted, oxygen-independent biophysical membrane rupture. However, tissue optical attenuation at 690 nm remains a fundamental physical boundary that necessitates interstitial fiber placement for deep lesions. Concurrently, recent advances in bioengineered nano-photoimmunotherapy (nano-PIT) and organelle-targeted photodynamic/photothermal platforms deliberately execute alternative inflammatory non-apoptotic pathways, such as pyroptosis, cuproptosis, and ferroptosis, and provoke cytosolic leakage of mitochondrial DNA that engages the cGAS-STING innate immune axis. Concurrently, NIR-PIT comprehensively remodels the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) by selectively depleting regulatory T cells (Tregs), myeloid-derived suppressor (MDSCs) cells, and cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), thereby deconstructing desmoplastic stroma, lowering interstitial fluid pressure (IFP), and driving the Super-Enhanced Permeability and Retention (SUPR) effect. Photically released mitochondrial DNA further engages the cytosolic cGAS-STING pathway, stimulating type I interferon signaling and dendritic cell cross-presentation. In selected preclinical models, this biophysical collapse promotes immunogenic cell death (ICD) and tumor microenvironment remodeling. When combined with systemic immunotherapies, NIR-PIT has demonstrated the potential to prime antitumor immunity and elicit abscopal responses in responsive syngeneic models; however, this immune conversion is not universal and is heavily constrained by tumor mutational burden, baseline antigen presentation fidelity, and diverse immunosuppressive networks. Translating these paradigms into clinical practice requires advancing 3D microphysiological models, implantable light technologies, and multi-component dosimetry frameworks.

Article.Authors: Dodina M.; Pavlova P.; Kuzkokova P.; Krasnyi A.; Shtil A.; Ivanov R.; Minskaia E.

A key driver of this resistance is transcriptional reprogramming, during which androgen receptor (AR) activity shifts from ligand-dependent signaling to reactivation via splice variants such as AR-V7 and eventually to AR-negative states. The oncogene c-MYC plays a pivotal role through context-dependent crosstalk with AR, suppressing canonical AR-dependent transcription while promoting its own oncogenic program. This reprogramming is sustained by dysregulation of RB1/E2F, NF-κB, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, WNT/β-catenin, and Hippo/YAP/TAZ pathways, alongside N-MYC and L-MYC activation, forming an interconnected network driving phenotypic plasticity. This review focuses on cyclin-dependent kinases 8 and 19 (CDK8/19), components of the Mediator complex kinase module, as potential regulators of epigenetic plasticity in PCa capable of modulating both AR-dependent and AR-independent transcription. Preclinical studies show that CDK8/19 inhibition suppresses castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) xenograft growth, restores ADT sensitivity, and additively enhances enzalutamide even in AR-V7-expressing resistant models, though the mechanisms of CDK8/19-mediated AR regulation remain largely undefined. We analyze the signaling pathways driving AR activity changes during PCa progression, evaluate potential mechanisms of CDK8/19-mediated AR regulation, and assess the therapeutic potential of CDK8/19 inhibitors with ADT.

Article.Title: Multidimensional Roles of Deubiquitinases in Tumor Glycolytic Reprogramming
Article.Authors: Zhao J.; Zhao Z.; Zang S.; Guo X.; Zhang J.; Yang J.; Mu X.; Li B.; Du J.; Xu G.; Qi L.; Zhang J.; Chen J.; Jin J.; Ye Z.
Article.Abstract: Tumor glycolytic reprogramming is an important metabolic hallmark of malignant tumors and plays a key role in sustaining tumor cell proliferation, adapting to microenvironmental changes, and promoting tumor progression. Studies have shown that DUBs can not only directly affect glycolysis by regulating the stability and functional status of key glycolytic enzymes, glucose transporters, and upstream transcriptional regulators, but also indirectly regulate glucose metabolism through signaling pathways such as AMPK, mTOR, HIF-1, and PI3K/AKT. In addition, DUBs can participate in the interplay between tumor metabolism and the immune microenvironment by affecting lactate production in tumor cells, metabolic adaptation of immune cells, and immune checkpoint signaling. Notably, glucose metabolism-related products and changes in metabolic status can also reciprocally regulate the expression and function of DUBs through mechanisms such as lactylation, O-GlcNAcylation, and phosphorylation, suggesting that bidirectional feedback regulation may exist between the two. Drugs targeting DUBs have shown potential to interfere with glycolysis and inhibit tumor progression in some preclinical tumor models; however, their clinical translation still faces challenges, including context-dependent mechanisms of action, inhibitor selectivity, and safety. This article systematically reviews the molecular mechanisms by which DUBs regulate tumor glycolytic reprogramming, with a focus on their roles in metabolic signal transduction, interactions with the tumor immune microenvironment, and metabolic feedback regulation, and summarizes the research progress and existing issues in related targeted intervention strategies, aiming to provide new insights for mechanistic studies of tumor metabolic reprogramming and precision therapy.

Article.Title: Electrochemical Performance of Citric Acid-Modified α-MnO2 Cathode for Aqueous Zinc-Ion Batteries
Article.Authors: Yu H.; Jia Y.; Liu M.; Li M.; Zhang X.; Han W.
Article.Abstract: Aqueous zinc-ion batteries (AZIBs) are considered promising for large-scale energy storage owing to their intrinsic safety, low cost, and environmental friendliness. α-MnO2, with its unique 2 × 2 tunnel structure, is regarded as one of the most promising cathode materials for zinc-ion batteries; however, its cycling stability is poor due to the disproportionation and dissolution of Mn3+ and structural collapse. Results show that the citric acid modification does not change the main crystal structure of α-MnO2, and SEM images reveal that both the pristine and modified samples present nanorod morphology. Electrochemical tests demonstrate that after 100 cycles at 0.5 A·g−1, the MnO2@CA electrode still retains a discharge-specific capacity of about 200 mAh·g−1 with a capacity retention of about 90%, while the pristine α-MnO2 electrode decays to about 75 mAh·g−1. At 0.1 and 0.2 A·g−1, MnO2@CA delivers higher specific capacities than pristine α-MnO2, and it also shows better capacity recovery after the current density returns to 0.1 A·g−1. At high rates, the rate performance is somewhat limited by solid-state diffusion/concentration polarization after low-rate activation, while the long-term cycling stability is significantly improved. Kinetics analysis indicates that the electrode process is dominated by diffusion control, while the capacitive contribution increases monotonically with scan rate (from about 7% to 19%) but remains minor compared with the diffusion contribution. Citric acid modification is proposed to stabilize Mn species through chelation, thereby suppressing Mn dissolution, and alleviating structural stress, thereby effectively enhancing the cycling stability and low-rate discharge capacity of the α-MnO2 cathode.

Article.Title: The Role of Fatty Acid-Binding Protein 4 in Pregnancy Complications and Fetal Health
Article.Authors: Mierzyński R.; Poniedziałek-Czajkowska E.; Świda K.; Mierzyńska K.
Article.Abstract: Fatty acid-binding protein 4 (FABP4) is an adipokine involved in regulating lipid metabolism, glucose homeostasis, and inflammatory processes. Altered circulating FABP4 concentrations have been associated with insulin resistance, adipose tissue dysfunction, and endothelial abnormalities. Growing evidence suggests that FABP4 dysregulation may contribute to impaired maternal metabolic and vascular adaptation during pregnancy, although the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. FABP4 has been implicated in the pathophysiology of several pregnancy-related conditions, including maternal obesity, gestational diabetes mellitus, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, preeclampsia, and recurrent pregnancy loss. Circulating FABP4 has also emerged as a potential biomarker for the early identification of women at increased risk of pregnancy-related metabolic and vascular complications, potentially improving risk assessment and providing earlier preventive or therapeutic interventions. This review summarizes current evidence on the role of FABP4 during pregnancy and its potential involvement in the pathophysiology of pregnancy-related complications, with particular emphasis on its biological functions, diagnostic and prognostic potential, and emerging therapeutic implications. Further mechanistic and prospective clinical studies are needed to determine whether FABP4 is a clinically useful biomarker and to clarify its potential as a therapeutic target in the management of pregnancy-related complications.

In a yeast two-hybrid analysis, we found that the N-terminal region of MSL1, primarily amino acids 66–85 and the coiled-coil domain, interacts with many DNA-binding transcription factors. The coiled-coil domain of Drosophila virilis MSL1 (vCC) retains the ability to interact with Drosophila melanogaster MSL2 but not with zinc finger proteins. Expression of a double mutant of MSL1 (MSL1Δ20vCC), in which amino acids 66–85 (Δ20) have been deleted and the coiled-coil domain has been replaced with the vCC domain, significantly reduced dosage compensation in males due to decreased binding of the MSL complex to the X chromosome. Substitution of MSL1 with MSL1vCC in females ectopically expressing MSL2 also significantly reduced recruitment of the MSL complex to the X chromosome. Altogether, these results indicate a key role of the N-terminal region of MSL1 not only in the assembly of the MSL complex but also in its recruitment to the X chromosome in males.

Article.Title: Effects of Flunarizine and Lutein on Atezolizumab-Associated Ovarian Alterations in Rats
Article.Authors: Esenkaya U.; Sezgin E.; Haciyeva S.; Suleyman B.; Ozkaraca M.; Gungor A.; Coban T.; Suleyman H.
Article.Abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), including atezolizumab, enhance antitumor immune responses by interfering with inhibitory immune checkpoint signaling. Atezolizumab targets programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1), thereby disrupting its interaction with programmed death-1 (PD-1). Although ICIs have improved cancer treatment outcomes, their potential associations with ovarian alterations remain insufficiently understood. This study aimed to compare ovarian biochemical, hormonal, histopathological, and immunofluorescence outcomes following the co-administration of flunarizine or lutein with atezolizumab in rats. Twenty-four female Wistar rats were randomly assigned to four groups (n = 6 per group): healthy control (HG), atezolizumab (ATZ), flunarizine plus atezolizumab (FUAZ), and lutein plus atezolizumab (LTAZ). Ovarian oxidative stress markers (MDA, tGSH, SOD, and CAT), inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α and IL-1β), serum anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) and prolactin levels, histopathological alterations, and immunofluorescence intensities of COX-1, COX-2, IL-1β, and IL-6 were evaluated. Compared with HG, the ATZ group exhibited increased MDA, TNF-α, and IL-1β levels and decreased tGSH, SOD, CAT, and serum AMH levels (p < 0.05). Histopathological examination revealed more pronounced follicular degeneration, parenchymal edema, and hyperemia in the ATZ group, whereas these alterations were milder in the FUAZ group and moderate in the LTAZ group. Immunofluorescence analysis demonstrated reduced COX-1 and increased COX-2, IL-1β, and IL-6 intensities in the ATZ group compared with HG. Both co-administration groups showed higher COX-1 and lower COX-2, IL-1β, and IL-6 intensities than the ATZ group. Several biochemical, histopathological, and immunofluorescence outcomes in the FUAZ group were closer to HG values than those in the LTAZ group. Serum prolactin levels differed significantly only between the ATZ and FUAZ groups in pairwise comparisons. Atezolizumab administration was associated with ovarian oxidative, inflammatory, and histopathological alterations. Co-administration of flunarizine or lutein was associated with differences in several evaluated parameters, with more favorable findings observed in the FUAZ group at the selected doses. However, the absence of appropriate antibody controls and adjunct-only groups limits causal attribution and precludes conclusions regarding independent protective efficacy.

Article.Title: Integrating QTL Mapping and Candidate-Region Association to Investigate Kernel Size and Weight in Sweet Corn
Article.Authors: Ma C.; Song J.; Qu J.; Zheng H.; Li T.; Li S.; Yu D.; Gu W.; Wang H.; Li K.; Zhao Y.; Zhao Z.; Vicente F.; Xie Y.; Guan Y.
Article.Abstract: Sweet corn is widely cultivated for fresh consumption and processing, and kernel size and weight are important yield-related traits. However, the genetic architecture of these traits in sweet corn remains poorly understood. In this study, the SHL01 × SHL03 recombinant inbred line (RIL) population was used to investigate the genetic basis of kernel size and weight-related traits using a high-density SNP-based genetic map. Quantitative trait loci (QTL) mapping was conducted in two environments and using the best linear unbiased estimates (BLUEs), followed by candidate-region association analysis to identify candidate genes. A total of 11 unique QTLs were identified from 12 detection records across the two environments and the BLUE dataset. Among them, seven unique QTLs, corresponding to eight detection records, were located on chromosome 7. Several QTLs were located near previously reported loci for kernel-related traits, suggesting a partially shared genetic basis between sweet corn and field corn. Candidate-region association analysis further characterized the major QTL regions and highlighted five potential candidate genes. Among them, Zm00001d020325 (HAK23), encoding a putative potassium transporter, was supported by functional annotation and available expression information, but its haplotypes were not significantly associated with HKW. In contrast, haplotypes defined by variants in neighboring Zm00001d020323 differed in HKW, with the GG haplotype showing the highest mean value. Because these analyses were conducted in overlapping populations, the haplotype results are exploratory. Together, these findings characterize genomic regions associated with mature-kernel traits in sweet corn and identify candidates for further validation.

Article.Title: Large-Scale Prospective Virtual Screening Using a Co-Folding-Rescoring Workflow for NPM1-TYK2 Inhibitor Discovery
Article.Authors: Tian W.; Zhang X.; Zhang O.; Hu R.; Ye Y.; Chen S.; Zheng J.; Zhang H.; Chai X.; Qu W.; Wang H.; Li D.; Kang Y.; Hou T.; Pan P.
Article.Abstract: Conventional large-scale structure-based virtual screening typically relies on fixed-receptor docking, in which ligand poses are sampled against a predefined receptor conformation. Protein-ligand co-folding models can instead generate candidate complex conformations by jointly modeling ligand placement and local receptor-ligand structural adaptation. Although recent benchmark studies have demonstrated the promise of AlphaFold3-like approaches for retrospective virtual screening, their practical application to target-specific, large-scale prospective screening with experimental validation remains limited. Here, we developed and prospectively applied a co-folding-rescoring workflow for NPM1-TYK2 inhibitor discovery. Using an in-house set of 4608 compounds experimentally annotated in Ba/F3-NPM1-TYK2 cells, we evaluated 13 pipelines combining AlphaFold 3, Protenix, Glide, or AutoDock Vina pose generation with scoring functions or confidence metrics. AlphaFold 3 followed by AutoDock Vina rescoring achieved the numerically highest BEDROC value, closely comparable to Protenix + Vina, and was selected for screening a commercial library of more than 300,000 compounds. AF3-generated complex conformations were subsequently rescored with Vina and prioritized by physicochemical assessment, clustering, and binding-mode inspection. Of 30 compounds tested experimentally, FV13 was identified as a cell-active primary hit, with a TYK2 kinase IC50 of 21.70 μM and a Ba/F3-NPM1-TYK2 cellular IC50 of 17.07 μM. Subsequent analog exploration yielded TX14, exhibiting an approximately 9.4-fold improvement in biochemical TYK2 inhibitory potency (IC50 = 2.31 μM). Additional selectivity profiling and Western blot analyses further characterized these compounds and indicated attenuation of downstream STAT5 phosphorylation at higher concentrations. Together, these findings demonstrate the feasibility of integrating co-folding, empirical rescoring, and target-specific experimental data for large-scale prospective hit discovery.

Article.Title: Quercetin Suppresses LCN2 and Restores Autophagy via the MAPK/ERK–mTOR Pathway in Bovine Endometrial Epithelial Cells and Attenuates Fibrotic Remodeling in LPS-Induced Mouse Endometritis
Article.Authors: Zhao L.; Chen X.; Zhou Y.; Tuniyazi M.; Shang Q.; Gao J.; Zhang M.; Duan H.; Wang X.; Xiao L.
Article.Abstract: Bovine endometritis frequently progresses to endometrial fibrosis, a leading cause of implantation failure and infertility in dairy cows, yet the upstream events that disrupt endometrial autophagy during uterine inflammation remain poorly defined, and the anti-fibrotic target of quercetin (Que) in the bovine endometrium is unknown. We therefore combined data-independent acquisition (DIA) proteomics of healthy and fibrotic bovine endometria (n = 4 per group) with network pharmacology, molecular docking and a cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA), gain- and loss-of-function studies in TGF-β1-stimulated primary bovine endometrial epithelial cells (BEECs), and a 48 h LPS-induced mouse endometritis model in female C57BL/6 mice. LCN2 was markedly upregulated in fibrotic endometria and was prioritized among five candidate targets; docking predicted binding within the LCN2 pocket, and CETSA showed increased thermal stability of LCN2, consistent with target engagement. In BEECs, LCN2 overexpression activated MAPK/ERK–mTOR signaling, suppressed autophagic flux and promoted epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), whereas LCN2 silencing reversed these phenotypes. Quercetin dose-dependently reduced LCN2 abundance and MAPK/ERK–mTOR phosphorylation, restored autophagic flux and reversed TGF-β1-induced EMT, and ERK inhibition abolished the LCN2-driven phenotype. In LPS-challenged mice, oral quercetin lowered uterine LCN2, recovered autophagy markers and reduced collagen deposition and endometrial damage. These preclinical findings associate LCN2 with impaired endometrial autophagy and EMT and suggest that quercetin may attenuate this cascade; binding affinity, LCN2 dependency and efficacy in cattle were not established and require validation in larger cohorts, purified-protein binding assays and chronic bovine models.

Article.Abstract: Autoimmune diseases (AIDs), a group of diseases induced by dysfunction of the immune system, are currently prompting the search for novel intervention strategies. Article.Title: Position and Strand Identity of G-Quadruplex Motifs Are Associated with Distinct Functional Signatures in Plants
Article.Authors: Kaluzhny D.; Krupskaya D.; Moskalenko O.; Pushkova E.; Melnikova N.; Dmitriev A.
Article.Abstract: Putative G-quadruplex (G4) sequences have been linked to transcriptional regulation in individual plant species, but a systematic, comparative view across the plant kingdom has been lacking. In this study, we analyzed putative G4-forming sequences (PQS) near transcription start sites (TSSs) in 70 plant species spanning over 1.2 billion years of evolutionary divergence, from algae to angiosperms. Using the G4Hunter algorithm, putative G4 motifs were mapped and scored separately on the coding and template DNA strands. This strand-resolved analysis identified four position/strand categories, among which template-strand motifs downstream of the TSS were the most abundant and resistant to an increase in the G4Hunter threshold. The majority of PQS-positive genes (62.4%) carry a motif in only one category, although combinatorial patterns involving two or more categories also occur. Gene Ontology enrichment analysis of Arabidopsis thaliana homologs tested in each species revealed two main recurrent patterns of modest effect size: downstream template-strand motifs were associated with chloroplast and mRNA-binding terms, and upstream template-strand motifs were associated with transcription factor activity and regulation of transcription, whereas downstream coding-strand motifs showed a weaker signal. At the level of individual genes, position-specific G4s recurred among homologs more often than expected at random, mostly downstream, where this may partly reflect the conservation of the coding sequence. These associations, based on computational prediction, provide a starting point for prioritizing candidate G4 elements for experimental validation of their role in transcriptional control in plants.

Article.Title: TGF-β1 Inhibition, Cytokine Modulation, and Clinical Response to Seleno-L-Methionine Plus Axitinib and Pembrolizumab in Treatment-Naïve Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma
Article.Authors: Kroll M.; Zakharia Y.; Maciel Barbosa F.; Fiorin de Vasconcellos V.; Rieth J.; Milhem M.; Capella M.; Rustum Y.
Article.Abstract: Metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) remains largely incurable, and the efficacy of pembrolizumab plus axitinib may be limited by hypoxia-associated signaling, immunosuppressive cytokines, and metabolic reprogramming involving the TGF-β1/HIF axis. Seleno-L-methionine (SLM) is a pharmacologic inhibitor of this axis and its downstream effectors, including PD-L1 and VEGF. In a phase I/II pilot study (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05363631), patients with newly diagnosed metastatic ccRCC received SLM twice daily for 14 days, then once daily with standard-dose axitinib; pembrolizumab was added on day 15. Twelve patients were treated and evaluable for safety (six at 5000 µg, six at 6000 µg SLM); ten were evaluable for response. The objective response rate was 70% (complete response 40%, partial response 30%). Of the four patients with CR, two had favorable and two had intermediate International Metastatic Renal Cell Carcinoma Database Consortium disease. Grade 3 hypertension was documented in 58.3%, about twice the pivotal-trial rate, without treatment discontinuations or new toxicities. SLM increased plasma selenium and produced time-dependent inhibition of TGF-β1 and modulation of immune-related cytokines (CXCL13, IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-6, IL-8). In this pilot study, SLM combined with axitinib and pembrolizumab showed time-dependent TGF-β1 inhibition, cytokine modulation, and encouraging antitumor activity without treatment-limiting toxicity, supporting further investigation of SLM for targeting the TGF-β1/HIF-driven immunosuppressive microenvironment in ccRCC.

Article.Title: The Emerging Role of CYP17A1 in Diabetes and Related Metabolic Disorders
Article.Authors: Alhalwachi Z.; Zainalabedin M.; Alhayki D.; Alsultan A.; Abdullahi S.; Alnahwi K.; Butler A.; Hasan A.
Article.Abstract: CYP17A1 (cytochrome P450 17A1) is a key steroidogenic enzyme that catalyzes 17α-hydroxylase and 17,20-lyase reactions, controlling glucocorticoid and androgen production. Emerging evidence suggests that CYP17A1 is not only essential for adrenal and gonadal steroidogenesis, but could also contribute to obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and hypertension. Genetic studies have associated CYP17A1 variants with fasting glucose, type 2 diabetes risk, arterial stiffness, and metabolic syndrome traits. In mouse models, obesity induces hepatic CYP17A1 expression and 17-hydroxyprogesterone overproduction, which activates glucocorticoid receptor signaling, promotes hepatic gluconeogenesis, and exacerbates insulin resistance and hyperglycemia. CYP17A1 has also been linked to adipose tissue dysfunction, altered steroid signaling, and redistribution of fat from visceral to subcutaneous depots. This review summarizes CYP17A1 structure, regulation, protein interaction networks, and its roles in insulin resistance, adipose tissue biology, steroid excess, and vascular complications. It also discusses CYP17A1 genetic variation and the therapeutic potential and limitations of CYP17A1 inhibition and glucocorticoid receptor modulation in diabetes and related metabolic disorders.

Article.Title: Circulating microRNAs Associated with Insulin Resistance in South Asian and European Adults with Type 2 Diabetes (T2D): A Systematic Review and Mapping of Ethnic Patterns
Article.Authors: Kimber T.; Hunter D.; Akam E.; Singh M.; Singh P.; Mastana S.
Article.Abstract: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is a global crisis affecting 589 million adults, with South Asian populations particularly vulnerable, developing T2D earlier and at lower BMIs than Europeans. Insulin resistance, measured by HOMA-IR, is central to T2D pathogenesis. Circulating microRNAs are stable biomarkers implicated in insulin signalling, but no systematic review has compared their associations with insulin resistance across South Asians and Europeans. To identify microRNAs associated with HOMA-IR in adults with T2D and explore whether association patterns differ between South Asians and Europeans. A PRISMA-compliant systematic review searched six databases (PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, bioRxiv, medRxiv). Eligible studies reported statistical associations between circulating serum/plasma microRNA and HOMA-IR in adults with T2D. Bias risks were assessed using an adapted domain-based tool. A qualitative synthesis was conducted because of the differences in methodology. The review was registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF). A total of 14 studies were included (9 European, 5 South Asian), reporting 29 associations across 21 microRNA species, with 12 reaching statistical significance (p < 0.05). The strongest finding was that miR-122 positively associated with log HOMA-IR in a large European prospective cohort. Co-directional associations for miR192 and miR-194 suggested a hepatic microRNA cluster in Europeans. The miR-29 family and miR-192 emerged as cross-ethnic signals. Associations reported in South Asian populations included miR-128 and miR-374a-5p. Circulating microRNAs showed consistent positive associations with HOMA-IR, supporting biomarker potential. Cross-ethnic comparison was not possible within the included studies, revealing a gap in the literature rather than true ethnic differences. Multi-ethnic, methodologically standardised studies are needed, prioritising miR-122, miR-192, the miR-29 family, miR-128, and miR-374a-5p.

Article.Title: Phenotypic Diversity and Genome-Wide Association Analysis of Decaploid Camellia hainanica Germplasm from Hainan Island
Article.Authors: Chen T.; Yu J.; Chen J.; Lin S.; Tana W.; Ling P.
Article.Abstract: Camellia hainanica is an endemic woody oil species from Hainan Island, but the phenotypic and genomic bases of its agronomic and ornamental variation remain poorly understood. Genome-wide association analysis identified 9 significant SNPs (−log10(P) > 8.63) associated with petal number, flower diameter, locule number, and flower density (3, 1, 3, and 2 SNPs, respectively), including a flower-diameter signal on GWHERBT00000039 and signals on GWHERBT00000008 and GWHERBT00000036. These results integrate phenotypic and genomic evidence for C. hainanica and provide germplasm resources and preliminary candidate regions for further validation and ornamental improvement alongside fruit-trait evaluation.

Article.Title: Maternal Angiogenic Profiles in Preeclampsia-Associated Versus Isolated Fetal Growth Restriction or Small-for-Gestational-Age Pregnancies: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Article.Authors: Kim M.; Lee E.; Lee H.; Choi A.
Article.Abstract: Maternal angiogenic imbalance is a hallmark of preeclampsia (PE), but whether it differs between PE-associated and isolated fetal growth restriction (FGR)/small-for-gestational-age (SGA) pregnancies is unclear, particularly before clinical recognition. Analyses were stratified by sampling context and pooled as Hedges’ g using random-effects models. Twenty-three studies (630 PE-associated, 1476 isolated FGR/SGA pregnancies) were included. The sFlt-1 difference was larger after clinical recognition in the test for subgroup differences (p = 0.002) but not in meta-regression (p = 0.064), and this between-context contrast is therefore reported as exploratory; the PlGF difference was similar in both contexts. These group-level differences do not establish individual-level prediction, discrimination or threshold performance. PE-associated and isolated FGR/SGA should therefore be distinguished in biomarker research, and angiogenic thresholds derived in suspected PE require validation before application to normotensive FGR/SGA.

Article.Title: TSPO and LRBA Expression Is Associated with Acute Renal Allograft Rejection: An Integrative Transcriptomic Analysis
Article.Authors: Yi S.; Zhu Q.; Chen S.
Article.Abstract: Acute renal transplant rejection causes allograft injury and affects long-term graft survival. Mitophagy helps maintain mitochondrial homeostasis and regulate immune function, but its relationship with acute rejection remains unclear. An exploratory TSPO/LRBA two-gene model showed modest discrimination between rejection and non-rejection samples. Higher model scores were associated with poorer graft survival. An exploratory analysis of the model was then performed in peripheral blood. Functional and single-cell analyses linked these genes to monocyte/macrophage populations, antigen presentation, T-cell signaling, and inflammatory pathways. Virtual knockout analysis predicted changes in antigen presentation, phagocytosis, and allograft rejection pathways. Quantitative PCR confirmed increased TSPO and decreased LRBA expression in mouse renal allografts with acute rejection. Together, these findings identify TSPO and LRBA as new candidate mitophagy-associated biomarkers linked to monocytes/macrophages and support further investigation of their associations with acute renal transplant rejection.

Article.Title: Congenital Pain-Insensitivity Syndromes in Perioperative Anesthesia and Analgesic Target Identification
Article.Authors: Mckenzie A.; Raman D.; Shukla N.; Bittar T.; Fransis N.; Dombrower R.; Theeraphapphong N.; Mckenzie S.; Hoang Y.; Abd-Elsayed A.
Article.Abstract: Congenital insensitivity to pain (CIP) comprises rare genetic disorders characterized by the absence of perception of noxious stimuli from birth. Despite their shared clinical phenotype, CIP syndromes arise from distinct molecular defects that differentially affect nociceptor development, ion channel function, and autonomic regulation. Pathogenic variants in genes, including NTRK1, SCN9A, and PRDM12, define key mechanisms of human nociception. NTRK1-associated CIP with anhidrosis results from disrupted nerve growth factor signaling, leading to loss of small-diameter sensory fibers, impaired thermoregulation, and autonomic instability. SCN9A- and PRDM12-associated forms affect sodium channel function or nociceptor development; autonomic involvement is generally less prominent but requires assessment in each patient. This narrative review synthesizes the genetic and neurodevelopmental basis of CIP syndromes and examines their implications for perioperative management and the development of analgesics. By correlating genotype-specific mechanisms with clinical phenotypes, CIP syndromes help to identify key components of nociceptive pathways. These rare disorders highlight molecular targets for precision analgesia and demonstrate how genetic characterization may guide perioperative risk assessment and the development of targeted pain therapies.

Article.Title: Drug Design Studio (DDS) 4.0: A Nano-Pharmaceutical Platform for Modelling of Drug–Drug Complexation and Drug–Nanocarrier Encapsulation and Interactions
Article.Authors: Soliman M.
Article.Abstract: Once a candidate molecule has been designed, its therapeutic value in practice is often decided not by its intrinsic potency but by whether it can be formulated—dissolved, stabilised and delivered. Modern pharmaceutics addresses this with nanoscale carriers (cyclodextrins, dendrimers, polymeric nanoparticles, micelles, liposomes and carbon nanomaterials, etc.) and with carrier-free solid-form engineering such as pharmaceutical cocrystals. Predicting, before the bench, whether a given drug will associate with a chosen carrier, in what geometry, and through which specific interactions is therefore of central practical importance, yet it remains fragmented, and expertise-intensive: the researcher must generate three-dimensional conformers, place the guest into a host cavity or onto its surface, minimise the assembly with a molecular-mechanics force field that correctly retains inter-molecular terms, and most importantly analyse the different interaction forces and estimate the binding affinities and solvent effects—each step in a different tool and none accessible to a typical formulation scientist. Here, we present the Nano Bio-Pharmaceutical Modelling module of Drug Design Studio (DDS), an integrated platform that models both drug–nanocarrier and carrier-free drug–drug complexes in one interface. From a SMILES string and a built-in carrier library, DDS generates conformers, runs a deterministic, geometry-aware global search (regime-adaptive random-restart and basin-hopping Monte-Carlo-minimization), and reports an interaction energy decomposed into van der Waals, electrostatic and non-polar terms under a gas-phase or implicit-water model, with hydrogen-bond, hydrophobic and π-stacking profiles, 2D/3D interaction maps, and selectable stoichiometry and thoroughness tiers. We validate the module at two levels over twenty-nine complexes spanning four association regimes. First, mode reproduction: this recovers the experimentally established association geometry across all four regimes—cyclodextrin inclusion, dendrimer-surface complexation, carbon-nanomaterial adsorption and carrier-free drug–drug cocrystals. Second, quantitative agreement: across twelve α-, β- and γ-cyclodextrin inclusion complexes, the predicted implicit-water interaction energy correlates with the experimental binding free energy at Pearson r = 0.85 (p < 0.001; Spearman ρ = 0.73), rising from r = 0.73 in the gas phase—evidence that the implicit-solvent treatment captures the dominant energetic determinants of aqueous binding and tracks the experimental thermodynamic trend (a correlation and correct ranking). The Nano module shares one application and compute engine with the docking, covalent/non-covalent virtual-screening, network-pharmacology and QSAR modules of earlier DDS releases. DDS is publicly and freely accessible software for academic use.

Article.Title: Molecular Science of Eicosapentaenoic Acid (EPA) Omega-3 Fatty Acid Using Nannochloropsis oceanica as a Model Organism
Article.Authors: Stephens E.; Thomas-Hall S.; Galea V.; Heimann K.
Article.Abstract: The EPA-rich marine microalga Nannochloropsis oceanica provides insight into EPA biosynthesis via the characterized Δ6-desaturase pathway, positioning this microalga for both experimental research and sustainable production solutions for non-fish oil-derived EPA oils. This review constructs a comprehensive molecular-to-clinical framework demonstrating how the chemical structure of eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) determines its biological activities, i.e., the specific positioning of the Δ17 double bond governs competitive enzymatic metabolism with arachidonic acid (ARA), yielding attenuated 3-series and 5-series eicosanoids while uniquely enabling E-series resolvin biosynthesis. Metabolic pathway modulation (AMPK, NF-κB, and SREBP-1c) translate biochemical events into transcriptional reprogramming. Sustained alterations in gene expression, membrane composition, and inflammatory mediator profiles manifest as clinical benefits across cardiovascular disease, metabolic disorders, inflammatory conditions, and psychiatric illnesses. The pleiotropic nature of EPA effectssimultaneously anti-inflammatory, TAG-lowering, anti-arrhythmic, insulin-sensitizing, and pro-resolving — arises not from independent mechanisms but from coordinated, multi-level integration. The ARA:EPA ratio emerges as the unifying quantitative biomarker, integrating dietary intake, competitive membrane incorporation, eicosanoid biosynthetic balance, and tissue-level inflammatory tone into a single metric predictive of disease risk and therapeutic response. Lowering this ratio through EPA supplementation represents a systems-level intervention: simultaneously reducing pro-inflammatory mediator production, enhancing resolution capacity, improving metabolic flexibility, and stabilizing cellular energetics.
