Article.Title: Extracellular Vesicle-Mediated Angiogenesis in Peripheral Artery Disease: Context-Dependent Effects in Ischemic Limbs and Atherosclerotic Plaques
Article.Authors: Tamaru Y.; Yoshioka Y.; Kikuchi S.; Ochiya T.
Article.Abstract: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) is most commonly caused by atherosclerotic arterial stenosis or occlusion, which reduces downstream tissue perfusion and causes tissue ischemia. In response to ischemia, reparative angiogenesis is activated and may support tissue perfusion recovery and skeletal muscle protection. In contrast, neovascularization within atherosclerotic plaques may promote intraplaque hemorrhage and plaque destabilization. Thus, angiogenesis has dual roles in PAD-related ischemia and atherosclerotic plaques. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are membrane-bound particles that carry various cargo, including proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, and metabolites. Through the transfer of bioactive cargo and surface-mediated signaling, EVs can modify recipient-cell functions and thereby influence angiogenic signaling. Investigation of EV-mediated communication may therefore help elucidate the mechanisms underlying angiogenic regulation in vascular disease. In addition, disease-promoting EVs may be therapeutically targeted, whereas engineered EVs may be developed as therapeutic agents or delivery platforms. Recent studies have shown that EVs regulate angiogenic responses in preclinical murine hindlimb ischemia models. However, these effects in ischemic limbs and the potential involvement of EVs in atherosclerotic plaque neovascularization have rarely been reviewed in an integrated manner. This narrative review discusses these contrasting angiogenic processes from a context-dependent perspective. Understanding this context dependency may help develop EV-based strategies that promote functional vascular repair in ischemic tissues while suppressing or normalizing pathological neovascularization in atherosclerotic plaques.

Article.Authors: Iguasnia Portilla D.; Castillo Castillo I.; Franco Figueroa V.; Fernández Cabrera H.; Romero Chala S.; Sobieschi I.; Cordero H.; Fernández Pereira L.

Circulating B cells were preserved before thymectomy and throughout 16 years of subsequent follow-up, with maintained class-switched memory B cells despite persistent antibody deficiency. T-cell differentiation abnormalities were present despite preserved absolute counts. Although preserved B cells do not exclude Good syndrome under existing definitions, the present observation should be considered hypothesis-generating and supports further studies evaluating potential biological heterogeneity among patients diagnosed with Good syndrome. This case highlights the need for consensus diagnostic criteria that consider the temporal relationship between both conditions, B-cell numbers, and the accompanying immune abnormalities, rather than relying on the coexistence of thymoma and hypogammaglobulinemia alone.

Article.Title: Molecular and Translational Anti-Inflammatory Strategies After Abdominal and Liver Surgery: From Immunonutrition to Cell-Based Therapies
Article.Authors: Pietrzyk B.; Pierzchała W.; Mikolajczyk J.; Lis P.; Heliasz A.; Kaczmarczyk B.
Article.Abstract: Postoperative inflammation influences recovery after abdominal and liver surgery. This narrative review critically synthesizes clinical and translational evidence on inflammation-modulating strategies using a structured search of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library for publications from 2015 to 2025. Case reports, pediatric studies, and publications lacking clinical or translational relevance were excluded. Immunonutrition and early enteral nutrition are the most established approaches, with benefits for postoperative recovery and infectious complications. Perioperative corticosteroids in liver resection and short-course antibiotics following adequate source control offer procedure- and indication-specific benefits. Emerging interventions, including microbiota modulation, N-acetylcysteine, activation of nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2/heme oxygenase-1 signaling, and cell-based therapies, show biological promise but lack sufficient high-quality clinical evidence for routine implementation. Established strategies should be integrated into Enhanced Recovery After Surgery pathways according to patient risk and surgical context. Personalized management requires prospective validation of emerging therapies and candidate biomarkers, including interleukin-6, C-reactive protein, and heme oxygenase-1, with standardized assays and sampling schedules.

Article.Title: Mitochondrial ROS and Mitophagy in Intervertebral Disc Degeneration: Mechanistic Interplay and Links to Regulated Cell Death
Article.Authors: Wang L.; Cao K.; Cheng H.; Fang Z.
Article.Abstract: Intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD) develops through interacting mechanical, matrix, nutritional, inflammatory and age-related processes. Mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) and mitophagy participate in some of these contexts, but current evidence does not place mitophagy failure at the start of every degenerative trajectory. Most mechanistic studies have been performed in nucleus pulposus (NP) cells. In these models, mechanical overload, inflammatory mediators and oxidant stress can depolarize mitochondria, disturb fission–fusion balance and increase mtROS. Mitophagy can limit injury when damaged cargo is selected and delivered through a competent lysosomal pathway; accumulation of pathway markers during blocked flux, or mitochondrial clearance that is not matched by renewal, need not be protective. The most extensive mechanistic literature concerns apoptosis and senescence. Evidence linking mitochondrial quality control to pyroptosis and ferroptosis is growing but remains model-dependent, whereas direct evidence for necroptosis is comparatively sparse. We use a capacity-matching framework to organize these findings around damage burden, cargo selection, lysosomal completion and mitochondrial renewal within the regional metabolic constraints of the disc. This is an interpretive framework rather than a newly identified pathway. Its purpose is to define testable conditions under which mitophagy is likely to be protective, insufficient or maladaptive, while preserving the distinction between NP-derived evidence and the more limited evidence from annulus fibrosus and cartilage endplate cells.

Article.Authors: Truffin D.; Marchand F.; Chatelais M.

Spectral Nile Red analysis further revealed distinct patterns of neutral-lipid- and phospholipid-associated fluorescence, indicating oxysterol-specific remodeling of intracellular lipid compartments. In contrast, oxLDL was the strongest inducer of neutral lipid accumulation and classical foam-cell formation in macrophages. Although 27HC increased intracellular 7KC levels, it induced comparatively limited effects on viability, oxidative stress, and macrophage functions. Moreover, oxLDL promoted a distinct macrophage activation state and altered polarization trajectories depending on the timing of exposure. These findings demonstrate that major oxysterols exert distinct and complementary biological effects across vascular and immune cell populations, highlighting their differential contribution to atherosclerotic plaque development and progression, and support the development of therapeutic approaches targeting multiple oxysterol species rather than a single oxidized cholesterol derivative.

Article.Title: Host Ubiquitin-Specific Proteases Regulate All Stages of Herpesvirus Infection
Article.Authors: Maarouf M.; Peterson C.; Mohni K.
Article.Abstract: Herpesviruses are a large group of double-stranded-DNA viruses that replicate their genomes in the nucleus, forming large replication compartments during lytic infection. Herpesviruses are known to modulate host DNA replication and DNA damage-repair proteins to promote their replication. Ubiquitination is a cellular process that can alter protein stability, localization, and availability, including that of multiple proteins involved in genome maintenance. Ubiquitin-specific proteases (USPs) are a class of deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) that counter this process by removing ubiquitin chains, thus acting as another level of regulation. Proteins from each of the three herpesvirus subfamilies (alpha-, beta-, and gammaherpesviruses) have been reported to interact with at least one host USP, and USP7 in particular is reported as a target in representatives of all three subfamilies. In this review, we give an up-to-date summary of herpesviruses–USPs interactions, with special emphasis on DNA replication, and how these interactions could shape infection outcomes. We also examine published proteomic datasets for herpesvirus-driven host-proteome modulation and offer a framework for future directions to prioritize potentially important, understudied USPs. Lastly, we visit herpesvirus-encoded DUBs and highlight their roles in viral replication by remodeling ubiquitin signaling, discussing viral DUBs and virus–USP interfaces as proposed antiviral targets.

Article.Title: Genetically Predicted Blood DNA Methylation Reveals Putative Regulatory Signals Associated with ALS Risk
Article.Authors: Zhao T.; Hoffman M.; Wu G.; Belzil V.
Article.Abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder whose genetic architecture and molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood, particularly in sporadic disease. To investigate whether genetically regulated DNA methylation may help interpret ALS susceptibility, we conducted a methylome-wide association study of genetically predicted blood methylation using the PrediXcan framework. CpG-specific models from the ARIES and Understanding Society cohorts were applied to ALS genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics from 27,205 cases and 110,881 controls of European ancestry. Using S-PrediXcan, we evaluated 192,378 unique CpG sites. At nominal p < 0.05, 3741 CpGs were associated with ALS risk using ARIES models and 13,127 using Understanding Society models. After Bonferroni correction, 25 CpGs across eight genomic regions remained significant, including signals near established ALS and ALS–frontotemporal dementia loci (C9orf72, TBK1, SCFD1, and MOB3B). Three CpGs mapped to WHAMM at 15q25.2, a region not previously implicated by ALS GWAS. Predicted methylation was positively associated with risk at 18 CpGs and inversely associated at seven. Complementary whole-blood transcriptome-wide association analysis identified 11 significant genes, including C9orf72. Together, these findings prioritize regulatory candidates for functional investigation without establishing that methylation changes cause ALS.

Article.Title: Serial Tumor-Agnostic Plasma Profiling with a Compact NGS Panel During First-Line Therapy for Newly Diagnosed Metastatic Colorectal Cancer
Article.Authors: Zakharova G.; Zauzolkov O.; Khristichenko A.; Lyadov V.; Gaziev I.; Shaban N.; Emelyanova A.; Sekacheva M.; Lyadova M.; Buzdin A.
Article.Abstract: Plasma circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) profiling may complement tissue hotspot testing and reveal molecular changes during treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC). We prospectively studied 39 patients with newly diagnosed unresectable mCRC receiving first-line therapy. Cell-free DNA was collected before treatment and after two and four cycles and analyzed using a 10 kb, 10-gene hybrid-capture sequencing panel with molecular barcodes and error correction. Baseline oncogenic variants were detected in 32 of 35 evaluable patients (91.4%). Compared with routine tissue PCR for shared RAS/BRAF targets, plasma testing showed 84.2% sensitivity (16/19) and 100% specificity (19/19) in the intention-to-test cohort, compared with 88.2% sensitivity (15/17) and 100% specificity (17/17) among technically evaluable samples. Three activating KRAS variants (L19F, A59T, and A146T) lay outside the tissue assays’ target regions; patients carrying these alterations received anti-EGFR therapy. Patients with metastases in two or more organs had more detectable oncogenic alterations than those with one metastatic site (median, three versus two; adjusted q = 0.00184; rank-biserial correlation = 0.687). Serial sampling revealed divergent trajectories of individual variants in nine patients. Early reductions in plasma variant allele frequencies tended to be greater among partial responders, although associations with radiological response were not significant after multiple testing correction. Compact tumor-agnostic plasma sequencing provides complementary molecular information, but its clinical utility requires further validation.

Article.Title: Molecular Dynamics Simulations Reveal a Broadly Open Solution Ensemble for the DNA Holliday Junction: Mg2+ Crossover Bridging and Weak Force-Field Sensitivity
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Zhou Y.
Article.Abstract: Holliday junctions, four-way DNA crossovers central to DNA origami and key intermediates of homologous recombination, must be accurately modeled for rational DNA-nanodevice design, yet their solution conformational ensemble remains incompletely characterized. We characterize this ensemble for the experimental junction d(TCGGTACCGA)4 by all-atom molecular dynamics, comparing the AMBER force fields parmbsc1, OL21, and OL24 in OPC water with matched ionic conditions. In every force field, the junction explores a broad, nearly flat inter-arm-angle landscape, with <1 kcal/mol variation across inter-arm angles of 2–90°: the open state is favored by 0.45–0.63 kcal/mol, the crystallographic-like inter-arm angle occurs in 2–5% of frames, and the crossover remains coaxially stacked whether open or compact. A Mg2+ ion occupies the crossover pocket in 92–94% of frames, specifically bridging the A- and C-strand phosphates (Li–Merz CM Mg2+ set). Stacking-isomer exchange between the A/C-continuous and crystallographic B/D isomers proceeds at ~0.5 ns−1 in this minimal short-arm construct, independent of force field, with A/C-continuous favored ~2:1. parmbsc1 yields a more open junction than OL21 and OL24, which reproduce the crystallographic inter-arm angle of 39–43°; the sugar-pucker shift targeted in OL24 is also visible at the junction. These results establish a force-field-robust baseline for simulation-guided design of crossover-containing nanostructures.

Article.Title: Integrative Single-Cell and Radiomics Analyses Identify N-Acetylneuraminate Synthase (NANS)-High Signature Associated with Adverse Prognosis and Immune Remodeling in Glioblastoma
Article.Authors: Chen J.; Wu Q.; Cardenas H.; Bernard K.; Berglund A.; Sun Y.; Macaulay R.; Mulé J.; Etame A.
Article.Abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is characterized by marked heterogeneity and an immunosuppressive microenvironment. N-acetylneuraminate synthase (NANS) contributes to tumor-associated metabolic regulation, but its relationship with GBM and its immune profile remains unclear. This study aimed to characterize the prognostic and immune relevance of NANS and develop an MRI radiomics model for noninvasive prediction of NANS-high GBM. Prognostic genes were screened across TCGA-GBM and two CGGA cohorts. Bulk transcriptomic and single-cell RNA sequencing analyses were used to evaluate NANS expression, patient survival association, and cellular localization. NANS-high bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) were characterized using functional enrichment and CellChat analyses. A NANS-high BMDM signature was validated in TCGA-GBM for immune infiltration and ligand–receptor axis activity. Drug sensitivity and CMap analyses were performed. MRI radiomics features were extracted from preprocessed T1 contrast-enhanced and FLAIR images, and an elastic net logistic regression model was constructed to predict NANS-high BMDM signature status. NANS was identified as a prognostic macrophage-associated biomarker in GBM and was enriched in BMDMs. NANS-high BMDMs showed enrichment of mTORC1 signaling, oxidative phosphorylation, unfolded protein response, glycolysis, hypoxia, and protein secretion programs. Cell–cell communication analysis revealed enhanced outgoing signaling toward malignant tumor states and T-cell subsets, with LGALS9-centered interactions representing the dominant differential communication program. In TCGA-GBM, the NANS-high BMDM signature correlated with increased macrophage infiltration, broad immune infiltration, and elevated LGALS9 and PLAU axis scores. Drug sensitivity analyses suggested potential vulnerabilities involving PI3K/mTOR and MAPK/ERK pathways. The radiomics model selected six MRI features and distinguished NANS-high from NANS-low tumors with an AUC of 0.795 (95% CI, 0.652–0.939); bootstrap validation showed a mean AUC of 0.793 (95% CI, 0.637–0.922). NANS-high BMDMs define a prognostically adverse and potentially targetable macrophage-associated phenotype in GBM. MRI radiomics may noninvasively predict this NANS-high BMDM state, supporting imaging-based risk stratification and therapeutic selection.

Article.Title: RyR2 Gain-of-Function Increases Ca2+ Spark and Ca2+ Wave Activity in Vascular Smooth Muscle Cells
Article.Authors: Alves D.; Zhai Q.; Lu L.; Chu Z.; Tsvetkov D.; Chen S.; Gollasch M.; Kassmann M.
Article.Abstract: Ca2+ sparks in vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) regulate vascular function, and their dysregulation with ageing may contribute to vascular disease. These localized Ca2+ signals originate from ryanodine receptors (RyRs) and can initiate propagating Ca2+ waves that modulate vascular tone. However, it is still unclear which RyR isoform (RyR1, RyR2, or RyR3) primarily drives these Ca2+ signals in arterial VSMCs, as all three are present. The RyR2 contribution to vascular Ca2+ signaling was analyzed using Ca2+ sparks and waves in arterial VSMCs isolated from mice carrying the RyR2R4496C mutation. Intracellular Ca2+ signals were recorded using a fluorescent Ca2+ indicator in VSMCs from both young and older mice. Caffeine-evoked Ca2+ responses and contractions were measured to assess RyR-mediated SR Ca2+ release and vascular reactivity. VSMCs from young RyR2R4496C mice exhibited a significantly higher frequency of Ca2+ sparks and a greater percentage of cells displaying Ca2+ sparks and propagating Ca2+ waves compared with controls. The RyR2R4496C mutation enhanced RyR2 sensitivity to caffeine, resulting in larger increases in intracellular [Ca2+]i and arterial contractions in older mice. These findings demonstrate that RyR2 gain-of-function increases Ca2+ spark and Ca2+ wave activity in VSMCs, supporting a role for RyR2 in the regulation of local and propagating Ca2+ signals. Dysregulated RyR2 activity may therefore contribute to altered vascular Ca2+ signaling and could represent a potential mechanistic link to vascular dysfunction associated with ageing and metabolic stress.

Article.Title: Synergistic Anti-Zika Activity of Repurposed Statin and Clofibrate Combinations: Evidence from Oleic Acid-Mediated Metabolic Complementation
Article.Authors: Lee C.; Park S.; Lee G.; Moon H.; Choi J.; Lee J.; Martinez-Sobrido L.; Almazán F.; Ryu E.; Baek Y.; Park J.
Article.Abstract: Zika virus (ZIKV) substantially relies on host lipid metabolism, presenting a prime target for host-directed antivirals. To identify host-directed antiviral interventions while circumventing interferon-mediated transcriptomic masking, we curated a dual-virus (dengue and ZIKV) gene signature to query the Connectivity Map. Top lipid-lowering candidates were validated using a reporter virus (rZIKV-Venus) and an authentic wild-type (WT) ZIKV in Vero E6 cells—a model deliberately selected for its interferon deficiency to isolate pure metabolic responses. Dose–response screening of 67 prioritized compounds identified atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, and clofibrate as potent ZIKV inhibitors. Statin–clofibrate combinations exhibited strong synergy, with fractional inhibitory concentration index (FICI) values of 0.203 (atorvastatin–clofibrate) and 0.117 (rosuvastatin–clofibrate) for the 4:1 clofibrate-to-statin ratio and an optimized selectivity index. Mechanistically, exogenous oleic acid supplementation induced significant metabolic complementation, significantly restoring both host lipid droplet (LD) abundance and ZIKV replication readouts suppressed by the dual treatment. Relative LD intensity strongly correlated with viral intensity in both models (Pearson r = 0.951 and 0.956, respectively; both p < 0.0001). These findings demonstrate that concurrent pharmacological modulation of host lipid metabolism exerts synergistic anti-ZIKV effects, highlighting highly curated transcriptomic repurposing as a mechanistic prioritization strategy for host-directed antiviral discovery.

Article.Title: A Tailored Sequencing Approach for Identifying SARS-CoV-2 Variants in Challenging Samples from Mink
Article.Authors: Giza A.; Iwan E.; Bomba A.; Orłowska A.; Smreczak M.; Pietruk M.; Chudzik A.; Olejnik M.; Domańska-Blicharz K.
Article.Abstract: High-throughput sequencing (HTS) is an essential tool for genomic surveillance of infectious agents, including SARS-CoV-2 in farmed mink. However, sample quality varies, hindering high-quality sequencing results. In this study, six mink-origin SARS-CoV-2-positive samples were sequenced using two hybrid-capture methods (commercial and custom) and a shotgun metagenomic approach. All methods consistently identified SARS-CoV-2 variants. The metagenomic approach yielded the lowest mapping rate (up to 0.35%), breadth of coverage (97–100%), depth of coverage (9–932×), and mean mapq (30–59), and one sequence did not meet the quality criteria. In contrast, both hybrid-capture methods achieved higher mapping rates (47–99%), breadth of coverage (99.9–100%), and depth of coverage (508–115,846×). The custom hybrid-capture approach was selected because of its superior coverage uniformity, the lowest number of ambiguous bases (N), adjustability to low RNA levels and degraded material, and streamlined laboratory workflow. To further evaluate its applicability, it was applied to 35 clinical samples collected as part of routine genomic surveillance. This method generated sequencing data with high mapping rates (median 95%), depth of coverage (median 13,238×), breadth of coverage (median 100%), and mean mapq (median 60). These findings demonstrate that the custom hybrid-capture approach is a useful tool for genomic surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 in mink-origin samples.

Article.Title: Computational Discovery of Plant-Derived Peptides with Therapeutic Potential: A Scoping Review
Article.Authors: Maphumulo S.; Mpofana N.; Ojewole E.
Article.Abstract: Computational methods are increasingly applied to the discovery of plant-derived peptides, but the extent, composition and reporting practice of this literature have not been mapped. Following PRISMA-ScR and Joanna Briggs Institute guidance, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect and PubMed were searched for records published between 2021 and 2026. Of 5062 unique records, 593 were screened at title and abstract, 88 full texts were assessed, 80 sources met all five eligibility criteria and 79 were charted. Overall, 49 (62.0%) were primary studies, 12 (15.2%) described a tool or database and 18 (22.8%) were narrative reviews. Antimicrobial peptides were the commonest class (33, 41.8%), followed by antioxidant (21, 26.6%) and ACE-inhibitory peptides (18, 22.8%). Only 11 sources (13.9%) trained and evaluated a model of their own, whereas 23 (29.1%) combined prediction with molecular docking. Of 61 empirical sources, 14 (23.0%) reported at least one quantitative prediction-task performance figure and 13 (21.3%) benchmarked a named comparator; the metrics used were not mutually comparable. Moreover, 18 of 62 applicable sources (29.0%) confirmed their own prediction experimentally; 70 (88.6%) named a plant source, most often Arabidopsis thaliana; and 8 (10.1%) linked their material to documented traditional medicine. No source applied machine learning to African plant peptides, an absence within the literature sampled rather than proof that none exists.

Article.Title: Real-Time Automated Fluorescence Imaging Assay for Quantifying GFP-Expressing Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis
Article.Authors: Badia-Bringué G.; Prado-López A.; Alonso-Hearn M.
Article.Abstract: Measurement of Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis (MAP) load within macrophages using a mycobacterial growth inhibition assay (MGIA) is an accurate indicator of host immune control of MAP infection. Real-time fluorescent microscopy allows the continuous analysis of infected cells and the quantification of fluorescence intensity, which directly correlates with concentration of fluorescent bacteria. The objective of this study was to develop an automated and real-time live-cell imaging assay using the IncuCyte SX1® platform for quantifying green fluorescence protein (GFP)-expressing MAP (MAP-GFP) within infected macrophages. The fluorescence of serially diluted free MAP-GFP was quantified using the IncuCyte SX1® demonstrating that the fluorescence signal of 3 × 107 CFU was significantly different from lowest MAP concentrations. Significant differences between uninfected and infected BOMAC cells (MOI; 1:10) in DMEM-F12, DMEM-F12 supplemented with fetal bovine serum (FBS), and RPMI-1640 supplemented with FBS were observed, indicating the suitability of these culture media for measuring MAP-GFP-host cell interaction in the IncuCyte SX1®. For the optimization of the MOI and cell density, bovine monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) and the BOMAC cells were seeded at different cell densities and infected with MAP-GFP at different MOIs. After 2 h of infection, the supernatant was removed, the cells were washed three times with HBSS, and fresh RPMI-1640 supplemented with FBS was added to the cells. Then, the fluorescence was quantified in the IncuCyte SX1® at different times p.i. Our results demonstrated that MAP phagocytosis is pathogen number- and cell density-dependent. Overall, the results showed that infection of 1 × 106 cells at an MOI of 1:10 maintained a stable fluorescence signal of approximately 400 to 500 GCU ⋅ μm2/image across 2 h to 4 days p.i. In addition, good correlations between MAP-GFP (logCFUs) estimated in the BACTEC MGIT™ 960 system and fluorescence intensity measured in the IncuCyte SX1® were observed for free MAP-GFP bacilli and from MAP-GFP within infected BOMAC cells, r = 0.79 and r = 0.78, respectively. In conclusion, real-time fluorescent microscopy enables continuous monitoring of MAP-GFP within infected macrophages.

Article.Title: Preliminary Evaluation of the Anticancer Activity of a PGK1 Small Molecule Inhibitor in Ishikawa Endometrial Cancer
Article.Authors: Cao H.; Xue S.; Xue M.; Li F.; Feng L.; Zheng W.; Ding H.; Zhang T.
Article.Abstract: To investigate the roles of a phosphoglycerate kinase 1 (PGK1) small-molecule inhibitor in Ishikawa endometrial cancer. The role of a PGK1 small molecule inhibitor in endometrial cancer was identified by cell viability, transwell, cell cycle, and apoptosis analyses. The expression levels of PGK1 in cancer cells treated with various concentrations of the PGK1 small molecule inhibitor at 48 h and 72 h were determined via Western blotting. Xenograft mouse models were established through subcutaneous tumor transplantation, and immunofluorescence analysis of PGK1 and apoptosis in tumor tissue was performed. The results of the cell counting kit-8 (CCK-8) assay revealed that NG52 inhibited the activity of human endometrial carcinoma Ishikawa, HEC-1-A, and HEC-1-B cells in a concentration-dependent manner. Moreover, NG52 significantly reduced the migration ability of the Ishikawa cell line in a dose-dependent manner. Flow cytometry (FCM) demonstrated that NG52 affected the survival of endometrial carcinoma cells by arresting the cell cycle at the G1 phase and inducing apoptosis in a dose-dependent manner. Western blot analysis also revealed that the apoptosis-inducing effects of NG52 were accompanied by a reduction in PGK1 expression after 48 h and 72 h of NG52 treatment. Moreover, NG52 partially suppressed tumor growth in a human Ishikawa xenograft model, and transferase dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL) showed an increasing trend of NG52-treated tumor tissue apoptosis, with a decreasing trend in PGK1 expression in the treatment group. NG52, a PGK1 small molecule inhibitor, can serve as a structural basis for developing potential anti-endometrial carcinoma agents. The findings are limited to the preliminary preclinical activity of NG52, and further mechanistic, pharmacologic, efficacy, and safety studies are warranted before improved PGK1 inhibitors can proceed to clinical translation.

Article.Title: Evaluation of Dihydropyridine Derivatives as Aldose Reductase Inhibitors: Enzymatic Screening, Molecular Docking and Ex Vivo Assessment of a Selected Compound in a Lens Model
Article.Authors: Alonso-Hurtado K.; Méndez-Pérez T.; Hernández-Gallegos Z.; Cajero-Juárez M.; Navarro-Santos P.; Virgen-Ortíz J.; Martínez-Pacheco M.
Article.Abstract: Aldose reductase (AR) is a key enzyme in the polyol pathway and has been widely implicated in the development of diabetic complications, including cataract formation. In this work, a series of structurally modified 1,4-dihydropyridine (DHP) derivatives were evaluated as potential AR inhibitors. The compounds were obtained with high purity and subjected to enzymatic screening, exhibiting IC50 values ranging from 1.11 ± 0.07 to 55.34 ± 0.06 µM. The unsubstituted DHP scaffold exhibited intrinsic activity, whereas substitution at the 4-phenyl ring modulated inhibition in a nonlinear manner, reflecting the combined influence of steric and electronic factors on enzyme interactions. Kinetic analysis revealed mixed-type inhibition, indicating that the inhibitory behavior of the DHP derivatives cannot be explained solely by simple competition with the substrate. Molecular docking using the AR–NADP complex identified favorable binding poses and interactions with residues involved in ligand recognition and stabilization, although no direct correlation was observed between predicted docking scores and experimental inhibitory potency. A representative compound (DHP3, IC50 = 1.11 ± 0.07 µM) was elected for ex vivo evaluation in a rabbit lens model under hyperglycemic conditions. Treatment reduced glucose-induced lens opacity by 89.1%, estimated by image-based analysis, and decreased sorbitol accumulation by 57.48% relative to hyperglycemic control, indicating modulation of the polyol pathway at the tissue level. In contrast, no significant changes were detected in calcium content. These findings support the potential of DHP derivatives as a scaffold for aldose reductase inhibition and highlight their ability to attenuate early alterations associated with hyperglycemia in lens tissue. Further studies are required to expand biological validation and optimize their inhibitory profile.

Article.Title: Ovariectomy Exacerbates Chronic Constriction Injury-Induced Neuropathic Pain Through Dysregulation of Spinal Estrogen Receptor Balance in Rats
Article.Authors: Chan Y.; Lin S.; Huang C.; Zheng T.; Wang Y.; Tsai Y.
Article.Abstract: Estrogen depletion after menopause has been associated with altered pain sensitivity; however, the spinal mechanisms linking estrogen deficiency to neuropathic pain remain incompletely understood. This study investigated whether ovariectomy (OVX)-induced estrogen depletion exacerbates chronic constriction injury (CCI)-induced neuropathic pain and whether this effect is associated with changes in spinal estrogen receptor alpha (ERα) and estrogen receptor beta (ERβ) expression. Female Sprague Dawley rats underwent OVX or sham surgery, followed 5 weeks later by median nerve CCI or sham CCI. Mechanical withdrawal thresholds and thermal withdrawal latencies were evaluated using von Frey filaments and the plantar test, respectively. ERα and ERβ expression in the spinal dorsal horn was assessed via immunofluorescence staining and Western blotting. Selective ERα and ERβ agonists were administered intrathecally to examine their effects on OVX/CCI-induced pain behaviors. Plasma estradiol levels were significantly reduced after OVX, and OVX rats developed mechanical and thermal hypersensitivity. Rats in the OVX/CCI group exhibited more pronounced pain behaviors than those in the Sham/CCI group, indicating that OVX exacerbated CCI-induced neuropathic pain. In the spinal dorsal horn, ERα expression was increased in the OVX/Sham, Sham/CCI, and OVX/CCI groups, with the greatest increase observed in the OVX/CCI group. In contrast, ERβ expression was decreased in the Sham/CCI and OVX/CCI groups, with no significant difference between these groups. Intrathecal administration of an ERα agonist further aggravated mechanical allodynia and thermal hyperalgesia in OVX/CCI rats, whereas an ERβ agonist attenuated these pain behaviors. These findings suggest that OVX-induced estrogen depletion exacerbates CCI-induced neuropathic pain, potentially through a shift toward ERα-dominant signaling relative to ERβ in the spinal dorsal horn. Selective modulation of ERα and ERβ may therefore represent a potential therapeutic approach for chronic pain exacerbated by estrogen depletion.

Article.Title: Vitamin K2 and Cardiovascular Calcification: Mechanistic Foundations, Conflicting Clinical Evidence, and Unresolved Questions
Article.Authors: Kothari C.; Chowdhary R.; Babazade S.; Egoavil A.; Abuirmaileh W.; Kapadia S.; Wimalawansa S.
Article.Abstract: Cardiovascular calcification is an active, complex process involving osteogenic transformation, inflammation, extracellular vesicle release, and impaired mineral buffering. These changes result from mineral imbalance and reduced levels of calcification inhibitors. Vitamin K supports the γ-carboxylation of matrix Gla protein (MGP) and other mineralization inhibitors, though some calcification defenses do not depend on vitamin K. Vitamin K deficiency and warfarin therapy increase circulating dephosphorylated-uncarboxylated MGP (dp-ucMGP), which is linked to greater vascular calcification. Preclinical studies demonstrate that disruption of the vitamin K-MGP axis promotes calcification. Supplementation with vitamin K1 or K2 can reduce, prevent, or partially reverse mineralization in certain animal models. In contrast, evidence from human studies is less consistent. Observational studies have identified an association between menaquinone (vitamin K2) intake and cardiovascular outcomes, but causality has not been established. Most randomized trials have shown neutral results for aortic-valve and chronic kidney disease-associated calcification, while the VitaK-CAC and DANCODE studies reported slower progression of coronary artery calcium in selected populations with moderate or severe baseline coronary calcification. These discrepancies may be due to differences in calcification phenotypes, disease stage, vitamin K forms, dosing regimens, vitamin D status, renal function, and response to vitamin K antagonists such as warfarin. Coronary intimal, valvular, and arterial medial calcification should be regarded as phenotypically distinct entities. This review evaluates the mechanistic, preclinical, and clinical evidence linking vitamin K2 to cardiovascular calcification and highlights population groups that warrant further clinical investigation. Large, adequately powered, and phenotype-specific clinical trials are needed to determine whether appropriately dosed vitamin K2 is a safe and cost-effective intervention for slowing valvular and vascular calcification.

Article.Title: Conserved Hepatospora eriocheir Sequences in Chinese Mitten Crabs from Poland, Germany and Belgium: A Comparative Molecular Study
Article.Authors: Stachnik M.; Normant-Saremba M.; Ewers C.; Keirsebelik H.; Schoelynck J.
Article.Abstract: Hepatospora eriocheir is an obligate intracellular microsporidian associated with the Chinese mitten crab, Eriocheir sinensis, an important aquaculture species in Asia and an invasive species in Europe. We investigated parasite sequence variation in crabs from three European regions: the Vistula Lagoon in the Baltic Sea (Poland) and the Elbe and Scheldt catchments draining into the North Sea (Germany and Belgium). Among 57 crabs examined, 26 infections were confirmed by small subunit ribosomal RNA (SSU rRNA) sequencing, including 17 newly identified infections among 42 specimens collected in 2022. The parasite groups comprised 13 Polish, eight German and five Belgian infections. Their SSU rRNA sequences were identical across a 794-position shared core, and all 26 newly generated arginyl-tRNA synthetase (ArgRS) sequences were identical across 624 nucleotides and matched the British reference KU695717. Both parasite gene fragments were identical across four host mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase subunit I (COI) haplotypes; the Eriocheir japonica-associated haplotype was detected only in Belgian crabs in this sample. The study provides the first specimen-linked, sequence-confirmed molecular characterisation of infections in the sampled German and Belgian crab populations, together with new Polish infections from 2022 and a comparative two-locus reference dataset. The repeated Baltic detection, combined with shared Polish–German host COI haplotypes and existing evidence of North Sea–Baltic connectivity, is consistent with the arrival of infected migrating crabs, although the parasite’s precise source remains unresolved.

Article.Title: Biomodulators and Skin Boosters in Skin Rejuvenation: Mechanisms, Applications, and Future Perspectives
Article.Authors: Ding Z.; Jin C.; Ming H.; Shim J.; Huy V.; Chien P.; Heo C.
Article.Abstract: Biomodulators and skin boosters comprise heterogeneous preparations whose biological activity and clinical effects require separate evaluation. This structured narrative review distinguishes mechanistic plausibility from human comparative findings for skin aging, skin quality, and atrophic acne scars. A reproducible PubMed/MEDLINE search completed on 16 October 2026, followed by predefined screening, source retrieval, and eligibility adjudication, identified 159 comparative reports, each contributing one specified result. Risk-of-bias assessments classified 123 results as High and 36 as Some concerns; none was Low overall. Selected formulations and procedure-assisted regimens showed benefits for particular outcomes, whereas other comparisons were null or discordant. Hydration, tissue remodeling, clinical appearance, and patient satisfaction were treated as distinct outcomes. Retrospective result selection, heterogeneous interventions and outcomes, four access-unresolved reports, and the absence of a prospective protocol constrain confidence. Clinical claims should remain specific to the product, protocol, indication, comparator, and outcome investigated.

Article.Title: Functional Characterization of ClHSP22.9 Promoter from Wild Watermelon (Citrullus lanatus) Reveals Heat- and Drought-Inducible Transcriptional Activity
Article.Authors: Munir R.; Hussain I.; Jan N.; Ali B.; Munir I.; Ali W.; Khan R.; Iqbal A.
Article.Abstract: Small heat shock proteins (sHSPs) are essential components of the plant proteostasis network under environmental stress; however, the cis-regulatory mechanisms underlying stress-responsive expression of individual sHSP genes remains insufficiently depicted. Here, we characterized the promoter of ClHSP22.9 from wild watermelon (Citrullus lanatus subsp. cordophanus) and evaluated its transcriptional responsiveness under different abiotic stresses. A semi-quantitative RT-PCR analysis revealed that ClHSP22.9 transcripts were strongly induced by heat, dehydration, and salinity treatments, whereas cold treatment caused comparatively limited transcriptional alterations. A 1482 bp promoter region upstream of the transcription start site was isolated using thermal asymmetric interlaced PCR (TAIL-PCR) and partially overlapping primer-based PCR (POP-PCR). An in silico promoter analysis identified multiple predicted stress and hormonal-associated cis-regulatory elements, including two heat shock elements (HSEs). Three serial 5′ promoter deletion fragments (−1482, −1012, and −522 bp) were fused to the GUS reporter gene and functionally analyzed in transgenic Brassica napus. Under heat stress, the −1482 and −1012 bp promoter fragments exhibited strong reporter activation, whereas deletion to −522 bp significantly reduced promoter activity, indicating that the −1012 to −522 bp region contributes substantially to maximal heat-responsive transcription. Furthermore, the −1012 bp proHSPII fragment retained an inducible GUS expression under heat, drought, and combined heat and drought stress conditions. These findings identify an important region within the ClHSP22.9 promoter and establish the −1012 bp promoter fragment as a promising candidate stress-responsive regulatory sequence for further mechanistic characterization and potential application in plant biotechnology.

Article.Title: Maternal Immune Activation by Lipopolysaccharide Reduced Parvalbumin Levels and Increased Perineuronal Nets in the Prefrontal Cortex Without Inducing Schizophrenia-like Behavioral Deficits in PV-Cre Long-Evans Rats
Article.Authors: Vojtechova I.; Tuckova K.; Kutna V.; Jelinkova B.; Skalova K.; Lebedeva M.; Khodak A.; Machacek T.; Petrasek T.
Article.Abstract: Models of maternal immune activation (MIA) often lead to parvalbumin-positive (PV+) interneuron deficits and behavioral alterations resembling autism or schizophrenia. We aimed to characterize the effects of MIA in PV-Cre Long-Evans rats. Pregnant dams received 8 lipopolysaccharide injections (1 mg/kg), on alternating days, starting with gestational day 7. The offspring behavior was tested from postnatal day 5 to adulthood, with tasks assessing motor development, anxiety, exploration, social behavior and sensorimotor gating. Morphological changes in the brain, density of PV+ interneurons and perineuronal nets in the prefrontal cortex, as well as the quantity of PV protein were measured at selected timepoints. We found that MIA in PV-Cre Long-Evans rats failed to elicit the expected schizophrenia- or autism-like deficits. Decrease in PV protein in the prefrontal cortex was present without corresponding decrement of PV+ interneurons, with a paradoxical increase in perineuronal net counts. PV-Cre Long-Evans rat line reacts to the MIA protocol very differently than Wistar rats in previously published studies and is suboptimal for studies of schizophrenia- or autism-like behavioral deficits. Genetic background seems to be an important factor for the outcome in MIA rodent models.

Article.Title: Development of Hydrogel-Cellulose Nanofiber Hybrid Scaffolds for Potential Cutaneous Wound-Healing Applications
Article.Authors: Edwards J.; Prevost N.; Lassiter H.; Hamel K.; Easson M.; Jordan J.; Rogers E.; Robinson J.; Frazier T.; Sanchez C.
Article.Abstract: Cellulose nanofibrils (CNFs) and TEMPO-oxidized cellulose nanofibrils (TOCNFs) are hydrated, high-aspect-ratio biomaterials with tunable physicochemical properties, whereas human-derived extracellular matrix (ECM) hydrogels provide matrix-associated biochemical cues. In this study, CNF- and TOCNF-based hybrid scaffolds incorporating human ECM hydrogel components were developed and evaluated in vitro as platforms relevant to cutaneous wound repair. Hybrid formulations gelled at physiological temperature and exhibited formulation-dependent shear-thinning behavior, elastic properties, protein release/leaching profiles, and porous fibrillar microstructures. Selected formulations supported cell-associated metabolic activity of human dermal fibroblasts and adipose-derived stromal/stem cells under two-dimensional and three-dimensional culture conditions. Additional exploratory studies demonstrated qualitative compatibility with adipogenic culture and condition-dependent changes in wound-gap width. In the absence of in vivo validation and confirmatory biological assays, these findings are interpreted as proof-of-concept rather than evidence of wound-healing efficacy. Overall, the results demonstrate the feasibility of combining CNF or TOCNF structural networks with human-derived ECM hydrogels to generate hybrid scaffolds with wound-relevant material properties and preliminary cytocompatibility, supporting further mechanistic and preclinical evaluation.

Article.Title: Pyrrolocytosine as a Fluorescent Sensor of RNA–Small Molecule Interactions
Article.Authors: Coulson T.; Valdez G.; Widom J.
Article.Abstract: Fluorescent base analogues have proven to be valuable probes of RNA structure. Pyrrolocytosine (pC), an analogue of cytosine, exhibits highly environment-sensitive fluorescence within RNA and is strongly quenched in hydrogen-bonded contexts. In this work, we incorporated pC into the aptamer domain of the B. subtilis guanine riboswitch to determine if this quenching mechanism could allow for sensing of RNA–small molecule interactions. We utilized complementary fluorescence spectroscopy methods to understand the functional impacts and ligand sensitivity of pC substitutions distal to and within the binding pocket. We found that pC substitution within a static structural region exhibits the expected ligand-independent fluorescence properties. When placed in the ligand binding pocket, pC exhibits a moderately decreased affinity for the ligands guanine (G) and hypoxanthine (Hx) while maintaining high specificity for G. We found that pC behaves as a turn-off sensor, with distinct changes in fluorescence upon G or Hx binding. These differences are dependent on the number of hydrogen bonds formed with pC and are resolvable in both time-dependent and steady-state fluorescence measurements. Our results show that pC can be used to study RNA–small molecule interactions and can discriminate between similar ligands even when they have identical binding modes.

Article.Title: A Decision-Centric Benchmark of Enrichment and Potency Ranking in CNN-Rescored Molecular Docking
Article.Authors: Lai Y.; Huang H.
Article.Abstract: Virtual screening answers two different questions with one number: enrichment, separating actives from background molecules, and potency ranking, ordering actives by measured activity. We benchmarked both for the same score on the same compounds across five CNS binding sites (SERT, GABAA benzodiazepine site, 5-HT1A, σ1, and NMDA MK-801 pore), docking ChEMBL actives, inactives, and property-matched decoys with Uni-Dock and GNINA under a held-out normalisation/evaluation split, plus an experimentally characterised negative probe excluded from all fitting. Ranking, evaluated among pChEMBL ≥ 7 actives, was negligible for every target (median Spearman ρ = 0.020) and was not recovered by data-quality filtering, multivariate null models, scaffold-aware resampling, strict assay–site matching with rebuilt decoys, or stricter curation. Enrichment proved strongly benchmark-dependent: an apparent ΔAUC gain of +0.153 against molecular weight-matched decoys decreased to ≤0.05 once the decoys were matched to seven descriptors, and the residue was not robust to compound resampling. A classifier using no structural information separated the same actives from the same decoys at ROC-AUC 0.959–0.993, and cognate ligand redocking reproduced the crystallographic pose as the top-ranked solution for one of five targets. Benchmark enrichment should not be equated with protein-specific recognition; the benchmark, the poses, and the ranking require separate validation.

Article.Title: Beyond Mesothelioma: From Diagnostic Biomarker to Therapeutic Opportunity—The Emerging Role of MTAP in Cancer
Article.Authors: Diluvio A.; Lucà S.; Iavarone L.; Masola V.; Fiorelli A.; Morgillo F.; D’Abbronzo G.; Franco R.
Article.Abstract: Methylthioadenosine phosphorylase (MTAP) loss is an emerging biomarker in several human malignancies, mainly due to its frequent co-deletion with CDKN2A on chromosome 9p21. Beyond its diagnostic value, MTAP deficiency has important biological consequences, including metabolic reprogramming, immune microenvironment modulation, and increased dependency on PRMT5-related pathways. This review summarizes the current evidence on MTAP alterations across different tumor types. The role of MTAP immunohistochemistry as a practical surrogate for CDKN2A homozygous deletion is discussed, together with its advantages and interpretative limitations. In addition, the potential predictive relevance of MTAP loss for immunotherapy, antifolate-based treatments, and novel PRMT5-targeted strategies is explored. Overall, MTAP assessment represents a promising tool in modern diagnostic pathology and precision oncology, bridging morphology, molecular alterations, and therapeutic decision-making.

Article.Title: From Oxyntomodulin to Retatrutide: A Translational Review of Metabolic Polyagonism
Article.Authors: Saldívar-Cerón H.; Maldonado-Trejo D.; Chavez-Castañeda Q.; Mercado-Guzmán A.; León-Barrita A.; López-García I.; Hernández-Solís A.; Ramírez-Mendoza A.; Terrazas-Delgado D.; Castañeda-Ramírez A.; Quiñones-Lara E.; Jay-Jímenez B.; Pozo-Molina G.; León-Cabrera S.
Article.Abstract: Oxyntomodulin (OXM), an endogenous proglucagon-derived peptide with dual glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) and glucagon receptor (GCGR) agonism, provides a physiological precedent for contemporary multi-receptor pharmacology. Recognition that GCGR signaling regulates not only hepatic glucose production but also amino acid turnover, lipid metabolism, substrate oxidation, and energy expenditure prompted the development of engineered GLP-1R/GCGR co-agonists, including cotadutide, mazdutide, survodutide, and pemvidutide. Retatrutide extends this strategy by integrating GIPR, GLP-1R, and GCGR agonism within a single long-acting peptide and has produced substantial improvements in body weight, glycemic control, and cardiometabolic parameters in phase 2 and phase 3 trials. This review examines the evolutionary and structural relationships of the proglucagon–Class B1 GPCR system, OXM biosynthesis and receptor pharmacology, the mechanistic rationale for therapeutic GCGR agonism, and the molecular and clinical development of dual and triple agonists. We further address receptor balance, the GIPR agonism–antagonism paradox, receptor-specific causal attribution, and the unresolved limitations of translating molecular pharmacology into durable clinical benefit. Finally, we propose an Activity–Exposure–Context framework for interpreting polyagonist pharmacology and discuss prospective enteroinsular phenotyping using standardized mixed-meal testing as a testable strategy to investigate interindividual variability in therapeutic response.

Article.Title: ssDNA Wrapping of Single-Walled Carbon Nanotubes and the Role of Sequence Periodicity: A Critical Review
Article.Authors: Al Nissafi L.; Emjeida M.; Venkatesan R.; Vetcher A.
Article.Abstract: Noncovalent hybrids of single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) and single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) are central to chiral sorting and near-infrared biosensing, yet no quantitative rule connects the periodicity of a natural sequence to the geometry of a given nanotube. Earlier reviews treat the sequence as a tool for sorting or sensing; this critical review asks what the published evidence up to 2026 establishes about periodicity. We compare base–wall affinities from calculation, calorimetry and force spectroscopy; the periods reported by cryo-electron microscopy, scanning tunnelling microscopy, atomic force microscopy (AFM) and X-ray scattering in solution; the recognition sequences used for single-chirality sorting; and the few studies of genomic DNA. The experimental order of base affinities depends on the method and on whether the surface is flat or curved. Helical pitches of 1.6–3.3 nm, spacings of 8.6–14.3 nm between strands in solution and the AFM period of about 14 nm are different quantities. Recognition depends on sequence pattern, length, chiral angle and handedness in addition to diameter. To our knowledge, base spacing at fixed composition has been varied only in covalently cross-linked hybrids; for noncovalent wrapping, this test is still missing. We outline the next experiments and the reporting standards and open data they require.

Article.Title: Hormone-Mediated Signaling of Reactive Oxygen Species Under Abiotic Stress
Article.Authors: Fedoreyeva L.; Bursakov S.; Molchanova T.; Muratova O.; Zakharova E.
Article.Abstract: Abiotic stresses trigger the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in various subcellular compartments of plant cells, where they perform a dual function: acting as cytotoxic agents during acute stress and as highly specific signaling modulators under mild or chronic stress. However, the fundamental question of how the cell distinguishes between toxic and signaling ROS pools—and how phytohormones coordinate this distinction—remains unresolved. This review re-examines the molecular logic of the hormone-redox interface, focusing on the post-translational modifications of NADPH oxidases (RBOHs) and antioxidant enzymes as a key mechanism for the rapid tuning of signals. Moving beyond traditional linear cascade models, we propose the concept of a “dynamic hormonal code,” in which abscisic acid acts as the primary initiator of apoplastic ROS bursts via SnRK2-dependent phosphorylation, while salicylates and jasmonates modulate the duration and amplitude of these bursts, thereby determining the outcome—ranging from programmed cell death to systemic resistance. Known mechanisms of the hormonal code have been established (e.g., ABA → SnRK2 → RBOH; SA/JA antagonism mediated by NPR1; and the redox relay involving PRXIIB/GPX3 → ABI2). This review goes beyond simple hormone combinatorics by proposing a conceptual framework: the hormonal code encodes ROS signals through parameters of time, amplitude, and cellular compartment. Particular attention is paid to recent discoveries regarding the roles of auxin and brassinosteroids in reconfiguring chloroplast redox homeostasis during flooding and heat shock. Generalizing these data, we propose an integrated model of spatiotemporal regulation that explains how feedback loops involving ROS, Ca2+ waves, and hormone receptors facilitate systemic acclimation. Thus, targeting key crosstalk nodes—specifically SnRK2 and TOR kinase complexes—offers new strategies for engineering stress-resilient crops in the face of climate change.

Article.Title: Exercise Modalities, Training Dose, and Circulating Myostatin and Follistatin in Adults: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis
Article.Authors: Qiao C.; Yang C.; Guo S.; Yang S.; Wang Y.
Article.Abstract: Exercise-associated changes in circulating myostatin (MSTN) and follistatin (FST) across training modalities remain uncertain. The review included 79 reports from 78 study families; 39 studies contributed primary effects. Exercise was associated with lower MSTN (57 effects; 33 studies; Hedges’ g = 1.25, 95% CI 0.68–1.82) and higher FST (42 effects; 23 studies; g = 1.58, 95% CI 0.92–2.23). Heterogeneity remained high and reference-model prediction intervals crossed zero. Excluding extreme effects attenuated the pooled magnitudes. Graph-exclusion and leave-one-study-out analyses retained positive average-effect intervals. Exploratory modality and dose analyses did not establish superiority or an optimal prescription. GRADE certainty was low for both outcomes. Exercise may alter circulating MSTN and FST, but assay differences, retrieval restrictions and heterogeneous protocols limit interpretation. These findings do not establish a confirmed intracellular mechanism or validated clinical surrogate endpoint.

Article.Title: 2B9-Fc Ameliorates Immune Thrombocytopenia by Suppressing STAT1-Mediated M1 Macrophage Polarization and Expanding Regulatory T Cells
Article.Authors: Yang S.; Xing S.; Shen X.; Zhu W.; Ge M.; Xiao H.; Yu K.; Yu Z.
Article.Abstract: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is an autoimmune bleeding disorder in which enhanced platelet destruction and impaired platelet production coexist, and a substantial proportion of patients remain refractory to available therapies. Here, we evaluated 2B9-Fc, a thrombopoietin (TPO) mimetic peptide engineered from a cyclic peptide with high affinity for both human and mouse c-MPL, in passive (anti-CD41 monoclonal antibody R300) and active (guinea pig anti-mouse platelet serum, GP-APS) immunization male C57BL/6J and humanized c-MPL receptor transgenic mouse models of ITP. 2B9-Fc (500 μg/kg, subcutaneously) significantly elevated peripheral platelet counts in both models (p < 0.01), without affecting WBC, RBC, or hemoglobin, and alleviated skin purpura and bleeding scores in the active model. In humanized c-MPL receptor transgenic (MT) mice, 2B9-Fc promoted CD41+ megakaryocyte generation in vitro and sustained platelet recovery in vivo through day 14. These results indicate that 2B9-Fc ameliorates ITP and is associated with promotion of megakaryocyte maturation and restoration of immune tolerance, likely involving inhibition of STAT1-mediated M1 polarization and Treg expansion, supporting its potential for clinical translation.

Article.Title: Raffinose in Brassica Crops: Integrating Plant Stress Physiology, Food Quality, Nutrition and Precision Breeding
Article.Authors: Czernicka M.; Czernicka M.
Article.Abstract: Raffinose-family oligosaccharides (RFOs) have nutritional and physiological significance that cannot be inferred from concentration alone. In Brassica, interpretation of their food value and definition of breeding targets require consideration of edible organ, environmental history, analytical resolution, and intended use. This critical review integrates evidence on RFO composition, plant physiology, food quality, and nutrition with an evidence-weighted assessment of conventional breeding, genetic transformation, and new genomic techniques. Direct Brassica experiments are distinguished from evidence derived from soybean and Arabidopsis and from prospective applications. Direct studies demonstrate that RFO metabolism in Brassica is manipulable, but they do not support a universal strategy for improving vegetable or meal quality. Genome-editing studies in soybean further show that reductions in total RFOs may coexist with increased raffinose and that lower RFO concentrations do not themselves demonstrate nutritional benefit. Tissue-specific regulation may offer a route to balance seed composition with stress responses, although genotype-dependent regeneration remains an important constraint. A three-tier framework is therefore proposed in which raffinose is interpreted as a stress-responsive metabolite, a potential food-quality indicator, and a context-dependent nutritional component. Compound-specific phenotyping, functional validation, and product-relevant physiological testing should precede deployment of low-RFO or stress-responsive Brassica material.

Article.Abstract: Saussurea involucrata is a medicinal plant rich in flavonoids, but the glycosyltransferases (GTs) responsible for flavonoid glycosylation in this species remain largely uncharacterized. Recombinant proteins were expressed in Escherichia coli as soluble maltose-binding protein (MBP) fusions and purified. In vitro enzymatic assays showed that SiUGT03 catalyzed the 3-O-glucosylation of quercetin to isoquercetin (quercetin-3-O-glucoside), whereas SiRhaT68-1 catalyzed the 1,6-rhamnosylation of isoquercetin to rutin. Among the substrates tested, SiUGT03 was active only toward the flavonols quercetin and kaempferol, while SiRhaT68-1 was active toward isoquercetin and one of the four tested flavone 7-O-glucosides, diosmetin-7-O-glucoside. These results, obtained from separate in vitro assays, demonstrated that the two enzymes catalyze two consecutive terminal glycosylation steps of rutin biosynthesis and represent promising candidates for further exploration of rutin biosynthesis in S. involucrata.

Article.Authors: Dan Y.; Shelef O.; Buzhor M.; Shimon L.; Satchi-Fainaro R.; Shabat D.; Adler-Abramovich L.
Article.Abstract: The interplay between distinct molecular building blocks in multicomponent supramolecular systems can lead to co-assembly or self-sorting, yet distinguishing between these modes of organization remains challenging. These findings establish fluorophore-conjugated short peptides as intrinsically traceable building blocks for investigating multicomponent supramolecular organization, while highlighting that fluorophore conjugation can simultaneously enable visualization and influence the assembly.

Article.Title: Targeted Regulation and Treatment Application of Liquid–Liquid Phase Separation in Human Diseases
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Xu Q.; Liu Y.; Yao K.; Chen N.; Sui G.; Li D.; Zheng J.
Article.Abstract: Liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) is widely recognized as a fundamental mechanism underlying the formation of membraneless organelles, which are critical for maintaining spatiotemporal precision in cellular function. Dysregulation of LLPS has become increasingly recognized as a key driver underlying the development of multiple human diseases, thereby establishing this process as a rapidly growing focus in biomedical research. In this review, we examine the contributions of LLPS to cellular pathophysiology. We start by outlining the fundamental biophysical and molecular principles that govern LLPS formation. We further explore how aberrant phase transitions contribute to disease mechanisms across different organ systems. Building on this mechanistic framework, we assess current and potential therapeutic strategies aimed at targeting LLPS for clinical intervention. Overall, this review aims to synthesize current understanding of LLPS in disease etiology and to highlight its potential as a novel target for future therapeutic development.

Article.Title: The Impact of Intratumoral Bacterial Response to Vaccine Therapy in Cancer Treatment
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Sun Z.; Qi H.; Zhao D.; Xing X.; Jiang J.; Gao T.
Article.Abstract: Therapeutic Human papillomavirus (HPVs) vaccines are designed to enhance the immunogenicity of HPV and promote the elimination of tumor cells effectively. Mounting evidence implies that tumor-resident microbiomes may influence therapeutic outcomes through immune modulation. In this study, we evaluated whether the intratumoral microbiota affects the efficacy of the therapeutic HPV vaccine. We analyzed RNA sequencing data from tumor tissues of C57BL/6N female mice treated with a DNA vaccine incorporating HPV16 E6/E7 antigens fused with the chemokine CCL11. Microbial community data were acquired using the PathSeq bioinformatics pipeline. Alpha diversity was estimated using the Shannon index and the number of observed taxonomic features, while beta diversity was assessed via principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) based on Bray–Curtis distance. Linear discriminant analysis Effect Size (LEfSe) analysis was performed to identify differentially abundant microbial taxa. Immune cell infiltration was characterized using the xCell deconvolution method. The analysis revealed significant divergence in both the alpha- and beta-diversity metrics of intratumoral microbiota, associated with treatment responsiveness. Vaccinated groups exhibited enriched abundances of the phyla Proteobacteria, together with a concomitant reduction in Firmicutes and Actinobacteria, and were associated with a positive response to cancer immunotherapy. Additionally, intratumoral microbiome composition and diversity correlated with the increased infiltration of CD8+ T cells, natural killer T (NKT) cells, and myeloid cells. This study identifies intratumoral microbiota remodeling as a key feature of therapeutic HPV vaccine response. The observed coordination between bacterial signatures and immune cell infiltration is associative and raises the hypothesis that intratumoral bacteria may modulate, rather than drive, antitumor immunity. These findings support the development of intratumoral microbiota profiling and highlight the potential for microbiota-targeted strategies to enhance cancer immunotherapy efficacy.

Article.Title: Thylakoid Nanoarchitecture and Photosystem II Energy Partitioning in Response to Treatment with Huminatrin Concentrate “Boron”
Article.Authors: Bukhanov E.; Gaevsky N.; Poznakhareva O.; Tikhomirov A.; Ushakova S.; Shabanov V.
Article.Abstract: Photosynthetic acclimation involves coordinated changes in the structural organization and functional activity of the photosynthetic apparatus. However, the structural basis underlying enhanced photosynthetic activity following biostimulant treatment under non-stress conditions remains insufficiently understood. In the present study, we investigated the effects of exogenous application of the humic-boron fertilizer Huminatrin Concentrate “Boron” on the structural and functional organization of the photosynthetic apparatus in spring rapeseed (Brassica napus L.) cv. Siberian. Thylakoid and granum architecture was characterized using transmission electron microscopy and quantitative morphometric analysis, whereas photosynthetic function was assessed using pulse-amplitude-modulated (PAM) chlorophyll fluorescence. Huminatrin treatment was associated with changes in granum organization, including a reduction in the stacking repeat distance (SRD), as well as increases in the apparent electron transport rate (ETR) and the effective quantum yield of photosystem II (PSII) photochemistry (Y(II)). Redistribution of PSII excitation energy was accompanied by a decrease in the regulatory quantum yield in PSII (Y(NPQ)) and an increase in the non-regulated energy loss in PSII (Y(NO)). These changes occurred without evidence of pronounced PSII photoinhibition, indicating that the observed changes in PSII photochemistry were not a response to experimentally induced stress. Structural and functional changes were accompanied by increases in plant and leaf biomass. Taken together, these findings indicate that leaf biostimulation is associated with coordinated remodeling of thylakoid architecture and PSII excitation-energy partitioning under the experimental conditions studied.

Article.Title: Selective PAC1 Receptor Antagonist, PA-810-04 Attenuates Oxaliplatin-Induced Hyperexcitability and Coordinated Firing in Cultured Dorsal Root Ganglion Neurons
Article.Authors: Arima T.; Takahama K.; Suetsugu K.; Kobae Y.; Iwai H.; Takasaki I.; Kurihara T.; Terazono H.
Article.Abstract: Oxaliplatin-induced peripheral neuropathy (OIPN) is a major dose-limiting adverse effect of chemotherapy, and dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons are its principal targets. Although pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP)/PAC1 receptor signaling has been implicated in neuropathic pain, its contribution to the oxaliplatin-induced hyperexcitability of primary sensory neurons remains unknown. We used a dual-axis multi-electrode array (MEA) platform quantifying the total spike count (TSC) and synchronous spike ratio (SSR), indices of overall activity and coordinated firing. Short-term oxaliplatin exposure produced concentration-dependent increases in TSC and SSR in cultured DRG neurons, which were significantly attenuated by the selective PAC1 receptor antagonist, PA-810-04. Similarly, conditioned medium from oxaliplatin-treated satellite glial cell (SGC)-enriched cultures increased TSC and SSR in naïve DRG neurons, and these effects were suppressed by PA-810-04. Exogenous PACAP alone increased TSC concentration-dependently, with only a modest effect on SSR, as a positive control. These findings identify a PA-810-04-sensitive component of early oxaliplatin-induced hyperexcitability in primary sensory neurons, while the proposed neuron–glia mechanism remains hypothetical. They also provide a quantitative in vitro approach for investigating neuron–glia interactions in early OIPN and evaluating PAC1-targeted candidates.

Article.Title: Immunometabolic Memory in Obesity: Nutritional Drivers, Persistence, and Reversibility
Article.Authors: Reytor-González C.; Zambrano-Villacres R.; Andrade Mejia N.; Duran-Agüero S.; Simancas-Racines D.
Article.Abstract: Obesity reshapes immune function across adipose tissue, circulation, and hematopoietic compartments. Weight reduction improves cardiometabolic health, yet emerging evidence indicates that prior obesity can leave persistent cellular, transcriptional, and epigenetic changes. Whether nutrition can reverse this biological imprint remains uncertain. We conducted a critical narrative review informed by structured searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library, and Epistemonikos, complemented by backward and forward citation tracking. We prioritized mechanistic human studies, controlled dietary interventions, longitudinal weight-loss studies, and experiments that tested persistence after stimulus withdrawal or response to re-exposure. Evidence was interpreted according to biological compartment and study design rather than pooled statistically. Obesogenic exposures can alter innate immune metabolism, inflammasome signaling, hematopoiesis, and chromatin states. Animal studies provide the strongest evidence that these changes can persist after weight normalization and amplify responses during weight regain. Human studies show incomplete normalization of adipose immune states, persistent adipocyte programs, and durable methylation changes in T lymphocytes after weight loss. Dietary interventions can lower inflammatory tone and modify immune metabolism, microbial metabolites, and lipid mediator pathways, but no dietary pattern has been shown to erase established obesity-associated immune memory in humans. An evidence map built on a core set of 47 studies showed that experimental work dominates the induction, persistence and re-challenge domains, whereas human evidence clusters in post-weight-loss remodelling and dietary modulation; human re-challenge data were absent and no study provided a direct test of reversal in humans. Obesity-associated immunometabolic memory appears to be distributed across hematopoietic, immune, adipose, stromal, and microbial compartments. Nutrition can modulate mechanisms implicated in this persistence, but human evidence of reversal is lacking, and whether pharmacologically induced weight loss leaves a comparable imprint has not been tested. Mechanistic trials should separate energy deficit, diet composition, adiposity change, and weight-loss modality and include a weight-stable follow-up and functional re-challenge where feasible.

Article.Title: A Comparative Analysis of Microglial and Astrocyte Transplantation in an Amyloid-Induced Rat for Alzheimer’s Disease
Article.Authors: Curecheriu L.; Iliescu B.; Stanciu G.; Mazarianu I.; Szilagyi A.; Gogu M.; Ciorpac M.; Balmus I.; Tutu P.; Horodincu L.; Daraban Bocaneti F.; Hritcu O.; Pasca A.; Tamba B.; Turliuc M.
Article.Abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is recognized as a neuroglial disorder in which dysregulated glial responses contribute to cognitive decline. We investigated whether intrahippocampal transplantation of primary glial cells modifies cognitive trajectories in an amyloid-induced rat model of AD. Sprague–Dawley rats received bilateral hippocampal injections of pre-aggregated Aβ1–42, followed by transplantation of primary astrocytes (AA) or microglia (AM). Memory was assessed using the Y-maze and novel object recognition (NOR) tests. Body weight and serum IL-6 and TNF-α were monitored for adverse effects, and GFAP, S100, Iba1 and TREM2 immunolabeling was quantified with QuPath. Mixed-effects models showed significant session and group x session effects on Y–maze spatial novelty recognition. Both treated groups improved compared with AD animals, with a stronger late effect in the AM group and a significant group × session × sex interaction. In the NOR test, both treated groups outperformed AD animals at the final session, without differences between them. GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein) immunoreactivity was reduced in the AM group but remained elevated in the AA group, while TREM2 increased after microglial and decreased after astrocyte transplantation. No adverse effects were detected in the monitored parameters. Intrahippocampal glial transplantation, particularly with microglia, may influence cognitive trajectories in established amyloid pathology.

Article.Title: An Epigenetically Remodeled EMT–Inflammatory Clone Associated with Spatial Immune Exclusion in Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma
Article.Authors: Lan R.; Weng L.; Cao B.; Li A.; Zhang J.; Shi H.; Yang L.; Lv Y.
Article.Abstract: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) exhibits intra-tumoral heterogeneity and spatial complexity that restrict immune infiltration, yet the malignant populations driving spatial immune exclusion remain elusive. We integrated scRNA-seq, paired scATAC-seq, spatial transcriptomics, and multiple bulk cohorts to identify the malignant subpopulation driving ccRCC progression. Multi-omics analyses, including malignancy inference, epigenomic profiling, cell–cell communication, and spatial modeling, characterized its molecular features and clinical relevance. We identified a malignant subpopulation co-activating epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) and inflammatory programs, termed the aggressive EMT–inflammatory clone (AEIC). AEIC exhibited pronounced genomic instability, enhanced stemness, and poor prognosis across multicenter cohorts (p < 0.001). Chromatin accessibility revealed a MAZ/RUNX1-centered network driving key AEIC signature genes such as TGFBI and COL6A2. Cell–cell communication analysis suggested AEIC interacts with NK_CD16− cells via the COL6A2–(ITGA1+ITGB1) axis. Spatial analyses showed AEIC-enriched regions forming an extracellular matrix-rich barrier associated with NK_CD16− cell exclusion, M2-like macrophage polarization, and increased genomic instability. Finally, an AEIC-derived 16-gene signature stratified prognosis across independent cohorts and was associated with distinct drug-sensitivity patterns, including increased predicted sensitivity to Bortezomib and AZD4547. Overall, AEIC is associated with spatial and epigenetic remodeling in ccRCC, and the AEIC-derived signature supports prognostic stratification and further exploration of potential therapeutic vulnerabilities associated with the AEIC phenotype.

Article.Title: Construction of a GCSCs-Related Prognostic Risk Model Based on Transcriptomic Data
Article.Authors: Hu X.; Fan S.; Liu N.; Fan M.; Wu Y.; Shi G.; Su Y.; Liu L.; Chen X.
Article.Abstract: Gastric Cancer Stem Cells (GCSCs) contribute to tumor progression and treatment resistance, but their heterogeneity and tumor microenvironment interactions remain unclear. We analyzed GSE163558 single-cell RNA-sequencing data from 10 gastric cancer samples and integrated GCSC-related genes with The Cancer Genome Atlas Stomach Adenocarcinoma (TCGA-STAD) training cohort (n = 448) and two independent external validation cohorts, GSE62254 (n = 300) and GSE84437 (n = 483), to construct and validate a six-gene prognostic risk model. Cell–cell communication, metabolic activity, immune infiltration, immunotherapy response, and drug sensitivity were evaluated. Nine cell populations, including a putative GCSC population, were identified. GCSCs showed higher inferred oxidative phosphorylation activity and extensive predicted interactions with tumor-associated cells. The model stratified patients into distinct prognostic groups. High-risk tumors exhibited enrichment of progression-related pathways, including epithelial–mesenchymal transition, and distinct immune features. In PRJEB25780 (n = 78), higher risk scores were associated with immunotherapy non-response, whereas an exploratory analysis of GSE91061 (n = 49) showed a similar trend. The model may support prognostic stratification and provide insights into potential associations with therapeutic response, pending prospective validation.

Article.Title: Physiological and Transcriptome Analysis of Polygonatum cyrtonema Under Continuous Drought Stress
Article.Authors: Xu X.; Cheng S.
Article.Abstract: Against the backdrop of global warming and the increasingly uneven distribution of water resources, drought has emerged as a critical abiotic stressor limiting the growth and quality formation of medicinal plants. In this study, Polygonatum cyrtonema was subjected to a continuous drought treatment experiment by withholding water for 5, 10, and 20 days, alongside a well-watered control (CK), to preliminarily investigate its physiological responses and transcriptomic alterations under water-deficit conditions. Physiological measurements revealed that prolonged drought stress significantly increased the concentrations of malondialdehyde (MDA) and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) in leaves, accompanied by elevated in superoxide dismutase (SOD) and peroxidase (POD) activities, as well as increased chlorophyll content. RNA-seq analysis identified a substantial number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs), with 11,835, 12,110, and 11,416 DEGs in the D5, D10, and D20 vs. CK comparisons, respectively, including 6133 shared core DEGs. KEGG enrichment analysis indicated that these DEGs were primarily involved in starch and sucrose metabolism, phenylpropanoid biosynthesis, and plant hormone signal transduction. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) identified a specific gene module (black module) containing 1681 genes that was highly positively correlated with drought duration (r = 0.95). Protein–protein interaction (PPI) network analysis of this module highlighted several candidate hub genes, including WRKY33 (BMK_Unigene_251623), EDA39 (BMK_Unigene_034545), OHP (BMK_Unigene_221621), and RD20 (BMK_Unigene_149641). Furthermore, genes within the black module were significantly enriched in metabolic pathways such as anthocyanin, phenylpropanoid, and isoflavonoid biosynthesis, as well as phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan, arginine, and proline metabolism. RT-qPCR validation confirmed the expression patterns of these candidate genes, supporting the reliability of the transcriptomic data. Collectively, these findings provide transcriptomic insights into the continuous drought response in P. cyrtonema, and identify candidate genes and pathways for future functional validation and stress-resilience improvement in this species.
