Article.Title: Recent Developments in Chemo-Photodynamic Nanoplatforms for Glioblastoma Treatment
Article.Authors: Woźnicki P.; Aebisher D.
Article.Abstract: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) remains one of the most difficult malignant brain tumours to treat due to its infiltrative nature, cellular heterogeneity, resistance to treatment and limited drug penetration across the blood–brain barrier. The combination of photodynamic therapy (PDT) with chemotherapy within a single nanoplatform offers the possibility of integrating the photogeneration of reactive oxygen species with the cytotoxic action of chemotherapeutic agents, whilst improving their coordinated delivery to tumour cells. This review summarises the latest nanoparticle-based strategies combining PDT and chemotherapy in the treatment of GBM. The literature published between January 2025 and August 2026 was identified using the PubMed, Web of Science and Scopus databases. The systems analysed included photoreactive organic nanoaggregates, ZnO-based nanocomposites, lipid nanocarriers, dual-targeting liposomes and platforms based on covalent organic frameworks. These nanoplatforms enabled various forms of therapeutic integration, including light-triggered drug release, co-encapsulation of photosensitisers and chemotherapeutic agents, targeting of mitochondria, and targeting of glioma cells and blood–brain barrier models via ligands. The available studies have generally demonstrated increased cytotoxicity following photoactivation, and selected systems have shown synergistic effects between chemotherapy and PDT. However, the available evidence is insufficient to support the translational readiness of the currently reported chemo-PDT nanoplatforms. Three of the five systems were evaluated only in vitro, only one was investigated in an orthotopic glioma model, and several studies relied on surrogate metabolic assays or irradiation conditions of limited relevance to deep intracranial disease. The current literature should therefore be regarded primarily as proof-of-concept evidence for coordinated chemo-PDT delivery rather than as evidence of clinically applicable therapy. Progress towards clinical relevance will require platforms designed around realistic light-delivery constraints, the hypoxic GBM microenvironment, brain-relevant delivery routes and therapeutically meaningful in vivo endpoints.

Article.Title: Fibrin Clot Properties in Aneurysmal Coronary Artery Disease: CARE-ANEURYSM Study
Article.Authors: Chmiel J.; Kopytek M.; Dąbrowski M.; Iwańczyk S.; Musiał K.; Woźniak P.; Chmiel J.; Partyka Ł.; Ząbczyk M.; Natorska J.; Musiałek P.
Article.Abstract: Coronary artery ectasias and aneurysms (CAEAs) are present in up to 5% of patients undergoing coronary angiography. Recent studies indicated an independent association between CAEA and the risk of myocardial infarction but the underlying mechanisms have not yet been elucidated. We evaluated the relationship between CAEA and fibrin clot properties in 60 consecutive CAEA subjects and 60 clinically/angiographically matched controls enrolled across three tertiary centers. Fibrin clot permeability coefficient (Ks), clot lysis time (CLT), and levels of 3-nitrotyrosine, an oxidative stress marker, were assessed. Among patients with CAEA, 52 (86.7%) were male, the median age was 66.0 (59.5–74.1) years, and 30 (50.0%) had concomitant coronary artery disease. Compared with controls, CAEA subjects had 14% lower Ks (p = 0.036), 25% longer CLT (p = 0.001), and 21% higher 3-nitrotyrosine levels (p = 0.002). Multivariable regression analysis showed an association of CAEA with lower Ks, longer CLT, and higher 3-nitrotyrosine levels (all p < 0.05). In CAEA patients, 3-nitrotyrosine levels correlated with Ks (r = −0.31, p = 0.016) and CLT (r = 0.27, p = 0.037). With increasing CAEA peak-to-reference diameter ratio, Ks decreased (p-trend = 0.017), and 3-nitrotyrosine levels increased (p-trend = 0.002). In conclusion, we found that CAEA is independently associated with unfavorably altered fibrin clot properties, reflected by denser clot structure and reduced susceptibility to fibrinolysis. Our findings suggest that oxidative stress may contribute to unfavorable modification of fibrin clot properties in CAEA. With an increase in CAEA size, there is an increase in oxidative stress and worsening of the fibrin clot phenotype (CARE-ANEURYSM, NCT05183373).

Article.Title: The Oral–Gut–Systemic Axis in Periodontitis: Microbiome Dysbiosis, Immune Crosstalk and Translational Perspectives
Article.Authors: Mochol M.; Kulig H.; Rączka A.; Lipski M.; Marek E.; Schuster L.; Dammaschke T.; Mazurek-Mochol M.
Article.Abstract: Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease associated with subgingival dysbiosis and altered host response. Although it is usually considered a local disease of the tooth-supporting tissues, it may also interact with distant mucosal and systemic compartments. One possible explanation is the oral–gut–systemic axis. In this model, oral bacteria, microbial products and inflammatory mediators are swallowed and reach the gastrointestinal tract. In susceptible hosts, these signals may affect gut microbial ecology, epithelial barrier integrity, mucosal immunity and microbial metabolite pathways. Human studies show links between periodontitis, altered oral and gut microbial communities, oral–gut microbial signatures and systemic metabolomic changes. Experimental studies provide stronger mechanistic support. They suggest that periodontal pathogens, particularly Porphyromonas gingivalis, may promote gut dysbiosis, barrier dysfunction, endotoxemia, inflammasome activation, T helper 17/regulatory T cell (Th17/Treg) imbalance and changes in metabolite signaling pathways. Candidate pathways include aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) signaling, suppression of G protein-coupled receptor 109A (GPR109A), short-chain fatty acid-related pathways and trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) metabolism. Inflammatory bowel disease is currently the most developed disease-specific model. Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), rheumatoid arthritis, cardiometabolic metabolite pathways and gastrointestinal cancer models are less mature extensions. This review summarizes current evidence and identifies the need for longitudinal studies, strain-level source tracking, multi-omics, immune phenotyping and disease-specific intervention studies. At present, the concept is biologically plausible, but clinical translation remains premature.

Article.Title: Actions of Pharmaceutical Lactones and Lactams on the Enzymes with Lactonase Activity: In Silico Prediction and In Vitro Study
Article.Authors: Efremenko E.; Domnin M.; Sarapina A.; Zagidulina A.
Article.Abstract: Pharmaceutical pollutants that contain lactone or lactam rings in their structure are frequently detected in wastewater. Enzymes with lactonase activity, synthesized by the microorganisms in aerobic activated sludge, are expected to be able to participate in the hydrolysis of these pharmaceutical pollutants, but the actual activity of many lactonases towards such compounds remains poorly characterized. In this work, a systematic molecular docking study of 12 enzymes and 39 pharmaceutical pollutants (β-lactam antibiotics, macrolides, coumarins, statins) was undertaken. The binding affinity, active-site occupancy, total enzyme surface occupancy and geometric characteristics of the molecules (the distance from the catalytic nucleophile to the carbonyl carbon of the lactone ring, and the attack angle formed between the nucleophilic atom of the enzyme and the C–N/C–O bond of the substrate) were evaluated in silico for a set of hydrolases displaying lactonase activity (AidC, AaL, hexahistidine-tagged organophosphate hydrolase (His6-OPH), etc.) and metallo-β-lactamases (MβLs) (NDM-1, MIM-1, SAM-1). Lactamases exhibited favorable intermolecular interaction geometry for the majority of β-lactams. No enzyme was found that satisfied the geometric criteria corresponding to the biodegradation of macrolides. With coumarins, only Paraoxonase PON2 provided an optimal geometry of biocatalysis; however, this enzyme is absent from activated sludge but may be of interest for in vivo applications. For several statins widely used in practice, combinations with enzymes having virtually ideal geometry for biocatalysis were identified: AidC/rosuvastatin lactone, AaL/lovastatin, His6-OPH/mevastatin, and PON2/simvastatin. For the first time, several pharmaceutical lactones were identified in silico and confirmed in vitro as inhibitors of MβL and His6-OPH. Competitive inhibition of NDM-1 by lactone-containing signaling molecules of Gram-negative bacteria present in activated sludge was revealed for the first time both in silico and in vitro. The obtained results‘ may be taken into account when implementing monitoring of biological stages at water treatment stations and improve the efficiency of water purification. The revealed characteristics of MβL inhibition by macrolides may be taken into account as one of possible explanations for the effective application of β-lactams in combinations with macrolides known from multiple paratactical investigations.

Article.Title: Contrasting Effects of Chitosan Molecular Modifications on the Properties of Fish Gelatin Hydrogels
Article.Authors: Nikiforova A.; Abramov V.; Skvortsova P.; Akhmadiyarov A.; Rakipov I.; Sorokin A.; Lavlinskaya M.; Zueva O.; Holyavka M.; Derkach S.; Zuev Y.
Article.Abstract: The limited water solubility of chitosan, which necessitates acidic conditions for its dissolution, restricts its application in food and pharmaceutical systems. To overcome this limitation, we chemically modified a chitosan molecule by introducing hydrophilic groups and compared three chitosan forms—unmodified chitosan, its quaternary ammonium derivative, and a graft copolymer with poly-N-vinylpyrrolidone, with respect to their effect on the structural and mechanical properties of fish gelatin hydrogels. An experimental study combining NMR relaxometry and water self-diffusion measurements, scanning electron microscopy, and rheology revealed a distinct supramolecular architecture of gelatin–chitosan hydrogel network for different chitosan modifications. The NMR data gave information on the molecular mobility of water as a marker of hydrogel structure to elucidate molecular basis for the observed rheological properties. Unmodified chitosan maximally reinforces gelatin network and enhances its thermorheological stability. Chitosan grafting with poly-N-vinylpyrrolidone produces a fine-pored xerogel structure with higher thermorheological stability, possibly through a non-cooperative reinforcement mechanism. The quaternary ammonium derivative results in a heterogeneous xerogel morphology with weak mechanical strength and low gel–sol transition temperature. These findings establish the structure–property correlation, demonstrating that chitosan modification governs the molecular network architecture and macroscopic performance of gelatin-based hydrogels, providing molecular-level insights into the behavior of fish gelatin–chitosan systems.

Article.Title: Central Nervous System Toxoplasmosis Beyond HIV in Patients with Hematologic Malignancies: A Contemporary Narrative Review and Illustrative Case Synthesis
Article.Authors: Łanocha A.; Pawelec-Pęciak O.; Kot K.; Machaliński B.; Kosik-Bogacka D.; Łanocha-Arendarczyk N.
Article.Abstract: Toxoplasmosis is an important opportunistic infection in immunocompromised individuals, typically resulting from reactivation of latent Toxoplasma gondii infection. CNS toxoplasmosis, most commonly presenting as toxoplasmic encephalitis (TE), is rare in patients with hematologic malignancies and after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). It is nevertheless life-threatening and likely underrecognized. This narrative review integrates molecular, immunological, clinical, and transplant-related evidence on T. gondii persistence and reactivation, treatment-associated immune dysfunction, diagnosis, management, prophylaxis, and molecular surveillance. Risk reflects cumulative immunosuppression, particularly impaired T-cell reconstitution, lymphocyte-depleting therapy, corticosteroid exposure, cytopenias, hypogammaglobulinemia, and absent or ineffective prophylaxis. Typical ring-enhancing lesions, positive serology, and detectable T. gondii DNA in cerebrospinal fluid may all be absent. Diagnosis therefore requires integration of immune and treatment history, magnetic resonance imaging, molecular testing, and, when necessary, histopathology. When clinical suspicion is high, empiric therapy should not be delayed; however, diagnostic specimens should be obtained whenever feasible, and evaluation for alternative diagnoses should proceed in parallel. In seropositive allogeneic HSCT recipients, trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis with quantitative PCR surveillance remains the best-established preventive strategy.

Article.Title: A Double-Edged Sword: The Dichotomous Roles of Dendritic Cell Subsets in Shaping CD8+ T Cell Immunity and Tolerance Within the Tumor Microenvironment
Article.Authors: Gao G.; Chen K.
Article.Abstract: Dendritic cells (DCs) function as a double-edged sword in tumor immunity, capable of both activating and tolerizing CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs). While conventional type 1 dendritic cells (cDC1s) are well-established mediators of cross-presentation for initiating anti-tumor CTL responses, existing reviews—largely overlook the tolerogenic potential of cDC1s and the context-dependent immunostimulatory capacity of cDC2s, monocyte-derived DCs (moDCs), and plasmacytoid DCs (pDCs). Furthermore, no prior synthesis has systematically reconciled the divergent functions of DC subsets across steady-state versus inflammatory conditions, migratory versus resident phenotypes, and human versus mouse model systems. The tumor microenvironment (TME) and tumor-derived exosomes further drive DCs toward an immunosuppressive phenotype, facilitating immune escape. Here, we establish a multi-dimensional framework that dissects the dichotomous roles of diverse DC subsets in regulating CTL immunity and tolerance, resolving key biological contradictions—including recent in vivo evidence that cDC2s can cross-present immune-complexed antigens via a WDFY4-dependent pathway shared with cDC1s—an activity that complements, but does not replace, the cDC1-restricted cross-presentation of cell-associated antigens. We also provide a hierarchical analysis of strategies to restore DC-mediated anti-tumor activity, extending the DC–CTL regulatory paradigm to autoimmunity and solid organ transplantation. A comprehensive summary table categorizes DC-based therapeutic approaches by clinical development stage. By elucidating this dynamic balancing mechanism, we offer refined insights for optimizing cancer immunotherapy design and cross-disciplinary therapeutic applications.

Article.Title: CATCH-EVseq, an Ultra-Sensitive Capture Assay to Monitor Human Enterovirus RNA
Article.Authors: Germain A.; Hanson M.
Article.Abstract: The detection of low-abundance viral RNA in chronic or persistent infections remains a major challenge in virology, constrained by the sensitivity and specificity of traditional methods. One such infection, chronic enterovirus (EV) infection, has been proposed as a potential underlying factor in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis (ME), although this hypothesis remains debated. Supporting evidence for EVs as a viral trigger includes historical spatiotemporal overlaps between ME outbreaks and poliomyelitis epidemics, frequent reports of “flu-like” illness at disease onset, seasonal outbreaks patterns, and serological findings. To address the problem of EV detection, we developed CATCH-EVseq, an ultra-sensitive platform built on the CATCH framework. By integrating high-throughput sequencing with cDNA capture using 49,847 probes targeting 3410 EV genomes, CATCH-EVseq achieved a detection limit in artificially created samples as low as one copy in a microgram of RNA for two out of three biological replicates. Additionally, spike-in controls allow for rigorous validation of the capture and sequencing throughout the CATCH-EVseq procedure. When applied to a small number of blood samples from both ME patients and healthy controls, CATCH-EVseq detected no EV RNA, either in direct assays or after in vitro viral amplification. While these results do not support the presence of circulating EV RNA in the blood of individuals with ME, they do not rule out persistent infection in other tissues or organs. Critically, CATCH-EVseq establishes a robust, ultra-sensitive framework for future investigations of low-level EV persistence in biopsies, post-mortem tissues, or other clinical contexts where chronic enterovirus infection is suspected.

Article.Title: Multiscale Interactome Analysis Prioritizes Candidate Herbs and Compounds for Diabetic Retinopathy
Article.Authors: Ahn Y.; Chae J.; Han S.; Lee W.; Park C.
Article.Abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR), a leading cause of preventable vision loss among working-age adults, arises from chronic hyperglycemic injury to the retinal microvasculature; current interventions such as anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) injection are largely reactive, and mechanism-anchored herbal options remain undefined. We constructed a multiscale interactome and applied a biased random-walk diffusion model to prioritize herbal candidates, candidate compounds, and mechanisms for DR. Herb–ingredient records were drawn from OASIS; ingredient targets from DrugBank, TTD, and STITCH; and disease genes from DisGeNET. For each herb and compound, we computed diffusion profiles, correlated them with the DR profile, and assessed target-overlap significance by hypergeometric test. Eleven herbs combining high correlation (top 5%) with significant overlap (p < 0.05) were retained, led by Pini Koraiensis Semen (0.0263), Benincasae Exocarpium (0.0183), and Veratri Rhizoma Et Radix (0.0162); none had been previously investigated for DR. CASP3 emerged as a target shared by all eleven herbs, and enrichment analysis highlighted the advanced glycation end product–receptor for AGE (AGE–RAGE), TNF, IL-17, and NF-κB pathways alongside apoptosis and reactive-oxygen-species responses. Compound-level analysis recovered evidence-supported quercetin, resveratrol, oleic acid, luteolin, and diosgenin and nominated tectorigenin and cucurbitacins as novel candidates. This framework recapitulates known DR biology and elevates testable multi-target leads that warrant experimental validation for diabetic retinopathy.

Article.Title: SGLT2 Inhibition Combined with Zn Supplementation Protects the Liver-Pancreas Axis in Experimental Type 2 Diabetes
Article.Authors: Anton I.; Solcan C.; Mititelu-Tartau L.; Amalinei C.; Poroch M.; Poroch V.; Buca B.; Tartau C.; Pelin A.; Jitareanu A.; Boldeanu M.; Botnariu G.
Article.Abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is associated with chronic hyperglycemia, inflammation, and progressive hepatic and pancreatic dysfunction. Although sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors exert metabolic and organ-protective effects, their ability to preserve pancreatic architecture and attenuate diabetes-associated hepatic injury, particularly combined with nutritional interventions, remains insufficiently explored. This study investigated the protective effects of dapagliflozin (DAPA) and empagliflozin (EMPA), alone or combined with zinc (Zn), on hepatic and pancreatic alterations in experimental diabetes. Methods: Diabetes was induced in male Sprague–Dawley rats using streptozotocin (STZ) and high fat diet (HFD). Diabetic animals received DAPA, EMPA, Zn, or SGLT2 inhibitor–Zn combinations for four weeks. Hepatic biochemical parameters, lipid profile, histopathology, pancreatic morphometry, and insulin immunoreactivity were evaluated. Diabetes induced hepatic and pancreatic alterations, including elevated liver injury markers, hepatocellular degeneration, reduced islet number and β-cell density, and diminished insulin immunoreactivity. DAPA and EMPA attenuated these changes, with greater improvements following Zn combination therapy. EMPA + Zn produced the most favorable response, improving hepatic architecture, reducing VCAM-1, ICAM-1, and NF-κB expression, preserving islet morphology, increasing β-cell density, and enhancing insulin immunoreactivity. SGLT2 inhibitors attenuated diabetes-associated hepatic and pancreatic alterations in this experimental model, while Zn supplementation was associated with additional tissue-preserving effects, particularly when combined with EMPA. These findings support further investigation of combined SGLT2 inhibition and Zn supplementation as an experimental approach to diabetes-associated organ injury; however, their clinical relevance remains to be established.

Article.Title: Three Cases of Levodopa–Carbidopa Responsive Nocturnal Akinesis in Male Children of an Inbred Family in Rural Baluchistan, Pakistan
Article.Authors: Akram J.; Ghaffar A.; Usmani M.; Shareef U.; Ahmed Z.; Riazuddin S.; Riazuddin S.
Article.Abstract: After more than 9 years of follow-up, we describe three affected male siblings from a consanguineous family (PKSOK) in rural Baluchistan, Pakistan, who presented with levodopa–carbidopa responsive nocturnal akinesia associated with tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency. The affected individuals also show delayed motor milestones, mild intellectual disability, speech and psychomotor delay, without epilepsy, spasticity, cerebellar ataxia, or daytime motor weakness. The marked improvement in nocturnal motor symptoms following levodopa–carbidopa (100 mg/25 mg) treatment raised the possibility of an underlying disorder of dopamine biosynthesis. Exome sequencing of the two affected siblings (IV:16 and IV:18) revealed twenty rare (frequency < 0.001) homozygous coding variants shared between them. However, segregation analysis with the disease phenotype ruled out the potential involvement of all these twenty variants. Therefore, we extended the analysis beyond the coding region variants to non-coding variants, which revealed a homozygous variant, c.-70G>A, in the regulatory region of TH (tyrosine hydroxylase). The c.-70G>A variant has been previously reported in three studies; however, our study represents the first report in the South Asian population. Our study also expands the phenotypic spectrum of disorders associated with variants in TH and highlights the importance of considering variants in regulatory regions of TH in patients with atypical but levodopa-responsive neurological phenotypes.

Article.Title: Serum Proteomic Profiling by SomaScan Aptamer Array Identifies Candidate Predictive and Monitoring Biomarkers of Distant Recurrence in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer
Article.Authors: Kim J.; Tanaka S.; Fosah E.; Jinno C.; Kim H.; Prathifkumar T.; Fukui Y.; Kawanishi K.; Kawashima M.; Masuda N.; Levy J.; Fujii T.; You S.; Furuya H.
Article.Abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) lacks a blood-based biomarker for predicting or monitoring distant recurrence. We profiled 39 serum samples from 38 women (10 healthy controls; 12 non-recurrent [NR]; eight diagnosis-timepoint samples from patients who later recurred [DR-DIG]; nine recurrence-timepoint samples [DR-REC]) using the SomaScan v5.0 aptamer platform). Public tumor-tissue transcriptomic cohorts were used for supportive and exploratory analyses. No protein reached a false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05 for NR vs. DR-DIG; granzyme A (GZMA) and endoplasmic reticulum aminopeptidase 1 (ERAP1) showed the strongest nominal signals. For DR-DIG vs. DR-REC, 38 aptamers (37 proteins) reached FDR < 0.05, enriched for RNA-binding and nuclear-envelope proteins; this signature was retained in leave-one-out and storage-adjusted analyses. Higher GZMA mRNA was associated with longer recurrence-free survival in two independent cohorts (hazard ratio [HR] = 0.795, p = 0.018; HR = 0.186, p = 0.0057). Monitor genes showed near-chance concordance with metastatic tissue, and the source of the signature could not be resolved. An exploratory four-gene elastic-net panel reached a concordance index of 0.613 internally but 0.559 externally. GZMA is a candidate serum biomarker of TNBC recurrence risk, and the monitor signature is a preliminary observation. Both require protein-level validation in independent, prospectively collected serum cohorts.

Article.Title: Thyroid Eye Disease in the Teprotumumab Era: Pathophysiology, Clinical Activity Assessment, and an Updated Therapeutic Landscape
Article.Authors: Shooshani T.; Cherupalla B.; Durand A.; Aung M.
Article.Abstract: Thyroid eye disease (TED), the principal extrathyroidal manifestation of Graves’ disease, is an autoimmune orbitopathy. The pathophysiology involves aberrant thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor (TSHR) and insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF-1R) signaling on orbital fibroblasts, leading to glycosaminoglycan accumulation, adipogenesis, inflammatory edema, and extraocular-muscle enlargement. The active phase is typically self-limited yet medically modifiable, characterized primarily by inflammation, edema, and tissue expansion, whereas chronic inactive disease is dominated by fibrosis and fixed structural change. This US-oriented review aims to provide updates in the field through 2026: (1) summarizing the molecular pathophysiology linking thyroid autoimmunity to orbital remodeling and current drug targets; (2) discussing activity-versus-severity assessment, with appraisal of the Clinical Activity Score (CAS); and (3) explaining the complementary roles of different structural and functional imaging modalities in the evaluation and management of TED. We then follow the therapeutic ladder, from conservative measures through the employment of glucocorticoids and steroid-sparing immunosuppression to the use of targeted biologics. We give particular attention to IGF-1R inhibition, including the use of teprotumumab and veligrotug, and to post-approval results, including otologic and metabolic adverse-event burden, recurrence, treatment sequencing, and the emerging efficacy of the treatment of chronic and low-activity disease. The CAS’s limited inter-observer reliability identifies additional reproducible activity measures as an open need.

Article.Title: Scaffolds and Artificial Augmentations for Tendon Repair
Article.Authors: Kordahji G.; Yakoby D.; Kaplan B.
Article.Abstract: Tendon injuries are common musculoskeletal disorders that represent a significant clinical challenge due to the limited regenerative capacity of tendon tissue. Although surgical repair remains the standard treatment for severe tendon injuries, healed tendons rarely regain the structural and mechanical properties of native tissue, often resulting in impaired function and an increased risk of re-injury. Recent advances in tissue engineering have introduced biologically active and biomimetic strategies aimed at enhancing tendon healing and promoting functional regeneration. This narrative review summarizes current knowledge of tendon injuries and highlights emerging tissue engineering strategies for tendon repair and regeneration. Emphasis is placed on the design and application of natural and synthetic polymers, scaffold engineering, and the key biological and mechanical characteristics required for successful tendon regeneration. In addition, recent developments in drug delivery systems, mesenchymal stem cell-based therapies, and artificial tendon technologies are discussed. These emerging approaches offer promising alternatives and adjuncts to conventional treatments, with the potential to improve tendon healing and functional recovery. However, further studies are required to optimize these technologies, establish their long-term safety and efficacy, and facilitate their translation into routine clinical practice.

Article.Title: High-Entropy Alloy-Engineered ZnIn2S4 Photocatalyst for Efficient In Vitro Eradication of MRSA and Inhibition of Biofilm Formation via ROS-Mediated Mechanisms
Article.Authors: Chen X.; Zhou T.; Wen C.; Zhang Y.; Wang H.; Wei J.
Article.Abstract: Antibiotic-resistant bacterial infections, particularly those caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), pose a critical clinical challenge and necessitate alternative non-antibiotic antimicrobial strategies. Herein, a high-entropy alloy-modified ZnIn2S4 (HEA–ZIS) photocatalytic nanoplatform was rationally engineered and evaluated for in vitro antibacterial performance. FeCoNiCuZn high-entropy alloy nanoparticles were uniformly anchored onto hierarchical ZnIn2S4 nanoflowers via a combined solvothermal–impregnation strategy. Structural and physicochemical characterizations reveal that the intrinsic flower-like morphology is well retained, while HEA incorporation induces lattice distortion, multivalent metal states, and interfacial charge redistribution. The optimized 3%HEA–ZIS exhibits potent antibacterial activity against MRSA under visible light, achieving 98.30% inactivation and a 5.91-log reduction, with a low minimum bactericidal concentration (0.30 mg mL−1). It also demonstrates strong antibiofilm activity by inhibiting MRSA biofilm formation, reducing biofilm biomass by over 84%, while maintaining good in vitro biosafety. Mechanistic studies reveal enhanced light absorption, improved charge separation, and accelerated interfacial electron transfer, promoting efficient oxygen activation. Electron paramagnetic resonance and in situ DRIFTS analyses identify a cascade reactive oxygen species (ROS) pathway responsible for the enhanced antibacterial efficacy. Overall, this work provides insights into high-entropy alloy-engineered semiconductor nanoplatforms and demonstrates their potential as promising biomedical nanomaterials for non-antibiotic antimicrobial applications.

Article.Title: Construction and Characterization of Rabbit scFv Antibodies Targeting Fibronectin by Phage Display Technology
Article.Authors: Chiang Y.; Juang J.; Yang Y.; Leu S.; Liu J.; Tsai B.; Mao Y.; Yen F.; Chiang J.; Andriani V.; Thenaka P.; Tan T.; Shen T.; Lee C.
Article.Abstract: Fibronectin (FN) is a multifunctional glycoprotein involved in extracellular matrix remodeling, tumor progression, tissue repair, and host–pathogen interactions. Despite its biological and clinical relevance, FN-binding antibodies derived from non-rodent species remain comparatively less explored. Here, one rabbit was immunized with full-length recombinant human FN, eliciting a robust antibody response confirmed by ELISA and Western blotting. Two rabbit-derived single-chain variable fragment (scFv) phage-display libraries were constructed from peripheral blood mononuclear cells, yielding 5.5 × 107 and 5.0 × 107 transformants for the short- and long-linker formats, respectively. After four rounds of biopanning, phage ELISA confirmed enrichment, and sequence analysis grouped selected clones into five short-linker and four long-linker groups. Seven purified scFvs displayed distinct ELISA binding profiles. Fiber-optic particle plasmon resonance (FOPPR)-based kinetic analysis yielded apparent equilibrium dissociation constants (KD,app) of 11.21–432.06 nM, with FN-L13 showing the lowest KD,app. Analytical size-exclusion chromatography indicated predominantly monomeric scFvs. Five scFvs recognized a high-molecular-weight band consistent with fibronectin in mouse plasma by Western blotting. ELISA showed preferential FN binding, with generally low reactivity toward human serum albumin (HSA) and collagens I, III, and IV, although FN-S1 and FN-L1 showed detectable fibrinogen reactivity. These findings support rabbit-derived FN-binding scFvs as research reagents for future FN-related assay development and mechanistic studies.

Article.Title: CPR-Centered Redox Interactions Between Cytochrome P450 Oxidoreductase and Cytochrome c Oxidase: Potential Pharmacological Implications
Article.Authors: Ponamarev V.
Article.Abstract: The intracellular pool of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) is a limited resource for which multiple enzyme systems compete. Among these systems, microsomal NADPH-cytochrome P450 oxidoreductase (CPR, POR) plays a central role in electron transfer to cytochrome P450 enzymes and can also reduce other redox-active electron acceptors in vitro. This review analyzes the molecular basis of competition between CPR-mediated cytochrome P450 reduction and cytochrome c reduction in vitro and discusses whether this can be extrapolated to an indirect interplay between CPR and cytochrome c oxidase (COX) in intact cells. In vitro, reduced cytochrome c (Fe2+) acts as a competitive inhibitor of NADPH-dependent cytochrome P450 reduction, apparently by binding to an overlapping site on CPR. However, CPR and COX are physically separated by subcellular compartmentalization, and cytosolic and mitochondrial NADPH pools are largely separate; therefore, CPR and COX should not be considered direct competitors for a common NADPH pool under physiological conditions. Potential pharmacological implications include modulation of drug metabolism, cellular energy homeostasis, and toxicity when both systems are challenged, but these remain hypothetical and require direct flux measurements in intact cells.

Article.Title: Immunomodulatory Effects of Fractional CO2 Laser and Narrowband UVB in Stable Non-Segmental Vitiligo
Article.Authors: Frączek A.; Czerwińska J.; Załuski D.; Owczarczyk-Saczonek A.
Article.Abstract: Stable non-segmental vitiligo is sustained by persistent autoimmune responses involving tissue-resident memory T (TRM) cells, impaired regulatory T-cell (Treg) function, and chronic cytokine-mediated inflammation. Although fractional carbon dioxide (CO2) laser and narrowband ultraviolet B (NB-UVB) phototherapy are widely used to induce repigmentation, their immunomodulatory mechanisms remain incompletely understood. In this prospective, non-randomized exploratory study, 19 patients with stable non-segmental vitiligo received either monthly fractional CO2 laser monotherapy or fractional CO2 laser combined with NB-UVB phototherapy for 6 months. Serum IL-15 and IL-17A concentrations were quantified by ELISA at baseline, 3 months, and 6 months. Double immunofluorescence was performed to evaluate cutaneous TRM- and Treg-associated markers (CD4, CD8, CD25, CD49a, CD69, CD103, FOXP3) together with melanocyte-associated markers (MITF and c-KIT). Longitudinal differences between treatment groups were assessed using linear mixed-effects models with treatment-by-time interactions. Serum IL-15 and IL-17A concentrations decreased significantly over time in both treatment groups. At 6 months, IL-15 concentrations did not differ significantly from those in healthy controls in either group, whereas IL-17A concentrations did not differ significantly from healthy-control values in the fractional CO2 laser monotherapy group but remained significantly higher in the combination-treatment group. Cutaneous analyses demonstrated longitudinal changes in selected TRM- and Treg-associated markers and melanocyte-associated markers, with MITF showing the most pronounced increase. Several cutaneous immune markers remained significantly different from healthy-control values after 6 months. No statistically significant treatment-by-time interactions were detected for IL-15, IL-17A, or the evaluated dermal and epidermal markers. Fractional CO2 laser monotherapy and fractional CO2 laser combined with NB-UVB were both associated with longitudinal changes in circulating inflammatory cytokines and selected cutaneous immune- and melanocyte-associated markers in patients with stable non-segmental vitiligo. Persistent abnormalities in several cutaneous immune markers suggest that treatment did not fully restore the cutaneous immune-marker profile within the 6-month observation period. Given the small sample size and non-randomized exploratory design, the absence of statistically significant treatment-by-time interactions should not be interpreted as evidence of therapeutic equivalence, non-inferiority, or absence of an additional effect of NB-UVB.

Article.Title: Store-Operated Calcium Entry Inhibitors: Structural Diversity, Mechanisms of Action, and Optimization Strategies
Article.Authors: Zakharova A.; Grekhnev D.; Kaznacheyeva E.; Vigont V.
Article.Abstract: Store-operated calcium entry (SOCE) is a ubiquitous calcium influx pathway critically involved in numerous physiological processes. Dysregulated SOCE contributes to the pathogenesis of cardiovascular disorders, cancer, and neurodegenerative diseases, making SOCE modulators promising therapeutic candidates. This review provides an overview of the major chemical classes of classical SOCE inhibitors that target Orai and STIM proteins. We focus on structure–activity relationships (SARs), mechanisms of action, strategies for enhancing inhibitory potency and selectivity, and discuss the limitations and side-effect profiles of these compounds. This comprehensive analysis identifies SOC channels as promising therapeutic targets and outlines future directions for rational drug design and the development of clinically viable SOCE modulators.

Article.Title: To Be or Not to Be—Thymocyte Survival and Death in the Thymic Medulla
Article.Authors: Zúñiga M.
Article.Abstract: The T cells of the mammalian immune system have a tricky challenge. They must recognize foreign antigen as “other” or “non-self” but in the context of self, while also being tolerant to the body’s own molecules and tissues. T-cell receptor (TCR) gene rearrangement occurs in the cortex of the thymus and generates receptors of relatively random specificity. The developing T cells (thymocytes) are screened in two stages, both of which are Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC)-based. The first, positive selection, occurs in the thymic cortex where cortical thymic epithelial cells (cTECs) display self MHC + self-peptides. Thymocytes that can bind to self MHC + self-peptide then migrate to the corticomedullary junction, where they undergo negative selection. Here, they encounter antigenic peptides characteristic of peripheral tissue proteins presented by medullary antigen-presenting cells (APCs). Among the most intriguing APCs in the medulla are the mimetic medullary thymic epithelial cells (mimetic mTECs). These mimetic APCs express peripheral antigens under the direction of specific transcription factors. During negative selection, most thymocytes whose TCRs bind too well to self MHC + self-peptide die by apoptosis. However, a small proportion of autoreactive thymocytes escape negative selection and instead “alternatively” differentiate into specialized cell types that are self-tolerant and even enforce self-tolerance. The CD4 and CD8 coreceptors, which bind to MHC II and MHC I, respectively, play crucial roles in positive and negative selection. With CD8, there is an added level of complexity because there are two forms of CD8, only one of which can promote signaling through the TCR. Upon binding to MHC, CD4 and CD8 initiate signal transduction through the TCR. The strength of signal transduction through the TCR and through co-stimulatory CD28 determines the outcome of TCR-MHC + peptide binding. Signal transduction occurs within the immunological synapse and is regulated by kinetic proofreading mechanisms. In summary, negative selection involves interactions between developing thymocytes and a variety of medullary APCs. These molecular interactions occur at specialized membrane domains that bring together the components of the TCR signaling apparatus, which are subject to kinetic proofreading. Together, the regulatory mechanisms occurring in developing thymocytes and in medullary APCs generate a T-cell arsenal that is tolerant of self and active against foreign entities.

Article.Title: Normalization Strategies for miRNA RT-qPCR in Blood-Derived Samples in Obesity Research: Current Practices and Methodological Considerations
Article.Authors: Pustovalova A.; Nikolaeva A.; Kalinkin A.; Sigin V.
Article.Abstract: Reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) is widely used to quantify circulating microRNAs, but reliable interpretation depends on appropriate data normalization. In obesity research, selecting reference RNAs for measurements in whole blood, blood cells, plasma, and serum is challenging because of biological heterogeneity and preanalytical variability. This review summarizes normalization strategies used in RT-qPCR studies of blood-derived samples from participants with overweight or obesity. We examine commonly used endogenous reference RNAs, including U6 snRNA and miR-16-5p, and assess the rationale for their selection and the available validation evidence in relation to sample matrix and cohort characteristics. The review evaluates normalization practices and the quality and reporting of reference-RNA validation in obesity-related studies, with particular attention to the biological comparison being made. No candidate, algorithmic ranking, or fixed panel size is considered universally applicable. Candidate selection, the number of references, and the normalization scale should be justified for the intended comparison. The review provides practical guidance for designing and reporting validation of reference small non-coding RNAs and process controls in study cohorts with overweight or obesity, with recommendations qualified by the available evidence.

Article.Title: Dihydromyricetin and Neuroinflammation: Implications for CNS Disorders and Therapeutic Development
Article.Authors: Skinner S.; Aleman E.; Berges A.; Kim K.; Kantilal D.; Asatryan L.; Davies D.
Article.Abstract: Dihydromyricetin (DHM) is a bioactive polyphenol with broad therapeutic potential, including strong anti-inflammatory activity. Importantly, DHM has been shown to cross the blood–brain barrier (BBB), enabling pharmacological activity within the central nervous system (CNS) and positioning it as a candidate for CNS disorders in which neuroinflammation plays a central role, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and stroke. Therapeutics such as DHM, which address neuroinflammation, are of increasing interest. Across CNS disease models, DHM’s effects show recurring convergence on NF-κB suppression, NLRP3 inflammasome inhibition, and autophagy regulation, alongside context-specific mechanisms involving oxidative stress, ferroptosis, neurotrophic signaling, and peripheral gut–CNS communication. This review examines the evidence for DHM as a neuroinflammatory modulator, focusing on the mechanisms by which it exerts its therapeutic effects. By doing so, we aim to support its translational potential as a natural product for improving human health.

Article.Title: Profiling Systemic IgG-Targeted Gut Microbiota Reveals Disease Activity-Associated Bacterial Signatures in Ulcerative Colitis
Article.Authors: Takahashi K.; Nakayama-Imaohji H.; Tada A.; Emmanuel M.; Mino Y.; Ishikawa H.; Kuwahara T.
Article.Abstract: Aberrant systemic IgG responses to the gut microbiota may be implicated in the pathogenesis of ulcerative colitis (UC). In this study, we investigated IgG-targeted bacteria and their predicted functional characteristics in UC. Using fecal samples and autologous sera from 37 patients with UC and 4 healthy controls, we profiled IgG-targeted bacteria under in vitro conditions using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. To correct for background bacterial abundance, we calculated the IgG+ Probability Score (IPS), which integrates the sample-specific IgG-binding rate to isolate candidate IgG-targeted taxa. Systemic IgG responses were selectively targeted at specific bacterial taxa rather than uniformly directed toward the entire gut microbiota. Active UC and elevated systemic inflammatory markers were associated with increased IPS in oral-associated commensals, including Granulicatella, as well as mucin-degrading taxa. Predictive functional profiling indicated the predicted enrichment of pathways hypothesized to be related to host-derived mucin degradation, capsular polysaccharide biosynthesis, and amino acid biosynthesis. Furthermore, exploratory Random Forest models using IPS features highlighted candidate taxa that differed among clinical parameters (UC exacerbation, Clinical Activity Index, and C-reactive protein), although their classification performance was not independently validated. In conclusion, our in vitro profiling indicates that systemic IgG in UC has the capacity to selectively target specific bacterial taxa associated with disease activity and systemic inflammation. Analyzing the IgG-targeted microbiota via IPS profiling deepens our understanding of host–microbiota interactions in UC and provides a valuable framework for evaluating candidate immune-targeted bacteria associated with disease activity.

Article.Title: N, S-Functionalized Magnetic Rice Husk Biochar for Flucloxacillin Sodium Adsorption: Regeneration and Water-Matrix Effects
Article.Authors: Pandey P.; Dhiman M.; Białowiec A.; Pokhriyal A.; Bahukhandi K.; Kaur P.; Igwegbe C.
Article.Abstract: Rice husk-derived biochars with progressively modified surface properties were investigated for adsorbing flucloxacillin sodium (FLX-Na) from aqueous solution. Four materials—rice husk biochar (RHB), nitrogen-functionalized RHB (N-RHB), magnetic nitrogen-functionalized RHB (MN-RHB), and magnetic nitrogen/sulfur-functionalized RHB (MN,S-RHB)—were prepared and characterised using morphological, structural, textural, and surface-chemical techniques. The sequential preparation routes produced materials with different surface areas, pore structures, and surface functionalities. FLX-Na adsorption increased in the order RHB < MN-RHB < N-RHB < MN, S-RHB, with the highest equilibrium adsorption capacity obtained for MN,S-RHB (118.6 mg g−1). Because chemical activation and a higher carbonisation temperature were introduced only for MN,S-RHB, the higher uptake is interpreted as an effect of the combined modification route rather than being attributed specifically to N/S co-doping. Kinetic and equilibrium data were described using several empirical models, with the pseudo-second-order and Sips models giving the highest coefficients of determination among the tested fits. The adsorption capacity of MN,S-RHB decreased from 84.60 ± 1.30 mg g−1 in deionised water to 60.30 ± 1.80 mg g−1 in a mixed inorganic/humic-acid matrix, corresponding to 71.3% capacity retention. Spectroscopic changes after adsorption were consistent with changes in the surface chemical environment, while the matrix experiments indicated that coexisting inorganic ions and dissolved organic matter influenced adsorption performance. These results show that the combined physicochemical modification route altered the adsorption behaviour of rice husk-derived biochar under the investigated conditions.

Article.Title: TLR2 Signaling in Myeloproliferative Neoplasms: Pathophysiological Roles, Mutation-Dependent Heterogeneity, and the Differential Efficacy of Ruxolitinib
Article.Authors: Pokhrel A.; Hakobyan N.; Wang J.
Article.Abstract: Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) is a versatile pattern-recognition receptor of the innate immune system that recognizes both pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) and endogenous danger-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs). Philadelphia chromosome-negative myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs)—clonal hematopoietic stem-cell disorders that include essential thrombocythemia (ET), polycythemia vera (PV), and myelofibrosis (MF)—are characterized by persistent inflammation and an increased risk of thrombosis. Dysregulated TLR2 signaling has emerged as a potentially important mediator of this chronic thrombo-inflammatory state. Findings from our group and others suggest that TLR2 may have a particularly prominent role in promoting inflammatory cytokine production, platelet–leukocyte interactions, endothelial dysfunction, and thrombotic complications in MPNs. Our findings are also consistent with evidence that NF-κB-mediated proinflammatory signaling, in addition to constitutive JAK/STAT activation, contributes substantially to MPN pathogenesis. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of TLR2 biology and examine its contribution to the thrombo-inflammatory milieu of MPNs, with particular emphasis on its potential utility as a biomarker and a therapeutic target. Ruxolitinib, a JAK1/2 inhibitor, markedly reduces symptom burden and splenomegaly in JAK2-mutant MPNs, particularly PV and MF; however, it has limited efficacy in CALR-mutant or triple-negative ET. This differential therapeutic response may reflect divergent downstream signaling pathways and may also be related to dysregulated TLR2 signaling. Furthermore, hyperactive TLR2 signaling in MPNs may help explain the incomplete ability of ruxolitinib to suppress thrombo-inflammatory responses. Therefore, combined TLR2-targeted therapy and ruxolitinib may represent a more effective therapeutic strategy for future MPN trials. Overall, however, we consider the TLR2-mediated thrombo-inflammatory response in MPNs to be an amplifier of inflammation rather than a primary disease driver.

Article.Title: The Role of SOD1 and Oxidative Stress in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: An Overview
Article.Authors: Gómez-Pérez C.; Ramírez-García M.; Yescas-Gómez P.
Article.Abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a rapidly progressing neurodegenerative disorder that selectively affects motor neurons. The median survival time after diagnosis is 2 to 5 years. Oxidative stress (OS), driven mainly by reactive oxygen species (ROS), plays a central role in motor neuron (MN) degeneration. In this narrative review, we analyse the pathogenic role of SOD1 variants and their contribution to OS in ALS. SOD1 mutations alter the Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase enzyme, thereby promoting oxidative damage and triggering neuroinflammatory cascades via the MAPK, NF-κB and Nrf2/ARE signalling pathways. We also discuss emerging proteomic and machine-learning biomarkers, as well as the current therapeutic landscape. Riluzole and edaravone are approved treatments, while AMX0035 was approved in 2022 but withdrawn in 2024. Masitinib and EPI-589 remain investigational. In the realm of genetic therapies, the antisense oligonucleotide tofersen received accelerated FDA approval in 2023 for SOD1-ALS, primarily due to its ability to reduce plasma neurofilament light chain levels. However, the clinical benefit remains modest. RNA interference has reached human trials, while CRISPR/Cas9 remains in the preclinical stage. Both approaches have shown promising results in experimental models. Further research into ALS pathogenesis is needed to develop treatments that integrate antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and gene-editing strategies.

Article.Title: Topographic Expression of IL-1β and Inflammasome-Associated Proteins in Lesional, Perilesional, and Distant Hidradenitis Suppurativa Skin
Article.Authors: Lewandowski M.; Górska-Ponikowska M.; Jakubczyk-Słabicka A.; Świerczewska Z.; Barańska-Rybak W.
Article.Abstract: Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a chronic inflammatory skin disease characterized by recurrent nodules, abscesses, draining tunnels, and scarring. Dysregulated IL-1 and inflammasome-associated pathways have been implicated in its pathogenesis, but their spatial distribution beyond clinically apparent lesions remains incompletely characterized. Skin samples were obtained from eight biologic-untreated patients with HS, six patients receiving adalimumab, and five healthy controls. In HS, matched 6 mm full-thickness biopsies were obtained from the same axilla at an active inflammatory lesion (0 cm), clinically normal-appearing skin 2 cm from the visible lesion edge, and clinically uninvolved skin 10 cm from the lesion edge. Protein abundance was assessed by Western blot. Primary topographic effects were evaluated using mixed-design ANOVA with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction, supplemented by non-parametric and exploratory contrast analyses. No protein showed an FDR (false discovery rate)-significant overall site effect or cohort × site interaction in the primary analysis. In biologic-untreated HS, IL-18 showed an FDR-significant topographic effect (q = 0.0444), with higher expression at 0 cm than at 10 cm (q = 0.0469). An exploratory post hoc 2-versus-10 cm analysis identified a highly concordant IL-1β pattern: expression was higher at 2 cm in 7/8 biologic-untreated and 6/6 adalimumab-treated patients. Fisher’s combined probability remained significant after BH correction across the four proteins evaluated for this contrast (p = 0.00421, q4 = 0.0168), whereas comprehensive correction across all 12 protein × contrast combinations yielded q12 = 0.0505 and did not meet q < 0.05. Overall, 13/14 patients showed the same direction (92.9%; exact 95% CI 66.1–99.8%). IL-18 provided the clearest FDR-supported secondary topographic finding. IL-1β showed a highly concordant but hypothesis-generating perilesional-to-distant spatial pattern, whereas total NLRP3 and caspase-1 did not show robust FDR-adjusted spatial variation.

Article.Title: DeepAVPred: A Deep Learning Framework Integrating RECM-DWT and BiGRU for Accurate Antiviral Peptide Prediction
Article.Authors: Fida H.; Zhang H.; Ahmad B.; Lin H.; Ma C.; Huang C.; Fan Z.
Article.Abstract: Viral infections continue to pose a significant global health challenge. Antiviral peptides (AVPs) have emerged as promising therapeutic agents owing to their high specificity, favorable safety profiles, and broad-spectrum antiviral activity. However, experimental AVP identification is time-consuming and costly, while existing computational predictors often have limitations in predictive accuracy and feature representation. Here, we propose DeepAVPred, a deep learning-based framework for AVP identification. DeepAVPred integrates complementary sequence descriptors to capture physicochemical properties and pairwise residue interactions. We present a novel feature representation, the Residue Energy Content Matrix augmented with a Discrete Wavelet Transform (RECM-DWT). RECM-DWT characterizes multi-scale patterns in residue-energy information and complements conventional sequence descriptors by providing wavelet-derived features across multiple resolution levels. The integrated features are then modeled using an attention-based Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (BiGRU) network to learn contextual dependencies and informative sequence patterns. On the AVPtrain dataset, DeepAVPred achieved strong performance in 10-fold cross-validation, with an accuracy of 0.990, a Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) of 0.980, and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.993. On the independent test dataset, AVPtest, DeepAVPred achieved an accuracy of 0.942, an MCC of 0.886, and an AUC of 0.949. These results demonstrate the predictive performance of DeepAVPred and support its potential as a computational framework for prioritizing candidate antiviral peptides for further experimental validation.

Article.Title: A Quantum Mechanism-Centered Review of Carbon Dot-Based Theranostics
Article.Authors: Cheng I.; Contreras G.; Yeh T.
Article.Abstract: Despite advances in drug discovery, effective delivery and precise imaging still pose significant obstacles. Scientists have turned to zero-dimensional nanomaterials like carbon dots (CDs) to enable precision drug delivery. Due to their multidisciplinary appeal, there is extensive research on both the physical properties and biological applications of CDs, yet the fields rarely complement each other. This review applies a quantum-mechanistic framework to better understand CDs and unify the relationship between electronic structure, photophysical behavior, and theranostic performance. We first highlight the theranostic advantages of CDs over quantum dots, then discuss the quantum mechanisms behind a CD’s imaging capabilities, including surface states, excitation-dependent photoluminescence, and the electronic origins of photostability. Through this physical lens, we then evaluate the effect of different precursors and doping strategies during synthesis on electronic structure and how dots are engineered to load, release, and track therapeutic cargo. Photodynamic therapy and surface functionalization strategies are also evaluated. Finally, we address the significance of renal clearance and translational bottlenecks such as heterogeneity.

Article.Title: Molecular Dynamics-Guided Triage of Approved Drugs Against Escherichia coli Resistance Targets Nominates Capmatinib, Metergoline and Nilotinib as Candidates for Experimental Testing
Article.Authors: Abdelsayed M.; Boulaamane Y.
Article.Abstract: Virtual screening ranks compounds by scoring functions that correlate with molecular size, and hit lists are rarely benchmarked against compounds of established activity. We screened 2070 approved drugs against four Escherichia coli targets selected by pocket-druggability triage (FabI, LpxC, DHFR and GyrB), with each docking protocol validated by redocking its native ligand (RMSD 0.50–0.69 Å). Per target, the two top-scoring compounds and a reference inhibitor were simulated for 100 ns in triplicate (12 complexes, 3.6 μs). Docking did not recover the references: trimethoprim ranked 762/2068 and novobiocin 576/2069, while top-ranked compounds were large, promiscuous drugs recurring across unrelated targets. Pose triage failed, too: all twelve complexes retained 43–87% of initial contacts, contact-loss time separated targets, not compounds, and MM-GBSA favoured the reference at one target of four. Persistent hydrogen bonding separated the reference from the hits at three of four targets, by 2–9-fold, although the GyrB result rests largely on one replicate. Benchmarking each hit against its reference nominates three candidates for experimental testing: capmatinib at DHFR, metergoline at FabI and nilotinib at LpxC. Capmatinib ranks highest on these computational criteria, with the highest pocket retention (87%) and an MM-GBSA energy with no detectable difference from trimethoprim’s at n = 3 (absence of evidence for a difference, not evidence of equivalence). In this small panel, carrying a known active through the same pipeline was therefore more informative than docking score, pose stability or end-point rescoring. The nominations are hypotheses: no experimental validation was performed, and generality would require multiple actives and property-matched decoys per target.

Article.Authors: Iwasa Y.; Hori K.; Nakajima T.; Yokota Y.; Yamazaki S.; Hori Y.; Uehara T.; Takumi Y.

Article.Title: Enzymatic Hydrolysate of Red Yeast Rice Accelerates Diabetic Wound Healing in Mice: Association with Modulation of Inflammatory, Matrix-Remodeling, and Angiogenesis-Related Markers
Article.Authors: Du Y.; Ma W.; Chang X.; Wang S.; Zeng R.; Wu N.
Article.Abstract: Delayed healing of diabetic wounds arises from a self-sustaining pathological microenvironment featuring persistent inflammation, excessive matrix degradation, impaired angiogenesis, and insufficient collagen deposition, and current single-process interventions remain unsatisfactory. Red yeast rice, produced by fermentation of rice with Monascus spp., is a traditional fermented product with documented anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activities; however, its direct extract is dominated by macromolecular and bound-state constituents with low release efficiency and poor skin permeation, which restricts its topical application. In this study, an enzymatic hydrolysate of red yeast rice (RYR-EH) was prepared by composite enzymatic hydrolysis, and the compositional changes induced by hydrolysis were characterized by widely targeted UPLC-MS/MS metabolomics. A total of 810 metabolites were detected, among which 199 showed differential accumulation after hydrolysis (179 upregulated and 20 downregulated; FC ≥ 2 or ≤0.5, VIP ≥ 1, and p < 0.05); the differential metabolites were significantly enriched (FDR < 0.05) in purine metabolism, nucleotide metabolism, ABC transporters, and the cGMP-PKG signaling pathway, a pattern consistent with hydrolysis-driven release of free amino acids, small peptides, and other low-molecular-weight constituents. In type 2 diabetic mice induced by a high-fat diet combined with low-dose streptozotocin, topical RYR-EH (2% and 5%) significantly accelerated the closure of full-thickness excisional wounds, with the 5% formulation showing more advanced closure than the 2% formulation and an effect approaching that of recombinant human epidermal growth factor (rhEGF). At the day-14 endpoint, RYR-EH treatment was associated with enhanced re-epithelialization, lower TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β levels in both wound tissue and serum, reduced MMP-2 and MMP-9 immunoreactivity, reduced Ki67-positive cellularity in the late-stage wound bed, increased Collagen I/III deposition, and increased VEGF/CD31 immunoreactivity. These results demonstrate that RYR-EH exerts multi-process reparative effects on diabetic wounds, simultaneously attenuating inflammation, restraining excessive matrix degradation, promoting angiogenesis, and restoring collagen deposition, and support RYR-EH as an effective multi-process topical agent for diabetic wound healing.

Article.Title: Gangliosides in Cutaneous Melanoma: Molecular Mechanisms, Translational Evidence Gaps, and Preclinical Natural-Compound Leads
Article.Authors: Koo D.; Kim K.; Kim J.; Yun H.; Song E.; Kim M.; Ryu J.; Kim J.; Kim S.; Lee H.; Choo Y.
Article.Abstract: Cutaneous melanoma remains lethal once metastatic despite advances in immune checkpoint blockade and BRAF/MEK-directed therapy. Gangliosides are surface-accessible sialylated glycosphingolipids that regulate membrane organization, adhesion, and signaling, representing potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets. This narrative review evaluated the translational readiness of ganglioside-directed strategies in cutaneous melanoma, without assuming that evidence from other GD2- or GD3-positive cancers is directly transferable. We synthesized melanoma-specific evidence on GD3-linked focal adhesion signaling, p130Cas/paxillin activity, PI3K–AKT and MAPK outputs, and distinct phenotypes associated with GD3, GD2, and GM3. We then applied an evidence-gated framework distinguishing melanoma clinical evidence, melanoma preclinical evidence, cross-tumor translational evidence, and hypothesis-generating claims. Direct contemporary clinical evidence in melanoma remains limited. Antibody, cellular, and biosynthetic enzyme strategies require diagnostic-quality antigen profiling, demonstration of surface accessibility and functional dependency, and prospective monitoring for antigen escape and neurotoxicity. Natural compounds, particularly quercetin, are mechanistic probes or formulation-enabled leads: a 2024 study reported reduced GM3/GD3 abundance and FAK/paxillin/AKT signaling in melanoma cell lines, but high in vitro concentrations and the lack of pharmacokinetic or in vivo validation preclude therapeutic conclusions. We proposed a minimum evidence package and go/no-go criteria for clinical translation, specifying experiments needed to advance ganglioside biology into biomarker-defined melanoma interventions.

Article.Title: Whole-Genome Sequencing in Diagnostics of Unsolved Cases of Inherited Retinal Diseases
Article.Authors: Ogorodova N.; Stepanova A.; Geletskaia P.; Kadyshev V.; Zinchenko R.; Kuznetsova S.; Khalanskaya O.; Monakhova A.; Beskorovainy N.; Zabnenkova V.; Ryzhkova O.; Severinov K.; Bychkov I.; Polyakov A.; Kutsev S.; Shchagina O.
Article.Abstract: The study purpose was to assess the diagnostic value of whole-genome sequencing (WGS) in identifying candidate genetic variants in patients with inherited retinal diseases (IRDs). We investigated 107 unrelated Russian patients with retinal diseases who carried single pathogenic variants in any of nine common autosomal recessive IRD genes (ABCA4, USH2A, EYS, CRB1, RPE65, CNGB3, CNGA3, CEP290, and GUCY2D). WGS was performed for all patients; candidate splice variants were functionally validated using minigene assays. The total diagnostic yield was 40.2% (43/107). In 25.2% of cases (27/107), the diagnosis was established by identifying a second variant in one of the following candidate genes: EYS (n = 9), USH2A (n = 8), ABCA4 (n = 5), CNGB3 (n = 3), CRB1 and CEP290 (n = 1 each). In 15.0% of cases (16/107), the diagnosis was reclassified by variants in alternative IRD genes (autosomal dominant, X-linked, mitochondrial, or syndromic). The majority of second variants detected in AR cases were CNVs (55.5%, 15 patients), followed by non-coding variants (26.0%, seven), structural rearrangements (14.8%, four) and exonic point variant (3.7%, one). Two recurrent CNVs were observed: a gross deletion of exons 22–24 in USH2A (n = 4) and a deletion partially affecting exon 19 of EYS (n = 4). Structural variants were mostly represented by delINV rearrangements (n = 5). Minigene assays confirmed that three novel deep intronic variants (in CHM, EYS, and CEP290) and one non-canonical splice-acceptor variant in USH2A which disrupt splicing, causes pseudoexon inclusion with premature termination or in-frame exon skipping respectively. Thus, WGS improves the diagnostic yield in IRDs by detecting variants missed by targeted sequencing, supporting its clinical utility in ophthalmologic practice.

Article.Title: Recent Advances in Lipid Nanoparticles for Cancer Vaccines: From Antigen Delivery to Personalized Immunotherapy
Article.Authors: Rachamala H.; Angom R.; Marepally S.
Article.Abstract: In recent years, lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have shown great promise as highly flexible delivery systems for cancer vaccines, which enable effective cargo delivery and allow for controlling their distribution, cell-targeting ability and immunogenicity. Innovations in ionizable lipid chemistry, biodegradable formulations, RNA engineering and LNP design resulted in improvements in RNA encapsulation, endosomal escape, delivery outside the liver, and targeting of lymphoid organs and antigen-presenting cells. All these achievements led to an expansion of strategies for developing cancer vaccines from using only mRNA to personal neoantigen vaccines, self-amplifying RNA (saRNA), circular RNA (circRNA), peptide/protein vaccines, and multi-purpose platforms that combine antigen delivery and modulation of the immune system. LNPs are also studied as tools for altering the tumor microenvironment (TME) and boosting anti-tumor immunity through local delivery of cytokines and innate immune modulators. Preliminary clinical results with personalized mRNA neoantigen vaccines show strong potential for this approach. However, inflammatory toxicity, suitability for repeated dosing, off-target delivery, difficulties with large-scale production, formulation stability, personalized production schedule and regulatory issues are still significant challenges. New biodegradable and PEG-free formulations, innovations in manufacturing and lyophilization technology, and AI-based approaches in lipid screening could help overcome some of these problems.

Article.Title: Compartment-Specific Transcriptional Remodelling Defines Denervation and Geriatric Muscle Regeneration
Article.Authors: Tong W.; Yu Q.; Yang R.; Shao C.; Yang G.; Wang Z.
Article.Abstract: Neuromuscular decline involves motor, junctional, myofibre and niche dysfunction, but whether these components remodel as a coordinated system is unresolved. We harmonised 654,053 locally audited single-cell or single-nucleus profiles from two human ageing cohorts and four mouse studies spanning denervation, injury, reinnervation and exercise, retaining the donor, animal or library as the inferential unit. Denervation produced 4311 cell-type-specific differential-expression results, with the largest number of detected gene effects in type IIB myonuclei. Competitive animal-pseudobulk testing identified eight FDR-supported compartment–programme results; six denervation-sensitivity results remained supported after each single-gene deletion, whereas the FAP matrix-inflammatory and type IIB junctional results were gene-sensitive. During geriatric regeneration, all eight annotated broad compartments varied over time, and 26 of 34 analysis-defined biologically applicable compartment–programme tests were significant after FDR correction. Tests of human ageing, restricted age-by-time interactions and mitochondrial perturbation did not survive multiplicity correction. The human results are hypothesis-generating, and neither RNA scores nor predicted cell communication establish functional recovery. This resource supports compartment-specific transcriptional responses within denervation and geriatric injury designs; it does not establish a conserved recovery axis across the six contexts.

Article.Title: Sexually Dimorphic Glutamatergic Control of R-Spondin 1 and R-Spondin 3 Neurons in Hypothalamic Reproductive and Metabolic Nuclei
Article.Authors: Topal G.; Yurtseven D.; Akbulut N.; Gul Z.; Udum D.; Yalcin M.; Eyigor O.
Article.Abstract: R-spondin 1 (RSPO1) and R-spondin 3 (RSPO3) contribute to reproductive development and feeding regulation, but their hypothalamic glutamatergic regulation remains unclear. We hypothesized that NMDA and non-NMDA receptor mechanisms contribute to hypothalamic RSPO neuronal activation. Given steroid-sensitive hypothalamic glutamatergic signaling, we compared activation and antagonist-mediated attenuation between sexes. Adult male and metestrous female Sprague–Dawley rats received kainic acid or AMPA with or without CNQX pretreatment, or NMDA with or without MK-801 pretreatment. RSPO/c-Fos labeling assessed activation in the supraoptic (SON), paraventricular (PVN), and arcuate (ARC) nuclei; ELISA assessed accompanying changes in serum RSPO concentrations. All agonists activated both populations in all nuclei. Only kainate-induced PVN RSPO3 activation differed between sexes (females, 89.3%; males, 72.8%; unadjusted p = 0.039), an isolated finding among 18 agonist comparisons. Antagonists attenuated all responses, although activation remained above control in 17 of 36 conditions. Females showed greater attenuation in selected kainate and NMDA conditions in the SON and PVN. Serum changes did not parallel neuronal activation. These findings support NMDA and non-NMDA receptor involvement and sex-dependent attenuation of RSPO neuronal activation. Given the central feeding effects of RSPOs, their sex-dependent glutamatergic regulation within neuroendocrine nuclei may contribute to sex differences in metabolic control.

Article.Title: Architect or Destroyer: The Diversity of Glucocorticoid Receptor Signaling Pathways in the Brain
Article.Authors: Shkarina L.; Khaybullina R.; Primak A.; Bozov K.; Dzhauari S.; Karagyaur M.
Article.Abstract: Glucocorticoids (GCs), acting through the glucocorticoid (GR) and mineralocorticoid (MR) receptors, are essential for brain development, stress adaptation, and metabolic homeostasis, yet their signaling exhibits context-dependent diversity yielding either beneficial or detrimental outcomes. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the multifaceted mechanisms through which GR integrates hormonal, metabolic, and stress signals to modulate transcriptional programs in the brain. We highlight three key levels of GR regulatory complexity: the diversity of DNA GR-binding motifs, GR-mediated epigenetic remodeling, and rapid non-genomic cascades. Clinical and experimental data reveal that while physiological GC levels are critical for normal maturation and function, excess or chronic exposure, especially during sensitive developmental windows, can disrupt neurogenesis, synaptogenesis, and myelination, predisposing individuals to cognitive, affective, and neurodegenerative disorders. We discuss promising therapeutic strategies based on selective modulation of MR/GR balance, interference with specific co-regulatory complexes, and targeted manipulation of DNMT/TET/HDAC cascades. Unlike most existing reviews—which address either (a) the MR–GR interaction as a whole receptor system, (b) non-genomic effects in isolation from genomic ones, or (c) the clinical manifestations of stress-associated disorders without an in-depth mechanistic analysis of GR targets—our manuscript attempts to integrate these three levels of GR regulation into a unified hierarchical system (binding motifs → epigenetic remodeling → the conditional nature of the boundary between genomic and non-genomic GR effects). We aim to explicitly demonstrate how these levels jointly determine cell-specific outcomes, rather than describing them in parallel as independent mechanisms. However, critical gaps remain in understanding the precise assembly of GR-co-regulator complexes in defined neuronal and glial populations, as well as the feasibility of selectively engaging beneficial GR signaling branches without systemic suppression of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis. Addressing these questions is essential for developing next-generation therapies that harness GR’s architectural potential while avoiding its adverse or unwanted consequences.

Article.Title: Delivery of 3-O-Ethyl-L-Ascorbic Acid from Radiation-Crosslinked Hydrogels to Promote Extracellular Matrix Production in Fibroblasts
Article.Authors: Rokita B.; Adamus-Wlodarczyk A.; Olejnik A.; Czechowska-Biskup R.; Skibska B.; Kadlubowski S.; Ulanski P.; Wach R.
Article.Abstract: L-ascorbic acid is a bioactive compound widely used in dermatology and cosmetology, owing to its antioxidant properties and essential role in collagen biosynthesis. However, its poor chemical stability in aqueous formulations considerably limits its incorporation into hydrogel-based delivery systems. In the present study, a radiation-crosslinked hydrogel based on poly(N-vinylpyrrolidone), poly(ethylene glycol) and agar was developed as a carrier for 3-O-ethyl-L-ascorbic acid (EvitC), a stabilized vitamin C derivative, for topical application. The influence of EvitC on hydrogel formation, physicochemical properties, release characteristics and long-term stability was investigated. In parallel, the biological safety and activity of EvitC and EvitC-containing hydrogel were evaluated using human dermal fibroblasts. Cell metabolic activity was assessed using the XTT assay and further supported by the qualitative evaluation of cell viability using Live/Dead staining, while extracellular matrix production was assessed using the Col-F assay. Hydrogels containing 0.1% EvitC exhibited advantageous essential properties, such as gel fraction, swelling capacity and mechanical properties while maintaining the sustained release of the biologically active compound. The components of the hydrogel matrix effectively protected EvitC during radiation processing and storage, thereby confirming the overall stability of the formulation. Neither EvitC nor hydrogel extracts induced cytotoxic effects under all tested conditions. Furthermore, the prolonged exposure of fibroblasts to hydrogel extracts resulted in a moderate but statistically significant increase in ECM-associated Col-F, i.e., collagen- and elastin-associated fluorescence. These findings support the potential of the developed radiation-crosslinked hydrogel as a stable and cytocompatible platform for the topical delivery of EvitC. The combination of favorable physicochemical properties, formulation stability and excellent biological performance highlights its potential for the development of advanced hydrogel-based skin care formulations.

Article.Title: Enhancing Exosome Production from Adipose-Derived Stem Cells via Arachidonic Acid Priming for Diabetic Wound Healing
Article.Authors: Cai Y.; Wang J.; Zhang R.; Che D.; Xie J.; Cao D.
Article.Abstract: Adipose-derived stem cell (ADSC)-derived exosomes are promising for regenerative therapy. However, their clinical translation is hindered by limited secretion yield and reduced functional potency. Mechanistically, transcriptomic and functional analyses revealed that AA promoted multivesicular body and intraluminal vesicle formation through CHMP1B upregulation and facilitated exosome release through Rab27b, and knockdown of either gene impaired the corresponding process. Proteomic profiling further showed that AA-Exos were enriched in wound-repair-related cargo, particularly interleukin-8 (IL-8/CXCL8). In high-glucose-challenged endothelial cells, AA-Exos enhanced proliferation and migration and reduced apoptosis by activating FAK/AKT/ERK signaling, whereas IL-8 neutralization attenuated these effects. In a diabetic mouse model, AA-Exos accelerated wound closure and improved tissue perfusion, angiogenesis, and collagen deposition. Taken together, AA priming enhances exosome production while improving their therapeutic function, suggesting a practical strategy to strengthen the translational potential of ADSC-derived exosomes for diabetic wound regeneration.

Article.Title: Effect of Nitrogen Concentration on Growth and Fatty Acid Composition in the Freshwater Diatom Stephanocyclus meneghinianus
Article.Authors: Selezneva A.; Gololobova M.; Krivova Z.; Kezlya E.; Kulikovskiy M.; Starikov A.; Maltsev Y.
Article.Abstract: Microalgae can alter their growth rate and metabolic pathways in response to nutrient concentration in the medium, particularly nitrogen, one of their most important components. Article.Title: Molecular Mechanisms of Candida albicans Adhesion to Maxillofacial Silicone Elastomers: Integrating Candidate Molecular Pathways with Material Surface Properties
Article.Authors: Hamarsha A.; Atatra M.; Watted N.; Irekeola A.; Sulaiman M.; Hasbullah N.
Article.Abstract: Colonisation of maxillofacial prostheses by Candida albicans is conventionally attributed to surface roughness, porosity, and wettability properties that explain where cells accumulate rather than why particular surfaces promote biofilm formation. This review reinterprets the in vitro literature on C. albicans adhesion to maxillofacial silicone elastomers through the underlying molecular events. Nine eligible studies identified through searches of PubMed, Scopus, and ScienceDirect conducted on 31 March 2026 were appraised with the QUIN tool and mapped onto a six-stage molecular cascade: surface conditioning, reversible attachment, adhesin engagement, morphogenesis, matrix assembly, and antifungal tolerance. Three conclusions emerged. First, C. albicans senses topography through mechanically gated calcium channels and converts mechanical contact into hyphal commitment; roughness is therefore a morphogenetic cue that surface finishing can withhold. Second, the tested agents—silver nanoparticles, chitosan, thymol, and carvacrol, and a Lactobacillus brevis-derived biosurfactant—engage distinct molecular targets and are not mechanistically interchangeable. Third, most included studies evaluated silicone without salivary conditioning, whereas the clinical interface is an acquired salivary pellicle that supplies both adhesion receptors and antimicrobial peptides. All studies fell within the medium risk-of-bias band (50.0–62.5%). Pellicle-conditioned models and molecular readouts are required. The mechanistic interpretations discussed in this review are derived from the broader C. albicans literature and have not been directly demonstrated on maxillofacial silicone elastomers.
