Article.Title: From Gene-Based Breeding to Haplotype-Based Breeding for Rice (Oryza sativa) Improvement in the Genomics Era
Article.Authors: Nguyen T.; Ho A.; Chu H.; Chuong N.; Anik T.; Dong G.; Sulieman S.; Nguyen N.; Jogaiah S.; La H.; Tran L.
Article.Abstract: Rice (Oryza sativa L.) improvement increasingly uses genome-scale variation, but breeding decisions remain trait-oriented and depend on genetic architecture, recipient background, target environment, and selection resources. This review assesses when phased haplotype information adds value beyond causal-gene markers, single-nucleotide polymorphism assays, phenotypic selection, and genomic prediction. Reported configurations for yield, grain quality, nutrition, biotic resistance, and abiotic-stress adaptation are evaluated according to population structure, carrier frequency, effect uncertainty, haplotype-by-background interaction, haplotype-by-environment interaction, linkage drag, transferability, assay availability, and current breeding use. A three-tier hierarchy classifies configurations as Candidate, Validated, or Breeder-Ready. Most reported favorable haplotypes remain Candidate targets, fewer have controlled genetic validation, and few sequence-defined multi-variant haplotypes have documented use in active breeding programs. Practical deployment requires stable sequence nomenclature, accessible donors, diagnostic assays, elite-background and multi-environment evaluation, cost analysis, and donor-segment recovery. Graph pangenomes, phased long-read assemblies, causal reconstruction, and prospective comparisons with current selection methods can improve future assessment. Haplotype information has greatest value when phase improves a defined breeding decision and increases target-environment performance, annual genetic gain, selection efficiency, or cultivar delivery.

Article.Title: Targeting EGR1 Attenuates CCL2 Expression in Inflammatory Keratinocytes and Allergic Skin Inflammation
Article.Authors: Choi Y.; Jung E.; Han J.; Shin S.
Article.Abstract: Early growth response 1 (EGR1) is a zinc-finger transcription factor involved in inflammatory gene regulation, but the extent to which pharmacological inhibition of EGR1 DNA-binding activity influences inflammatory transcriptional responses in keratinocytes remains incompletely understood. Here, we explored the transcriptional effects of pharmacological EGR1 inhibition in tumor necrosis factor-α (TNFα)-stimulated HaCaT keratinocytes. RNA sequencing was employed as an exploratory, hypothesis-generating screen using three structurally related EGR1 inhibitors (IT21, IT23, and IT25) to identify candidate genes showing concordant expression patterns across the three pharmacological perturbations. This exploratory analysis suggested broader changes in inflammation-associated transcriptional programs and identified several leukocyte-recruiting chemokines among the candidate genes. CCL2 was selected as a representative candidate for independent biological and mechanistic validation. IT25 treatment and EGR1 knockdown attenuated TNFα-induced CCL2 expression, while promoter–reporter analysis, EGR1-binding site mutagenesis, EGR1 overexpression, and chromatin immunoprecipitation supported EGR1-dependent transcriptional regulation of CCL2 in keratinocytes. Furthermore, topical IT25 treatment attenuated house dust mite-induced atopic dermatitis-like skin inflammation and was associated with reduced epidermal CCL2 expression and inflammatory cell infiltration in vivo. Collectively, these findings establish EGR1-dependent regulation of CCL2 in inflammatory keratinocytes and support further investigation of EGR1 DNA-binding activity as a pharmacological target in cutaneous inflammation.

Article.Title: Nutritional Programming via Maternal Protein Restriction Mitigates Long-Term Consequences of Acute Kidney Injury
Article.Authors: García-Ortuño L.; Barragán K.; Caldiño-Bhon R.; Luna E.; Pérez-Villalva R.; Bobadilla N.
Article.Abstract: The kidney is highly sensitive to prenatal and early-life environmental influences. Maternal protein restriction (MPR) can alter renal development and may modify susceptibility to chronic kidney disease (CKD) following acute kidney injury (AKI). We investigated whether MPR during gestation and/or lactation influences the progression from AKI to CKD after renal ischemia–reperfusion (IR) in rat offspring. Fifty Wistar pregnant rats were fed a control (20% casein) or protein-restricted (10% casein) diet during gestation, with diets maintained or switched during lactation, generating four maternal nutritional groups (CC, CR, RC, and RR). At 280–330 g body weight, offspring from these groups were randomly assigned to left renal IR plus right nephrectomy (CC + IR, CR + IR, RC + IR, and RR + IR) or right nephrectomy alone (CC, CR, RC, and RR). Renal outcomes were assessed in two independent cohorts of rats at 7 days and 5 months after surgery. Offspring from MPR during gestation and/or lactation (CR + IR, RC + IR, and RR + IR) showed reduced susceptibility to AKI-to-CKD progression compared to the CC + IR group, characterized by attenuated proteinuria, absence of glomerular hypertrophy, and minimal renal fibrosis. This protective phenotype was associated with reduced oxidative stress and endoplasmic reticulum stress, as indicated by lower 4-HNE, CHOP, and BiP, together with enhanced post-ischemic repair reflected by lower urinary KIM-1 and Hsp72 excretion. MPR during gestation and/or lactation induces a persistent renal phenotype in the offspring that confers resistance to AKI-to-CKD progression, potentially through modulation of oxidative and endoplasmic reticulum stress. These findings highlight developmental nutritional programming as a previously underappreciated determinant of renal resilience in offspring after AKI and provide a basis for investigating nutritional and developmental mechanisms that may be targeted to prevent CKD after AKI.

Article.Title: CYBA Gene Polymorphisms, Lipid Parameters and Atherogenic Indices: A Cohort Study of Healthy Individuals Without Prior Lipid-Lowering Therapy
Article.Authors: Niemiec P.; Nowak T.; Wrona J.; Iwanicka J.; Iwanicki T.; Jarosz A.; Górczyńska-Kosiorz S.; Balcerzyk-Matić A.
Article.Abstract: Single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the CYBA gene, encoding the p22phox subunit of vascular NADPH oxidases, have been associated with atherosclerosis-related disorders. Notably, the G allele/GG genotype of rs13306296 was associated with the least favorable lipid profile across multiple parameters, preferential binding of thirteen TFs, and increased CYBA expression in aorta and heart tissues. Article.Title: Genome-Informed Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP) Assays for Detection and Differentiation of Ralstonia pseudosolanacearum Phylotypes I and III
Article.Authors: Karakkat B.; Huang Q.; Nunziata S.; Yasuhara-Bell J.
Article.Abstract: The Ralstonia solanacearum species complex (RSSC) causes bacterial wilt in a broad range of economically important hosts. The RSSC has been reclassified into three species, of which R. solanacearum sequevars 1 and 2 in phylotype IIB are designated as Select Agents in the U.S. Many rapid tests for “R. solanacearum” target the RSSC and thus cross-react with R. pseudosolanacearum, which is endemic to the U.S. To avoid false positive identifications and unnecessary triggering of Select Agent measures, four portable LAMP-based screening assay variations were developed and validated for specific detection of R. pseudosolanacearum: real-time LAMP assays for detection of R. pseudosolanacearum (1) and differentiation of R. pseudosolanacearum phylotypes I and III in the AmpliFire® Isothermal Fluorometer (2) or Genie® III (3), and a colorimetric LAMP for detection of R. pseudosolanacearum (4). All assays demonstrated high sensitivity (10–50 colony-forming units (CFU)/reaction) and specificity; 100% analytical specificity and selectivity based on 177 RSSC isolates (81 phylotype I, 70 phylotype II, 15 phylotype III and 11 phylotype IV) and 53 non-RSSC bacterial pathogens on relevant hosts and soil, and 100% diagnostic specificity and sensitivity based on testing inoculated plants and a Euphresco sample panel. The assays presented here represent useful diagnostic tools that can be deployed on-site to aid domestic survey and detection efforts.

Candidate prioritization identified phosphorylation events for future validation. Article.Title: Microplastics and the Kidney: A Narrative Review of Human Evidence, Molecular Mechanisms of Cell Injury, and Future Directions
Article.Authors: La Porta E.; Gentile M.; Quaglia M.; Ducoli S.; Massardo S.; Verzola D.; Mancianti N.; Esposito P.
Article.Abstract: Microplastics (MPs) are widespread environmental contaminants, but their potential effects on kidney health remain poorly defined. As an organ continuously exposed to circulating particles and involved in their urinary elimination, the kidney may represent both a target of MP toxicity and a route of excretion. In this narrative review, we examine current evidence linking MPs to kidney injury, integrating experimental, mechanistic, and human data. Particular attention is given to the early events governing particle–cell interactions. After exposure, micro- and nanoplastics acquire an eco- and biomolecular corona that modifies their surface properties, cellular recognition, uptake, and biodistribution. Following internalization through phagocytic and endocytic pathways, particles may accumulate within endolysosomal compartments and interact with intracellular structures, disrupting cellular homeostasis. In renal cells, these events converge on mitochondrial dysfunction, reactive oxygen species generation, endoplasmic reticulum stress, inflammatory signaling, altered autophagy, and regulated cell death. Several interconnected pathways have been implicated, including Keap1–Nrf2/ARE and NF-κB signaling, MAPK and IRE1/XBP1-mediated stress responses, ACSL4–GPX4-related ferroptosis, and TGF-β1-related profibrotic signaling. Human studies have detected MPs in urine and kidney tissue and provide preliminary evidence linking MP burden with early markers of kidney damage, although current findings remain limited by small study populations and substantial methodological heterogeneity. Patients with chronic kidney disease, particularly those receiving dialysis, may represent a population of special interest because potentially altered renal handling may coexist with repeated exposure to polymer-based medical devices and dialysis fluids. Despite this potential relevance, data on MP exposure and accumulation in CKD and dialysis patients remain remarkably scarce. We finally discuss the limitations of current experimental models and analytical methods and the need for standardized biomonitoring, more environmentally relevant particles and exposure concentrations, and detection strategies capable of reaching the nanoscale, including artificial intelligence-assisted analysis. Overall, available evidence provides a mechanistic basis for MP-induced kidney injury, but its clinical relevance and contribution to human kidney disease remain to be established.

Article.Title: Evolutionary and Functional Conservation of Topologically Associating Domain Boundaries in Rice Genomes
Article.Authors: Geyman O.; Kurbidaeva A.
Article.Abstract: Traditional evolutionary analysis has relied primarily on one-dimensional (1D) sequencing data, but recent advances in three-dimensional (3D) genomics allow for deeper investigation of how genome architecture shapes evolutionary divergence. Here, we characterize boundary conservation at different levels, from highly conserved to species-unique. We apply TCBF, a relatively novel and underutilized tool for TAD boundary conservation analysis, alongside a suite of complementary analyses, including gene ontology, RNA-seq, sequence conservation, and epigenetic profiling. Our approach not only validates canonical evolutionary relationships reflected in sequence data but also novel patterns unique to 3D genome organization. Most notably, our study uncovers strong associations between highly conserved TAD boundaries and RNA metabolism-related genes, as well as other genetic and epigenetic signatures, and a contrasting absence in minimally conserved boundaries. To our knowledge, we created the first phylogenetic reconstruction derived from topological domain data in plants, which demonstrated a strong similarity between 3D and 1D genomic evolutionary relationships. Overall, our work presents an approach that integrates the 3D genome structure into evolutionary genomics, addressing a critical and underexplored dimension of comparative plant genomics.

Article.Title: Molecular Genetics and Reproductive Genomic Medicine in Cleft Lip and Palate: Current Evidence, Preimplantation Testing, and Clinical Translation—A Narrative Review
Article.Authors: Fan R.; Shen H.; Liu Y.; Ji T.; Zhang L.; Ma X.
Article.Abstract: Cleft lip and palate (CLP) is a common congenital craniofacial anomaly with heterogeneous clinical manifestations and complex etiologies. Current evidence indicates that CLP arises from the combined effects of Mendelian syndromic disorders, rare pathogenic variants, common susceptibility loci, non-coding regulatory variants, epigenetic regulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and maternal environmental exposures. Although reconstructive surgery and multidisciplinary care remain central to treatment, families with recurrent CLP or a family history of orofacial clefts increasingly seek reproductive counseling and genetic risk assessment before pregnancy. Preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) may provide a clinically meaningful option when a pathogenic variant, chromosomal abnormality, or clearly defined familial haplotype is identified. However, most non-syndromic CLP cases are polygenic or multifactorial, and the application of preimplantation genetic testing for polygenic disorders (PGT-P) remains limited by modest predictive accuracy, population-specific transferability, embryo-number constraints, incomplete penetrance, variants of uncertain significance, and uncertain long-term clinical utility. This narrative review summarizes the clinical phenotypes and genomic architecture of CLP, evaluates the principles and current limitations of preimplantation genetic testing for monogenic disorders (PGT-M) and PGT-P, and discusses psychosocial and ethical issues in reproductive decision-making. We propose that PGT for CLP should be positioned as part of a stepwise counseling framework rather than as a universal preventive strategy. Future progress will depend on standardized phenotyping, multi-ancestry genomic databases, functional validation of candidate variants, transparent risk communication, and shared decision-making that respects both reproductive autonomy and the uncertainty of genomic prediction.

Article.Title: Inflammatory Burden Shapes Antioxidant Adaptation and Immunometabolic Remodeling in LPS-Activated BV-2 Microglial Cells
Article.Authors: Barbalace M.; Rinaldi I.; Mantini M.; Zallocco L.; Ronci M.; Di Cintio F.; Attanzio A.; Prata C.; Malaguti M.; Hrelia S.; Giusti L.; Angeloni C.
Article.Abstract: Neuroinflammation is a hallmark of numerous neurodegenerative diseases and is characterized by profound inflammatory, metabolic, and redox alterations in activated microglia. Although lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated BV-2 cells represent one of the most widely used in vitro models of neuroinflammation, a comprehensive understanding of the coordinated molecular adaptations underlying this model remains incomplete. Functional enrichment analysis identified Nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) as the most significantly activated upstream regulator, a prediction consistent with engagement of an adaptive antioxidant program. Interestingly, analysis of increasing LPS concentrations revealed that antioxidant responses were not proportional to the inflammatory stimulus. Expression of NRF2-controlled antioxidant enzymes progressively increased for LPS concentrations up to 500 ng/mL, but declined at 1000 ng/mL LPS, whereas pro-inflammatory mediators remained continuously upregulated. This pattern is consistent with the attenuation of antioxidant adaptation under the highest inflammatory burden tested. Together, these findings demonstrate that the BV-2/LPS model is characterized by a dynamic interplay between inflammatory, redox, metabolic, lysosomal, endocytic, and cytoskeletal pathways, providing a more comprehensive characterization to support the interpretation and experimental use of this neuroinflammatory model.

Article.Title: Genome-Wide Identification and Characterization of the Rboh Gene Family in Populus trichocarpa Reveals PtrRbohB Positively Regulates Adventitious Root Development
Article.Authors: Shi R.; Ding Y.; Guo P.; Shang F.; Cao S.
Article.Abstract: Adventitious roots (ARs) are essential for clonal vegetative propagation of woody tree species. Collectively, this study provides the direct genetic evidence that Rboh regulates AR formation in poplar, and identifies PtrRbohB as a key positive regulator of AR development. These findings enrich our understanding of woody plant AR formation and provide candidate genes for molecular breeding of poplar rooting traits.

Article.Title: Urinary Metabolomics in Bladder Cancer: A Scoping Review of Current Evidence and Translation Implications
Article.Authors: Carapito Â.; Amaro F.; Roque A.; Carvalho F.; Pinto J.; Guedes de Pinho P.
Article.Abstract: Bladder cancer (BC) diagnosis and surveillance currently rely largely on invasive cystoscopy, making urine an attractive non-invasive biofluid for discovering metabolic biomarkers, given its direct contact with the bladder urothelium. This review provides a comprehensive and critical synthesis of the literature on urinary metabolomic profiling in BC, summarising metabolites and metabolite panels associated with the disease, their relevant metabolic pathways, and diagnostic performance. A search was conducted in PubMed, complemented by records from reference lists of relevant reviews. After screening, 30 original studies comparing urinary metabolomic profiles between BC patients and cancer-free controls were included, encompassing diverse analytical platforms and statistical approaches. A wide range of urinary metabolites were reported to be altered between BC patients and controls, of which 52 were recurrently identified in at least two independent studies. Increased levels of taurine, valine, lactate, adenosine monophosphate and adipate were among the most consistent metabolic alterations, whereas the levels of citrate, glycerol, creatinine, and several dicarboxylic acids and acylcarnitines were consistently decreased. Other metabolites, such as hippurate, tyrosine, and histidine, showed variable trends in their levels. These alterations may reflect metabolic processes associated with tumour growth, energy reprogramming, lipid metabolism, and oxidative stress adaptation. Most studies also proposed multi-metabolite panels combining metabolites to discriminate BC patients from controls, achieving sensitivity and specificity up to 100% and AUC up to 0.983, while fewer studies explored panels for tumour stage and grade discrimination, with more modest performance. Overall, urinary metabolomics reveals a broad, biologically coherent set of metabolic alterations associated with BC, but methodological heterogeneity and limited independent validation still hinder clinical translation. Larger, harmonised, prospectively validated studies integrating multi-omics and machine learning are needed to establish robust urinary biomarkers for BC.

Article.Authors: Cai H.; Xie G.; Liu H.; Chen Y.; Li H.; Wan J.; Deng Z.

In a 160-sample bulk RNA-seq cohort, TOP2A was overexpressed in high-grade and recurrent tumors, and elevated TOP2A mRNA was significantly associated with shorter progression-free survival (PFS). IHC on 154 specimens confirmed TOP2A protein overexpression, and FISH on 27 specimens demonstrated focal TOP2A copy-number gain enriched in high-grade cases. Copy-number gain was concordant with TOP2A mRNA levels. Article.Authors: Urbanowicz T.; Kowalewski M.; Suwalski P.; Raffa G.
Article.Abstract: Heart transplantation transfers not only donor alloantigens and functional myocardium but also a pre-existing tissue environment shaped by resident immune, vascular, stromal, and parenchymal populations. Donor-resident macrophages, endothelial cells, fibroblasts, extracellular matrix, and tissue-resident lymphocytes constitute an immunologically active myocardial niche that encounters ischemia–reperfusion injury and recipient immune effectors immediately after implantation. Experimental and human studies demonstrate the dynamic coexistence and replacement of donor- and recipient-derived immune populations, with recipient cells acquiring phenotypes within the graft microenvironment. We distinguish transient donor-tissue activation from genuine tissue immune memory, which would require persistence of an exposure-induced molecular or functional state and an altered response to a subsequent challenge. Potential mechanisms include trained innate immunity, epigenetic and metabolic reprogramming, endothelial inflammatory memory, and persistent stromal–immune interactions. We propose that allograft biology be investigated at the level of the donor–recipient immune pair and outline longitudinal single-cell, spatial, and cell-of-origin approaches to test this concept in human heart transplantation.

Article.Title: Is Aging a Failure to Resolve? Integrating Damage Responses, Regenerative Decline, and Geroscience Interventions
Article.Authors: Chmielewski P.; Strzelec B.
Article.Abstract: Biological aging is accompanied by persistent tissue-damage signaling, chronic inflammation, extracellular matrix remodeling, cellular senescence, and declining regenerative capacity. Taken together, these features resemble an injury response that is repeatedly initiated but fails to progress reliably through clearance, reconstruction, and functional recovery. This resemblance motivated the proposal that aging is a wound that never starts healing. Here, we develop that proposal into a testable failed-resolution framework in which some age-related dysfunction reflects damage responses that exceed organ-specific capacities for intracellular quality control, efferocytosis, immune termination, matrix normalization, and cell replacement. Its central predictions are that (i) impaired recovery kinetics will forecast functional decline beyond established measures of biological age, (ii) restoring resolution will improve tissue function beyond suppressing inflammatory markers, and (iii) efficacy will depend on treatment phase and tissue-specific failure mode. We specify which age-related processes lie outside the framework and propose measurements spanning damage burden, danger sensing, resolution competence, regenerative reserve, organ function, and recovery after standardized challenge. Supporting evidence is predominantly preclinical, whereas human studies provide mechanistic findings, target engagement, or domain-specific effects. Failed resolution thus offers a falsifiable research program for testing tissue recovery as a therapeutic target in aging.

Article.Authors: Cortes-Camacho F.; Zambrano-Vásquez O.; García-Arroyo F.; Aréchaga-Ocampo E.; Castañeda-Sánchez J.; Manzur-Sandoval D.; Roldan-Gómez F.; Valle-Mondragón L.; Aparicio-Trejo O.; Martínez-Olivares C.; Hernández-Pando R.; Gonzaga-Sánchez J.; Sánchez-Lozada L.; Osorio-Alonso H.

Likewise, the increases in angiotensin II and nitric oxide concentrations in the hearts and kidneys were attenuated (p < 0.05). These effects appear to be mediated by the modulation of key proteins involved in vascular tone, uric acid metabolism, oxidative stress, inflammation, and regulation of transcription factors involved in carbohydrate and lipid metabolism.

Article.Title: Translational Potential of the Epoxyeicosatrienoic Acid Pathway in Neurological Disorders
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; He Z.
Article.Abstract: Neurological disorders represent a leading cause of global disability and mortality. Given that current single-target therapies often fail to halt disease progression or cross the blood–brain barrier (BBB), novel therapeutic strategies are urgently needed. Endogenous lipid networks offer promising targets. They are major structural components of the central nervous system (CNS) that provide multi-target neuroprotection essential for homeostasis and can bypass BBB restrictions naturally or via brain-penetrant small-molecule modulation. Among these lipids, arachidonic acid (AA) accounts for approximately 20% of total neuronal fatty acids. Upon cellular activation, while the cyclooxygenases (COXs) and lipoxygenases (LOXs) pathways yield pro-inflammatory mediators targeted by classic drugs, the cytochrome P450 (CYP450) cascade generates protective epoxyeicosatrienoic acids (EETs), which serve as fundamental regulators of systemic and neural homeostasis. Within the CNS, EETs act as crucial protectors of the neurovascular unit (NVU) by regulating cerebral blood flow (CBF), maintaining BBB integrity, and promoting angiogenesis. Furthermore, they actively mitigate neuroinflammation by suppressing microglial activation, reducing oxidative stress, and inhibiting neuronal apoptosis. Through these multifaceted mechanisms, alongside the enhancement of neurogenesis and synaptic plasticity, EETs effectively protect the brain against ischemic stroke, neurodegenerative diseases, and other neurological insults. Consequently, this article comprehensively reviews the physiological roles, underlying mechanisms, and regulatory factors of EETs in the nervous system. Ultimately, by highlighting the translational potential of targeted soluble epoxide hydrolase (sEH) inhibition and EET elevation, this review aims to pave the way for innovative neuroprotective therapies.

Article.Title: Prediction of Tumor Complete Response Using Genomic and Clinical Data in Solid Cancer Undergoing Definitive Radiation Therapy
Article.Authors: Chang J.; Jung S.; Lee D.
Article.Abstract: In this retrospective, single-center observational study, targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) was performed on pre-radiation therapy (RT) tumor specimens to identify genomic features associated with RT response and clinical outcomes. This study included 77 eligible patients with esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC, n = 23), non-human papilloma virus-related head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC, n = 24), and rectal adenocarcinoma (RAC, n = 30) treated between 2014 and 2020. Treatment was employed for definitive aim (chemoradiotherapy or pre-operative chemoradiotherapy followed by radical surgery). Treatment response was assessed using clinical and pathological criteria and was dichotomized as complete response (CR) versus non-CR. Targeted NGS was performed using a customized panel composing 161 genes. A total of 1263 nonsynonymous somatic variants were identified across 153 genes. The most commonly altered genes were TP53 (70.1%), APC (41.6%), NOTCH1 (41.6%), KMT2C (39.0%), NOTCH3 (36.4%), and NOTCH2 (35.1%). Overall, 25 (32.5%) and 52 patients (67.5%) were classified as CR and non-CR, respectively. APC (P = 0.008), KMT2C (P = 0.018), and KRAS (P = 0.012) alterations were associated with non-CR, whereas CD274 (P = 0.003), MSH3 (P = 0.011), and NOTCH3 (P = 0.048) alterations were associated with CR. KRAS alterations occurred exclusively in RAC, and most concurrent APC–KMT2C alterations in non-CR tumors were also observed in RAC, suggesting that these associations may partly reflect tumor type-specific genomic backgrounds. An exploratory pooled model incorporating age and six candidate genomic variables achieved a cross-validated area under the curve of 0.867 for CR prediction. In survival analysis, alterations in CCND1, CXCL9, ERCC6, LIF, and RAD51B were independently associated with poor recurrence-free survival. Pre-RT tumor genomic profiling identified candidate features associated with RT response and recurrence-free survival in this heterogeneous cohort. The pooled genomic associations and prediction model should not be interpreted as pan-cancer biomarkers or predictors and require validation in larger, independent, cancer-specific cohort.

Article.Title: Targeted DNA Sequencing Reveals Distinct Rare-Variant Profiles in Pulmonary Hypertension Associated with Chronic Lung Diseases
Article.Authors: Bosacoma A.; Garcia A.; Madrigal I.; Lozano J.; Sidorova J.; Aguilar D.; Blanco I.; Roger Y.; Tura-Ceide O.; Sardiné-Rama A.; Martín-Ontiyuelo C.; Rodríguez-Chiaradía D.; López-Meseguer M.; Hernandez-Gonzalez F.; Ribas J.; Pomares X.; Santos S.; Molina-Molina M.; Fernández-Hernández R.; Peinado V.; Barberà J.
Article.Abstract: The mechanisms underlying the development and severity of pulmonary hypertension (PH) in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and interstitial lung disease (ILD) remain poorly understood. To investigate the contribution of genetic factors, we performed targeted sequencing of PH-related genes in 63 patients with COPD, 51 with ILD, and 38 with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension (IPAH), stratifying COPD and ILD patients according to PH severity, assessed by right heart catheterisation. Patients with ILD-associated PH harboured fewer genetic variants than those without PH, whereas an opposite trend was observed in COPD-associated PH. Variants of uncertain significance (VUS) in PAH-associated genes (BMPR2, BMPR1B) were identified in two out of 28 patients with severe COPD-PH and in one with nonsevere ILD-PH (SMAD9). VUS in extracellular matrix-related genes (THBS1, LOXL2) were also identified in four patients with severe COPD-PH, and in inflammatory-related genes (TNFAIP6) in two patients with ILD-PH. Pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants in PAH-associated genes were exclusive to IPAH. We conclude that there is limited genetic overlap between COPD-PH and ILD-PH, with a stronger genetic contribution to PH in COPD, particularly in its severe form, where a subset of patients carries VUS in PAH-associated genes or genes involved in vascular remodelling.

Article.Title: Diagnostic and Predictive CSF Biomarkers in Idiopathic Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (iNPH): A Systematic Review
Article.Authors: Procopio E.; Accattatis A.; Stroscio C.; Guzzi G.; Lavano A.; La Torre D.; Della Torre A.
Article.Abstract: Idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH) is a progressive disorder clinically characterized by Hakim’s triad: gait disturbance, cognitive impairment, and urinary incontinence. iNPH treatment consists of neurosurgical implantation of a ventriculoperitoneal CSF diversion, whose outcome depends on an early and correct diagnosis. Currently, there is no specific diagnostic test to perform preoperatively. Still, the combination of neurological examination, gait analysis, neurocognitive evaluation, and the tap test is useful to suggest when surgery is indicated. Our systematic review aims to identify diagnostic and outcome predictor CSF biomarkers (BM) in iNPH. The present systematic review was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library databases were first consulted in April 2025 and updated in May 2026. Studies were selected using the terms “idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus” and “CSF biomarkers” under Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) as inclusion criteria. The eligibility of a record was defined according to the study title and abstract. The QUADAS-2, QUIPS, ROBINS-I V2, and RobVis tools were used to assess the risk of bias. Ninety-nine records were included in this systematic review. Amyloid proteins (Aβ40-42), followed by tau (τT, τP−181) and neuroinflammatory proteins were the most frequently CSF BM analyzed in patients with iNPH. ELISA was the most used method to measure BM in CSF samples. Forty-seven records investigated the potential diagnostic role of CSF BM; comparisons were frequently made among iNPH, Alzheimer’s disease (AD), and healthy control CSF samples. Regarding outcome prediction, 28 records examined CSF BM, with heterogeneous comparisons such as lumbar versus ventricular CSF or shunted versus non-shunted iNPH CSF samples, including healthy controls and iNPH. Seven records proposed both the diagnostic and predictive role of some CSF biomarkers, especially for tau proteins and Aβ42. On the other hand, 17 records concluded that neither a diagnostic nor a predictive role could be proposed for the CSF BM they analyzed. However, these records increased knowledge about an iNPH CSF pattern. Collecting and analyzing CSF samples from iNPH patients can be advantageous in differential diagnosis with other similar neurodegenerative disorders, especially AD, and therefore a predictor of neurosurgical outcomes. Combined biomarker panels should be integrated in standardized protocols, measuring: Aβ42, Aβ42/Aβ40, p-tau, total tau, ADAβ42/p-tau, L-PGDS, NFL and NRGN.

Article.Title: Cachexia and Sarcopenia in Patients with Coexisting Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease and Pulmonary Tuberculosis
Article.Authors: Oskin D.; Kotlyarov S.
Article.Abstract: Malnutrition, loss of muscle mass, and reduced muscle strength are common but underrecognized conditions in tuberculosis (TB) and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). These abnormalities may persist after completion of TB treatment, and a normal or elevated body mass index does not exclude muscle depletion. Unlike the extensively studied conditions of hyperglycemia and obesity, the catabolic end of the spectrum of metabolic disturbances in coexisting TB and COPD remains insufficiently investigated. This narrative review focuses on cachexia and sarcopenia in patients with coexisting TB and COPD (TB–COPD). It examines the roles of systemic inflammation, immunometabolic remodeling, mitochondrial dysfunction, disturbances in protein metabolism and endocrine regulation, and ceramide signaling. Because direct evidence in TB–COPD is scarce, findings from TB or post-tuberculosis lung disease without confirmed COPD and from COPD alone are used as indirect evidence, and the level of evidence is indicated for each mechanism. The diagnostic approach is organized around current clinical guidelines and includes assessment of nutritional status, diagnosis of malnutrition using the Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition (GLIM) criteria, identification of sarcopenia using European Working Group on Sarcopenia in Older People 2 (EWGSOP2) or Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia (AWGS) criteria, pulmonary function testing to distinguish post-tuberculosis airflow obstruction from COPD, and evaluation for reversible causes of muscle weakness. The main treatment approaches are correction of malnutrition, pulmonary rehabilitation, and treatment of the underlying respiratory disease. The effectiveness of interventions is assessed through changes in muscle strength, physical performance, body weight, and body composition. The evidence base for patients with coexisting TB and COPD remains limited; most studies have investigated each disease separately. The efficacy of pharmacological agents targeting the molecular mechanisms of muscle wasting has not been established in this population. Priorities for future research include prospective assessment of muscle function in TB–COPD cohorts and the development of personalized strategies for nutritional and rehabilitation support.

Article.Title: Genome-Wide Identification of the Castanea mollissima MADS-Box Gene Family and Its Potential Roles in Female Flower Development Based on Transcriptomic and Morphological Analyses
Article.Authors: Zeng L.; Hu X.; Yang H.; Song J.; Guo R.; Zhang H.; Zhang J.; Guo C.
Article.Abstract: Castanea mollissima is an important woody food crop in China. Late, sparse, and unstable female flower differentiation constrains the development of the chestnut industry. Here, two more-female cultivars, ‘Longquanzhuang No. 2’ (LQ) and ‘Yanqiu’ (YQ), and the control cultivar ‘Yanshanzaofeng’ (ZF) were sampled at five stages after budbreak (7–35 d) for morphological observation and transcriptome sequencing. Morphological divergence became evident at 21 d after budbreak. Transcriptome analysis identified 2223 differentially expressed genes specific to the LQ–ZF comparison at 21 d and 791 inter-cultivar differentially expressed genes shared across 21–35 d. GO enrichment analysis showed significant enrichment in transcription factor activity and related pathways. Transcription factor prediction identified MADS-box genes as candidates, and 60 MADS-box members were identified in Chinese chestnut. These comprised 29 Type I members and 31 Type II members, with the latter classified into 13 subfamilies. Integrated analysis of gene-expression patterns and predicted protein interactions showed that more Type II genes were differentially expressed in female flowers and that expression patterns differed between the more-female cultivars and the control. The contrasting expression patterns of putative positive and negative CmMADS regulators may be associated with differences in female flower developmental capacity among these cultivars. RT-qPCR analysis of four representative CmMADS genes showed that genes expressed at higher levels in female flowers generally increased during development, consistent with the transcriptome data. These findings reveal morphological divergence and dynamic CmMADS expression during female flower development in two more-female chestnut cultivars and a control cultivar, providing a basis for investigating the underlying molecular regulatory network, but functional validation is currently limited to transcriptome-level prediction, requiring further experimental verification.

Article.Title: Genome-Wide Identification of the TCP Gene Family in Tetraploid Potato and Analysis of Their Potential Roles in Tuber Development
Article.Authors: Li Y.; Mei L.; Ma Y.; Zhao L.; Wang J.; Wang F.
Article.Abstract: Potato tuber formation is a complex developmental process regulated by coordinated interactions among multiple phytohormones and genes. TEOSINTE BRANCHED1/CYCLOIDEA/PROLIFERATING CELL FACTOR (TCP) transcription factors play important roles in plant growth, development and responses to environmental stimuli; however, their specific functions in tuber development in tetraploid potato remain poorly understood. In this study, we performed genome-wide identification and systematic characterization of the TCP gene family in tetraploid potato, integrated transcriptome profiling, quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR), protein–protein interaction prediction and weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) to identify candidate genes potentially associated with tuber development. A total of 57 StTCP genes were identified across 29 chromosomes and classified into eight subfamilies. Members within the same subfamily generally shared similar gene structures, conserved motifs and protein domains, whereas their promoter regions contained abundant cis-acting elements associated with light and phytohormone responses, growth and development, and stress responses. Expression profiling revealed distinct StTCP expression patterns under temperature stress and across tuber developmental stages. Eight StTCP genes exhibited pronounced stage-specific expression across the four developmental stages, and their expression trends were broadly supported by quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR). In particular, StTCP42, StTCP55, and StTCP57 showed significantly higher expression at the stolon hook stage than at the other stages (p < 0.05), whereas StTCP20 was significantly upregulated at the subapical swelling stage (p < 0.05). Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) of RNA-seq data from the four developmental stages identified 27 co-expression modules. The turquoise, dark red, pink, and green modules were significantly and positively associated with the stolon hook, subapical swelling, initial tuber formation, and tuber formation stages, respectively; the turquoise module showed the strongest positive correlation with the stolon hook stage (r = 0.997, false discovery rate (FDR) = 2.77 × 10−10). Notably, StTCP42 and StTCP57 were both highly expressed at the stolon hook stage and were assigned to the turquoise module. StTCP42 further exhibited high module membership (kME = 0.930) and gene significance (GS = 0.937, p = 6.79 × 10−6), providing convergent evidence for its association with early tuber development by the transcriptomic, qRT-PCR, and co-expression evidence. This study systematically characterised the TCP gene family in tetraploid potato and identified several candidate genes potentially associated with tuber development, particularly StTCP42 and StTCP57. These findings provide a foundation for future functional studies aimed at elucidating the roles of TCP transcription factors in potato tuber formation and development.

Article.Title: Age and Neuroimmune Diseases
Article.Authors: Yu Z.; Huang X.; Zhang H.; Shi F.
Article.Abstract: Abstract With the aging population accelerating, age has become a core factor influencing the clinical phenotypes, treatment responses, and prognoses of neuroimmune diseases (NDs), including those affecting the central nervous system (CNS) and peripheral nervous system (PNS). This cross-disease review summarizes the shared and specific age-related characteristics of NDs, focusing on the pathological basis of immunosenescence and neurodegeneration underlying age-related ND progression. We extract the clinical manifestations, immune and neural mechanisms of elderly ND patients, and evaluate the challenges and individualized adjustment principles of therapeutic strategies for this population. We explore the age-related immune dysregulation features between NDs and other systemic autoimmune diseases (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), type 1 diabetes (T1D)). This review aims to construct a cross-disease framework for the precision management of NDs in the aging era, identify research gaps and future directions, and emphasize age-adapted intervention strategies for optimizing the prognosis of elderly ND patients.

Article.Title: Thrombospondin 2 Promotes Neuropathic Pain by Mediating Nav1.7 Membrane Anchoring in Mouse Primary Sensory Neurons
Article.Authors: Wei J.; Wang Y.; Zhao Z.; Chen H.; Chang S.; Yang Q.; Wang H.; Liu X.; Zhou X.; Li X.; Zhang J.; Liang L.
Article.Abstract: Thrombospondin 2 (TSP2), a member of the thrombospondin family of extracellular matrix proteins, mediates critical cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions. However, its potential roles in neuropathic pain remain unclear. We demonstrate that TSP2 is specifically expressed in isolectin B4-negative dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons. Following lumbar 4 (L4) spinal nerve ligation (SNL), TSP2 expression was upregulated in both injured (L4) and uninjured (L3) DRGs. Notably, siRNA-mediated TSP2 knockdown attenuated SNL-induced pain hypersensitivity during the development phase, but not during the maintenance phase, of neuropathic pain. Conversely, neuron-specific TSP2 overexpression in the DRG alone was sufficient to produce enhanced nociceptive behavior. Mechanistically, SNL enhanced the interaction between TSP2 and Nav1.7, promoting Nav1.7 membrane anchoring in the L3 and L4 DRGs and thereby increasing DRG neuronal excitability. These findings establish TSP2 as a novel Nav1.7-interacting protein and a potential therapeutic target for preventing chronic neuropathic pain.

Article.Title: Neural Stem Cell Therapies for Central Nervous System Regeneration: Advances, Challenges, and Integrative Technologies
Article.Authors: Marei H.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Neural stem cells (NSCs) are promising candidates for central nervous system (CNS) regeneration because they self-renew and differentiate into neural lineages. Advances in genome engineering, extracellular vesicles (EVs), biomaterials, organoids, single-cell technologies, and precision medicine have expanded approaches for characterizing, engineering, delivering, and evaluating NSC-based therapies for neurological disorders. CRISPR/Cas9 and related platforms may enable more precise modification of NSC function, while NSC-derived EVs offer potential cell-free strategies. Engineered hydrogels and three-dimensional scaffolds may improve cell survival, engraftment, migration, and integration. Organoids and single-cell omics provide increasingly detailed models of cellular heterogeneity and lineage specification. However, clinical translation remains limited by immune compatibility, tumorigenic risk, manufacturing standardization, graft survival and integration, and regulatory requirements. Rigorous preclinical validation, standardized manufacturing, appropriately designed clinical trials, long-term safety monitoring, and harmonized regulatory frameworks are required before routine clinical application.

Article.Title: Systematic Microcircuit Reconfigurations Underlie Early Experience-induced Visual Cortical Plasticity
Article.Authors: Yao L.; Shang Z.; Ji Z.; Meng M.; Wang F.; Gu X.; He M.; Wu S.; Zhang X.
Article.Abstract: Experience-dependent reorganization of neuronal connections during the postnatal critical period is essential for the functional maturation of the developing primary visual cortex (V1). However, the systematic reconfigurations across microcircuit synapses underlying experience-dependent plasticity are poorly defined. Using paired whole-cell recordings from excitatory pyramidal cells and three other major classes of interneurons (INs) within layers 2/3 and 4 in the developing mouse V1 monocular region, we found that monocular deprivation (MD) for one day in juvenile mice transiently reconfigures local excitatory synapses onto inhibitory INs that specifically express parvalbumin (PV) or vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP). In contrast, prolonged MD predominantly strengthens inhibitory synaptic transmission from somatostatin (SST)-expressing INs to PV-INs and VIP-INs across both layers. A physiologically based microcircuit model further recapitulated MD-induced activity changes in visual responses across layer 2/3 neurons in vivo. We provide a detailed microcircuit framework that contributes to the experience-dependent regulation of visual function.

Article.Title: Transcranial Evoked Potentials are Minimally Influenced by Afferent Feedback From Peripheral Muscle Contraction
Article.Authors: Marco M.; Andrea G.; Andrea F.; Carlo P.; Giorgio L.; Rocchi L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Transcranial magnetic stimulation with electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) investigates cortical reactivity, yet the contribution of sensory feedback from muscle twitches to the recorded signals remains debated. We combined M1 TMS-EEG with electromyography, accelerometry, and peripheral electrical stimulation to dissociate central and peripheral contributions. We compared EEG responses across trials yielding large versus small motor outputs, while peripheral stimulation isolated pure afferent components. Bayesian analysis revealed that larger motor outputs covaried with distinct EEG morphologies uniformly across all time windows—including those too early for peripheral feedback—indicating that spontaneous fluctuations in baseline motor cortex excitability drive both responses. Conversely, isolated muscle contraction produced delayed (> 65 ms), markedly smaller EEG responses with distinct spatiotemporal profiles. We conclude that sensory feedback from muscle twitches contributes minimally to TMS-evoked EEG responses, which instead primarily reflect the baseline excitability state of the stimulated cortex.

Article.Title: Distinct Contributions and Sensorimotor Encoding of PV and FoxP2 Neurons in the External Globus Pallidus during Perceptual Decision-making
Article.Authors: Pu X.; Ren J.; Xie T.; Zou K.; Xu J.; Li Y.; Liu D.; Yao H.
Article.Abstract: The external globus pallidus (GPe), the central nucleus of the basal ganglia, comprises diverse cell types, including parvalbumin (PV) and forkhead box protein P2 (FoxP2) neurons. Their roles in movement regulation and sensory processing are well established; however, their contribution to perceptual decision-making remains unclear. Using a Go/No-Go visual task in mice, we found that optogenetic activation of either population impaired performance, whereas PV inhibition, but not FoxP2 inhibition, disrupted behavioral accuracy. Electrophysiological recordings showed that PV and FoxP2 neurons differentially encoded visual stimuli, licking movements, and trial outcomes. FoxP2 inhibition produced minimal changes in the spontaneous firing of substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) neurons. PV inhibition altered spontaneous SNr firing and, together with PV activation, altered task-evoked SNr activity, reducing the preference for reward-predicting stimuli in one subpopulation and unrewarded outcomes in another. These findings reveal the distinct roles of GPe PV and FoxP2 neurons in shaping perceptual decisions and modulating basal ganglia output.

Article.Title: Neuroplastin Suppresses Seizures by Downregulating Endophilin A1 to Promote Internalization of GluA1-AMPA Receptors: Therapeutic Implications of Arbutin
Article.Authors: Li S.; Chen M.; Zheng S.; Wei X.; Sun L.; Wei L.; Lu Y.; Ma M.; Wu Y.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Status epilepticus (SE) is a critical neurological disorder characterized by an imbalance between excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmission. α-Amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptors (AMPARs) mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission, whereas internalization of GluA1-containing AMPARs regulates neuronal excitability. Although neuroplastin (Np) modulates neuronal excitability, its role in GluA1-AMPAR internalization in epilepsy remains unclear. Using single-cell transcriptomics, virtual knockout, in vitro and in vivo epilepsy models, patch-clamp, biochemistry, and behavioral tests, we identified Endophilin A1 (EndoA1) as a key target through which Np regulates GluA1 internalization. In epilepsy models, EndoA1 was upregulated, surface GluA1 levels increased, and receptor internalization was reduced. EndoA1 knockdown decreased the amplitude and frequency of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs), promoted GluA1 internalization, prolonged seizure latency, and shortened seizure duration. Np overexpression reduced EndoA1 expression, facilitated GluA1 internalization, and suppressed hyperexcitability, whereas EndoA1 knockdown rescued the Np knockdown-induced phenotype. Network pharmacology and molecular docking studies identified arbutin as an EndoA1-targeting compound that reduced hyperexcitability, mEPSC amplitude, and surface GluA1 in a concentration-dependent manner. These findings establish the Np–EndoA1–GluA1 axis as a key epileptic pathway, whereby Np negatively regulates EndoA1 to promote GluA1-AMPAR internalization and suppress excitability. Arbutin, which targets EndoA1, exerts anti-epileptic effects by modulating excitatory transmission.

Article.Title: Spatiotemporal Resolution for Neurodegenerative Diseases: Linking Proteinopathy, Cellular Vulnerability, and Disease Trajectories
Article.Authors: Dong M.; Wang C.; Chen Z.; Ding S.; Peng L.; Jiang H.
Article.Abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDs) are a heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by selective and progressive degeneration of specific neuronal populations, often accompanied by glial dysfunction. Despite extensive investigation, proposed pathogenic models remain insufficient to fully explain selective vulnerability and stereotyped spatiotemporal patterns of neurodegeneration across diseases. Spatial omics technologies preserve anatomical context and enable interrogation of cell-type composition, molecular heterogeneity, and intercellular interactions within neural systems. In this review, we synthesize current concepts and technological advances in spatial omics and discuss how these approaches are reshaping our understanding of NDs. Spatial omics provides an integrative framework for linking pathological protein aggregation with selective cellular vulnerability, microenvironment-dependent interactions, and disease progression across molecular, cellular, and anatomical scales. We highlight emerging insights into pathology-associated gene modules, neuron-glia interactions, and mechanisms underlying regional vulnerability. Finally, we discuss multimodal data integration and future directions for translating spatially resolved molecular maps into mechanistic understanding.

Article.Title: Theta-Band Temporal Interference Stimulation Modulates Food Reward Prediction Error Encoding in Individuals with Elevated Food Addiction Symptoms
Article.Authors: Wen Y.; Wang M.; Dong X.; Gola M.; Liu Q.; Tu Y.; Li Y.
Article.Abstract: Prediction error (PE) signals support feedback evaluation and adaptive updating, and are closely linked to medial frontal theta dynamics, particularly within dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC)-centered networks. However, evidence linking these oscillatory mechanisms to the modulation of PE encoding remains limited. Here, we tested whether theta-band modulation of a dACC-centered medial frontal network altered trial-level PE encoding during food-reward processing. In a single-blind, sham-controlled pre-post design, individuals with elevated food addiction symptoms performed a food incentive-delay task while undergoing electroencephalographic recordings combined with theta-band temporal interference stimulation. Single-trial analyses revealed that feedback-related negativity (FRN) amplitudes varied as a function of both behavioral and model-derived prediction errors. Critically, theta-band modulation altered FRN-PE coupling, with the effect most pronounced for unfavorable outcomes, whereas anticipatory activity remained unchanged. These findings support the hypothesis that theta-band modulation can alter feedback-related PE encoding within this population and task context.

Article.Title: Cystatin C and its Role in the Neuro-Glial-Vascular Unit: Implications for Cerebrovascular Diseases and Neurodegeneration
Article.Authors: Li M.; Wang Z.; Huang Z.; Guo X.; Wang Q.; Wei X.
Article.Abstract: Cystatin C (CysC) is emerging as a key regulator and intercellular signaling mediator within the neuro-glial-vascular unit (NGVU). This review comprehensively examines its multifaceted roles across NGVU components, detailing mechanisms by which CysC preserves blood-brain barrier integrity, modulates neuroinflammation, and influences pathological protein aggregation. Rather than providing a merely descriptive catalogue, we emphasize its context-dependent nature. In cerebrovascular and neurodegenerative diseases, CysC exhibits functional duality along the neuron-glia axis, either restraining or perpetuating inflammation and proteinopathy depending on cellular context and disease stage. Similarly, along the endothelial-oligodendrocyte precursor cell crosstalk, its coordination of angiogenesis and myelination may shift from protective to detrimental under chronic hypoperfusion. We evaluate its dual utility as a clinical biomarker and therapeutic target, addressing challenges in brain delivery, target selectivity, and safety. This integrative synthesis provides a critical perspective on unresolved controversies and future research priorities regarding CysC in neurological disorders.

Article.Title: Normative Modeling of Amygdala Subfields and Disease-Specific Vulnerabilities Across Neurological Disorders
Article.Authors: Zhang C.; Bai L.; Shi D.; Li W.; Ai L.; Ao F.; Bai Y.; Bai Y.; Bao H.; Cai Q.; Cao J.; Chai L.; Chen F.; Chen F.; Chen K.; Chen Y.; Cheng D.; Cole J.; Cui Z.; Dai H.; Deng D.; Du X.; Du Y.; Duan X.; Fu Y.
Article.Abstract: As an integrative center of the limbic system, the amygdala and its subfields participate in diverse neural functions and demonstrate heterogeneous structural changes in various neurological disorders. In this study, three-dimensional T1-weighted MRI data from 22,258 healthy participants were analyzed using normative modeling to establish normative references for the volumes of the amygdala and its subfields. These models elucidated the developmental and aging curves of the amygdala and identified distinct ages at peak volume across subfields, ranging from 24.6 to 43.7 years. Based on these references, individual centile scores were calculated for 4132 patients with mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, cerebral small vessel disease, multiple sclerosis, and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder. These centile scores not only captured disease-specific deviation patterns of the amygdala subfields but also demonstrated utility in disease classification. Moreover, the centile scores correlated with clinical measures of cognitive function, emotional state, and motor performance across disorders. These findings suggest that normative references of the amygdala subfields provide insights into cross-disease alteration patterns and offer potential neuroimaging biomarkers to aid differential diagnosis and clinical assessment.

Article.Title: Cellular senescence changes and their association with brain structure in schizophrenia and major depressive disorder
Article.Authors: Okada N.; Seitz-Holland J.; Ikegame T.; Omileke F.; Kiyota M.; Shoji E.; Mori S.; Morita S.; Koshiyama D.; Satomura Y.; Koike S.; Jinde S.; Yagishita S.; Kamiya K.; Abe O.; Shenton M.; Kubicki M.; Kasai K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Individuals with schizophrenia (SZ) and major depressive disorder (MDD) may experience accelerated biological aging, potentially linked to cellular senescence and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). While the SASP index has been reported to be elevated in MDD, its status in SZ and its relationship with brain structure remain unclear. This study investigated whether the SASP index, a composite biomarker-based measure, is elevated in SZ and MDD, and examined its associations with brain-predicted age difference (brain-PAD) and regional brain morphology across SZ, MDD, and healthy controls (HCs). A total of 119 subjects (29 individuals with SZ, 40 individuals with MDD, and 50 HCs) underwent both peripheral blood collection and MRI scanning. First, across all subjects, the effects of diagnostic groups on SASP indices were assessed. Second, associations between age-adjusted SASP indices and brain-PAD were examined within each diagnostic group. Third, exploratory analyses tested associations between SASP indices and subcortical volumes as well as cortical thickness and surface area in each diagnostic group. We found a significant main effect of diagnostic group on SASP indices and significantly elevated SASP indices in both SZ and MDD. Although no significant associations were observed between SASP indices and brain-PAD in any diagnostic group, negative associations were identified in SZ between SASP indices and the surface area of the left transverse temporal gyrus and the right inferior frontal gyrus pars triangularis, regions that play pivotal roles in auditory and language processing alterations observed in SZ. These findings suggest that SASP-related processes may contribute to the neural underpinnings of SZ through localized, rather than global, alterations in brain structure.

Article.Title: Reduced attenuation of neural activation during fear extinction learning in patients with anxiety disorders: a delayed fear extinction fMRI study
Article.Authors: Qian Z.; Yang Y.; Richter J.; Domschke K.; Koelkebeck K.; Deckert J.; Herrmann M.; Plag J.; Ströhle A.; Wittchen H.; Pittig A.; Hamm A.; Arolt V.; Dannlowski U.; Schneider S.; Margraf J.; Rief W.; Lueken U.; Kircher T.; Ridderbusch I.; Straube B.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Clarifying the patterns of neural activation during fear extinction in anxiety disorders (ADs) is essential for advancing our understanding of inhibitory learning. However, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly characterized in large, heterogeneous cohorts of patients. Utilizing a delayed fear extinction fMRI paradigm, this study examined neural responses in 280 patients with ADs — comprising panic disorder, agoraphobia, panic disorder with agoraphobia, social anxiety disorder, and multiple specific phobias — compared to 103 healthy controls (HC). The attenuation of neural activation to conditioned fear (CS+) and safety (CS−) stimuli from early versus late extinction was compared between groups. Subjective ratings of US-expectancy, arousal, and valence were also collected. In a whole-brain voxelwise analysis, patients showed significantly reduced attenuation of neural activation across both CS+ and CS− relative to HC from early compared to late phases of extinction learning. This pattern was observed in a broad network, encompassing the insular cortex (IC) and bilateral supplementary motor area (SMA), among other regions. No interaction between group and stimulus type was observed. Region-of-interest analysis of the left anterior insular cortex confirmed that reduced attenuation in this region represents a robust neural signature of altered extinction learning in ADs. Furthermore, patients reported persistently higher fear expectancy and arousal than HC, consistent with sustained alterations in threat-related processing following extinction training. Together, these findings highlight altered extinction-related neural attenuation as a transdiagnostic feature of ADs, offering novel insights into the neural mechanisms underlying fear extinction.

Article.Title: Effects of chronic oxytocin administration on white matter microstructure in autistic adults: a pilot pharmaco-neuroimaging DTI study
Article.Authors: Heemels R.; Deferm W.; Boets B.; Alaerts K.
Article.Abstract: Intranasal oxytocin is a promising therapeutic approach for social and stress-regulatory difficulties in autism spectrum disorder. However, there is limited understanding regarding whether chronic administration regimes can induce neuroplastic changes at the brain’s anatomical level and how such microstructural changes might underlie clinical-behavioral effects. This placebo-controlled pilot assessed the effects of a four-week oxytocin regimen (24 IU daily) on white matter microstructure in 27 young adult men with autism. Diffusion tensor imaging was performed at baseline, post-treatment, and after four-week and one-year retention periods. Tractography focused on fractional anisotropy (FA) in amygdala-centered tracts associated with socio-emotional processing: the bilateral Inferior Longitudinal Fasciculus (ILF), Inferior Fronto-Occipital Fasciculus (IFOF), and Uncinate Fasciculus (UF). Following four weeks of oxytocin administration, a spatially selective impact of intranasal oxytocin administration was demonstrated, indicating bilateral improvements in UF integrity and a hemispherically lateralized pattern of changes for the ILF and IFOF tracts, with FA increases predominantly emerging in the right hemisphere, while reductions were evident in left-sided segments. Especially for bilateral UF and right IFOF, the observed changes were clinically relevant, correlating with enhanced social responsiveness and reduced feelings of avoidant attachment. In conclusion, exploratory findings from this pilot neuroimaging trial suggest that a four-week oxytocin regimen may induce long-lasting neuroplastic changes in white-matter tracts relevant to behavioral improvements in adult men with autism. These hypothesis-generating findings may inform future confirmatory trials. Further investigation of the neuroplastic changes associated with oxytocin’s clinical and behavioral effects may help refine oxytocin-based interventions, not only for autism but also for other neuropsychiatric conditions in which oxytocin is being explored as a potential therapeutic option.

Article.Title: Control of whole-body glucose metabolism by central lactate in the presence of antipsychotics
Article.Authors: Pereira S.; d’Orchymont F.; Tong J.; Au E.; Singh R.; Wu S.; Beroncal E.; Choi J.; Li D.; Humber B.; Chaudhry T.; Alijaniaram M.; Agarwal S.; Vernon A.; Giacca A.; Andreazza A.; Vasdev N.; Hahn M.
Article.Abstract: The brain-liver axis is important in maintaining whole-body glucose homeostasis. Antipsychotics are used to treat schizophrenia, but one of their side-effects is disruption of metabolism. We previously reported that the antipsychotics olanzapine and haloperidol block the ability of central glucose to stimulate whole-body glucose metabolism and suppress glucose production by the liver (EGP, endogenous glucose production). Both effects by central glucose require the conversion of glucose to lactate centrally. In the current study, we therefore examined whether antipsychotics affect the ability of central lactate to stimulate whole-body glucose metabolism and suppress EGP. Using our previous model of central (third ventricle to target the hypothalamus) infusion, acute subcutaneous administration of antipsychotics, and the pancreatic euglycemic clamp in rats, we found that olanzapine completely inhibited the ability of central lactate to stimulate whole-body glucose metabolism and partially blocked central lactate-induced suppression of EGP. Since activation of the hypothalamus-liver axis of glycemic control requires central glucose and lactate to be metabolized, relevant pathways were also investigated. The adverse effects of olanzapine on central lactate sensing were not associated with decreased levels of citrate, a tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediate, in the hypothalamus or robust alterations in hypothalamic mitochondrial complex I activity assessed with the positron emission tomography tracer [ 18 F]BCPP-EF. In summary, olanzapine impairs the ability of central lactate to control whole-body glucose metabolism and partially inhibits suppression of EGP by central lactate.

Article.Title: Impaired outcome-based decision-making in human cocaine addiction
Article.Authors: Lim T.; Cardinal R.; Mak E.; Ersche K.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Despite rising global rates for cocaine addiction, treatments options are limited. Psychological treatments remain the standard option but have only modest effectiveness. One major barrier to treatment success is that patients often make disadvantageous decisions that go against recovery, highlighting the need for strategies to support decision-making. Converging evidence indicates that decision-making deficits in cocaine addiction are driven by impaired processing of outcomes and risks. We investigated how patients with cocaine addiction use explicit outcomes and risk information to guide decision-making. One-hundred-and-five patients with moderate-to-severe cocaine use disorder (CUD) and 80 healthy control volunteers completed a decision-making task in which reward, loss, and probability information were provided explicitly. A subset of participants underwent diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging to investigate the orbitofronto-striatal white matter tracts that underpin decision-making. We used generalized linear mixed-effects models to determine how rewards, losses, and probability influence decisions, and combined probabilistic tractography with principal component analysis to characterize the white matter tracts. We found that patients incorporated explicit probability information into their decisions to the same degree as control participants but showed reduced integration of outcomes. Notably, patients were less likely to integrate losses into their decisions than rewards. Although orbitofronto-striatal white matter tracts did not differ between groups, individual variability predicted the extent to which reward and loss information guided decisions, irrespective of diagnosis. Overall, these findings reveal fundamental challenges in using outcomes, particularly negative ones, to guide decision-making in patients with CUD, emphasizing the need for additional support to promote adaptive choices during recovery.

Article.Title: Temporal imprecision of the self in drug-free psychosis: Abnormal infraslow phase dynamics and brain complexity
Article.Authors: Chen I.; Ao Y.; Catal Y.; Liu C.; Hwang T.; Lin Y.; Hsieh M.; Chien Y.; Hwu H.; Lechner S.; Liu C.; Northoff G.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Self-disturbance is a core feature of schizophrenia (SCZ) and may emerge during the prodromal phase. Temporal imprecision has recently been proposed as a core neural mechanism in schizophrenia, primarily demonstrated in faster EEG frequency ranges. Whether such imprecision extends to infraslow brain dynamics in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and relates to self-disturbance in early psychosis remains unknown. Here, we examined resting-state fMRI data from drug-free early psychosis patients (EP drug-free, n = 31, scanned before and after medication) and 31 healthy controls (HC). Brain dynamics were quantified using sample entropy (SampEn) and instantaneous peak frequency (PF) in regions associated with different layers of self-processing (interoceptive, exteroceptive, and mental). Compared to controls, EP drug-free showed higher SampEn and slower mean PF with greater variability than HC, particularly in the regions of the exteroceptive self. Moreover, EP drug-free exhibited a decoupling between SampEn and PF, whereas HC showed strong correlations. Both SampEn and PF significantly contributed to diagnostic classification, and increased SampEn was associated with greater severity of negative, disorganized, and anxiety/depression symptoms. Together, these findings indicate abnormal infraslow brain dynamics in early psychosis, characterized by increased neural complexity and disrupted temporal organization. This temporal imprecision, particularly within the exteroceptive self, may represent a key mechanism linking altered brain dynamics to self-disturbance and psychopathology in early psychosis.

Article.Title: Treating diagnostic frameworks as information systems: normative implications and opportunities
Article.Authors: Millroth P.
Article.Abstract: The DSM-5 and ICD-11 are not just clinical manuals; they are information architectures. Every time a clinician applies diagnostic criteria, every time a researcher aggregates symptoms into a diagnostic variable, and every time a committee drafts a revision, they operate on the same basic object: a coded system for transmitting information about mental states. Yet no one has applied information theory [ 1 ] to evaluate the architecture of diagnostic systems themselves. Existing applications of information-theoretic thinking in psychiatry — model-selection criteria such as AIC and BIC — assess how well statistical models fit covariance data; they say nothing about the efficiency of the diagnostic code itself. This Viewpoint argues that information theory (henceforth, IT) — the elsewhere highly influential mathematical framework developed by Shannon to characterize the capacity and efficiency of communication systems [ 1 ] — provides what is currently missing: a principled, quantitative basis for designing, evaluating, and reforming diagnostic frameworks and the instruments that operationalize them. The case for this reframing is not merely theoretical. Diagnostic quality, the product of validity and reliability in the DSM-5 and ICD-11 is, by available estimates, remarkably poor -essentially entailing that the majority of variability stems from measurement error or other irrelevant factors [ 2 , 3 ].

Article.Title: A precision health approach to medication management in neurodevelopmental conditions: a model development and validation study using four international cohorts
Article.Authors: Vandewouw M.; Niroomand K.; Bokadia H.; Lenz S.; Rapley J.; Arias A.; Crosbie J.; Trinari E.; Kelley E.; Nicolson R.; Schachar R.; Arnold P.; Iaboni A.; Lerch J.; Penner M.; Baribeau D.; Anagnostou E.; Kushki A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Psychotropic medications are commonly prescribed to children with neurodevelopmental conditions, but responses vary widely, prescribing is largely off-label, and the expertise required is concentrated in specialized programs. We developed artificial intelligence models to predict prescribing patterns of stimulants, anti-depressants, and anti-psychotics. Feasibility was established in research cohorts by predicting cross-sectional medication use from the Child Behaviour Checklist, with training and internal testing in the Province of Ontario Neurodevelopmental network ( N =598) and external testing in the Healthy Brain Network ( N =1,764) and Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development ( N =2,396) studies. Clinical evaluation used electronic medical records (EMRs) from the Psychopharmacology Program ( N =312) at Holland Bloorview Kids Rehabilitation Hospital to predict the medication class prescribed at a follow-up visit (∼3 months later). In all cohorts, the modelled outcome was the clinician’s prescribing decision, which reflects clinician judgement, family preference, tolerability, and access to care in addition to expected effectiveness, and does not directly measure treatment response or clinical benefit. In the research cohorts, internal testing achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (median [IQR]) of 0.75 [0.73,0.80] for stimulants, 0.83 [0.78,0.87] for anti-depressants, and 0.79 [0.72,0.86] for anti-psychotics, and external testing confirmed generalizability. In the EMR cohort, values were 0.84 [0.81,0.88] for stimulants, 0.82 [0.77,0.87] for anti-depressants, and 0.87 [0.83,0.91] for anti-psychotics. Findings demonstrate that AI can accurately learn expert prescribing patterns and predict medication prescribing decisions, supporting the potential of data-driven tools to guide personalized medication management for neurodevelopmental conditions.

Article.Title: Counteracting the overestimation of effect size in mass-univariate brain-wide association studies using cross-validation
Article.Authors: Goltermann J.; Winter N.; Gruber M.; Fisch L.; Richter M.; Grotegerd D.; Dohm K.; Meinert S.; Leehr E.; Böhnlein J.; Kraus A.; Thiel K.; Winter A.; Flinkenflügel K.; Leenings R.; Barkhau C.; Ernsting J.; Berger K.; Minnerup H.; Straube B.; Alexander N.; Jamalabadi H.; Stein F.; Brosch K.; Wroblewski A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Background Brain-wide association effects are commonly overestimated in psychiatric neuroimaging research, leading to low replicability and generalizability of findings, and ultimately to poor translation to clinical utility. Cross-validation is currently not standardly used in univariate neuroimaging analyses but could pose a potential counteracting measure for this problem. Methods We systematically evaluated the benefit of a cross-validation procedure to expose inflated effect size estimates in mass-univariate voxel-based analysis, using body mass index (BMI) as an example predictor for gray matter. A total of n = 3401 MRI scans from a psychiatric cohort were used to investigate the impact of applying cross-validation on effect size estimates across a range of sample sizes and across different localizations with a range of underlying pooled effect sizes. Results BMI was negatively associated with gray matter density with a maximum underlying effect size of R ² p = 0.036 (in the full sample of n = 3401). However, without cross-validation, effects were substantially overestimated in small samples, with effect sizes ranging up to R ² p = 0.535. Even with an underlying null-effect, effect size estimates up to R ² p = 0.429 were reached in samples with n = 25. Applying cross-validation revealed that these inflated effects in small samples did not generalize to novel data. A minimum sample size of n = 100 was required for largest brain-wide effects to start generalizing, while samples with n = 400 were needed for smaller effects to generalize. This ‘point of initial generalizability’ was not reached for underlying null effects, even with the maximum available sample of n = 3401. Conclusions Results suggest that cross-validation is an effective measure to expose overestimated effects in small samples and thus could help to counteract low replicability and generalizability in brain-wide mass-univariate association studies. Open-source code is provided for practical implementation.

Article.Title: Temporal cortical gray matter volume relates to symptom improvement during cognitive behavioral therapy for depression
Article.Authors: Schöniger K.; Kamrla R.; König P.; Zwiky E.; Küttner A.; Scheiwe G.; Andreev J.; Hamann J.; Brückner A.; Pletsch S.; Wittig E.; Selle J.; Gussew A.; Deistung A.; Tüscher O.; Wohlgemuth W.; Redlich R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a first-line treatment for depression, yet treatment responses vary considerably. Understanding neurobiological factors associated with symptom improvement may help elucidate mechanisms underlying therapeutic change. This study investigated whether baseline cortical gray matter volume (GMV) is associated with reductions in depressive symptom severity during CBT. Therefore, n = 52 patients with unipolar affective disorders and at least mild depressive symptoms (according to BDI-II) and n = 42 healthy controls underwent clinical assessments and structural MRI at baseline; depressive symptom severity was reassessed after six months of outpatient CBT. Multiple regression analyses examined associations between pre-treatment cortical GMV and reductions in depressive symptoms under false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Additional models included anxiety, perceived stress, and childhood trauma as predictors. Compared to controls, patients exhibited significantly higher depressive symptom severity at baseline and greater symptom reduction over time (all p < 0.001). Within patients, baseline GMV of the right middle temporal gyrus (MTG) was significantly associated with symptom reduction (baseline–follow-up; β = 0.55, p FDR = 0.033). Right MTG volume accounted for additional variance in symptom reduction beyond established clinical variables (Δ R ² = 0.15). Group differences in GMV did not remain significant following FDR correction. These findings suggest that temporal gyrus GMV is associated with symptom improvement following CBT in unipolar depression, extending the focus beyond traditionally emphasized limbic regions. Preserved temporal morphology may support cognitive and emotional processes engaged during CBT, underscoring the relevance of temporal cortical structure for understanding the neurobiological correlates of psychotherapy response.
