Article.Title: Plasma cytokines associated with anxiety comorbidity in adult epilepsy
Article.Authors: Wang K.; Li L.; Yang Y.; Li Z.; Zheng Y.; Liu Y.; Wang T.; Jin L.; Luo Y.; Shan Y.; Zhao G.
Article.Abstract: Background: Anxiety comorbidity in epilepsy may reflect altered immune-brain communication, but the peripheral cytokine profile associated with this phenotype remains insufficiently characterized. We examined plasma cytokine alterations in adult epilepsy and explored whether immune-clinical modelling could identify a stable comorbidity-related signature. Methods: We retrospectively enrolled 124 adults with epilepsy, including 35 with anxiety comorbidity and 89 without. Plasma concentrations of 12 cytokines (IFN-α, IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-2, IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IL-12p70, and IL-17A) and routine hematological parameters were evaluated. Cytokines were measured using a multiplex bead-based flow fluorescent immunoassay. Group comparisons, univariable logistic regression, LASSO regression with bootstrap stability selection, and multivariable logistic regression were performed. Model performance was assessed as an exploratory integrative framework. Results: Patients with anxiety comorbidity had significantly lower plasma IFN-α levels than those without anxiety comorbidity (P = 0.001). In the final four-variable model, lower IFN-α (adjusted OR 0.20, 95% CI 0.05-0.67; P = 0.009) and lower mean corpuscular hemoglobin (adjusted OR 0.79, 95% CI 0.65-0.94; P = 0.009) were independently associated with anxiety comorbidity. IL-4 showed a positive association, whereas IL-17A showed an inverse association. The model showed moderate discrimination and acceptable calibration. Conclusions: Anxiety comorbidity in adult epilepsy is associated with peripheral cytokine alterations, particularly reduced plasma IFN-α. These findings suggest type I interferon-related immune dysregulation within a broader peripheral immune-network imbalance. Prospective validation and mechanistic studies are warranted.

Article.Title: Beyond classification accuracy: Building trustworthy artificial intelligence for clinical electroencephalography
Article.Authors: Hu S.; Huang Y.; Zhang J.
Article.Abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) remains important in clinical neuroscience because it records brain activity as a time-resolved physiological process. It offers millisecond temporal resolution, can be used at the bedside and supports prolonged monitoring. Artificial intelligence (AI) has expanded EEG analysis through automated pattern recognition, representation learning, large-scale screening and decision support in epilepsy, sleep medicine, cognitive disorders, psychiatric conditions, intensive care, disorders of consciousness and anaesthesia monitoring. High classification accuracy in a research dataset, however, is not clinical readiness. EEG signals are shaped by physiological state, artefacts, acquisition systems, preprocessing choices and clinical context. Labels may come from expert annotations, diagnostic categories, behavioural scales, treatment responses or long-term outcomes, and these sources do not always define the same biological target. This review argues that EEG-AI translation should be judged by the strength of its evidence, not by technical performance alone. We examine why EEG is valuable yet hard to standardize, how EEG features can serve as candidate biomarkers, and why translational maturity differs across clinical scenarios. We then discuss the evidence gaps behind high-performing models, focusing on target validity, data leakage, confounding, external validation and clinically aligned metrics. Finally, we argue for clinical understandability rather than model interpretability alone, and for human-machine workflows rather than isolated classifiers. Future EEG-AI systems should be assessed by whether their outputs are biologically plausible, externally generalizable, understandable to clinicians and safe in real-world care.

Article.Title: Alterations in brain magnetic susceptibility in children with growth hormone deficiency: A quantitative susceptibility mapping study
Article.Authors: Lin L.; Cheng Y.; Gao X.; Huang S.; Deng C.; Qiu H.; Yang Z.; Qian L.; Chen Q.; Su S.
Article.Abstract: Objectives: Brain magnetic susceptibility in children with growth hormone deficiency (GHD) has not been well characterized. This study investigated regional magnetic susceptibility differences between children with GHD and typically developing (TD) children using quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM). Methods: Forty children with GHD and 40 typically developing (TD) children were recruited in this prospective study. QSM images were reconstructed using the MEDI toolbox, and regional susceptibility values were extracted using the Automated Anatomical Labeling atlas. Group differences in regional QSM values were assessed using analysis of covariance. The associations between significantly altered QSM values and clinical variables were evaluated using Spearman correlation. Results: Compared with TD children, children with GHD showed significantly higher QSM values in left amygdala (mean difference = 4.088 ppb, 95% CI [0.421, 7.755], Cohen's d = 0.50, PFDR = 0.028), bilateral putamen (left: mean difference = 2.285 ppb, 95% CI [0.210, 4.360], Cohen's d = 0.49, PFDR = 0.028; right: mean difference = 2.039 ppb, 95% CI [-0.093, 4.171], Cohen's d = 0.43, PFDR = 0.043), and left pallidum (mean difference = 4.440 ppb, 95% CI [0.956, 7.924], Cohen's d = 0.57, PFDR = 0.030), and significantly lower QSM values in the bilateral mid-cingulate cortex (left: mean difference = -0.806 ppb, 95% CI [-1.577, -0.035], Cohen's d = -0.47, PFDR = 0.040; right: mean difference = -0.781 ppb, 95% CI [-1.538, -0.023], Cohen's d = -0.46, PFDR = 0.045) and right lingual gyrus (mean difference = -1.829 ppb, 95% CI [-2.743, -0.915], Cohen's d = -0.89, PFDR < 0.001). In the GHD group, QSM values in left putamen (r = -0.356, P uncorrected = 0.024, PFDR = 0.104) and left amygdala (r = -0.364, P uncorrected = 0.021, PFDR = 0.104) were negatively correlated with serum insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), whereas QSM values in the right mid-cingulate cortex were positively correlated with IGF-1 (r = 0.414, P uncorrected = 0.008, PFDR = 0.104). However, these IGF-1-QSM associations did not remain statistically significant after adjustment for age and BMI. Conclusions: These preliminary findings indicate regional alterations in brain magnetic susceptibility in pediatric GHD; however, the observed IGF-1-QSM associations require confirmation in larger, adequately adjusted longitudinal studies. Article.Title: Crocin attenuates dopaminergic neuronal injury in 6-OHDA-induced PD rats: Associations with mitochondrial protection and p38/p53 signaling
Article.Authors: Cui H.; Li H.; Wang Y.; Han Y.; Tan J.; Li J.; Li X.; Zhang J.; Wang T.; Du W.; Wang Y.; Tan Y.; Zhao Q.
Article.Abstract: Background: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the degeneration of dopaminergic (DA) neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc). Crocin (CRO) has been reported to possess antioxidant and neuroprotective properties. However, whether its neuroprotective effects are associated with preserved mitochondrial integrity and alterations in p38/p53 signaling remains unclear. Methods: A unilateral rat model of PD was established by stereotaxic injection of 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) into the right striatum. Rats were randomly assigned to four groups: control, 6-OHDA, 6-OHDA+CRO (30 mg/kg), and 6-OHDA+levodopa (L-DOPA; 50 mg/kg). Motor function was evaluated using the beam balance, rotarod, and cylinder tests. Nissl staining was performed to quantify neurons in the SNc, while tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) immunohistochemistry was used to assess DA neurons in the SNc and DA fibers in the striatum. Mitochondrial ultrastructure was examined using transmission electron microscopy(TEM), and mitochondrial function was assessed by measuring ATP content and mitochondrial complex I activity in substantia nigra (SN) tissue. Oxidative stress markers were measured in serum and tissues from the SN and striatum using commercial assay kits. Protein levels of TH, p53, total and phosphorylated p38, Bax, Bcl-2, and caspase-3 were determined by Western blotting. Results: CRO treatment significantly ameliorated 6-OHDA-induced motor deficits (p < 0.01, p < 0.001, p < 0.0001) and attenuated reductions in TH-positive neuron counts in the SNc (p < 0.01) and striatal TH optical density (p < 0.01). TEM revealed that CRO alleviated mitochondrial ultrastructural damage and increased the mitochondrial aspect ratio (p < 0.001). These improvements were accompanied by increased ATP content (p < 0.01) and mitochondrial complex I activity (p < 0.05) in SN tissue. Furthermore, CRO increased CAT activity and GSH levels while reducing MDA levels in serum, SN, and striatum (p < 0.05, p < 0.01, p < 0.001), while SOD activity increased significantly in both brain regions (p < 0.0001). Western blot analysis showed that CRO increased TH protein expression (p < 0.01), reduced the p-p38/p38 (p < 0.05) and Bax/Bcl-2 (p < 0.05) ratios, and decreased p53 (p < 0.05) and caspase-3 (p < 0.01) protein levels compared with the 6-OHDA group. Conclusions: CRO attenuated motor deficits and nigrostriatal DA damage in a 6-OHDA-induced rat model of PD. These neuroprotective effects were associated with reduced oxidative stress, preserved mitochondrial morphology and function, and decreased p38 phosphorylation and p53 expression. These findings support further investigation of CRO as a potential neuroprotective compound for PD.

Article.Title: Neuroprotective effects of calcitriol after experimental ischemic stroke induction via modulation of glutamate excitotoxicity, MMP-9 activity, and oxidative stress
Article.Authors: Rahmatipour S.; Bayat R.; Rezvani Z.; Vahidinia Z.; Tameh A.
Article.Abstract: Background: Ischemic stroke triggers detrimental cascades, including glutamate excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation. This study evaluated the neuroprotective potential of calcitriol during the acute phase of stroke, focusing on inflammatory damage and modulation of glutamate transporters. Methods: Male Wistar rats underwent 1-h middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) and were assigned to Sham, tMCAO + Vehicle, and tMCAO + Calcitriol groups. Calcitriol (1 μg/kg) was administered at 30 min, 24 h, and 48 h post-stroke. After 72 h, behavioral outcomes, infarct volume, and histological alterations in cortical region were assessed utilizing Nissl staining. Cortical mRNA expression of glutamate-aspartate transporter (GLAST), glutamate transporter-1 (GLT-1), and excitatory amino acid transporter 3 (EAAT3) was evaluated via RT-PCR. Serum Matrix Metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9) activity was measured using gelatin zymography, and oxidative stress biomarkers malondialdehyde (MDA), total antioxidant capacity (TAC), and nitric oxide (NO) were quantified in the penumbra. Molecular docking simulations explored calcitriol-MMP-9 binding affinity. Results: Calcitriol significantly reduced infarct volume, improved neurobehavioral scores, and mitigated morphological neuronal damage. It elevated TAC while suppressing MDA and NO levels. In line with docking simulations predicting a moderate binding affinity of -6.5 kcal/mol, a marked decrease in serum MMP-9 enzymatic activity was observed. Furthermore, calcitriol treatment significantly reduced GLAST, GLT-1, and EAAT3 cortical gene expression compared to the untreated ischemia group. Conclusion: Calcitriol administration attenuates acute ischemic brain injury. This neuroprotective effect is associated with parallel downregulations of glutamate transporter gene expression, suppression of penumbral oxidative stress, and reduced serum MMP-9 enzymatic activity.

Article.Title: State-separated analysis for L-DOPA response in hemiparkinsonian 6-OHDA rats
Article.Authors: Kim J.; Kang S.; Park J.; Lee Y.; Park J.; Lee K.; Yu J.; Kim E.; Jang H.; Kim S.; Rah J.; Choi J.
Article.Abstract: Analysis of responses to L-3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine (L-DOPA) in hemiparkinsonian rodent models can enhance understanding of Parkinson's disease (PD). Traditionally, these responses have been classified into medication OFF and ON states, with ON defined as the period after sufficient time has elapsed following drug administration. However, this binary classification may lead to neurophysiological analyses that overlook interindividual variability in the onset and duration of therapeutic effects. Although measuring plasma L-DOPA concentrations has been proposed to quantify this variability, technical difficulties in direct measurement limit the application of this approach. Here, we investigated whether acute L-DOPA responses can be quantitatively distinguished into behavioral states without direct plasma measurements, and whether these states correspond to neurophysiological dynamics. Using quantitative analysis of rotation direction in hemiparkinsonian rat model, we classified L-DOPA responses into four temporally distinct states: OFF, early contralateral rotation (ECR), rotational pause (RP), and late contralateral rotation (LCR). These behaviorally defined states exhibited statistically distinct neurophysiological profiles, characterized by simultaneously measured subthalamic firing rates and striatal dopamine levels. Although single-unit activity was insufficient to decode state transitions, neural population activity enabled robust decoding via a support vector machine (SVM). Furthermore, linear dynamical system modeling revealed transition-specific trajectories in a low-dimensional state space, suggesting that state transitions are represented by coordinated population dynamics. These findings demonstrate that temporal variability in L-DOPA responses can be identified behaviorally, providing a neurophysiologically validated framework that extends the conventional binary classification into a multi-state transition for PD research.

Article.Title: Sirt1 modulates p53‑acetylation‑dependent Yy2‑Elf‑1‑associated NLRP3‑relevant signaling in CUMS‑evoked aggravated Alzheimer’s disease‑related phenotypes
Article.Authors: Chai F.; Shan Q.; Hu Y.; Liu L.; Zou J.; Xia G.; Wang Y.
Article.Abstract: Depressive disorder (DD) is recognized as an important comorbidity of Alzheimer's disease (AD) and is associated with aggravated cognitive impairment and neuroinflammatory responses; however, the underlying molecular mechanisms remain largely unknown. This study investigated the role of the Sirtuin 1 (Sirt1)/p53 acetylation/Yin-Yang 2 (Yy2)/E74-like ETS transcription factor 1 (Elf-1)/NLR family pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3) axis in DD-associated AD phenotypes and evaluated the effects of resveratrol intervention. Bioinformatics analysis, CoIP-MS, ChIP-seq, and dual-luciferase assays were applied to identify and validate the regulatory relationships among these molecules. APP/PS1 double-transgenic mice subjected to chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) and LPS-stimulated BV2 microglia were used as in vivo and in vitro models. Behavioral tests demonstrated that CUMS-induced depressive-like stress aggravated cognitive deficits and depression- and anxiety-related behavioral abnormalities in AD mice. Sirt1 expression was decreased, whereas acetylated p53 (ac-p53), Yy2, Elf-1, and NLRP3 levels were elevated in the hippocampus of DD + AD mice and activated BV2 microglia, accompanied by enhanced inflammatory and oxidative stress responses. Resveratrol treatment reduced p53 acetylation, suppressed the Yy2/Elf-1/NLRP3 pathway, alleviated inflammatory and oxidative stress responses, and improved behavioral deficits. Yy2 overexpression partially reversed the effects of resveratrol treatment. Collectively, our findings suggest that reduced Sirt1 expression promotes p53 acetylation and activates the Yy2/Elf‑1‑associated NLRP3‑relevant axis (the regulatory link between Elf‑1 and NLRP3 requires further experimental validation), contributing to neuroinflammatory responses and behavioural deficits in CUMS‑aggravated AD‑related phenotypes. Resveratrol treatment partially restored Sirt1‑related signalling and ameliorated these pathological manifestations, although further studies are required to determine its therapeutic potential and exclude Sirt1‑independent effects.

Article.Title: CD55-targeted modulation of C3-mediated microglia polarization improves perioperative neurocognitive disorders in male mice
Article.Authors: Tian Q.; Zhang H.; Zhang X.; Huang H.; Sun R.; Cui S.; Shao J.; Song L.; Qie X.
Article.Abstract: Background: Perioperative neurocognitive disorders (PND) are common postoperative complications driven by neuroinflammation and an imbalance in microglial M1/M2 polarization. Complement component 3 (C3) is elevated in PND, while CD55 inhibits C3 activation. Whether CD55 regulates PND via C3 remains unclear. Methods: A PND mouse model and an lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced BV2 model were established. Lentivirus-mediated CD55/C3 overexpression was performed. Cognitive function, neuronal injury, inflammation, microglial polarization, and CD55/C3 expression were assessed using behavioral tests, HE staining, ELISA, immunofluorescence, RT-qPCR, and WB. Results: PND mice exhibited cognitive impairment, hippocampal neuronal damage, elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines and C3, and reduced CD55 expression. Overexpression of CD55 improved cognitive function, alleviated damage and inflammation, and suppressed C3. It also restored the balance of M1/M2 markers in BV2 cells. Overexpression of C3 reversed the protective effects of CD55 both in vitro and in vivo. Conclusion: CD55 alleviates PND by regulating complement C3, which may be related to promoting the polarization of microglia toward the M2 phenotype. We have preliminarily identified a potential regulatory target for PND.

Article.Title: Oxytocin receptor activation enhances SK channel-mediated afterhyperpolarization in MPOA neurons of maternally experienced mice
Article.Authors: Ma G.; Yang X.; Huang Q.; Li J.; Mao H.; Xue Q.; Hu E.; Wu S.; Qi C.; Wang W.
Article.Abstract: Maternal experience induces significant behavioral changes; however, the underlying cellular mechanisms within the medial preoptic area (MPOA), a central hub for regulating maternal behavior, remain poorly understood. Here, we combined behavioral assays (e.g., pup retrieval, crouching, nesting, and grooming) with in vitro whole-cell patch-clamp recordings to examine how maternal experience alters the intrinsic excitability of MPOA neurons and to identify the underlying mechanisms. Adult female mice were divided into three groups: virgin females, dams (experienced dams), and co-housed virgins (virgins co-housed with a dam and her pups for five days). Maternal behavior and the intrinsic properties of MPOA neurons were assessed in all three groups. We first compared virgin females with experienced dams, and then tested whether the maternal experience-dependent changes in MPOA neurons were reproduced in co-housed virgins by social co-housing. Our results revealed that MPOA neurons from both dams and co-housed virgins exhibited reduced excitability and increased afterhyperpolarization (AHP) amplitude. This enhancement was mediated by small-conductance calcium-activated potassium (SK) channels, as it was abolished by the SK channel blocker apamin. Furthermore, direct application of an oxytocin receptor agonist to MPOA neurons from virgin females induced similar functional changes, replicating the physiological profile observed in dams. Notably, this oxytocin-induced enhancement of SK channel activity was observed in glutamatergic, but not GABAergic, MPOA neurons, indicating that the effect is not uniform across cell types. These findings suggest that oxytocin modulates SK channel activity to reduce the excitability of a subpopulation of MPOA neurons. Because this effect was prominent in VGLUT2-positive neurons, it may facilitate maternal behavior by reducing the activity of neurons that restrain maternal behavior, a candidate mechanism by which hormonal and experiential signals converge on MPOA excitability.

Article.Title: Glutamatergic Dysfunction in Major Depressive Disorder: From Receptor and Glial Abnormalities to Circuit Pathology and Mechanism-Based Therapeutic Strategies
Article.Authors: Chen X.; Chen Q.; Long Y.; Huang S.; Li C.; Zhu D.; Ben X.
Article.Abstract: Major depressive disorder is a heterogeneous psychiatric disorder that cannot be fully explained by classical monoamine-deficiency models. Increasing evidence indicates that glutamatergic dysfunction provides a central framework for linking molecular, glial, synaptic, and circuit-level abnormalities in depression. This narrative review focuses on glutamatergic dysregulation as the organizing mechanism of major depressive disorder. We summarize core abnormalities involving context-dependent N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor dysfunction, impaired α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor-mediated synaptic plasticity, altered metabotropic glutamate receptor signaling, and disrupted astrocytic excitatory amino acid transporter 2-mediated glutamate clearance. These changes converge on excitation-inhibition imbalance, leading to unstable cortical-limbic activity and contributing to emotional dysregulation, anhedonia, cognitive impairment, and impaired stress adaptation. We further discuss upstream mechanisms that regulate glutamatergic dysfunction, including brain-derived neurotrophic factor/mammalian target of rapamycin signaling, neuroinflammation, epigenetic regulation, and microbiota-gut-brain axis-related peripheral crosstalk. At the circuit level, we emphasize abnormalities in the prefrontal cortex-amygdala, amygdala-nucleus accumbens, prefrontal cortex-hippocampus, and lateral habenula pathways. We also consider how monoaminergic and opioid systems modulate glutamate-dependent synaptic and reward-circuit plasticity. Finally, we review therapeutic implications, including ketamine and related N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor modulators, α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor facilitation, astrocyte-targeted strategies, anti-inflammatory interventions, circuit-based neuromodulation, and biomarker-guided patient stratification. By centering diverse pathological findings around glutamatergic dysfunction, this review provides a focused mechanistic framework for understanding major depressive disorder and developing precision, mechanism-based treatments.

Article.Title: ATP-sensitive potassium channel openers inhibit the formation of neutrophil extracellular traps to protect against neuroinflammation in ischemic stroke
Article.Authors: Shi D.; Jin H.; Liao J.; Zhou S.; Zhang N.; Zhao Y.
Article.Abstract: Neuroinflammation is a key contributor to brain injury and poor functional recovery after ischemic stroke, yet no clinically approved therapy targets the neutrophil extracellular trap (NET)-cGAS-STING axis that drives it. This study investigates the effects of the clinically used K-ATP channel opener nicorandil on neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation and evaluates its potential to attenuate NET-cGAS-STING-associated neuroinflammation. A mouse model of middle cerebral artery occlusion and reperfusion (MCAO/R) and BV-2 microglial cell oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R) were used to assess NET formation, cGAS-STING pathway activation, inflammatory responses, and neurological injury. Significant increases in NET markers, such as MPO-DNA and CitH3, were found in plasma and brain tissue after MCAO/R. This was accompanied by elevated TNF-α, IL-6、IL-1β, brain edema, neuronal apoptosis, and neurological deficits. Both DNase I-mediated NET degradation and Nicorandil treatment reduced NET formation, suppressed microglial activation, lowered phosphorylation of STING and TBK1, and alleviated brain infarction, neuronal death, and impairment. In vitro, exogenous NETs enhanced OGD/R-induced cGAS-STING activation and IL-1β release, effects reversed by DNase I and Nicorandil. In summary, extracellular DNA associated with NETs promotes microglial cGAS-STING activation and contributes to neuroinflammatory injury after stroke. Nicorandil exerts neuroprotective effects by inhibiting the upstream formation of NETs and attenuating this signaling axis, suggesting a promising and readily translatable therapeutic strategy for ischemic stroke.

Article.Title: Characterizing White Matter and Structural Brain Network Alterations in Children with Growth Hormone Deficiency Using Diffusion Tensor Imaging
Article.Authors: Wang X.; Tan H.; Lin D.; Zhang G.; Li K.; Wang J.; Zheng H.; Wang H.; Zheng W.
Article.Abstract: Purpose: To characterize white matter microstructure and structural brain network topology in children with growth hormone deficiency (GHD) using diffusion tensor imaging and explore their associations with clinical indicators. Methods: A total of 77 short-stature children (GHD = 50, idiopathic short stature [ISS] = 27) and 40 healthy controls (HC) underwent 3D-T1WI and DTI. Nineteen participants were excluded due to poor data quality (10 in the GHD group, 4 in the ISS group, and 5 in the HC group), yielding a final analytical cohort of 40 children with GHD, 23 with ISS, and 35 healthy controls. Tract-Based Spatial Statistics and graph-theoretical analysis were applied to characterize white matter microstructure and network topological properties. Clinical metrics including bone age and pituitary volume were collected. Results: Children with GHD showed reduced fractional anisotropy together with elevated mean and radial diffusivity relative to controls. Children with ISS showed elevated mean and radial diffusivity without a reduction in fractional anisotropy, and their diffusivity elevations exceeded those observed in the GHD group. Graph-theoretical analysis revealed that the GHD group had significantly higher global efficiency and lower characteristic path length than the HC group, as well as lower clustering coefficient than the ISS group. Rich-club findings were contingent on both the method used to define core nodes and the connection retention thresholds applied to backbone networks. Nodal analysis identified significantly higher betweenness centrality of the left insula in ISS compared with both the GHD and HC groups. Significant associations were observed between white matter microstructural properties, network connectivity, and clinical variables, including age, bone age, and bone age delay. Conclusion: Children with GHD exhibit altered white matter microstructure and global organization of the structural brain network, which differed from the pattern observed in ISS, and these imaging measures were associated with age, bone age, and bone age delay; given the cross-sectional design, causal inference remains unwarranted.

Article.Title: Cognitive impairment in age-related hearing loss: linking brain structure, glymphatic function, and molecular mechanisms
Article.Authors: Xing C.; Du Y.; Xia Y.; Li S.; Xu X.; Salvi R.; Chen G.; Chen Y.; Xiao Y.
Article.Abstract: The neurobiological mechanisms of cognitive impairment in age-related hearing loss (ARHL) remain unclear. This study examined multi-level neural mechanisms from macroscale gray matter (GM) structure, microscale glymphatic function, and imaging transcriptomics. Sixty-nine ARHL patients and 76 controls underwent multimodal MRI and neuropsychological assessments. Glymphatic function was assessed via DTI-ALPS index and choroid plexus volume (CPV). Transcriptomic analysis using Allen Human Brain Atlas identified molecular pathways and key genes linked to GM atrophy. ARHL patients showed GM atrophy in right amygdala, left inferior frontal gyrus, and orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), but increased volume in left cerebellum. They also exhibited reduced ALPS index and enlarged CPV. Mediation analysis showed a significant indirect effect of glymphatic function on visual memory via right amygdala volume. Transcriptomics revealed enrichment in axonogenesis, energy metabolism, and protein ubiquitination, with key drivers including SMURF1 and GAD1. ARHL-related cognitive decline may follow a cascade from sensory deprivation to glymphatic dysfunction, involving energy metabolism, protein homeostasis, and axonal remodeling, ultimately leading to degenerative atrophy and compensatory adaptation in specific brain networks.

Article.Title: Smiling Muscle Stimulation Alters Neural Processing During Emotional Face Comparison
Article.Authors: Baker J.; Lisi M.; Elsenaar A.; Mehu M.; Korb S.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Within embodied and predictive-processing frameworks, emotional face perception is informed by bodily states, such as proprioceptive facial feedback. In line with this, our earlier work showed that activation of smiling muscles with facial neuromuscular electrical stimulation (fNMES) can induce a happiness bias in emotional face perception, and reduce visual face processing demands. Here, we extended this research to examine whether the same facial muscle stimulation biases the emotional representation of a face when it serves as a perceptual template (prime) for comparison with a following target face. In a delayed matching-to-sample task, 53 participants judged which of two sequentially presented faces appeared happier (or more female, in a control sex task). On half of trials, fNMES was applied bilaterally to the zygomaticus major during encoding of the prime face. Performance was held constant using an adaptive staircase. fNMES altered comparison judgments only when emotion was task-relevant, flattening the relation between emotion difference and choice. Across tasks, fNMES reduced N170 amplitudes and increased Early Posterior Negativity (EPN) differences between happy and sad faces. The prime EPN predicted choice only when emotion was task-relevant, whereas fNMES modulated emotion effects on the target N170 only in the control task. Facial feedback may thus increase the perceptual salience of emotion-relevant information, with task-dependent consequences for decisions.

Article.Title: How Habitual Language Mode Shapes Self-Stigma Perception Process in Deaf Individuals: Evidence from an Event-Related Potentials Study
Article.Authors: Huang J.; Li Y.; Wang T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Deaf individuals often experience public stigma from the hearing majority due to communication barriers, which may further evolve into internalized self-stigma. However, how habitual language mode shapes self-stigma-related processing remains unclear. In the present study, 20 signing deaf and 21 oral deaf individuals completed a semantic priming task while event-related potentials (ERPs) were recorded. Deaf-identity (“I am deaf”) primes were presented subliminally or supraliminally before positive and negative trait words. Among oral deaf participants, negative words elicited a larger N400 than positive words under supraliminal priming, while a negative-over-positive LPC effect emerged in the no-priming and subliminal conditions but disappeared under supraliminal priming. Signing deaf participants showed no N400 valence effect but exhibited a negative-over-positive LPC effect across all conditions. These findings provide no clear evidence of self-stigma in either group. Instead, they suggest that habitual language mode and conscious accessibility of deaf identity jointly shape the temporal dynamics of self-evaluative processing, potentially reflecting different ways of resisting the internalization of negative societal evaluations. Signing deaf individuals may derive protection from a culturally and collectively grounded Deaf identity, whereas oral deaf individuals may rely more on individualized, self-protective processing to prevent negative evaluations from being incorporated into the self.

Article.Title: Understanding Audiovisual Affective Processing: Behavioral Effects and Neural Underpinnings
Article.Authors: Gao C.; Green J.; Shinkareva S.; Yan R.; Xu Z.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Emotional signals are typically conveyed jointly through vision and audition. This article reviews behavioral, electrophysiological, and neuroimaging evidence on audiovisual affective processing, addressing what its core effects are, when they unfold, and where they occur in the brain. Congruent audiovisual cues often facilitate emotion recognition, although benefits vary across emotions, tasks, measures, and unimodal comparisons. Audiovisual input can also shape affective appraisals and subjective emotional experience. Modality dominance is context-dependent, varying with cue reliability and the affective dimension judged. Cross-modal influences can persist when one modality is task-irrelevant, suggesting limited goal dependence. Electrophysiological findings reveal audiovisual affective interactions at both early and later stages of neural processing. Neuroimaging work implicates posterior superior temporal cortex (pSTC) within a distributed network of sensory, subcortical, and frontal regions. Building on this evidence, we consider Anderson's information integration theory as a computational framework for characterizing modality-related and value-dependent contributions to affective judgments. We propose a hypothesis-generating dual-pathway framework predicting that reliability-related changes in cue influence will covary with sensory-pSTC interactions, whereas value-dependent changes will additionally involve amygdala and prefrontal systems. These hypotheses concern relative rather than exclusive network contributions and require direct testing through independent manipulations of cue reliability and affective value.

Article.Title: When Fakes Feel Real: Behavioral and Neural Mechanisms of Deepfake Hyperrealism in Younger and Older Adults
Article.Authors: Washburn S.; Lin T.; Zhu M.; Faulkner R.; Cahill B.; Lighthall N.; Ebner N.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Deepfakes are designed to mimic real people and constitute an emerging exploitation threat. They are potent methods of fraud as humans detect deepfake images at near or below chance levels, and deepfakes are frequently perceived as more real even than real images (deepfake hyperrealism). Anterior insula (aINS) function is implicated in processing salient, untrustworthy cues suggesting that low aINS recruitment during deepfake perception may underlie experiences of deepfake hyperrealism. Further, aging may confer increased experiences of deepfake hyperrealism, given increased susceptibility to deception and reduced aINS sensitivity to deceptive stimuli with age. Here, 156 participants (62 younger: 18-37 years, 94 older: 60-89 years) evaluated the realness of real and deepfake face images while undergoing fMRI. Behavioral results revealed deepfake hyperrealism in both age groups, with these effects more pronounced in older adults. Our imaging results indicated lower aINS activation was associated with higher realness ratings and aINS activity was also lower for deepfake than real images in both younger and older adults. These findings provide additional support for deepfake hyperrealism in perception, underscoring the threat of deepfakes as a method of exploitation across adulthood. Results also support that muted aINS response to deepfakes constitutes a neuromechanism in deception vulnerability.

Article.Title: mPFC-Dependent Valuation Shapes Information Sharing: Causal Evidence from tDCS and a Dyadic Social Media Paradigm
Article.Authors: Li Y.; Zhang Y.; Wang J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Information sharing drives the spread of both accurate and misleading content, yet its psychological and neural mechanisms remain unclear. We investigated whether perceived self- and social relevance influence sharing through downstream content evaluations, and whether this process depends on medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) function. In a dyadic social media paradigm, 186 participants were assigned to anodal, cathodal, or sham tDCS over the mPFC. Senders judged 30 science news items (15 true and 15 false) on truthfulness, self-relevance, social relevance, interestingness, and importance before deciding whether to share each item with a real receiver. Structural equation modeling showed that self- and social relevance predicted sharing indirectly through evaluations of interestingness, importance, and truthfulness. mPFC stimulation did not reliably change sharing rates, but altered evaluative processing: it reduced perceived interestingness, and anodal stimulation produced a significant negative indirect pathway to sharing through reduced interestingness. Multi-group analyses indicated that these valuation pathways were invariant across true and false news. On the receiver side, social endorsement increased reading of shared items but had little effect on post-reading evaluations. Together, these findings support a causal contribution of mPFC-targeted neuromodulation to evaluative processing relevant to sharing, with limited evidence for a direct effect on sharing behavior.

Article.Title: Social relationship is associated with distinct patterns of inter-brain synchrony and directed connectivity during interpersonal coordination
Article.Authors: Han H.; Zhao Z.; Lin L.; Li C.; Jin X.
Article.Abstract: Abstract How social relationship and effector pairing relate to behavioral coordination and inter-brain interaction during joint timing remains unclear. Using functional near-infrared spectroscopy hyperscanning during a dyadic synchronization-continuation task, we examined 21 romantic couples and 23 stranger dyads performing hand-hand and hand-foot coordination. Romantic partners showed smaller tapping deviations than strangers during continuation, while hand–foot coordination was associated with greater tapping variability. Motor-region inter-brain synchrony (IBS) was greater in romantic partners than in strangers. True-dyad IBS exceeded the pseudo-dyad baseline in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, corresponding differences were not detected in the motor cortex or left temporoparietal junction. Dynamic IBS analysis identified two recurrent configurations differing in synchrony strength and global efficiency, but state-transition frequency did not differ significantly between relationship groups. Granger-causality-based directed connectivity was stronger overall in stranger dyads, with female-to-male values exceeding those in the reverse direction. Together, these findings indicate that social relationship is associated with contrasting patterns of motor-region synchrony and directed connectivity, while effector pairing is associated with behavioral variability.

Article.Title: Effect of calcium carbonate on the thermodynamics and kinetics of lead sulfide carbothermic reduction
Article.Authors: Moldabayeva G.; Tazhiyev Y.; Baimbetov B.; Dauletbakova A.; Shayakhmetova R.; Koishina G.; Jumankulova S.; Lentschke J.; Iskendirov A.; Seitkaliyeva M.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The effect of calcium carbonate on the thermodynamics and apparent kinetics of lead sulfide (PbS) carbothermic reduction was investigated in the PbS–Na 2 CO 3 –C and PbS–Na 2 CO 3 –CaCO 3 –C systems at 800–1100 °C. Thermodynamic analysis included Gibbs free energy calculations and multiphase equilibrium modeling, while kinetic behavior was evaluated through time-resolved gas analysis and TG–DTG–DSC measurements. Equilibrium calculations revealed predominant Na 2 S formation in the CaCO 3 -free system and CaS formation in the CaCO 3 -containing system. At 800 °C, the calculated equilibrium amount of metallic lead increased from 804.29 to 999.83 mol upon CaCO 3 addition, based on 1000 mol of initial PbS. Sodium carbonate remained largely unconsumed in the CaCO 3 -containing system. Experimental results demonstrated a pronounced temperature-dependent effect of CaCO 3 . At 800 °C, the apparent reaction extent (α app ) was 70.6% with CaCO 3 and 74.9% without it. At 900, 1000, and 1100 °C, α app reached 96.4%, 97.9%, and 99.5%, respectively, in the CaCO 3 -containing system, accompanied by higher apparent reaction rates. The corresponding apparent activation energies were 32.0 and 52.9 kJ·mol − 1 , indicating stronger temperature sensitivity with CaCO 3 addition. These findings demonstrate that CaCO 3 modifies sulfur distribution and the apparent kinetic behavior of PbS-containing systems.

Article.Title: Contextual constraints and shot quality in elite Olympic curling
Article.Authors: Wang H.; Chen Y.; Zhang Z.; Ning C.; Wang L.; Zhu T.; Sun R.; Mu L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Curling is a turn-based team sport in which shot selection and execution occur under changing match contexts. Using official shot-by-shot data from the Milano Cortina 2026 Olympic Winter Games, this study examined contextual associations with shot selection and shot quality and within-match process differences between winning and losing teams. The dataset comprised 18,402 shots from 147 matches, including 18,358 shots with valid official success percentages. Descriptive analyses, chi-square tests, paired winner–loser comparisons, match-level difference logistic regression, mixed-effects models and supplementary post-match classification models were applied. Shot-type distribution was significantly associated with shot phase, hammer status, score state, event type and critical-end status, with the largest associations observed for shot phase and hammer status. Winning teams showed higher success percentages in late-phase and take-out-family shots and in the study-defined pressure context (late-match, close-score situations). They also had more favourable stealing-related outcomes; psychological pressure was not directly measured. In the multivariable match-level model, late-phase success difference and net stolen-end difference remained associated with match outcome. Across the primary and sensitivity mixed-effects analyses, shot phase, event type, score state and critical-end status showed comparatively consistent associations with shot quality. These findings suggest that context-specific shot-quality measures and end-level scoring outcomes describe aspects of within-match performance differences not summarized by overall shot success alone. The results represent observational post-match associations rather than causal effects or evidence of generalizable pre-match prediction.

Article.Title: Effects of recycled PET aggregate size and replacement level on hot mix asphalt performance
Article.Authors: Mohammadi R.; Ameri M.; Karamroudi M.; Jarrahi A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The increasing accumulation of plastic waste has intensified the need for sustainable reuse strategies in construction materials. This study investigates the feasibility of using recycled polyethylene terephthalate (rPET) from post‑consumer bottles as a partial replacement for natural aggregates in hot mix asphalt (HMA) using the dry mixing method, emphasizing the influence of particle size and replacement level on HMA performance. rPET particles with natural‑aggregate‑like physical characteristics were produced and sieved into standard size fractions to function as rPET aggregates. The adhesion behavior and mechanical properties of rPET aggregates were evaluated and compared with limestone aggregates used in this study under different temperature conditions. HMA performance was assessed through dynamic creep tests (flow number and permanent deformation) at 40 °C, and moisture susceptibility and indirect tensile fatigue tests at 25 °C. To investigate the effect of particle size, 10% of natural aggregates (by volume) were replaced with rPET aggregates in five size ranges from ≤ 0.3 to 19 mm, and the most effective range was used to determine the optimum replacement level. The results showed that at medium-to-high temperatures, rPET had better interfacial adhesion with bitumen than with limestone, and rPET aggregates performed better in the LAA and AIV tests. Optimal performance was achieved using 4.75–12.5 mm rPET aggregates, where 18% replacement increased creep resistance by 57% and reduced moisture susceptibility by 7%, while 16% replacement improved fatigue life by 295%. These findings demonstrate that rPET aggregates provide an environmentally sustainable alternative for enhancing HMA performance.

Article.Title: Joint latent class mixed model trajectories of estimated glomerular filtration rate related to mortality and physical activity in older adults
Article.Authors: Weinmayr G.; Braisch J.; Klenk J.; Denkinger M.; Dallmeier D.; Rothenbacher D.; Peter R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Deterioration of renal function occurs with age, leading in many individuals to chronic kidney disease, considerable disability and premature mortality. The trajectories of kidney function decline and potential protective factors remain poorly understood, especially in older individuals. We therefore investigated eGFR-decline trajectories related to mortality as well as the influence of physical activity patterns on trajectory membership in a population-based cohort of older individuals. 1,506 community-dwelling adults aged $$\:\ge\:$$ 65 years were recruited in 2009 and followed up for up to three times. Trajectories of eGFR-decline and their relation with mortality were determined using joint latent class models. The association of physical activity (PA) and sedentary behavior (SB), determined by accelerometer measurements at baseline, with class-membership was studied with logistic regression. There were 2,812 observations on eGFR. We identified two trajectories, one starting with a lower mean baseline eGFR value and showing a stronger decline over time and higher mortality. In adjusted models, we found robust inverse associations of time spent in PA and total steps with being in this trajectory (Odds ratios with 95%-confidence intervals of 0.72 [0.60, 0.87] for 10 min and 0.73 [0.62, 0.86] for 1000 steps); SB was positively associated with this trajectory (2.51 [1.65, 3.81] for 100 min). PA was negatively and SB was positively associated with the worse trajectory. This may indicate that interventions for increasing PA may potentially be viable strategies to prevent impaired renal function and slow age-related functional decline in older individuals and should be investigated in future studies.

Article.Title: Specifics of the growth of lithium-doped KCl single crystals by the Bridgman method in an argon atmosphere
Article.Authors: Shunkeyev K.; Sagimbayeva S.; Kenzhebayeva A.; Ubaev Z.; Beketova G.; Zhumabayev D.
Article.Abstract: Abstract A purification and growth process for alkali halide crystals (AHCs) is demonstrated using KCl: Li as a model system and employing an experimental crystal growth setup manufactured by Across International, USA. The process involves the following sequential stages: (i) deposition of a thin pyrolytic carbon coating (pyrolysis) onto the inner surface of a quartz ampoule in order to suppress the adhesion of molten alkali halide compounds (AHCs) to the ampoule walls; (ii) generation of a high vacuum (10 –6 Тоrr) inside the quartz reactor to purify the alkali halide raw materials from oxygen-containing impurities; (iii) establishment of an argon atmosphere (1.1–1.3 bar) and the quartz ampoule shielding as a technological approach for suppressing the evaporation of aggressive halogen vapors. Flame photometry, absorption spectroscopy, and luminescence spectroscopy analyses demonstrate that the KCl crystal matrix was purified from oxygen-containing impurities (OH) down to 0.2 ppm, divalent impurities (Me 2+ ) down to 0.1 − 0.3 ppm, and alkali-metal homolog cations (Li + , Na + ) down to 1–3 ppm. Unique capabilities of the facility were further realized in the growth of KCl single crystals doped with hygroscopic lithium ions. Enhanced scintillation and dosimetric properties of KCl: Li crystals were demonstrated.

Article.Title: A systematic review and meta analysis of early exercise based cardiac rehabilitation in patients hospitalized with acute heart failure
Article.Authors: Zhang X.; Luo Z.; Yang M.; Huang W.; Wang Y.; Yu P.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Early exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation (ExCR) has been increasingly investigated in patients hospitalized with acute heart failure (AHF), but its effects on functional recovery and whether these effects vary across selected study-level characteristics remain uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effects of ExCR initiated during hospitalization on functional capacity in patients with AHF and to explore potential differences according to rehabilitation delivery model, World Bank country income classification, and study-level mean age. PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and CNKI were searched from inception to May 2026. Randomized controlled trials were eligible if they enrolled adults hospitalized with AHF, initiated a structured ExCR program during hospitalization, compared ExCR with usual care or no structured exercise intervention, and reported 6-minute walk distance (6MWD). The primary outcome was 6MWD, secondary outcomes included health-related quality of life (HRQoL), clinical events and safety. Random-effects models were used, and subgroup analyses were considered exploratory. Twelve independent randomized controlled trials were included. Early ExCR significantly improved 6MWD compared with control group (mean difference [MD] 54.44 m, 95% CI 35.62 to 73.26; I² = 60%). Exploratory subgroup analyses showed no statistically significant differences according to rehabilitation delivery model, World Bank country income classification, or study-level mean age. ExCR also showed potential benefits for disease-specific HRQoL, whereas evidence for HF-related readmission and all-cause mortality remained inconclusive. Sensitivity analyses supported the robustness of the primary 6MWD finding, although the certainty of evidence was rated as low because of risk of bias and inconsistency. Early ExCR initiated during hospitalization may improve functional capacity in patients with AHF. Exploratory subgroup analyses did not identify significant effect modification by rehabilitation delivery model, World Bank country income classification, or study-level mean age. However, the exact magnitude of benefit should be interpreted cautiously, and larger, methodologically rigorous trials are needed to clarify optimal delivery strategies and long-term clinical effects.

Article.Title: Estimating dispersal, survival and population size of wild Aedes aegypti in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania using self-mark-release-recapture method
Article.Authors: Tenywa F.; Makame H.; Moore J.; Dogan O.; Mapipi H.; Smith T.; Chitnis N.; Moore S.; Felber L.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Aedes -borne arboviral diseases represent a major global public health challenge, with vector control remaining the primary preventive strategy because there are no available antivirals or universal vaccines for most of these infections. This study quantified dispersal, survival time and population size of Aedes aegypti using a mosquito mark-release-recapture (MMRR) approach to generate ecological parameters required for implementing a release-based approaches for Ae. aegypti control. Wild Ae. aegypti pupae were placed beneath a marking unit covered with fluorescent dust-coated cloth-grids. Marked mosquitoes were recaptured within a 250 m radius using BG-sentinel traps, Prokopack aspirators, resting buckets and gravid traps. The overall mean distance travelled (MDT) was 94.5 m (95% CI 83.4–105.7) and the maximum distance travelled was 156 m. The average life expectancy (ALE) was 13.5 days (95% CI 12.2–14.8), with an average probability of daily survival (PDS) of 0.93 (95% CI 0.92–0.94). Survival analysis showed that approximately 80% of male and female Ae. aegypti survived up to 10 days. The estimated population size was 1195 mosquitoes/ha. These findings demonstrate that Ae. aegypti exhibit limited dispersal and survive beyond dengue virus’ average extrinsic incubation period (EIP) of 7–12 days, providing ecological conditions conducive to sustain arboviral transmission. The results also provide critical parameters for optimizing release-based control strategies.

Article.Title: Effects of an intensive firefighter training program on a simulated fire-escape staircase climb
Article.Authors: Sanchis C.; Martí-Martí J.; Miñana J.; Navarro-Martínez D.; Zahonero J.; Monleón C.
Article.Abstract: Abstract To evaluate the effects of a four-week intensive training program on weighted stair-climb performance, 18 participants (17 men, 1 woman) completed 16 training sessions combining strength, power, and endurance work. Pre- and post-intervention assessments included a loaded fire-escape staircase climb test, incremental VO₂max test, 30-s Wingate test, submaximal squat test, anthropometric measures, and the ANTI-Vea attentional task. Linear mixed models were used to assess intervention effects; effect sizes were expressed as Cohen's d . Stair-climb time decreased significantly after training (EMC: −1.26 s; d = − 0.88). Post-intervention performance was predicted by a composite Strength Score ( β std = − 0.65) and Wingate Score ( β std = − 0.35; model R ² = 0.86). High-load squat velocity and power, estimated 1RM, and Wingate mean power improved significantly (all d > 0.67), whereas VO₂max, ventilatory thresholds, and body mass remained unchanged. ANT-I mean reaction time improved ( d z = − 0.59), with a shift from a linear to a quadratic vigilance decrement pattern. In conclusion, four weeks of intensive firefighter training improved stair-climb performance primarily through neuromuscular and anaerobic adaptations. Training programs targeting this task should prioritize explosive strength at task-relevant loads and anaerobic endurance, while dedicated cognitive training may be required to improve higher-order vigilance components.

Article.Title: Application of spectral preprocessing and machine learning models for discriminating nitrogen levels in cucumber production
Article.Authors: Sabzi S.; Azadbakht M.; Vahedi Torshizi M.; Pourdarbani R.
Article.Abstract: Nitrogen is one of the most essential macronutrients for plant growth, and its improper management can reduce fertilizer use efficiency while causing significant economic and environmental consequences. In this study, a hyperspectral imaging–based machine learning framework was developed and evaluated to classify different nitrogen fertilizer levels in cucumber leaves (cv. Super Arshiya-F1). Nitrogen treatments consisted of 30%, 60%, and 90% additional nitrogen applied to a nutrient solution with a base concentration of 2 g L⁻¹. Seventy-two hours after treatment application, a total of 300 leaves were collected from the treated plants, and hyperspectral images were acquired in the spectral range of 400–1100 nm, producing 327 spectral bands for each sample. To enhance signal quality and examine the influence of spectral preprocessing on class separability, three preprocessing techniques—Savitzky–Golay filtering, Multiplicative Scatter Correction (MSC), and Gaussian normalization—were applied exclusively to the training dataset and subsequently transferred to the independent test set. Three machine learning algorithms, including Support Vector Machine (SVM), Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), and Decision Tree (DT), were evaluated using a 75/25 training–testing split along with five-fold cross-validation for model optimization. The results demonstrated that SVM consistently achieved the highest classification performance across all scenarios. The best results were obtained without preprocessing and with Gaussian normalization, both reaching an overall accuracy of 94%, an F1-score of approximately 0.94, and a ROC–AUC exceeding 0.98. In contrast, LDA showed moderate performance, while DT yielded the lowest classification accuracy. These findings highlight the strong potential of integrating hyperspectral imaging with SVM for accurate discrimination of nitrogen levels and for supporting efficient nutrient management in crop production systems.

Article.Title: Profilin-regulated actin polymerization dynamics at high monomer concentrations
Article.Authors: Heydenreich L.; Funk J.; Bieling P.; Kierfeld J.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Actin polymerization in the cytoskeleton drives crucial dynamical biological processes such as cell motility and morphogenesis. Recent experiments 1 show that binding to profilin plays a crucial role in controlling the maximal polymerization speed of F-actin at cellular actin concentrations. These experiments are successfully described by a four reaction kinetic model, which predicts a Michaelis-Menten-like saturation of growth speed at high profilin-actin concentrations. In this work, we further analyze the four reaction model in terms of master equations and using the concept of two polymerization cycles, a pure actin cycle and a profilin-actin cycle and propose further experimental setups to gain access to all kinetic rates of the model. We find that varying the profilin excess leads to a profilin-dependent Michaelis constant for the growth speed. For polymerization against an external force, we identify a unique stall force as an indicator of energetically balanced profilin-driven polymerization, i.e., for the absence of coupling to other chemical processes providing energy input. Calculating length diffusivity (or Fano factor) we show that actin growth becomes much more precise by profilin-regulation and almost reaches precision bounds set by thermodynamic uncertainty relations.

Article.Title: Maternal autophagy contributes to grain yield in maize
Article.Authors: Tang J.; Wan X.; Myers A.; Avin-Wittenberg T.; Vollbrecht E.; Bassham D.
Article.Abstract: Maize ( Zea mays ) is an important crop species that is cultivated worldwide, and increasing maize yield is one of the major goals of plant breeding. The subcellular degradation and recycling pathway known as autophagy is involved in many plant developmental processes including vegetative growth, reproductive development, seed development, and senescence. Here, we demonstrate that maize autophagy-defective atg10 mutants have delayed flowering and reduced kernel size, weight and number, leading to reduced grain yield. Reciprocal crosses between mutant and parental lines indicate that, in contrast to the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana , the maternal maize plant genotype is the major contributor to the kernel phenotype in atg10 mutants, rather than the seed genotype.

Article.Title: Expression patterns of Slc38a4 and mmu-miR-6948-3p in a murine model of metastatic triple-negative breast cancer
Article.Authors: Farzamfar P.; Salehi Z.; Mashayekhi F.; Khodayari S.
Article.Abstract: SLC38A4 (SNAT4), a system A amino acid transporter, contributes to nutrient uptake and metabolic regulation, but its role in the progression of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is unclear. We examined the expression of Slc38a4 and its predicted regulatory miRNA, mmu-miR-6948-3p , in primary tumors, invasive mammary tumors, and lung metastases in a murine TNBC model. RNA-sequencing data (GSE150928) from primary mammary tumors and lung metastases were analyzed to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs), followed by functional enrichment, protein–protein interaction (PPI) network analysis, and miRNA–mRNA target prediction. Eighteen female BALB/c mice implanted with 4T1 TNBC cells were grouped into those with primary mammary tumors and those with lung metastases. Expression of Slc38a4 and mmu-miR-6948-3p was measured by quantitative real-time PCR (qRT–PCR). Public human datasets (TCGA, MET500, DepMap) were also examined. In the RNA-seq data, Slc38a4 was upregulated in lung metastases relative to primary tumors (logFC = 3.93) and was assigned to a PPI cluster enriched for amino acid transport and vesicle trafficking. qRT–PCR confirmed higher Slc38a4 expression in lung metastases (6.23 ± 0.48 vs. 1.00 ± 0.08, P < 0.0001) and lower expression in invasive mammary tumors (0.51 ± 0.05 vs. 1.00 ± 0.08, P < 0.0001) than in primary tumors. Levels of mmu-miR-6948-3p did not differ significantly between groups. In human data, SLC38A4 mRNA was lower in breast tumors than in normal breast tissue, and DNA methylation showed no clear relationship with its expression. Slc38a4 expression depends on tissue context during TNBC progression, being lower in invasive mammary tumors and higher in lung metastases, and this pattern is not explained by changes in mmu-miR-6948-3p. Functional studies are needed to determine whether the increase in the lung drives colonization or is an adaptive response to it.

Article.Title: Investigating the intergenerational stress buffering effects of ethnic-racial identity in disaster-exposed parents and their children
Article.Authors: Knowles E.; Danzi B.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Disasters are a significant source of stress for parents, and people of color (POC) are disproportionately negatively impacted. Identifying protective factors is a necessary step toward promoting resilience and recovery in POC. Ethnic-racial identity (ERI) may protect against psychological stress for disaster-exposed POC. The purpose of this study was to identify how families of color (FOC) were affected by a disaster and evaluate ERI as a protective factor for POC and their children. It was hypothesized that FOC would report greater distress compared to White families and that ERI would mitigate distress in FOC. Parents ( N = 218) exposed to a hurricane reported on their family’s hurricane experiences, ERI, and parent and child psychological functioning. FOC parents reported greater hurricane-realted distress compared to White parents. ERI did not diminish the association between hurricane adversity and distress in parents. FOC children experienced greater distress compared to White counterparts. Child and parent distress were positively associated with one another. ERI was found to buffer the relationship between parent distress and child distress, such that these symptoms were mitigated. These findings highlight the impact of disaster exposure on FOC and describe how ERI may diminish negative outcomes for these families.

Article.Title: Parent-metabolite PBPK model of methotrexate to inform pediatric extrapolation, transporter-mediated drug–drug interactions, and renal impairment
Article.Authors: Dette C.; Marok F.; Alberg V.; Dings C.; Selzer D.; Schwab M.; Kotnik B.; Dolžan V.; Yildiz D.; Bittenbring J.; Remke M.; Lehr T.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Methotrexate (MTX) is widely used in treating chronic inflammatory diseases and in chemotherapy for both adult and pediatric patients. Its pharmacokinetics are complex, as MTX is a substrate of multiple transporters. Particularly during high-dose chemotherapeutic use, it is associated with severe toxicities including reversible kidney impairment and hematological toxicity. Physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling offers a mechanistic approach to predict drug pharmacokinetics and guide dosing, especially in pediatric applications where clinical data is limited. A whole-body parent-metabolite PBPK model of MTX and 7-hydroxymethotrexate was developed in PK-Sim ® (version 12.1) for intravenous and oral administration in adults and children. Model development used 42 MTX and 16 metabolite plasma concentration-time profiles and showed strong predictive performance, with 53/58 area under the plasma concentration-time curve and 38/39 maximum plasma concentration values within a 2-fold range of observed data. Pediatric extrapolation incorporating transporter ontogeny yielded adequate predictions. Drug-drug interaction simulations for five perpetrator drugs met established acceptance criteria, and renal impairment simulations revealed markedly increased exposure in the high-dose setting. The model will be made publicly available to support dose optimization across clinical scenarios.

Article.Title: Effects of maximum teleportation distance on wayfinding in virtual reality: the role of optical flow cues
Article.Authors: Zhao Y.; Li Q.
Article.Abstract: Instantaneous teleportation reduces simulator sickness risk by omitting continuous viewpoint motion but may impair spatial orientation. Previous research has generally examined maximum teleportation distance and optical-flow transitions separately, leaving their combined effects during wayfinding unclear. We conducted a 2 (teleportation type: no optical flow vs. brief optical flow) × 3 (maximum teleportation distance: 5, 15, and 25 m) mixed-design experiment with 60 participants who completed route-exploration and unguided-return tasks in a virtual urban environment. Wayfinding performance and experience were assessed using sketch maps, navigation measures, the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire, and semi-structured interviews. Sketch-map scores were lower at 25 m than at 5 and 15 m. Navigation time was longer at 5 m than at 25 m, and mean navigation time per teleportation increased across the 5-, 15-, and 25-m conditions. No significant between-type differences or type × distance interactions were detected for sketch-map or navigation measures. Simulator sickness scores were low across conditions. The aligned rank transform analysis indicated effects of teleportation type, distance, and their interaction that were not consistently reproduced by other approaches, leaving insufficient evidence for a stable simulator-sickness effect. Interview responses suggested that shorter-distance teleportation facilitated environmental observation, whereas longer-distance teleportation was perceived as easier to operate. The 25 m condition combined shorter navigation time with lower sketch-map scores. Distance conditions were paired with fixed scene variants, and the fixed 0.3 s transition coupled displacement with translation speed. The possible trade-off between traversal efficiency and environmental learning therefore remains specific to the tested configurations.

Article.Title: Hormonal dynamics in contrasting bearing habits of mango grafted on different rootstocks
Article.Authors: Vittal H.; Sharma N.; Sharma R.; Pandey R.; Singh N.; Ali A.; Singh N.; Kumar R.; Dubey A.; Mishra G.; Nirgude M.; Lata S.; Dilip S.; Gaikwad K.
Article.Abstract: Mango productivity is heavily dependent on the physiological transition from vegetative to reproductive growth, yet the integrated role of rootstock-mediated hormonal crosstalk in regulating these reproductive traits remains poorly understood. This study evaluated hormonal profiles and reproductive traits in regular-bearing ‘Amrapali’ and alternate-bearing ‘Dashehari’ grafted onto four rootstocks. Eight scion–rootstock combinations were evaluated with three biological replicates each. Leaf and bud concentrations of indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), gibberellic acid (GA 3 ), zeatin and abscisic acid (ABA) were quantified using high-performance liquid chromatography, alongside assessments of flowering traits. Hormonal concentrations exhibited scion × rootstock × tissue interactions, with Kurukkan-associated bud IAA exceeding leaf concentrations in Amrapali (10.37 versus 4.92 ng g⁻ 1 ) and Dashehari (9.93 versus 1.40 ng g⁻ 1 ). Bud GA₃ also exceeded leaf concentrations under Kurukkan in both cultivars, whereas ABA showed contrasting tissue distributions. Amrapali/Olour produced the highest total flower number (1,077.33 per panicle), whereas Amrapali/PAM-2 exhibited the greatest hermaphrodite flower number (372.67 per panicle) and proportion (38.78%). Exploratory correlations associated bud zeatin with male flower number in Amrapali (r = 0.963, P = 0.037) and bud ABA with panicle length in Dashehari (r = 0.962, P = 0.038). These findings indicate rootstock-associated hormonal and reproductive variation without establishing causal relationships.

Article.Title: Quantum-resistant blockchain-assisted federated secure cancer diagnosis framework using hierarchical window pattern cognition network
Article.Authors: Asmeen S.; Chenam V.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Breast cancer is still a major cause of cancer mortality in women, and the development of efficient, reliable and explainable diagnostic systems capable of inter-hospital data sharing while maintaining privacy of data is essential. This study proposes a Hierarchical Window Pattern Cognition Network for breast cancer diagnosis using the Breast Histopathology Images (IDC Regular Patches) dataset. The workflow starts with data collection, then the Patient-Level Data Partitioning process by applying patient identifiers to avoid training-testing overlap. The framework uses CLAHE and data augmentation, image normalization and image resizing to enhance the image consistency. The network learns hierarchical histological and cellular morphological patterns by the modules: Global Histological Representation, Cellular Morphology Learning, Adaptive Tissue Fusion and Diagnostic Probability Estimation. A federated learning framework with five clients uses Federated Averaging (FedAvg) to aggregate models and share model updates securely. The security layer uses an AES-256-GCM encryption algorithm, a SHA3-512 hashing algorithm, and a mechanism simulating those of CRYSTALS-Kyber and CRYSTALS-Dilithium for cryptographic security. Record-integrity verification is supported by a local hash-chain audit log, and predictions of the model are explained with visual and feature-level explanations by using GradCAM + + and SHAP. The proposed centralized model achieved an accuracy of 94.23%, precision of 94.00%, recall of 94.47%, F1-score of 94.24%, and ROC-AUC of 0.9651. These findings highlight the promise of combining the histopathology classification, privacy-preserving federated learning, cryptographic protection, tamper-evident audit logging and explainable artificial intelligence within a unified diagnostic framework.
Article.TopicFields: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > AI in cancer detection; Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence > Privacy-Preserving Technologies in Data; Computer Science > Information Systems > Blockchain Technology Applications and Security

Article.Title: Electroencephalographic patterns of equine sleep: comparative description and neurophysiological implications of recumbent and standing sleep
Article.Authors: Oliveira T.; Basile R.; Souza B.; Vicentini Y.; Barbosa A.; Baccarin R.
Article.Abstract: Abstract The present study aimed to describe and compare the electroencephalographic patterns of sleep in horses during recumbent and standing positions, identifying the cortical dynamics and spectral characteristics associated with each stage. Eight clinically healthy adult horses were monitored through polysomnographic EEG recordings, using a double-banana montage with subcutaneous needle electrodes. Sleep stages were classified according to spectral and morphological criteria analogous to human scoring standards, with one sleep cycle analyzed per horse. REM sleep was posture-dependent, with complete paradoxical patterns observed only in recumbent horses. In standing animals, a REM-like state was identified, marked by rapid eye movements but cortical hypoactivation and absence of muscle atonia. Quantitative analysis revealed that N1 and N2 accounted for approximately 90% of total sleep duration, while N3 and REM represented smaller fractions. Standing horses exhibited longer light sleep stages and a smaller proportion of N3 sleep. These findings demonstrate that equine sleep architecture is highly posture-dependent, and behavioral postures such as sternal or lateral recumbency cannot be reliably used as proxies for specific EEG sleep stages. The study provides a methodological framework to support future investigations and facilitate comparisons of equine sleep physiology across studies and species.
Article.TopicFields: Neuroscience > Cognitive Neuroscience > Sleep and Wakefulness Research; Veterinary > Equine > Veterinary Equine Medical Research; Veterinary > Small Animals > Veterinary Pharmacology and Anesthesia

Article.Title: A Bayesian Functional Kriging framework for spatial interpolation of PM2.5 concentration profiles
Article.Authors: Baseer A.; Khalefa M.; Ismael W.; Hussain I.; Basheer A.
Article.Abstract: Air pollution, especially fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ), is a major global public health problem, causing breathing difficulties, lung disease, heart problems, and premature death. Predicting PM 2.5 concentrations at unobserved locations is essential in environmental science, especially with sparse observational data. This study introduces a new Bayesian Functional Kriging (BFK) model to predict PM 2.5 concentration profiles across Pakistan’s most populous province, using MERRA-2 reanalysis data at 17 city locations across Punjab. The BFK framework combines three methodologies: Functional Data Analysis (FDA), where continuous temporal curves model discrete PM 2.5 concentration profiles through B-spline smoothing; Functional Kriging (FK), in which functional data are used for spatial prediction of curve-valued observations; and Bayesian hierarchical modeling using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling for parameter estimation. Prior empirical distributions are assumed for all parameters of interest: mean, partial sill, nugget effect, and spatial range, while posterior estimates are derived via a hybrid Gibbs-Metropolis algorithm within Gibbs sampling. Cross-validation results show that BFK is significantly better than the FK method, with RMSE and MAE differences of 30.9% (from 16.88 µg/m 3 to 11.66 µg/m 3 ) and 29.9% (from 13.03 µg/m 3 to 9.14 µg/m 3 ), respectively. In addition, we used the proposed model to estimate temporal variation in PM 2.5 concentration at five locations not sampled during data collection: Vehari, Sialkot, Attock, Khanewal, and Okara. We found that pollution is much higher in the southern areas than in the northern ones. These findings underscore BFK’s utility as a statistically principled and practically effective tool for air quality monitoring and environmental policy.

Article.Title: Predictors of prolonged hospitalization among children admitted with severe pneumonia in Southeast Ethiopia: a retrospective follow-up study
Article.Authors: Redwan M.; Belete B.; Abdeta G.; Gebremeskel T.; Demissie A.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Background Severe pneumonia remains a primary driver of pediatric morbidity in Sub-Saharan Africa. Prolonged hospital stay (PHS) escalates healthcare expenditure and strains referral hospital resources. This study aimed to evaluate the magnitude, clinical determinants, and model performance of factors associated with PHS among hospitalized pediatric severe pneumonia cases in Southeast Ethiopia. Methods A hospital-based retrospective follow-up study was conducted at Asella Referral and Teaching Hospital, analyzing 395 systematically sampled pediatric cases (aged 3 months to 14 years) admitted with severe pneumonia. Multivariable binary logistic regression was executed with model diagnostics, including Variance Inflation Factors (VIF), Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit, and Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Results The magnitude of prolonged hospital stay (> 7 days) was 42.0% (95% CI 37.2–46.8). In the multivariable model, independent clinical predictors included presence of comorbidities (Adjusted OR [aOR] = 4.02; 95% CI 2.42–6.67; p < 0.001), care-seeking delay > 48 hours (aOR = 3.89; 95% CI 2.35–6.42; p < 0.001), history of previous pneumonia (aOR = 3.23; 95% CI 1.81–5.74; p < 0.001), partial vaccination status (aOR = 3.03; 95% CI 1.73–5.32; p < 0.001), and underlying malnutrition (aOR = 2.44; 95% CI 1.15–5.18; p = 0.021). The multivariable explanatory model demonstrated good discriminative performance (AUC = 0.804, 95% CI 0.759–0.848) and good model calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow p = 0.612). Conclusions Over four in ten pediatric severe pneumonia admissions experience prolonged hospitalization. Early triage, prompt care-seeking, complete routine immunization, and nutritional interventions may reduce prolonged hospitalization and should be prioritized in similar referral settings.

Article.Title: Hidden baseline heterogeneity can mask treatment effects in randomized xenograft studies
Article.Authors: Gül N.; Hekim N.
Article.Abstract: Abstract Randomization and standardized analytical workflows are central to preclinical oncology, yet they do not necessarily ensure biological comparability at baseline. Using a real-world xenograft efficacy dataset generated under standard CRO conditions, we show that biologically meaningful treatment effects can remain statistically undetected when baseline heterogeneity is not explicitly considered. Although treatment groups appeared balanced at study entry by conventional summaries, baseline tumour volume exhibited latent structure within the cohort. Pooled group-level analyses reported no significant treatment effect, whereas baseline-aware evaluation of tumour growth trajectories revealed a responder subpopulation whose signal was masked by aggregation. This discrepancy did not arise from deficiencies in experimental conduct or data quality, but from limitations of pooled inference in the presence of structured baseline variability. Extending this framework to publicly available xenograft datasets, we observed that baseline tumour volume heterogeneity is common under routine preclinical workflows and can similarly alter efficacy interpretation. Together, these findings indicate that baseline tumour burden represents a biologically consequential source of hidden heterogeneity and that baseline-aware analytical strategies can improve the sensitivity and interpretability of preclinical efficacy assessment without deviation from standard experimental practice.
Article.TopicFields: Mathematics > Statistics and Probability > Statistical Methods in Clinical Trials; Veterinary > Small Animals > Animal testing and alternatives; Veterinary > Small Animals > Veterinary Oncology Research

Article.Title: Virus induced cochlear inflammation alters stria vascularis function and auditory development
Article.Authors: Smith M.; Hirose K.; Britt W.
Article.Abstract: Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is the most common viral infection acquired in utero and a leading cause of sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL). In previous studies utilizing a murine model of SNHL that follows congenital CMV infection (cCMV), virus-induced cochlear inflammation has been shown to result in SNHL that develops in the absence of histopathology in the sensory neuroepithelium but is associated with the dysregulation of a number of deafness related genes (DRG). In this study, virus-induced cochlear inflammation was shown to dysregulate the expression of multiple DRG that have been shown to contribute to ion and metabolite transport within stria vacularis (SV). In addition, cochlear inflammation in virus-infected mice resulted in the loss of barrier functions of the SV that have also been linked to SNHL. Decreased expression of these DRG in infected animals was associated with SNHL that was similar to that observed in genetically engineered murine models with deletion of these DRG. Together, these results argue that virus-induced inflammation can lead to dysregulation of host genes associated with barrier and ion transport function of the SV, thus providing further insight into potential mechanisms of SNHL that follow virus infections during early auditory development.
