Article.Title: Quantifying the impact of age-related hearing loss on neural signatures of target selection and distractor suppression
Article.Authors: Solmssen N.; Stockar F.; Alavash M.; Popov T.; Wöstmann M.; Obleser J.; Preisig B.
Article.Abstract: Listeners with hearing loss (HL) often report difficulties in separating relevant target sound from irrelevant distraction. These difficulties in auditory selective attention might be caused by inefficient neural mechanisms underlying target selection and distractor suppression. In this registered report, we tested whether neural and behavioural signatures of target selection and distractor suppression were selectively impaired in 30 older listeners with HL, compared to 32 older listeners with normal hearing (NH) and 33 young NH listeners. For this purpose, we used an auditory pitch discrimination task that allowed to dissociate changes in neural alpha activity (∼8-12Hz) and microsaccade direction in response to target selection and distractor suppression due to spatial separation. Our results show that neural signatures of spatial attention may be relatively preserved in individuals with mild-to-moderate hearing loss. Specifically, we found no conclusive evidence that hearing loss affects either target-related or distractor-related alpha lateralization. In contrast, distractor-related, but not target-related, alpha lateralization diminished with age. Furthermore, we found no conclusive evidence that single-trial alpha lateralization predicts listening accuracy or confidence. We found that attentional modulation of microsaccade rate occurred independently of directional bias and alpha lateralization. Microsaccade rate, but not microsaccade direction, was significantly increased during lateral distractor suppression compared to target selection, and we observed no oculomotor pattern mirroring neural alpha lateralization. Collectively, these findings suggest that aging more strongly affects the neural signature of distractor suppression than that of target selection.

Article.Title: Gaze guides language comprehension in adults in a simulated social environment
Article.Authors: Zappa A.; Osokina P.; Fargier R.; Cerda-Company X.; Panisello S.; Anderssen N.; Zambrana I.; Rodriguez-Fornells A.; Slater M.
Article.Abstract: Multimodal cues are crucial for real-life language comprehension. While gaze-following is a well-established mechanism in early language acquisition, its role in adult language comprehension - especially under challenging conditions - remains relatively unexplored. Here, we used a novel immersive and embodied virtual reality (VR) paradigm to examine whether referential gaze facilitates comprehension of unfamiliar spoken words in a noisy environment. Participants interacted with virtual agents whose gaze behavior varied in referential informativeness. Explicit feedback ensured that gaze-guided comprehension outcomes could be disentangled from informational content. Behavioral and eye-tracking data showed that participants identified spoken input more accurately when the teacher’s gaze reliably signaled the intended referent, and when they actively followed it. This facilitative effect of gaze emerged early and persisted across tasks. These findings highlight the enduring role of social gaze mechanisms in adult language comprehension, particularly in ambiguous or noisy contexts. They have important implications for a multimodal and situated language processing perspective, showing that gaze-following plays a meaningful role in real-world comprehension.

Article.Title: Beyond the Microbial Hypothesis: Shared Genetic, Osteoimmune and Vascular Mechanisms in the Oral–Brain Axis Linking Periodontitis and Alzheimer's Disease
Article.Authors: Kabbashi S.; Ahmed M.; Chetty M.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Periodontitis, a chronic inflammatory disease of the tooth‐supporting tissues, is increasingly linked to Alzheimer's disease ( AD ), yet mechanistic accounts of this ‘oral–brain axis’ have been dominated by microbial translocation and the gingipain hypothesis. This review argues that the convergence between periodontitis and AD extends well beyond microbes, integrating shared genetic, osteoimmune and vascular‐inflammatory mechanisms that are rarely considered together. Genetic susceptibility reaches beyond APOE ε4 to the osteoprotegerin (OPG) axis, with APOE ε4 linking the two conditions through impaired amyloid‐β clearance, blood–brain barrier dysfunction and altered lipid handling. The OPG/RANK/RANKL system emerges as a bone–brain (osteoimmune) interface, in which OPG shows a dual‐role paradox, reduced locally in periodontal bone loss yet elevated systematically in AD , while soluble RANKL displays neuroprotective properties. Because OPG acts as a decoy receptor for RANKL, we hypothesise that elevated OPG in AD limits RANKL‐dependent microglial amyloid‐β clearance. Endothelial dysfunction, reflected in circulating endocan, provides a shared vascular readout that is raised in both diseases and responsive to periodontal therapy. We propose that these genetic, microbial and vascular inputs converge on microglial priming and trained immunity, a unifying immunological node through which chronic peripheral inflammation may act during the decades‐long preclinical phase of AD . Current evidence nonetheless remains predominantly associative, causality is unproven and mechanistic data rely heavily on animal models. The oral–brain axis is therefore best regarded as a promising yet still unproven framework in which osteoimmune and vascular pathways, and candidate biomarkers such as endocan, represent underexplored targets for future longitudinal and interventional research.

Article.Title: Cortical Adaptation to Muscle Fatigue Does Not Alter Early Proprioceptive Processing in Primary Sensorimotor Cortex
Article.Authors: Chen J.; Mujunen T.; Li F.; Nikander R.; Piitulainen H.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Muscle fatigue potentially interferes with proprioceptive afference from peripheral “movement sensors”—the proprioceptors, which may hinder crucial sensorimotor integration and thus movement performance. However, little is known about how muscle fatigue affects cortical processing of proprioceptive afference. Twenty‐four healthy volunteers (30.7 ± 6.5 years) participated in the experiment, which included magnetoencephalography (MEG) recordings during 2‐Hz passive ankle‐joint rotations, and fatigue tasks comprised of isometric ankle plantarflexion. Corticokinematic coherence (CKC) between linear foot acceleration and MEG signals was examined before (PRE) and ~3 min after (POST) the fatigue tasks to compare the cortical proprioceptive processing. CKC peaked in the gradiometer pairs above the foot region of the primary sensorimotor (SM1) cortex in each participant. CKC strength did not show significant difference between PRE and POST at 2 Hz (0.30 ± 0.12 vs. 0.30 ± 0.14, p = 0.981) or its first harmonic at 4 Hz (0.38 ± 0.14 vs. 0.37 ± 0.13, p = 0.724). However, 4‐Hz MEG power was ~30% lower in POST than in PRE. Surprisingly, fatigue‐induced increase of alpha and beta power was observed bilaterally in SM1 hand regions during the ankle movements. Our results indicate that the early processing of proprioceptive afference from the ankle joint was negligibly affected by muscle fatigue or the effect recovered rapidly. The fatigue elevated alpha and beta power while diminishing neuronal activity at the 4‐Hz harmonic frequency, which may reflect a compensatory mechanism for asynchronous proprioceptive afference by enhancing cortical inhibitory control.

Article.Title: Mitochondria‐Associated Membranes as a Convergent Hub of Brain Aging: From Neurodegeneration to Cerebral Ischemia
Article.Authors: Li M.; Xu D.; Li Y.; Zhao Q.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Brain aging is the principal risk factor for both neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs) and cerebral ischemic disorders, yet the subcellular mechanisms linking these conditions remain incompletely defined. Mitochondria‐associated membranes (MAMs)—specialized contact sites between the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and mitochondria—sit at the intersection of two well‐established hallmarks of aging, mitochondrial dysfunction, and loss of proteostasis, making them an attractive mechanistic node for understanding age‐related brain decline. In this review, we propose a MAM‐centered framework that unifies neurodegenerative and ischemic brain pathology under the broader paradigm of brain aging. We first summarize the molecular architecture of MAMs and their core functions in neuronal Ca 2+ transfer, mitochondrial dynamics, lipid metabolism, inflammasome assembly, and autophagic quality control, together with emerging evidence from non‐neuronal brain cells. We then examine how MAM dysfunction intersects with five hallmarks of aging—mitochondrial dysfunction, loss of proteostasis, disabled macroautophagy, chronic inflammation (inflammaging), and altered intercellular communication—drawing on evidence from physiological aging and cellular senescence models. Next, we discuss disease‐specific roles of MAMs in cerebral ischemia and in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and Huntington's disease. A central theme emerges: Rather than a unidirectional decline of MAMs, brain aging is associated with a loss of MAM homeostasis, in which both insufficient and excessive ER–mitochondria coupling can be pathological and the shared deficit is the failure to maintain contact‐site function within an optimal range. Finally, we consider age‐relevant therapeutic and biomarker strategies targeting MAMs and their potential translation into geriatric neurology. To our knowledge, this is the first review to integrate MAM biology across physiological brain aging, cerebral ischemia, and the four major NDDs within a single homeostatic framework, offering a unified perspective on the mechanisms of age‐related brain decline.

Article.Title: Traditional Chinese Medicine Targeting the Ischemic Cascade in Ischemic Stroke: Multitarget Mechanisms and Therapeutic Potential
Article.Authors: Song Y.; Yang M.; Wang S.; Chen Y.; Dong P.; Han H.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Ischemic stroke (IS) remains a major cause of mortality and long‐term disability worldwide. Increasing evidence indicates that injury progression after cerebral ischemia is closely associated with dysfunction of the neurovascular unit (NVU). Following ischemia, a series of interconnected pathological events, including metabolic failure, excitotoxicity, calcium dysregulation, oxidative injury, inflammation and cell death, contribute to progressive neuronal and vascular damage. Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) has been increasingly investigated as a source of multicomponent interventions for IS. Experimental studies indicate that bioactive compounds, extracts and classical formulas may influence multiple components of the ischemic cascade, including energy metabolism, glutamate excitotoxicity, Ca 2+ homeostasis, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation and regulated cell death. These effects have been associated with pathways including AMPK/SIRT1, PI3K/Akt, Nrf2/HO‐1, NF‐κB and NLRP3. However, modulation of multiple pathways does not necessarily establish pharmacological synergy or superiority over single‐target interventions. This review summarizes TCM interventions targeting the ischemic cascade, with a primary focus on studies published between 2015 and 2025. Particular attention is given to the strength of mechanistic evidence, treatment timing, experimental models, pharmacologically active constituents, safety and clinical translation. By critically evaluating both mechanistic findings and current limitations, this review provides a framework for assessing the evidence and translational potential of TCM‐derived neuroprotective strategies in IS.

Article.Title: Cognitive Cerebellum Structure and Functional Connectivity in Relation to Executive Functions in Obsessive‐Compulsive Disorder
Article.Authors: Rosales Mondragón C.; Barbosa Luna M.; Ricardo Garcell J.; Alcauter Solórzano S.; Salvador Cruz J.; Corona Márquez B.; López Lazo L.; Pasaye E.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Obsessive‐compulsive disorder (OCD) has been primarily linked to abnormalities within the cortico–striato–thalamo–cortical circuit; however, recent evidence suggests that the posterior cerebellum may contribute to the executive dysfunction observed in the disorder. Functional connectivity results revealed a mixed pattern, including focal hyperconnectivity (e.g., left Crus I with primary auditory cortex; left Crus II with occipital cortex) and widespread intracerebellar hypoconnectivity. In addition, significant Group × executive‐function interactions ( p ‐family‐wise error < 0.05) emerged mainly for bilateral Crus I (Global Executive Index and working memory/flexibility) and left lobule VI (inhibition/decision‐making), indicating that the relationship between cerebellar connectivity and executive performance differs in OCD relative to controls. Article.Title: Protective Role of Netrin‐1 in the Female Nucleus Accumbens Following Amphetamine Exposure in Adolescence
Article.Authors: Teixeira M.; MacGowan D.; Avramescu R.; Zhu A.; Niu Z.; Mahmud A.; Hernandez G.; Flores C.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Adolescence is a period of mesocorticolimbic dopamine remodelling, when exposure to drugs of abuse can alter axon targeting and synaptic maturation. In adolescent male rodents, amphetamine causes dopamine axon mistargeting and long‐term cognitive deficits via downregulation of the Netrin‐1/DCC guidance system. In females, compensatory Netrin‐1 protein upregulation in the nucleus accumbens protects against these effects. How Netrin‐1 expression in the nucleus accumbens is regulated and what role it plays in local synaptic architecture remain unclear. Here, we mapped Netrin‐1 mRNA ( Ntn1 ) across development in nucleus accumbens medium spiny neurons, assessed the role of dopamine D1 and D2 receptor signalling in Netrin‐1 protein expression and examined whether Netrin‐1 maintains medium spiny neuron dendritic spine architecture following adolescent amphetamine exposure. In adolescent females, systemic blockade of either D1 or D2 receptors reduced nucleus accumbens Netrin‐1 protein levels under both baseline and amphetamine‐exposed conditions. Although amphetamine did not alter Ntn1 mRNA in the nucleus accumbens, it increased its expression in the ventral tegmental area, suggesting a potential contribution from afferent projections. These findings indicate that Netrin‐1 upregulation in adolescent females is dopamine‐dependent and may protect against amphetamine‐induced circuit disruption, possibly involving pre‐ and postsynaptic mechanisms.

Article.Title: Time to Move Upstream? A Framework for Expanding the Focus of Freezing of Gait to Prodromal, Subclinical, and Pre‐FOG Stages
Article.Authors: Hausdorff J.; Ehgoetz Martens K.; Gilat M.; Nonnekes J.; Mancini M.; McKay J.; Ginis P.; Adams J.; Mammen J.; Howe E.; Lewis S.; Horak F.; Nieuwboer A.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Freezing of gait (FOG) is one of the most disabling motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease, yet a fundamental question remains unresolved: why does FOG occur at any given moment? Most research has focused on studying FOG once it is already manifest. The present work aims to synthesize recent observations and propose a conceptual framework in which FOG reflects a dynamic process unfolding across multiple stages and time scales. Subtle changes in gait dynamics and physiology can precede episodes by several seconds (Stage −1), and experimental paradigms show that individuals without clinically recognized freezing may exhibit brief episodes under sufficiently sensitive conditions (Stage −2). At longer time scales, prospective studies indicate that vulnerability to freezing may be detectable years before onset (Stage −3). This framework reflects the idea that FOG emerges from progressive instability across interacting motor, cognitive, autonomic, and environmental systems, rather than as an isolated event. The proposed framework includes a prodromal stage, a subclinical stage, an immediate prefreezing state, and the freezing episode itself (Stage 0). This framework integrates findings from wearable sensing, physiology, and clinical studies and emphasizes that FOG remains latent in Stage −3, may be elicited only under specific conditions in Stage −2, and becomes manifest as instability evolves toward imminent and overt freezing (Stages −1 and 0, respectively). Reframing FOG as a multistage process that includes an upstream phase raises new questions regarding mechanisms, classification, and intervention, and may, ultimately, inform strategies aimed at predicting and preventing freezing rather than simply reacting to it.

Article.Title: Effects of Short‐Term Breathwork on Respiration and Cognitive Performance in a Discrimination Task
Article.Authors: Hehemann L.; Stetza L.; Kayser C.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Respiration is a unique physiological process that can operate automatically but can also be deliberately used to modulate the bodily state. Importantly, respiration is deeply intertwined with neural processes, influencing functions from arousal and attention to executive control. Although structured respiration (breathing practice) has been exploited for centuries, the immediate consequences of short periods of structured respiration for sensation and cognition remain poorly understood. The present explorative study examined how brief, 1‐min episodes of structured respiration affect respiration and performance in a subsequent sensory‐cognitive task. Across two experiments, participants engaged in structured breathing practices that manipulated either respiratory frequency (slow breathing vs. fast breathing) or the inhalation–exhalation ratio (short inspiration–long expiration and long inspiration–short expiration) prior to performing a visual emotion discrimination task. Immediately after breathing practice, participants' respiration deviated from their baseline: Each technique resulted in specific deviations of respiratory frequency, inhalation–exhalation ratio, or the occurrence of atypical respiratory cycles, suggesting technique‐specific returns to regular respiration. During the subsequent discrimination task response accuracy and reaction times did not differ between breathing practices. However, we observed transient changes in reaction times immediately following all practices, suggesting a brief facilitation of attentional or sensorimotor responsiveness following conscious breathing. Our findings indicate that even brief, consciously controlled respiration can transiently influence cognitive performance, highlighting the role of voluntary respiratory modulation in shaping brain function and behavior.

Article.Title: Photoperiodic Regulation of SK Channels in Dorsal Raphe Serotonin Neurons
Article.Authors: Giannoni‐Guzmán M.; Zepeda J.; Kamitakahara A.; Magalong V.; Levitt P.; Grueter B.; McMahon D.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Day length, or seasonal photoperiod, shapes mood and affective behaviors, but the neural mechanisms underlying these effects are still being defined. Serotonin neurons of the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN) are critical regulators of affective behaviors, and photoperiod modulates their excitability and ongoing activity. Here, we investigated the influence of seasonal photoperiod on the function and expression of small conductance calcium‐activated potassium (SK) channels, which mediate the after‐hyperpolarizing potential (AHP) in dorsal raphe serotonin neurons. Building on previous work demonstrating that long summer‐like photoperiod increases serotonergic neuron excitability and decreases AHP amplitude, we hypothesized that day length influences SK channel activity, thereby contributing to differences in neuronal excitability observed between Long, Equinox, and Short photoperiod conditions. Using multielectrode array recordings from DRN slices, we found a significant, dose‐dependent increase in spike rate upon application of the SK channel inhibitor apamin, indicating that SK channels indeed influence the spike rate of dorsal raphe serotonin neurons. In addition, whole‐cell recordings from DRN neurons in slices demonstrated that SK channel–mediated AHP currents were smaller in amplitude in Long photoperiod mice compared to Short and Equinox photoperiod mice. However, we found no significant differences in mRNA levels of the SK3 subunit ( Kcnn3 ) in DRN serotonin neurons across photoperiod conditions as determined by single‐molecule fluorescence in situ hybridization. Overall, these findings indicate that photoperiod modulates SK channel function in DRN serotonin neurons, possibly through posttranscriptional mechanisms, contributing to the increase in serotonin neuron excitability observed in long summer‐like photoperiods.

Article.Title: Differential NMDA‐Evoked Excitatory and Inhibitory Neuronal Responses Under In Vivo and Ex Vivo Conditions in 5xFAD Mice
Article.Authors: Lee S.; Park T.; Chung S.; Suh M.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Alzheimer's disease (AD) is associated with profound disturbances in neuronal activity. While spontaneous neuronal hyperactivity is a well‐established feature of AD, how the disease affects stimulus‐evoked responses of excitatory and inhibitory neurons remains unclear. Prior studies examining stimulus‐evoked activity have reported conflicting results, describing both exaggerated and blunted responses, which has hindered a coherent understanding of how neuronal activity is evoked by stimulation in AD. The objective of this study was to determine how experimental context influences stimulus‐evoked neuronal responses in AD and to define cell‐type‐specific alterations in excitatory and inhibitory neurons within the same disease model. We examined N ‐methyl‐D‐aspartate (NMDA)‐evoked calcium responses in the 5xFAD mouse model under ex vivo and in vivo conditions using two‐photon calcium imaging. Excitatory and inhibitory neuronal populations were analyzed, enabling assessment of stimulus‐evoked response amplitude and kinetics across experimental contexts. In acute brain slices, NMDA stimulation elicited exaggerated peak responses and altered response kinetics in excitatory neurons from AD mice, whereas inhibitory neurons showed preserved peak amplitude but a significantly delayed time to peak. In contrast, under in vivo conditions, NMDA‐evoked responses were markedly attenuated in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons. Thus, the same AD model exhibited opposing stimulus‐evoked response profiles depending on experimental context. These findings demonstrate that stimulus‐evoked neuronal dysfunction in AD is context‐dependent and cannot be inferred from a single experimental modality. Our results indicate that AD‐related alterations in neuronal responsiveness reflect changes in how inputs are recruited and transformed, rather than a uniform shift toward hyperexcitability or hypoexcitability, underscoring the need for integrative, multimodal approaches to define neuronal dysfunction in neurodegenerative disease.

Article.Title: Structural and EEG Motor Networks Distinguish Level of Motor Impairment After Stroke
Article.Authors: Zhou Z.; Wodeyar A.; Cramer S.; Srinivasan R.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT The objective of this study was to determine how structural and EEG‐based functional connectivity jointly distinguish levels of motor impairment after stroke. We estimated patient‐specific (1) structural connectivity using MRI‐derived lesion models and (2) functional connectivity using source‐localized EEG, guided by each patient's structural connectome. Analyses focused on the brainstem and three motor‐related cortical regions bilaterally: primary motor cortex (M1), dorsal premotor cortex (PMd), and supplementary motor cortex (SMA). Network analysis metrics (degree centrality, average efficiency, betweenness centrality) were applied to structural and functional data, contrasting motor networks between patients with high (H) and low (L) upper extremity motor function. Structural disconnection of the brainstem from M1 and PMd carried the highest probability of low motor status. All network measures were elevated in the H group compared to the L group across motor‐related regions, indicating a globally strengthened motor network organization associated with better motor function. Functional connectivity revealed convergent but distinct patterns. In the delta band (1–3 Hz), ipsilesional motor regions showed stronger connectivity in the H group. In the beta band (14–29 Hz), contralesional motor regions demonstrated enhanced connectivity in H patients, consistent with prior evidence that contralesional motor regions may contribute to motor function after ipsilesional injury. We also introduced a novel metric, motor betweenness centrality, to quantify the role of nonmotor regions in rerouting motor‐related communication. Almost all new hubs identified structurally were associated with lower motor status, suggesting less efficient network organization in more impaired patients. Thus, preservation of direct motor pathways supports better motor status, while reliance on alternative, less efficient routes correlates with worse outcomes. By contrast, EEG routing revealed that H patients recruited proximal cortical hubs, while L patients relied on distant, inefficient ones, highlighting functional network organization not evident in the structural analysis. These patterns suggest that more local network organization, rather than more distributed rerouting, is associated with better motor status within the motor system. In summary, multimodal network properties reliably identified key motor ROIs predictive of motor status. This concordance suggests that EEG‐based metrics, particularly delta‐ and beta‐band connectivity, are associated with lesion‐derived structural disruption and complementary features of motor‐network organization. Structural connectivity damage within motor circuits defines the extent of network disruption associated with motor impairment, while EEG functional connectivity provides complementary information about network organization measured at the time of assessment. Together, these measures characterize different aspects of motor network integrity after stroke.

Article.Title: Chronic Mild Stress in Male Wistar‐Kyoto Rats Induces Long‐Term Hippocampal Plasticity Impairments Differentially Reversed by Acute and Chronic Ketamine Treatment
Article.Authors: Loizeau V.; Jesic M.; Kuster R.; Hugel S.; Barbelivien A.; Lecourtier L.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Chronic stress induces strong alteration of hippocampal synaptic plasticity, impairing long‐term potentiation and facilitating long‐term depression, processes thought to be involved in the pathophysiology of depression. Ketamine, a noncompetitive antagonist of the N ‐methyl‐D‐aspartate receptor, has emerged as a fast‐acting antidepressant whose action is believed to involve restoring impaired plasticity, though its sustained effects are elusive. Here, we investigated how chronic mild stress and subsequent acute and chronic ketamine treatments modulate synaptic plasticity in the Schaffer collateral pathway in the dorsal hippocampus of stress‐vulnerable Wistar‐Kyoto rats. Adult male rats were subjected to 4 weeks of chronic mild stress and vulnerability was determined through behavioral performance in the forced swim and elevated plus maze tests. Stress‐vulnerable rats received saline or either an acute or chronic subanesthetic dose of ketamine (10 mg/kg), and hippocampal slices were harvested for synaptic plasticity investigation. Conversely to what occurred in nonstressed rats, in stress‐vulnerable rats treated with saline, neither long‐term potentiation (LTP) nor long‐term depression (LTD) could be induced following high‐frequency and low‐frequency stimulation, respectively. Acute ketamine restored normal LTP but not LTD, while chronic ketamine restored LTD but not LTP. These findings highlight complex temporal dynamics in the modulation of hippocampal synaptic plasticity by ketamine following chronic stress and demonstrate that acute and chronic treatment regimens differentially affect the induction of LTP and LTD.

Article.Title: Glycogen Synthase Kinase‐3β as a Central Regulator of Alzheimer's Disease: Mechanistic Insights and Therapeutic Perspectives
Article.Authors: Kifayat S.; Kifayat W.; Chauhan S.; Zehra A.; Kaushik R.; Najmi A.; Parvez S.; Ali J.; Akhtar M.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurological condition marked by cognitive decline, memory impairment, extracellular amyloid‐β (Aβ) accumulation, and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs). Among the multiple molecular pathways involved in AD pathogenesis, glycogen synthase kinase‐3β (GSK‐3β) has emerged as a crucial signaling regulator due to its extensive contribution to neuronal survival, synaptic plasticity, metabolism, and cellular stress responses. Growing evidence suggests that abnormal activation of GSK‐3β contributes not merely to classical AD hallmarks, including tau hyperphosphorylation and amyloidogenesis, but is also linked to mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, autophagic impairment, ferroptosis, insulin resistance, and oxidative stress through modulation of the Nrf2 pathway. These findings place GSK‐3β as a crucial molecular hub linking different pathogenic pathways in AD. This review outlines the structural attributes along with regulatory mechanisms of GSK‐3β and extensively explores its involvement in AD pathophysiology. Specific emphasis is given to evolving mechanisms, such as metabolic dysregulation, ferroptosis, and antioxidant signaling pathways. Additionally, current breakthroughs in therapeutic targeting techniques such as ATP‐competitive inhibitors, non–ATP‐competitive inhibitors, allosteric modulators, natural chemicals, and clinically studied medicines are emphasized. The translational difficulties linked to selectivity, blood–brain barrier permeability, and clinical efficacies are also explored. Collectively, this review reinforces the therapeutic relevance of GSK‐3β and indicates potential opportunities for creating effective disease‐modifying therapies in AD.

Article.Title: Opioid Modulation of Major Neurotransmitter Systems: Acute, Chronic, and Withdrawal Effects
Article.Authors: Novakova D.; Pritulova E.; Novotny J.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Opioids are widely used in clinical practice for the management of moderate‐to‐severe acute and chronic pain. However, their use is associated with the development of tolerance and physical dependence, often followed by a withdrawal syndrome upon discontinuation. The mechanisms underlying opioid dependence and withdrawal are highly complex and remain incompletely understood. These processes involve multiple regions of the central nervous system and are accompanied by widespread alterations in neuronal signaling pathways. Neurotransmitters, which are essential for communication between neurons, play a critical role in opioid addiction and withdrawal. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of the major neurotransmitter systems, their involvement, and the changes that occur during acute and chronic opioid exposure. Particular attention is also given to the consequences of opioid discontinuation. Overall, this review summarizes current knowledge of the molecular mechanisms underlying both the acute and long‐term effects of opioids on key neurotransmitter systems in the brain.

Article.Title: Integrative Evolutionary and Structural Analysis of GBA1 Provides Insights Into Mutation‐Specific Effects Associated With Parkinson's Disease
Article.Authors: Mustafa S.; Abbasi A.; Mughal K.; Batool F.; Malik M.; Khalid R.; Abbasi A.; Bao Y.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT GBA1 encodes lysosomal acid β‐glucosidase (glucocerebrosidase [GCase]), a key lysosomal enzyme and one of the most important genetic factors in Parkinson's disease (PD). Yet how different GBA1 variants influence PD‐related molecular pathology remains incompletely understood. Here, we integrated phylogenetic, comparative sequence, structural, docking, and molecular dynamics analyses to identify evolutionarily constrained features of GBA1 that may influence its interaction with α‐synuclein (SNCA) and thereby contribute to PD pathogenesis. Phylogenetic reconstruction indicated that GBA1 originated early in bilaterian evolution and was maintained as a single‐copy gene in the sampled taxa, consistent with strong functional constraint. Sequence‐based analyses across sarcopterygian lineages further supported pervasive purifying selection, especially within the TIM barrel catalytic domain. Comparative structural analyses highlighted a conformationally sensitive segment spanning Residues 379–389, which includes catalytic and neighboring residues and showed recurrent involvement in both mammalian evolution and PD‐associated mutant proteins. Docking and molecular dynamics simulations of wild‐type and mutant GBA1–SNCA complexes indicated that PD‐associated substitutions can remodel hydrogen‐bond networks and influence the conformational landscape of the GBA1–SNCA complex in a mutation‐specific manner. Although no statistically significant differences in global structural or energetic properties were detected, individual variants exhibited distinct patterns of conformational deviation, flexibility, and interaction dynamics relative to wild type. In particular, Residues 387–389 emerged as part of a structurally responsive region linked to altered GBA1–SNCA association. Together, these findings highlight candidate structural determinants for future experimental studies of GBA1‐associated neurodegeneration.

Article.Title: Inferior Frontal Gyrus Alterations in Freezing of Gait in Parkinson's Disease Without Evidence for Overall Hemispheric Lateralization: A Systematic Review and Activation Likelihood Estimation Meta‐Analysis
Article.Authors: Taniguchi S.; Deckmyn H.; Gilat M.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Freezing of gait (FOG) is one of the most debilitating motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease (PD). Prior studies have suggested a potential right‐hemispheric preference in the pathophysiology of FOG. Yet, there is limited evidence regarding which brain regions are most consistently associated with FOG and whether these alterations indeed show right‐hemispheric lateralization. We aimed to identify brain regions associated with FOG based on multimodal neuroimaging findings and to examine their hemispheric lateralization. A systematic review across multiple neuroimaging modalities was performed, followed by an activation likelihood estimation (ALE) coordinate‐based meta‐analysis to assess convergent brain alterations in PD patients with FOG (freezers) versus those without FOG (nonfreezers). Hemispheric lateralization was assessed using the distribution of reported stereotactic coordinates. The systematic review included 108 articles, of which 33 were included in the primary ALE meta‐analysis. We identified a significant convergent cluster in the right inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) pars opercularis/dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in PD freezers compared with nonfreezers. No evidence of overall hemispheric lateralization was observed based on the distribution of reported coordinates. Our findings identify the right IFG as a consistent neural correlate of FOG, potentially reflecting heightened frontal recruitment, with no clear evidence of hemispheric lateralization. The lack of further consistency in brain regions could reflect the known heterogeneity in the pathophysiology of FOG.

Article.Title: Differential Cellular Dynamics of Platelet‐Derived Growth Factor Receptor β Cells and Macrophages After Complete Spinal Cord Transection in Neonatal and Juvenile Rats
Article.Authors: Takiguchi M.; Tamaji R.; Funakoshi K.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Lesion morphology after complete spinal cord transection (CST) varies depending on the time of injury. Following CST, the stumps are connected by fibrous tissue in adult and juvenile rats, whereas they are connected by thin meningeal tissue in neonatal rats. Here, we compared the cellular dynamics after CST in neonatal and juvenile rats to investigate factors contributing to the morphologic differences between the two groups. The intensity of PDGFRβ‐positive structures associated with fibrotic scar formation at the lesion core was significantly higher in juvenile CST rats than in neonatal CST rats. In neonatal rats, the intensity gradually decreased, whereas in juvenile rats it peaked at 7 days and then decreased. Pro‐inflammatory CD11c‐positive macrophages were abundant in the lesion core 2 days after CST, then rapidly decreased in both neonatal and juvenile CST rats. Anti‐inflammatory CD163‐positive macrophages in the lesion core were significantly more abundant in neonatal CST rats than in juvenile CST rats and remained elevated until 14 days after CST. Neonatal CST rats exhibited less fibroblast accumulation and higher CD163‐positive macrophage density in the lesion core compared with juvenile CST rats. These differences may be associated with morphologic differences in the lesion core between the two groups. CD163‐positive macrophages in the neonatal CST rats may primarily promote meningeal remodeling rather than fibrous tissue proliferation leading to fibrous scar formation.

Article.Title: The Glial Firestorm: Targeting Ferroptotic Microglia–Astrocyte Crosstalk in Intracerebral Hemorrhage
Article.Authors: Guo P.; Chen H.; Li N.; Liu D.
Article.Abstract: ABSTRACT Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) causes substantial mortality and disability, with secondary injury extending beyond the initial hematoma. This narrative review examines the working hypothesis that ferroptotic microglia amplify a neurotoxic astrocyte response after ICH. In the iron‐rich hemorrhagic milieu, microglial iron loading and impaired antioxidant defenses favor lipid peroxidation, whereas inflammatory astrocyte states marked by LCN2, C3, and MMP3 contribute to barrier dysfunction and neuronal injury. Findings from ICH and related experimental models suggest that oxidized lipids, extracellular vesicles, and inflammatory mediators could connect these responses. Reactive astrocytes may then reinforce myeloid oxidative stress through altered iron handling, glutamate clearance, and complement signaling. Ferroptosis must be considered alongside apoptosis, necroptosis, and pyroptosis, and resident microglia share erythrophagocytic and iron‐handling functions with infiltrating monocytes/macrophages. These overlapping processes limit the attribution of mixed myeloid signals to a single lineage or death pathway. The proposed bidirectional circuit remains a framework for testing rather than an established sequence in ICH. Therapeutic interception could combine early control of iron‐dependent lipid injury with later astrocyte modulation through STAT3 or PPAR‐γ, provided that beneficial hematoma clearance is preserved. High‐resolution spatiotemporal mapping, lineage‐resolved experiments, and sex‐specific analyses are needed to identify the relevant cells and treatment windows. Targeting this glial interaction may complement neuroprotection, but its therapeutic value requires direct experimental and clinical validation.

Article.Title: Rimonabant reveals reward- and anxiety-related behavioral effects of N-arachidonoyl dopamine (N-ADA) in mice
Article.Authors: Colis-Arenas O.; Navarro-Montellano K.; López-Lariz C.; Romero-Guevara R.; Marichal-Cancino B.
Article.Abstract: The endovanilloid N-arachidonoyl dopamine (N-ADA) is a lipid mediator associated with nociception and inflammation, but its effects on reward and anxiety remain unclear. We examined the behavioral impact of subacute N-ADA pre-exposure on conditioned place preference (CPP) and anxiety-like behavior in the circular open-field test (COF), assessed both under basal conditions and after acute CB1 blockade/GPR55 modulation with rimonabant. Male BALB/c mice were pre-exposed for four days to either vehicle (10% ethanol) or N-ADA (0.1 mg/kg). A counterbalanced CPP protocol was then conducted over eight days. Place preference was assessed before and after rimonabant administration (0.1 mg/kg), and anxiety-like behavior was evaluated using the COF following rimonabant. N-ADA exposure alone did not significantly modify place preference compared to baseline (p > 0.05). However, following rimonabant administration, N-ADA-exposed mice displayed a significant increase in preference for the drug-paired compartment (p < 0.05) and increased anxiety-like behavior in the COF (p < 0.05). These findings indicate that prior exposure to N-ADA can influence reward- and anxiety-related behaviors specifically under conditions of CB1 blockade/GPR55 modulation. The results support the modulatory role of N-ADA on reward- and anxiety-related behaviors at the dose tested, indicating an interaction with endocannabinoid signaling (or other rimonabant-sensitive mechanisms).

Article.Title: Anterior insular cortex neurostimulation modulates sensory hypersensitivity and pain-related emotional behaviors in a rat model of chronic neuropathic pain
Article.Authors: Acunha R.; Medeiros P.; Machado H.; Sbragia L.; Coimbra N.; Maione S.; de Freitas R.
Article.Abstract: Background and aims: Chronic neuropathic pain (NP) is frequently accompanied by anxiety- and depression-like behaviors that contribute to functional impairment. The insular cortex plays a central role in pain processing and interoceptive regulation, with the anterior insular cortex (AIC) critically involved in integrating sensory inputs with emotional and behavioral responses. However, whether direct modulation of AIC activity can simultaneously regulate sensory hypersensitivity and pain-related emotional behaviors remains unclear. This study investigated the effects of electrical neurostimulation of the AIC (eAIC) on chronic NP and associated affective disturbances. Methods: Male Wistar rats were subjected to chronic constriction injury (CCI) of the sciatic nerve to induce NP or to a Sham procedure. Twenty-one days after surgery, an independent group of animals received a single session of eAIC neurostimulation delivered via stereotaxically implanted electrodes at low-frequency deep brain stimulation parameters (20 μA, 100 Hz, 15 s). Mechanical and cold allodynia, as well as anxiety- and depression-like behaviors, were subsequently evaluated using established behavioral paradigms. Results: The eAIC significantly attenuated mechanical and cold allodynia in CCI rats. In parallel, eAIC reduced anxiety-like and depression-like behaviors without altering general locomotor activity. These effects were selectively observed in neuropathic animals and were not detected in SHAM-operated controls. Conclusion: These findings demonstrate that AIC activity regulates both sensory hypersensitivity and pain-related emotional behaviors in chronic NP. By showing concurrent modulation of nociceptive and affective dimensions, this study provides physiological evidence supporting the AIC as a key cortical node linking pain processing to emotional behavior and underscoring its relevance for integrative neuromodulatory strategies.

Article.Title: Impact of testosterone on daily wheel running in female rats
Article.Authors: Craft R.; Morgan M.
Article.Abstract: Sex differences in daily activity have been attributed to the actions of gonadal steroid hormones. We tested this hypothesis by measuring the impact of male-typical levels of testosterone (T) on female rats' daily activity. Analyses were conducted on pooled data from three studies in which adult female Sprague-Dawley rats were implanted with blank or T-filled capsules (and adult males were implanted with blank capsules); home cage wheel running activity was measured 23 h/day before and for 3 weeks after capsule implantation. Approximately 75-80% of running occurred during the dark phase of the light-dark cycle in all groups, throughout the study. Before capsule implantation, the total number of wheel revolutions was significantly higher in females than males at the end of the light phase and during most of the dark phase; running speed and duration of daily running were higher in females compared to males. During the 3 weeks after capsule implantation, dark phase (and end-of-light phase) wheel revolutions, and average and maximum running speeds increased in all groups; however, T exposure blunted females' running increases during the second half of the dark phase, such that running during that period was similar to that of males by week 3. T also decreased the duration of females' active time, primarily by shifting offset of wheel running earlier, making it comparable to that in males. T non-significantly decreased females' running speeds. These results indicate that, within 3 weeks, T defeminizes females' daily activity in multiple ways. Thus, in addition to producing myriad physiological changes, male-typical levels of T also alter females' locomotor behavior.

Article.Title: Human milk oligosaccharide supplementation in post-weaning rats fed a high fat/sucrose diet affects glutamate receptor gene expression in the nucleus accumbens and amygdala
Article.Authors: Noye Tuplin E.; Fernandes T.; Lowry D.; Cho N.; Sales K.; Patterson R.; Reimer R.
Article.Abstract: The consumption of human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs), a key component of breast milk, during early life has been shown to have long-lasting impacts on metabolic processes, immune system function, and nervous system development. The long-term effects of early-life HMO supplementation on behaviours that are associated with metabolic processes, such as food preferences and food choices, and mental health conditions, such as anxiety and depression, are less clear. The present study examined the effects of post-weaning supplementation with two common HMOs, 2'-fucosyllactose (2'FL) and 3'sialyllactose (3'SL), on anxiety-like behavior, sucrose consumption, food preference, and glutamate receptor gene expression in adulthood in Sprague-Dawley rats. We also assessed whether HMO supplementation could attenuate any changes in glutamate receptor gene expression or behavior associated with a high-fat/sucrose (HFS) diet. The present study demonstrated that the effects of HMO supplementation are both sex and dose-dependent, with changes in glutamate receptor gene expression in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) representing the most prominent changes. Effects on sucrose intake were modest and sex-specific, with H/HFS females consuming less sucrose than H/AIN females on the first, but not second, day of testing. This effect was most evident in females that received the high-HMO diet before the HFS challenge and was accompanied by lower GluR1 and GluR2 gene expression in the NAc. Rats fed a HFS diet displayed a preference for palatable food, regardless of early HMO exposure, which may be the result of changes to incentive salience or "wanting" for palatable foods. The findings of this study show a potential link between early-life HMO supplementation, behaviour, and the expression of genes related to synaptic plasticity.

Article.Title: The impact of postweaning food texture on swallow function in the juvenile Ts65Dn mouse model of Down syndrome
Article.Authors: Singhal G.; Sitko J.; Fisher E.; Cullins M.; Connor N.; Glass T.
Article.Abstract: Background: Children with Down syndrome (DS) often show feeding and swallowing difficulties, including prolonged reliance on soft diets. The Ts65Dn mouse model mirrors oromotor challenges in DS, yet the impacts of extended postweaning periods of soft food conditions are not well understood. We examined whether a soft food condition from postnatal day (P)21-P34 alters oral motor behaviors, weight, swallow function, and hypoglossal nucleus BDNF expression in Ts65Dn vs. euploid controls, hypothesizing that soft food would impact these outcomes. Methods: Male and female Ts65Dn and euploid littermates were assigned to hard or soft food (HF, SF) from P21-P34. Daily body weight and water intake were recorded. Videofluoroscopic swallow studies (VFSS) measured swallow rate, inter-swallow interval (ISI), jaw excursion rate (JER), and jaw cycle swallow ratio. ProBDNF and mature BDNF were quantified in hypoglossal nucleus at P35. Water consumption was analyzed at the cage level, and BDNF outcomes were analyzed using generalized linear models. Data were analyzed using mixed effects and three-way ANOVA with Sidak post hoc correction (α = 0.05). Results: Ts65Dn weighed significantly less than euploid control at P21 and P34. Mice in all genotype groups licked significantly more water in the HF condition than in the SF condition. VFSS revealed a significant genotype effect on ISI, with higher ISI in Ts65Dn than euploid mice. A sex x food texture x genotype interaction was detected for JER, with female Ts65Dn HF mice showing lower JER than female euploid HF mice. None of the overall models for proBDNF, mature BDNF, or the mature BDNF/proBDNF ratio reached statistical significance, although predictor level associations were observed for sex with proBDNF and food condition with mature BDNF. Conclusions: Soft diets did not worsen genotype specific differences in VFSS measures. Predictor level BDNF findings were exploratory because the corresponding overall models were not statistically significant.

Article.Title: Appetite responses over 24 hours before and after 12-weeks of resistance exercise in older male adults: Secondary data analysis of a randomised trial
Article.Authors: Griffen C.; Renshaw D.; Hattersley J.; Weickert M.; Duncan M.; Broom D.
Article.Abstract: Background: Despite resistance exercise (RE) being a key component of landmark recommendations for weight control, there is still a paucity of data on the effects of RE on appetite. The aim of this study was to examine the effects of 12-weeks of RE on appetite. Methods: Thirty-three older men (age: 67 ± 4 years; BMI: 25.4 ± 2.4 kg/m2) were included in this secondary pooled data analysis of a 12-week randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, 4-arm parallel group trial. In the present analysis, RE (2x/week at 80% 1RM; n = 17) and no exercise (NE; continue habitual physical activity; n = 16) groups were pooled and compared to one another. Appetite profile was measured over 24 h inside a metabolic chamber at baseline and post 12-weeks using visual analogue scales (VAS). Area under the curve (AUC) was calculated using the trapezoidal method. Significance was set at p < 0.05. Results: No significant group-by-time (p ≥ 0.08) or group-by-time-by-time point (p ≥ 0.10) differences occurred between groups for VAS hunger, satiety, fullness, prospective food consumption, or composite appetite score. Similarly, no significant differences were observed for 24-h VAS AUC for hunger (p = 0.35), satiety (p = 0.58), fullness (p = 0.41), prospective food consumption (p = 0.21), or composite appetite score (p = 0.40). Discussion: The present study found no statistical effect on appetite following 12-weeks of RE in older adult males. RE should continue to be undertaken throughout the life course and be included as part of physical activity recommendations for optimal health in older adults due to the many physical, mental health and functional benefits.

Article.Title: Changes in food reward are associated with improvements in metabolic markers and eating behaviors after bariatric surgery
Article.Authors: Lachance A.; Toro V.; Legault M.; Gagnon P.; Pelletier M.; Biertho L.; Provencher V.; Iceta S.; Tchernof A.; Picard F.; Michaud A.
Article.Abstract: Background: Bariatric surgery improves metabolic health and eating behaviors. However, its impact on food reward, particularly liking and wanting, remains poorly understood. Objective: To characterize changes in explicit and implicit food reward following sleeve gastrectomy and to examine their associations with metabolic health and eating behaviors. Methods: Food reward was assessed before and 4 months after surgery using the Leeds Food Preference Questionnaire. Eating behaviors, assessed with the Three-Factor Eating Questionnaire, and glycemic and lipid profiles were measured at both time points. Linear mixed-effects models were used to assess changes in food reward and their associations with metabolic and behavioral outcomes. Lower implicit wanting for high-fat sweet foods was significantly associated with improvements in eating behaviors and insulin-like growth factor binding protein 2 (IGFBP-2), a marker of glucose metabolism. Exploratory mediation analyses showed that implicit wanting for high-fat sweet foods accounted for 16 to 18% of the association between IGFBP-2 and changes in eating behaviors. Conclusion: Sleeve gastrectomy is associated with reduced motivational drive for high-fat sweet foods, while hedonic appreciation remains stable. These findings suggest that post-surgical metabolic adaptations may improve the control of food intake, in part by modulating implicit motivation for high-fat sweet foods.

Article.Title: Estradiol attenuates cardiac apoptosis and modulates cardiovascular remodeling in ovariectomized female rats with 6-hydroxydopamine-induced parkinsonism
Article.Authors: de Campos B.; Borges F.; Ariza D.; de Jager L.; Reginato G.; Gonçalves A.; Martins Novais Padrão A.; Fonseca H.; Pinge-Filho P.; Crestani C.; Martins-Pinge M.
Article.Abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a chronic neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc) and reduced striatal dopamine concentrations. In addition to its characteristic motor manifestations, PD is associated with nonmotor complications, including cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction, orthostatic and postprandial hypotension, and blood pressure instability. The lower prevalence of PD in women has prompted investigation into the potential protective effects of female sex hormones. In this study, we evaluated cardiovascular function, autonomic modulation, cardiac and vascular morphology, and apoptosis in ovariectomized female rats with 6-OHDA-induced parkinsonism treated with estradiol. Wistar rats underwent bilateral ovariectomy and received estradiol (1 mg/kg) or almond oil as the vehicle for 13 consecutive days. Six days later, the animals underwent femoral artery catheterization, and mean arterial pressure (MAP) and heart rate (HR) were recorded after 24 h. The 6-OHDA lesion reduced striatal dopamine concentrations by more than 50%, confirming the induction of parkinsonism. No significant group differences were detected in MAP, HR, autonomic variability, or baroreflex sensitivity. However, parkinsonism reduced left ventricular wall thickness, increased apoptosis in both ventricles, and decreased cardiac and aortic collagen content. Estradiol increased left ventricular wall thickness and partially attenuated ventricular apoptosis and the parkinsonism-associated alteration in aortic elastin. These findings indicate that 6-OHDA-induced parkinsonism produces cardiac and aortic structural alterations that are not reflected in basal cardiovascular or autonomic measurements and, estradiol may modulate selected cardiac alterations. Although the underlying mechanisms and translational relevance require further investigation, our findings suggest potential clinical relevance for postmenopausal women with Parkinson's disease.

Article.Title: Probiotics attenuate AlCl₃-induced Alzheimer’s disease via gut–brain axis modulation and suppression of NF-κB/NLRP3 neuroinflammation
Article.Authors: Elfiky A.; Shahy E.; Mahmoud A.
Article.Abstract: Disruptions along the brain-gut-microbiota axis significantly contribute to Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis. This study evaluated the therapeutic potential of a multi-strain probiotic mixture in mitigating cognitive decline, neuroinflammation, and amyloid pathology in an AD rat model. In the present study, after induction of AD in rats by oral administration of AlCl3 (50 mg/kg) for 28 days, followed by oral treatment with a probiotic mixture (109 log CFU/ml) for 42 days. Behavioral assessments were conducted during the final week. Histological analysis revealed marked reductions in hippocampal β-amyloid deposition and substantial restoration of colonic mucosal barrier integrity. Blautia abundance was strongly negatively correlated with NF-κB expression. Mechanistically, probiotics suppressed neuroinflammation by down-regulating pro-inflammatory cascades TNF-α, NLRP3, IL-1β, and NF-κB activation. Furthermore, treatment suppressed amyloidogenic processing via decreased APP mRNA and enhanced Aβ clearance through upregulation of LRP1 and modulation of AGER. These findings provide integrative evidence that probiotics exert neuroprotective and immunomodulatory effects, supporting their translational potential as a preventive strategy against AD-related cognitive decline.

Article.Title: Functional involvement of HMGB1-related neuroinflammation in depression and its modulation by intermittent theta-burst stimulation(iTBS)
Article.Authors: Zhang Y.; Xin S.; Zhang K.; Zhang Y.; Wang L.; An C.
Article.Abstract: Purpose: Intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS) is widely used for its rapid antidepressant efficacy in clinical practice. However, its underlying neuroimmune mechanisms and objective biomarkers of treatment response remain largely unexplored. High mobility group box 1 (HMGB1), a critical driver of neuroimmune interactions in stress-related disorders, may link peripheral inflammation to central pathological processes in depression and may serve as a potential therapeutic target. Therefore, we aimed to explore the functional involvement of HMGB1 in depression and whether HMGB1-related inflammatory signaling is modulated by iTBS. Methods: We measured circulating HMGB1 levels in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD). In mice exposed to chronic restraint stress (CRS) or lipopolysaccharide (LPS), HMGB1/TLR4/NF-κB signaling and neuroinflammatory responses in the prefrontal cortex were assessed. Glycyrrhizic acid (GA), a well-established HMGB1 antagonist, was used to determine the functional relevance of HMGB1. iTBS-mediated antidepressant effects were assessed via behavioral tests and HMGB1-related inflammatory signaling analysis. Results: HMGB1 was markedly upregulated in patients and in depressive‑like mouse models, accompanied by activation of the HMGB1/TLR4/NF-κB signaling pathway and increased neuroinflammation. GA alleviated depressive-like behaviors. iTBS reversed behavioral deficits and suppressed HMGB1-associated inflammatory signaling. Conclusion: HMGB1 is functionally involved in depression, and the therapeutic effects of iTBS are associated with suppression of HMGB1-related neuroinflammatory signaling. These findings suggest that HMGB1 may have potential as a biomarker for monitoring the biological effects of iTBS, warranting further investigation into its role in treatment response.

Article.Authors: dos Santos I.; dos Santos H.; Ribeiro J.; Leite J.; de Abreu A.; Mendonça M.; da Silva E.; Colombari E.; Pedrino G.; Gomes R.; Fajemiroye J.; Lima P.; Perelló M.; Marques S.; Xavier C.

Article.Title: Distinct behavioral and electrophysiological correlates of sleep disturbance during verbal and spatial working memory tasks
Article.Authors: Wang P.; Xie C.; Chen Y.; Wang K.
Article.Abstract: Associations between sleep disturbance and working memory (WM) vary across tasks and outcome measures. This study examined behavioral and electrophysiological correlates of subjective sleep disturbance during verbal working memory (VWM) and spatial working memory (SWM) in university students. Sixty-one participants were classified using Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) scores into a sleep disturbance group (n = 28) and a normal sleep group (n = 33) and completed separate verbal and spatial 2-back tasks with event-related potential (ERP) recording. VWM false alarm rates (FAR) were also higher, although the absolute difference was small. Higher PSQI scores were associated with lower VWM ACC and d' and higher FAR. The sleep disturbance group showed lower VWM P3 amplitude averaged across the analyzed electrode sites and longer P3 peak latency at Oz. No significant group-related effects were detected for VWM median reaction time or N2 measures, or for SWM behavioral and ERP measures. These findings link subjective sleep disturbance to lower ACC and discrimination during verbal updating, accompanied by differences in later task-related electrophysiological processing. Future longitudinal and intervention studies with matched tasks and objective sleep measures could clarify the temporal and causal relationships underlying these associations.

Article.Title: Exploring the reconfiguration effects of physical fatigue on the gradient space of brain function based on EEG
Article.Authors: Yang G.; Chi P.; Zhao S.
Article.Abstract: Objective: This study examined how physical fatigue reorganizes the low-dimensional structure of EEG functional connectivity using three embedding approaches. Results: PCA showed increased beta-band G1 scores over the central scalp region and decreased scores over the occipital region, together with reduced alpha-band G3 over the central region. LE showed increased theta-band G3 over the central region. PCA displacement exhibited a significant frequency band × scalp region interaction, driven by greater alpha-band occipital displacement. Theta-band λ1-λ3 increased with PCA but decreased with DM, whereas LE showed no significant eigenvalue changes. The PCA-derived beta-band central ΔG1 was positively correlated with exhaustive exercise duration (r = 0.50, p = 0.004). Conclusions: Physical fatigue induces frequency-, region-, component-, and method-specific reorganization of the low-dimensional structure of scalp-level EEG functional connectivity. PCA was particularly sensitive to spatially differentiated gradient changes, while LE and DM captured complementary aspects of fatigue-related reorganization. The association between central beta-band ΔG1 and exercise duration further suggests potential behavioral relevance of gradient.

Article.Title: The effect of positive emotions on psychophysiological recovery and performance in athletes - investigating the undoing-hypothesis
Article.Authors: Zajonz P.; Sascha Leisterer-Härtig N/A.; Sylvain Laborde N/A.; Legerlotz K.; Wolfarth B.; Franziska Lautenbach N/A.
Article.Abstract: Athletes have to cope with psychosocial and physiological stressors, requiring recovery to ensure subsequent performance. According to the undoing-hypothesis, positive emotions (PE) may enhance psychophysiological recovery. The present two studies investigated the undoing hypothesis and its benefits for athletes' cognitive (Study 1; n = 60) and motor (Study 2; n = 30) performance. After a combined psychosocial-physiological stressor, participants either completed a five-minute PE induction (music; imagination exercise) or were assigned to a resting condition. Emotions, perceived stress-recovery, and physiological parameters (e.g., heart rate, heart rate variability, cortisol) were assessed. In Study 1, inhibition and cognitive flexibility were measured once. In Study 2, hand force and jump height were measured using a pre-posttest design. Due to the lack of psychological stress responses and successful PE induction, no conclusions could be drawn regarding the undoing hypothesis. Nevertheless, the present study provides valuable methodological insights into the challenges of testing the undoing hypothesis in athletes. These insights can inform the design and implementation of future studies and thereby contribute to advancing research on the undoing hypothesis in athletic populations.

Article.Title: Intermittent fasting as a therapeutic strategy in Alzheimer’s disease: Understanding of brain-derived neurotrophic factor modulation
Article.Authors: Shrirame D.; Tatode A.; Dabhade D.; Taksande J.; Taksande B.; Kakade O.; Umekar M.
Article.Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease with amyloid-beta (Aβ) plaques, tau tangles, neuroinflammation, and oxidative stress, and it causes cognitive impairment and neuronal loss. The pharmacological treatment is of limited effectiveness, therefore the interest in novel approaches such as intermittent fasting (IF). IF, a nutritional regimen of periodic caloric restriction, has shown a potential to modulate neurodegenerative alterations by metabolic and molecular mechanisms. This review presents the implications of IF in the etiopathogenesis of AD, specifically in controlling brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). BDNF is a major neurotrophin that plays a key role in synaptic plasticity, neuronal survival, and cognition. Evidence indicates that BDNF is drastically decreased in AD, therefore enhancing disease progression. IF enhances BDNF expression via mechanisms such as improved mitochondrial function, increased ketone body production, and reduced systemic inflammation. Preclinical studies indicate that IF not only upregulates BDNF but also alleviates key AD pathologies, including Aβ deposition and tau hyperphosphorylation. Additionally, clinical data highlight the cognitive benefits of IF and its role in modulating metabolic health, although studies specifically linking IF, BDNF and AD in humans remain limited. This review underscores the need for further research to determine optimal IF protocols and clarify its long-term impact on AD progression. IF's ability to modulate BDNF and other neuroprotective pathways positions it as a promising non-pharmacological intervention for AD management. By bridging metabolic health and neuroprotection, IF offers potential therapeutic synergy for mitigating AD's complex etiopathogenesis.

Article.Title: Openness to experience modulates the neural dynamics of semantic processing
Article.Authors: Li B.; Huang C.; Lin Q.; Huang H.
Article.Abstract: Personality fundamentally shapes language processing, yet the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying this relationship remain poorly understood. Openness to experience (Openness), as measured by the NEO Five-Factor Inventory (NEO-FFI), has been associated with enhanced creativity and engagement with novel semantic information. This study examined how openness modulates the neural dynamics of semantic processing using event-related potentials (ERPs) during a semantic category verification task. Participants evaluated category relatedness across the four levels of semantic structure, including high typicality (HT), low typicality (LT), related violations (RV), and nonrelated violations (NRV). Neural responses exhibited the expected graded pattern, with N400 amplitudes becoming more negative as semantic relatedness decreased. Critically, higher Openness was associated with greater N400 differentiation between related and nonrelated violations, an effect uniquely predicted by Openness beyond the remaining four personality traits. Follow-up analyses revealed that this differentiation was primarily driven by enhanced N400 responses to nonrelated violations rather than by reduced responses to related violations. This pattern is inconsistent with a simple facilitation account in which higher Openness uniformly eases semantic processing. Instead, it suggests that Openness is associated with heightened sensitivity to semantic mismatch or more sustained semantic evaluation when incoming information is incompatible with an activated context. Behavioral performance was comparable across participants; the observed neural differences were not accompanied by detectable differences in task success. Together, these findings establish that Openness is systematically related to variation in the neural dynamics of semantic processing, while highlighting the need to clarify the underlying cognitive mechanisms and contributions of other individual differences.

Article.Title: The effect of concurrent application of the deep brain stimulation of the nucleus accumbens and cannabidiol injection during extinction period on reinstatement of METH-induced conditioned place preference in extinguished rats
Article.Authors: Mohammadi M.; Zendehdel M.; Haghparast A.
Article.Abstract: Methamphetamine (METH) is a potent stimulant drug that significantly alters the function of the central nervous system (CNS). METHS's abuse may be linked with a variety of psychiatric disorders, primarily by affecting the reward system. Cannabidiol (CBD), a primary cannabinoid component of the Cannabis plant, has been shown to affect the reward system, suggesting it for modulating addictive behaviors. On the other hand, deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the nucleus accumbens (NAc), one of the most significant brain regions implicated in mediating rewards, is effective in alleviating drug-seeking behaviors. The present research aimed to evaluate the effects of low-frequency DBS, CBD, and a combination of both on the extinction and reinstatement of METH-induced conditioned place preference (CPP). CBD was injected into the lateral ventricle at doses of 2.5, 5, and 10 μg/5 μL, and low-frequency DBS (10 Hz, for 30 min) was administered to the NAc, both during the extinction phase. The results showed CBD (10 µg/5 µL) or DBS facilitated extinction. DBS decreased mean extinction latency but did not differ significantly from CBD (10 µg/5 µL) alone. The combination groups at all tested CBD doses showed reduced mean extinction latency compared with the control groups; only the 10 µg/5 µL combination group differed significantly from DBS alone. However, neither CBD (10 µg/5 µL) alone nor DBS altered the CPP score on the reinstatement day. Combination of DBS and CBD administration (at all doses) significantly decreased the CPP score on the reinstatement day. In conclusion, it can be suggested that CBD may be beneficial for alleviating METH-induced reinstatement in combination with DBS, while both alone had no effect.

Notably, this early-life central reward transcriptional suppression persisted into adulthood in males but not in females. Our results indicate that maternal HF diet and MT treatment influence HF diet and low-concentration sucrose preferences in adult offspring in a sex-specific manner, which may be associated with altered gene expression in the central reward system and the peripheral taste perception pathways.

Article.Abstract: Anorexia nervosa (AN) is characterized by marked metabolic, behavioral, and neurobiological alterations. Although neuroinflammation and microglial activation have been suggested to contribute to its pathophysiology, preclinical evidence remains inconsistent and appears to depend on the experimental conditions and brain regions examined. Here, we asked whether the two core components of the activity-based anorexia (ABA) paradigm, food restriction and voluntary hyperactivity, are associated with distinct regional patterns of Iba1 immunoreactivity across neural circuits involved in energy balance, cognition, and reward, and whether these alterations relate to the behavioral and metabolic severity of the model. Using the ABA rat model, we quantified the percentage of Iba1-positive area in the prefrontal cortex, dorsal and ventral hippocampus, anterior cingulate cortex, nucleus accumbens, caudate putamen, amygdala, and the arcuate and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus. ABA animals displayed an overall reduction in Iba1 immunoreactivity, with significant decreases in the hippocampus and paraventricular nucleus. Conversely, food restriction alone increased Iba1 coverage in the arcuate nucleus, whereas voluntary physical activity selectively enhanced Iba1 immunoreactivity in reward-related areas, particularly the nucleus accumbens. These findings indicate that starvation and hyperactivity induce distinct, region-specific changes in Iba1 immunoreactive coverage, potentially reflecting alterations in microglial responses that may differentially affect hypothalamic, cognitive, and reward-related circuits implicated in AN pathophysiology.

Article.Title: Gene-environment interaction in transgenic rats overexpressing human DISC1: effects of early social isolation on behavioral domains
Article.Authors: Pedroso-Fidelis G.; Avila F.; Nani J.; Porta L.; Bertagna N.; Rodolpho B.; Lee R.; Cruz F.; Hayashi M.
Article.Abstract: Early-life social isolation (SI) is a well-established environmental stressor associated with persistent behavioral alterations relevant to psychiatric disorders. Whether SI interacts with neurodevelopmental brain abnormalities to modify behavioral vulnerability remains unclear. We investigated the effects of post-weaning SI in transgenic rats overexpressing full-length human Disrupted-in-Schizophrenia 1 (tgDISC1), a model characterized by DISC1 protein aggregation, impaired dopamine homeostasis, and abnormal neuronal migration. Male wild-type (WT) and tgDISC1 rats were housed individually or in groups from postnatal day 21 for 28 consecutive days and evaluated using behavioral tests assessing stress-coping, self-care, locomotor activity, anxiety-like behavior, contextual fear memory, and social behavior. SI reduced grooming behavior, shortened the latency to the first immobility episode in the forced swim test, and decreased contextual freezing regardless of genotype, whereas locomotor activity and anxiety-like behavior were unaffected. Genotype-dependent differences were observed in anxiety-related measures, showing distinct performances in the Open Field and Elevated Plus Maze tests. In the social interaction test, SI selectively altered social preference, revealing a significant gene × environment interaction, indicating that neurodevelopmental brain abnormalities specifically modulated the effects of early-life SI on social behavior. Together, these findings demonstrate that early-life SI induces selective behavioral alterations, whereas DISC1-related dysfunction selectively influences the behavioral consequences of SI in the social domain rather than conferring generalized vulnerability. These results highlight the value of multidomain behavioral phenotyping in gene × environment models and identify social behavior as a sensitive marker of DISC1-related susceptibility to early-life stress, with implications for the developmental origins of psychiatric disorders.

Article.Title: Leuprolide acetate, a GnRH agonist, preserves cerebellar integrity and motor coordination in a rat model of hepatic encephalopathy
Article.Authors: Gutiérrez-Esparza B.; González-Torres M.; Quintanar-Stephano A.; Calderón-Vallejo D.; Martínez-Saldaña M.; Murillo-Sánchez M.; Quintanar J.
Article.Abstract: Patients with hepatic encephalopathy (HE) experience both cognitive and motor coordination alterations, which lead to a decrease in quality of life. During the progression of this disease, the cerebellum is one of the most affected brain regions due to elevated blood ammonia levels that cause neuronal damage and contribute to motor dysfunction. Leuprolide acetate (LA), a gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) receptor agonist, has demonstrated neurotrophic effects in various regions of the central nervous system. Therefore, this study evaluated the potential neurotrophic effect of LA on the cerebellum in a rat model of HE induced by portocaval anastomosis (PCA). For the experimental design, male Wistar rats were divided into three groups: SHAM, PCA with saline solution (PCA+SS), and PCA treated with LA (PCA+LA). Motor function was assessed using rotarod and open field tests. Histological assessment of the cerebellum was performed using H&E staining, while immunoreactivity of the apoptotic markers caspase-8 and caspase-3 were analyzed to evaluate apoptosis. In addition, the expression of proteins associated with neuronal integrity and recovery, including NF200, neurabin II, and BDNF, were examined. The results showed that LA administration significantly improved motor coordination. Treated animals exhibited reduced neuronal loss in the Purkinje and granular layers, decreased activation of caspase-8 and caspase-3, and increased expression of neurabin II and BDNF. Collectively, these findings indicate that LA has therapeutic potential to attenuate cerebellar neuronal damage and promote functional recovery during HE.

Article.Title: Reduced locomotor activity in juvenile ICR and BALB/c mice exposed to early-life sleep restriction
Article.Authors: Ueno H.; Arai R.; Tanaka Y.; Kitano E.; Takahashi Y.; Mori S.; Murakami S.; Wani K.; Matsumoto Y.; Okamoto M.; Ishihara T.
Article.Abstract: Sleep during early life is essential for normal brain development, and its disruption is implicated as a risk factor for later behavioral abnormalities. We previously reported that chronic postnatal sleep restriction in C57BL/6N mice impairs parvalbumin interneuron development and produces anxiety-like behavior and persistent reductions in locomotor activity into adulthood. Whether these behavioral consequences extend to other genetic backgrounds remains unclear. Here, male ICR (outbred) and BALB/c (inbred) mice underwent daily sleep restriction by gentle handling from postnatal day 8 to 21, and body weight, open-field behavior, and social interaction were assessed thereafter; body weight and open-field behavior were reassessed at 8 weeks of age following return to standard housing. During the juvenile period, sleep restriction reduced total distance traveled in the open field in both strains, without a significant strain × treatment interaction. Significant interactions were found for body weight and time in the central area, both of which were altered in ICR but not in BALB/c mice. In the social interaction test, sleep restriction reduced locomotion and the number of contacts in both strains. At 8 weeks of age, the reduction in total distance traveled remained detectable across strains, and no other measure was affected. BALB/c mice differed from ICR mice in most measures irrespective of treatment. These findings indicate that early-life sleep restriction reduces locomotor activity in both strains, whereas its effects on body weight and central-area exploration were strain-specific. Because sleep was not directly measured and restriction relied on gentle handling, contributions of handling stress cannot be excluded.
