Article.Title: Automated Proofreading of Digitally Reconstructed Neural Morphology Enhances Accuracy, Scalability, and Standardization
Article.Authors: Emissah H.; Tecuatl C.; Ascoli G.
Article.Abstract: Background: The rapid expansion of large-scale neuroscience datasets has increased the need for automated, accurate, and standardized quality control (QC). Manual proofreading of 3-dimensional neural morphology (SWC files) remains labor-intensive, error-prone, and non-scalable. We developed and evaluated a fully automated, machine-learning–driven QC pipeline to standardize neural reconstructions, detect and correct structural anomalies, and rectify dendritic labeling in pyramidal neurons. Methods: We developed an end-to-end, cloud-deployed pipeline for automated QC, correction, and standardization of SWC-formatted neural morphologies. The framework integrates deterministic structural normalization, topology repair, geometric correction, quantitative morphometric analysis, and graph-based dendritic relabeling within a containerized React/Flask architecture deployed on Amazon Web Services. Rule-based algorithms systematically detect, classify, and correct structural irregularities including overlapping nodes, spurious side branches, non-positive radii, disconnected components, and anomalously long parent-child connections. A graph convolutional network, trained on Sholl-derived features from 20,500 pyramidal neurons, performs dendritic relabeling. Model training employed an 80/10/10 train–validation–test split with adaptive learning-rate scheduling and distributed execution across ten runs to evaluate stability and reproducibility. The pipeline generates images of the final product and computes quantitative morphometrics using L-Measure. Results: All neural reconstructions were processed without manual intervention. Automated normalization and topology repair improved structural consistency and standardized neuronal morphologies for quantitative analysis and visualization while preserving topological and morphological continuity throughout the correction process. Dendritic relabeling achieved a test classification accuracy of 99.51%, calculated from 2040 correctly classified neurons out of 2050 test neurons (2040/2050 × 100 = 99.51%). The test dataset comprised a separate 10% partition of the 20,500-neuron dataset, resulting from the 80/10/10 training–validation–test split, with no overlap between the three subsets. The mean validation accuracy across ten training runs also reached 99.51% at the final epoch, with class-weighted precision of 0.978 and recall of 0.977. Validation accuracy increased rapidly during the initial epochs, exhibited a transient decrease at epoch 15 and subsequently recovered and stabilized by epoch 50. Enforcing a single apical dendritic tree per neuron improved anatomical consistency without reducing classification performance. Distributed training completed all runs in approximately 25 hours, demonstrating scalability and reproducibility for large datasets. Conclusions: We present an automated, cloud-scalable open-source pipeline for standardizing neural reconstructions and performing biologically consistent dendritic classification with high accuracy. The automated correction and relabeling procedures do not alter or compromise the size or unaffected morphological detail of the original SWC files, ensuring geometric fidelity and compatibility with downstream analysis tools. This open-access framework provides a robust foundation for high-throughput neural morphology curation and large-scale neuroanatomical analysis.

Article.Title: Resting-State EEG Graph Analysis Reveals Enhanced Alpha-Band Integration in High-IQ Individuals: The MENSA-Connect Project
Article.Authors: Moci M.; Zauli A.; Iacovelli C.; Reale G.; Garbuglia M.; Cacciatore E.; De Grandis M.; Tomaino A.; Rossi S.; Caliandro P.
Article.Abstract: Background: To assess whether resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) connectivity differs between high-intelligence individuals (MENSA members) and controls using graph-theory metrics: clustering coefficient, characteristic path length, and small-worldness. Methods: Resting-state 64-channel EEG data were recorded in 29 MENSA participants and 20 controls. Functional connectivity was estimated using Lagged Linear Coherence across delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands. Graph-theory measures were computed using sLORETA and the Brain Connectivity Toolbox. Between-group comparisons were performed using the Mann–Whitney U test; p-values were corrected for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure, and effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals were calculated. Results: Compared with controls, MENSA participants showed significantly lower characteristic path length in the alpha band (Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) critical value = 0.004), indicating greater global network integration. In the beta band, they showed a higher clustering coefficient (BH critical value = 0.008), reflecting greater local specialization; together with a higher characteristic path length (BH critical value = 0.013), suggesting reduced global communication. No significant group differences were observed in small-worldness across frequency bands. Conclusions: High-Intelligence Quotient (IQ) individuals show a frequency-dependent resting-state cortical organization, characterized by enhanced alpha-band integration and increased beta-band local specialization. These findings support a nuanced neural-efficiency model of intelligence without changes in small-world architecture. Given the cross-sectional and observational design, these findings should be regarded as associative rather than causal and require replication in larger, independent samples. These findings indicate frequency-specific differences in functional network organization, although their cognitive implications remain to be established.

Article.Title: The Glymphatic System: From Basic Research Advances to Non-Invasive Brain Stimulation Applications-A Narrative Review
Article.Authors: Jiang Z.; Yue W.; Zhang Y.; Yu S.; Wang H.; Luo T.
Article.Abstract: The glymphatic system (GS) is a pathway for waste clearance in the brain and a promising therapeutic target for neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and Parkinson’s disease (PD). GS function is governed by multiple interacting factors, such as aquaporin-4 (AQP4) polarization, cerebral arterial pulsatility, and the integrity of meningeal lymphatic vessels (MLVs). Despite growing recognition of the importance of the GS, effective strategies to actively and non-invasively enhance glymphatic function have long been lacking. In recent years, non-invasive neuromodulatory approaches—most notably focused ultrasound (FUS), repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), and transcranial photobiomodulation (tPBM)—have emerged as novel strategies to modulate GS activity. Growing evidence suggests that these interventions can enhance glymphatic transport by influencing key regulatory mechanisms, including cerebrovascular dynamics, AQP4 expression and localization, and meningeal lymphatic drainage. In this review, we summarize current experimental advances in non-invasive, external alterations of the GS, discuss underlying mechanisms and translational challenges, and highlight the therapeutic potential of GS modulation in neurological diseases characterized by impaired waste clearance. However, further research about the function and dysfunction of the GS in humans is needed to evaluate the findings from animal studies and thereby fill the translational gap in the human pathophysiology of the GS.

Article.Title: Epigenetic Gene-Environment Interactions in Parkinson’s Disease
Article.Authors: Zhang K.; Chen G.; Jia J.; Zeng X.
Article.Abstract: Background: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder, characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra. While genetic mutations and environmental exposures have both been established as risk factors for PD, emerging evidence has implicated epigenetic modifications as key mediators of gene-environment interactions involved in the pathogenesis of PD. Objective: This review aims to systematically characterize the epigenetic regulatory mechanisms that bridge the effects of environmental neurotoxicants and genetic susceptibility in PD, providing a comprehensive synthesis of the current understanding of their functional crosstalk at a molecular level. Key Findings: Environmental factors drive the pathogenesis of PD through abnormal DNA methylation, dynamic imbalances in histone modification, and non-coding RNA regulatory networks. Here, we detail the mechanisms by which environment-induced epigenetic shifts give rise to the dysregulation of key PD-associated genes, including SNCA, PRKN (PARK2), PARK7 (DJ-1), and LRRK2. This epigenetic dysregulation subsequently exacerbates downstream pathological events, such as mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired autophagy, endoplasmic reticulum stress, and neuroinflammation. Conclusion: Systematically exploring epigenetic gene-environment interactions offers detailed insight into the etiology of PD. Given the potential reversibility of specific epigenetic modifications, targeting these pathways may offer a prospective avenue for neuroprotective research. However, further rigorous investigation remains essential to evaluate the clinical viability of these mechanisms as reliable biomarkers or therapeutic targets.

Article.Title: Neural Mechanisms of Smartphone Addiction: A Systematic Review of Neuroimaging and Related Neurophysiological/Neurostimulation Studies
Article.Authors: Liu H.; Li T.; Hu R.; Yang P.; Lei Y.; Liu X.
Article.Abstract: Background: The rapid integration of smartphones into daily life has undeniably brought immense convenience, but it has also introduced challenges, particularly in the form of problematic smartphone use (often referred to as smartphone addiction). This form of behavioral dependence has been linked to significant impairments in physiological, psychological, and social domains. Methods: In this systematic review, we investigated the neural underpinnings of smartphone addiction through various brain imaging techniques, with a particular emphasis on studies employing functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), electroencephalography (EEG), functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and complementary neurostimulation as well as neurophysiological methods. Relevant data were retrieved from major academic databases—including CNKI, PubMed, and Web of Science—using a thorough keyword-based search strategy. A total of 41 studies were analyzed and categorized according to their research methods, participant characteristics, targeted populations, and key findings. Results: We identified a consistent association between smartphone addiction and alterations in brain structure and activity, as well as its co-occurrence with a range of mental health challenges. Conclusion: These findings collectively underscore the pressing need for further research into the neurobiological mechanisms of smartphone addiction and the development of targeted interventions to mitigate its adverse effects. Article.Title: Effects of Transcranial Ultrasound Stimulation on Neural Electrical Activity in the Paraventricular Thalamus of Rats Under Etomidate Anesthesia
Article.Authors: Zhao L.; Yuan Y.; Cui G.; Chi C.; Qin M.; Liu Z.
Article.Abstract: Background: Transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) has been shown to modulate recovery from propofol anesthesia. Etomidate is also widely used as an anesthetic in clinical practice. Therefore, further investigation is needed to clarify whether TUS modulates thalamic neural electrical activity under etomidate anesthesia. Methods: In this study, we applied TUS to the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus (PVT) in etomidate-anesthetized rats. Local field potentials (LFPs) from the PVT and electromyography (EMG) signals from cervical muscles were recorded to analyze anesthesia recovery time, time-frequency characteristics, power spectral density, and sample entropy (SampEn). Results: The recovery time from anesthesia was significantly shorter in the TUS group than in the sham group. TUS also induced significant changes in LFPs metrics during emergence, including: a significant decrease in mean absolute power (MAP) in the 4–8 Hz band and increases in the 30–60 Hz, 60–100 Hz, 100–140 Hz, and 140–200 Hz bands; a reduction in relative power (RP) in the 4–8 Hz band and elevations in the 30–60 Hz and 60–100 Hz bands; and a significant increase in SampEn across the 1–200 Hz frequency spectrum. Conclusion: TUS effectively modulated the relative power, mean absolute power, and SampEn of LFPs during the transition from anesthetized to awake states in etomidate-anesthetized rats.

Article.Title: AIM2 Promotes Neuronal Apoptosis Through NF-κB Activation in an OxyHb-Induced In Vitro Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
Article.Authors: Ji H.; Mao T.; Chen Y.; Jin Z.; Yan T.; Jin H.
Article.Abstract: Background: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) induces early brain injury (EBI) characterized by neuronal apoptosis, inflammation, and neurological dysfunction, yet the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Although absent in melanoma 2 (AIM2) has been implicated in post-SAH pathology, its role in neuronal injury remains unclear. Methods: Transcriptomic analyses of Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) datasets (GSE36791 and GSE73378) were performed to investigate the association between AIM2 and nuclear factor κB (NF-κB)-related signaling. An oxyhemoglobin (OxyHb)-induced in vitro SAH model, Aim2 knockdown, and Rela co-silencing experiments were used to evaluate neuronal apoptosis, viability, and NF-κB activation. In vivo validation was performed in SAH brain tissues. Results: Transcriptomic analyses showed a positive association between AIM2 expression and NF-κB signaling. In OxyHb-treated neurons, AIM2 expression and p65 phosphorylation were increased, accompanied by enhanced neuronal apoptosis and reduced viability. Aim2 knockdown attenuated NF-κB activation, reduced neuronal apoptosis, and improved cell viability, whereas co-silencing of Aim2 and Rela exerted stronger neuroprotective effects. Aim2 silencing showed limited effects on pyroptosis-related responses, and in vivo analyses further supported a positive association between AIM2 expression and NF-κB activation after SAH. Conclusions: AIM2 contributes to OxyHb-induced neuronal apoptosis, at least in part, through NF-κB signaling. These findings provide new insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying EBI after SAH.

Article.Title: Smad4 Regulates the Developmental Coordination of Cortical Neurons via the CXCL12-CXCR4 Axis
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Zhang Y.; Li Y.; Han W.; Shan B.; Wang Y.; Chen B.; Guo R.
Article.Abstract: Background: The functional assembly of neural circuits during cortical development relies on the precise spatiotemporal coordination of excitatory projection neurons and inhibitory interneurons. Here, we show that SMAD family member 4 (SMAD4) is required for this developmental coordination. Methods: We performed conditional deletion of Smad4 in pallial progenitors and evaluated the spatial distribution and number of Glutamic acid decarboxylase 67-green fluorescent protein positive (Gad67-GFP+) interneurons in the embryonic and adult cortex. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was utilized to assess transcriptomic changes in the Smad4-deficient cortex. Further in vivo expression validation and functional assessments were conducted using a C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 12 (Cxcl12)-Discosoma red fluorescent protein (DsRed) reporter line and Cxcl12 loss-of-function mutants, respectively. Results: Conditional deletion of Smad4 in pallial progenitors disrupts the spatial distribution and overall number of Gad67-GFP+ interneurons in both the embryonic and adult cortex. scRNA-seq revealed a marked reduction in Cxcl12 expression within the mutant cortex, while its receptor, C-X-C chemokine receptor type 4 (Cxcr4), remained normally expressed in interneurons. We confirmed this downregulation in vivo using the Cxcl12-DsRed reporter line. Functionally, Cxcl12 loss-of-function mutants phenocopy the interneuron migration deficits seen in Smad4 mutants. Conclusions: Our results uncover a projection neuron-derived SMAD4-CXCL12 signaling cascade that regulates CXCR4-dependent interneuron migration, providing a molecular basis for the cross-talk between these two distinct neuronal lineages.

Article.Title: Enkephalin Treatment Reduces Elevated Brain Glia in Mice With Experimental Autoimmune Encephalomyelitis
Article.Authors: Kumari R.; Zagon I.; McLaughlin P.
Article.Abstract: Background: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic, autoimmune disorder that culminates in severe motor and cognitive deficits. The progression of the disease is associated with inflammation and demyelination of the brain and spinal cord. Activation and proliferation of glia, including astrocytes and oligodendrocytes, in the brain are hallmarks. Persons with MS (PwMS) have significantly low levels of the neuropeptide [Met5]-enkephalin (Met5-Enk), also termed Opioid Growth Factor (OGF) that is an inhibitory growth factor and modulates cellular homeostasis. Treatment with low doses of naltrexone, an opioid antagonist that blocks the receptor OGFr, is reported to decrease inflammation, neutralize pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion, and stabilize disease progression. Intermittent blockade of OGFr with low doses of naltrexone stimulates serum enkephalin levels. In this investigation, brains of mice with experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) were treated with low dose naltrexone (LDN) or OGF/Met-Enk and examined for reactive astrocytes and oligodendrocytes. Methods: Female C57BL/6J mice were inoculated with myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG35–55) to induce EAE. At the initial appearance of clinical behavioral symptoms, mice were randomized to receive 10 mg/kg [Met5]-enkephalin (OGF/Met-Enk), 0.1 mg/kg naltrexone (LDN), or 0.1 mL phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) daily. At 35 days post EAE induction, mice were euthanized, and the brains were removed and prepared for immunohistochemistry. The corpus callosum, subventricular zone, and dentate gyrus were stained with glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and adenomatous polyposis coli protein (APC) antibodies to detect astrocytes and oligodendrocytes, respectively. Results: The number of reactive astroglia in EAE brains was elevated relative to the number in normal mouse brains. Daily treatment with OGF/Met-Enk reduced GFAP-positive cells in all 3 brain regions, and LDN reduced astrocyte number in the corpus callosum and subventricular zone. Astrocytes in treated EAE mice had process lengths that were comparable with those in normal mice, suggesting less reactivity. The numbers of oligodendrocytes in the corpus callosum of EAE+LDN mice were significantly reduced relative to EAE+PBS tissues. Conclusions: These results demonstrate quantitative changes in reactive glia in EAE mouse brains following treatment with OGF/Met-Enk and LDN and corroborate other studies showing that OGF/Met-Enk and LDN treatment increase plasma enkephalins, reduce inflammation and decrease pro-inflammatory cytokines.

Article.Title: Electroacupuncture Inhibits Neuronal Ferroptosis in MCAO/R Model Mice by Regulating the GSK-3β/NRF2 Signaling Pathway
Article.Authors: Xia W.; Zhao R.; Li X.; Xu C.; Dong J.; Li S.; Xu Y.; Han Y.
Article.Abstract: Background: Neuronal ferroptosis following acute ischemic stroke (AIS) contributes to ischemic brain injury and is regulated by nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2), a key regulator of antioxidant defense and iron homeostasis. Whether electroacupuncture (EA) suppresses neuronal ferroptosis by regulating NRF2 stability and nuclear translocation through upstream glycogen synthase kinase 3 beta (GSK-3β) remains unclear. We investigated whether EA inhibits neuronal ferroptosis and alleviates ischemic brain injury by modulating the GSK-3β/NRF2 axis. Methods: Middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion (MCAO/R) models were established in C57BL/6 and conditional Nrf2-knockout mice. The GSK-3β inhibitor laduviglusib (CHIR-99021; CHIR), the ferroptosis inhibitor ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1), and conditional Nrf2 knockout were used to investigate the anti-ferroptotic mechanism of EA and the regulatory hierarchy between GSK-3β and NRF2. Reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR), western blotting, and immunofluorescence were used to examine the GSK-3β/NRF2 pathway and ferroptosis-related molecules. NRF2 nuclear localization, neuronal nuclei (NeuN) /acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4 (ACSL4) double immunofluorescence, and co-immunoprecipitation were used to assess NRF2 nuclear translocation, neuronal ferroptosis, and the GSK-3β–NRF2 interaction, respectively. Results: EA inhibited GSK-3β activity after MCAO/R, restored NRF2 protein expression, promoted nuclear accumulation, and upregulated NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1). EA also downregulated ACSL4 and transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1), upregulated glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) and solute carrier family 7 member 11 (SLC7A11), reduced NeuN/ACSL4-colocalized neurons, decreased ferrous iron (Fe2+) and malondialdehyde (MDA) levels, and increased superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity, glutathione (GSH) content, and the GSH/oxidized glutathione (GSSG) ratio. CHIR and Fer-1 produced similar anti-ferroptotic effects, and co-immunoprecipitation confirmed GSK-3β–NRF2 interaction. Conditional Nrf2 knockout did not affect EA- or CHIR-mediated GSK-3β phosphorylation but markedly attenuated their effects on NQO1, SLC7A11, GPX4, and TfR1. EA also alleviated mitochondrial ultrastructural damage, reduced cerebral infarction and Fluoro-Jade B (FJB)-positive neurons, and improved neurological function and motor coordination in MCAO/R mice. Conclusion: These findings identify the GSK-3β/NRF2 axis as an important regulatory mechanism of regulating neuronal ferroptosis after MCAO/R and support EA as a potential therapeutic strategy for alleviating neuronal ferroptosis and cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury through GSK-3β inhibition and NRF2 activation.

Article.Title: Dynamics of Sleep Architecture and Nocturnal Oxygen Saturation During Acclimatization at Intermediate Altitude: A Longitudinal Observational Study in Elite Athletes
Article.Authors: Varesco G.; Van Cutsem J.; Pattyn N.; Bourrel N.; Bieuzen F.; Simonelli G.
Article.Abstract: Background: Athletes typically undergo training camps living and sleeping at intermediate altitudes (1500–2500 m). Hypoxia reshapes sleep through central circuits regulating arousal, chemoreflex gain and sympathetic outflow. However, the relationship between peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) and sleep architecture and how it co-evolves during acclimatization, is unclear. Methods: We tested whether SpO2 differs across sleep stages at intermediate altitude and whether its recovery is stage specific. Seventeen mogul-ski athletes (seven women) travelled from Montréal (Canada) to Tignes (France) for a 2-week altitude training camp (AltitudeCamp; 2100 m) in June 2025. During the first week (6 nights) and the last night of AltitudeCamp, athletes were provided with a validated ring pulse oximeter and an electroencephalography (EEG) headband. We evaluated the changes in sleep stage distribution across successive nights, scored on 30-second epochs and synchronized with oximetry data. Model estimates are reported as mean ± Standard Error (SE), raw data as mean ± Standard Deviation (SD). Results: Average total sleep time was 429 ± 47 min (mean ± SD) and did not change during AltitudeCamp (p = 0.939). Across the first week, %N3 decreased logarithmically (β = −2.35 ± 0.72%/ln (night), p = 0.002) and %Rapid eye movement sleep (REM) increased logarithmically (β = 3.13 ± 0.88%/ln (night), p < 0.001), with no changes in %Wake, %N1, or %N2. SpO2 was lower during AltitudeCamp (95.2 ± 0.3%) than measures obtained in normoxia (98 ± 0.4%; p < 0.001), and overnight heart rate (HR) was 7 ± 2 beats per minute (bpm) higher than the habitual 58 ± 3 bpm observed in normoxia (p = 0.005). Wake SpO2 increased by 0.13 ± 0.01 percentage points per night (p < 0.001), with faster recovery in N1 (0.19 ± 0.02 percentage points/night; p = 0.006) and REM (0.23 ± 0.01 percentage points/night; p < 0.001), while N2 and N3 did not differ from Wake. HR declined by 0.79 bpm/night during Wake, similar to N3 (p = 0.26), but larger than the decline in N1 (p = 0.024) and REM (p < 0.001). In N2, HR did not evolve during the first week at altitude. Conclusions: At intermediate altitude, nocturnal SpO2 and HR show sleep-stage-specific dynamics that mirror central ventilatory and autonomic adaptation to hypoxia. Our data suggest that acclimatization is not uniform across sleep stages, and that the first 2 nights after ascent may capture the most rapid adjustments despite similar total sleep duration. Sleep therefore offers a heterogeneous and ecologically valid index of central nervous system (CNS) acclimatization, which can be monitored longitudinally with wearable EEG–oximetry.

Article.Title: A Neuro-endocrine-immune Network Perspective on Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation for Metabolic Dysregulation in Schizophrenia
Article.Authors: Tang H.; Luo C.; Chen J.
Article.Abstract: Individuals with schizophrenia (SCZ) frequently exhibit glycolipid metabolic disorders. This clinical issue cannot be fully explained by the high metabolic risk associated with antipsychotic medications alone. It is increasingly recognized to involve complex multi-system interactions, particularly those linking the central nervous system with peripheral endocrine and immune regulation. Existing interventions have shown limited efficacy, underscoring the need for novel adjunctive strategies. Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), a non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) technique that modulates cortical excitability, has accumulated preliminary evidence for metabolic regulation in non-psychiatric populations and has generated several mechanistic hypotheses. However, direct evidence regarding its efficacy in SCZ remains limited, and the lack of comparison with existing interventions has hindered the recognition of its neurobiological mechanisms and potential advantages. Current challenges include methodological limitations, outcome heterogeneity, and insufficient mechanistic understanding, highlighting the need for further research and standardization of this clinical intervention. In light of these gaps, we synthesize the latest evidence on the metabolic and weight regulatory effects of tDCS, and further propose an integrative neuro-endocrine-immune network framework to conceptualize how central neuromodulation may influence peripheral metabolic regulation through interconnected biological systems. Moreover, we identify key methodological limitations in current tDCS research and outline directions for improvement, aiming to enhance the quality of future direct evidence. This framework provides a theoretical direction for future interventional studies applying tDCS to glycolipid metabolic disorders in SCZ, while acknowledging that further direct evidence is still warranted.

Article.Title: A Lightweight EEG-Based Alzheimer’s Disease Detection Framework on an Edge-Computing Platform Toward Future Intelligent Digital Twin Systems
Article.Authors: Alqahtani A.; Al-Ahmadi S.; Soudani A.
Article.Abstract: Background: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) progresses slowly through several stages until the patient reaches full cognitive decline. The electroencephalography (EEG) alterations associated with AD often emerge before symptom onset, suggesting that accessible and repeated EEG-based assessment could facilitate earlier detection and longitudinal monitoring. However, this type of assessment requires an AD detection model operating on edge-computing platforms within the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT). At present, many existing AD detection models rely on complex deep learning architectures with numerous parameters, which significantly limit their practicality for on-edge deployment. Methods: We propose an on-edge AD detection framework comprising a lightweight dilated hybrid deep learning (DHDL) model with a channel selection approach to reduce the computational and power demands on the evaluated edge-computing platform. A key architectural component is the inclusion of dual-granularity dilated temporal convolutions. This method expands the receptive field at two scales to capture both short- and long-term temporal features from EEG signals without increasing the number of parameters. Subsequently, several hybrid lightweight layers extract distinct temporal and spatial features and are integrated with attention mechanisms. Additionally, our channel selection approach first forms an initial subset of EEG channels guided by individual channel classification accuracy, and then iteratively refines the selected channels using hill-climbing optimization. Here, we evaluated our framework on two publicly available EEG datasets recorded for the same group of subjects (n = 48 subjects): a conventional closed-eye (CE) dataset and a more challenging open-eye (OE) dataset. Validation followed a subject-independent Leave-2-Subjects-Out (L2SO) cross-validation protocol. Real-time deployment was tested on an edge-computing platform. Results: The proposed framework achieved 92.56% accuracy for the CE dataset and 75.15% accuracy for the OE dataset. Inference required 10.45 ms and 8.23 ms per segment for the CE and OE datasets, respectively, and consumed 9.69 mJ and 6.95 mJ of energy per segment, respectively. Conclusions: These results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed framework as a real-time, on-edge inference module for AD detection. Although a complete intelligent digital twin system is not implemented in this work, the proposed framework can serve as an inference component for future digital twin systems, supporting early AD detection and progression monitoring.

Article.Title: Salidroside alleviates MPP <sup>+</sup> -induced injury and mitochondrial fission in PC12 cells by mediating the HDAC6/MST1/MIEF1 axis
Article.Authors: Zhao R.; Chen L.; Li X.; Mao X.; Zhou Y.; Shen J.
Article.Abstract: Objective: To investigate the protective effects of salidroside (SAL) against MPP+-induced injury and mitochondrial fission in PC12 cells and to explore the involvement of the HDAC6/MST1/MIEF1 signaling axis. Methods: NGF-differentiated PC12 cells were exposed to MPP+ to establish a cellular model of Parkinson's disease-related injury and subsequently treated with SAL. Cell viability, apoptosis, inflammatory cytokines, oxidative stress, mitochondrial membrane potential, ATP production, mitochondrial morphology, and mitochondrial fission-related proteins were evaluated. HDAC6 promoter activity, the interaction between HDAC6 and MST1, and MST1 acetylation were analyzed. The mechanistic role of the HDAC6/MST1/MIEF1 axis was further examined using HDAC6 knockdown and MST1 or MIEF1 overexpression. Results: SAL significantly improved cell viability, reduced apoptotic nuclear changes and the levels of IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α, and alleviated oxidative stress by decreasing reactive oxygen species and malondialdehyde levels while increasing superoxide dismutase activity. SAL also restored mitochondrial membrane potential and ATP production, increased mitochondrial length, and decreased the expression of the mitochondrial fission-related proteins DRP1, FIS1, and MFF. Mechanistically, SAL enhanced HDAC6 promoter activity and increased HDAC6 expression, while reducing MST1 and MIEF1 expression. HDAC6 interacted with MST1 and regulated its acetylation. The protective effects of SAL were markedly attenuated by HDAC6 knockdown or MST1/MIEF1 overexpression. Conclusion: SAL alleviates MPP+-induced cellular injury, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and excessive mitochondrial fission in PC12 cells through an HDAC6-dependent mechanism involving the MST1/MIEF1 axis. These findings support further investigation of this pathway in physiologically relevant models of Parkinson's disease.

Article.Title: Serum CitH3 and PTX3 levels for early prediction of acute respiratory distress syndrome following severe traumatic brain injury
Article.Authors: Wang Y.; Lang M.; Zhen C.; Liu B.; Pang Z.; Yang Y.
Article.Abstract: Objective: To evaluate the predictive value of serum citrullinated histone H3 (CitH3) and pentraxin 3 (PTX3) for acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) after severe traumatic brain injury (sTBI). Methods: This prospective observational study enrolled 395 consecutive sTBI patients admitted between April 2025 and February 2026. Patients were categorized into ARDS (n = 111) and non-ARDS (n = 284) groups. Serum CitH3 and PTX3 were measured by ELISA. Candidate predictors were selected by LASSO regression. Spearman correlation, multivariable logistic regression, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were performed. The DeLong test, category-free net reclassification improvement (NRI), and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI) assessed incremental predictive value over the conventional model. Results: Serum CitH3 and PTX3 were significantly higher in the ARDS group (both p < 0.001) and were positively correlated with each other but negatively with oxygenation indices and albumin. Multivariable analysis identified pulmonary contusion, shock, fluid balance within 12 h of admission, APACHE II and SOFA scores, and elevated CitH3 and PTX3 as independent risk factors (all p < 0.05), whereas a higher GCS score and elevated albumin were protective. Their combination yielded an AUC of 0.841, superior to either alone. When added to the conventional model, biomarkers increased the AUC from 0.926 to 0.943 (p = 0.025), with category-free NRI of 0.554 (95% CI: 0.320-0.778, p < 0.001) and IDI of 0.072 (95% CI: 0.040-0.105, p < 0.001). Conclusion: Combined serum CitH3 and PTX3 demonstrate early predictive potential for ARDS after sTBI but require external validation.

Article.Title: Myrtenol mitigates seizure activity and oxidative imbalance in a mouse model of PTZ-induced seizure
Article.Authors: Rasouli F.; Hojjat S.; Shakeri F.
Article.Abstract: Aim: Pentylenetetrazole (PTZ)-induced seizures are strongly associated with oxidative imbalance, and the monoterpenoid alcohol myrtenol has been proposed to exert antioxidant and neuroprotective effects. This study investigated whether myrtenol attenuates PTZ-evoked seizure activity and oxidative disturbances in the mouse hippocampus and cerebral cortex. Methods: Sixty male mice were assigned to six groups: control, PTZ-only, three myrtenol pretreatment doses (25, 50, 100 mg/kg), and diazepam. Seizure susceptibility was evaluated by measuring latencies to minimal clonic and generalized tonic-clonic seizures following PTZ administration. Oxidative stress markers, including malondialdehyde (MDA), nitric oxide (NO), superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase (CAT), and total thiol content, were quantified in brain homogenates. Results: PTZ reliably induced seizures and oxidative alterations. Myrtenol pretreatment increased seizure latencies in a dose-dependent manner, although diazepam produced the greatest protection. Myrtenol, particularly at 100 mg/kg, reduced PTZ-induced elevations in MDA and NO, restored SOD and CAT activities, and improved thiol levels, with effects approaching those of diazepam. Lower myrtenol doses produced partial or nonsignificant biochemical improvements. Conclusion: These findings indicate that myrtenol mitigates PTZ-induced seizure expression and oxidative stress, with the highest dose demonstrating the most consistent neuroprotective profile.

Article.Title: Trans-vatabnet: transcriptomic signatures for Parkinson’s disease detection using deep learning
Article.Authors: Vishwakarma P.; Vishwakarma P.; Avanti S.
Article.Abstract: Background: Early detection of Parkinson's disease (PD) is essential for timely clinical intervention. However, transcriptomic-based diagnosis faces challenges associated with high-dimensional gene expression data, redundant features, class imbalance, and limited interpretability. Objective: This study proposes TransVaTabNet, an integrated framework for PD detection and biomarker identification using transcriptomic analysis, deep learning, and explainable artificial intelligence. Methods: RNA-seq data were preprocessed using low-expression gene filtering, Trimmed Mean of M-values (TMM) normalization, and voom transformation. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified using limma-voom, followed by stage-specific gene analysis and functional enrichment to investigate disease-associated pathways. A Variational Autoencoder (VAE) generated compact latent representations, while the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) addressed class imbalance. TabNet classified the derived features using sequential attention, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) supported model interpretation and potential biomarker identification. Results: Evaluation on the GSE216281 RNA-seq dataset achieved an Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC) of 90.95%, outperforming the classical machine learning models evaluated in this study.Conclusion: TransVaTabNet combines dimensionality reduction, attention-based classification, and explainability to support PD detection and potential biomarker discovery. The framework offers an interpretable approach to identifying disease-associated transcriptomic patterns and may support future precision diagnostic research.

Article.Title: Benchmarking 3D U-Net variants for volumetric segmentation of the substantia nigra and brain ageing related analysis using 7T MRI
Article.Authors: Haridhas A.; Alfred L.
Article.Abstract: Unlabelled: Objective: Accurate segmentation of the substantia nigra (SN) is essential for assessing its structural integrity and volumetric changes in Parkinson's disease and brain aging. However, it remains challenging due to SN's small size, deep location, and low contrast on conventional MRI. This study benchmarked six U-Net variants baseline 3D U-Net, ResU-Net, SE-U-Net, Attention U-Net, U-Net++, and U-Net 3+ for SN segmentation using ultra-high-field 7 T MRI. Methods: T1-weighted MP2RAGE images from the ATAG dataset (53 healthy subjects: 31 train, 7 validation and 15 test). Six architectures were evaluated: 3D U-Net, ResU-Net, SE-U-Net, Attention U-Net, U-Net++, and U-Net 3+.Performance was evalauted with Dice score, IoU, 95% HD95, ASSD, and also age-stratified analysis was considered for analysing the robustness of model across young, middle-aged, and elderly cohorts. Results: While ResU-Net achieved the highest overlap metrics (Dice = 0.763, IoU = 0.618), where the baseline 3D U-Net outperformed all variants in boundary accuracy (HD95 = 13.85 mm, ASSD = 20.15 mm). The U-Net 3+ and SE-U-Net complex models relatively underperformed, indicated that architectural complexity does not enhance the segmentation performance of small subcortical structures. Descriptive Age-stratified analysis shows, ResU-Net maintained consistent performance across different age groups and 3D U-Net revealed strong age-invariance, however no statistically significant age-group differences were exhibited. Conclusions: This study findings demonstrates architecture selection influences overlap, boundary detection and volume estimation small-structure segmentation and highlights the importance of evaluating model robustness to demographic variability. The findings offer a methodological benchmark for developing reliable SN volumetry tools for neurodegenerative research.

Article.Title: Multimodal based Brain Tumor Classification using Clustered Federated Learning in Edge based IoT Network
Article.Authors: C R.; B M.
Article.Abstract: A brain tumor is characterized by the uncontrolled growth of cells that causes a severe impact on the quality of life. Nowadays, various methods based on multimodal medical images are used to identify brain tumors. Meanwhile, these methods require extensive amounts of labeled information to identify disease tissues and often encounter various challenges based on privacy and accuracy. This paper establishes a Taylor-based Focal Log-cosh Entropy Network (TFLE-Net) to classify brain tumors from demographic data and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) images by utilizing clustered federated learning in an edge-based Internet of Things (IoT) network. The detection process is executed in clustered federated learning concerning two entities: server and nodes. In a local training model, an input MRI scan is pre-processed, further brain tumor areas are segmented, and then, the mining of various features is performed. Simultaneously, the normalization of input demographic data is done, and the suitable features are selected using information gain. Further, the extracted features and chosen features are subjected to TFLE-Net to classify brain tumors. Additionally, the TFLE-Net yielded Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.057, Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 0.047, True Positive Rate (TPR) of 97.789%, and accuracy of 96.987%.
